case_title: E-Homes Infrastructure Private Limited vs. New Okhla Industrial Development Authority & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: E-Homes Infrastructure Private Limited acted as the Resolution Applicant; New Okhla Industrial Development Authority (NOIDA) is the Lessor/Creditor; Neo Infrastructure Private Limited is the Corporate Debtor (Sub-Lessee); M/s Brys International Private Limited is a collaborating entity/Corporate Debtor; and Bank of Baroda acted as Financial Creditor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: NOIDA executed a 90-year lease deed on 17.01.2012 with M/s Logix Builders & Promoters Pvt. Ltd. for commercial Plot No. SC 01/A, Sector 150, Noida. A tripartite Sub-Lease Deed was executed on 15.04.2013 between NOIDA, Logix, and Neo Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. Subsequently, on 13.07.2013, Neo Infrastructure and Logix executed a Collaboration Agreement transferring development and sales rights to Brys International Pvt. Ltd. for Rs. 20 Crores without obtaining prior approval from NOIDA. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Bank of Baroda initiated Section 7 proceedings against both entities; NOIDA submitted its claim in Neo Infrastructure's CIRP, which was admitted by the CoC on 15.05.2019 for Rs. 443,066,019/- with a 26.95% voting share. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP against Brys International was initiated on 31.01.2019 and against Neo Infrastructure on 01.02.2019. The Resolution Applicant submitted separate parallel resolution plans on 15.10.2019. NOIDA filed CA No. 2488 of 2019 on 13.11.2019. CoC approved both plans on 28.02.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Clauses II(k), III.14(h), and III.14(p) of the Sub-Lease Deed mandating prior written lessor permission for any assignment, role change, or further sub-lease; Clauses 3 and 4 of the unapproved Collaboration Agreement dated 13.07.2013; and Clause 5.2.1 of the Resolution Plans making approval of each plan conditionally interdependent on the other. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NOIDA filed CA No. 2488/2019 in CP (IB) 875 (PB)/2018 seeking directions to reject composite/interdependent schemes and stay voting. The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT New Delhi Bench) allowed NOIDA's application on 21.02.2022 on the grounds that Neo Infrastructure violated lease deed terms by transferring development/sales rights without lessor approval.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT had jurisdiction under Section 60(5) of the IBC to adjudicate NOIDA's application regarding contractual lease violations and interdependent resolution plans; whether CA No. 2488/2019 became infructuous upon subsequent CoC approval of the resolution plans; and whether a composite, interdependent resolution plan spanning two distinct corporate debtors is permissible without a formal consolidation order.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An adjudicating authority retains jurisdiction under insolvency law to reject or restrain interdependent and conditional resolution schemes submitted across separate corporate debtors when such schemes deal with proprietary leasehold assets in breach of statutory or contractual restrictions and absent any substantive consolidation order. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60(5)(c) confers jurisdiction over questions of priorities or law/facts arising out of or in relation to insolvency proceedings; this empowers tribunals to halt unauthorized CIRP consolidation attempted via contingent contractual clauses in resolution plans. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of contractual clauses revealed that transfer of rights was explicitly contingent on the lessor's prior written permission; without it, the transfer is void and cannot form the asset base of a resolution plan. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because no procedural consolidation of the two CIRPs had been ordered, the submission of mutually interdependent plans was an unauthorized contrivance attempting to circumvent lease restrictions, justifying the lower bench's intervention.
operative_order: The Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 424 of 2022 along with companion appeals is dismissed; the Adjudicating Authority's order dated 21.02.2022 is affirmed. No order as to costs.
summary: E-Homes Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. challenged an order of NCLT New Delhi allowing an application by NOIDA restraining composite resolution plans[cite: 1]. Neo Infrastructure held leasehold rights from NOIDA requiring lessor approval for transfers, yet executed a collaboration agreement transferring rights to Brys International without sanction[cite: 1]. Both entities underwent separate CIRPs[cite: 1]. The appellant submitted interdependent resolution plans conditional upon mutual approval[cite: 1]. NCLAT held that absent an order of consolidation, introducing interdependent resolution plans to transfer lease rights without lessor sanction was impermissible[cite: 1]. The tribunal affirmed NCLT's jurisdiction under Section 60(5) and dismissed the appeal, holding that subsequent CoC approval did not render NOIDA's challenge infructuous[cite: 1].

case_title: Department of State Tax vs. Zicom Saas Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is the Department of State Tax (through the Deputy Commissioner of State Tax), acting as an Operational Creditor; Respondent No. 1 is Zicom Saas Pvt. Ltd., the Corporate Debtor; and Respondent No. 2 is the Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Assessment and statutory levy of state value-added tax dues under the Maharashtra Value Added Tax Act, 2002 against the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant lodged a total tax claim of Rs. 43,72,97,479/-, out of which the Resolution Professional verified and admitted Rs. 36,68,12,729/-. In the final approved resolution plan, the Appellant was allocated 1% of its admitted claim amount. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: No statutory demand notices or recall notices under the IBC were extracted in the text of the judgment; the appeal challenged the plan approval order dated 16.12.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Admitted claim schedule of Rs. 36,68,12,729/- verified during CIRP, the terms of the approved Resolution Plan providing 1% payout, and statutory provisions under Section 37 of the MVAT Act, 2002. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Following approval by the CoC, the RP moved an application for approval of the resolution plan, which was approved by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Mumbai Bench, Court-III) vide order dated 16.12.2021. The Appellant appealed against the 1% allocation.
legal_issues: Whether statutory tax dues under Section 37 of the Maharashtra Value Added Tax Act, 2002 create a first charge elevating the tax department to a secured creditor akin to Section 48 of the GVAT Act interpreted in Rainbow Papers, and whether allocating 1% to such claim violates Section 30(2)(b) read with Section 53 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A statutory first charge provision in state legislation that is expressly made subject to central enactments is subordinate to the priority distribution waterfall prescribed under central insolvency legislation, keeping the taxing authority within the class of unsecured operational creditors. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 37 of the MVAT Act explicitly incorporates the phrase 'subject to any provision regarding creation of first charge in any Central Act', which distinguishes it from unconditional first-charge clauses; the waterfall mechanism under Section 53 of the IBC constitutes such central statutory regulation governing distribution priorities. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Comparison of statutory texts showed the absence of absolute priority language found in Rainbow Papers, establishing the tax department's status as an Operational Creditor. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The state tax claim is governed by Section 53's waterfall, making the 1% plan allocation legally compliant under Section 30(2)(b).
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 246 of 2022 is dismissed without costs, and the Adjudicating Authority's plan approval order dated 16.12.2021 is affirmed.
summary: The Department of State Tax challenged an NCLT Mumbai order approving a resolution plan for Zicom Saas Pvt. Ltd., where the department received 1% of its admitted tax claim of Rs. 36.68 Crores[cite: 2]. The Appellant argued it was a secured creditor pursuant to Rainbow Papers and Section 37 of the Maharashtra Value Added Tax Act, 2002[cite: 2]. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, distinguishing Rainbow Papers because Section 37 of the MVAT Act is expressly subject to central enactments creating a first charge[cite: 2]. Consequently, Section 53 of the IBC overrides the state provision, maintaining the department's status as an operational creditor and rendering the 1% payout legally compliant[cite: 2].

case_title: Pooja Ramesh Singh vs. State Bank Of India And Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Pooja Ramesh Singh is the Suspended Director of Essel Infraprojects Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/Corporate Guarantor); State Bank of India is the Financial Creditor; M/s Spanco Nagpur Discom Ltd. (SND Ltd.) is the Principal Borrower. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: SND Ltd. availed term loan and working capital credit facilities from SBI under agreements dated 25.02.2013 and 01.03.2013, supported by combined corporate guarantees executed by Essel Infraprojects Ltd., subsequently renewed on 17.07.2018 and afresh on 17.05.2019 for up to Rs. 186.60 Crores. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed against the Corporate Guarantor amounted to Rs. 1,77,37,02,868.74/-. SND Ltd.'s account was classified as NPA on 05.12.2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: SND Ltd. became NPA on 05.12.2019; SBI issued loan recall and guarantee invocation notice on 01.10.2020 granting 7 days to pay (expiring 08.10.2020); Section 7 petition CP(IB) No. 543 of 2021 was filed on 10.05.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Terms of the Guarantee Deed dated 17.05.2019 (Clauses 1, 13, 14, and 20) specifying that liability arose 'forthwith on demand'; recall-cum-invocation notice dated 01.10.2020 calling for payment within 7 days; and Part IV of the petition disclosing invocation on 01.10.2020. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: SBI filed a Section 7 petition against Essel Infraprojects Ltd. The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Mumbai Bench, Court V) admitted the application on 01.03.2023, holding that default occurred on 05.09.2019 (prior to NPA) and was not barred by Section 10A.
legal_issues: Whether the date of default for a corporate guarantor under an 'on-demand' guarantee is identical to the date of default of the principal borrower, and whether the guarantee invocation notice dated 01.10.2020 triggered default on 08.10.2020, squarely attracting the bar under Section 10A of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When a corporate guarantee is explicitly structured as payable on demand, the guarantor's default arises only upon failure to comply with a formal demand notice, rather than automatically on the date the principal borrower defaults. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Default under Section 3(12) requires that the debt has become 'due and payable and is not paid'; in an 'on-demand' contract, the debt becomes payable by the guarantor only after a demand is served, making the date of default independent from the borrower's default. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Construction of clauses 1, 13, and 20 of the guarantee instrument proved it was an on-demand contract; hence non-payment within 7 days of the 01.10.2020 demand fixed the default on 08.10.2020. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: As the default occurred on 08.10.2020, within the Section 10A prohibited period (25.03.2020 to 25.03.2021), the Section 7 petition was statutorily barred.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed, and the impugned order dated 01.03.2023 passed by the Adjudicating Authority admitting the Section 7 petition is set aside.
summary: Pooja Ramesh Singh, Suspended Director of Essel Infraprojects Ltd. (Corporate Guarantor), appealed an NCLT Mumbai order admitting SBI's Section 7 insolvency petition[cite: 3]. The principal borrower, SND Ltd., became NPA on 05.12.2019[cite: 3]. SBI invoked the corporate guarantee via demand notice dated 01.10.2020 allowing seven days for payment[cite: 3]. The Adjudicating Authority held the default occurred on 05.09.2019, bypassing Section 10A[cite: 3]. NCLAT reversed the decision, holding that under an on-demand guarantee, the guarantor's default arises only after the notice period expires—here, on 08.10.2020[cite: 3]. Since this fell within the prohibited window under Section 10A of the IBC, the application was barred and was set aside[cite: 3].

case_title: Vijay Kumar Pasricha vs. Manish Kumar Gupta (IRP in Umang Realtech Pvt. Ltd.)
appeal_number: I.A. No. 2187 of 2021 in Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 926 of 2019
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Vijay Kumar Pasricha is an allottee/homebuyer in 'Monsoon Breeze II' (Applicant); Manish Kumar Gupta is the Interim Resolution Professional; and Umang Realtech Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Booking and Builder Buyer's Agreement dated 26.09.2014 for apartment T-301 in the 'Monsoon Breeze II' project, Sector-78, Gurugram, with possession due by 29.06.2018. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Upon failure to deliver possession, Haryana RERA ordered a refund of Rs. 49,47,725/- with 10.75% interest per annum on 10.01.2019; subsequent execution proceedings led to attachment orders for Rs. 76,68,788/- on 12.02.2021. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 CIRP application against the Corporate Debtor was admitted on 20.08.2019 in CP (IB) 1564 (PB)/2018; the Appellate Tribunal introduced 'Reverse CIRP' for 'Winter Hills-77' on 04.02.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: HARERA decree dated 10.01.2019; attachment order dated 12.02.2021; and IRP's affidavit dated 28.08.2021 before RERA Appellate Tribunal claiming enterprise-wide moratorium over the Corporate Debtor despite project-specific reverse CIRP. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 application was admitted on 20.08.2019 by NCLT New Delhi. On 04.02.2020, NCLAT disposed of CA (AT) (Ins.) No. 926 of 2019 by instituting project-specific 'Reverse CIRP' for 'Winter Hills-77'. The Applicant filed I.A. 2187 of 2021 seeking clarification that Section 14 moratorium is restricted solely to the Winter Hills-77 project.
legal_issues: Whether the statutory moratorium declared under Section 14 of the IBC applies globally to the entire corporate entity or can be restricted solely to a single real estate project when a project-specific 'Reverse CIRP' mechanism is judicially instituted.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In real estate insolvencies where an exceptional, project-specific 'Reverse CIRP' is instituted, the resultant moratorium under Section 14 can be deemed confined solely to that specific project to ensure other distinct projects continue operations unhindered. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Although Section 14 fundamentally contemplates a company-wide moratorium over all assets, the sui generis framework of 'Reverse CIRP' accommodates project-level segregation so that unrelated project assets and creditors remain unaffected. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Analysis of the earlier directions dated 04.02.2020 revealed CIRP was expressly confined to 'Winter Hills-77', excluding claims of creditors from separate projects. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Due to the extraordinary circumstances of the reverse CIRP framework, the moratorium was clarified as confined exclusively to 'Winter Hills-77', while clarifying this does not disrupt general enterprise-wide moratorium principles.
operative_order: Interlocutory Application bearing I.A. No. 2187 of 2021 in Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 926 of 2019 is disposed of, clarifying that the moratorium under Section 14 is confined exclusively to the Winter Hills-77 project. No costs.
summary: An allottee of 'Monsoon Breeze II', Vijay Kumar Pasricha, filed a clarification application in the disposed appeal regarding Umang Realtech Pvt. Ltd., wherein NCLAT had earlier instituted a project-specific 'Reverse CIRP' for 'Winter Hills-77'[cite: 4]. The IRP claimed that despite project-specific CIRP, Section 14 moratorium applied company-wide, hindering RERA recovery orders in other projects[cite: 4]. NCLAT clarified that under the peculiar facts of this reverse CIRP, the Section 14 moratorium was deemed restricted solely to the 'Winter Hills-77' project[cite: 4]. NCLAT emphasized that while an enterprise-wide moratorium remains fundamental under Section 14, reverse CIRP operates as a tailored exception[cite: 4].

case_title: Winifred John & Ors. vs. Kumar Rajan, Resolution Professional of Hindustan Newsprint Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mrs. C.G. Vijayalakshmi, Mrs. Winifred John, and other former employees/workmen are Appellants; Shri Kumar Rajan is Respondent No. 1 (RP); Hindustan Newsprint Limited (HNL) is Respondent No. 2 (Corporate Debtor); the Committee of Creditors is Respondent No. 3; and Kerala Industrial Infrastructure Development Corporation (KINFRA) is Respondent No. 4 (Successful Resolution Applicant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Employment contracts, wage obligations, and statutory retiral/social security benefit entitlements under the EPF & MP Act, 1952 and Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Admitted claim of secured financial creditors was Rs. 209.09 Crores against a liquidation value of Rs. 162.70 Crores; total claims admitted were Rs. 518.5540 Crores. The approved resolution plan proposed only a 35.13% payout towards admitted Provident Fund (PF) and Gratuity claims of employees/workmen, treating them at par with secured creditors. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application TIBA/03/KOB/2019 was admitted on 28.11.2019; CoC approved KINFRA's plan on 24.12.2020 with a 92.72% vote; and the Adjudicating Authority approved the plan on 29.01.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Admitted claim sheets showing full verification of PF claims (Rs. 3,046.32 Lakhs), workmen gratuity (Rs. 2,961.46 Lakhs), and employee gratuity (Rs. 1,410.75 Lakhs), alongside plan allocation tables offering only 35.13%. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kochi Bench allowed IA(IBC)/21/KOB/2021 on 29.01.2021 approving KINFRA's plan. Appellants appealed under Section 61 asserting violation of Section 30(2)(e) due to partial PF/gratuity payment.
legal_issues: Whether a resolution plan providing only 35.13% payout towards statutory Provident Fund and Gratuity dues complies with Section 30(2)(e) of the IBC, and whether the absence of a separate physical fund maintained by the Corporate Debtor exempts the Successful Resolution Applicant from paying such retiral dues in full.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Statutory dues owed to workmen and employees on account of Provident Fund and Gratuity do not form part of the debtor's estate and must be satisfied in full by the Successful Resolution Applicant, irrespective of whether a separate physical fund was created or maintained by the corporate debtor prior to insolvency. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Reading Section 30(2)(e) with Section 36(4)(a)(iii), all sums due towards provident fund, pension, and gratuity are statutorily protected and placed entirely outside the Section 53 waterfall mechanism; allocating a discounted percentage violates statutory provisions. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying the precedent in Jet Aircraft Maintenance Engineers Welfare Association, the absence of a dedicated pre-existing fund on the corporate balance sheet does not eliminate the mandatory statutory liability. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Truncating PF and gratuity dues to 35.13% breached Section 30(2) of the Code; the SRA is legally obligated to satisfy the unpaid balance in full up to the insolvency commencement date.
operative_order: The appeals are allowed in part; the Successful Resolution Applicant is directed to make payment of the unpaid balance of Provident Fund, Gratuity Fund, and statutory retiral dues to the workmen/employees up to the CIRP commencement date after adjusting amounts already disbursed under the Plan.
summary: Appellants, ex-employees of Hindustan Newsprint Limited, challenged an NCLT Kochi order approving KINFRA's resolution plan, which allocated only 35.13% toward their verified Provident Fund and Gratuity dues[cite: 5]. The RP and SRA argued that because the liquidation value was insufficient to reach operational creditors under Section 53, and no specific statutory funds were maintained, the 35.13% allocation was valid within commercial wisdom[cite: 5]. NCLAT rejected these defenses, citing Section 36(4)(a)(iii) and following the Jet Aircraft precedent[cite: 5]. The tribunal held that PF and gratuity dues are excluded from the liquidation waterfall and must be paid in full[cite: 5]. The appeals were allowed in part with directions to the SRA to pay the balance[cite: 5].

case_title: Shapoorji Pallonji Finance Pvt. Ltd. vs. Rekha Singh
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Shapoorji Pallonji Finance Pvt. Ltd. is the Financial Creditor (NBFC)[cite: 6]; Rekha Singh (along with Siddharth Singh and Ajay Kumar Singh) is the Personal Guarantor / Respondent[cite: 6]; Jumbo Finvest (India) Ltd. (JFIL) is the Principal Borrower (NBFC / Financial Service Provider)[cite: 6]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A credit facility of Rs. 25 Crores was sanctioned to JFIL pursuant to a Facility Agreement dated 27.03.2018[cite: 6], for which the Respondents executed individual Deeds of Personal Guarantee on 27.03.2018 in favour of the Appellant[cite: 6]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Rs. 24,86,50,000/- was disbursed[cite: 6]. Following default in repayment of principal and interest instalments, a recall notice claimed Rs. 11,92,91,681/-[cite: 6], and the default amount stated in Part III of the Section 95 application as of 17.05.2021 was Rs. 11,94,50,226/-[cite: 6]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Recall notice was issued on 27.01.2021[cite: 6]; dishonoured repayment cheques were returned in February 2021[cite: 6]; demand notice invoking the guarantees was issued on 02.03.2021[cite: 6]; Section 95 petitions were filed on 03.06.2021[cite: 6]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Facility Agreement and Personal Guarantee Deeds dated 27.03.2018[cite: 6]; dishonoured cheques[cite: 6]; demand notices[cite: 6]; audited balance sheet of JFIL as on 31.03.2020 reflecting total assets exceeding Rs. 600 Crores (with Note 17 detailing loan receivables of Rs. 487.80 Crores)[cite: 6]; and MCA Notification dated 18.11.2019[cite: 6]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed CP No. (IB) 25/95/JPR/2021 before NCLT Jaipur Bench[cite: 6]. Respondents filed IA No. 229/JPR/2021 challenging maintainability[cite: 6]. The Adjudicating Authority allowed the IA on 22.02.2022 and dismissed the company petitions on the ground that JFIL's asset size was only Rs. 487 Crores (under Note 17), falling below the Rs. 500 Crore threshold required to qualify as a Corporate Debtor under the Section 227 Notification[cite: 6].
legal_issues: Whether the qualifying asset size threshold of Rs. 500 crore under MCA Notification dated 18.11.2019 is limited to loan receivables or includes total current and non-current assets[cite: 6]; whether subsequent asset depletion during the pendency of proceedings divests the Adjudicating Authority of jurisdiction[cite: 6]; and whether an application under Section 95 can be initiated against personal guarantors of an eligible FSP absent an ongoing CIRP against the principal borrower[cite: 6].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Statutory asset thresholds determining the applicability of insolvency laws to financial service providers encompass the aggregate of all balance sheet assets rather than isolated receivable sub-categories, and subject-matter jurisdiction established at the time of petition filing is not extinguished by subsequent asset devaluation[cite: 6]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The term 'asset size of Rs. 500 crore or more' in MCA Notification dated 18.11.2019 issued under Section 227 of the IBC signifies total assets (both current and non-current) on the last audited balance sheet[cite: 6]. Under Section 60(1), an application under Section 95 is maintainable against a personal guarantor before the NCLT having territorial jurisdiction without requiring the pre-existence of a CIRP against the corporate debtor under Section 60(2)[cite: 6]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of JFIL's audited balance sheet for the year ending 31.03.2020 established total assets of Rs. 603.92 Crores, demonstrating that Note 17 reflected only loan receivables (Rs. 487.80 Crores) and was erroneously treated by the lower bench as total asset size[cite: 6]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because JFIL satisfied the Rs. 500 Crore threshold on the date of petition filing, it constituted a Corporate Debtor under Section 227, rendering the Section 95 petitions against its personal guarantors maintainable[cite: 6].
operative_order: Company Appeals (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 397, 398, and 399 of 2022 are allowed[cite: 6]. The impugned order dated 22.02.2022 is set aside[cite: 6]. The company petitions under Section 95 are held maintainable and revived before the Adjudicating Authority to proceed in accordance with law[cite: 6].
summary: Shapoorji Pallonji Finance Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Jaipur order dismissing its Section 95 insolvency petitions against personal guarantors of Jumbo Finvest (India) Ltd. (JFIL), an NBFC[cite: 6]. The Adjudicating Authority held that JFIL's asset size was Rs. 487 Crores based on Note 17 (loan receivables), falling short of the Rs. 500 Crore threshold under the Section 227 Notification[cite: 6]. NCLAT set aside the order, holding that asset size encompasses total assets (both current and non-current), which exceeded Rs. 600 Crores in JFIL's audited balance sheet[cite: 6]. Furthermore, subsequent asset devaluation does not divest the tribunal of jurisdiction[cite: 6]. The petitions were held maintainable and revived[cite: 6].

case_title: Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. vs. Anuj Jain & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. (EARCL) is the Appellant (Assignee of Yes Bank / Secured Creditor)[cite: 7]; Anuj Jain is Respondent No. 1 (RP of Ballarpur Industries Ltd.)[cite: 7]; Committee of Creditors of Ballarpur Industries Ltd. is Respondent No. 2[cite: 7]; Finquest Financial Solutions Pvt. Ltd. is Respondent No. 3 (Successful Resolution Applicant)[cite: 7]; BILT Graphic Paper Products Ltd. (BGPPL) is the Principal Borrower[cite: 7]; and Ballarpur Industries Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor (Mortgagor/Corporate Guarantor)[cite: 7]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Yes Bank extended Term Loan-I of Rs. 150 Crores (01.09.2015) and Term Loan-II of Rs. 250 Crores (04.05.2016) to BGPPL[cite: 7]. The Corporate Debtor mortgaged 621 acres in Choudwar, Orissa, as security and executed a Corporate Guarantee dated 22.06.2016 for Term Loan-II[cite: 7]. Yes Bank assigned its debt and securities to EARCL on 30.09.2016[cite: 7]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: EARCL lodged Form C claiming Rs. 133,24,05,045/- under Term Loan-II[cite: 7]. However, BGPPL committed no repayment default, and the corporate guarantee was never invoked[cite: 7]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP against the Corporate Debtor commenced on 17.01.2020[cite: 7]; public announcement was made on 23.01.2020[cite: 7]; EARCL filed Form C on 05.02.2020[cite: 7]; RP classified EARCL under 'Other Creditors' at a notional value of Re. 1 on 19.10.2020[cite: 7]; final list of creditors was published on 24.12.2020[cite: 7]; CoC approved the resolution plan on 14.04.2022 with an 88% majority[cite: 7]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Term loan agreements, mortgage deed, Corporate Guarantee dated 22.06.2016, Form C, list of creditors assigning Re. 1 value[cite: 7], and public notice dated 03.05.2022 stating that the resolution plan provided for the sale of the 621-acre Choudwar land free of encumbrance to pay CoC financial creditors[cite: 7]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: EARCL filed IA No. 1311/2022 seeking rejection of Finquest's plan and protection of its mortgage[cite: 7]. NCLT Mumbai Bench-III rejected IA No. 1311/2022 and approved the resolution plan in IA No. 1143/2022 on 31.03.2023 on the grounds that BGPPL had not defaulted and Regulation 37 permitted dealing with encumbered assets[cite: 7].
legal_issues: Whether a resolution plan can extinguish the security interest/mortgage of a third-party secured creditor who submitted a claim admitted at notional value of Re. 1 without default by the principal borrower[cite: 7], and whether Regulation 37 of the CIRP Regulations empowers the CoC to sell assets free of encumbrances without the consent of such secured creditor[cite: 7].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Corporate debtor assets subject to security interests may be sold, transferred, or modified free of encumbrances under an approved resolution plan without requiring the individual consent of a third-party secured creditor who submitted to and participated in the CIRP[cite: 7]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 37(b) and (d) of the CIRP Regulations expressly authorize a resolution plan to provide for the sale of assets 'whether subject to any security interest or not' and the 'satisfaction or modification of any security interest'[cite: 7]. Sections 52 and 53 apply strictly to liquidation proceedings, while Section 14(1)(c) prevents the enforcement of any security interest during CIRP[cite: 7]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where a creditor files a claim in Form C and accepts its admission as an 'Other Creditor' at a notional value of Re. 1 without judicial challenge, its security interest is subsumed within the CIRP, rendering Jaypee Kensington inapplicable since the creditor did not remain outside the process[cite: 7]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The commercial wisdom of the CoC to extinguish the mortgage and utilize the asset for corporate rejuvenation is valid under Regulation 37, especially where the underlying debt is being serviced by the principal borrower who remains liable to provide alternative security[cite: 7].
operative_order: Company Appeals (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 517 & 518 of 2023 are dismissed without costs, affirming the NCLT Mumbai orders dated 31.03.2023[cite: 7].
summary: Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. appealed an order of NCLT Mumbai approving a resolution plan for Ballarpur Industries Ltd., which extinguished Edelweiss's mortgage over 621 acres in Choudwar, Odisha[cite: 7]. The Corporate Debtor had mortgaged the land for loans availed by its group company, BILT Graphic Paper Products Ltd., which had not defaulted[cite: 7]. Edelweiss's claim was admitted as 'Other Creditor' at notional value Re. 1[cite: 7]. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that under Regulation 37 of the CIRP Regulations, a resolution plan can provide for the sale or modification of assets subject to security interests without separate creditor consent, distinguishing Jaypee Kensington since Edelweiss had participated in the CIRP[cite: 7].

case_title: Srei Equipment Finance Limited vs. Kalpataru Properties Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: I.A. No. 130 of 2023 in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 37 of 2023
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: SREI Equipment Finance Limited is the Appellant (Financial Creditor / CoC member)[cite: 8]; Kalpataru Properties Pvt. Ltd. is Respondent No. 1[cite: 8]; Shree Ram Urban Infrastructure Limited is Respondent No. 2 (Corporate Debtor represented by RP Pankaj Ramandas Majithia)[cite: 8]; and the Official Liquidator, Bombay High Court is Respondent No. 3[cite: 8]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: MOU dated 28.06.2004 executed between the Corporate Debtor, Respondent No. 1, and Vijay Infrastructure Technology Pvt. Ltd. for the sale of 20,955.40 sq. meters of land at Plot No. 5A, Lower Parel, Mumbai[cite: 8]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Following contractual disputes, an Arbitral Award dated 29.08.2016 directed specific performance for conveyance of the plot to Respondent No. 1 upon deposit of balance sale consideration of Rs. 75,30,00,000/-[cite: 8]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 CIRP against Corporate Debtor was admitted on 06.11.2019 in CP (IB) No. 494/MB/2019[cite: 8]; Supreme Court dismissed challenges to the Arbitral Award on 16.10.2020[cite: 8]; NCLT passed the conveyance order on 08.10.2021[cite: 8]; Appellant filed Intervention IA 2623/2021 in companion Appeal 880/2021 on 17.11.2021[cite: 8]; IA 2623/2021 was rejected on 03.01.2023[cite: 8]; instant appeal was e-filed on 07.01.2023[cite: 8]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: MOU dated 28.06.2004, Arbitral Award dated 29.08.2016, Supreme Court orders dated 14.11.2022 and 09.12.2022 in Civil Appeal No. 7050/2022[cite: 8], and NCLAT judgment dated 03.01.2023 in Appeal 880/2021 rejecting the intervention application on merits[cite: 8]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent No. 1 filed IA No. 1921/2021 seeking directions to the RP to execute the conveyance deed, which NCLT Mumbai allowed on 08.10.2021[cite: 8]. Indiabulls Housing Finance appealed in Appeal 880/2021, wherein Appellant filed an intervention application[cite: 8]. On 03.01.2023, NCLAT dismissed Appeal 880/2021 as withdrawn and rejected Appellant's IA[cite: 8]. Appellant then filed Appeal No. 37/2023 with IA No. 130/2023 seeking condonation of a 400+ day delay under Section 14 of the Limitation Act[cite: 8].
legal_issues: Whether the period spent pursuing an intervention application in another party's appeal can be excluded under Section 14 of the Limitation Act to condone an appeal delay of over 400 days under Section 61 of the IBC[cite: 8], and whether the prior rejection of an intervention application constitutes an inability to entertain due to defect of jurisdiction or other cause of like nature[cite: 8].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The exclusionary benefit of Section 14 of the Limitation Act cannot be claimed when the prior legal proceeding was entertained, considered, and dismissed on its merits rather than being aborted due to a defect of jurisdiction or other cause of a like nature preventing adjudication[cite: 8]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The statutory expression 'unable to entertain it' in Section 14 refers to the court's inability to grant a trial or examine merits due to formal jurisdictional defects[cite: 8]; it does not cover situations where an application is heard on its merits and relief is denied[cite: 8]. Under Section 61(2) proviso of the IBC, appellate delay beyond the statutory 15-day condonable period cannot be relaxed[cite: 8]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the NCLAT judgment dated 03.01.2023 showed that the bench fully examined the merits of the intervenor's claims before dismissing the application[cite: 8]; moreover, choosing to intervene in another creditor's appeal instead of filing an independent statutory appeal defeated the requirement of due diligence[cite: 8]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the prior proceeding was adjudicated on merits, the essential criteria of Section 14 were unsatisfied, rendering the 400-day delay in filing the appeal incapable of condonation[cite: 8].
operative_order: I.A. No. 130 of 2023 praying for condonation of delay is dismissed; consequently, the Memo of Appeal in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 37 of 2023 is rejected[cite: 8].
summary: SREI Equipment Finance Ltd. filed an application seeking condonation of a delay exceeding 400 days in filing an appeal under Section 61 of the IBC against an NCLT Mumbai order directing conveyance of land to Kalpataru Properties[cite: 8]. The appellant claimed benefit under Section 14 of the Limitation Act, arguing it was diligently prosecuting an intervention application in another creditor's appeal before NCLAT[cite: 8]. NCLAT rejected the application, holding that Section 14 applies only when a proceeding fails due to defect of jurisdiction or like cause preventing trial on merits[cite: 8]. Because the intervention application was entertained and rejected on merits, Section 14 was inapplicable, rendering the appeal barred by limitation[cite: 8].

case_title: Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Limited vs. Uniworth Textiles Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Limited (ARCIL) is the Financial Creditor / Appellant (Assignee of ICICI and IFCIL)[cite: 9]; Uniworth Textiles Limited (UTL) is the Corporate Debtor / Respondent[cite: 9]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: IFCIL and ICICI extended term loans aggregating Rs. 41.50 Crores in 1992 (agreements registered on 09.03.1995 and 12.12.1996)[cite: 9]. ICICI assigned its debt to ARCIL on 31.03.2004, and IFCIL assigned its debt to ARCIL on 12.01.2007[cite: 9]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed in the Section 7 petition was Rs. 2,05,83,38,883/-[cite: 9]. The loan account was declared NPA on 31.08.2007[cite: 9]. DRT Nagpur allowed OA No. 162/2014 under Section 19 of the RDB Act on 04.12.2018 in favour of ARCIL[cite: 9]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: SICA reference initiated in 2004 before BIFR was abated by AAIFR on 22.05.2013[cite: 9]; DRT proceeding filed on 05.09.2014[cite: 9]; OTS proposals were submitted on 19.09.2016, 11.11.2016, and 22.01.2018[cite: 9]; settlement was revoked on 22.11.2018[cite: 9]; Section 7 petition CP (IB) No. 1593/KB/2018 was filed on 27.11.2018[cite: 9]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Loan agreements, assignment deeds, AAIFR abatement order dated 22.05.2013[cite: 9], OTS correspondence agreeing to pay Rs. 21 Crores for UTL[cite: 9], part payments of Rs. 51.10 Crores by the group[cite: 9], and balance sheet disclosures acknowledging indebtedness from 2006-07 to 2018-19 despite adverse remarks in Directors' Reports[cite: 9]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench dismissed the Section 7 petition on 17.03.2020 on limitation grounds, refusing to exclude the SICA period and holding that disputed balance sheet entries did not constitute acknowledgments under Section 18[cite: 9].
legal_issues: Whether the period during which proceedings were pending before BIFR and AAIFR is excludable under Section 22(5) of SICA read with Section 5 of the Limitation Act for filing a Section 7 application[cite: 9], and whether balance sheet entries coupled with caveats in Directors' Reports and OTS letters constitute valid acknowledgment of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act[cite: 9].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Statutory suspension of legal remedies under special industrial sickness legislation entitles a creditor to exclusion of time when calculating limitation under the insolvency code, and consistent balance sheet entries together with compromise offers renew the limitation period under Section 18 despite qualifying riders in management reports[cite: 9]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 22(5) of SICA suspends the running of limitation during the subsistence of inquiry or appeal under Section 22(1); such period constitutes 'sufficient cause' under Section 5 of the Limitation Act read with Section 238A of the IBC[cite: 9]. Under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, balance sheets and OTS offers constitute valid written acknowledgments of liability[cite: 9]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Following Bishal Jaiswal, balance sheets must be reviewed alongside notes and reports; isolated caveats disputing debt in 3 out of 13 balance sheets do not negate continuous admissions of debt and restructuring negotiations evidenced by OTS letters[cite: 9]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Excluding the SICA period up to 22.05.2013 and reckoning successive acknowledgments through OTS letters and balance sheets up to 2018, the Section 7 petition was filed well within the three-year limitation period[cite: 9].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 991 of 2020 is allowed; the impugned order dated 17.03.2020 is set aside; and the matter is remanded to the Adjudicating Authority for adjudication on merits. Parties directed to appear on 28.07.2023[cite: 9].
summary: Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Limited appealed an NCLT Kolkata order dismissing its Section 7 petition against Uniworth Textiles Limited on grounds of limitation[cite: 9]. The Corporate Debtor's account was declared NPA in 2007, but SICA proceedings were pending before BIFR and AAIFR until abatement on 22.05.2013[cite: 9]. Thereafter, Uniworth acknowledged debts in balance sheets and OTS settlement letters[cite: 9]. NCLAT allowed the appeal, holding that the period during which legal proceedings were suspended under SICA must be excluded under Section 22(5) read with Section 5 of the Limitation Act[cite: 9]. Furthermore, balance sheet entries and OTS letters constituted valid acknowledgments under Section 18, bringing the application well within limitation[cite: 9].

case_title: Greater Noida Industrial Development Authority vs. Roma Unicon Designex Consortium & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Greater Noida Industrial Development Authority (GNIDA) is the Appellant (Lessor/Statutory Authority)[cite: 10]; Roma Unicon Designex Consortium is Respondent No. 1 (SRA for Earth Towne)[cite: 10]; Earth Infrastructures Limited is the Corporate Debtor (Developer/Holding Company)[cite: 10]; Earth Towne Infrastructures Pvt. Ltd. is the Subsidiary/Lessee (Special Purpose Company)[cite: 10]; Alpha Corp Development Pvt. Ltd. is SRA for Earth Sapphire Court and Earth Techone[cite: 10]; Flat Buyers Associations are Intervenors/Respondents[cite: 10]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: GNIDA allotted Plot No. GH-04, Sector-01, Greater Noida, and executed a registered 90-year lease deed dated 01.09.2010 in favour of Earth Towne Infrastructures Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 10]. An unregistered Development Agreement dated 09.09.2010 was executed between Earth Towne and Corporate Debtor granting development rights[cite: 10]. Similar lease deeds existed for Neo Multimedia and Nishtha Software[cite: 10]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Outstanding dues claimed by GNIDA against Earth Towne were Rs. 148,37,46,148/- as of September 2019, which escalated to Rs. 215,87,18,190/- as of 31.03.2022[cite: 10]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 CIRP against Earth Infrastructures Ltd. commenced on 06.06.2018[cite: 10]; GNIDA submitted Form C on 18.09.2019[cite: 10]; CoC approved Roma Unicon's plan on 26.08.2019 and Alpha Corp's plan on 11.11.2019[cite: 10]; NCLT approved the plans on 05.04.2021 and 08.06.2021[cite: 10], and directed GNIDA to transfer land on 07.12.2021[cite: 10]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Registered lease deeds prohibiting transfer without lessor approval and full payment of dues[cite: 10]; unregistered development agreements[cite: 10]; Information Memorandum of June 2019[cite: 10]; default notices by GNIDA[cite: 10]; and resolution plan provisions waiving GNIDA dues and directing mandatory transfer of leasehold title[cite: 10]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Delhi Bench-III approved resolution plans for Earth Towne on 05.04.2021 and Earth Sapphire Court/Techone on 08.06.2021, and allowed IA 4235/2021 on 07.12.2021 ordering GNIDA to transfer the land[cite: 10]. GNIDA appealed all three orders under Section 61[cite: 10].
legal_issues: Whether assets of a subsidiary company (leasehold land) can be treated and transferred as assets of the holding company in CIRP under Section 18 of the IBC[cite: 10], and whether a resolution plan can extinguish statutory lessor dues and order the transfer of leasehold land without the statutory authority's prior consent[cite: 10].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Assets of a subsidiary company cannot be treated as assets of a holding company undergoing insolvency resolution, and a resolution plan cannot transfer third-party statutory leasehold property or extinguish lessor dues without the express prior approval of the lessor authority[cite: 10]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Explanation (b) to Section 18(1) of the IBC explicitly excludes the assets of an Indian or foreign subsidiary from the assets of the corporate debtor[cite: 10]. Section 7 of the UP Industrial Area Development Act, 1976 and Regulation 37 mandate that transfer of leasehold rights is contingent upon compliance with lease conditions and statutory permissions[cite: 10]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of registered lease deeds established that title and leasehold rights vested exclusively in the subsidiary SPCs, whereas unregistered development agreements conferred only permissive license rights for construction, not proprietary ownership[cite: 10]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Inclusion of GNIDA's leased land in the resolution plans and the unilateral waiver of its statutory dues violated the IBC and state law, requiring the approval orders to be set aside[cite: 10].
operative_order: Appeals are allowed; orders dated 05.04.2021, 08.06.2021, and 07.12.2021 are set aside[cite: 10]. GNIDA is directed to recalculate dues without penal interest within 15 days and is made a party to CIRP[cite: 10]. RP is directed to publish a fresh Form-G with conditions requiring prior approval and payment arrangements with GNIDA[cite: 10]. CIRP is extended by six months[cite: 10].
summary: Greater Noida Industrial Development Authority (GNIDA) appealed NCLT New Delhi orders approving resolution plans for Earth Infrastructures Ltd., which transferred GNIDA's leased lands to resolution applicants and extinguished its dues[cite: 10]. The lands were leased to special purpose subsidiaries, but the corporate debtor executed unregistered development agreements[cite: 10]. NCLAT allowed the appeals and set aside the approvals, holding that under Explanation (b) to Section 18(1) of the IBC, subsidiary assets cannot be treated as assets of the holding company[cite: 10]. Leased lands could not be transferred without GNIDA's statutory consent[cite: 10]. NCLAT directed GNIDA to recalculate dues without penal interest and ordered a fresh resolution process[cite: 10].

case_title: M.K. Rajagopalan vs. S. Rajendran, Resolution Professional of Vasan Health Care Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M.K. Rajagopalan is the Petitioner/Appellant (Unsuccessful Prospective Resolution Applicant / Third Party)[cite: 11]; S. Rajendran is Respondent No. 1 (Resolution Professional of Vasan Health Care Pvt. Ltd.)[cite: 11]; ASG Hospital Private Ltd. is Respondent No. 2 (Successful Resolution Applicant)[cite: 11]; and Vasan Health Care Pvt. Ltd. (VHCPL) is the Corporate Debtor[cite: 11]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Submission and comparative competitive evaluation of corporate resolution plans pursuant to Expression of Interest during the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of VHCPL[cite: 11]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: ASG Hospital Private Ltd. submitted the winning resolution plan offering infusion of funds amounting to Rs. 400 Crores for distribution to stakeholders[cite: 11]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP of VHCPL expired on 10.03.2022 (inclusive of exclusions and extensions)[cite: 11]; the CoC approved ASG Hospital's plan by a 97% voting majority[cite: 11]; NCLT Chennai Division Bench-I approved the plan via order dated 03.02.2023 in IA(IBC)/288(CHE)/2022 in CA/1/IB/2017[cite: 11]; the plan was implemented and funds were transferred with management assumed by a new Board on 06.03.2023[cite: 11]; the instant appeal and leave application IA No. 215 of 2023 were heard and disposed of on 17.03.2023[cite: 11]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Voting records demonstrating 97% CoC approval[cite: 11]; email communications proving Appellant's voluntary participation in the second plan revision without contemporaneous protest[cite: 11]; reconstitution of Board records on 06.03.2023[cite: 11]; and non-joinder of Corporate Debtor VHCPL as a party respondent[cite: 11]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant's interlocutory objections in IA No. 507/2022 were rejected by NCLT Chennai[cite: 11]. Following approval of ASG Hospital's plan on 03.02.2023[cite: 11], Appellant filed IA No. 215/2023 seeking leave as a third party to maintain Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS) No. 58/2023 under Section 61 of the IBC[cite: 11].
legal_issues: Whether an unsuccessful resolution applicant qualifies as a 'person aggrieved' under Section 61(1) of the IBC with locus standi to appeal the approval and implementation of a successful resolution applicant's plan, and whether leave can be granted to rewind a concluded CIRP after plan implementation and fund infusion[cite: 11].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An unsuccessful resolution applicant is not a stakeholder or privy to an approved resolution plan and lacks locus standi to maintain an appeal under Section 61 as a 'person aggrieved' to challenge the commercial approval or implementation of a competing resolution plan[cite: 11]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 31(1) binds the corporate debtor, its employees, members, creditors, and guarantors to the approved plan; an unsuccessful prospective bidder falls outside this defined class of stakeholders[cite: 11]. Section 61(1) restricts appellate rights exclusively to 'aggrieved persons' possessing an enforceable legal right or injury directly stemming from the impugned order[cite: 11]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Having willingly submitted to the revised bidding process to maximize value without contemporary protest, a bidder is precluded from belatedly claiming procedural unfairness after the CIRP has concluded, the plan is implemented, and the statutory timeline has expired[cite: 11]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the appellant is not a stakeholder or privy to the plan and the corporate debtor was not impleaded, the leave application was sans merits, rendering the main appeal incompetent and not maintainable[cite: 11].
operative_order: IA No. 215 of 2023 seeking leave to appeal is dismissed[cite: 11]; consequently, Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS.) No. 58 of 2023 is not entertained and is rejected[cite: 11]. Connected pending IA Nos. 213 and 214 of 2023 are closed without costs[cite: 11].
summary: Petitioner M.K. Rajagopalan, an unsuccessful resolution applicant in the CIRP of Vasan Health Care Pvt. Ltd., sought leave under IA No. 215 of 2023 to appeal against an NCLT Chennai order approving the resolution plan submitted by ASG Hospital Pvt. Ltd., which had infused Rs. 400 Crores[cite: 11]. The petitioner argued he had a vested interest as a bidder who had suffered in the process[cite: 11]. NCLAT dismissed the leave application and rejected the appeal, holding that an unsuccessful resolution applicant is not a stakeholder under Section 31(1) nor a 'person aggrieved' under Section 61(1) of the IBC[cite: 11]. Furthermore, having participated in the plan revisions, the petitioner had no locus to challenge the approved plan[cite: 11].

case_title: Kapil Wadhawan vs. Piramal Capital & Housing Finance Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Kapil Wadhawan is the Appellant (Ex-Promoter of Dewan Housing Finance Corporation Limited)[cite: 12]; Piramal Capital & Housing Finance Ltd. (Piramal) is Respondent No. 1 (Successful Resolution Applicant)[cite: 12]; R. Subramaniakumar is the Administrator/RP appointed by RBI[cite: 12]; and Dewan Housing Finance Corporation Limited (DHFL) is the Corporate Debtor[cite: 12]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process initiated against DHFL under the IBC read with the FSP Rules, 2019, culminating in an approved resolution plan[cite: 12]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Avoidance applications under Sections 43, 44, 45, and 66 impugned preferential, undervalued, and fraudulent transactions undertaken by the erstwhile promoters involving substantial sums of public money[cite: 12]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: RBI superseded the Board and CIRP was admitted on 03.12.2019[cite: 12]; CoC approved Piramal's resolution plan on 15.01.2021[cite: 12]; the Administrator filed various avoidance IAs before and two IAs shortly after CoC voting[cite: 12]; NCLT Mumbai approved the plan on 07.06.2021 in IA No. 449/2021[cite: 12]; Piramal filed substitution applications (including IA 3128/2022) in 2021-2022[cite: 12]; NCLT allowed the substitution orders on 09.02.2023[cite: 12]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Clauses 2.13.2 and 2.13.3 of Part A of the approved resolution plan empowering Piramal to pursue pending avoidance applications and retain recoveries or distribute net proceeds to financial creditors[cite: 12]; substitution applications filed by Piramal[cite: 12]; and orders of the Adjudicating Authority dated 07.06.2021 and 09.02.2023[cite: 12]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Piramal filed IA No. 3128 of 2022 in IA No. 338 of 2021 seeking to substitute its name in place of the erstwhile Administrator to pursue avoidance applications post-CIRP[cite: 12]. The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Mumbai Bench-II) allowed the application on 09.02.2023[cite: 12]. The ex-promoter appealed against the substitution orders[cite: 12].
legal_issues: Whether avoidance applications filed under Sections 43, 45, and 66 survive the conclusion of CIRP and approval of a resolution plan, and whether a Successful Resolution Applicant can be substituted in place of the Resolution Professional/Administrator to pursue such pending avoidance applications pursuant to terms in an approved resolution plan[cite: 12].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Avoidance and fraudulent trading proceedings are independent of and survive the conclusion of the corporate insolvency resolution process, and a successful resolution applicant may be substituted to pursue such pending applications where expressly authorized by the terms of an approved resolution plan[cite: 12]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 26 dictates that avoidance applications filed under Section 25(2)(j) do not affect CIRP proceedings, reflecting legislative intent to maintain separate tracks[cite: 12]. Sections 30 and 31 make an approved resolution plan legally binding on all stakeholders, including the corporate debtor and ex-promoters; thus, contractual assignment of litigation rights to the resolution applicant in the plan is legally binding[cite: 12]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Following the Delhi High Court Division Bench ruling in Tata Steel BSL v. Venus Recruiter, avoidance actions primarily benefit creditors and protect against unjust enrichment; hence, timelines under Regulation 35A are directory and do not render post-voting or post-approval pursuits infructuous[cite: 12]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The substitution was an authorized implementation of the binding approved resolution plan rather than an unlawful delegation of statutory powers, meaning the ex-promoter had no basis to prevent the pursuit of suspect transactions[cite: 12].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 437 of 2023 and companion appeals are dismissed, affirming the NCLT Mumbai orders dated 09.02.2023 allowing the substitution of Piramal Capital & Housing Finance Ltd. to pursue the avoidance applications[cite: 12].
summary: Kapil Wadhawan, ex-promoter of DHFL, challenged NCLT Mumbai orders substituting Piramal Capital & Housing Finance Ltd. in place of the erstwhile Administrator to pursue pending avoidance applications filed under Sections 43, 45, and 66 of the IBC[cite: 12]. Wadhawan argued that the Administrator was persona designata and that avoidance applications became infructuous upon CIRP completion[cite: 12]. NCLAT dismissed the appeals, relying on Section 26 and the Delhi High Court's ruling in Tata Steel BSL[cite: 12]. NCLAT held that avoidance actions survive CIRP, and under Section 31, the approved resolution plan (which expressly empowered Piramal to pursue avoidance applications) is legally binding, permitting the substitution[cite: 12].

case_title: The Rathna Textile Mills Private Limited & Ors. vs. V.R.A.R. Ramakrishnan
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Rathna Textile Mills Pvt. Ltd. (Company) is Appellant No. 1[cite: 13]; Smt. Vasantha Kokilam, R. Angappa Murali, R. Senniappa Sridhar, R. Vidyadhar, and Smt. Senni Girija (legal heirs of Late T.S. Rathnasabapathy) are Appellants No. 2 to 6[cite: 13]; and V.R.A.R. Ramakrishnan is the Respondent / Original Petitioner (50% Shareholder and Founding Director)[cite: 13]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Close family private limited company incorporated with 800 equity shares held equally (400 shares each) between the Respondent and his brother, Late T.S. Rathnasabapathy, holding 9.345 acres of dry land at Palladam, Coimbatore, as its sole asset[cite: 13]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The company never commenced business[cite: 13]; the ancestral management unilaterally allotted 420 shares to Late T.S. Rathnasabapathy on 05.02.1996 and further allotted 200 shares (total 620 shares) to Appellants 2 to 6, reducing the Respondent's 50% holding to a minority without offering rights shares[cite: 13]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: ROC issued show cause notice in 1989[cite: 13]; voluntary winding up CP No. 117/1995 was filed in 1995 and withdrawn on 16.09.2005 with liberty to pursue civil suit O.S. No. 17254/2005[cite: 13]; City Civil Court dismissed the suit on 02.04.2012 relegating parties to CLB[cite: 13]; Form 32 co-opting Appellants 4 & 5 and removing Respondent as Director was filed on 01.12.2005[cite: 13]; sole land asset was sold on 14.11.2005[cite: 13]; company petition CP No. 8/2008 was filed before CLB in April 2008[cite: 13]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Lack of postal proof of service/acknowledgment for board meeting notices in 1995[cite: 13]; Form 32 filings dated 01.12.2005[cite: 13]; Sale Deed dated 14.11.2005 executed without notice[cite: 13]; and ROC notice dated 09.12.1998 confirming no business operations[cite: 13]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent filed CP No. 8/2008 under Sections 397/398 of the Companies Act, 1956[cite: 13]. NCLT Bengaluru allowed the petition on 11.10.2018, setting aside the board proceedings, invalidating the allotment of 620 shares, declaring Form 32 filings null and void, and restoring the 50:50 shareholding[cite: 13]. Appellants appealed under Section 421[cite: 13].
legal_issues: Whether a petition alleging continuous oppression and mismanagement under Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956 is barred by limitation when interlinked corporate acts (illegal allotment, secret board meetings, removal of director, and disposal of sole asset) culminate within three years of filing[cite: 13], and whether board meetings held without notice to a 50% shareholder-director and without quorum are null and void[cite: 13].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Corporate actions characterized by lack of notice, absence of statutory quorum, exclusion of a 50% shareholder-director, covert share allotments diluting equality, and unilateral alienation of the company's sole asset constitute a continuous chain of oppression and mismanagement that is not barred by limitation or forum shopping[cite: 13]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Applications under Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956 are maintainable against a continuous course of oppressive conduct even if originating in isolated past acts, provided the effects of such wrongful acts persist up to the petition date[cite: 13]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: In the absence of registered post acknowledgment receipts demonstrating valid service of board meeting notices on a 50% director, and given the total absence of valid quorum, board resolutions purporting to allot shares or co-opt directors are legally void[cite: 13]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The allotment of 620 shares, the removal of the respondent, and the clandestine sale of company land were invalid and rightly set aside by the NCLT[cite: 13].
operative_order: The Company Appeal (AT) No. 403/2018 (TA No. 81/2021) is dismissed without costs, affirming the NCLT Bengaluru order dated 11.10.2018[cite: 13].
summary: Appellants appealed an NCLT Bengaluru order setting aside an illegal share allotment of 620 shares, Form 32 director filings, and unilateral sale of company land in a petition filed under Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956 by Respondent V.R.A.R. Ramakrishnan[cite: 13]. The Appellants claimed the petition was barred by limitation and amounted to forum shopping[cite: 13]. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the filing of Form 32 removing the respondent and the secret sale of the sole land asset in late 2005 formed a continuous chain of oppression up to the petition's filing in 2008[cite: 13]. Further, board meetings conducted without proof of notice and without quorum were null and void[cite: 13].

case_title: M/S Smartworks Coworking Spaces Private Limited vs. M/S Turbot HQ India Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s Smartworks Coworking Spaces Private Limited is the Appellant / Operational Creditor[cite: 14]; M/s Turbot HQ India Private Limited is the Respondent / Corporate Debtor[cite: 14]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Office Service Provider Agreement dated 17.08.2018 providing flexi-office space and full corporate infrastructure services at Kolkata on a monthly fee of Rs. 3,52,000/- plus taxes, with a mandatory lock-in period of 36 months running from 01.10.2018 to 30.09.2021[cite: 14]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Following premature termination, the claimed operational debt towards the unpaid lock-in period was Rs. 1,05,32,126/-, which increased with interest and charges to Rs. 1,28,95,402/- in the Section 8 demand notice[cite: 14]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Agreement executed on 17.08.2018; Corporate Debtor took possession on 01.10.2018; Corporate Debtor sent early termination email on 04.06.2019 effective September 2019; Operational Creditor issued demand notice under Section 8 on 18.08.2020; Corporate Debtor replied on 05.11.2020 disputing liability; Section 9 application was filed on 09.10.2020[cite: 14]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Service Agreement dated 17.08.2018 specifying a 36-month lock-in under Clause 1.4; email dated 04.06.2019 terminating the contract mid-term; monthly fee payments made up to July 2019; and Section 8 demand notice and reply[cite: 14]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed CP (IB) No. 181/CB/2020 under Section 9 of the IBC[cite: 14]. NCLT Cuttack Bench rejected the application on 08.04.2022, holding that lock-in period dues do not constitute an operational debt and that the agreement was inadmissible because it was unstamped and unregistered[cite: 14].
legal_issues: Whether unpaid office fees for the unexpired lock-in period arising from premature breach of a flexi-coworking services agreement constitute an 'operational debt' under Section 5(21) read with Section 3(6)(b) of the IBC, and whether an unstamped, unregistered service agreement bars initiation of Section 9 proceedings[cite: 14].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Claims arising from breach of contract for the provision of shared office spaces and business amenities during a contractual lock-in period constitute operational debt under the IBC, and formal deficiencies regarding stamp duty or registration do not negate debt where the contract was acted upon[cite: 14]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 3(6)(b) and Section 3(11), a 'claim' includes a right to remedy for breach of contract giving rise to a right to payment; this constitutes an 'operational debt' under Section 5(21) as confirmed by the Larger Bench in Jaipur Trade Expocentre[cite: 14]. A service agreement conferring no interest or title in immovable property is not compulsorily registrable under Section 17(b) of the Registration Act, 1908[cite: 14]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The execution and performance of the contract were uncontroverted because the corporate debtor occupied the premises and paid fees until July 2019; summary IBC proceedings do not require discarding an acted-upon commercial agreement over stamp paper technicalities[cite: 14]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt claimed was a valid operational debt, and the default occurred upon premature unilateral termination during the lock-in period, warranting admission under Section 9[cite: 14].
operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the order dated 08.04.2022 is set aside[cite: 14]. The Adjudicating Authority is directed to pass an order of admission under Section 9 within one month, during which parties may enter into a settlement[cite: 14].
summary: M/s Smartworks Coworking Spaces Pvt. Ltd. appealed an NCLT Cuttack order rejecting its Section 9 application against M/s Turbot HQ India Pvt. Ltd. for unpaid office fees during a 36-month lock-in period[cite: 14]. The NCLT had held that lock-in dues do not constitute an operational debt and that the underlying agreement was inadmissible due to being unstamped and unregistered[cite: 14]. NCLAT allowed the appeal, holding that under Section 3(6)(b) and the Larger Bench ruling in Jaipur Trade Expocentre, unpaid license/service fees for breach of contract qualify as operational debt[cite: 14]. Furthermore, the service contract created no estate in immovable property requiring registration, and technical stamp defects did not defeat summary IBC proceedings[cite: 14].

case_title: Zhejiang Industrial Group Co. Ltd. vs. Al Badr Seafoods Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Zhejiang Industrial Group Co. Ltd. (China) is the Appellant / Operational Creditor[cite: 15]; Al Badr Seafoods Private Limited (India) is the Respondent / Corporate Debtor (Confirming Party/Guarantor)[cite: 15]; and Al Badr Sarl (Tunisia) is the Buyer / Associate Enterprise[cite: 15]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Sale and supply of Frozen Precooked Skip Jack Tuna Loins shipped to Tunisia under Sales Contracts dated 24.05.2019 and 26.06.2019, followed by a Tripartite Settlement Agreement dated 16.07.2020 whereby Al Badr Sarl agreed to pay USD 1,000,000 in 10 equal monthly instalments of USD 100,000, with the Corporate Debtor acting as Confirming Party/Guarantor[cite: 15]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default was claimed for USD 1,121,450 (Rs. 8,52,78,758.79)[cite: 15]. In Part IV, the Appellant claimed default dates based on original invoices (16.09.2019, 07.10.2019, and 14.10.2019), but under the Settlement Agreement, default on the first instalment occurred on 01.08.2020[cite: 15]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Invoices raised in June-July 2019[cite: 15]; Settlement Agreement executed on 16.07.2020[cite: 15]; first instalment fell due on 31.07.2020 and defaulted on 01.08.2020[cite: 15]; Demand Notice under Section 8(1) issued on 30.04.2021[cite: 15]; Corporate Debtor replied on 14.05.2021 denying liability and signature authority[cite: 15]; CP (IB)/45/KOB/2022 filed under Section 9[cite: 15]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Unstamped Sales Contracts and Settlement Agreement dated 16.07.2020[cite: 15]; Bills of Lading showing goods delivered to Tunisia rather than India[cite: 15]; invalid Power of Attorney executed in China and stamped improperly after arrival in India in violation of Section 18 of the Stamp Act[cite: 15]; and Section 8 reply dated 14.05.2021 raising pre-existing disputes[cite: 15]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed CP (IB)/45/KOB/2022 under Section 9[cite: 15]. NCLT Kochi Bench dismissed the petition on 03.05.2023 on the grounds that default under the settlement agreement occurred on 01.08.2020 (barred by Section 10A), breach of a settlement agreement does not constitute operational debt, and the petition was founded on invalid, unstamped documents[cite: 15].
legal_issues: Whether the date of default under a settlement agreement supersedes original invoice dates, bringing the default within the suspended period under Section 10A of the IBC[cite: 15]; whether default of instalment payments under a settlement agreement qualifies as an 'operational debt' under Section 5(21)[cite: 15]; and whether an application under Section 9 can be maintained on the basis of an invalid Power of Attorney and unstamped instruments[cite: 15].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where underlying commercial debts merge into a formal settlement agreement, the date of default is determined strictly by the breach of the settlement schedule; if this breach occurs during the statutory moratorium window prescribed under Section 10A, the application is barred, and defaults under settlement agreements do not constitute operational debt[cite: 15]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 10A creates a blanket prohibition against filing Sections 7, 9, or 10 petitions for any default occurring between 25.03.2020 and 24.03.2021[cite: 15]. A failure to pay settlement instalments does not qualify as an operational debt under Section 5(21) because it does not directly represent the provision of goods or services[cite: 15]. Instruments not stamped in accordance with Section 18 of the Indian Stamp Act and Section 34 of the Kerala Stamp Act are legally unenforceable in summary IBC proceedings[cite: 15]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Al Badr Sarl defaulted on the first settlement instalment on 01.08.2020, demonstrating that the creditor's reliance on 2019 invoice dates was an artifice to evade Section 10A[cite: 15]. Additionally, goods were delivered outside India to a foreign buyer, establishing pre-existing disputes[cite: 15]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The actual default occurred squarely within the Section 10A prohibited window, and the debt lost its operational character upon settlement, justifying dismissal of the Section 9 petition[cite: 15].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS.) No. 272 of 2023 is dismissed at the admission stage without costs, affirming the dismissal order dated 03.05.2023 passed by the NCLT Kochi Bench[cite: 15].
summary: Zhejiang Industrial Group Co. Ltd. appealed an NCLT Kochi order dismissing its Section 9 petition against Al Badr Seafoods Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/Guarantor) for tuna fish supplies delivered to an associate entity in Tunisia[cite: 15]. Following non-payment, the parties entered into a Tripartite Settlement Agreement on 16.07.2020, but the first instalment due on 31.07.2020 was defaulted on 01.08.2020[cite: 15]. NCLAT affirmed the dismissal, holding that the default arose under the settlement on 01.08.2020, falling squarely within the Section 10A suspended period[cite: 15]. Furthermore, breach of a settlement agreement does not constitute an operational debt under Section 5(21), and the petition relied on improperly stamped and unauthorized documents[cite: 15].

case_title: Jagdish Kumar Parulkar, Liquidator for Kapil Steels Ltd. vs. M/s Indore Steel & Alloys Private Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Jagdish Kumar Parulkar is the Liquidator for Kapil Steels Ltd. (Appellant/Corporate Debtor); M/s Indore Steel & Alloys Pvt. Ltd. (ISAPL) is Respondent No. 1; M/s Patni Carbides Pvt. Ltd. (PCPL) is the original lessee; Madhya Pradesh Financial Corporation (MPFC) is the secured lender; M/s Powerage Towers Ltd. (PTL) is a group entity purchaser; and Madhya Pradesh Industrial Development Corporation Ltd. (MPIDCL) is Respondent No. 6 (Lessor)[cite: 16]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: PCPL held 10,219 sq. meters of industrial land at Pithampur under a 99-year lease from MPIDCL dated 07.02.1987, on which it constructed a tin shed[cite: 16]. Upon PCPL's loan default, MPFC auctioned the land and executed a conditional sale deed dated 23.02.2010 in favour of the Corporate Debtor for Rs. 60,01,001/- (paid by a third party, ACME Fero Alloys)[cite: 16]. Clause 6 required the Corporate Debtor to get the lease transferred and registered with MPIDCL within six months, failing which MPIDCL could reallot the land[cite: 16]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Corporate Debtor failed to pay balance transfer dues of Rs. 20,49,216/- demanded by MPIDCL on 15.06.2011 and never registered the lease deed[cite: 16]. On 01.02.2020, the suspended management sold the tin shed to PTL for Rs. 7,81,000/-[cite: 16]. PTL sold the shed to ISAPL on 13.11.2020 for Rs. 11,72,220/-, and ISAPL paid Rs. 38,09,748/- directly to MPIDCL for leasehold rights[cite: 16]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 petition was filed on 10.12.2018; the Corporate Debtor entered CIRP on 28.07.2020 and liquidation on 01.10.2021[cite: 16]. ISAPL executed the amended lease deed with MPIDCL on 02.12.2020[cite: 16]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Conditional sale deed dated 23.02.2010 (Clause 6); demand notice dated 15.06.2011; sale deed dated 01.02.2020; registered sale deed for tin shed dated 13.11.2020; amended lease deed dated 02.12.2020; and MP State Industrial Land and Building Management Rules, 2019 (Rule 19)[cite: 16]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: ISAPL filed IA No. 96/2021 to protect possession, and the Liquidator filed IA No. 04/2022 under Sections 43, 45, 49, and 66 to reverse the transfer[cite: 16]. NCLT Indore Bench disposed of both on 05.05.2022, holding the Corporate Debtor's rights had lapsed and restraining the Liquidator from interfering with ISAPL's possession[cite: 16].
legal_issues: Whether the Corporate Debtor acquired valid, enforceable leasehold rights over industrial land under an unregistered, conditional auction sale deed without executing a lease with the lessor authority, and whether the subsequent direct transfer of leasehold rights by the statutory lessor to a third party constitutes an avoidable or fraudulent transaction under Sections 43, 45, 49, or 66 of the IBC[cite: 16].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In the absence of a registered instrument as mandated by property and registration statutes, an auction purchaser acquires no enforceable title or leasehold rights over immovable property, and the statutory lessor's reallocation of such lapsed rights to a bona fide purchaser for value cannot be impugned as an avoidable, preferential, or fraudulent transaction under insolvency law[cite: 16]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 and Section 17(1)(d) of the Registration Act, 1908, a lease exceeding one year can be created only by a registered instrument[cite: 16]. Failure to comply with mandatory statutory conditions and non-payment of lessor dues causes the allotment to lapse by efflux of time, placing the land outside the scope of Sections 43, 45, 49, and 66 of the IBC[cite: 16]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Liquidators must display professional restraint; mere suspicion of collusion between the debtor's ex-management and subsequent purchasers is insufficient without concrete evidence to invalidate a transparent transfer of property rights executed directly by a public authority[cite: 16]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor never acquired leasehold rights from MPIDCL, and ISAPL legally acquired title and possession directly from MPIDCL through banking channels, making the Liquidator's avoidance application untenable[cite: 16].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs, affirming the order dated 05.05.2022 passed by NCLT Indore Bench[cite: 16].
summary: The Liquidator of Kapil Steels Ltd. appealed an NCLT Indore order refusing to set aside the transfer of leasehold industrial land to M/s Indore Steel & Alloys Pvt. Ltd. (ISAPL)[cite: 16]. The Corporate Debtor had purchased the leasehold in an MPFC auction in 2010 but failed to clear dues or execute a registered lease with MPIDCL within the stipulated six months[cite: 16]. MPIDCL subsequently transferred the leasehold directly to ISAPL under MP Rules, 2019[cite: 16]. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that absent a registered lease deed under Section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act, the debtor never held leasehold rights[cite: 16]. Consequently, ISAPL's direct transaction with MPIDCL was valid and outside Sections 43, 45, 49, and 66 of the IBC[cite: 16].

case_title: M/s IFCI Limited vs. Sutanu Sinha, RP of IVRCL Chengapalli Tollways Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s IFCI Limited is the Appellant (Investor/CCD Holder); Sutanu Sinha is Respondent No. 1 (RP of IVRCL Chengapalli Tollways Ltd.); Asset Care Reconstruction Enterprise Ltd. (ACRE) is Respondent No. 2 (Sole CoC Member/Assignee of Senior Lenders); IVRCL Ltd. is the Sponsor/Holding Company; and IVRCL Chengapalli Tollways Ltd. (ICTL) is the Corporate Debtor (SPV/Concessionaire)[cite: 17]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Under a Concession Agreement dated 25.03.2010 with NHAI, ICTL undertook a toll highway project[cite: 17]. IFCI subscribed to Compulsorily Convertible Debentures (CCDs) of Rs. 125 Crores issued by ICTL under a Debenture Subscription Agreement (DSA) and Share Buy Back Agreement dated 14.10.2011, treated as part of the equity component approved by NHAI[cite: 17]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellant submitted a claim of Rs. 525,04,21,889/- (including interest) in Form C as a Financial Creditor[cite: 17]. Under the DSA, interest was payable solely by the sponsor IVRCL, and the buy-back/put option was on IVRCL, not the Corporate Debtor[cite: 17]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CCD conversion period lapsed on 09.11.2017; CIRP was admitted on 20.04.2022 in CP(IB)/28/2022 filed by ACRE; Appellant submitted Form C on 09.05.2022; RP rejected the claim on 09.08.2022; Appellant challenged the rejection via IA No. 1465/2022 on 30.11.2022; CoC approved the resolution plan with 100% vote on 08.03.2023[cite: 17]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Concession Agreement dated 25.03.2010 defining CCDs as equity; DSA dated 14.10.2011 (Clause 2.1 fastening coupon interest on sponsor IVRCL); Common Loan Agreement; and the fact that IFCI had its corporate guarantee claim of Rs. 663.08 Crores admitted in the liquidation of IVRCL[cite: 17]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant challenged the RP's rejection of its claim as a financial debt before NCLT Hyderabad Bench-II in IA(IBC)/1465/2022[cite: 17]. The Adjudicating Authority dismissed the IA on 14.03.2023, holding that CCDs are equity instruments and not financial debt[cite: 17].
legal_issues: Whether Compulsorily Convertible Debentures (CCDs) that matured prior to insolvency admission constitute a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC or remain equity instruments, and whether coupon interest obligations undertaken solely by a sponsor/holding company impart the character of a financial debt against the concessionaire corporate debtor[cite: 17].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A debenture that is compulsorily and mandatorily convertible into shares does not postulate any repayment of principal and is an equity instrument rather than a loan or debt, and contractual coupon liabilities borne exclusively by a third-party sponsor cannot transform such equity into a financial debt of the corporate debtor under insolvency law[cite: 17]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 5(8) of the IBC, a financial debt requires a disbursement against consideration for the time value of money owed by the debtor; where project documents and financing structures categorize CCDs as the project's equity component with exit limited to equity conversion or third-party sponsor buy-back, no debtor-creditor relationship arises qua the corporate debtor[cite: 17]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying the Supreme Court doctrine in Narendra Kumar Maheshwari and Sahara India, an instrument that compulsorily converts to shares without principal repayment is equity; subsequent default does not alter its intrinsic legal nature[cite: 17]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CCDs matured and converted to equity in 2017, and because ICTL had no obligation to repay the principal or pay interest, IFCI held the status of an investor rather than a financial creditor[cite: 17].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 108 of 2023 is dismissed without costs, affirming the order dated 14.03.2023 passed by the NCLT Hyderabad Bench[cite: 17].
summary: IFCI Limited appealed an NCLT Hyderabad order upholding the Resolution Professional's rejection of its Rs. 525 Crore financial creditor claim against IVRCL Chengapalli Tollways Ltd. (ICTL) based on Compulsorily Convertible Debentures (CCDs)[cite: 17].
