IFCI argued that failure to convert the CCDs and non-payment of interest converted the instrument into a financial debt[cite: 17]. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that CCDs do not postulate principal repayment and constitute equity instruments under Supreme Court precedent[cite: 17]. Since project agreements classified the CCDs as equity and interest payment was the sole obligation of sponsor IVRCL, the debt lacked time value of money qua ICTL, excluding IFCI from being a financial creditor under Section 5(8)[cite: 17].

case_title: Gp. Capt. Atul Jain (Retd.) vs. Tripathi Hospital Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Gp. Capt. Atul Jain (Retd.) is the Appellant (Applicant/Alleged Financial Creditor); Tripathi Hospital Pvt. Ltd. (THPL) is Respondent No. 1 (Corporate Debtor); Dr. B.K. Tripathi (BKT) is Respondent No. 2 (MD); Dr. Nidhi Tripathi (NT) is Respondent No. 3 (Director); and M/s Heritage Hospitals Ltd. is Respondent No. 9 (Auction Purchaser in SARFAESI)[cite: 18]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Alleged oral loan of Rs. 40 Lakhs advanced at 18% interest for construction of the Corporate Debtor's hospital[cite: 18]. Funds were not transferred to THPL, but routed through personal accounts: Rs. 20 Lakhs transferred to one D.K. Chaturvedi (and other third-party accounts) and Rs. 20 Lakhs transferred directly into the personal savings bank accounts of BKT and NT at Noble Bank, Noida[cite: 18]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed principal loan of Rs. 40 Lakhs plus interest; BKT had previously made two interest payments of Rs. 2.5 Lakhs each to the Appellant from his individual account[cite: 18]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application CP (IB) No. 457/ALD/2019 was filed in 2019 following legal recovery notices served on BKT and NT in their personal capacities[cite: 18]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bank transfer receipts to intermediary D.K. Chaturvedi and personal accounts of BKT/NT; NeSL Information Utility Report marked 'Deemed to be Authenticated'; WhatsApp and SMS messages; and personal interest payment cheques[cite: 18]. There was no written loan agreement or direct transaction with THPL[cite: 18]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed a Section 7 petition to initiate CIRP against THPL[cite: 18]. NCLT Allahabad Bench dismissed the petition on 25.06.2020, holding that no documents proved disbursement to the Corporate Debtor and no financial debt was established under Section 5(8)[cite: 18].
legal_issues: Whether personal loan disbursements made to the individual bank accounts of promoters/directors or third-party intermediaries constitute a 'financial debt' disbursed to the corporate debtor under Section 5(8) of the IBC, and whether the corporate veil can be pierced to establish financial creditor status under Section 5(7)[cite: 18].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An applicant cannot trigger corporate insolvency resolution under Section 7 of the IBC unless it establishes a direct debtor-creditor relationship with the corporate entity; personal loans extended to directors, promoters, or intermediaries do not constitute financial debt owed by the corporate debtor[cite: 18]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 5(7) read with Section 5(8) and Section 7(1), the existence of a financial debt disbursed to the corporate debtor against the consideration for the time value of money is a mandatory prerequisite[cite: 18]. The Explanation to Section 7 allowing reliance on default to other creditors applies only after the applicant independently establishes its own financial creditor status qua the corporate debtor[cite: 18]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Following Radha Exports v. K.P. Jayaram, loans to directors in their personal capacity cannot be shifted onto the company[cite: 18]. Piercing the corporate veil is an exceptional doctrine that cannot be used to salvage informal, opaque, and undocumented private lendings[cite: 18]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because no funds were disbursed to THPL and no written contract existed with the corporate debtor, the applicant was not a financial creditor, rendering the Section 7 petition unmaintainable[cite: 18].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, affirming the dismissal order dated 25.06.2020 passed by NCLT Allahabad Bench, with liberty to pursue other civil recovery remedies[cite: 18].
summary: Gp. Capt. Atul Jain (Retd.) appealed an NCLT Allahabad order dismissing his Section 7 petition against Tripathi Hospital Pvt. Ltd. (THPL)[cite: 18]. The Appellant claimed he advanced Rs. 40 Lakhs for hospital construction, but the money was transferred to an intermediary and to the personal bank accounts of the Managing Director and Director[cite: 18]. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that under Section 5(8) and Supreme Court precedent in Radha Exports, a loan given to promoters or directors in their individual capacity does not constitute a financial debt owed by the corporate debtor[cite: 18]. Absent direct disbursement or privity of contract with the corporate person, corporate veil piercing could not be invoked, rendering the Section 7 petition unmaintainable[cite: 18].

case_title: Ramdas Dutta vs. IDBI Bank Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Ramdas Dutta is the Appellant (Suspended Director of Saraju Flour Mills Pvt. Ltd.); IDBI Bank Limited is Respondent No. 1 (Financial Creditor); and Pankaj Kumar Tibrewal is Respondent No. 2 (Interim Resolution Professional)[cite: 19]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Cash credit facility sanctioned by IDBI Bank to Saraju Flour Mills Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor) for Rs. 8,50,000/-, subsequently enhanced to Rs. 15,54,000/-, secured by personal guarantees and hypothecation[cite: 19]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed default was Rs. 15,22,21,838.58/- (including interest as of 01.08.2019)[cite: 19]. The date of default disclosed on affidavit was 31.08.2013, and the loan account was declared NPA on 31.03.2014[cite: 19]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Date of default: 31.08.2013[cite: 19]; Date of NPA: 31.03.2014[cite: 19]; Three-year limitation under Article 137 expired on 31.08.2016[cite: 19]; Alleged credit entry of Rs. 2.75 Lakhs: 29.03.2017[cite: 19]; OTS offer accepted: 29.12.2018 and approved on 11.01.2019[cite: 19]; Section 7 petition CP(IB) No. 1749/KB/2019 was filed on 18.10.2019[cite: 19]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Part IV omission of default date; Bank's Supplementary Affidavit dated November 2021 specifically declaring 31.08.2013 as the date of default; bank statement reflecting a deposit of Rs. 2.75 Lakhs on 29.03.2017 without any signed writing from the debtor; and an OTS proposal submitted in 2018-2019[cite: 19]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench-I admitted the Bank's Section 7 petition on 26.08.2022, holding that the 2017-2018 balance sheet entries and the 2019 OTS extended limitation under Section 18[cite: 19]. The Suspended Director appealed against admission[cite: 19].
legal_issues: Whether a financial creditor can alter the date of default to the date of NPA to save limitation under Section 7 of the IBC, and whether part-payments or OTS proposals executed after the expiry of the three-year limitation period can revive a barred debt under Sections 18 or 19 of the Limitation Act[cite: 19].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The limitation period for filing an insolvency application under Section 7 of the IBC commences strictly from the date of default and not from the date of NPA declaration, and neither an acknowledgment under Section 18 nor a part-payment under Section 19 of the Limitation Act can revive a debt once the three-year period has expired[cite: 19]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963, the right to apply accrues upon the occurrence of default[cite: 19]. The date of default cannot be shifted to the date of NPA[cite: 19]. For Section 18, an acknowledgment must be made before the expiration of the prescribed limitation period[cite: 19]. Under Section 19, part-payment extends limitation only if made within the limitation period and evidenced by a writing signed by or in the handwriting of the payer[cite: 19]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Following Shanti Conductors, a simple bank deposit entry unsupported by a contemporaneous signed writing by the debtor fails the evidentiary test under Section 19[cite: 19]. Because the three-year window from 31.08.2013 expired on 31.08.2016, the 2017 credit entry, 2017-18 balance sheet, and 2019 OTS occurred after limitation had already expired[cite: 19]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt was time-barred prior to the filing of the Section 7 petition, rendering the order of admission illegal[cite: 19].
operative_order: The appeal is allowed, and the impugned admission order dated 26.08.2022 passed by NCLT Kolkata Bench-I is set aside[cite: 19].
summary: Ramdas Dutta, Suspended Director of Saraju Flour Mills Pvt. Ltd., appealed an NCLT Kolkata order admitting IDBI Bank's Section 7 petition[cite: 19]. The Bank's supplementary affidavit specified the date of default as 31.08.2013 and NPA as 31.03.2014, while the petition was filed on 18.10.2019[cite: 19]. The Bank relied on a 2017 part-payment and a 2019 OTS proposal to assert the debt was within limitation[cite: 19]. NCLAT set aside the admission order, holding that limitation begins from the date of default, not NPA[cite: 19]. Since three years expired on 31.08.2016, the subsequent unsigned 2017 bank entry and 2019 OTS could not revive a time-barred debt under Sections 18 or 19 of the Limitation Act[cite: 19].

case_title: Naresh Kumar Aggarwal vs. CFM Asset Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Naresh Kumar Aggarwal is the Appellant (Shareholder of Corporate Debtor); CFM Asset Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. is Respondent No. 1 (Assignee Financial Creditor); Dipti Ranjan Nath is Respondent No. 2 (IRP); M/s Action Ispat and Power Pvt. Ltd. is the Principal Borrower; and M/s Nikhil Footwears Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor (Corporate Guarantor)[cite: 20]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: State Bank of India and consortium lenders sanctioned credit facilities to the Principal Borrower, restructured under Master Restructuring Agreements in 2013 and 2016[cite: 20]. The Corporate Debtor executed a Deed of Guarantee on 30.09.2013 in favour of SBICAP Trustee Company Ltd. to secure the debt[cite: 20]. SBI assigned its debt and underlying securities to CFM Asset Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. via an Assignment Agreement dated 18.01.2021[cite: 20]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Upon default by the Principal Borrower, Section 7 CIRP was admitted against the Principal Borrower on 23.03.2022 in CP (IB) No. 1096/2018[cite: 20]. The Corporate Debtor failed to pay the guaranteed debt, leading to CIRP initiation against it in CP (IB) No. 106(ND)/2022[cite: 20]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Deed of Guarantee: 30.09.2013; CIRP admitted against Principal Borrower: 23.03.2022; Assignment Agreement executed: 18.01.2021; Section 7 petition CP(IB) No. 106(ND)/2022 admitted against the Corporate Guarantor on 28.02.2023[cite: 20]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Master Restructuring Agreements; Deed of Guarantee dated 30.09.2013; Assignment Agreement dated 18.01.2021; and MCA modification of charge records registering CFM as charge holder[cite: 20]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CFM filed a Section 7 petition against Corporate Guarantor Nikhil Footwears Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 20]. NCLT New Delhi Court-IV admitted the petition on 28.02.2023[cite: 20]. The Appellant shareholder appealed against the admission order[cite: 20].
legal_issues: Whether an assignment of financial debt to an Asset Reconstruction Company under Section 5 of the SARFAESI Act requires mandatory registration under the Registration Act to maintain a Section 7 IBC petition, and whether the admission of a Section 7 petition against the principal borrower bars simultaneous initiation of CIRP against the corporate guarantor for the same debt[cite: 20].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An assignment of financial debt executed in favour of a registered Asset Reconstruction Company under Section 5 of the SARFAESI Act operates under a statutory legal fiction deeming the ARC to be the lender, dispensing with general registration requirements, and the pendency or admission of insolvency proceedings against the principal borrower does not bar simultaneous CIRP against the corporate guarantor[cite: 20]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(1) of the SARFAESI Act begins with a non-obstante clause overriding other laws; under Section 5(2), an ARC acquiring financial assets is deemed to be the lender, vesting in it all rights to file a Section 7 petition[cite: 20]. Following the Supreme Court ruling in Laxmi Pat Surana, the liability of the surety under Section 128 of the Contract Act is co-extensive, giving the financial creditor the right to proceed against both borrower and guarantor in equal measure[cite: 20]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Assignment Agreement complied with Section 5(1)(b) of the SARFAESI Act, and charges were duly registered with the MCA; precedents requiring registration for ordinary NBFC assignments do not apply to statutory ARC acquisitions[cite: 20]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: CFM was a deemed lender entitled to maintain the petition, and the simultaneous CIRP against the corporate guarantor was legally valid, justifying admission under Section 7[cite: 20].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 470 of 2023 is dismissed without costs, affirming the admission order dated 28.02.2023 passed by NCLT New Delhi Court-IV[cite: 20].
summary: A shareholder of Nikhil Footwears Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Guarantor) appealed an NCLT New Delhi order admitting a Section 7 petition filed by CFM Asset Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 20]. The appellant contended that the underlying assignment agreement from SBI was unregistered and that CIRP had already been initiated against the principal borrower, Action Ispat and Power Pvt. Ltd., for the same debt[cite: 20]. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that an acquisition of debt by an ARC under Section 5 of the SARFAESI Act operates with a non-obstante clause deeming the ARC as the lender, exempting it from general registration requirements[cite: 20]. Under Laxmi Pat Surana, simultaneous proceedings against the principal borrower and corporate guarantor are maintainable due to co-extensive liability[cite: 20].

case_title: Thyagaraja vs. The Church of South India Trust Association & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Mr. Thyagaraja (a communicant member of the unregistered Church of South India); Respondent No. 1 is The Church of South India Trust Association (CSITA), a Section 8 charitable company incorporated on 20.06.1947; Respondent No. 12 is Mr. John S. Dorai (the original Petitioner who filed the company petition); and Respondents No. 2 to 11 are individual respondents/officials. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CSITA was incorporated to hold and administer church properties and assets for the benefit of the members of the Church of South India across multiple southern states; membership in CSITA involves a distinct four-tier electoral system where parish members elect diocesan and synod council delegates, who then elect CSITA members. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: No financial loan or debt default metrics are involved; the grievance pertains to alleged statutory non-compliances, lapses in conducting biennial synod elections since 13.01.2016, and alleged oppression and mismanagement under Section 241 of the Companies Act, 2013. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The biennial synod expired on 13.01.2016 without fresh elections; a preliminary maintainability application (CA/12/2016) was filed questioning locus standi; an interim order by NCLT was passed on 18.11.2016; Madras High Court disposed of revision proceedings on 22.11.2018 granting liberty to approach NCLAT. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Madras High Court's directions in WP No. 21343/2011 ordering inspection under Section 209-A of the Companies Act, 1956; RoC inspection reports suggesting SFIO investigation; the Register of Members of CSITA showing the absence of the names of the petitioner, the appellant, and the 24 consentors. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CP/02/2016 was filed under Section 241 by John S. Dorai with 24 consentors; NCLT Chennai dismissed the petition via order dated 20.01.2020 in CA/171/2019 holding the petition non-maintainable as the petitioner and consentors were not registered members under Section 2(55) and could not claim Section 244 waiver.
legal_issues: Whether a communicant member of an unregistered religious church body has locus standi to maintain an oppression and mismanagement petition or an appeal against a Section 8 company (CSITA) without being an entered member on its Register of Members under Section 2(55), and whether statutory waiver under Section 244 can be granted to a non-member.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A person cannot be recognized as a member entitled to invoke oppression and mismanagement remedies under Section 241 unless their name is duly entered into the company's Register of Members in accordance with Section 2(55), and statutory waiver of qualifying thresholds under Section 244 is impermissible for non-members having zero membership status. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 2(55) strictly restricts membership to subscribers, written applicants entered into the register, and beneficial depository owners; Section 244(1) provides judicial discretion to waive numerical qualifying percentage thresholds (from 1 to 10) for existing members, but cannot be extrapolated to waive membership itself (zero membership) to confer standing upon non-members. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict verification of the company's Register of Members and Articles of Association governing the electoral hierarchy, requiring affirmative proof of admission to the register rather than general religious or communicant affiliation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appellant was not a party to the original company petition, had not traversed the multi-layered electoral ladder to become a registered member of CSITA, and therefore possessed no locus standi under Sections 241 and 244 to maintain the appeal or challenge internal management.
operative_order: Company Appeal TA No. 15/2021 (Comp. App. (AT) No. 235/2020/TR) is dismissed. No order as to costs.
summary: Mr. Thyagaraja appealed against the NCLT Chennai order dismissing CP/02/2016, which had alleged oppression and mismanagement within the Church of South India Trust Association (CSITA) under Section 241 of the Companies Act, 2013. The Appellant, a church communicant member, claimed representative standing under Order 1 Rule 8 CPC. The NCLAT held that locus standi under Section 241 strictly requires entry in the Register of Members pursuant to Section 2(55). Furthermore, the statutory waiver under Section 244 permits reducing qualifying thresholds for existing members but cannot confer standing upon non-members. Finding that the Appellant was neither a registered member nor an original petitioner, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Raghavendra Joshi vs. Axis Bank Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Raghavendra Joshi is the suspended Director of the Corporate Debtor (M/s. Khadkeshwar Hatcheries Ltd.); Axis Bank Limited is the Financial Creditor; Mr. Amit Chandrashekar Poddar is the Interim Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial credit facilities extended by Axis Bank Limited to M/s. Khadkeshwar Hatcheries Ltd. between the years 2004 and 2016. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Outstanding claimed default amount in the Section 7 petition was Rs. 15,55,87,365/-; account declared NPA on 19.07.2016; loan recall notice issued for Rs. 8,65,76,698/-; Information Utility recorded date of default as 26.09.2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Loan recall notice dated 15.12.2016; Section 13(2) SARFAESI notice issued on 28.02.2017; Corporate Debtor's OTS letter submitted on 04.12.2019; OTS sanctioned by Bank on 14.02.2020 for Rs. 5 Crores against Rs. 12,80,11,496/- dues; revision request on 13.03.2020; OTS withdrawn on 25.01.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Audited balance sheets of the Corporate Debtor acknowledging debt across FY 2018-19, FY 2019-20, and FY 2020-21; Information Utility records establishing default on 26.09.2019; OTS letters dated 14.02.2020, 13.03.2020, and 25.01.2021 confirming default prior to the Section 10A cutoff. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Axis Bank filed a Section 7 IBC application before NCLT Mumbai Bench (Court No. III); NCLT admitted the petition on 20.06.2023, rejecting the Corporate Debtor's Section 10A defense as default occurred prior to 25.03.2020.
legal_issues: Whether a Corporate Debtor whose loan default and NPA classification occurred prior to 25.03.2020 can claim statutory immunity under Section 10A of the IBC on the ground that a default in installment payments under an interim OTS sanction occurred during the Section 10A prohibited window.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory bar under Section 10A applies solely to original defaults arising on or after 25.03.2020 and cannot be invoked to shield pre-existing or continuing defaults that originated prior to the statutory cut-off date, even if a subsequent OTS proposal fails during the protected period. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The Explanation to Section 10A expressly clarifies that the section does not apply to any default committed before 25.03.2020; a default under an OTS sanction does not reset or erase antecedent defaults when the OTS itself was defaulted upon prior to 25.03.2020 and subsequently withdrawn. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification of the default timeline on the Information Utility record and statutory debt acknowledgments in audited financial balance sheets pursuant to Section 18 of the Limitation Act. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the Corporate Debtor defaulted on 26.09.2019, continuously acknowledged debt in subsequent balance sheets, and committed defaults under the OTS prior to 25.03.2020, Section 10A was inapplicable and the Section 7 petition was rightly admitted.
operative_order: The Company Appeal (AT) Insolvency No. 914 of 2023 is dismissed. The Adjudicating Authority's admission order is affirmed. No order as to costs.
summary: The Appellant, a suspended Director of Khadkeshwar Hatcheries Ltd., appealed against the NCLT Mumbai order admitting Axis Bank's Section 7 IBC application for a default exceeding Rs. 15.55 Crores. The Appellant contended that since the default under a One-Time Settlement (OTS) sanctioned on 14.02.2020 occurred during the Covid-19 period, the petition was barred under Section 10A of the IBC. The NCLAT held that Section 10A bars only defaults arising on or after 25.03.2020 and does not shield continuing or pre-existing defaults originating beforehand. Relying on Information Utility records and balance sheet acknowledgments, the NCLAT affirmed admission and dismissed the appeal.

case_title: M/s. Jhanvi Rajpal Automotive Pvt. Ltd. vs. R.P. of Rajpal Abhikaran Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s. Jhanvi Rajpal Automotive Pvt. Ltd. is the Lessee/Appellant; Mrs. Teena Saraswat Pandey is the Resolution Professional of the Corporate Debtor (Rajpal Abhikaran Pvt. Ltd.); Agarwal Real City Pvt. Ltd. is the Successful Resolution Applicant (SRA). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Tenancy/lease of ground floor commercial premises at Niranjanpur, Dewas Naka, Indore, owned by the Corporate Debtor, initially leased under an unregistered deed on 01.11.2018 for Rs. 50,000/- monthly rent; subsequent lease executed by RP on 17.09.2021 expiring on 31.12.2021. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Failure to pay rent from September 2021 to December 2021, and failure to vacate the premises upon lease expiry on 31.12.2021 and expiry of the 15-day notice period. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 26.03.2021; 16th CoC meeting on 06-08.12.2021 resolved to terminate lease; RP issued 15-day eviction notice on 21.12.2021; Appellant replied on 29.12.2021 undertaking to vacate within 10 days of plan approval; NCLT approved the SRA's Resolution Plan on 25.08.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Lease deed dated 17.09.2021 (Clauses 2, 11, 18) containing 15-day notice eviction covenants; Appellant's reply letter dated 29.12.2021 unconditionally undertaking to vacate within 10 days of plan approval; approved Resolution Plan requiring possession for implementation. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP filed I.A. No. 200/2022 under Section 60(5) for eviction; NCLT Indore allowed the application on 11.11.2022 directing the Appellant to vacate within 15 days with police assistance if necessary.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT) possesses statutory jurisdiction under Section 60(5) read with Section 18(1)(f) of the IBC to direct eviction of a tenant whose lease has expired to implement an approved Resolution Plan, or whether the RP is mandated to file civil eviction proceedings under state rent control legislation (MP Accommodation Control Act, 1961).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority possesses jurisdiction under Section 60(5) to order the summary eviction of an occupant from corporate debtor property where the lease has expired, the corporate debtor undisputedly holds title, and vacation is necessary to implement a binding resolution plan, without compelling recourse to civil rent control laws. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 18(1)(f)(ii) and Section 25, the IRP/RP has a statutory duty to take custody and control of assets owned by the corporate debtor, whether in possession or not; Section 60(5) provides wide powers overriding contrary general laws to prevent frustration of the time-bound CIRP. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Clear, unclouded ownership title of the corporate debtor over the asset and the indisputable contractual expiry of the underlying lease agreement. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the corporate debtor's title was undisputed, the lease had expired on 31.12.2021, and the appellant had given a written undertaking to vacate upon approval of the plan, requiring civil proceedings under the MP Accommodation Control Act would frustrate the IBC's objects; hence, the NCLT rightly ordered eviction.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1417 of 2022 is dismissed. The NCLT Indore order dated 11.11.2022 is upheld.
summary: The Appellant, a tenant in premises owned by Corporate Debtor Rajpal Abhikaran Pvt. Ltd., appealed an NCLT Indore order directing it to vacate the premises to facilitate implementation of an approved resolution plan. The Appellant argued that the Adjudicating Authority lacked jurisdiction to direct eviction and that the RP was required to institute regular eviction proceedings under the MP Accommodation Control Act, 1961. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, ruling that under Sections 18(1)(f) and 60(5) of the IBC, the NCLT possesses full jurisdiction to recover unclouded property whose lease has expired to avoid defeating the time-bound resolution process, especially in light of the Appellant's prior undertaking to vacate.

case_title: Westcoast Infraprojects Private Limited vs. Mr. Ram Chandra Dallaram Choudhary, Liquidator of Anil Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Westcoast Infraprojects Private Limited is the Successful Auction Purchaser/Appellant; Mr. Ram Chandra Dallaram Choudhary is the Liquidator of the Corporate Debtor (Anil Limited). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Statutory e-Auction sale of industrial land owned by Anil Limited (in liquidation) conducted on 14.03.2022 pursuant to an e-Auction Sale Notice dated 28.02.2022 on an 'as is where is, what is there is, whatever there is and non-recourse' basis. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Bid price was Rs. 3,73,00,00,000/-; Appellant paid Rs. 15,00,00,000/- as EMD and part-payment of Rs. 1,75,00,000/-, but failed to deposit the balance consideration of Rs. 3,56,25,00,000/- within the mandatory 90-day statutory period expiring on 26.06.2022. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: E-auction held 14.03.2022; sale confirmation letter issued 28.03.2022; 30-day interest-free window expired 27.04.2022; 90-day statutory window expired 26.06.2022; Liquidator cancelled sale and forfeited deposits on 28.06.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Tender document clauses 4.6(f), 4.10(b), and 4.11 permitting automatic cancellation and forfeiture; communication dated 17.06.2022 alleging defective title due to revenue records reflecting the corporate debtor's previous name ('Anil Products Limited'); fresh Certificate of Incorporation dated 23.09.2010 proving change of name; Deputy Collector's transfer permission dated 20.08.2022. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed I.A. No. 578/2022 before NCLT Ahmedabad seeking a 30-day extension and quashing of the cancellation letter dated 28.06.2022; NCLT Ahmedabad dismissed the application with Rs. 5 Lakhs cost on 06.09.2022.
legal_issues: Whether the forfeiture of Earnest Money Deposit (EMD) and part consideration by a Liquidator upon an auction purchaser's failure to deposit balance sale consideration within the mandatory 90-day period violates Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, and whether an un-mutated earlier corporate name in revenue records constitutes a defective title justifying non-payment.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 has no application to statutory auctions where forfeiture is carried out under the terms and conditions of a public auction document prior to the execution of a final sale agreement, and statutory forfeiture terms framed under liquidation regulations are strictly enforceable. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The second proviso to Clause 1(12) of Schedule I of the Liquidation Process Regulations, 2016 is mandatory; balance sale consideration must be paid within 90 days, failing which cancellation and forfeiture automatically operate; a change of name certified under the Companies Act does not alter property ownership or create a defect in title. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict adherence to caveat emptor principles outlined in the auction process document and verification of statutory compliance within the non-extendable 90-day timeline. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Liquidator acted within statutory authority in cancelling the sale and forfeiting the deposited sums upon the Appellant's default beyond 90 days; alleged discrepancies in revenue records did not dilute corporate title.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1258 of 2022 is dismissed, confirming the NCLT Ahmedabad order dated 06.09.2022. No order as to costs.
summary: Westcoast Infraprojects emerged as the highest bidder (Rs. 373 Crores) in an e-auction for land owned by Anil Limited (in liquidation). After paying Rs. 16.75 Crores, the Appellant failed to pay the balance consideration within the mandatory 90-day period, claiming that revenue records reflected the debtor's prior corporate name ('Anil Products Limited') and that forfeiture violated Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that Section 74 does not apply to forfeitures under public auction terms framed under the IBBI Liquidation Regulations, that the 90-day timeline is mandatory, and that a corporate name change does not constitute a defect in title.

case_title: Mr. Arun Chadha, Liquidator of Pawan Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. vs. Ramesh Kumar Suneja & Ors. (with connected appeal)
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 747 of 2021 & Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 748 of 2021
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. Arun Chadha is the Liquidator of Pawan Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Ramesh Kumar Suneja, Savitri Suneja, and Pankul Suneja are suspended Directors/Promoters; Bajaj Finance Ltd. is the non-related Lender; SAKS Developers LLP is a related entity; Skyland International Pvt. Ltd. and S. Kumar & Co. Pvt. Ltd. are related co-borrowers. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Two loan facilities (Rs. 3.46 Cr and Rs. 5.81 Cr) availed from Bajaj Finance Ltd. on 28.02.2017 with the Corporate Debtor mortgaging its Noida commercial unit; and an unnotarized MoU dated 30.08.2018 under which the Corporate Debtor transferred Rs. 1,02,09,360/- to SAKS Developers LLP for real estate development. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total loan disbursed was Rs. 9.28 Cr utilized exclusively by promoter co-borrowers rather than the Corporate Debtor; corporate funds of Rs. 1,02,09,360/- diverted under the MoU; Corporate Debtor was already in default of financial debts. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 CIRP initiated on 04.04.2018; NCLAT stayed/set aside CIRP on 07.08.2018; Supreme Court restored CIRP on 30.11.2018; MoU executed on 30.08.2018; liquidation ordered on 05.02.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Registered Form CHG-1 creating an exclusive first charge over Noida property; Independent Statutory Auditor's report showing guarantees exceeding 60% of net worth in breach of Section 186; MoU executed on UP stamp paper with incomplete profit-sharing terms between father and son sharing identical registered offices. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Liquidator filed avoidance applications (I.A. 2499/2020 and I.A. 2496/2020); NCLT New Delhi on 30.07.2021 held the mortgage valid applying a 1-year lookback period, but ordered refund of Rs. 1.02 Cr from SAKS Developers.
legal_issues: Whether the creation of an exclusive mortgage over corporate debtor property to secure credit for related parties constitutes a preferential transaction under Section 43 attracting a two-year lookback period despite the lender being an unrelated party, and whether a fund transfer executed during an interim judicial stay on CIRP constitutes an avoidable preferential transfer.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In assessing preferential transactions under Section 43, the court must identify the ultimate beneficiaries of the encumbrance; if corporate property is pledged to secure borrowings benefiting related parties, the transaction is governed by the two-year lookback period under Section 43(4)(a) irrespective of whether the immediate lender is a non-related entity. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Applying the Anuj Jain doctrine, the terms 'corporate debtor' and 'transferee' in Section 43(3)(a) must be read conjunctively ('and'); transfers executed outside ordinary business that enrich related parties at the expense of general creditors fall squarely within Section 43(2), and restoration of CIRP by the Supreme Court revives the lookback computation to cover interim periods. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of fund flow trails and beneficiary identities, combined with statutory auditor red flags indicating ultra vires corporate guarantees without reciprocal consideration. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The mortgage executed on 28.02.2017 was a preferential transaction within the two-year lookback period designed to siphon security to related individuals; similarly, the fund diversion of Rs. 1.02 Cr under the suspicious MoU was correctly ordered to be refunded.
operative_order: The Liquidator's appeal (Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 747/2021) is allowed. The Adjudicating Authority's finding upholding the mortgage is reversed, Form CHG-1 is cancelled, and the Noida property is restored unencumbered to the liquidation estate. The promoters' appeal (Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 748/2021) challenging the refund of Rs. 1,02,09,360/- is dismissed. No costs.
summary: The Liquidator and suspended directors filed cross-appeals against an NCLT order adjudicating avoidance applications under Sections 43 and 66 of the IBC. The Corporate Debtor had mortgaged its Noida commercial property to Bajaj Finance Ltd. to secure loans utilized by its directors/affiliates and transferred Rs. 1.02 Crores to a related LLP during a brief stay on CIRP. The NCLAT held that because the ultimate beneficiaries were related parties, the two-year lookback period under Section 43(4)(a) applied to the mortgage despite the lender being unrelated. The mortgage was annulled, the unencumbered asset was restored to the liquidation estate, and the refund order of Rs. 1.02 Crores was upheld.

case_title: Vistra ITCL (India) Ltd. vs. Torrent Investments Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. (with connected appeal)
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 132, 133 & 134 of 2023 with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 139 of 2023
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Corporate Debtor is Reliance Capital Limited (under CIRP with RBI-appointed Administrator Mr. Y. Nageswara Rao)[cite: 6]; Appellants are Vistra ITCL (India) Ltd. (debenture trustee and financial creditor representing lenders) and IndusInd International Holdings Ltd. (IIHL, resolution applicant)[cite: 6]; Respondent No. 1 is Torrent Investments Pvt. Ltd. (resolution applicant)[cite: 6]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Reliance Capital Limited where Administrator reissued RFRP on 22.10.2022 and conducted a Challenge Mechanism on 21.12.2022 under Regulation 39(1A) to optimize resolution plan values[cite: 6]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor carried admitted financial debt of approximately Rs. 25,000 Crores against an estimated liquidation value of Rs. 13,000 Crores[cite: 6]; during the 21.12.2022 Challenge Mechanism, IIHL stopped at round 3 with an NPV bid of Rs. 8,110 Crores, while Torrent bid up to round 4 with an NPV bid of Rs. 8,640 Crores[cite: 6]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 06.12.2021[cite: 6]; Challenge Mechanism conducted on 21.12.2022[cite: 6]; IIHL sent revised draft offer of Rs. 9,000+ Crores on 23.12.2022[cite: 6]; Torrent filed IA No. 1/2023 on 31.12.2022[cite: 6]; CoC resolved with a 98% majority on 06.01.2023/10.01.2023 to hold an extended Challenge Mechanism[cite: 6]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Clauses 3.17.17, 4.2.4, 4.2.9, 4.3.7, and 4.4.4 of the RFRP explicitly reserving the CoC's unconditional right to negotiate, modify, annul, or reissue bidding terms prior to voting[cite: 6]; Administrator's email dated 21.12.2022 indicating Torrent's NPV bid of Rs. 8,640 Crores[cite: 6]; subsequent revised upfront and deferred cash flow proposals submitted by both applicants on 06.01.2023[cite: 6]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Torrent filed IA No. 1/MB/C-I/2023 challenging post-challenge negotiations and the proposed second round[cite: 6]; NCLT Mumbai allowed the application on 02.02.2023, declaring the challenge concluded on 21.12.2022 and prohibiting the CoC from holding an extended challenge mechanism or entertaining revised bids beyond the 21.12.2022 figures[cite: 6].
legal_issues: Whether the conclusion of a Challenge Mechanism under Regulation 39(1A)(b) of the CIRP Regulations imposes a statutory bar on the Committee of Creditors preventing further negotiations or an extended Challenge Mechanism for value maximization prior to voting on resolution plans under Section 30(4), and whether the highest bidder in a challenge process acquires a vested right to have its plan put to vote without further price discovery[cite: 6].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A challenge mechanism conducted under procedural insolvency regulations does not vest any absolute or enforceable legal right in the highest bidder, nor does it extinguish or circumscribe the commercial wisdom and statutory autonomy of the Committee of Creditors to negotiate further, solicit revised terms, or conduct extended rounds for maximizing the value of the corporate debtor's assets prior to voting[cite: 6]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 39(1A) is a procedural mechanism enabling the Resolution Professional to seek modifications or utilize a challenge process, but it does not repeal or restrict the CoC's substantive power under Section 30(4) or Regulation 36B(7) to evaluate feasibility, viability, and financial adequacy, or to reject sub-optimal plans[cite: 6]; the right of the CoC to negotiate under RFRP clauses remains operative post-challenge[cite: 6]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the reservation of rights clauses in the RFRP and Challenge Mechanism Process Note, alongside CoC minutes demonstrating a reasoned assessment that the received bids were sub-optimal compared to the liquidation value and corporate debt[cite: 6]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in interdicting the resolution process and restraining the CoC; the CoC was well within its commercial wisdom and contractual rights to declare the bids sub-optimal and conduct an extended challenge mechanism[cite: 6].
operative_order: The appeals are allowed and the impugned order of NCLT Mumbai dated 02.02.2023 is set aside[cite: 6]. IA No. 1/MB/C-I/2023 and IA No. 99/MB/C-I/2023 filed by Torrent are rejected[cite: 6]. It is declared that the CoC is fully empowered under the RFRP to negotiate further and conduct an extended Challenge Mechanism[cite: 6]. A 30-day exclusion period is granted to complete the CIRP[cite: 6]. Parties shall bear their own costs[cite: 6].
summary: Vistra ITCL (India) Ltd. and IndusInd International Holdings Ltd. (IIHL) appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order that restrained the Committee of Creditors (CoC) of Reliance Capital Limited from conducting an extended challenge mechanism after Torrent emerged with the highest Net Present Value (NPV) bid of Rs. 8,640 Crores on 21.12.2022[cite: 6]. The NCLAT set aside the NCLT's order and allowed the appeals, ruling that Regulation 39(1A) of the CIRP Regulations does not extinguish the CoC's statutory autonomy or commercial wisdom under Section 30(4) of the IBC[cite: 6]. The Tribunal held that an auction applicant possesses no vested right to force a vote, and the CoC retains the right under its Request for Resolution Plan (RFRP) to conduct further negotiations and extended bidding rounds to achieve asset value maximization[cite: 6].

case_title: IDBI Bank Ltd. vs. Indian Oil Corporation Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: IDBI Bank Ltd. is the Appellant/Guarantor Bank[cite: 7]; Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. (IOCL) is Respondent No. 1/Principal Beneficiary[cite: 7]; Mr. Ashwini Mehra is the Resolution Professional of the Corporate Debtor (Punj Lloyd Ltd., PLL)[cite: 7]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Advance Bank Guarantees (ABGs) issued by IDBI Bank on behalf of Punj Lloyd Ltd. to secure a mobilization advance of Rs. 107 Crores and 10% supply payments for IOCL's EPCC-2 package of the 'Aishwarya Project' at Haldia Refinery[cite: 7]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Bank Guarantees No. 160127IBGA00005 for Rs. 49,44,58,134/- and No. 160127IBGA00014 for Rs. 29,47,64,102/- (aggregating approximately Rs. 78.92 Crores) were encashed on 22.10.2021[cite: 7]; Punj Lloyd Ltd. owed an admitted overall debt of approximately Rs. 13,200 Crores[cite: 7]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced against Punj Lloyd Ltd. under Section 7 in CP (I.B) No. 731/PB/2018[cite: 7]; Corporate Debtor sought interim relief before an Arbitral Tribunal under Section 17 of the Arbitration Act, which was dismissed on 21.10.2021[cite: 7]; BGs encashed on 22.10.2021[cite: 7]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Unconditional and irrevocable Bank Guarantee agreements payable on demand without demur[cite: 7]; Arbitral Tribunal order dated 21.10.2021 finding no irretrievable harm or established fraud[cite: 7]; letters alleging that Punj Lloyd Ltd. agreed not to proportionally reduce the guarantee amount against recovered mobilization advances without the Bank's consent[cite: 7]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Resolution Professional filed IA No. 2184 of 2020 before NCLT New Delhi seeking to stay encashment of the BGs[cite: 7]; NCLT dismissed the application on 31.05.2021 holding that bank guarantees are outside the moratorium[cite: 7]; IDBI Bank appealed the dismissal under Section 61 of the IBC[cite: 7].
legal_issues: Whether unconditional and irrevocable Advance Bank Guarantees (ABGs) can be lawfully invoked and encashed during the pendency of a CIRP moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC, and whether allegations of contractual modification or fraud between the beneficiary and the corporate debtor justify interdicting encashment before the NCLT[cite: 7].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An unconditional and irrevocable bank guarantee payable on demand creates an independent obligation on the issuing bank that can be validly invoked and encashed notwithstanding the imposition of a corporate insolvency moratorium, as third-party guarantee contracts are exempted from the statutory stay[cite: 7]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14(3)(b) of the IBC explicitly excludes a surety in a contract of guarantee to a corporate debtor from the scope of the moratorium under Section 14(1)[cite: 7]; bank guarantees represent assets of the issuing bank, not of the corporate debtor, and their invocation is protected under the 2018 IBC amendment[cite: 7]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Fraud vitiating a bank guarantee must be established fraud of an egregious nature directly known to the bank, and mere contractual disputes or unadjudicated claims regarding advance adjustments are legally insufficient to interdict payment[cite: 7]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the bank guarantees were unconditional, irrevocable, and payable on demand, and the Arbitral Tribunal's rejection of interim relief against encashment had attained finality without any actionable fraud substantiated by the Bank, the dismissal of the avoidance application by the NCLT was lawful[cite: 7].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 543 of 2021 is dismissed. No order as to costs[cite: 7].
summary: IDBI Bank appealed against the NCLT New Delhi order dismissing an application that sought to restrain Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. (IOCL) from encashing two Advance Bank Guarantees totaling Rs. 78.92 Crores issued on behalf of Corporate Debtor Punj Lloyd Ltd.[cite: 7] The Bank contended that the mobilization advance had already been recovered, that IOCL and the debtor altered payment terms fraudulently without its concurrence, and that ABGs cannot be invoked during the Section 14 moratorium[cite: 7]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that under Section 14(3)(b) of the IBC, bank guarantees are excluded from the moratorium[cite: 7]. The Tribunal affirmed that unconditional bank guarantees payable on demand must be honored independent of contractual disputes[cite: 7].

summary.case_title: Amanjyot Singh Gulati vs. Navneet Kumar Jain & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Amanjyot Singh Gulati is the Personal Guarantor/Appellant[cite: 8]; Navneet Kumar Jain is the Resolution Professional[cite: 8]; Arun Chadha is the Resolution Professional of the Corporate Debtor (M/s. Gulati Retail India Ltd.)[cite: 8]; Punjab & Sind Bank and ICICI Bank Ltd. are the Financial Creditors[cite: 8]; Smt. Inderjit Kaur Bagga is a co-guarantor/mortgagor[cite: 8]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities availed by the Corporate Debtor (Gulati Retail India Ltd.) from Punjab & Sind Bank and ICICI Bank, secured by personal guarantees and an equitable mortgage over immovable property in Faridabad furnished by Inderjit Kaur Bagga[cite: 8]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed under a SARFAESI notice claiming Rs. 2,83,43,314.56 with interest from 01.10.2013[cite: 8]; mortgaged property was auctioned to recover part of the loan, leaving an unrecovered balance of Rs. 76.48 Lakhs[cite: 8]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Bank issued notice under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act on 04.10.2013[cite: 8]; Corporate Debtor filed Section 10 CIRP application admitted on 30.07.2019[cite: 8]; Appellant filed Section 94 application registered as (IB)-957(ND)2020[cite: 8]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: SARFAESI Section 13(2) notice dated 04.10.2013 addressed to borrowers and guarantors[cite: 8]; Report of the Resolution Professional recommending rejection of the Section 94 petition due to lack of a guarantee invocation notice and expiration of limitation under Article 55 of the Limitation Act, 1963[cite: 8]; absence of any specific demand or invocation notice issued against the Appellant for the balance sum[cite: 8]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed an application under Section 94 of the IBC before NCLT New Delhi (Bench-II) to initiate insolvency resolution against himself as Personal Guarantor[cite: 8]; NCLT dismissed the petition via order dated 23.05.2022 in IA-4356/2022 relying on the RP's report[cite: 8].
summary.legal_issues: Whether a general demand notice issued under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act for enforcing a mortgage over a co-guarantor's property amounts to an invocation of personal guarantee sufficient to constitute a default under Section 94 of the IBC, and whether a guarantor can initiate insolvency against himself nine years after such notice when the creditor took no recovery steps[cite: 8].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A general statutory demand notice issued under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act to enforce a specific mortgage does not automatically constitute an actionable invocation of a personal guarantee for initiating personal insolvency under Section 94 of the IBC where the creditor has not taken steps to enforce the personal guarantee or demand the deficit balance[cite: 8]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: While the definition of 'borrower' under Section 2(f) of the SARFAESI Act includes a guarantor for the enforcement of security interest under Section 13(2), invocation of a guarantee requires an express demand; a lapse of nine years without recovery steps leaves only an alleged technical default that is time-barred and insufficient to trigger Section 94[cite: 8]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of whether the creditor formally issued an invocation of personal guarantee and actively initiated recovery proceedings for the unpaid balance against the guarantor[cite: 8]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The creditor bank never invoked the personal guarantee against the Appellant nor initiated recovery proceedings for the balance Rs. 76.48 Lakhs, rendering the Section 94 application devoid of adequate foundation[cite: 8].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 961 of 2022 is dismissed[cite: 8]. The order dated 23.05.2022 passed by NCLT New Delhi is affirmed[cite: 8]. No order as to costs[cite: 8].
summary.summary: The Appellant, a Personal Guarantor of Corporate Debtor Gulati Retail India Ltd., appealed against the NCLT New Delhi's dismissal of his Section 94 application seeking to initiate personal insolvency resolution against himself[cite: 8]. The Appellant claimed he defaulted following a Section 13(2) SARFAESI notice issued by Punjab & Sind Bank on 04.10.2013[cite: 8]. The NCLAT affirmed the dismissal, observing that the SARFAESI notice was issued primarily to enforce an equitable mortgage of another co-guarantor and did not constitute an active invocation of the Appellant's personal guarantee[cite: 8]. Since the bank had taken no recovery steps against the Appellant for over nine years, no valid foundation for insolvency existed[cite: 8].

summary.case_title: Southern Power Distribution Company of Andhra Pradesh Limited vs. Gavi Siddeswara Steels (India) Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Southern Power Distribution Company of Andhra Pradesh Limited (APCPDCL), a state-owned distribution licensee and operational creditor[cite: 9]; Respondent No. 1 is Gavi Siddeswara Steels (India) Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor) represented by Bharat Kumar (Successful Resolution Applicant)[cite: 9]; Respondent No. 2 is Punjab National Bank (lead Financial Creditor)[cite: 9]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of high-tension electricity to the industrial manufacturing unit/premises of the Corporate Debtor in Anantapur District, Andhra Pradesh, subject to the General Terms and Conditions of Supply approved by APERC[cite: 9]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Pre-CIRP outstanding electricity dues owed to the Appellant; Resolution Plan provided nil payment to the operational creditor based on liquidation value under Section 30(2)(b)[cite: 9]; total payment of Rs. 20.32 Crores was earmarked for Financial Creditors and CIRP costs[cite: 9]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process initiated under Section 7 in CP (IB) No. 673/07/HDB/2018[cite: 9]; CoC approved the resolution plan with 100% voting share[cite: 9]; NCLT Hyderabad approved the plan on 13.12.2019 in IA No. 1079 of 2019[cite: 9]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Approved Resolution Plan allocating nil distribution to statutory/operational creditors based on Section 53 waterfall[cite: 9]; Clause 8.4 of the General Terms and Conditions of Supply requiring full settlement of past arrears before restoration of electric supply to premises[cite: 9]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Resolution Professional filed IA No. 1079 of 2019 for plan approval; NCLT Hyderabad Bench-I approved the plan on 13.12.2019 holding that under amended Section 31(1), the plan is binding on state authorities even if nil payment is allotted[cite: 9]; Appellant appealed under Section 61 asserting its right to recover pre-CIRP electricity arrears under state regulations[cite: 9].
summary.legal_issues: Whether a state electricity distribution utility can demand the payment of pre-CIRP electricity dues from a Successful Resolution Applicant as a condition precedent for restoring power supply under state electricity regulatory terms, or whether Section 238 of the IBC overrides such regulations and extinguishes past claims upon approval of a Resolution Plan[cite: 9].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: By virtue of the non-obstante mandate of Section 238 of the IBC, the provisions of an approved Resolution Plan override contrary statutory conditions or recovery regulations framed under state electricity laws, extinguishing pre-CIRP claims not accommodated under the approved plan[cite: 9]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 31(1) of the IBC establishes that an approved resolution plan is binding on the Central Government, State Governments, and local authorities[cite: 9]; regulations under the Electricity Act, 2003 conditioning service connection on the payment of past arrears conflict with Section 53 distribution priorities and are overridden pursuant to Section 238[cite: 9]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Harmonious reading of Section 30(2) and Section 238 confirming that failure to pay pre-CIRP claims where liquidation value for operational creditors is nil does not invalidate a compliant plan[cite: 9]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The issue stands squarely covered by prior precedent (Damodar Valley Corporation and Eastern Power Distribution Company); the Appellant cannot insist on pre-CIRP dues before restoring power supply[cite: 9].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 258 of 2021 is dismissed[cite: 9]. The NCLT order dated 13.12.2019 in IA No. 1079 of 2019 is affirmed[cite: 9]. IA No. 550 of 2021 is closed[cite: 9]. No costs[cite: 9].
summary.summary: Southern Power Distribution Company of AP appealed an NCLT Hyderabad order approving a Resolution Plan for Gavi Siddeswara Steels (India) Pvt. Ltd., which allocated nil recovery to operational creditors[cite: 9]. The Appellant contended that under Clause 8.4 of its General Terms and Conditions of Supply approved by APERC and the Supreme Court's ruling in TSSPDCL v. Srigdhaa Beverages, electricity dues attach to the premises and cannot be waived[cite: 9]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that Section 238 of the IBC overrides inconsistent provisions of the Electricity Act, 2003, and an approved plan binds the State Government under Section 31(1)[cite: 9].

summary.case_title: Ram Prakash Gupta vs. Radhey Shyam Sharma & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Ram Prakash Gupta is the Appellant/Disputed Director[cite: 10]; Radhey Shyam Sharma is Respondent No. 1/Original Petitioner and founding 50% shareholder[cite: 10]; M/s Shreemat Mahavir Buildcom Pvt. Ltd. is Respondent No. 2/Company[cite: 10]; Smt. Alka Gupta (Appellant's wife) is Respondent No. 3/Director[cite: 10]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Real estate development and land parcel transactions in Jaipur; the Company was incorporated on 20.12.2004 with authorized/paid-up capital of Rs. 1,00,000/- held equally (5,000 shares each) between Respondent No. 1 and Archana Bhansali, whose shares were subsequently transferred to Respondent No. 3 in 2005[cite: 10]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Illegal increase of authorized share capital from Rs. 1,00,000/- to Rs. 2,00,000/- in 2008 and allotment of 1,000 additional shares exclusively to the Appellant, reducing Respondent No. 1's 50% controlling holding to a 25% minority without board authorization or consent[cite: 10]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Form-32 appointing Appellant filed on 15.06.2008[cite: 10]; EGM dated 21.06.2010 authorizing litigation against Suresh Saharan[cite: 10]; Civil Suit No. 02/2010 filed before Civil Judge Jaipur[cite: 10]; Counterclaim filed in 2013[cite: 10]; Company Petition CP-118(ND)/2013 filed before CLB in 2013[cite: 10]; EGM dated 05.11.2016 removing Respondent No. 1 as Director during petition pendency[cite: 10]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Admission of Appellant during testimony in Civil Suit No. 02/2010 that no board meeting took place in the presence of Respondent No. 1 to approve his directorship[cite: 10]; lack of statutory notices of board meetings under Section 286[cite: 10]; fabricated Form-32 without supporting board resolutions[cite: 10]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent No. 1 filed CP-118(ND)/2013 under Sections 397/398 of the Companies Act, 1956 alleging oppression and equity dilution[cite: 10]; NCLT New Delhi allowed the petition on 20.12.2019, setting aside Appellant's directorship, cancelling the share increase, and restoring 50:50 shareholding[cite: 10].
summary.legal_issues: Whether the appointment of a director and dilution of a 50% majority shareholder's stake through an increase in share capital, conducted without issuing mandatory board meeting notices under Section 286 of the Companies Act, 1956, constitutes an act of oppression and mismanagement, and whether the petition was barred by limitation[cite: 10].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The allotment of additional shares executed with the sole object of converting an existing majority shareholder into a minority, combined with the induction of a director without proof of valid statutory notice and quorum, constitutes a continuing act of oppression and breach of fiduciary duty[cite: 10]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 286 notice requirements are mandatory; any board meeting convened without notice in writing to all directors is null and void, rendering resolutions passed therein legally invalid[cite: 10]; continuous oppression is not defeated by a plea of limitation[cite: 10]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The burden of proof rests on the majority/board to establish proper service of notice and valid statutory compliance for board meetings[cite: 10]; admissions in judicial cross-examination confirming the absence of meeting quorum are fatal to claims of regular appointment[cite: 10]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because no documentary proof existed establishing a valid board meeting or notice to appoint the Appellant, the NCLT rightly annulled his directorship and reversed the capital increase to restore 50% equity to each founding bloc[cite: 10].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 183 of 2020 is dismissed[cite: 10]. The NCLT New Delhi order dated 20.12.2019 in CP-118(ND)/2013 is affirmed[cite: 10]. No order as to costs[cite: 10].
summary.summary: Ram Prakash Gupta appealed against the NCLT New Delhi order in CP-118(ND)/2013 setting aside his appointment as Director of M/s Shreemat Mahavir Buildcom Pvt. Ltd. and reversing an increase in share capital that had diluted founding shareholder Radhey Shyam Sharma from 50% to 25%[cite: 10]. The Appellant claimed the petition was barred by limitation due to five years of acquiescence[cite: 10]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that issuance of shares to convert a majority into a minority without issuing mandatory board meeting notices under Section 286 of the Companies Act, 1956 constitutes continuous oppression[cite: 10]. Affirming the NCLT, the Tribunal cancelled the excess shares and restored equal 50% shareholding[cite: 10].

summary.case_title: Indiabulls Housing Finance Limited vs. Revital Realty Private Limited
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Indiabulls Housing Finance Limited is the Financial Creditor/Appellant; Revital Realty Private Limited is the Corporate Debtor/Respondent[cite: 11]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan facility of Rs. 85 Crores sanctioned on 05.02.2016 and formalized via Loan Agreement dated 22.02.2016, with full disbursement completed on 09.05.2016; terms provided a repayment moratorium on principal until 19.07.2017[cite: 11]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor defaulted on the July 2018 installment payable on 19.08.2018; entire remaining facility was recalled with Rs. 85 Crores-linked dues falling due upon expiry of recall period on 28.03.2022[cite: 11]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Loan disbursed on 09.05.2016; repayments made by debtor from 02.06.2016 to 24.01.2019 adjusted toward dues up to 19.07.2018; installment default on 19.08.2018; Loan Recall Notice issued on 25.03.2022 with deadline of 28.03.2022; Section 7 application filed on 04.04.2022[cite: 11]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Loan Account No. S000239453; Clauses 3.1.1, 12.1.1, and 12.2 of the Loan Agreement; RTGS and cheque payment records proving credit adjustments up to 19.07.2018; Loan Recall Notice dated 25.03.2022[cite: 11]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed CP (IB) 283 (ND)/2022 under Section 7 on 04.04.2022; NCLT New Delhi (Bench-V) dismissed the petition at threshold on 23.05.2022 holding it barred by limitation, presuming the date of loan disbursement (09.05.2016) to be the date of default[cite: 11].
summary.legal_issues: Whether the limitation period of three years under Article 137 of the Limitation Act for filing an application under Section 7 of the IBC begins on the date of loan disbursement, the date of the first installment default, or each subsequent continuing default/loan recall date, and whether the Supreme Court's Covid-19 limitation exclusion applies[cite: 11].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The date of disbursement cannot be treated as the date of default; a financial creditor is not obligated to initiate insolvency on the very first default, and every subsequent default or acceleration of the debt pursuant to a loan recall notice provides a fresh cause of action and computation period for limitation[cite: 11]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 3(12) and Section 7(1) of the IBC, default occurs only when an amount is due and payable and remains unpaid; treating the date of loan disbursement as the date of default is a patent error[cite: 11]; furthermore, the exclusion period from 15.03.2020 to 28.02.2022 established by the Supreme Court in Suo Motu WP No. 3/2020 applies to Section 7 filings[cite: 11]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the loan ledger entries showing the actual date when repayment installments fell due and remained unpaid, considered alongside the terms of the loan contract[cite: 11]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The default occurred either on 19.08.2018 or upon expiry of the recall notice on 28.03.2022, both of which fall within the permissible limitation period when applying the Supreme Court's Covid-19 limitation exclusion for the application filed on 04.04.2022[cite: 11].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 994 of 2022 is allowed[cite: 11]. The order dated 23.05.2022 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench-V is set aside[cite: 11]. The Section 7 application is revived to be heard on merits in accordance with law[cite: 11]. No costs[cite: 11].
summary.summary: Indiabulls Housing Finance Limited appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order dismissing its Section 7 IBC application against Revital Realty Private Limited as barred by limitation[cite: 11]. The NCLT had incorrectly identified 09.05.2016 (the date of full loan disbursement) as the date of default[cite: 11]. The NCLAT set aside the dismissal and revived the petition, holding that disbursement cannot constitute default under Section 3(12)[cite: 11]. The Tribunal clarified that repayments were credited through 19.07.2018, making 19.08.2018 the first installment default and 28.03.2022 the loan recall default, both of which fell well within limitation after applying the Supreme Court's Covid-19 limitation exclusion[cite: 11].

summary.case_title: Jindal Stainless Ltd. vs. Mr. Shailendra Ajmera, Resolution Professional of Mittal Corp Ltd. & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Jindal Stainless Ltd. (JSL) is the Resolution Applicant/Appellant[cite: 12]; Mr. Shailendra Ajmera is the Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor Mittal Corp Ltd. (Respondent No. 1)[cite: 12]; Shyam Sel and Power Limited (SSPL) is a competing Resolution Applicant (Respondent No. 2)[cite: 12]; Committee of Creditors is Respondent No. 3[cite: 12]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP of Mittal Corp Limited wherein RFRP was issued on 11.04.2022 and six resolution plans were received; CoC in its 12th meeting adopted a multi-round Challenge Process mechanism to optimize resolution plan values[cite: 12]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor was undergoing CIRP; during the 15.07.2022 Challenge Process, seven bidding rounds were held until Rimjhim Ispat emerged as the highest bidder and JSL exited in round 3; all applicants were required to submit final binding compliance plans by 18.07.2022[cite: 12]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 10.11.2021[cite: 12]; Challenge Process held on 15.07.2022[cite: 12]; final plans submitted by 18.07.2022[cite: 12]; SSPL submitted revised unsolicited financial proposals on 19.07.2022, 25.07.2022, and 29.07.2022[cite: 12]; 17th CoC on 03.08.2022 resolved to commence voting on the four compliant plans from 05.08.2022 to 26.08.2022[cite: 12]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Challenge Process Rules (Clauses 3 to 9) providing that the last revised financial proposal is binding and prohibiting post-closure revisions[cite: 12]; Resurgent India qualitative/quantitative evaluation matrix scores (JSL: 84.50, RIL: 78.62, SSPL: 69.73)[cite: 12]; SSPL's unsolicited post-challenge offer emails[cite: 12]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: SSPL filed IA 2193/2022 before NCLT Mumbai seeking direction to place its post-closure revised offer before CoC[cite: 12]; NCLT Mumbai on 11.08.2022 allowed the application without detailed reasoning and directed CoC to consider SSPL's revised plan, halting ongoing voting[cite: 12].
summary.legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority can direct the Committee of Creditors to consider an unsolicited, post-closure revised resolution plan submitted by an applicant after the formal completion of a Swiss Challenge/Challenge Process under Regulation 39(1A) and after the CoC had already resolved to commence voting[cite: 12].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a challenge mechanism is formally concluded under agreed rules and the CoC in its commercial wisdom resolves to put compliant resolution plans to vote, the Adjudicating Authority cannot interfere to compel consideration of an unsolicited, late revised financial offer submitted by a single applicant post closure[cite: 12]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 39(1A) permits a challenge mechanism to enable applicants to improve their plans, and Clause 7 of the approved Challenge Rules bars unilateral revisions after closure; the paramount status of the commercial wisdom of the CoC under Section 30(4) encompasses the choice to abide by its concluded challenge and proceed with voting within statutory timelines[cite: 12]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification that equal opportunity was provided to all prospective applicants during the seven bidding rounds and adherence to the agreed non-negotiation clause post-closure[cite: 12]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred in disrupting the voting process that commenced on 07.08.2022 to entertain an unsolicited bid submitted outside the challenge process rules[cite: 12].
summary.operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 1058 of 2022 is allowed[cite: 12]. The order dated 11.08.2022 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench in IA 2193/2022 is set aside[cite: 12]. Voting on the four compliant plans shall resume and be completed within one month, with CIRP extended to 28.02.2023[cite: 12].
summary.summary: Jindal Stainless Ltd. appealed an NCLT Mumbai order directing the CoC of Mittal Corp Ltd. to consider a revised, post-challenge offer submitted by competing bidder Shyam Sel and Power Ltd. (SSPL)[cite: 12]. The CoC had previously conducted a seven-round Challenge Process under Regulation 39(1A) of the CIRP Regulations, received final binding plans, and begun voting on 07.08.2022[cite: 12]. The NCLAT set aside the NCLT's direction and allowed the appeal, holding that once a challenge mechanism is concluded and the CoC elects to proceed with voting, an individual applicant has no legal right to submit late unsolicited revisions[cite: 12]. The Tribunal ordered voting to resume immediately[cite: 12].

summary.case_title: Tejinder Pal Setia vs. Kone Elevator India Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Tejinder Pal Setia is the Suspended Director of the Corporate Debtor (M/s. Future Colonizer and Construction Pvt. Ltd. / Jade Business Park project entity); Kone Elevator India Pvt. Ltd. is the Operational Creditor/Respondent No. 1; Sanjeev Chadha is the Assignee/Respondent No. 3; Intervenors are 55 Homebuyer Allottees[cite: 14]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply, installation, testing, and commissioning of 4 passenger elevators for the Fashion Technology Park/Jade Business Park project in Mohali, Punjab, initially contracted on 05.02.2013 and novated via fresh contract dated 14.03.2015[cite: 14]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total claimed operational debt was Rs. 92,70,000/-; three cheques issued in 2015 for Rs. 10.30 Lakhs, Rs. 36.05 Lakhs, and Rs. 36.05 Lakhs were dishonoured; Corporate Debtor acknowledged debt on 12.07.2013 and 25.11.2015[cite: 14]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Form 3 Demand Notice issued on 15.10.2018 and dispatched on 18.10.2018; Section 9 application filed on 03.04.2019; Settlement Agreement executed on 27.09.2021 for Rs. 60 Lakhs (Rs. 25 Lakhs paid, Rs. 35 Lakhs unpaid); debt assigned to Respondent No. 3 on 03.02.2023[cite: 14]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Postal receipts and delivery tracking confirming delivery of Demand Notice at Registered Office; letter of acknowledgment dated 25.11.2015; three dishonoured cheques; signed Settlement Agreement dated 27.09.2021 expressly admitting default and the 15.10.2018 Demand Notice[cite: 14]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed Section 9 application CP (IB) No. 248/Chd/Chd/2019; NCLT Chandigarh admitted the petition on 27.02.2023 upon breach of settlement; Suspended Director appealed the admission order[cite: 14].
summary.legal_issues: Whether a Section 8 demand notice issued in Form 3 without invoices is defective when the operational debt is based on contracts, written acknowledgments, and dishonoured cheques; whether demand notice delivered at the registered office constitutes valid service; and whether an operational creditor can prosecute Section 9 upon a debtor's breach of an interim settlement agreement[cite: 14].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A Section 8 demand notice issued in Form 3 without invoices is legally valid and complete when the operational debt is founded upon contractual agreements, written acknowledgments, and dishonoured cheques rather than contemporaneous invoice disputes[cite: 14]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Rule 5(1) of the Adjudicating Authority Rules, an operational creditor has the statutory option to deliver either a demand notice in Form 3 or a notice in Form 4 with attached invoices; where liability is acknowledged via contracts and dishonoured negotiable instruments, Form 3 suffices[cite: 14]; breach of a formal settlement agreement revives the right to proceed for the full acknowledged debt[cite: 14]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Postal speed post dispatch receipts and online postal tracking reports confirming delivery at the debtor's registered office establish valid statutory service[cite: 14]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor acknowledged the operational debt in letters and the Settlement Agreement, defaulted on payment installments, and was properly served with Demand Notice, fully justifying the Section 9 admission[cite: 14].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 262 of 2023 is dismissed[cite: 14]. The NCLT Chandigarh admission order dated 27.02.2023 is affirmed[cite: 14]. The interim deposit of Rs. 35 Lakhs deposited by the Appellant is directed to be returned[cite: 14]. No order as to costs[cite: 14].
summary.summary: Tejinder Pal Setia, Suspended Director of the Corporate Debtor, appealed against an NCLT Chandigarh order admitting a Section 9 IBC application filed by Kone Elevator India Pvt. Ltd. for an unpaid debt of Rs. 92.70 Lakhs[cite: 14]. The Appellant contended that the Demand Notice was defective as it was issued in Form 3 without accompanying invoices, that service was ineffective, and that the debt assignment was invalid[cite: 14]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that Form 3 is legally valid where the debt is anchored in contracts, dishonoured cheques, and written acknowledgments[cite: 14]. Furthermore, the debtor had admitted the debt and notice in a subsequent Settlement Agreement, which it breached by failing to pay balance installments[cite: 14].

summary.case_title: Carissa Investments LLC vs. Indu Techzone Private Limited & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Carissa Investments LLC (Mauritius) is the Shareholder/Appellant[cite: 15]; Indu Techzone Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor (Respondent No. 1) represented by RP Krishna Komaravolu[cite: 15]; Prudent ARC Limited is the Financial Creditor/Assignee (Respondent No. 2)[cite: 15]; Edelweiss ARC (EARC) is the intermediate Assignor[cite: 15]; IDFC Ltd. is the original native lender[cite: 15]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Rupee Loan Agreement dated 08.09.2008 for a credit facility of Rs. 60 Crores disbursed by IDFC Ltd., assigned to EARC on 24.12.2013 and subsequently assigned to Prudent ARC on 04.09.2020[cite: 15]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Loan classified as NPA on 13.10.2013; EARC filed OA No. 721 of 2015 before DRT Hyderabad claiming Rs. 49,12,33,998/-; settlement reached on 12.03.2018 for Rs. 15,00,12,830/- payable in three tranches, where the third tranche of Rs. 10 Crores defaulted on 31.03.2020[cite: 15]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account declared NPA on 13.10.2013; Settlement letter executed on 12.03.2018; third tranche payment fell due and defaulted on 31.03.2020; Prudent ARC filed Section 7 application on 03.07.2021[cite: 15]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Part IV of the Section 7 application expressly declaring 31.03.2020 as the date of default; DRT settlement letter dated 12.03.2018 fixing the third installment date as 31.03.2020; Assignment Agreements dated 24.12.2013 and 04.09.2020[cite: 15]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Prudent ARC filed CP(IB) No. 207/7/HDB/2021 under Section 7; NCLT Hyderabad admitted the petition on 07.02.2022 holding that financial debt was admitted and payable; Appellant shareholder appealed the admission order under Section 61[cite: 15].
summary.legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 7 of the IBC can be maintained when the default date set out in Part IV of the application is 31.03.2020, falling squarely within the statutory bar imposed under Section 10A of the IBC[cite: 15].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 10A of the IBC, no application for the initiation of CIRP can ever be filed for any default arising on or after 25.03.2020 up to 24.03.2021, and this statutory prohibition operates as an absolute bar to admission[cite: 15]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Following the Supreme Court ruling in Ramesh Kymal, Section 10A contains a non-obstante clause overriding Sections 7, 9, and 10; its proviso explicitly mandates that 'no application shall ever be filed' for defaults occurring during the covered period; continuation of default past the protected year does not remove the bar for a default that arose within the period[cite: 15]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the date of default specifically crystalized in Part IV of the Section 7 petition and the governing terms of the underlying settlement agreement[cite: 15]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the creditor's application specifically specified the default date as 31.03.2020 under the third installment of the settlement, the petition was hit by the statutory embargo of Section 10A and was legally non-maintainable[cite: 15].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 124 of 2022 is allowed[cite: 15]. The impugned admission order of NCLT Hyderabad dated 07.02.2022 in CP(IB) No. 207/7/HDB/2021 is set aside, and the Section 7 petition is dismissed[cite: 15]. No order as to costs[cite: 15].
summary.summary: Carissa Investments LLC, a shareholder of Indu Techzone Pvt. Ltd., appealed an NCLT Hyderabad order admitting a Section 7 IBC petition filed by Prudent ARC Limited[cite: 15]. The petition was predicated on the default of the third installment under a DRT settlement agreement, which fell due and was defaulted on 31.03.2020[cite: 15]. The NCLAT set aside the admission order and dismissed the Section 7 petition, holding that under Section 10A of the IBC and the Supreme Court precedent in Ramesh Kymal, no insolvency petition can ever be filed for a default occurring between 25.03.2020 and 24.03.2021[cite: 15].

summary.case_title: Vishwajeet Subhash Jhavar vs. IDFC First Bank Limited & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Vishwajeet Subhash Jhavar is the Suspended Director of Marvel Realtors & Developers Limited (Corporate Debtor); IDFC First Bank Limited is the Financial Creditor (Respondent No. 1); Manoj Kumar Mishra is the Interim Resolution Professional (Respondent No. 2); Catalyst Trusteeship Limited is the Intervener/Third-Party Financial Creditor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities extended by IDFC First Bank Limited to Marvel Realtors & Developers Limited. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default committed on credit facilities leading to the initiation of Section 7 proceedings; specific quantum not detailed in order; settlement reached between parties via Settlement Letter dated 08.05.2023. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 23.12.2022; NCLAT stayed CoC formation on 04.01.2023; Catalyst Trusteeship submitted Form C claim on 04.01.2023; Settlement Letter executed on 08.05.2023; settlement brought on record by affidavit dated 09.05.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Settlement Letter dated 08.05.2023 executed between IDFC First Bank and the Corporate Debtor; Appellant's undertaking to pay unpaid CIRP costs and IRP fees; Intervener's Form C claim dated 04.01.2023. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 application CP (IB) 646 (MB)/2022 admitted by NCLT Mumbai Bench-I on 23.12.2022; Suspended Director appealed under Section 61; NCLAT stayed CoC constitution before taking the settlement on record.
