summary.legal_issues: Whether the Appellate Tribunal can exercise inherent powers under Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016 to close CIRP and set aside a Section 7 admission order pursuant to a settlement between the corporate debtor and the petitioning financial creditor prior to the constitution of the Committee of Creditors (CoC), notwithstanding objections and claims filed by third-party financial creditors before the IRP.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Prior to the formal constitution of the Committee of Creditors, an application for withdrawal and closure of corporate insolvency proceedings following a settlement between the corporate debtor and the original petitioning creditor cannot be stifled merely due to the filing or anticipation of claims by third-party creditors. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Applying the Swiss Ribbons and Ashok G. Rajani doctrines, inherent powers under Rule 11 of the NCLT/NCLAT Rules are exercisable to permit withdrawal/settlement before the CoC is constituted; third-party creditors suffer no legal prejudice as they retain the independent statutory right to file fresh insolvency proceedings for their own claims. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Formal confirmation of settlement by the petitioning financial creditor, undisputed non-constitution of the CoC, and a binding undertaking to cover all accrued CIRP costs and IRP fees. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the CoC was never constituted and IDFC First Bank executed a valid settlement, the CIRP was terminated and the admission order set aside, reserving the intervener's right to pursue independent legal remedies.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 08 of 2023 is disposed of by taking the Settlement Letter dated 08.05.2023 on record, setting aside the NCLT Mumbai admission order dated 23.12.2022, and closing the CIRP against Marvel Realtors & Developers Limited. The intervener is granted liberty to initiate independent proceedings in accordance with law.
summary.summary: Vishwajeet Subhash Jhavar, Suspended Director of Marvel Realtors & Developers Limited, challenged an NCLT Mumbai order admitting IDFC First Bank's Section 7 IBC application. Before the Committee of Creditors (CoC) was constituted, the NCLAT stayed its formation and the parties executed a comprehensive settlement on 08.05.2023. Catalyst Trusteeship Limited intervened, opposing closure due to its pending Form C claims. The NCLAT held that settlements reached prior to CoC constitution cannot be blocked by third-party claims, as other creditors retain independent rights to initiate fresh insolvency actions. Exercising inherent powers under Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules, the Tribunal set aside the admission order and terminated CIRP.

summary.case_title: Ashmeet Singh Bhatia vs. Sundrm Consultants Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Ashmeet Singh Bhatia is the Appellant/Homebuyer in group entity Granite Gate Properties Pvt. Ltd.; Sundrm Consultants Pvt. Ltd. is the Financial Creditor/Respondent No. 1; M/s Three C Properties Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor/Respondent No. 2. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Sundrm Consultants Pvt. Ltd. filed a Section 7 IBC application claiming a default of Rs. 5 Crores against Three C Properties Pvt. Ltd., registered as C.P. (IB) No. 849 (PB)/2020. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Purported financial debt of Rs. 5 Crores claimed under the Section 7 petition, alleged by the Appellant to be collusive, malicious, and fraudulent to defeat homebuyers' recoveries. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application filed in 2020; Appellant filed IA No. 4971 of 2020 under Section 65 prior to admission; NCLT dismissed the IA on 31.05.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Pleadings in IA No. 4971 of 2020 alleging collusive, fraudulent litigation between Sundrm Consultants and the Corporate Debtor designed to defraud thousands of flat buyers. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi dismissed IA No. 4971 of 2020 on 31.05.2021 holding that Section 65(1) applications are maintainable only after a company petition is admitted and CIRP is initiated; Appellant appealed under Section 61.
summary.legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 65 of the IBC alleging fraudulent or malicious initiation of insolvency proceedings is maintainable immediately after an application under Section 7, 9, or 10 is filed, or whether it can only be entertained after the main petition is formally admitted and CIRP is initiated.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application under Section 65 challenging fraudulent or malicious initiation of insolvency proceedings is maintainable at the pre-admission stage immediately after an application under Section 7, 9, or 10 is filed, and its maintainability is not conditioned upon prior admission of the petition. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 5(11), 'initiation date' refers to the date an application is filed by the applicant, whereas under Section 5(12), 'insolvency commencement date' is the date of formal admission; the phrase 'If, any person initiates the insolvency resolution process' under Section 65 refers to the filing of the petition under Section 5(11) rather than its admission. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Harmonious statutory construction of definition clauses Sections 5(11) and 5(12) alongside the Supreme Court's ruling in Ramesh Kymal v. Siemens Gamesa. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT committed a patent error of law in equating 'initiation' with 'admission'; Section 65 applies at the inception of proceedings to prevent fraudulent invocations of the Code.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 557 of 2021 is allowed. The NCLT New Delhi order dated 31.05.2021 is set aside, and IA No. 4971 of 2020 is remanded back to the Tribunal to decide locus standi and substantive allegations on merits in accordance with law. Parties directed to appear on 10.04.2023.
summary.summary: Ashmeet Singh Bhatia, a homebuyer in a group company of Corporate Debtor Three C Properties Pvt. Ltd., appealed an NCLT New Delhi order dismissing his application under Section 65 of the IBC. The NCLT had held that Section 65 penalties for fraudulent or malicious initiation can only be considered after an insolvency petition is formally admitted. The NCLAT set aside the decision and allowed the appeal, ruling that 'initiation date' under Section 5(11) means the filing date of the petition, whereas 'commencement date' under Section 5(12) denotes admission. Consequently, Section 65 applications are fully maintainable at the pre-admission stage, and the matter was remanded to determine locus and merits.

summary.case_title: J.C. Flowers Asset Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. vs. Deserve Exim Pvt. Ltd.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: J.C. Flowers Asset Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. is the Financial Creditor/Appellant; Deserve Exim Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Guarantor/Corporate Debtor; Radius & Deserve Builders LLP is Borrower 1; Raghuleela Builders Pvt. Ltd. is Borrower 2. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Two Deeds of Guarantee dated 02.06.2015 executed by Deserve Exim Pvt. Ltd. securing term loan facilities of Rs. 500 Crores disbursed to Borrower 1 and Rs. 300 Crores disbursed to Borrower 2. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by Borrower 1 occurred on 01.08.2019 (NPA on 31.10.2019) with total dues of Rs. 514,89,16,795/-; default by Borrower 2 occurred on 01.02.2019 with total dues of Rs. 374,05,78,070/-; guarantees were invoked on 07.08.2020 and 26.06.2020 respectively. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Term loans disbursed between 2015 and 2016; principal borrower defaults on 01.02.2019 and 01.08.2019; Guarantee Deed for Borrower 2 invoked on 26.06.2020; Guarantee Deed for Borrower 1 invoked on 07.08.2020; Section 7 application filed citing invocation dates. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Guarantee Deeds dated 02.06.2015 containing Clauses 1 and 3 stipulating repayment 'on demand without demur'; demand notices invoking corporate guarantee issued on 26.06.2020 and 07.08.2020; Part IV entries explicitly listing invocation dates as default dates for the guarantor. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Financial Creditor filed Section 7 application; NCLT rejected the petition on 10.02.2023 holding it barred by Section 10A as guarantee invocations fell within the statutory suspension window; Financial Creditor appealed under Section 61.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the date of default on the part of a Corporate Guarantor is determined by the underlying default date of the principal borrower or by the date on which the guarantee is formally invoked by demand notice, and whether an insolvency application against the guarantor is barred under Section 10A when such invocation occurs between 25.03.2020 and 24.03.2021.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where a contract of guarantee stipulates repayment upon demand by the creditor, default on the part of the corporate guarantor arises only upon the issuance and receipt of the demand notice invoking the guarantee, rather than on the date of default by the principal borrower. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 10A of the IBC, no CIRP application can ever be filed for defaults occurring during the suspended period; because the liability of the guarantor crystallizes only upon demand/invocation, invocations made between 25.03.2020 and 24.03.2021 are irrevocably barred, irrespective of when the principal borrower defaulted. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of express covenants in the Deed of Guarantee (Clauses 1 and 3) requiring formal demand, and verification of default dates specified in Part IV of the Section 7 petition. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The guarantees were invoked on 26.06.2020 and 07.08.2020, falling squarely within the Section 10A prohibited period; inclusion of general indemnity clauses does not advance or alter the date of default.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 486 of 2023 is dismissed. The NCLT order dated 10.02.2023 rejecting the Section 7 application is affirmed.
summary.summary: J.C. Flowers Asset Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT order dismissing its Section 7 application against Corporate Guarantor Deserve Exim Pvt. Ltd. as barred by Section 10A of the IBC. The principal borrowers had defaulted in February and August 2019, but the Financial Creditor formally invoked the corporate guarantees on 26.06.2020 and 07.08.2020. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that under terms requiring repayment on demand, default by a guarantor occurs only upon guarantee invocation. Since both demand notices were served during the Section 10A suspension window (25.03.2020 to 24.03.2021), the petition was permanently barred.

summary.case_title: Mr. Sanjay Bhausaheb Bhange vs. Khushbu Dye-Chem Private Limited & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. Sanjay Bhausaheb Bhange is the Suspended Director of Bhange Organic Chemicals Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/Respondent No. 2); Khushbu Dye Chem Private Limited is the Operational Creditor/Respondent No. 1. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Agreement dated 24.06.2019 for conversion of supplied raw materials (imported Ethanol and Acetic Acid) into finished Ethyl Acetate; Operational Creditor incurred Rs. 11,17,19,527/- while Corporate Debtor delivered 15,00,635 kg of Ethyl Acetate valued at Rs. 9,82,22,873/-, resulting in a disputed balance of Rs. 1,34,96,652/- followed by an MoU dated 03.01.2020 with 18 post-dated cheques. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed operational debt of Rs. 1,36,11,373/- (including interest); 18 cheques deposited on 06.07.2021 were returned unpaid with the remark 'Payment stopped by drawer' on 07.07.2021. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Business Agreement executed 24.06.2019; MoU signed 03.01.2020; cheques returned 07.07.2021; Section 8 Demand Notice sent 30.07.2021; Section 9 application filed thereafter and heard ex-parte on 21.03.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Section 8 Demand Notice itself citing Operational Creditor's letter dated 15.06.2021 disputing 6 GST invoices raised by Corporate Debtor; Corporate Debtor's reply letter dated 19.07.2021 disputing amounts, asserting unpaid conversion charges, and demanding ledger reconciliation; multiple emails from December 2020 to May 2021 demanding account reconciliation. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed CP(IB) No. 1288(MB)/2021 under Section 9; NCLT Mumbai Bench-III set the Corporate Debtor ex-parte and admitted the petition on 25.04.2022; Suspended Director appealed under Section 61.
summary.legal_issues: Whether pre-existing disputes regarding contract terms, conversion rates, GST invoices, and account reconciliation raised prior to the issuance of a Section 8 demand notice render an application under Section 9 of the IBC non-maintainable under the Mobilox Innovations doctrine.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application under Section 9 of the IBC must be rejected if the corporate debtor raises a plausible, pre-existing dispute prior to the issuance of the demand notice that is supported by contemporaneous correspondence and is not a patently feeble or spurious defense. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8(2) and Section 9(5)(2)(d) mandate that the Adjudicating Authority reject an insolvency petition where a genuine factual dispute exists; the Tribunal cannot adjudicate the merits of commercial claims, conversion rate interpretations, or mutual accounting claims in summary proceedings. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The standard laid down in Mobilox Innovations: whether there is a plausible contention requiring investigation that is not spurious, hypothetical, or illusory, evidenced by written communications predating the Section 8 demand notice. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Extensive communications from December 2020 to July 2021, and the operational creditor's own admission in its demand notice disputing debtor invoices, established a genuine pre-existing dispute, making Section 9 admission improper.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 621 of 2022 is allowed. The NCLT Mumbai order dated 25.04.2022 is set aside, the appointment of the IRP is cancelled, and the Corporate Debtor is released from CIRP with immediate effect. IA No. 4364 is disposed of. No costs.
summary.summary: Mr. Sanjay Bhausaheb Bhange, Director of Bhange Organic Chemicals Pvt. Ltd., appealed an ex-parte NCLT Mumbai order admitting Khushbu Dye Chem's Section 9 IBC application for an operational debt of Rs. 1.36 Crores arising from a chemical processing contract and subsequent MoU. The Appellant demonstrated that prior to the Section 8 demand notice, the parties exchanged multiple communications disputing conversion calculations, unreleased labor charges, and conflicting GST invoices. The NCLAT allowed the appeal and quashed the CIRP, holding under the Mobilox test that substantial, genuine pre-existing disputes existed regarding the underlying debt, precluding summary insolvency adjudication.

summary.case_title: Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Company Ltd. vs. NRC Ltd. & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Company Ltd. (MSEDCL) is the Operational Creditor/Appellant; NRC Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor (Respondent No. 1); Successful Resolution Applicant is Respondent No. 2. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Electricity supply and associated distribution dues owed by the Corporate Debtor; approval of Resolution Plan during CIRP. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Pre-CIRP and resolution electricity dues; details not quantified in the delay condonation order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution Plan approved by NCLT on 13.03.2020; SRA filed Writ Petition against MSEDCL on 29.06.2022; Appeal filed before NCLAT on 22.11.2022 with a delay of 244 days. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Certified copy of the approval order dated 13.03.2020; SRA Writ Petition dated 29.06.2022 through which Appellant claimed first knowledge; IA No. 37 of 2023 seeking condonation of 244 days delay. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT approved the Resolution Plan for NRC Ltd. on 13.03.2020; Appellant filed Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 13 of 2023 on 22.11.2022 with IA No. 37 of 2023; NCLAT considered the delay condonation application.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the NCLAT possesses jurisdiction under the proviso to Section 61(2) of the IBC to condone a delay of 244 days in filing an appeal against a resolution plan approval order, and whether Section 17(1)(c) of the Limitation Act, 1963 can extend limitation for filing an appeal.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Appellate Tribunal has no statutory power or jurisdiction to condone any delay in filing an appeal under Section 61 of the IBC beyond the maximum period of 15 days provided in the proviso to Section 61(2). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(2) prescribes a strict 30-day limitation period with a proviso limiting condonation to a maximum of 15 days upon showing sufficient cause; Section 17(1)(c) of the Limitation Act, 1963 applies exclusively to suits and original applications seeking relief from mistake or fraud, and cannot be extended to enlarge the limitation period prescribed for statutory appeals. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict chronological computation of statutory limitation days from the date of the impugned order. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal was filed with an incurable delay of 244 days, well beyond the 15-day outer limit; lack of prior knowledge and reliance on Section 17(1)(c) do not confer jurisdiction on the Tribunal.
summary.operative_order: IA No. 37 of 2023 for condonation of delay is dismissed. Consequently, the Memo of Appeal in Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 13 of 2023 is rejected.
summary.summary: Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Company Ltd. appealed an NCLT order dated 13.03.2020 approving the Resolution Plan of NRC Ltd., filing the appeal on 22.11.2022 with a 244-day delay. The Appellant claimed it acquired knowledge of the order only on 29.06.2022 through a writ petition filed by the Successful Resolution Applicant, seeking relief under Section 17(1)(c) of the Limitation Act, 1963. The NCLAT rejected the appeal, holding that Section 61(2) of the IBC limits condonable delay to a maximum of 15 days beyond the initial 30 days. The Tribunal held that Section 17(1)(c) applies only to suits and applications, not appeals, leaving NCLAT without jurisdiction to condone delays exceeding 15 days.

summary.case_title: Akashganga Processors Pvt. Ltd. vs. Shri Ravindra Kumar Goyal & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Akashganga Processors Pvt. Ltd. is the Successful Resolution Applicant/Appellant; Shri Ravindra Kumar Goyal is the Resolution Professional (Respondent No. 1); Punjab National Bank is the Assenting Financial Creditor (Respondent No. 2); Respondent No. 3 is a Dissenting Financial Creditor; State Tax Department (Govt. of Gujarat), Central Excise (Govt. of India), Gujarat Industrial Development Corporation (GIDC), and Surat Municipal Corporation are Operational Creditors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Submission and approval of a Resolution Plan in the CIRP of the Corporate Debtor by the CoC with a 99.84% majority voting share. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Financial Creditors had admitted claims of Rs. 111,29,36,000/- and were allocated Rs. 7.52 Crores; liquidation value allocated to operational creditors was nil under Section 53; however, the plan earmarked Rs. 32,78,102/- conceded by Financial Creditors exclusively to GIDC and Surat Municipal Corporation to preserve going concern operations, allocating zero to statutory tax creditors. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution Plan approved by CoC on 06.08.2021; RP filed approval application IA No. 680 of 2021; NCLT rejected approval on 23.08.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: CoC voting minutes dated 06.08.2021 showing 99.84% approval; Information Memorandum reflecting statutory dues; Additional Affidavit of Punjab National Bank justifying allocation; attendance records of the 7th CoC meeting via video conference. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad rejected IA No. 680 of 2021 on 23.08.2022 holding the plan violative of Section 30(2)(e) and (f) due to inter-se discrimination among operational creditors; Successful Resolution Applicant appealed.
summary.legal_issues: Whether a Resolution Plan can allocate payments to select Operational Creditors to preserve the corporate debtor as a going concern while allocating nil to other statutory Operational Creditors whose liquidation value is nil, and whether the Adjudicating Authority should invalidate the entire plan or modify distribution on a pro-rata basis among all operational creditors.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: While financial creditors and operational creditors may receive differential treatment under a resolution plan, operational creditors inter-se within the same class cannot be subjected to discriminatory treatment in fund allocation, even under the justification of preserving the corporate debtor as a going concern. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Applying the Essar Steel doctrine, equitable treatment requires that similarly situated creditors within the same class be treated without unjust discrimination; however, non-compliance in inter-se distribution under Section 30(2) does not mandate total rejection of an approved plan if it can be cured by directing pro-rata distribution of the allocated pool. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the resolution plan allocation sheets against the Section 53 waterfall entitlement and verification of discrimination among operational creditors. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Rather than invalidating a plan approved by 99.84% CoC voting share, the allocated sum of Rs. 32,78,102/- must be distributed pro-rata among all four operational creditors to satisfy statutory parity under Section 30(2).
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1148 of 2022 is allowed. The NCLT order dated 23.08.2022 is modified, IA No. 680 of 2021 is allowed, and the Resolution Plan is approved subject to the modification that Rs. 32,78,102/- be distributed on a pro-rata basis among all Operational Creditors. No costs.
summary.summary: Akashganga Processors Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Ahmedabad order rejecting its CoC-approved Resolution Plan for the Corporate Debtor under Section 30(2)(e) and (f) of the IBC. Although operational creditors had nil liquidation entitlement, the plan allocated Rs. 32.78 Lakhs exclusively to GIDC and Surat Municipal Corporation to maintain going concern status, leaving tax authorities with zero. The NCLAT held that while differential treatment between financial and operational creditors is permissible under the Essar Steel doctrine, inter-se discrimination among operational creditors is prohibited. To prevent plan invalidation, the Tribunal modified the plan by directing pro-rata distribution of the Rs. 32.78 Lakhs among all operational creditors, thereby approving the plan.

summary.case_title: Pani Logistics vs. Vikas G. Jain & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Pani Logistics (through sole proprietor Kiran M. Jain) is an Unsecured Financial Creditor holding a 0.264% CoC vote share (Appellant); Vikas G. Jain is the Resolution Professional (Respondent No. 1); MTC Business Pvt. Ltd. is the Successful Resolution Applicant (Respondent No. 3). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of the Corporate Debtor resulting in approval of a Resolution Plan by the CoC with over 99% vote share. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Admitted secured financial creditor claims totaled Rs. 1,696.82 Crores (settled at Rs. 365.85 Crores or 21.56%); admitted operational creditor claims totaled Rs. 114.7 Crores (settled at Rs. 0.19 Crores or 0.0969%); Appellant's claims were partially rejected by the RP, with challenge applications pending. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution Plan approved by CoC with >99% voting share; NCLT Ahmedabad approved the plan in IA No. 314/(AHM)/2021 and rejected Appellant's objections in IA No. 431/(AHM)/2021 on 06.02.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Approved Resolution Plan allocating 0.0969% to operational creditors; Form H compliance certificate filed by RP; Performance Security Bank Guarantee of Rs. 10 Crores submitted under Regulation 36B(4A); RP's undertaking in affidavit dated 08.01.2023 creating an escrow mechanism for pending claims. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed IA No. 431/(AHM)/2021 objecting to plan approval based on insufficient performance security, pending claim disputes, and disproportionate allocation; NCLT Ahmedabad dismissed objections and approved the plan on 06.02.2023; Appellant appealed under Section 61.
summary.legal_issues: Whether a Resolution Plan approved by over 99% majority of the CoC can be challenged by a minority unsecured creditor on grounds of meager percentage allocation where liquidation value is not breached, and whether pending claim adjudications or allegations against a participating ARC invalidate plan approval.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in approving a resolution plan is paramount, and an approved plan cannot be challenged on the ground that the allocation to operational or unsecured creditors is meager, provided it is not less than the statutory liquidation value under Section 30(2)(b). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Judicial review of an approved resolution plan under Section 30(2) is strictly limited; where the RP undertakes to distribute pro-rata amounts from an escrow fund to creditors whose claims are subsequently admitted in pending interlocutory applications, the interests of disputed claimants are adequately protected without stalling implementation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Review of compliance with Section 30(2) requirements, Form H certification, and absence of proof that the plan allocated less than liquidation value. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The commercial wisdom of the CoC with >99% majority prevailed; pending claim applications were safeguarded by the escrow mechanism ordered by the NCLT.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 205 of 2023 is dismissed. The NCLT Ahmedabad orders dated 06.02.2023 in IA No. 314/(AHM)/2021 and IA No. 431/(AHM)/2021 are affirmed. No costs.
summary.summary: Pani Logistics, an unsecured financial creditor holding a 0.264% voting share, appealed an NCLT Ahmedabad order approving MTC Business Pvt. Ltd.'s Resolution Plan for the Corporate Debtor and rejecting its objection petition. The Appellant contended that operational creditors received an inequitable payout of only 0.0969% (Rs. 0.19 Crores against Rs. 114.7 Crores admitted), that performance security was insufficient, and that pending applications regarding rejected claims barred approval. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that under the Essar Steel doctrine, the CoC's commercial wisdom is non-justiciable provided the allocation is not below liquidation value. Furthermore, the RP's escrow undertaking adequately protected pending claim adjudications.

summary.case_title: Narayan Mangal vs. Vatsalya Builders & Developers Pvt. Ltd.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Narayan Mangal is the Financial Creditor/Appellant; Vatsalya Builders & Developers Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor/Respondent. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Settlement agreement entered into on 12.12.2019 under which the Corporate Debtor agreed to pay Rs. 71 Lakhs, of which Rs. 6 Lakhs was paid, leaving a balance principal debt of Rs. 65 Lakhs. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default occurred on 01.02.2020 upon dishonour of settlement cheques; Financial Creditor claimed total default of Rs. 1,00,59,922/- comprising principal of Rs. 65,00,000/- and interest of Rs. 35,59,922/- accrued from 13.12.2019 to 23.05.2022. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Settlement executed on 12.12.2019; default date occurred on 01.02.2020; Section 10A period operated from 25.03.2020 to 24.03.2021; Section 7 application filed on 25.05.2022 claiming Rs. 1,00,59,922/-. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Settlement Agreement dated 12.12.2019; dishonoured post-dated cheques; Part IV of Section 7 application specifying 01.02.2020 as the date of default; detailed interest calculation sheet showing interest accrual from 13.12.2019 to 23.05.2022. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Financial Creditor filed Section 7 application; NCLT Mumbai dismissed the petition on 09.01.2023 holding it was below the Rs. 1 Crore threshold under MCA Notification dated 24.03.2020, by excluding interest that accrued during the Section 10A period; Financial Creditor appealed.
summary.legal_issues: Whether interest accruing during the Section 10A statutory suspension period can be excluded when computing the Rs. 1 Crore minimum threshold limit under Section 4 of the IBC for a debt where default occurred prior to 25.03.2020.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where a default occurs prior to the Section 10A period and continues thereafter, Section 10A does not bar initiation of CIRP, and contractual interest accruing during the Section 10A period cannot be excluded when computing the mandatory threshold under Section 4 of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 10A prohibits filing insolvency applications exclusively for defaults arising on or after 25.03.2020; it does not freeze liability or extinguish the corporate debtor's obligation to pay interest on pre-existing defaults; interest continues to run and must be aggregated with principal to ascertain the threshold. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the date of default in Part IV and verification that the default occurred on 01.02.2020, prior to the Section 10A cut-off date. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The default occurred on 01.02.2020 and total dues including interest totaled Rs. 1,00,59,922/-, crossing the Rs. 1 Crore threshold; NCLT erred in holding the petition non-maintainable.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 294 of 2023 is allowed. The NCLT Mumbai order dated 09.01.2023 is set aside, and the Adjudicating Authority is directed to pass a fresh order admitting the Section 7 application within 30 days, granting parties liberty to settle within said period. No costs.
summary.summary: Narayan Mangal appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order dismissing his Section 7 IBC application against Vatsalya Builders & Developers Pvt. Ltd. for failing to meet the Rs. 1 Crore threshold. The debt originated from a settlement dated 12.12.2019 defaulted on 01.02.2020, with the claimed amount totaling Rs. 1,00,59,922/- (Rs. 65 Lakhs principal plus Rs. 35.60 Lakhs interest up to 23.05.2022). The Corporate Debtor argued that interest accrued during the Section 10A period should be deducted, reducing the claim below threshold. The NCLAT allowed the appeal, ruling that Section 10A does not apply to pre-existing defaults and does not extinguish interest liabilities accruing during that window, thereby satisfying the threshold.

summary.case_title: Talbot & Company vs. Austin Distributors Pvt. Ltd.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Talbot & Company (Partnership Firm) is the Operational Creditor/Appellant; Austin Distributors Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor/Respondent. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Work order dated 30.09.2015 for deployment of security guards and provision of security solutions at Corporate Debtor's premises, with monthly billing. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed operational debt of Rs. 8,17,678.54 plus interest of Rs. 1,46,052/- for unpaid security service invoices. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Security services engaged 30.09.2015; disputes raised via emails from 2016 to March 2019; purported acknowledgement email on 21.05.2019; Section 8 Demand Notice issued on 26.07.2019; reply to demand notice issued on 06.08.2019; Section 9 application CP(IB) No. 1801/KB/2019 filed in 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Contemporaneous email communications dated 26.02.2016, 10.11.2017, 02.10.2018, 12.03.2019, and 14.03.2019 from the debtor documenting deficient security, guard absenteeism, theft, and equipment damage; Appellant's replies dated 27.02.2016 and 29.08.2018 admitting staff misconduct; generic email dated 21.05.2019 from 'HR & Admn Dept' lacking specific employee authorization. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed Section 9 application; NCLT Kolkata Bench dismissed the petition on 18.10.2022 on the ground of plausible pre-existing disputes under Mobilox Innovations; Operational Creditor appealed.
summary.legal_issues: Whether contemporaneous emails complaining of service deficiency, employee negligence, theft, and damage exchanged prior to the Section 8 demand notice constitute a pre-existing dispute under Section 8(2) and Section 9(5)(2)(d) of the IBC, and whether a generic acknowledgement email from an administrative email ID overrides such pre-existing disputes.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application under Section 9 of the IBC must be rejected where contemporaneous correspondence predating the Section 8 demand notice reveals genuine, non-frivolous disputes concerning deficient performance and contractual breach, which cannot be cured or overridden by an ambiguous or unconventional acknowledgement. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Applying the Mobilox Innovations framework, the Adjudicating Authority in summary Section 9 proceedings is confined to examining whether a plausible, non-illusory dispute exists requiring trial; it cannot resolve disputed contractual quality issues or evaluate allegations of fraud regarding disputed balance confirmations. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Documentary proof of continuous, unaddressed customer complaints regarding security lapses and the operational creditor's written admissions of staff misconduct prior to the demand notice. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor established substantial pre-existing disputes regarding service quality and damages between 2016 and 2019; NCLT rightly dismissed the Section 9 application.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1470 of 2022 is dismissed. The NCLT Kolkata order dated 18.10.2022 is affirmed, reserving liberty to the Appellant to pursue ordinary legal remedies. No costs.
summary.summary: Talbot & Company appealed against an NCLT Kolkata order dismissing its Section 9 IBC petition filed against Austin Distributors Pvt. Ltd. for unpaid security service invoices amounting to Rs. 8.17 Lakhs plus interest. The Appellant claimed the debt was admitted via an email dated 21.05.2019. The Respondent demonstrated that between 2016 and March 2019, it had repeatedly complained via email regarding guard absenteeism, theft, and property damage caused by security negligence, which the Appellant had partially conceded. The NCLAT affirmed the dismissal under the Mobilox Innovations test, holding that genuine pre-existing contractual disputes existed prior to the Section 8 notice, rendering summary insolvency proceedings inapplicable.

summary.case_title: Dharmesh S. Jain vs. SREI Equipment Finance Limited & Anr. (with connected appeal)
summary.appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 697 of 2022 with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 698 of 2022
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Dharmesh S. Jain is the Suspended Director of Nirmal Lifestyle (Kalyan) Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/Appellant in Appeal No. 697); SREI Equipment Finance Limited is the Financial Creditor (Respondent No. 1); Dilipkumar Natvarlal Jagad is the IRP (Respondent No. 2); Appellants in Appeal No. 698 are 5 Homebuyers in the 'Lifestyle City, Kalyan' project. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan facility of Rs. 84,23,75,000/- disbursed pursuant to Loan Agreement and Personal Guarantee dated 05.08.2019 and Mortgage Deed dated 18.09.2019 for the development of the 'Lifestyle City, Kalyan' township project. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Defaults occurred on 05.02.2020 and 05.03.2020 totaling Rs. 1,12,73,387/- prior to the Section 10A cut-off, with subsequent defaults bringing total claimed default to Rs. 7,87,50,000/- as of 07.09.2020; IRP received total creditor claims aggregating Rs. 1,930.40 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Loan agreement executed 05.08.2019; first default on 05.02.2020; second default on 05.03.2020; Section 7 petition filed on 07.09.2020; NCLT Mumbai admitted Section 7 petition on 16.06.2022; NCLAT stayed CoC formation on 12.07.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Loan agreement and Mortgage Deed; default notices establishing pre-10A default of Rs. 1.12 Crores; IRP Status Reports revealing 30 registered buildings with MAHA RERA in stalled conditions with huge homebuyer claims; conditional in-principle letter from SWAMIH Investment Fund dated 03.06.2021 containing 37 unfulfilled conditions precedent. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Financial Creditor filed CP(IB) No. 1337/MB/2020; NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV admitted the application on 16.06.2022 holding that default of Rs. 1,12,73,387/- occurred prior to 25.03.2020 and exceeded the Section 4 threshold; Suspended Director and Homebuyers appealed.
summary.legal_issues: Whether a Section 7 application is maintainable based on defaults occurring prior to 25.03.2020 exceeding the statutory threshold, whether an offer to pay only the admitted pre-10A default amount can stave off CIRP, and whether insolvency of a multi-project real estate company should be managed under project-wise resolution principles.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An insolvency application under Section 7 is maintainable for defaults that accrued prior to the Section 10A cut-off date exceeding the statutory threshold, and an offer to deposit only the isolated initial default sum cannot defeat CIRP where massive corporate indebtedness and stalled projects persist. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 10A bars only defaults occurring between 25.03.2020 and 24.03.2021; defaults occurring on 05.02.2020 and 05.03.2020 stand outside the statutory bar; in real estate insolvencies, the CoC retains the discretion to adopt project-wise or building-wise resolution frameworks under the Umang Realtech doctrine to ensure home delivery. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Proof of debt disbursement, verification of default dates predating 25.03.2020 exceeding Rs. 1 Crore, and absence of concrete, unconditional financing to complete stalled constructions. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt and default exceeded the threshold prior to the Section 10A period, and conditional funding letters from SWAMIH did not cure default; the admission order was upheld with directions for project-wise resolution.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 697 and 698 of 2022 are dismissed. The NCLT Mumbai admission order dated 16.06.2022 is upheld. The IRP is directed to constitute the CoC within one week, and the CoC is granted liberty to explore interim finance and invite project-wise/building-wise resolution plans. The stay period from 12.07.2022 to date is excluded from CIRP. No costs.
summary.summary: A Suspended Director and five homebuyers appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order admitting SREI Equipment Finance's Section 7 IBC application against real estate debtor Nirmal Lifestyle (Kalyan) Pvt. Ltd. The debt arose from an Rs. 84.23 Crore loan facility, where defaults of Rs. 1.12 Crores occurred on 05.02.2020 and 05.03.2020. The Appellants contended that subsequent defaults were barred under Section 10A, offered to deposit Rs. 1.12 Crores, and cited conditional funding from the SWAMIH Fund. The NCLAT affirmed the admission order, holding that the initial defaults occurred prior to Section 10A and met the statutory threshold. To protect homebuyers across 30 stalled buildings, the Tribunal directed the CoC to explore project-wise resolution plans.

summary.case_title: Jindal Stainless Limited vs. Mr. Shailendra Ajmera, Resolution Professional of Mittal Corp Limited & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Jindal Stainless Limited (JSL) is the Resolution Applicant/Appellant; Mr. Shailendra Ajmera is the Resolution Professional of Mittal Corp Limited (Corporate Debtor/Respondent No. 1); Committee of Creditors of Mittal Corp Limited through Phoenix ARC Private Limited is Respondent No. 2; Shyam Sel and Power Limited (SSPL) is a competing Resolution Applicant[cite: 26]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Mittal Corp Limited initiated under the IBC where RFRP was issued on 11.04.2022, challenge process conducted on 15.07.2022, and final plans submitted on 18.07.2022[cite: 26]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Admitted debt during CIRP of Mittal Corp Limited; subsequent to challenge process, JSL offered INR 365 Crores, while financial creditors assigned debt to Phoenix ARC (holding 89.10% voting share) at Rs. 405 Crores; all plans were rejected by 89.10% vote share on 10.02.2023[cite: 26]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 10.11.2021; challenge process conducted on 15.07.2022; NCLAT ordered fresh voting in Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 1058 of 2022 on 18.01.2023; CoC meeting held on 25.01.2023; e-voting concluded and all plans rejected on 10.02.2023; fresh RFRP issued on 10.02.2023; IA No. 602/2023 filed on 14.02.2023[cite: 26]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Minutes of the 27th CoC meeting dated 10.02.2023 showing rejection of all four submitted resolution plans with 89.10% voting share; fresh RFRP reissued on 10.02.2023 under Regulation 36B(7); JSL's IA No. 602/2023 seeking cancellation of fresh RFRP[cite: 26]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed IA No. 602 of 2023 before NCLT Mumbai Bench-II to rescind the re-issued RFRP dated 10.02.2023; NCLT Mumbai rejected the application on 20.02.2023 holding CoC acted consistently with NCLAT's earlier order; Appellant appealed under Section 61[cite: 26].
summary.legal_issues: Whether the Committee of Creditors complies with an appellate direction to complete voting on existing resolution plans when it votes upon and rejects all submitted plans in its commercial wisdom, and whether the CoC possesses statutory authority under Regulation 36B(7) of the CIRP Regulations to reissue a fresh RFRP after rejecting all existing plans[cite: 26].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A judicial directive ordering the Committee of Creditors to put submitted resolution plans to vote mandates completion of the voting process but does not compel approval of any plan; where all plans are voted upon and rejected by the requisite majority, the statutory authority of the CoC to reissue a request for resolution plans under insolvency regulations remains unimpaired[cite: 26]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 36B(7) of the CIRP Regulations empowers the Resolution Professional, with the approval of the CoC, to reissue an RFRP if earlier plans are not found satisfactory; exercising commercial wisdom to reject sub-optimal plans is full compliance with an order directing voting[cite: 26]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of CoC minutes to verify that all compliant resolution plans received as of 18.07.2022 were duly placed before the CoC for voting without modifications before the decision to reissue RFRP was taken[cite: 26]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CoC duly complied with NCLAT's mandate by voting on all four plans on 10.02.2023, and upon rejecting them with an 89.10% voting share, was fully empowered under Regulation 36B(7) to reissue a fresh RFRP[cite: 26].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) Insolvency No. 356 of 2023 is dismissed, affirming the NCLT Mumbai order dated 20.02.2023, with liberty reserved to the Appellant to raise objections in IA No. 791/2023 before the Adjudicating Authority[cite: 26].
summary.summary: Jindal Stainless Limited appealed an NCLT Mumbai order rejecting its application (IA No. 602 of 2023) to cancel a re-issued Request for Resolution Plan (RFRP) dated 10.02.2023 for Corporate Debtor Mittal Corp Limited[cite: 26]. The Appellant contended that following a prior NCLAT order directing voting on plans received post-challenge, the CoC was obligated to approve an existing plan rather than reject all plans and reissue an RFRP[cite: 26]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that putting all plans to vote satisfies the judicial directive and that the CoC, upon rejecting all plans by 89.10% voting share in its commercial wisdom, has statutory power under Regulation 36B(7) of the CIRP Regulations to reissue an RFRP[cite: 26].

summary.case_title: Pr. Commissioner of Income Tax-1, Chandigarh vs. Sumat Gupta, RP of M/s International Mega Food Park Ltd.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Pr. Commissioner of Income Tax-1, Chandigarh is the Operational/Statutory Creditor and Appellant; Sumat Gupta is the Resolution Professional of M/s International Mega Food Park Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/Respondent); SIDBI is the original petitioning Financial Creditor[cite: 27]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Statutory income tax assessment and refund retention relating to the Corporate Debtor during its Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process initiated by SIDBI under Section 7 in CP (IB) No. 174/CHD/2018[cite: 27]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Retained income tax refund of Rs. 43,49,040/- with accrued interest which the Adjudicating Authority directed the Income Tax Department to refund to the Resolution Professional[cite: 27]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Order allowing refund passed by NCLT on 04.08.2022; Appeal filed before NCLAT with a delay of 59 days in filing and 23 days in re-filing; IA No. 4880 of 2022 filed for condonation of 59 days delay[cite: 27]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Certified copy of impugned order dated 04.08.2022; IA No. 4880 of 2022 citing procedural governmental delays; absence of any statutory ground extending limitation beyond the 15-day proviso window[cite: 27]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP filed IA No. 460 of 2020 under Section 60(5); NCLT Chandigarh Bench allowed the application on 04.08.2022 directing refund of Rs. 43,49,040/-; Appellant filed Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1531 of 2022 accompanied by IA No. 4880 of 2022 for condonation of delay[cite: 27].
summary.legal_issues: Whether the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal possesses statutory jurisdiction under the proviso to Section 61(2) of the IBC to condone a delay of 59 days in filing an appeal against an order passed by the Adjudicating Authority[cite: 27].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Appellate Tribunal has no jurisdiction or discretion to condone a delay in preferring an appeal under Section 61 of the IBC beyond the outer limit of 15 days provided in the statutory proviso to Section 61(2), irrespective of the merits or governmental character of the appellant[cite: 27]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(2) mandates a 30-day period for filing an appeal, and its proviso restricts condonable delay to an absolute maximum of 15 days upon demonstration of sufficient cause; in accordance with the Supreme Court ruling in National Spot Exchange Limited v. Anil Kohli, any delay exceeding 15 days is incurable[cite: 27]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Mathematical calculation of delay from the date of the impugned order to the date of physical/electronic filing of the appeal memo[cite: 27]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the appeal was filed with a delay of 59 days, which exceeds the statutory ceiling of 45 total days (30 + 15), the Tribunal lacks jurisdiction to entertain the condonation application[cite: 27].
summary.operative_order: IA No. 4880 of 2022 for condonation of delay is dismissed; consequently, Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1531 of 2022 along with IA No. 4879 of 2022 (stay) and IA No. 4855 of 2022 (delay in re-filing) is dismissed as not duly constituted[cite: 27].
summary.summary: The Pr. Commissioner of Income Tax-1, Chandigarh appealed an NCLT Chandigarh order dated 04.08.2022 directing the Income Tax Department to refund Rs. 43,49,040/- with interest to the Resolution Professional of International Mega Food Park Ltd.[cite: 27] The appeal was filed with an admitted delay of 59 days, and the Appellant sought condonation citing internal administrative and procedural delays[cite: 27]. The NCLAT dismissed the delay condonation application and consequently rejected the appeal as incompetent, holding under Section 61(2) of the IBC and the Supreme Court precedent in National Spot Exchange Ltd. v. Anil Kohli that the Tribunal's power to condone delay is strictly limited to 15 days beyond the initial 30-day window[cite: 27].

summary.case_title: Permali Wallace Pvt. Ltd. vs. Narbada Forest Industries Pvt. Ltd.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Permali Wallace Pvt. Ltd. is the Operational Creditor/Appellant; Narbada Forest Industries Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor/Respondent[cite: 28]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying supply transaction resulting in a Section 9 application filed in 2017, which was settled between the parties via a Settlement Agreement dated 07.11.2017 providing for payment of principal and interest[cite: 28]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor paid the entire principal operational debt of Rs. 1,74,16,527/- and Rs. 16,00,000/- towards interest out of Rs. 48,00,000/- agreed under settlement; Appellant subsequently filed a fresh Section 9 application claiming Rs. 1,28,00,000/- as unpaid balance interest[cite: 28]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: First Section 9 application filed in 2017 and withdrawn on settlement dated 07.11.2017; principal amount and partial interest paid; post-dated cheques for balance interest bounced; second Section 9 application filed thereafter[cite: 28]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Settlement Agreement dated 07.11.2017; proof of full payment of principal operational debt of Rs. 1,74,16,527/-; bank records showing payment of Rs. 16,00,000/- towards interest; disputed interest calculation of Rs. 1,28,00,000/-[cite: 28]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed Section 9 application for balance interest; NCLT Indore Bench rejected the application on 03.11.2022 holding that claims arising purely out of settlement agreements do not constitute operational debt and cannot be used for recovery; Operational Creditor appealed[cite: 28].
summary.legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 9 of the IBC is maintainable solely for the recovery of disputed unpaid balance interest arising out of a settlement agreement after the entire principal operational debt has been paid in full[cite: 28].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application under Section 9 of the IBC cannot be maintained or weaponized as a recovery mechanism solely for enforcing balance interest claims under a settlement agreement where the underlying principal operational debt stands fully satisfied[cite: 28]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Following the Supreme Court ruling in Swiss Ribbons, the IBC is not a recovery forum or money recovery proceeding; amounts claimed purely as balance default under terms of a settlement agreement after satisfaction of the principal do not constitute an operational debt within the scope of Section 5(21) for triggering corporate insolvency[cite: 28]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification of whether the principal debt for goods and services has been extinguished and whether the surviving dispute pertains exclusively to conflicting calculations of interest under a compromise deed[cite: 28]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the entire principal operational debt was paid and the petition sought recovery of disputed interest arising from a settlement agreement, the NCLT rightly held the Section 9 petition non-maintainable[cite: 28].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 36 of 2023 is dismissed. The NCLT Indore order dated 03.11.2022 rejecting the Section 9 application is affirmed. No costs[cite: 28].
summary.summary: Permali Wallace Pvt. Ltd. appealed an NCLT Indore order rejecting its Section 9 IBC application filed against Narbada Forest Industries Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 28] The parties had previously resolved a 2017 Section 9 petition via a settlement agreement dated 07.11.2017, pursuant to which the debtor paid the entire principal operational debt of Rs. 1.74 Crores and Rs. 16 Lakhs towards interest[cite: 28]. The Appellant filed a fresh Section 9 application seeking to recover Rs. 1.28 Crores as balance interest[cite: 28]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the IBC is an insolvency resolution mechanism rather than a debt recovery forum under the Swiss Ribbons doctrine, and an application solely to recover disputed interest arising from a settlement agreement is not maintainable[cite: 28].

summary.case_title: Commercial Tax Department vs. Mr. Sajjan Kumar Dokania & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Commercial Tax Department is the Statutory/Operational Creditor and Appellant; Mr. Sajjan Kumar Dokania is the Resolution Professional (Respondent No. 1); MS Soya Industries in consortium with Mr. Sanjay Chopra is the Successful Resolution Applicant (Respondents No. 2 & 3)[cite: 29]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Statutory commercial tax assessments against the Corporate Debtor; approval and implementation of a CIRP Resolution Plan allocating nil distribution to operational creditors[cite: 29]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unpaid statutory tax assessments; claim submitted in Form B on 01.06.2022 after CoC approval of the plan, which provided zero payout to operational creditors under Section 53[cite: 29]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 04.12.2020; public announcement made on 08.12.2020; CoC approved resolution plan of MS Soya consortium with 98.28% votes on 07.12.2021; Appellant submitted belated Form B claim on 01.06.2022; NCLT rejected claim application on 16.06.2022; NCLT approved Resolution Plan on 09.09.2022[cite: 29]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Form G publications dated 17.02.2020 and 11.10.2021; Information Memorandum mentioning tax liabilities; CoC minutes dated 07.12.2021 approving the plan; Form B claim dated 01.06.2022 filed as an operational creditor; complete disbursement of resolution funds to financial creditors[cite: 29]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP rejected belated claim on 01.06.2022; NCLT dismissed Appellant's challenge on 16.06.2022; NCLT approved the Resolution Plan on 09.09.2022; Commercial Tax Department appealed the approval under Section 61 relying on Rainbow Papers[cite: 29].
summary.legal_issues: Whether a statutory authority that fails to file its claim within the prescribed CIRP timelines can demand parity with secured financial creditors under Section 53 of the IBC on the strength of the Supreme Court's ruling in Rainbow Papers after the Resolution Plan has already been approved by the CoC and fully implemented[cite: 29].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A statutory authority cannot claim the benefit of secured creditor status or demand distribution under Section 53 if it fails to submit its claim within the statutory timelines prior to approval of the resolution plan by the Committee of Creditors[cite: 29]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The doctrine in State Tax Officer v. Rainbow Papers applies where claims are invited and filed during the initial stage of resolution; it cannot be extended to unsettle or rewrite a Resolution Plan that has already been approved by the CoC and implemented through fund disbursement before the belated claim is submitted[cite: 29]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the timeline of claim submission against the formal date of approval by the CoC and proof of complete implementation and disbursement of plan proceeds[cite: 29]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellant submitted its claim in Form B six months after the CoC approved the plan with 98.28% votes, and the plan has been fully implemented; NCLT committed no error in approving the plan[cite: 29].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1412 of 2022 and IA No. 4416 of 2022 are dismissed. No order as to costs[cite: 29].
summary.summary: The Commercial Tax Department appealed an NCLT order dated 09.09.2022 approving the Resolution Plan submitted by MS Soya Industries for the Corporate Debtor[cite: 29]. The Appellant argued that under the Supreme Court's Rainbow Papers ruling, it is a secured creditor entitled to parity with secured financial creditors under Section 53 of the IBC, notwithstanding its failure to submit a timely claim[cite: 29]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that Rainbow Papers cannot be invoked by a statutory department that lodged its Form B claim after the CoC had already approved the resolution plan with 98.28% votes[cite: 29]. Furthermore, because the plan was fully implemented and the funds disbursed, no interference was warranted[cite: 29].

summary.case_title: Priyal Kantilal Patel vs. IREP Credit Capital Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Priyal Kantilal Patel is the Suspended Director of the Corporate Debtor/Appellant; IREP Credit Capital Pvt. Ltd. is the Financial Creditor/Debenture Holder (Respondent No. 1); Interim Resolution Professional is Respondent No. 2[cite: 30]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Issuance and subscription of 18 fully paid up unrated, unlisted, secured, redeemable, non-convertible debentures ('Series Debentures') with redemption premium and penal interest, held by the Financial Creditor (representing 12% debenture holding)[cite: 30]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total claimed financial debt was Rs. 26,96,49,413/- as of 08.10.2021, comprising face value redemption of Rs. 18,00,00,000/-, redemption premium of Rs. 3,64,31,833/-, penal interest of Rs. 64,71,708/-, and interest of Rs. 4,67,45,872/-[cite: 30]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: First Section 7 application CP No. 45/IBC/NCLT/MB/MAH/2020 filed on 20.12.2019; Consent Terms entered into and earlier petition withdrawn; consent terms defaulted due to dishonoured cheques; fresh Section 7 application CP (IB) No. 1029 of 2021 filed based on original debt[cite: 30]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Debenture subscription agreements; Part IV particulars claiming Rs. 26.96 Crores; Clause 9 of the Consent Terms expressly reserving the Financial Creditor's right upon default to claim the entire outstanding debt under transaction documents; dishonoured post-dated cheques[cite: 30]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Financial Creditor filed fresh petition CP (IB) No. 1029 of 2021; NCLT Mumbai admitted the application on 10.10.2022; Suspended Director appealed under Section 61 arguing that breach of consent terms cannot sustain Section 7 proceedings[cite: 30].
summary.legal_issues: Whether a fresh application under Section 7 of the IBC is maintainable on the foundation of the underlying original financial debt after a corporate debtor defaults on consent terms entered into in a previously withdrawn company petition, and whether an individual debenture holder holding 12% debt has standing to initiate Section 7 without the consensus of other debenture holders[cite: 30].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The execution and subsequent breach of interim consent terms in an earlier withdrawn company petition does not extinguish the underlying financial debt, and the creditor is fully entitled to file a fresh Section 7 application founded upon the original financial contract and debt instruments[cite: 30]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Precedents establishing that breach of a pure settlement agreement is not a financial debt (e.g., Amrit Kumar Agrawal) apply strictly where the petition is founded solely on the compromise deed; they do not apply where the petition is grounded upon the original financial debt and transaction documents[cite: 30]; an individual debenture holder possesses independent statutory standing under Section 7 regardless of consensus among other holders[cite: 30]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of Part IV of the petition to verify whether the claim is framed around the underlying commercial debt rather than exclusively on the settlement instrument, and verification of non-waiver covenants in the consent terms[cite: 30]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The petition was founded upon the unredeemed non-convertible debentures and contractual dues, which retained their financial debt character upon breach of the consent terms; admission by NCLT was lawful[cite: 30].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) Ins. No. 1423 of 2022 and IA No. 4457 of 2022 are dismissed, affirming the NCLT Mumbai admission order dated 10.10.2022, with liberty reserved to the Appellant to explore Section 12A proceedings if settlement is reached[cite: 30].
summary.summary: Priyal Kantilal Patel, Suspended Director of the Corporate Debtor, appealed an NCLT Mumbai order admitting a Section 7 IBC application filed by debenture holder IREP Credit Capital Pvt. Ltd. for default of Rs. 26.96 Crores on 18 redeemable non-convertible debentures[cite: 30]. The Appellant contended that because an earlier petition had been withdrawn under consent terms which were subsequently breached, the filing of a fresh Section 7 petition was impermissible as breach of settlement terms does not constitute financial debt under Amrit Kumar Agrawal[cite: 30]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the petition was explicitly grounded on the original financial debenture contracts rather than the consent terms alone, leaving the financial debt intact[cite: 30].

summary.case_title: Vishal Agarwal vs. ICICI Prudential Real Estate AIF-I & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant: Vishal Agarwal, Erstwhile Director of Corporate Debtor (Gagan I-Land Township Pvt. Ltd.); Respondent No. 1: ICICI Prudential Real Estate AIF-I (Financial Creditor); Respondent No. 2: Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Debenture Subscription Agreement (DSA) executed between the parties wherein the Corporate Debtor issued debentures carrying periodic interest servicing obligations. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in servicing of quarterly interest for the quarters ending September 30, 2019 and December 31, 2019, as well as principal repayment claimed on August 31, 2020. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Corporate Debtor issued a restructuring request letter on September 9, 2021; Section 7 application was admitted on July 27, 2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor's letter dated September 9, 2021 acknowledging default in paying interest for quarters ending September 2019 and December 2019, requesting debt restructuring, capitalization/reduction of interest, and waiver of penal IRR; oral and written admissions; repeated adjournments sought before the Appellate Tribunal to propose a One Time Settlement (OTS). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT admitted the Financial Creditor's Section 7 application on July 27, 2022 holding that default occurred prior to the Section 10A blackout period; the Appellant appealed challenging maintainability under Section 10A.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the Section 7 CIRP application was barred by Section 10A of the IBC when principal repayment fell due on August 31, 2020, but defaults in interest payments under the Debenture Subscription Agreement had undisputedly occurred in September 2019 and December 2019 prior to March 25, 2020.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory bar under Section 10A of the IBC applies strictly and exclusively to defaults occurring within the prescribed period (March 25, 2020 to March 25, 2021); a corporate debtor cannot seek immunity under Section 10A by relying on a subsequent default date if an event of default had already occurred and was acknowledged prior to March 25, 2020. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 10A prohibits CIRP applications only for defaults arising during the period beginning March 25, 2020; an event of default triggered by non-payment of periodic interest before this window remains fully actionable. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Clear, unequivocal written admissions of default in commercial correspondence (such as debt restructuring requests) prior to the Section 10A threshold date conclusively establish an antecedent actionable default. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor having committed and acknowledged defaults in interest servicing for the quarters ending September 2019 and December 2019, the Section 7 petition was not hit by Section 10A, and admission of the petition was legally valid.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1016 of 2022 is dismissed without costs, affirming the Adjudicating Authority's order dated 27.07.2022 admitting the Corporate Debtor into CIRP.
summary.summary: The Appellant, an erstwhile director of Gagan I-Land Township Pvt. Ltd., appealed against the NCLT order admitting a Section 7 petition filed by ICICI Prudential Real Estate AIF-I, contending that the petition was barred under Section 10A of the IBC as the repayment date under the Debenture Subscription Agreement fell on 31.08.2020. The NCLAT held that the Corporate Debtor had explicitly admitted in its letter dated 09.09.2021 that it defaulted on interest payments for quarters ending September 2019 and December 2019. Because these actionable defaults occurred prior to the 25.03.2020 cutoff, Section 10A was inapplicable, and the appeal was dismissed.

summary.case_title: Tata Power Western Odisha Distribution Limited (TPWODL) & Anr. vs. Jagannath Sponge Private Limited
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants: Tata Power Western Odisha Distribution Limited (TPWODL) and its Executive Engineer (Electricity Distribution Licensee); Respondent: Jagannath Sponge Private Limited (Corporate Debtor, represented post-resolution by the Successful Resolution Applicant/Director Sh. Arun Kumar Gaindhar). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Power supply agreements for supply of electricity to the Corporate Debtor's industrial units (which agreements had been terminated with effect from 03.10.2013 and 01.02.2015). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total claimed electricity arrears of Rs. 13,46,19,931/- (also referred to as Rs. 13,56,19,931/-) accruing from disconnection in 2013 prior to CIRP initiation. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 CIRP initiated on April 20, 2019; Resolution plan approved by NCLT on August 6, 2021; Respondent applied for new electricity connection on August 5, 2022; Appellant issued demand letter for past dues on December 8, 2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Approved resolution plan containing specific waivers/reliefs directing electricity distribution companies not to raise demands for past dues and to treat new connection applications independently; failure of Appellant to submit any claim during CIRP; withdrawal of Appellant's prior appeal C.A.(AT) Ins. No. 1404 of 2022 challenging plan approval. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent filed IA (IB) No. 14/CB/2023 before NCLT Cuttack Bench seeking reconnection without paying past arrears; NCLT allowed the IA on April 18, 2023 declaring the demand invalid; Appellant appealed to NCLAT.
summary.legal_issues: Whether an electricity distribution licensee can demand payment of unpaid pre-CIRP electricity arrears as a condition precedent for granting a fresh electricity connection to a Successful Resolution Applicant whose resolution plan was duly approved under Section 31 of the IBC.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a resolution plan is approved under Section 31 of the IBC, all pre-CIRP claims and statutory dues owed to creditors who failed to submit their claims during the CIRP stand completely extinguished under the 'clean slate' doctrine, and no utility provider can condition fresh service upon clearance of extinguished historical dues. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Following the interpretation in Ghanashyam Mishra and Sons Pvt. Ltd., the approval of a plan under Section 31 binds all stakeholders, extinguishing all prior debts not forming part of the plan. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where an approved resolution plan expressly includes waivers forbidding electricity boards from raising past dues, and the creditor withdrew its statutory appeal against the approval order, the terms of the plan operate as res judicata and binding law. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The claimed arrears of Rs. 13,46,19,931/- were completely extinguished upon plan approval; hence, the direction to consider the application for a new electricity connection without insisting on pre-CIRP arrears was upheld.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 777 of 2023 is dismissed without costs, sustaining the NCLT Cuttack Bench order directing the Appellants to process the Respondent's service connection application without insisting on past arrears payable prior to 06.08.2021.
summary.summary: Tata Power Western Odisha Distribution Limited appealed an NCLT order directing it to process an application for electricity connection by Jagannath Sponge Private Limited without insisting on pre-CIRP arrears of Rs. 13,46,19,931/-. The appellant had terminated power supply agreements prior to CIRP and failed to submit a claim during the insolvency process, which culminated in an approved resolution plan granting clean slate relief. Relying on the Supreme Court ruling in Ghanashyam Mishra, the NCLAT held that all unsubmitted pre-CIRP dues stood extinguished upon approval under Section 31. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding the appellant cannot condition a fresh connection on past dues.

summary.case_title: Shrem Residency Private Limited vs. Shraman Estates Private Limited
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant: Shrem Residency Private Limited (Financial Creditor/Developer); Respondent: Shraman Estates Private Limited (Corporate Debtor/Land Owner). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Collaboration Agreement dated 31.08.2012, Addendum Agreement dated 31.12.2012, and Term Sheets dated 02.09.2012 and 31.12.2012 for development of 21 acres of land at Najafgarh, New Delhi, containing provisions for inter-corporate deposit (ICD)/loan of Rs. 6 Crores carrying interest @ 24% p.a. and refundable deposit of Rs. 1 Crore @ 18% p.a., secured by equitable mortgage and personal guarantees. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed on loan of Rs. 6 Crores (total default with interest calculated as on 31.03.2019 at Rs. 20,59,45,641/-) and refundable deposit of Rs. 1 Crore (total Rs. 3,05,27,174/-); default dates asserted as 01.02.2014, 03.04.2014, and 31.01.2013 respectively. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Default notices issued by Appellant on September 5, 2017 and April 2, 2019; Section 7 petition filed on May 16, 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bank account statements of HDFC Bank proving disbursement of Rs. 7 Crores and receipt of initial interest; Board resolutions of both companies passed in August 2012; balance sheet of the Corporate Debtor as on 31.03.2016 (signed on 27.08.2016) reflecting the amount under short-term borrowings; equitable mortgage deed and Form-A charge registration. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 application filed on 16.05.2019; NCLT New Delhi (Bench-II) dismissed the application on 01.10.2019 holding that discrepancies between the collaboration agreement and term sheets showed failure to prove terms of advancement, repayment, and default; Financial Creditor appealed to NCLAT.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the advancement of Rs. 6 Crores along with interest under term sheets read with a collaboration agreement constitutes a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC, and whether the NCLT erred in dismissing the Section 7 petition due to perceived inconsistencies between contractual documents despite uncontroverted evidence of disbursement, interest payment, and default.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In an application under Section 7 of the IBC, the Adjudicating Authority is solely required to determine the existence of a 'financial debt' disbursed against the time value of money and a corresponding 'default'; minor drafting variations or lack of reconciliation between underlying agreements and accompanying term sheets cannot defeat admission when disbursement, accrual of interest, and default are demonstrated by documentary evidence. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: An inter-corporate deposit bearing commercial interest disbursed for real estate acquisition satisfies the statutory threshold of 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Bank statements confirming disbursement, subsequent payments of interest, board resolutions, charge registration, and acknowledgment of borrowings in audited balance sheets constitute conclusive proof of financial debt and default, extending limitation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority misappreciated the evidence; the appellant established both debt and default, warranting admission into CIRP.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1336 of 2019 is allowed without costs; the impugned order dated 01.10.2019 is set aside, and the Adjudicating Authority is directed to admit the Section 7 application and proceed in accordance with law.
summary.summary: Shrem Residency Private Limited appealed an order of NCLT New Delhi dismissing its Section 7 application against Shraman Estates Private Limited. Under a collaboration agreement and term sheets, the appellant had disbursed Rs. 6 Crores as a loan carrying 24% interest p.a. and Rs. 1 Crore as a refundable deposit. The NCLT dismissed the petition citing irreconcilable terms between the collaboration agreement and term sheets. Setting aside the dismissal, the NCLAT held that bank statements, board resolutions, mortgage deeds, and balance sheet acknowledgments clearly proved the disbursement of financial debt and occurrence of default. The appeal was allowed with directions to NCLT to admit the petition.

summary.case_title: DCB Bank Limited vs. Mr. R. Sadasivan, Liquidator of Thiru Arooran Sugars Limited & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant: DCB Bank Limited (Lender/Financial Creditor); Respondent No. 1: Mr. R. Sadasivan (Liquidator of Corporate Debtor Thiru Arooran Sugars Limited); Respondent No. 2: State Bank of India; Respondent No. 3: Ramalingam Vadapathimangalam Tyagarajan (Suspended CMD). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Working Capital Consortium Agreement dated 30.09.2016 and a separate Non-Consortium Facility of Rs. 10,00,000,000/- granted on 29.11.2017 to the Corporate Debtor, under which the Appellant claimed a right of set-off/lien under Article 5. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Liquidator demanded refund of an unauthorized appropriation of Rs. 11,30,40,034/- made from Corporate Debtor accounts by the Appellant. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 CIRP admitted against Corporate Debtor on 07.06.2019; liquidation scheme approved on 02.05.2022; notice in IA/1341/2020 served on Appellant on 17.07.2021 and 22.07.2021; ex-parte order passed on 03.03.2022; recall application IA/419/2022 dismissed on 18.10.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Proof of valid service of notices to Head Office, Branch Office, and alternative offices on 17.07.2021 and 22.07.2021 across seven hearing listings between August 2021 and February 2022; notice demanding Rs. 11,30,40,034/- dated 25.03.2022 received by Bank on 28.03.2022. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Liquidator filed IA(IBC)/1341(CHE)/2020 seeking refund; Appellant remained ex parte and order was passed on 03.03.2022 directing refund; Appellant filed IA(IBC)/419(CHE)/2022 under Rule 49 to set aside the ex-parte order, which NCLT dismissed on 18.10.2022; Appellant appealed to NCLAT.
summary.legal_issues: Whether skeletal operations during the COVID-19 pandemic constitute 'sufficient cause' under Rule 49 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 to set aside an ex-parte order directing refund of Rs. 11,30,40,034/-, where multiple statutory notices were duly delivered to the bank's corporate, branch, and registered offices.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where statutory notices of proceedings are duly served at the proper and registered address of a commercial entity, a presumption of due service arises; generalized hardship such as skeletal staffing during the COVID-19 pandemic does not constitute 'sufficient cause' under Rule 49 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 if adequate time and multiple listings were afforded prior to adjudication. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 49(2) of the NCLT Rules, 2016 requires concrete demonstration that the party was prevented by 'sufficient cause' from appearing; administrative failure to track notices delivered to valid corporate addresses does not satisfy this legal standard. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Proof of physical/postal service of notice at several corporate and branch addresses without contest over multiple listing dates defeats any plea of denial of natural justice. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellant had reasonable notice and opportunity to contest IA/1341/2020, and the NCLT correctly dismissed the recall application under Rule 49.
summary.operative_order: Comp App (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 446 of 2022 is dismissed without costs, and pending stay application IA No. 1132/2022 is closed.
summary.summary: DCB Bank Limited appealed against orders of NCLT Chennai directing it to refund Rs. 11,30,40,034/- to the account of Corporate Debtor Thiru Arooran Sugars Limited and rejecting its application under Rule 49 of the NCLT Rules to set aside the ex-parte order. The bank claimed that due to COVID-19 lockdowns and skeletal staffing at its corporate and local offices, it failed to track the notices. The NCLAT held that notices were admittedly delivered to multiple offices of the bank across seven hearing dates, creating a presumption of due service. The plea of skeletal staffing did not constitute sufficient cause, and the appeal was dismissed.

summary.case_title: Continuous Dyeing & Printing Mills vs. Bhavika Apparels Pvt. Ltd.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant: Continuous Dyeing & Printing Mills (Operational Creditor); Respondent: Bhavika Apparels Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Work order dated 13.12.2018 placed by Corporate Debtor for job work printing and finishing of woven fabrics, for which GST invoices were raised between 04.01.2019 and 05.02.2019. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Outstanding operational debt claimed as Rs. 35,33,737/- as on 04.01.2019 (with varying claims of Rs. 40,24,320/-, Rs. 50,24,320/-, and Rs. 50,26,260/- based on interest computation); date of default linked to unpaid invoices from January 2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Debit notes sent on 05.02.2019; intimation letter issued on 19.08.2019; Corporate Debtor dispute notice issued on 23.08.2019; Civil Suit No. 517/2019 filed on 06.09.2019; Section 8 demand notice sent on 16.09.2019; reply to demand notice issued on 27.09.2019; Section 9 petition filed on 15.10.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Debit notes dated 31.01.2019; Corporate Debtor's detailed letter dated 23.08.2019 complaining of inferior fabric (10% contraction against 18% required) and 8% extra charges; pendency of Civil Suit No. 517/2019 in District Court. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 9 petition filed on 15.10.2019; NCLT New Delhi (Bench-IV) dismissed the application under Section 9(5)(ii)(d) on 21.12.2021 on grounds of pre-existing dispute; Operational Creditor appealed to NCLAT.
summary.legal_issues: Whether a communication raising quality defects and the prior institution of a civil suit regarding substandard goods before the issuance of a Section 8 demand notice constitutes a genuine pre-existing dispute under Section 8(2)(a) and Section 9(5)(ii)(d) of the IBC, mandating rejection of a Section 9 application.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1.
