ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: If a corporate debtor raises specific grievances regarding the quality of goods or services or institutes a civil suit prior to the service of a demand notice under Section 8, a bona fide pre-existing dispute is established, and the Adjudicating Authority must reject the Section 9 application without adjudicating the underlying merits of the contractual dispute. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 9(5)(ii)(d), receipt of a notice of dispute by the operational creditor prior to the Section 8 demand notice creates a mandatory bar to CIRP initiation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The dispute raised must not be spurious, hypothetical, or an afterthought; documented complaints specifying defects (e.g., fabric contraction variance) predating the Section 8 notice satisfy the test of a real, plausible dispute. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor's communication dated 23.08.2019 and the pending civil suit predated the Section 8 notice dated 16.09.2019, conclusively barring CIRP under Section 9(5)(ii)(d).
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 301 of 2022 is dismissed without costs, upholding the NCLT order dated 21.12.2021, while granting liberty to the Appellant to seek appropriate alternate legal remedies.
summary.summary: Continuous Dyeing & Printing Mills appealed against an order of NCLT New Delhi rejecting its Section 9 CIRP application against Bhavika Apparels Pvt. Ltd. The appellant claimed outstanding operational debt of over Rs. 35 Lakhs for textile printing services. The Corporate Debtor had raised specific quality objections regarding fabric shrinkage on 23.08.2019 and filed a civil suit on 06.09.2019, both prior to the Section 8 demand notice dated 16.09.2019. The NCLAT held that the dispute was not moonshine or spurious and satisfied Section 9(5)(ii)(d) of the IBC, affirming the rejection of the Section 9 application while preserving the appellant's right to pursue ordinary legal remedies.

summary.case_title: Vivek Parthi vs. H.S. Oberoi Buildtech Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant: Vivek Parthi (Erstwhile Resolution Professional); Respondent No. 1: H.S. Oberoi Buildtech Pvt. Ltd.; Respondent No. 2: Monitoring Committee; Intervenor: Earth Iconic Project (Home Buyers' Association). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of the Corporate Debtor wherein an approved Resolution Plan was undergoing implementation. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claim for non-payment of RP's success fee allegedly payable under the terms of the approved Resolution Plan (exact quantitative sum not specified in the order). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned order passed by NCLT on 13.04.2022 in IA No. 1056/2022 and IA No. 236/2022; Appellate disposal on 06.02.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Approved Resolution Plan; Minutes of the Committee of Creditors meetings (which respondents argued merely contained a passing note rather than an approved resolution for success fees); pending regulatory approval issues before the Director General, Town and Country Planning (DGTCP), Haryana delaying implementation. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed IA No. 236/2022 seeking release of success fee; NCLT dismissed IA No. 1056/2022 and IA No. 236/2022 as infructuous because the Appellant was not pressing for liquidation; Appellant appealed under Section 61.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the erstwhile Resolution Professional is entitled to claim and enforce payment of a success fee under an approved Resolution Plan when the implementation of the plan itself remains stalled due to pending regulatory approvals.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An erstwhile Resolution Professional cannot seek judicial enforcement of success fees or contractual fees linked to a resolution plan when the condition precedent—actual execution and operationalization of the resolution plan—remains incomplete due to regulatory impediments. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61 appellate review does not warrant directing contractual or plan-based disbursements where the foundational corporate resolution has not materialized on the ground. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Concrete proof of implementation hurdles (e.g., pending DGTCP clearances) negates premature financial recovery claims by insolvency professionals. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the plan had not been implemented, the appellate tribunal declined to issue directions, disposing of the appeal while preserving the RP's liberty to file a fresh application following implementation.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 793 of 2022 is disposed of without costs, granting liberty to the Appellant to file a fresh application before the Adjudicating Authority after plan implementation, to be decided after hearing the SRA, CoC, and Monitoring Committee without prejudice on merits.
summary.summary: Vivek Parthi, erstwhile Resolution Professional, appealed an NCLT order dismissing his application (IA No. 236/2022) for payment of a success fee claimed under an approved Resolution Plan. The Monitoring Committee and Home Buyers' Association objected, citing that the plan remained unimplemented due to pending approvals from the Director General, Town and Country Planning (DGTCP), Haryana, and that no formal resolution authorized such fees. The NCLAT held that because the resolution plan had not yet been implemented, no directions for payment could be issued. The appeal was disposed of with liberty to the appellant to approach the NCLT afresh once the plan progresses.

summary.case_title: Rajasthan State Mines & Minerals Ltd. vs. Parag Sheth & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant: Rajasthan State Mines & Minerals Ltd. (Respondent No. 3 before NCLT); Respondent No. 1: Parag Sheth (Resolution Professional of the Corporate Debtor); Respondents No. 2 & 3: Other co-respondents/suspended management. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Custody and possession of assets belonging to the Corporate Debtor allegedly lying at the commercial premises of the Appellant. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Failure/refusal by parties to identify and deliver possession of Corporate Debtor assets to the RP within the statutory CIRP framework. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution Professional filed IA/1115(AHM)2022; NCLT passed final directions on 19.12.2022; NCLAT final order passed on 17.02.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Case record showing that while an advance copy was served, no formal statutory notice was issued or served by the Tribunal to Appellant (Respondent No. 3) prior to passing peremptory directions to surrender premises and assets under threat of police assistance. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP filed IA/1115(AHM)2022 under the IBC seeking handover of assets; NCLT Ahmedabad Bench (Court-1) allowed the IA on 19.12.2022 ex-parte without notice; Appellant challenged the order for violation of natural justice.
summary.legal_issues: Whether an Adjudicating Authority can pass final, coercive directions requiring a third party to hand over assets lying in its premises to a Resolution Professional within one week without issuing and serving formal notice to that party.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An order directing dispossession or delivery of physical property entails adverse civil consequences and cannot be made without strictly issuing formal notice and affording a reasonable opportunity of hearing to the affected party, in compliance with natural justice. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Summary powers conferred under the IBC to assist the Resolution Professional do not dispense with fundamental procedural fairness or the requirement to serve formal notice prior to entering adverse final orders. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Absence of formal court notice or opportunity to file a reply affidavit before passing mandatory compliance orders invalidates the decision on procedural grounds alone. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The failure of the NCLT to issue notice to Respondent No. 3 before directing the handover of assets within a week rendered the impugned order legally unsustainable.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) Ins. No. 170 of 2023 is allowed; the impugned order dated 19.12.2022 is set aside, and IA/1115(AHM)2022 is revived before NCLT Ahmedabad for fresh adjudication with liberty to the Appellant to file a reply affidavit within three weeks.
summary.summary: Rajasthan State Mines & Minerals Ltd. appealed an order of NCLT Ahmedabad which allowed IA/1115(AHM)2022 filed by Resolution Professional Parag Sheth, directing the appellant to hand over assets of the Corporate Debtor within one week with police assistance. The appellant contended that this final order was passed without issuing notice or granting an opportunity to be heard. The NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority committed a fatal procedural error by passing coercive final directions without issuing formal notice. The NCLAT set aside the order and remitted the matter back to the NCLT to decide afresh after taking the appellant's reply on record.

summary.case_title: Sanjay Chaudhary vs. Dinesh Kumar Gupta
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant: Sanjay Chaudhary (Respondent No. 4 in NCLT proceedings); Respondent: Dinesh Kumar Gupta (Liquidator of the Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Liquidation proceedings of the Corporate Debtor involving recovery of funds and rectification of prior distribution orders. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Direction issued against the Appellant to refund specified monetary sums to the liquidation estate (exact sum not specified in the order). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Original order in IA No. 111 of 2022 passed on 22.12.2022; Liquidator filed rectification IA No. 384 of 2023; Impugned rectification order passed on 01.03.2023; Appellate order passed on 08.05.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Final order dated 22.12.2022 in IA No. 111 of 2022, which contained no monetary refund direction against the Appellant; Subsequent filing of IA No. 384 of 2023 under Rule 11 without impleading the Appellant or serving notice. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Liquidator obtained an order under Rule 11 on 01.03.2023 directing the Appellant to refund funds; Appellant appealed to NCLAT on grounds of breach of natural justice.
summary.legal_issues: Whether an Adjudicating Authority, under the guise of rectification/clarification under Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, can introduce a new substantive monetary liability/refund direction against an individual without issuing notice or granting an opportunity of being heard.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Any judicial order imposing substantive monetary liabilities or adverse financial directions on a party cannot be passed under inherent or rectification powers without providing notice and an opportunity to contest, regardless of whether it is styled as a mere clarification of a prior order. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Inherent powers under Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 cannot bypass the fundamental requirements of natural justice where an order acts to the prejudice of a party's rights. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The introduction of fresh liability not present in the original decree/order constitutes a prejudicial modification requiring strict notice. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The order dated 01.03.2023 having been passed in violation of audi alteram partem was unsustainable and required remand for de novo consideration.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 522 of 2023 is allowed; the impugned order dated 01.03.2023 is set aside, and IA No. 384 of 2023 is remitted to the Adjudicating Authority to pass fresh orders after hearing the Appellant, who is granted two weeks to file a reply.
summary.summary: Sanjay Chaudhary appealed an order dated 01.03.2023 passed by the NCLT on an application filed under Rule 11 by Liquidator Dinesh Kumar Gupta, which directed the appellant to refund monetary amounts. The appellant argued that the original order dated 22.12.2022 in IA No. 111 of 2022 contained no such direction, and the subsequent modification was passed ex-parte without notice. The NCLAT held that because the clarification created fresh prejudice and financial liability, the appellant was entitled to be heard in accordance with natural justice. The NCLAT set aside the impugned order and remitted the matter for fresh adjudication.

summary.case_title: UTI Employees Sai Samruddhi Cooperative Housing Society vs. Jayash Sangharajka & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant: UTI Employees Sai Samruddhi Cooperative Housing Society (Land Allottee/Stakeholder); Respondent No. 1: Jayash Sangharajka (Resolution Professional of Ornate Spaces Pvt. Ltd.); Other Respondents: PNB Housing Finance Ltd. and CoC members. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Real estate development project being executed by Corporate Debtor Ornate Spaces Pvt. Ltd. on land allotted to the Appellant Housing Society. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in completing development and delivering possession of real estate units pursuant to the development agreement. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV passed impugned orders dismissing interlocutory applications on 02.05.2023; NCLAT common disposal order passed on 02.06.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Interlocutory applications IA No. 651 of 2022 (seeking possession), IA No. 2074 of 2022, and IA No. 2232 of 2022 filed by the Society; approval application for Resolution Plan pending before NCLT; admitted fact that project possession resided with the Corporate Debtor. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV dismissed IA Nos. 651/2022, 2074/2022, and 2232/2022 on 02.05.2023 holding that the Society had no locus to oppose the resolution plan and could not recover possession; Society filed appeals Nos. 755, 757, and 758 of 2023.
summary.legal_issues: Whether a cooperative housing society whose land is being developed by a Corporate Debtor has locus standi to file objections against a pending Resolution Plan, and whether possession can be claimed from the Corporate Debtor during CIRP.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Stakeholders whose proprietary or developmental rights are directly impacted by a proposed resolution plan are entitled to have their objections heard by the Adjudicating Authority prior to plan approval under Section 31; however, substantive possession cannot be retrieved from a Corporate Debtor mid-CIRP in prejudice to the resolution estate. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 31 of the IBC contemplates comprehensive judicial scrutiny of objections raised by affected stakeholders before an Adjudicating Authority decides to approve or reject a plan. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Determination of stakeholder status in a real estate project justifies procedural locus to participate in the plan approval hearing, while leaving substantive merits open. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT's dismissal of the society's interlocutory applications regarding possession was upheld, but the society was granted two weeks to file objections to the pending resolution plan for independent adjudication.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeals (AT) (Ins.) Nos. 755, 757, and 758 of 2023 are disposed of; the NCLT orders dismissing the IAs are upheld, but the Appellant is granted two weeks' liberty to file objections to the pending Resolution Plan before NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV.
summary.summary: UTI Employees Sai Samruddhi Cooperative Housing Society appealed three orders of NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV dismissing its interlocutory applications (IA Nos. 651/2022, 2074/2022, and 2232/2022) concerning the CIRP of developer Ornate Spaces Pvt. Ltd. The NCLT had rejected the society's plea for possession and held it lacked locus to challenge the resolution plan. The NCLAT upheld the refusal to hand over possession from the Corporate Debtor but held that the society, as an affected stakeholder, is entitled to file objections to the plan. The NCLAT granted the appellant two weeks to lodge objections before the Adjudicating Authority and disposed of the appeals.

summary.case_title: Ome Prakash Verma vs. Amit Jain & Anr.
summary.appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 73 of 2023 & I.A. No. 300 of 2023
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant: Ome Prakash Verma (Suspended Director of Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1: Amit Jain (Resolution Professional); Respondent No. 2: Other Respondent. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) proceedings against the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Monetary metrics of the underlying default are not specified in the withdrawal order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 73 of 2023 along with I.A. No. 300 of 2023 listed for hearing and disposed of on 27.01.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Voluntary oral prayer and application made by the counsel for the Appellant seeking permission to withdraw the appeal. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed an appeal under Section 61 of the IBC against an adverse order of the Adjudicating Authority; at the preliminary hearing, the Appellant elected not to prosecute and prayed for withdrawal.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the Appellant is entitled to withdraw an appeal preferred under Section 61 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellant has the prerogative to unconditionally abandon or withdraw an appeal, and where such leave is sought, the appellate tribunal will dismiss the appeal as withdrawn without deciding the underlying merits. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Appellate jurisdiction under Section 61 terminates without substantive inquiry upon grant of permission to unconditionally withdraw the proceedings. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Unconditional oral prayer made by the appellant's counsel requesting withdrawal. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The prayer for withdrawal was allowed, concluding the proceedings by dismissing the appeal as withdrawn.
summary.operative_order: Prayer for withdrawal allowed; Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 73 of 2023 along with I.A. No. 300 of 2023 is dismissed as withdrawn.
summary.summary: The Appellant, Ome Prakash Verma (Suspended Director), filed an appeal under Section 61 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 challenging an order of the Adjudicating Authority involving Resolution Professional Amit Jain. During the hearing before the NCLAT Principal Bench, counsel for the Appellant prayed for permission to withdraw the appeal. The Appellate Tribunal allowed the prayer and formally dismissed the appeal as withdrawn without entering into the merits.

summary.case_title: Surinder Pal Singh & Ors. vs. Spaze Towers Pvt. Ltd.
summary.appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 354 of 2023 & I.A. No. 1157, 1195 of 2023
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants: Surinder Pal Singh & Ors. (Third-party Homebuyers/Intervenors); Respondent: Spaze Towers Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Purchase and allotment of real estate units by homebuyers in a project developed by the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in delivery or refund arising out of a pending Section 7 application initiated by another homebuyer (default amount unspecified in the order). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Court-IV, New Delhi) passed the impugned order on 26.08.2022; NCLAT dismissed the appeal on 27.03.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Applications for intervention (I.A. Nos. 3795/ND/2022 and 3796/ND/2022) filed by Appellants in a pending Section 7 proceeding; contention that Corporate Debtor previously settled with original applicants; admission that the main Section 7 petition was still at the pre-admission stage. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Homebuyers filed intervention applications before NCLT Court-IV, New Delhi in an unadmitted Section 7 petition; NCLT rejected the applications on 26.08.2022 holding third-party interventions impermissible prior to admission; Appellants appealed to NCLAT.
summary.legal_issues: Whether third-party homebuyers have a legal right to intervene in an insolvency petition filed under Section 7 of the IBC by another creditor before the Adjudicating Authority decides the question of admission.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application for intervention by third parties is impermissible and maintainable only post-admission of a Section 7 application; at the pre-admission stage, the lis is strictly between the petitioning financial creditor and the corporate debtor. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 of the IBC restricts the threshold determination of debt and default strictly to the petitioning creditor and the corporate debtor, with no locus for outside intervenors prior to an admission order. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The admitted procedural status of the Section 7 petition being unadmitted and pending determination of maintainability. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed no error in rejecting the intervention applications at the pre-admission stage, leaving the applicants liberty to file fresh applications only if the Section 7 petition is admitted.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 354 of 2023 is dismissed, granting liberty to the Appellants to file appropriate applications if the Section 7 petition is admitted.
summary.summary: Surinder Pal Singh and other homebuyers appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order rejecting their intervention applications (I.A. Nos. 3795/ND/2022 and 3796/ND/2022) in a Section 7 IBC proceeding initiated against Spaze Towers Pvt. Ltd. by another homebuyer. The appellants argued they should be permitted to intervene as the debtor had previously settled with other petitioners. The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's decision, ruling that third-party intervention is impermissible at the pre-admission stage of a Section 7 petition. The appeal was dismissed, granting liberty to apply afresh if the petition is subsequently admitted.

summary.case_title: Department of Town and Country Planning, Haryana vs. Manoj Kulshrestha & Anr.
summary.appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1325 of 2023 & I.A. No. 4605, 4698 of 2023
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant: Department of Town and Country Planning, Haryana; Respondent No. 1: Manoj Kulshrestha (Resolution Professional); Respondent No. 2: Other Respondent. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP proceedings involving town planning permissions, statutory development charges, or project approvals concerning the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Non-compliance or dispute regarding statutory town planning directions and liabilities (quantum not specified in the limitation order). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned order passed by NCLT on 10.06.2022; Appeal e-filed before NCLAT on 09.07.2023; Refiling delay of 65 days; Order rejecting appeal passed on 12.10.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: I.A. No. 4605 of 2023 explaining 65 days delay in refiling; I.A. No. 4698 of 2023 seeking condonation of filing delay for an appeal preferred more than one year after the impugned order date (10.06.2022 to 09.07.2023). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed an appeal along with applications for condonation of refiling delay and condonation of filing delay beyond the statutory 30-day period and 15-day extended period provided under Section 61(2).
summary.legal_issues: Whether the Appellate Tribunal has the statutory jurisdiction or power under the proviso to Section 61(2) of the IBC to condone a delay in filing an appeal exceeding the maximum allowable period of 15 days beyond the initial 30-day limitation window.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The appellate jurisdiction of the NCLAT to condone delay in filing an appeal against an NCLT order is strictly confined by statute to a maximum period of 15 days beyond the initial 30 days prescribed under Section 61(2); any appeal preferred beyond this 45-day outer limit cannot be condoned and must be rejected as barred by limitation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The proviso to Section 61(2) of the IBC is mandatory and exhaustive, completely ousting the application of Section 5 of the Limitation Act to extend time beyond the 15-day discretionary ceiling. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Calculation of the date of the impugned order (10.06.2022) against the date of e-filing (09.07.2023), revealing an inordinate filing delay far surpassing the 15-day outer limit. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Tribunal possesses no jurisdiction to condone filing delay beyond 15 days, warranting dismissal of the condonation application and rejection of the appeal memo.
summary.operative_order: I.A. No. 4605 of 2023 (refiling delay) is condoned; I.A. No. 4698 of 2023 (delay condonation) is dismissed; consequently, the Memo of Appeal is rejected.
summary.summary: The Department of Town and Country Planning, Haryana appealed against an NCLT order dated 10.06.2022 involving Resolution Professional Manoj Kulshrestha. The appeal was e-filed only on 09.07.2023, accompanied by an application for condonation of delay (I.A. No. 4698 of 2023). The NCLAT Principal Bench held that under the mandatory proviso to Section 61(2) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, its jurisdiction to condone delay is strictly limited to a maximum of 15 days after the 30-day period. Because the inordinate delay exceeded the statutory ceiling, the condonation application was dismissed and the memo of appeal was rejected.

summary.case_title: CA Harish Kumar T.K. & Ors. vs. National Financial Reporting Authority
summary.appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) No. 68 of 2023 with Company Appeal (AT) Nos. 87, 90 & 91 of 2023
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants: CA Harish Kumar T.K., CA Ayna Tamton, CA M. Baskaran, and CA Sam Varghese, Engagement Partners (EPs) at audit firm M/s K. Varghese & Co.; Respondent: National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA)[cite: 16]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Statutory branch audit engagements of 17 branches of Dewan Housing Finance Corporation Limited (DHFL) for FY 2017-18 assigned to the firm and conducted by the Appellants as EPs[cite: 16]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Regulatory misconduct proceedings arising out of alleged gross negligence and statutory violations in failing to report fraud and follow auditing standards during audits of DHFL branches amidst a broader Rs. 31,000 Crore fraud[cite: 16]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Audit file requisition issued on 10.08.2022; Show Cause Notices issued under Rule 11(1) of NFRA Rules on 07.12.2022; Impugned disciplinary orders passed between 31.03.2023 and 13.04.2023; Appeals dismissed on 01.12.2023[cite: 16]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Audit files and supplementary audit files produced to NFRA exhibiting an absence of documented audit plans, risk assessments, materiality determinations, and sampling procedures under SAs 210, 230, 300, 315, 320, 330, 500, 520, 530, and 700[cite: 16]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NFRA initiated suo-motu Audit Quality Review under Section 132(4) of Companies Act 2013, found Appellants guilty of professional misconduct, and imposed a monetary penalty of Rs. 1,00,000/- each along with one-year debarment; Appellants appealed to NCLAT challenging NFRA's retrospective jurisdiction and findings on merits[cite: 16].
summary.legal_issues: Whether NFRA possesses retrospective jurisdiction to investigate and penalize professional misconduct for audits conducted prior to the notification of Section 132(4) of the Companies Act, 2013, and whether statutory branch auditors are independently required to adhere to mandatory Standards on Auditing (SAs)[cite: 16].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Standards on Auditing (SAs) have mandatory statutory force and bind both principal and branch statutory auditors; statutory bodies established to enforce professional discipline over auditors can exercise jurisdiction over past audit conducts where the enactment constitutes a change of forum and the underlying misconduct was already prohibited under existing legal frameworks[cite: 16]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 132(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 is a non-obstante disciplinary provision conferring superior, overriding jurisdiction on NFRA over ICAI, operating retrospectively on adjectival/procedural grounds without infringing Article 20(1) of the Constitution[cite: 16]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Compliance with SAs is governed by the cardinal evidentiary principle 'work not documented is work not done'; verbal justifications or relying on prior years' unupdated audit templates cannot substitute contemporaneous documentation in the audit file[cite: 16]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellants failed to perform required risk assessment and documentation, and accepted branch appointments without verifying compliance with Sections 139 and 140, justifying NFRA's findings of professional misconduct[cite: 16].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) Nos. 68, 87, 90, and 91 of 2023 are dismissed without costs; all pending interlocutory applications are closed, and NFRA's orders imposing penalties of Rs. 1,00,000/- each and one-year debarment are sustained[cite: 16].
summary.summary: Engagement partners of M/s K. Varghese & Co. appealed NFRA orders holding them guilty of professional misconduct during the statutory branch audit of 17 branches of DHFL for FY 2017-18 and imposing monetary penalties and a one-year debarment[cite: 16]. The Appellants contended that NFRA lacked retrospective jurisdiction, that branch auditors have limited responsibilities, and that Standards on Auditing were substantially complied with[cite: 16]. The NCLAT held that NFRA has valid retrospective jurisdiction as a designated procedural forum, that Standards on Auditing are statutory and mandatory for branch auditors as well, and that failure to document compliance constitutes actionable professional misconduct[cite: 16]. Consequently, all appeals were dismissed[cite: 16].

summary.case_title: Jitendra Virwani vs. MRO-TEK Reality Limited & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant: Jitendra Virwani (Shareholder/CMD of Embassy Group); Respondent No. 1: MRO-TEK Reality Limited (Listed Corporate Debtor); Respondents No. 2 to 10: Erstwhile Promoters/Directors; Respondents No. 11 to 15: Umiya Builders & Developers and its proprietors/directors[cite: 19]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Postal ballot notice dated 10.11.2015 and special resolution passed on 22.12.2015 authorising Joint Development of the company's Hebbal land, followed by execution of Joint Development Agreement on 01.01.2016 with Respondent No. 11 and subsequent Share Purchase Agreement dated 19.05.2016[cite: 19]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Grievance centered on alleged corporate asset stripping and oppressive alienation of company undertaking rather than a conventional monetary debt default[cite: 19]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Postal ballot notice issued on 10.11.2015; special resolution passed on 22.12.2015; JDA executed on 01.01.2016; CP No. 486/BB/2018 filed before NCLT Bengaluru on 06.09.2018; dismissed by NCLT on 27.11.2019; appellate judgment passed on 04.10.2023[cite: 19]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Scrutinizer's report confirming 91.13% votes in favor of joint development; payment of Rs. 9 Crores non-refundable deposit by developer keeping the company solvent; completed commercial building generating monthly rental income of Rs. 1.25 Crores; SEBI's clearance of share acquisitions under Takeover Regulations[cite: 19]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed CP No. 486/BB/2018 under Sections 241-242 alleging oppression and mismanagement; NCLT Bengaluru dismissed the petition holding Appellant lacked clean hands and qualitative locus standi; Appellant appealed under Section 421[cite: 19].
summary.legal_issues: Whether the Appellant had locus standi and satisfied the qualitative eligibility test under Sections 241 and 244 of the Companies Act, 2013 to challenge corporate decisions implemented when his shareholding was below 10%, and whether entering into a joint development agreement approved by 91.13% majority constituted oppression and mismanagement[cite: 19].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In a petition alleging oppression and mismanagement under Section 241, the petitioner must satisfy not merely the quantitative shareholding threshold on the date of filing but also the qualitative test of bona fides and clean hands; a petitioner cannot challenge antecedent corporate transactions executed prior to acquiring the qualifying shareholding[cite: 19]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 102 of the Companies Act requires disclosure of material facts concerning the general nature of business to be transacted, but does not mandate disclosure of confidential preliminary commercial negotiations or unrelated future intentions of individual shareholders[cite: 19]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Demonstration of extensive forum shopping, parallel unmerited civil suits, and purchase of shares purely to weaponize litigation demonstrates unclean hands, barring equitable relief under Sections 241-242[cite: 19]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The joint development project was approved by 91.13% majority, proved financially beneficial to the company, and was free from illegality; the petition was rightly dismissed[cite: 19].
summary.operative_order: TA (AT) No. 94/2021 (Company Appeal (AT) No. 363/2019) is dismissed without costs; all connected pending interlocutory applications (IA Nos. 4295/2019, 4296/2019, and 517/2023) are closed[cite: 19].
summary.summary: Jitendra Virwani appealed against an NCLT Bengaluru order dismissing his petition under Sections 241-242 of the Companies Act, 2013 alleging oppression and mismanagement against MRO-TEK Reality Limited and its management[cite: 19]. The appellant challenged a joint development agreement for the company's Hebbal land and a subsequent promoter share sale[cite: 19]. The NCLAT held that while the appellant held over 10% shares on the date of filing, he held less than 5% when the cause of action arose and had purchased shares to engage in vexatious litigation[cite: 19]. Finding that the transaction was approved by 91.13% majority and yielded significant revenue, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal[cite: 19].

summary.case_title: Tridhaatu Kirti Developers LLP vs. Arihant Nenawati & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant: Tridhaatu Kirti Developers LLP (Third-party Real Estate Developer/Borrower); Respondent No. 1: Arihant Nenawati (Liquidator of Corporate Debtor Royal Refinery Pvt. Ltd.); Respondents No. 2 to 5: Suspended directors and connected parties[cite: 20]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan facility extended in 2017 by the Corporate Debtor (engaged in gold trading) to the Appellant for redevelopment of Kirti Cooperative Housing Society, which the Appellant claimed was orally converted into an investment of Rs. 20 Crores with a forfeiture clause[cite: 20]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unpaid outstanding loan balance of Rs. 8.95 Crores appearing on the audited ledger and balance sheet of the Corporate Debtor as on 31.03.2019[cite: 20]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Part payments of Rs. 50 Lakhs (19.07.2018), Rs. 55 Lakhs (24.09.2018), and Rs. 45 Lakhs (07.06.2019) made by Appellant; CIRP initiated on 13.11.2019; Section 66 application IA No. 1124/2020 filed on 20.07.2020; NCLT order passed on 21.01.2021[cite: 20]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor's audited financial ledger reflecting an admitted receivable of Rs. 8.95 Crores; total absence of any written contract, development agreement, or forfeiture agreement authorizing the Appellant to convert or forfeit the Corporate Debtor's loan[cite: 20]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Resolution Professional filed IA No. 1124/2020 under Section 66 of IBC alleging fraudulent trading; NCLT Mumbai Bench directed the Appellant to repay Rs. 8.95 Crores to the Corporate Debtor within two days; Appellant appealed under Section 61[cite: 20].
summary.legal_issues: Whether a third party who received corporate debtor funds as a loan can defeat recovery proceedings under Section 66 of the IBC by setting up an undocumented verbal agreement to convert the loan into an investment and unilaterally forfeiting the balance[cite: 20].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 66 of the IBC, establishing fraudulent trading or transactions designed to defraud creditors does not require the strict standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt applicable in criminal trials; where funds are siphoned or retained under a sham, unevidenced pretext, liability to contribute to the assets of the corporate debtor attaches[cite: 20]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 66(1) empowers the Adjudicating Authority to compel contributions from 'any persons who were knowingly parties to the carrying on of the business' with intent to defraud creditors, extending beyond directors to encompass third-party recipients of sham transactions[cite: 20]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: An unrecorded, undocumented verbal claim of loan conversion and forfeiture cannot rebut ledger accounts and audited balance sheets confirming an outstanding debt[cite: 20]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The retention of Rs. 8.95 Crores on the bogus defense of forfeiture constituted fraudulent conduct designed to defraud creditors, rendering the NCLT's repayment direction fully justified[cite: 20].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 95 of 2021 is dismissed, sustaining the NCLT Mumbai Bench order directing the Appellant to contribute and pay Rs. 8.95 Crores to the account of the Corporate Debtor[cite: 20].
summary.summary: Tridhaatu Kirti Developers LLP appealed an order of NCLT Mumbai Bench under Section 66 of the IBC directing it to pay Rs. 8.95 Crores to Corporate Debtor Royal Refinery Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 20] The appellant had received loans from the debtor in 2017 and claimed that pursuant to an oral agreement, the loan was converted into project investment and forfeited when the debtor failed to invest Rs. 20 Crores[cite: 20]. The NCLAT held that the alleged forfeiture agreement was completely undocumented and constituted a sham device to defraud creditors[cite: 20]. Finding clear evidence of admitted debt in audited accounts, the NCLAT affirmed that Section 66 applied and dismissed the appeal[cite: 20].

summary.case_title: Shankar Sundaram vs. M/s Amalgamations Ltd. & Ors.
summary.appeal_number: TA (AT) No. 18/2021 (Company Appeal (AT) No. 325/2019) with TA (AT) No. 114/2021 (Company Appeal (AT) No. 328/2019)
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant: Mr. Shankar Sundaram (10% shareholder of holding company Amalgamations Ltd. via inheritance from his mother); Respondent No. 1: M/s Amalgamations Limited (Holding Company); Respondents No. 2 & 3: A. Sivasailam (deceased) and A. Krishnamoorthy (Promoters/Managing Directors); Respondents No. 4 to 20/48: Direct and indirect operating subsidiaries (including Simpson & Co. Ltd., TAFE Ltd., Addisons Paints & Chemicals Ltd.); Respondents No. 21 to 26: Statutory auditors and family directors (including Mrs. Mallika Srinivasan)[cite: 21]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate governance and internal administration across a multi-tier group conglomerate comprising 38 operating subsidiaries across diverse manufacturing industries[cite: 21]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Oppression and mismanagement claimed regarding alleged disproportionate managerial remuneration/commissions paid to majority family directors in subsidiaries (escalating from Rs. 2 Crores in 1997-98 to over Rs. 850 Crores by 2018), resulting in reduced distributable profits/dividends to the holding company and its 10% shareholder[cite: 21]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Group founder died intestate on 18.04.1964; shares devolved equally among five legal heirs; Appellant inherited 10% in 1974; CP No. 94/1999 (TCP No. 1/2016) filed in 1999; CP No. 20/2012 (TCP No. 88/2016) filed in 2012; NCLT Chennai dismissed both on 18.09.2019; NCLAT final order passed on 06.10.2023[cite: 21]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Consolidated financial statements and AGM minutes from 1984 to 1999 showing Appellant attended and unanimously approved balance sheets, proposed dividends, and director appointments without protest; proof that managerial remuneration remained within the statutory 11% ceiling under the Companies Act; presence of significant third-party and foreign equity in subsidiaries[cite: 21]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai dismissed TCP Nos. 1/2016 and 88/2016 on 18.09.2019 holding that family shareholding did not create a quasi-partnership and no oppression occurred; Appellant appealed under Section 421[cite: 21].
summary.legal_issues: Whether a multi-tier family-owned corporate group can be treated as a quasi-partnership to enforce a legitimate expectation of directorship and equal remuneration across subsidiaries, whether payment of managerial remuneration within statutory limits constitutes oppression of minority shareholders, and whether a share buyout can be ordered under Sections 241-242 in the absence of a functional deadlock[cite: 21].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A corporate group cannot be treated as a quasi-partnership merely because shares were devolved equally among family members through inheritance, absent an antecedent partnership or explicit contractual understanding of joint management; payment of managerial remuneration within statutory limits does not constitute oppression of a shareholder, and a buyout of shares under equitable jurisdiction cannot be granted without a showing of lack of probity or complete functional deadlock[cite: 21]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Oppression under Section 241/397 must affect the petitioner strictly in their proprietary capacity as a shareholder and not in their personal aspirations as a director; lawful remuneration approved by general bodies under Section 152/Section 197 does not constitute an oppressive deprivation of dividends[cite: 21]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Continued attendance, approval, and adoption of annual consolidated accounts and dividends at successive AGMs without contemporaneous dissent operates as acquiescence, defeating subsequent allegations of continuous oppression[cite: 21]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The holding company and its subsidiaries operate profitably with distinct corporate personalities without any functional deadlock; hence, no ground for winding up on just and equitable principles or directed share buyout was established[cite: 21].
summary.operative_order: TA (AT) No. 18/2021 (Company Appeal (AT) No. 325/2019) and TA (AT) No. 114/2021 (Company Appeal (AT) No. 328/2019) are dismissed without costs; connected pending interlocutory applications (IA Nos. 580/2021 and 191/2022) are closed[cite: 21].
summary.summary: Shankar Sundaram, a 10% shareholder of holding company Amalgamations Limited by inheritance, appealed the dismissal of his oppression and mismanagement petitions against the company, its family directors, and 47 subsidiaries[cite: 21]. Sundaram alleged that majority family members extracted exorbitant directorial remuneration from profit-making subsidiaries while denying him board representation and adequate dividends[cite: 21]. The NCLAT held that Amalgamations Ltd. is not a quasi-partnership, legitimate expectation of directorship cannot arise without mutual agreement, and director remuneration within statutory ceilings does not violate shareholder proprietary rights[cite: 21]. In the absence of functional deadlock or lack of probity, the NCLAT declined to order a share buyout and dismissed the appeals[cite: 21].

summary.case_title: Google LLC & Anr. vs. Competition Commission of India & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants: Google LLC and Google India Pvt. Ltd. (Developers/Licensors of Android OS and GMS Suite); Respondent No. 1: Competition Commission of India (CCI); Respondents No. 2 to 4: Umar Javeed, Sukarma Thapar, and Aaqib Javeed (Informants/Android device users)[cite: 24]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Licensing of Android Operating System and proprietary applications to Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs) under Mobile Applications Distribution Agreements (MADA), Anti-Fragmentation Agreements / Android Compatibility Commitments (AFA/ACC), and Revenue Sharing Agreements (RSAs)[cite: 24]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Imposition of a monetary penalty of INR 1337.76 Crores calculated at 10% of average relevant turnover from Indian mobile operations for FYs 2018-19, 2019-20, and 2020-21 under Section 27(b)[cite: 24]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Information filed under Section 19(1)(a) on 28.08.2018; Section 26(1) prima facie order passed on 16.04.2019; DG report submitted on 29.06.2021; CCI final order passed on 20.10.2022; NCLAT appellate judgment passed on 29.03.2023[cite: 24]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Standard contract terms under MADA mandating pre-installation and prominent default placement of the entire 11-app GMS suite; ACC clauses preventing OEMs from manufacturing or distributing devices running Android Forks; RSAs conditioning search ad revenue sharing on exclusivity of Google Search; usage data showing Google's persistent >95% market share in relevant markets creating behavioral status quo bias[cite: 24]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CCI held Google dominant across five defined relevant markets and found abuse under Sections 4(2)(a)(i), 4(2)(b)(ii), 4(2)(c), 4(2)(d), and 4(2)(e), imposing a penalty of INR 1337.76 Crores and ten behavioral remedies under Section 27; Google appealed to NCLAT[cite: 24].
summary.legal_issues: Whether establishing abuse of dominant position under Section 4 of the Competition Act, 2002 requires an effects-based analysis demonstrating anti-competitive harm, whether MADA, AFA/ACC, and RSA restrictions constituted statutory abuse, and whether CCI exceeded its jurisdiction under Section 27 by directing Google to share proprietary APIs, host rival app stores on Play Store, allow uninstallation, and permit unrestricted sideloading without warnings[cite: 24].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: For establishing an abuse of dominant position under Section 4 of the Competition Act, the competition authority must conduct an effects-based analysis to determine whether the impugned conduct produces anti-competitive exclusionary or foreclosure effects; however, remedial directions under Section 27 must strictly correlate to proved infringements and cannot expropriate intellectual property or negate statutory security warnings absent an essential facilities finding[cite: 24]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The statutory scheme of Section 4 read with Section 18 requires proving anti-competitive harm; MADA's mandatory bundling of core apps violates Section 4(2)(a)(i) and 4(2)(d), AFA/ACC restrictions on Android forks violate Section 4(2)(b)(ii), and tying search/browser/video apps leverages dominance under Sections 4(2)(c) and 4(2)(e)[cite: 24]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Demonstrable barriers to entry, status quo bias caused by mandatory pre-installation, foreclosure of distribution channels, and market shares exceeding 95% establish anti-competitive market harm[cite: 24]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: CCI's findings of abuse and penalty calculation based on best estimates of relevant turnover from Indian mobile business were valid, but behavioral remedies compelling Google to share proprietary APIs (para 617.3), host rival app stores in Play Store (para 617.9), unrestrict sideloading warnings (para 617.10), and permit app uninstallation (para 617.7) lacked underlying infringement findings and were ultra vires[cite: 24].
summary.operative_order: Competition Appeal (AT) No. 01 of 2023 is allowed in part; the CCI order dated 20.10.2022 is upheld regarding findings of abuse and the monetary penalty of INR 1337.76 Crores, but directions at paragraphs 617.3, 617.7, 617.9, and 617.10 are quashed and set aside; the word 'provisional' regarding penalty is deleted, and Google is granted 30 days to pay the balance penalty and implement the remaining remedies[cite: 24].
summary.summary: Google LLC and Google India appealed a CCI order finding it guilty of abusing its dominant position in the Android mobile ecosystem under Section 4 of the Competition Act, 2002, which imposed a penalty of INR 1337.76 Crores and ten mandatory behavioural remedies[cite: 24]. The NCLAT held that an effects-based analysis demonstrating anti-competitive harm is necessary under Section 4 and affirmed that Google's mandatory pre-installation of GMS apps, anti-fragmentation restrictions on Android Forks, and search exclusivity agreements were anti-competitive[cite: 24]. However, the NCLAT struck down four remedial directions (sharing APIs, hosting third-party app stores on Play Store, allowing uninstallation of core apps, and restraining sideloading warnings) as unsupported by infringement findings, while upholding the remaining remedies and the penalty in full[cite: 24].

summary.case_title: Mahendra Kumar Agarwal vs. PTC India Financial Services Ltd. & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: PTC India Financial Services Ltd. (PFS) is the Financial Creditor; Mahendra Kumar Agarwal is the Appellant/Personal Guarantor; Gati Infrastructure Bhasmey Power Pvt. Ltd. (GIBPPL) is the Corporate Debtor/Principal Borrower; Devvart Rana is the Resolution Professional[cite: 1]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: PFS sanctioned financial assistance of Rs. 125,00,00,000 to the Corporate Debtor, out of which Rs. 116,07,13,161 was disbursed for its project, secured by an unconditional personal guarantee executed by the Appellant[cite: 1]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Corporate Debtor's account was classified as an NPA on 31.03.2018, with the date of default recorded in the Information Utility as 15.05.2017[cite: 1]. The claimed default amount was Rs. 1,76,75,60,935 as on 15.01.2020[cite: 1]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Lead lender IFCI issued a loan recall notice on 11.02.2019 demanding Rs. 150,08,42,949, followed by a personal guarantee invocation notice on 08.03.2019[cite: 1]. PFS subsequently issued a demand notice under Form B on 12.03.2020 demanding Rs. 1,76,75,60,935[cite: 1]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Core evidence comprised the Personal Guarantee Deed containing independent and continuing obligations, the default record deemed authenticated from the Information Utility, and demand/invocation notices[cite: 1]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: PFS filed the original Section 95 petition, CP (IB) No. 335/95/HDB/2020, on 06.08.2020[cite: 1]. NCLT Hyderabad Bench-I admitted the petition on 21.07.2022 and appointed a Resolution Professional, rejecting the guarantor's objection that NCLT lacked jurisdiction absent ongoing CIRP/liquidation against the Corporate Debtor[cite: 1].
summary.legal_issues: Whether the NCLT has jurisdiction under Section 60(1) of the IBC to entertain and initiate insolvency resolution proceedings under Section 95 against a personal guarantor to a corporate debtor when no Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) or liquidation proceeding is pending against the principal corporate debtor[cite: 1].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application for insolvency resolution against a personal guarantor to a corporate debtor is maintainable before the National Company Law Tribunal having territorial jurisdiction over the registered office of the corporate debtor under Section 60(1) of the IBC, irrespective of whether CIRP or liquidation proceedings are pending against the corporate debtor[cite: 1]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60(1) is the substantive provision conferring jurisdiction on the NCLT over corporate persons and personal guarantors[cite: 1]. The non-obstante opening phrase 'Without prejudice to sub-section (1)' in Section 60(2) demonstrates that sub-section (2) is supplemental to sub-section (1) and avoids split forums when CIRP is active; it does not restrict the substantive jurisdiction under Section 60(1) or make pending CIRP a condition precedent[cite: 1]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under Section 128 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, the liability of the surety is co-extensive with that of the principal debtor, granting the creditor an independent right to proceed against the guarantor without exhausting remedies against the principal debtor or establishing prior corporate insolvency[cite: 1]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority possessed valid jurisdiction to admit the Section 95 application against the personal guarantor under Section 60(1), and in fact CIRP petitions against the principal borrower were also pending before the tribunal[cite: 1].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS.) No. 8 of 2023 is dismissed, affirming the NCLT Hyderabad Bench-I admission order dated 21.07.2022[cite: 1]. No order as to costs[cite: 1]. Connected pending Interlocutory Applications are closed[cite: 1].
summary.summary: Financial Creditor PTC India Financial Services filed a Section 95 application against personal guarantor Mahendra Kumar Agarwal for a default of Rs. 1,76,75,60,935 arising from credit facilities sanctioned to Gati Infrastructure Bhasmey Power Pvt. Ltd[cite: 1]. The Adjudicating Authority admitted the petition and appointed a Resolution Professional[cite: 1]. The Appellant appealed, arguing that under Sections 60 and 179 of the IBC, insolvency against a personal guarantor can only be initiated before the NCLT if CIRP or liquidation is pending against the corporate debtor[cite: 1]. The NCLAT Chennai dismissed the appeal, holding that substantive jurisdiction vests under Section 60(1), which does not mandate ongoing CIRP against the principal debtor[cite: 1].

summary.case_title: Indian Sugar Mills Association vs. Competition Commission of India & Ors.
summary.appeal_number: Competition Appeal (AT) No. 103 of 2018 (with connected appeals)
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants comprise ethanol producers and the Indian Sugar Mills Association (ISMA); the Respondents include the Competition Commission of India (CCI) and ester/chemical manufacturing informants[cite: 2]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Joint tender floated by Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs) on 02.01.2013 for the procurement and supply of ethanol[cite: 2]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The CCI found sugar mills guilty of bid-rigging and cartelization under Section 3(1) read with Section 3(1)(d) of the Competition Act, 2002, and imposed monetary penalties capped up to 10% of their average turnover[cite: 2]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Final arguments before the CCI concluded on 22.08.2017; the CCI reserved orders on 22.08.2017; the CCI ordered supplementary investigation on 30.10.2017; the Director General's supplementary report was considered on 07.06.2018; the impugned final order was delivered on 18.09.2018[cite: 2]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Director General submitted an initial investigation report confined to UP depots, followed by a Supplementary Investigation Report covering Maharashtra depots; the CCI collected revenue details for FY 2011-12 to 2013-14 before deciding on the finding of contravention[cite: 2]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Multiple informations (Case Nos. 21, 29, 36, 47, 48, and 49 of 2013) were filed alleging cartelization[cite: 2]. The CCI passed the impugned order dated 18.09.2018 under Section 27 imposing penalties, which was challenged under Section 53B before the NCLAT[cite: 2].
summary.legal_issues: Whether the impugned final order of the CCI was vitiated by gross violation of natural justice under Section 36(1) of the Competition Act, 2002 due to an inordinate 13-month delay between reserving orders and pronouncement, resulting in only three members signing the order out of the five/six members who heard the case, and due to failure to grant an oral hearing on the Supplementary Investigation Report and the quantum of penalty[cite: 2].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In quasi-judicial proceedings, the fundamental tenet 'one who hears must decide' is mandatory; a final adjudicatory decision cannot be signed and pronounced by a truncated body of members when a larger coram heard the oral arguments, particularly where the truncation is occasioned by unexplained and inordinate delay[cite: 2]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 36(1) mandates that the CCI be guided by principles of natural justice[cite: 2]. Regulation 32 of the CCI (General) Regulations, 2009 requires all members who heard the matter to sign the order, and orders must be pronounced as far as practicable within 21 days[cite: 2]. Section 15(c) curatively covers procedural irregularities not affecting merits, but cannot salvage a fundamental failure of natural justice and jurisdictional defect arising from split coram and inordinate delay[cite: 2]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where a quasi-judicial body reserves judgment and delays pronouncement for 13 months, during which members retire, prejudice is established because the deliberative composition that heard the evidence is broken and natural justice is visibly undermined[cite: 2]. Furthermore, failure to provide oral hearing after receiving supplementary investigative reports violates mandatory procedural fairness[cite: 2]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The impugned order of the CCI suffered from fatal jurisdictional and procedural infirmities of coram non judice and denied natural justice, rendering it null, void, and non est in law[cite: 2].
summary.operative_order: The impugned order dated 18.09.2018 passed by the Competition Commission of India is set aside[cite: 2]. The batch of appeals is allowed and the matter is remanded to the CCI for constitution of an appropriate coram to conduct a fresh hearing on all issues, including the Supplementary Investigation Report and penalty[cite: 2]. FDRs deposited by the Appellants (10% penalty) are ordered to be released within 15 days[cite: 2].
summary.summary: Appellants, including Indian Sugar Mills Association and various sugar mills, appealed against a CCI order imposing penalties for alleged ethanol tender bid-rigging under Section 3 of the Competition Act, 2002[cite: 2]. The final arguments were heard by five members in August 2017, but the order was delivered 13 months later in September 2018 signed by only three members, as two members had demitted office[cite: 2]. Additionally, the CCI considered a Supplementary Investigation Report without providing an oral hearing[cite: 2]. The NCLAT held that the fundamental principle 'one who hears must decide' and Section 36 were violated[cite: 2]. Setting aside the order, the Tribunal remanded the matter for fresh hearing[cite: 2].

summary.case_title: Giriraj Enterprises & Ors. vs. Regen Powertech Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
summary.appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 323 of 2021 (with connected appeals)
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are customers, wind turbine purchasers, and operational creditors (including Giriraj Enterprises, TVH Energy Resource, Clean Wind Power, Echanda Urja, GAIL, and Sulochana Cotton Spinning Mills), as well as ARCIL (Financial Creditor) and the RP of RISPL; Respondents are Regen Powertech Pvt. Ltd. (RPPL - Holding Company) and Regen Infrastructure and Services Pvt. Ltd. (RISPL - Wholly Owned Subsidiary) through their respective Resolution Professionals[cite: 3]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: RPPL manufactured and supplied Vensys Wind Turbine Generators with long-term 10-year Operation and Maintenance (O&M) contracts transferred/assigned to RISPL under a Business Transfer Agreement dated 05.03.2014, with RPPL executing continuing Sponsor Support Undertakings and performance guarantees[cite: 3]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by both companies resulted in independent CIRP admissions: RPPL admitted on 09.12.2019 and RISPL admitted on 19.02.2020[cite: 3]. Appellants lodged substantial claims (e.g., Giriraj Enterprises for Rs. 25,18,56,602; Clean Wind Power holding an arbitral award for Rs. 12,10,55,648; Bhilwara Green for Rs. 21,26,95,018)[cite: 3]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Form G for RPPL was issued on 12.03.2020; Form G for RISPL on 15.10.2020; Mediator Justice K. Kannan submitted a mediation report on 23.04.2021 recommending a single resolution plan for both entities; RP of RISPL filed application IA/548/CHE/2021 for simultaneous CIRP on 18.05.2021[cite: 3]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Tripartite Assignment Agreements, Debenture Trust Deeds showing inter-corporate cross-guarantees, common directors, identical registered offices, common creditors (SBI, ARCIL), intertwined balance sheets, and shared manufacturing/repair infrastructure[cite: 3]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants and the RP of RISPL filed multiple applications seeking consolidation/simultaneous CIRP of RPPL and RISPL[cite: 3]. The NCLT Chennai Bench dismissed all applications on 01.11.2021, holding applicants lacked locus as operational creditors and that the tribunal lacked equity jurisdiction under the IBC to order consolidation[cite: 3].
summary.legal_issues: Whether wind turbine purchasers/O&M service recipients have locus standi as 'Operational Creditors' under Section 5(20) read with Section 5(21) of the IBC, and whether the NCLT has legal jurisdiction under Section 60(5) of the IBC and Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 to order substantive consolidation of CIRP of a holding company and its wholly owned subsidiary as a single economic unit to ensure value maximization[cite: 3].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Corporate insolvency resolution processes of a holding company and its wholly owned subsidiary may be substantively consolidated under Section 60(5) of the IBC where the entities function as a single economic unit with deeply intertwined operations, finances, and assets, and where separate resolutions would cause commercial death or asset value destruction[cite: 3]. Customers who pay advance amounts for supply or services qualify as operational creditors with standing[cite: 3]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(21) defines 'operational debt' broadly to encompass debts arising from contracts for goods and services irrespective of whether the creditor is a supplier or recipient[cite: 3]. Section 60(5)(c) confers wide residuary jurisdiction to decide any question of law or fact arising out of insolvency; ordering consolidation is an application of established legal principles on single economic units and value maximization, not an unauthorized exercise of equity jurisdiction[cite: 3]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Application of the Videocon/Radico Khaitan parameters: common control, common directors, common assets, common liabilities, financial interlacing, resource pooling, intricate links, and coexistence for survival[cite: 3]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The criteria for consolidation were fully satisfied by RPPL and RISPL; the NCLT erred in denying locus and refusing consolidation[cite: 3].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 323 of 2021 and connected appeals are allowed[cite: 3]. The common order dated 01.11.2021 passed by the NCLT Chennai Bench is set aside[cite: 3]. The Adjudicating Authority, NCLT Chennai Bench, is directed to proceed with the consolidated CIRP of RPPL and RISPL in accordance with law[cite: 3]. Connected interlocutory applications are closed[cite: 3].
summary.summary: Wind energy customers and operational/financial creditors appealed an NCLT Chennai order refusing to consolidate the CIRPs of holding company Regen Powertech Pvt. Ltd. (RPPL) and its wholly owned subsidiary Regen Infrastructure and Services Pvt. Ltd. (RISPL)[cite: 3]. NCLT had dismissed the applications holding that customers lacked locus as operational creditors and the tribunal possessed no equity jurisdiction for consolidation[cite: 3]. The NCLAT Chennai set aside the order, holding that under Supreme Court precedent, advance-paying service recipients are operational creditors with valid locus standi[cite: 3]. It held that ordering consolidation under Section 60(5) based on established parameters is a legal principle serving value maximization, not equity jurisdiction[cite: 3].

summary.case_title: Precious Energy Holdings Ltd. vs. State Bank of India & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: State Bank of India (Lead Lender) is the Financial Creditor; Coastal Energen Private Limited is the Corporate Debtor; Precious Energy Holdings Ltd. is the Appellant (Shareholder-cum-Investor/Promoter of the Corporate Debtor); Radhakrishnan Dharmarajan is the Interim Resolution Professional[cite: 5]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: SBI along with a consortium of lenders sanctioned and disbursed various credit facilities under Common Loan and Working Capital Facility Agreements to finance a thermal power plant project[cite: 5]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total disbursed amount stood at Rs. 3131.40 Crores; default occurred on 31.03.2017 when the account was declared NPA; total outstanding amount in default claimed was Rs. 2923,62,42,864.46 as on 06.09.2018 (including principal of Rs. 2442.83 Crores)[cite: 5]. Default as of 24.01.2022 was admitted at approximately Rs. 1458 Crores[cite: 5]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Section 7 application (IBA/757/2019) was filed on 03.10.2018; dismissed as withdrawn on 19.12.2019 with express liberty to reinstate upon OTS default; reinstated via IA/827/2020 on 05.11.2020[cite: 5]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Third Amended and Restated Common Loan Agreement dated 05.07.2016, Working Capital Facility Agreement dated 23.02.2017, Information Utility certificate showing 'Deemed to be Authenticated' default, and failed OTS proposals (including an in-principle LOI dated 14.02.2020 and unappropriated deposits kept in a 'No Lien Account')[cite: 5]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: SBI filed IBA/757/2019 under Section 7[cite: 5]. After the Corporate Debtor defaulted on OTS commitments, the petition was reinstated and subsequently admitted by NCLT Chennai Division Bench-I on 04.02.2022, initiating CIRP and imposing a moratorium[cite: 5].
summary.legal_issues: Whether a shareholder-cum-investor has locus standi as an 'aggrieved person' under Section 61(1) to challenge an admission order under Section 7, whether reinstatement of a previously withdrawn Section 7 petition upon failure of an OTS proposal is legally valid under Section 60(5) and Rule 11 of NCLT Rules, and whether Section 10A bars admission when the default date pre-dated the pandemic cut-off[cite: 5].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A shareholder or investor of a corporate debtor is not an 'aggrieved person' within the meaning of Section 61(1) of the IBC to maintain an appeal against an order admitting a Section 7 insolvency petition[cite: 5]. Reinstatement of a Section 7 application withdrawn with liberty upon failure of an OTS agreement is fully permissible under inherent powers[cite: 5]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 10A bars insolvency applications strictly for defaults occurring on or after 25 March 2020 and has no application to debts where the default occurred prior to the cut-off date[cite: 5]. Under Section 7(5), where financial debt exceeding the statutory threshold and default are proven and the application is complete, the Adjudicating Authority has the subjective judicial discretion to admit the petition[cite: 5]. An OTS proposal constitutes a clear acknowledgment of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963[cite: 5]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Once the Information Utility authenticated record and contractual loan documents establish default exceeding the threshold, and the borrower admits substantial unpaid dues, admission is justified in law[cite: 5]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor had committed default long prior to 25.03.2020; the OTS having failed, the Adjudicating Authority committed no illegality in restoring and admitting the Section 7 petition[cite: 5].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS.) No. 89 of 2022 is dismissed, affirming the NCLT Chennai admission order dated 04.02.2022[cite: 5]. The interim order granted on 11.03.2022 stands vacated[cite: 5]. All connected pending Interlocutory Applications are closed with no order as to costs[cite: 5].
summary.summary: Appellant Precious Energy Holdings, a shareholder/investor in Coastal Energen Pvt. Ltd., appealed the Section 7 admission order passed by NCLT Chennai on an application filed by State Bank of India for an unpaid default exceeding Rs. 2900 Crores[cite: 5]. The Appellant contended that the petition could not be reinstated after withdrawal, that payments were made towards an OTS proposal, and that Section 10A barred the proceedings[cite: 5]. The NCLAT Chennai held that the Appellant lacked locus standi under Section 61(1) as a mere investor[cite: 5]. It affirmed the admission, holding that pre-pandemic defaults are untouched by Section 10A, failed OTS negotiations serve as acknowledgments of debt, and reinstatement with liberty was valid[cite: 5].

summary.case_title: Gaurav Katiyar vs. Nisus Finance and Investment Managers LLP & Anr.
summary.appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 593 of 2021 (with connected appeals)
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Gaurav Katiyar is the Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor Earthcon Universal Infratech Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 6]; Nisus Finance and Investment Managers LLP and Beacon Trusteeship Ltd. are Financial Creditors/Debenture Holders/Trustees[cite: 6]; Earthcon Infracon Pvt. Ltd. (EIPL) is the Principal Borrower/Issuer Company[cite: 6]; Sanskriti Allottee Welfare Association and individual homebuyers are Real Estate Allottees/Unsecured Financial Creditors[cite: 6]; Saya Homes Pvt. Ltd. is the Successful Resolution Applicant[cite: 6]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Under Debenture Trust Deeds dated 13.06.2017, 20.12.2017, and 24.12.2018, EIPL raised funds totaling Rs. 52.50 Crores to acquire units in the Corporate Debtor's real estate projects (Casa Royal and Sanskriti), guaranteed by the Corporate Debtor and secured by unregistered Builder Buyer Agreements (BBAs) and Mortgage Deeds over 268 flats[cite: 6]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose under the DTD redemption schedule where principal repayments fell due from 31.03.2019[cite: 6]; EIPL transferred Rs. 51.79 Crores to the Corporate Debtor against flats valued at Rs. 115.50 Crores, with the Corporate Debtor executing an Offer to Purchase Agreement agreeing to buy back flats at double the price to service debenture debt[cite: 6]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Corporate Debtor was admitted into CIRP on 08.01.2020[cite: 6]; the RP published the Information Memorandum including all 268 flats on 14.01.2021[cite: 6]; the CoC approved the Resolution Plan of Saya Homes with 91.46% majority in the 8th meeting concluding on 03.05.2021 (with Nisus voting in favour)[cite: 6]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: DTDs, unregistered BBAs, irrevocable POAs, Transactional Audit Report dated 12.04.2021 identifying the arrangement as an undervalued/preferential sham loan transaction, and RoC charge forms[cite: 6]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Nisus and Beacon filed IA 1606/2021 under Section 60(5) seeking exclusion of the 268 flats from the IM[cite: 6]. NCLT Delhi Bench-III on 23.07.2021 directed the RP to exclude 205 flats covered by registered mortgage deeds from the Corporate Debtor's assets and reduce Nisus's voting share proportionally[cite: 6].
summary.legal_issues: Whether unregistered Builder Buyer Agreements and mortgage deeds executed pursuant to a Debenture Trust Deed amount to an absolute transfer of title of flats or constitute a secured loan financing transaction, whether the corporate veil can be lifted to ascertain the real nature of the transaction, and whether a financial creditor who voted to approve a resolution plan can subsequently seek modification of the Information Memorandum to exclude underlying units[cite: 6].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An unregistered Builder Buyer Agreement does not convey proprietary title or create an interest in immovable property under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 and Section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908[cite: 6]. Where transactions are structured through interlinked buyback agreements and escrow sweeps to secure debenture redemption, adjudicating authorities must lift the corporate veil to recognize the transaction as a financing loan rather than a genuine sale[cite: 6]. A financial creditor that deliberates and votes in favour of a CoC-approved resolution plan is estopped from seeking subsequent modifications of the Information Memorandum[cite: 6]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18(f) empowers the RP to take custody of the debtor's assets, and Explanation (a) excludes third-party assets only where genuine ownership vests outside[cite: 6]. Unregistered sales confer merely in personam contractual rights and cannot defeat statutory asset collation[cite: 6]. Under Section 29 read with CIRP Regulation 36, timelines are sacrosanct and the scheme of the IBC provides no latitude for post-approval amendments to the Information Memorandum[cite: 6]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Substance over form analysis, examining fund circularity, substantial undervaluation against market circle rates, and audit reports confirming that funds functioned as collateralized loans rather than genuine sale consideration[cite: 6]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The 205 flats formed part of the Corporate Debtor's asset pool; Nisus had already exercised its voting rights on the plan and was barred from excluding the assets, rendering the NCLT exclusion order unsustainable[cite: 6].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeals (AT) (Ins.) Nos. 593, 659, 694, 703, 736, and 912 of 2021 are allowed, and the order of the Adjudicating Authority dated 23.07.2021 excluding the 205 flats from the Corporate Debtor's asset pool is set aside[cite: 6]. Consequently, Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 656 of 2021 is dismissed[cite: 6]. No order as to costs[cite: 6]. Pending Interlocutory Applications are closed[cite: 6].
summary.summary: Financial creditors Nisus Finance and Beacon Trusteeship sought exclusion of 268 flats from the asset pool of Corporate Debtor Earthcon Universal Infratech, asserting ownership through unregistered Builder Buyer Agreements and mortgages under a Debenture Trust Deed[cite: 6]. The NCLT excluded 205 flats, prompting appeals by the Resolution Professional, the Committee of Creditors, and homebuyers[cite: 6]. The NCLAT Principal Bench allowed the appeals and set aside the exclusion, holding that an unregistered BBA does not convey immovable property title under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act[cite: 6]. Lifting the corporate veil, the Tribunal determined the arrangement was a secured loan transaction rather than a sale[cite: 6]. Furthermore, Nisus was estopped from altering the Information Memorandum after approving the resolution plan[cite: 6].

summary.case_title: SICOM Ltd. & Anr. vs. Kitply Industries Ltd. & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are SICOM Ltd. (Vendor/Financial Creditor) and SICOM ARC Ltd.[cite: 7]; Respondent No. 1 is Kitply Industries Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/Purchaser)[cite: 7]; other respondents are SICOM officers and directors[cite: 7]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Agreement for Sale dated 03.09.1998 executed between SICOM and Kitply for the sale of an industrial property at Village Takeghati, Igatpuri, District Nashik for Rs. 2,25,00,000, along with a subsequent Inter-Corporate Deposit of Rs. 8.90 Crores extended on 07.05.1999[cite: 7]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default occurred when Kitply failed to remit 31 monthly deferred payment installments culminating on 15.08.2001 and failed to repay the ICD[cite: 7]. SICOM recalled dues demanding Rs. 29,71,28,927 via legal notice dated 06.03.2010 and lodged a claim of Rs. 40,86,47,641 before the IRP[cite: 7]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: SICOM terminated the sale agreement and cancelled the OTS on 25.03.2009[cite: 7]; CIRP against Kitply was initiated by NCLT on 01.05.2018[cite: 7]; SICOM submitted Form C on 18.07.2018 and revised it on 27.08.2018[cite: 7]; NCLT approved SREI's Resolution Plan on 07.12.2018 settling SICOM's debenture claim for Rs. 31,000[cite: 7]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Registered Indentures of Mortgage of 1993 and 1995 showing SICOM's ownership title[cite: 7], Agreement for Sale dated 03.09.1998[cite: 7], termination/cancellation notice dated 25.03.2009[cite: 7], and Form C claim submissions[cite: 7]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Following approval of the Resolution Plan, Kitply filed IA No. 47/2020 under Section 60(5) and Section 74(3) to enforce clause 3.8 of the plan[cite: 7]. NCLT Guwahati Bench on 31.08.2021 allowed the application and directed SICOM to convey and transfer the Igatpuri Unit to Kitply within 45 days[cite: 7].
summary.legal_issues: Whether the NCLT in exercise of its jurisdiction under Section 60(5) of the IBC can direct an unpaid vendor to execute a conveyance deed and transfer immovable property to the Corporate Debtor pursuant to an approved resolution plan when the pre-CIRP agreement for sale was terminated and legal title remained vested with the third-party vendor under Section 18(1)(f) of the IBC[cite: 7].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, an agreement to sell does not create any interest in or charge on immovable property, and title passes only upon execution and registration of a conveyance deed[cite: 7]. Under Section 18(1)(f) read with Explanation (a) of the IBC, assets owned by a third party in possession of the corporate debtor under contractual arrangements are excluded from the debtor's asset pool; hence, the NCLT lacks residuary jurisdiction under Section 60(5) to adjudicate pre-existing contractual title disputes or direct transfer of title[cite: 7]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18(1)(f) limits the control and custody of the IRP/RP strictly to assets over which the corporate debtor possesses ownership rights[cite: 7]. Explanation (a) explicitly prohibits treating third-party property as corporate debtor assets[cite: 7]. Inclusion of disputed third-party property in an approved resolution plan cannot override property laws via Section 238 or Section 31(1) to divest a third party of title without a registered conveyance[cite: 7]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Standard of proof regarding transfer of title in immovable property requiring a registered sale deed; equitable protection of possession under Section 53A acts only as a defensive shield and does not confer ownership[cite: 7]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because legal title to the Igatpuri Unit remained with SICOM and the pre-CIRP termination dispute fell outside the summary jurisdiction of the IBC, NCLT exceeded its jurisdiction in directing SICOM to execute the conveyance deed[cite: 7].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 849 of 2021 is allowed without costs[cite: 7]. The impugned judgment and order dated 31.08.2021 passed by NCLT Guwahati Bench in IA No. 47/2020 in CP(IB) No. 02/GB/2018 is set aside[cite: 7].
summary.summary: Corporate Debtor Kitply Industries entered into a 1998 agreement to purchase the Igatpuri industrial unit from SICOM Ltd. but defaulted on deferred installments, leading SICOM to terminate the contract in 2009 while Kitply remained in possession[cite: 7]. In Kitply's subsequent CIRP, a resolution plan was approved settling SICOM's claim for Rs. 31,000 and stipulating transfer of the unit[cite: 7].
