Kitply applied under Section 60(5) and the NCLT Guwahati Bench ordered SICOM to convey the property[cite: 7]. On appeal, the NCLAT Principal Bench set aside the order, holding that under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, an agreement to sell does not confer title[cite: 7]. Under Section 18(1)(f) Explanation (a) of the IBC, the NCLT lacks jurisdiction to order conveyance of third-party property[cite: 7].

summary.case_title: P.P. Bafna Ventures Private Limited vs. Punjab National Bank & Ors.
summary.appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS.) No. 331 of 2022 (with Comp. App (AT) (CH) (INS.) No. 332 of 2022)
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is P.P. Bafna Ventures Pvt. Ltd. (Financial Creditor/Shareholder)[cite: 8]; Respondent No. 1 is Punjab National Bank (Sole Independent Financial Creditor in CoC)[cite: 8]; Purusottam Behera is the former IRP[cite: 8]; KVR Industries Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor[cite: 8]; Maligi Madhusudhana Reddy is the RP[cite: 8]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: On 29.12.2018, Appellant entered into an Inter Corporate Deposit Agreement (disbursing Rs. 12.55 Crores), a Business Management Agreement, and a Share Subscription and Shareholders Agreement (investing Rs. 2.45 Crores for 10% equity with two board nominee seats and affirmative voting rights)[cite: 8]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in debt servicing led the Appellant to trigger CIRP against the Corporate Debtor under Section 7[cite: 8]. The IRP admitted the claim and assigned the Appellant 53.87% voting rights while reducing PNB to 46.13%[cite: 8]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Admission of Corporate Debtor into CIRP on 18.02.2022[cite: 8]; Appellant's nominee directors allegedly booked resignation notices via courier on 11.02.2022[cite: 8]; nominee directors resigned from Appellant's board on 16.02.2022[cite: 8]; DIR-11 filed with RoC on 03.03.2022/04.03.2022[cite: 8]; CoC constituted on 15.03.2022[cite: 8]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Courier booking slips dated 11.02.2022 addressed to an incorrect PIN code (430016 instead of 530016) showing tracking status 'consignment status request could not be processed'[cite: 8], BMA showing joint factory management, SSHA conferring veto rights, and MCA portal records[cite: 8]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: PNB and the Corporate Debtor filed IA Nos. 53 and 54 of 2022 challenging the CoC constitution[cite: 8]. NCLT Amaravati Bench on 22.08.2022 declared the Appellant a related party under Section 5(24), ordered its exclusion from the CoC under Section 21(2), and directed reconstitution with PNB as sole member[cite: 8].
summary.legal_issues: Whether delivery failure of a director's resignation notice sent via courier to an erroneous address constitutes valid service under Section 168 of the Companies Act, 2013 and Section 27 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, and whether a financial creditor whose nominee directors resigned immediately prior to CIRP initiation remains a 'related party' disqualified from the Committee of Creditors under the first proviso to Section 21(2) of the IBC[cite: 8].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Resignation of a director under Section 168 of the Companies Act, 2013 takes effect only upon actual receipt of notice by the company; where notice fails to deliver due to dispatch to an erroneous address, directorship and related-party status do not cease[cite: 8]. A related-party financial creditor that divests or tenders resignation on the eve of CIRP to circumvent the statutory exclusion under the first proviso to Section 21(2) of the IBC remains debarred from the Committee of Creditors[cite: 8]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Service by post under Section 27 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 does not encompass private courier delivery, particularly where an incorrect PIN code is inscribed[cite: 8]. The first proviso to Section 21(2) debars related parties in praesenti, but under the Phoenix ARC principle, purposeful pre-CIRP contrivances designed to circumvent disqualification require treatment of the creditor as debarred to prevent sabotage of the resolution process[cite: 8]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Courier tracking records demonstrating non-delivery and PIN discrepancies rebut any presumption of service; extensive contractual control through affirmative voting rights under SSHA and factory operations under BMA establishes pervasive related-party nexus under Section 5(24)[cite: 8]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The resignation notices were never legally served; the nominee directors continued in office, rendering the Appellant a related party under Section 5(24) rightfully excluded from the CoC[cite: 8].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeals (AT) (CH) (INS.) Nos. 331 and 332 of 2022 are dismissed, confirming the NCLT Amaravati Bench order dated 22.08.2022[cite: 8]. No costs[cite: 8]. Connected pending Interlocutory Applications are closed[cite: 8].
summary.summary: Financial Creditor P.P. Bafna Ventures appealed an NCLT Amaravati order disqualifying it from the Committee of Creditors of KVR Industries as a 'related party' under Section 5(24) and Section 21(2) of the IBC[cite: 8]. The Appellant contended that its two nominee directors had resigned seven days prior to CIRP admission by booking notices via courier and filing DIR-11[cite: 8]. The NCLAT Chennai Bench dismissed the appeal, holding that the courier was dispatched to an incorrect PIN code, never delivered, and failed the service requirements of Section 168 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 8]. Applying the Supreme Court's Phoenix ARC ruling, the Tribunal held that eleventh-hour resignations engineered to circumvent Section 21(2) do not cleanse related-party status[cite: 8].

summary.case_title: G. Sundaravadivelu vs. Indian Overseas Bank & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is G. Sundaravadivelu, Suspended Director of Corporate Debtor INMA International Ltd.; Respondent No. 1 is Indian Overseas Bank (Financial Creditor); Respondent No. 2 is the Corporate Debtor through its IRP[cite: 9]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: IOB sanctioned and enhanced credit facilities including Modified Cash Credit of Rs. 13 Crores and Inland Letters of Credit of Rs. 6 Crores under Sanction Letter dated 27.09.2013, secured by personal guarantees and mortgage of immovable properties[cite: 9]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default occurred following the devolution of Letters of Credit paid by the Bank amounting to Rs. 5,94,36,318, resulting in account classification as NPA on 30.12.2014[cite: 9]; claimed default was Rs. 14,08,75,444.17 as of 15.10.2018; updated default under the DRAT decree stood at Rs. 4,29,94,004 as of 01.03.2022[cite: 9]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: SARFAESI Demand Notice issued on 27.01.2015[cite: 9]; DRT-II Chennai passed final order in OA 633/2016 on 30.05.2019[cite: 9]; DRAT Chennai modified the decree on 14.11.2019 awarding 9% interest from sanction[cite: 9]; Madras High Court issued interim injunction against coercive steps on 04.12.2019 in WP No. 33396/2019[cite: 9]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Loan agreements, sanction letters, Bankers Books Evidence Act certified statements, DRAT Chennai decree dated 14.11.2019, and records of unfulfilled OTS proposals[cite: 9]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: IOB filed Section 7 petition IBA/49/2019 on 10.09.2018[cite: 9]. Corporate Debtor argued that payments made complied with the initial DRT order, leaving no default, and that a High Court injunction against coercive recovery barred CIRP[cite: 9]. NCLT Chennai Special Bench-II admitted the petition on 13.04.2022[cite: 9].
summary.legal_issues: Whether the pendency of a High Court writ petition granting an interim injunction against coercive recovery steps bars the NCLT from admitting a Section 7 insolvency petition, and whether a decree from the DRAT modifying a debt with 9% interest establishes a subsisting financial debt and default exceeding the statutory threshold under Section 4 of the IBC[cite: 9].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Initiation of CIRP under Section 7 of the IBC is not a coercive recovery proceeding or a money execution suit, but an independent statutory mechanism for insolvency resolution; therefore, an interim order of a High Court restraining coercive steps does not interdict the NCLT from adjudicating and admitting a Section 7 application[cite: 9]. A decree passed by the DRAT determining debt and default serves as a conclusive platform establishing financial debt[cite: 9]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7(5)(a) confers judicial discretion to admit an application once satisfied that a default exceeding the Section 4 statutory threshold has occurred and the application is complete[cite: 9]. Disputes regarding quantum or counterclaims are extraneous at the stage of admission and remain preserved for adjudication during claims collation[cite: 9]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Production of contractual facility agreements, certified account ledgers, and a modified appellate decree of the DRAT demonstrating an unpaid amount exceeding Rs. 1 Lakh satisfies the statutory requirement of proving debt and default[cite: 9]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the DRT order merged into the DRAT order leaving an unpaid default of over Rs. 3.55 Crores, and the High Court injunction did not stay the DRAT decree or bar IBC proceedings, the admission order was legally valid[cite: 9].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS.) No. 143 of 2022 is dismissed, confirming the admission order dated 13.04.2022 passed by NCLT Chennai Special Bench-II[cite: 9]. No order as to costs[cite: 9]. Connected Interlocutory Application IA No. 330 of 2022 for stay is closed[cite: 9].
summary.summary: The Suspended Director of Corporate Debtor INMA International appealed a Section 7 admission order obtained by Indian Overseas Bank for defaults under cash credit and letter of credit facilities[cite: 9]. The Appellant contended that the debt was cleared under a DRT order, that a High Court writ petition had granted an interim injunction restraining coercive recovery, and that no default subsisted[cite: 9]. The NCLAT Chennai Bench dismissed the appeal, holding that the DRT order had merged into a DRAT appellate order establishing outstanding dues exceeding Rs. 4.29 Crores[cite: 9]. The Tribunal held that CIRP is a resolution process rather than coercive debt recovery, and the High Court's injunction did not stay the DRAT decree or bar Section 7 proceedings[cite: 9].

summary.case_title: The U.P. Glass Manufacturers Syndicate vs. Competition Commission of India & Ors.
summary.appeal_number: Competition Appeal (AT) No. 07 of 2023 (with Comp. App. (AT) Nos. 08, 09 & 10 of 2023)
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are The U.P. Glass Manufacturers Syndicate (UPGMS - MSME industry body), Independent Sugar Corporation Ltd. (unsuccessful resolution applicant), Geeta and Company, and HNG Industries Thozilalar Nala Sangam (workers union)[cite: 10]; Respondents are the Competition Commission of India (CCI), AGI Greenpac Ltd. (Acquirer), and Hindustan National Glass & Industries Ltd. (HNG - Target/Corporate Debtor through RP)[cite: 10]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Proposed combination via Form-II notice filed on 03.11.2022 under Section 6(2) by AGI to acquire 100% of HNG pursuant to a CIRP Resolution Plan approved by HNG's Committee of Creditors on 28.10.2022[cite: 10]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Merger of the two largest container glass manufacturers in India, which would result in a combined entity controlling over 60% market share[cite: 10]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Form-II notice submitted on 03.11.2022[cite: 10]; CCI issued Show Cause Notice under Section 29(1) on 10.02.2023[cite: 10]; AGI submitted its reply with voluntary modifications on 10.03.2023 and clarifications on 14.03.2023[cite: 10]; CCI approved the combination under Section 31(1) on 15.03.2023[cite: 10]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Market share reports, capacity utilization data, show cause notice expressing prima facie AAEC concerns, and voluntary remedy commitment by AGI to divest HNG's Rishikesh manufacturing plant to eliminate market overlap[cite: 10]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Third parties (including UPGMS) filed objections and sought inspection and hearings, which CCI disposed of on 22.02.2023[cite: 10]. CCI approved the combination on 15.03.2023 without directing publication under Section 29(2)[cite: 10]. Appellants filed appeals under Section 53B[cite: 10].
summary.legal_issues: Whether third-party industry associations have locus standi as 'aggrieved persons' under Section 53B of the Competition Act, whether Section 29(1) requires issuance of a show cause notice to both acquirer and target entities, and whether the CCI is statutorily mandated to order public advertisement under Section 29(2) once a prima facie opinion is formed under Section 29(1) even if voluntary modifications submitted under Regulation 25(1A) dispel AAEC concerns[cite: 10].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The term 'person aggrieved' under Section 53B must be interpreted broadly in public interest given the CCI's inquisitorial role[cite: 10]. In combination reviews, Section 29(2) mandates a second-stage prima facie opinion after receiving the response to the show cause notice; if voluntary modifications offered under Regulation 25(1A) resolve AAEC concerns, the Commission can approve the combination under Section 31(1) without directing publication or third-party consultations[cite: 10]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 29(1) uses 'parties to combination' in the plural, contemplating notice to both acquirer and target[cite: 10]. However, in an insolvency scenario where the target is in CIRP and the RP supports the acquisition, failure to formally issue notice to the target does not vitiate the approval[cite: 10]. Section 29(2) publication is conditional upon the CCI sustaining a prima facie opinion of AAEC post-reply[cite: 10]. Section 30 does not make full Section 29 inquiry mandatory where concerns are resolved[cite: 10]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Judicial restraint regarding expert economic regulatory bodies; the evaluation of structural divestiture (such as plant divestment) to alleviate horizontal market concentration is an inquisitorial exercise that will not be disturbed absent patent irrationality[cite: 10]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CCI followed valid statutory procedure in accepting the voluntary divestment of the Rishikesh plant and approving the combination under Section 31(1) without requiring public notice under Section 29(2)[cite: 10].
summary.operative_order: Competition Appeals (AT) Nos. 07, 08, 09, and 10 of 2023 are dismissed, upholding the CCI approval order dated 15.03.2023 in Combination Registration No. C-2022/11/983[cite: 10]. Parties shall bear their own costs[cite: 10].
summary.summary: Appellants challenged a Competition Commission of India order approving the combination of container glass manufacturers AGI Greenpac and Hindustan National Glass (HNG) under Section 31(1) of the Competition Act[cite: 10]. The Appellants contended that once the CCI formed a prima facie opinion under Section 29(1), public advertisement under Section 29(2) was mandatory, and that the target HNG was never served notice[cite: 10]. The NCLAT Principal Bench dismissed the appeals, holding that although UPGMS had locus standi, the CCI was not required to trigger Section 29(2) publication because AGI submitted voluntary modifications (divestment of the Rishikesh plant) under Regulation 25(1A) that dispelled AAEC concerns upon the second-stage evaluation[cite: 10].

summary.case_title: Real Estate Regulatory Authority vs. D.B. Corp Limited & Anr.
summary.appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1172-1173 of 2022 (with Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 1321 of 2022)
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Real Estate Regulatory Authority (Madhya Pradesh RERA) and Aquacity Consumer and Societies Welfare Society (association of 74 homebuyers) are Appellants[cite: 11]; D.B. Corp Ltd. is the Operational Creditor[cite: 11]; M/s AG8 Ventures Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor[cite: 11]; Anil Goel is the Interim Resolution Professional/Resolution Professional[cite: 11]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Between 29.09.2010 and 13.08.2019, Corporate Debtor entered into nine Barter Agreements with D.B. Corp Ltd. for print and media advertisement campaigns, wherein consideration comprised a Cash Component and a Barter Component (allotment and transfer of residential/commercial units in lieu of advertising services)[cite: 11]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor fully paid the Cash Component but allegedly failed to hand over 19 out of 41 units under the Barter Component valued at Rs. 5,25,89,000[cite: 11]. D.B. Corp claimed total default of Rs. 10,77,17,000 (including interest @ 18% p.a.) with default date asserted as 13.02.2020[cite: 11]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Form 3 Demand Notice issued on 13.01.2022[cite: 11]; Section 9 application filed on 02.02.2022[cite: 11]; RERA had previously revoked project registrations on 08.01.2022 and 23.03.2022 and directed deposit of Rs. 81 Crores[cite: 11]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Nine Barter Agreements[cite: 11], 210 invoices (containing CGST/IGST entries predating the 01.07.2017 GST Act)[cite: 11], Demand Notice dated 13.01.2022[cite: 11], RERA investigation orders under Section 35[cite: 11], and NCDRC refund orders upheld by Supreme Court[cite: 11, 12]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Indore Bench-I admitted the Section 9 application on 05.08.2022 based on Corporate Debtor's admission of liability to the extent of Rs. 5,25,89,000[cite: 11]. Appellants appealed under Section 61 challenging maintainability and alleging collusion[cite: 11].
summary.legal_issues: Whether a Real Estate Regulatory Authority (RERA) and an association of allottees have locus standi as 'aggrieved persons' under Section 61 of the IBC to appeal an admission order under Section 9, and whether a claim arising out of non-allotment/transfer of real estate units under the 'Barter Component' of a Barter Agreement constitutes an 'Operational Debt' involving a right to payment of money under Section 5(21) read with Section 8 and 9 of the IBC[cite: 11].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Statutory regulatory bodies charged with protecting public interest and homebuyer welfare associations have locus standi as aggrieved persons under Section 61 to challenge the admission of an insolvency application that affects their statutory enforcement or possessory entitlements[cite: 11]. A contractual obligation restricted to the transfer or allotment of immovable property under a barter arrangement does not constitute an operational debt; breach thereof creates a claim for specific performance or contractual breach, but not a right to monetary payment required to trigger Section 9[cite: 11]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The term 'claim' under Section 3(6) and 'operational debt' under Section 5(21), when read with Section 8 and 9, necessitates an underlying 'right to payment' in terms of money[cite: 11]. Following Jaypee Kensington, the statutory concept of 'payment' under the IBC strictly denotes payment in money and excludes discharge of obligations through barter or equivalent non-monetary means[cite: 11]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the Barter Agreement covenants showing separate cash and barter components; where the cash component is fully discharged and the unfulfilled commitment is strictly for unit transfers, the creditor cannot unilaterally convert a barter obligation into a monetary demand under Form 3[cite: 11]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because no operational debt sounding in monetary payment was owed to D.B. Corp Ltd., the Section 9 petition was non-maintainable and the Adjudicating Authority committed jurisdictional error in admitting it[cite: 11].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeals (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 1172-1173 of 2022 and 1321 of 2022 are allowed[cite: 11]. The order dated 05.08.2022 passed by NCLT Indore Bench admitting the Section 9 application in CP (IB)/26(MP)2022 is set aside[cite: 11]. All connected Interlocutory Applications are disposed of with no order as to costs[cite: 11].
summary.summary: D.B. Corp Ltd. filed a Section 9 application against real estate developer AG8 Ventures Ltd. claiming default of Rs. 10.77 Crores arising from unallotted residential units under the 'barter component' of advertising contracts[cite: 11]. The NCLT Indore Bench admitted the petition after the Corporate Debtor admitted non-delivery of 19 units[cite: 11]. RERA Madhya Pradesh and a homebuyers' association appealed under Section 61[cite: 11]. The NCLAT Principal Bench held that both Appellants had locus standi as aggrieved persons[cite: 11]. Setting aside the admission order, the Tribunal held that an unperformed barter obligation to allot flats does not constitute an 'operational debt' under Section 5(21) because the statutory scheme of Sections 8 and 9 mandates a right to payment in monetary terms, not an exchange of commodities or barter[cite: 11].

summary.case_title: SP Coal Resources Pvt. Ltd. vs. Indus Fila Limited & Ors.
summary.appeal_number: TA (AT) No. 13 of 2021 in Company Appeal (AT) (INS.) No. 850 of 2019
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: SP Coal Resources Pvt. Ltd. is the Appellant (Operational Creditor)[cite: 15]; Indus Fila Limited is Respondent No. 1 (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 15]; SPG Macrocosm Limited (through SPV Vision Textile) is Respondent No. 2 (Successful Resolution Applicant)[cite: 15]; SF Dyes is Respondent No. 3 (Operational Creditor who triggered CIRP)[cite: 15]; Udayraj Patwardhan is Respondent No. 4 (Resolution Professional)[cite: 15]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of imported coal by the Appellant to the Corporate Debtor over several years covered under 14 unpaid commercial invoices[cite: 15]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellant lodged a claim of Rs. 6,05,00,111; the RP admitted Rs. 3.53 Crores and disallowed the interest claim as it was unmentioned in the invoices[cite: 15]. Corporate Debtor's liquidation value was determined to be 'Nil', while assets as on insolvency commencement were estimated at Rs. 80.75 Crores[cite: 15]. SRA offered Rs. 50.70 Crores in full and final settlement[cite: 15]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated under Section 9 on 20.08.2018[cite: 15]; Resolution Plan submitted on 07.01.2019 and revised on 09.01.2019 and 11.01.2019[cite: 15]; CoC approved plan via e-voting with 69.04% majority on 15.01.2019[cite: 15]; NCLT approved plan on 10.05.2019[cite: 15]; RP communicated extinguishment of debt on 26.06.2019[cite: 15]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Approved Resolution Plan dated 07.01.2019[cite: 15], 14 coal supply invoices[cite: 15], CoC voting records (Form H)[cite: 15], and liquidation valuation reports reflecting nil value for operational creditors[cite: 15]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP filed IA No. 40 of 2019 seeking plan approval[cite: 15]. NCLT Bengaluru Bench approved the resolution plan on 10.05.2019[cite: 15]. Appellant appealed under Section 61 challenging the plan for allocating nil payment to operational creditors despite debtor assets valued at Rs. 80.75 Crores[cite: 15].
summary.legal_issues: Whether a resolution plan providing 'Nil' payment to operational creditors when the liquidation value payable to them under Section 53(1) is 'Nil' violates Section 30(2)(b) of the IBC, and whether the commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in accepting a plan below the book value of assets is open to judicial review[cite: 15].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A resolution plan that provides 'Nil' payout to operational creditors complies with Section 30(2)(b) of the IBC if their entitlement under Section 53(1) in the event of liquidation is also 'Nil'[cite: 15]. The principle of fair and equitable treatment requires non-discrimination among similarly situated creditors within the same class, and does not mandate parity between operational and financial creditors[cite: 15]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(2)(b) guarantees operational creditors a statutory minimum floor equivalent to the liquidation value they would receive under Section 53[cite: 15]. Where liquidation value is nil after accounting for higher-ranked secured financial debt and workmen dues, an allocation of nil does not violate the statute[cite: 15]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Scrutiny of the plan's compliance with Section 30(2) parameters and verification that all operational creditors were treated uniformly with nil allocation without intra-class discrimination[cite: 15]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The commercial wisdom of the CoC in approving the financial matrix and valuation of the resolution plan with a 69.04% majority is non-justiciable; the plan was fully implemented and suffered from no legal infirmity[cite: 15].
summary.operative_order: TA (AT) No. 13 of 2021 in Company Appeal (AT) (INS.) No. 850 of 2019 is dismissed, confirming the NCLT Bengaluru Bench approval order dated 10.05.2019 in IA No. 40 of 2019 in CP(IB) No. 136/BB/2017[cite: 15]. Connected Interlocutory Applications are closed[cite: 15].
summary.summary: Operational Creditor SP Coal Resources appealed the NCLT Bengaluru Bench approval of SPG Macrocosm's resolution plan for Indus Fila Limited, which allocated 'Nil' payment toward its admitted operational claim of Rs. 3.53 Crores[cite: 15]. The Appellant argued that the plan was discriminatory and failed value maximization because the Corporate Debtor possessed assets valued at Rs. 80.75 Crores while the resolution amount was only Rs. 50.70 Crores[cite: 15]. The NCLAT Chennai Bench dismissed the appeal, holding that under Section 30(2)(b), operational creditors are guaranteed only their liquidation value, which was 'Nil'[cite: 15]. The Tribunal held that equitable treatment applies within the class of creditors and the CoC's commercial wisdom regarding asset valuation is immune from judicial interference[cite: 15].

summary.case_title: Indus Motor Company Private Limited & Ors. vs. T.P. Anilkumar & Ors.
summary.appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) No. 204 of 2020 & Company Appeal (AT) No. 87 of 2020
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Indus Motor Company Private Limited (Appellant No. 1 / Company) along with its majority shareholders and directors, Mr. Pulikkal Veetil Abdul Wahab and family members (Appellants No. 2 to 6, 8), and Mr. Thomas Kuruvilla, CEO (Appellant No. 7); T.P. Anilkumar and three others are minority shareholders (Respondents No. 1 to 4 / Petitioners before NCLT). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) dated 31.03.2007 entered into between shareholders governing shareholding reorganization, internal management, collateral/capital contributions, and containing an arbitration agreement under Clause 18. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not an IBC default proceeding; Respondents alleged oppression and mismanagement involving diversion of funds, interest-free loans, related-party transactions, and quantified alleged losses and claims to the tune of Rs. 62,88,86,800. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Section 11 notice invoking arbitration under the MoU was issued on 06.06.2020; Section 8 application filed in 2020 during company petition proceedings; an interim order by NCLT was passed on 05.06.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: MoU dated 31.03.2007, financial statements spanning 10 years, Advocate Commissioner's report, and Kerala High Court's Section 11 referral order dated 10.01.2023 (subsequently stayed by the Supreme Court on 28.02.2023). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Minority shareholders filed CP/02/KOB/2020 before NCLT Kochi Bench under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013; Appellants filed I.A. 44/KOB/2020 under Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 to refer the dispute to arbitration; NCLT dismissed the Section 8 application on 15.09.2020 on the grounds of complex fraud allegations, non-bifurcation of claims, and lack of arbitral jurisdiction over statutory corporate reliefs; NCLT also passed an interim order on 05.06.2020 appointing a Forensic Auditor.
summary.legal_issues: Whether statutory company petitions alleging oppression, mismanagement, and fraud under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 are arbitrable under Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996; whether the cause of action and reliefs prayed for before NCLT can be bifurcated between arbitration and the Tribunal; whether NCLT had jurisdiction to order interim appointment of a Forensic Auditor under Section 242(4).
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An arbitral tribunal, being a private creature of contract, lacks jurisdiction to grant statutory in rem and equitable remedies reserved exclusively for statutory judicial fora; where a composite dispute contains non-arbitrable corporate governance grievances, bifurcation of causes of action is impermissible. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 applies strictly where the entire subject matter is covered by an arbitration agreement and capable of arbitral resolution; statutory remedies under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 (such as appointment of inspectors, forensic auditors, regulation of affairs, and removal of directors) fall within the exclusive plenary domain of the NCLT and cannot be circumscribed or referred to arbitration. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The court must look at the averments and reliefs framed in the company petition holistically rather than merely examining defense assertions; if allegations involve serious management fraud, oppression, and statutory non-compliances requiring complex evidentiary scrutiny and regulatory redress, the dispute is inherently non-arbitrable. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The reliefs sought under Sections 241 and 242 are outside the competence of an arbitral tribunal and cannot be bifurcated without frustrating proceedings; hence, the dismissal of the Section 8 application and the interim order appointing a forensic auditor were fully justified.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 204 of 2020 and Company Appeal (AT) No. 87 of 2020 are dismissed without costs. The interim stay order stands vacated, and all connected pending Interlocutory Applications are closed.
summary.summary: Appellants appealed orders of NCLT Kochi dismissing their Section 8 Arbitration and Conciliation Act application and directing an interim forensic audit in a petition alleging oppression and mismanagement under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013. Appellants argued that disputes were purely contractual under a 2007 MoU containing an arbitration clause. NCLAT dismissed both appeals, holding that an arbitral tribunal lacks jurisdiction to grant statutory remedies under Section 242, including appointment of inspectors, forensic auditors, and removal of directors. Furthermore, bifurcation of the subject matter between arbitration and the Tribunal is legally impermissible, making the company petition non-arbitrable.

summary.case_title: Real Estate Regulatory Authority vs. D.B. Corp Limited & Anr.
summary.appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1172-1173 of 2022 & Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1321 of 2022
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Real Estate Regulatory Authority, Madhya Pradesh (RERA - Appellant in Comp. App. 1172-1173/2022); Aquacity Consumer and Societies Welfare Society (Homebuyers' Association - Appellant in Comp. App. 1321/2022); M/s D.B. Corp Limited (Operational Creditor / Respondent No. 1); M/s AG8 Ventures Limited (Corporate Debtor / Respondent No. 2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Between 2010 and 13.08.2019, Corporate Debtor entered into nine Barter Agreements for media advertising with D.B. Corp Limited, where consideration comprised a cash component and a barter component (allotment and transfer of real estate units). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational Creditor claimed a default of Rs. 10,77,17,000 with 18% interest per annum, alleging debt fell due on 13.02.2020; Corporate Debtor paid cash components and discharged 22 units (value Rs. 6,47,47,000) but failed to convey 19 units valued at Rs. 5,25,89,000 out of total 41 units under the barter arrangement. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand Notice under Section 8 in Form 3 was issued on 13.01.2022 claiming Rs. 10,77,17,000; Section 9 application filed before NCLT Indore on 02.02.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Nine Barter Agreements (last dated 13.08.2019), 210 invoices issued between 2010 and 2019, RERA orders revoking project registration on 08.01.2022 and 23.03.2022 and imposing penalties for fund diversion, and Corporate Debtor's reply affidavit before NCLT admitting principal liability of Rs. 5,25,89,000. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 9 application CP (IB)/26(MP)2022 was admitted by NCLT Indore Bench on 05.08.2022 based on the Corporate Debtor's reply admitting liability, imposing a moratorium under Section 14 and appointing an IRP on 11.08.2022.
summary.legal_issues: Whether RERA and a registered Homebuyers' Association have locus standi under Section 61 of the IBC as 'aggrieved persons' to challenge an order admitting a Section 9 application against a real estate corporate debtor; whether non-discharge of an obligation to allot/transfer real estate units under a Barter Agreement constitutes an 'operational debt' involving a 'right to payment' of money under Sections 5(21), 3(6), 8, and 9 of the IBC.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Statutory regulatory authorities entrusted with protecting stakeholder interests and registered consumer societies whose statutory enforcement actions are halted by a moratorium have locus standi under Section 61 of the IBC; furthermore, a contractual obligation to transfer immovable property under a barter transaction does not constitute an operational debt sounding in money. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The terms 'claim' under Section 3(6) and 'operational debt' under Section 5(21), read with Sections 8 and 9, strictly require a 'right to payment' in terms of sum of money; following the Supreme Court's ruling in Jaypee Kensington, 'payment' under the Code refers solely to money transfer and not anything of equivalent value in the nature of barter. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the underlying contract's terms and conditions governs the character of the debt; if the agreement mandates satisfaction via allotment of units without a contractually enforceable clause automatically converting undelivered barter units into an unconditional pecuniary cash debt, no operational debt is established. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The failure of the Corporate Debtor to transfer 19 real estate units under the Barter Agreements entitled the creditor at best to remedies such as specific performance, but did not create an unpaid operational debt payable in money; hence, the Section 9 petition was non-maintainable and jurisdictionally defective.
summary.operative_order: Both Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1172-1173 of 2022 and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1321 of 2022 are allowed. The impugned orders dated 05.08.2022 and 11.08.2022 admitting the Section 9 application and appointing the IRP are set aside. All connected Interlocutory Applications are disposed of. Parties shall bear their own costs.
summary.summary: Appellants RERA Madhya Pradesh and a Homebuyers' Association challenged the NCLT Indore Bench's order admitting an application under Section 9 of the IBC filed by D.B. Corp Ltd. against real estate developer AG8 Ventures Ltd. The operational creditor alleged default based on unfulfilled obligations under Barter Agreements to transfer 19 residential/commercial units in exchange for advertising services. NCLAT held that both RERA and the Homebuyers' Association possess locus standi under Section 61 as aggrieved persons. On merits, NCLAT held that 'operational debt' under Sections 5(21), 8, and 9 strictly requires a right to monetary payment; breach of a barter arrangement to convey property does not generate an operational debt. The admission order was set aside.

summary.case_title: Vijay Kumar Singhania vs. Bank of Baroda & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Vijay Kumar Singhania, Suspended Director of Corporate Debtor Cygnus Splendid Limited (Appellant); Bank of Baroda (Financial Creditor / Respondent No. 1); Sunil Kumar Gupta (Interim Resolution Professional / Respondent No. 2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Term Loan of Rs. 9,02,50,000 and Cash Credit facility of Rs. 3,64,00,000 sanctioned to the Corporate Debtor by Bank of Baroda vide sanction letter dated 18.02.2014, secured by hypothecation and equitable mortgages. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Aggregate defaulted amount of Rs. 13,49,47,775.57 (Principal and Interest across both accounts as of 08.10.2022); Date of default specified as 13.03.2017 (date of NPA classification). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 13(2) of SARFAESI Act issued on 06.05.2017; OA No. 615 of 2017 filed before DRT-II New Delhi on 26.05.2017; Section 7 petition filed on 03.01.2023 (formally registered on 12.01.2023). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Certified statements of accounts and interest calculation sheets under Section 2A of the Bankers' Books Evidence Act, 1891; written One Time Settlement (OTS) offers submitted by the Corporate Debtor on 05.09.2019, 07.09.2019, 23.09.2019, 16.12.2019, 21.09.2020, and 03.11.2020 (including upfront deposits of Rs. 2 crores); Supreme Court COVID limitation exclusion orders. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 application CP No. (IB)-39(ND)/2023 was admitted by NCLT New Delhi Bench (Court-II) on 26.07.2023, holding that repeated OTS proposals constituted valid acknowledgments of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, and Banker's Book certificates constituted sufficient evidence of default under Regulation 2A of CIRP Regulations.
summary.legal_issues: Whether filing a record of default from an Information Utility under Regulation 20(1A) and 21 of the IBBI (Information Utilities) Regulations, 2017 is mandatory to maintain a Section 7 application; whether repeated OTS compromise letters written 'without prejudice' constitute valid acknowledgment of liability under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963; whether an ongoing counter-claim before DRT or a commercial suit constitutes a bar or 'pre-existing dispute' against Section 7 proceedings; whether a power of attorney holder can delegate filing authority under the principle of delegatus non potest delegare.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In an application under Section 7 of the IBC, record of default from an Information Utility is not an exclusive or mandatory mode of proof, and default can be established via alternate statutory evidence such as certified Banker's Books records; written OTS offers, notwithstanding the caption 'without prejudice', constitute unequivocal acknowledgments of liability extending limitation under Section 18. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 20(1A) of IBBI (Information Utilities) Regulations, 2017 cannot override Section 7(3)(a) of the Code or Rule 4 of the AAA Rules, 2016 read with Regulation 2A of the CIRP Regulations, 2016, which expressly specify alternate evidence of default; the concept of 'pre-existing dispute' under Section 8/9 is alien to Section 7, where the adjudicating authority only needs to ascertain existence of financial debt due and payable. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under the doctrine of ITC Ltd. v. Blue Coast Hotels Ltd., inserting the words 'without prejudice' in settlement correspondence does not negate the factual acknowledgment of debt under Section 18; certified statements of accounts under the Bankers' Books Evidence Act, 1891 satisfy the legal standard of proof of default under Regulation 2A(a). 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt was alive due to continuous OTS proposals culminating on 03.11.2020 and Supreme Court COVID exclusion directives; default was conclusively established through Banker's Book entries, rendering the Section 7 admission unimpeachable.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1058 of 2023 is dismissed. The interim protection granted on 18.08.2023 stands vacated. No order as to costs.
summary.summary: Appellant, a suspended director of Cygnus Splendid Limited, appealed against the NCLT New Delhi order admitting Bank of Baroda's Section 7 IBC application for a default of Rs. 13.49 crores. Appellant contended that absence of an Information Utility default record invalidated the application, the claim was time-barred since OTS proposals marked 'without prejudice' could not extend limitation, and pending counter-claims before DRT constituted a pre-existing dispute. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, ruling that Information Utility records are not mandatory when default is evidenced by certified Banker's Books statements under Regulation 2A, 'without prejudice' OTS proposals operate as valid acknowledgments of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, and counter-claims do not bar Section 7 proceedings.

summary.case_title: Jaydip Ghosh & Ors. vs. Niraj Agarwal & Ors.
summary.appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 839 of 2022 & Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 861 of 2022
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Jaydip Ghosh, Mahesh Kumar Khaitan, and Uttam Kumar Samanta (Appellants in Comp. App. 839/2022 / Suspended Directors of Corporate Debtor Castal Extrusion Pvt. Ltd.); T-RMC Private Ltd. (Appellant in Comp. App. 861/2022 / Unregistered Tenant & Unsuccessful Resolution Applicant); Niraj Agarwal (Resolution Professional / Respondent No. 1); Square Four Housing & Infrastructure Development Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant / Respondent No. 2); Vijaya Bank, now Bank of Baroda (Sole Member of CoC / Financial Creditor / Respondent No. 3). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate guarantee extended on 06.05.2013 by Corporate Debtor for loan facilities availed by flagship company Tantia Construction Pvt. Ltd. (TCL), secured by equitable mortgage over 2.209 acres of industrial freehold land at Mouza-Gopalpur, Rajarhat, 24 Parganas (North). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in the borrower loan account led to NPA classification on 10.03.2014; Bank invoked the corporate guarantee on 26.02.2018 demanding an outstanding amount of Rs. 57.34 crores plus interest. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 13(2) of SARFAESI Act issued on 10.03.2014; Section 13(4) possession notice issued on 01.08.2014; Section 7 IBC petition filed in March/April 2018 and admitted on 18.03.2020 / 19.03.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Post-default creation of unregistered, unstamped 5-year lease deeds dated 27.07.2014 and 26.07.2019 transferring 1.90 out of 2.209 acres of mortgaged land to related entity T-RMC at an undervalued monthly rent of Rs. 55,000 against a transactional audit fair rent of Rs. 4.85 lakhs; factory shut down for years, uninsurable, lacking valid factory license, and encumbered by 15 years of unpaid municipal taxes. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench vide order dated 29.06.2022 in IA(IB) No. 277/KB/2021 approved Respondent No. 2's Resolution Plan with 100% CoC approval and allowed IA No. 107/KB/2021 ordering eviction of T-RMC and payment of differential rent at Rs. 2,00,000/month.
summary.legal_issues: Whether suspended directors of the corporate debtor and an unsuccessful resolution applicant/tenant have locus standi under Section 61(1) of the IBC to challenge the approval of a resolution plan sanctioned by the CoC's commercial wisdom; whether a resolution plan providing for the alteration of the line of business from obsolete industrial manufacturing to real estate development complies with Section 5(26) of the IBC and Regulation 37 of the CIRP Regulations.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Neither suspended directors who are divested of management nor unsuccessful resolution applicants have any vested right or locus standi under Section 61(1) of the IBC to challenge a resolution plan approved by the commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors; furthermore, a resolution plan can alter or change the corporate debtor's business line to maximize asset value without violating the 'going concern' requirement. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(26) read with Regulation 37(a), (b), (ba), and (j) of the CIRP Regulations empowers a resolution applicant to restructure, transfer assets, or alter the portfolio of goods/services; 'going concern' does not rigidly bind the corporate debtor to continue an obsolete, closed, and economically unviable undertaking. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Clean hands doctrine applies to insolvency litigants; where parties enter into fraudulent, unstamped, and unregistered lease agreements post-NPA with related parties to sequester mortgaged assets, equitable challenges to resolution plans are barred. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CoC's 100% approval of the turnaround strategy converting dilapidated factory land into a viable residential project was an unassailable exercise of commercial wisdom, justifying dismissal of both appeals and referral of the fraudulent lease transactions to the police for investigation.
summary.operative_order: Both Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 839 of 2022 and Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 861 of 2022 are dismissed. Direction issued to forward a copy of the order to the Delhi Police Commissioner to investigate the creation and use of the fraudulent lease agreements dated 27.07.2014 and 26.07.2019 through the Economic Offences Wing.
summary.summary: Appellants, comprising suspended directors of Castal Extrusion Pvt. Ltd. and an alleged tenant/unsuccessful resolution applicant (T-RMC Pvt. Ltd.), challenged NCLT Kolkata's order approving a Resolution Plan submitted by Square Four Housing. The plan proposed converting the non-operational factory land into a commercial/residential project. NCLAT dismissed both appeals, holding that suspended directors and unsuccessful resolution applicants lack locus standi under Section 61(1) to assail an approved plan. Further, NCLAT held that changing the business line of an obsolete undertaking does not violate Section 5(26) or Regulation 37. Due to collusive, unregistered post-NPA leases executed with related parties, NCLAT directed the Delhi Police Commissioner to initiate a criminal inquiry.

summary.case_title: Pooja Rai & Ors. vs. Tata Steel BSL Limited & Ors.
summary.appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) No. 132 of 2021 & Company Appeal (AT) No. 150 & 151 of 2021
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Jatinder Singh Ahuja and 16 other minority shareholders of Tata Steel BSL Ltd. (Appellants in Comp. App. 132/2021); Pooja Rai, Authorized Representative of Unsecured Creditors (Tapas Kumar Malla and R&S Engineering Services) (Appellants in Comp. App. 150-151/2021); Tata Steel Limited (Transferee / Respondent No. 1); Bamnipal Steel Ltd. (Wholly Owned Subsidiary / Transferor Co. 1 / Respondent No. 2); Tata Steel BSL Limited, formerly Bhushan Steel Limited (Transferor Co. 2 / Respondent No. 3). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Composite Scheme of Amalgamation of Bamnipal Steel Limited and Tata Steel BSL Limited into and with Tata Steel Limited pursuant to Sections 230 to 232 of the Companies Act, 2013. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not an insolvency default action; in the creditors' appeal, R&S Engineering claimed pre-CIRP outstanding operational dues of Rs. 4,16,19,292, and Tapas Kumar Malla claimed Rs. 16,00,810 (totaling Rs. 4,32,20,102), against total corporate debt of Rs. 11,608.51 crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution plan of Bhushan Steel originally approved on 15.05.2018; joint amalgamation petition filed in 2021 after shareholder meeting held on 26.03.2021; Tribunal sanctioned the Scheme on 29.10.2021 with Appointed Date as 01.04.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Shareholder voting results showing 99.33% of equity shareholders and 90.93% of public shareholders voting in favor; independent valuation reports recommending a share swap ratio of 15:1; Benpos records establishing that 17 objecting shareholders held only 0.0699% shareholding, and objecting creditors represented only 0.04% of total outstanding debt. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench vide order dated 29.10.2021 in CP (CAA) No. 70/MB/2021 dismissed shareholder and creditor objection applications (CA 156/2021 and CA 261/2021) and sanctioned the composite scheme under Sections 230-232.
summary.legal_issues: Whether objecting shareholders holding less than 10% shareholding and creditors holding less than 5% total debt have locus standi under the proviso to Section 230(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 to challenge an amalgamation scheme; whether convening a meeting or obtaining consent affidavits of unsecured creditors under Section 230(9) is mandatory when the amalgamation scheme involves no compromise or arrangement with creditors under Section 230(1)(b).
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory thresholds established in the proviso to Section 230(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 (minimum 10% equity shareholding or 5% outstanding debt) are mandatory conditions precedent for maintaining objections against a compromise or arrangement scheme; miniscule stakeholders lack locus standi to stall a commercially prudent amalgamation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Where an arrangement is proposed exclusively between a company and its members under Section 230(1)(b) without proposing any sacrifice, haircut, or modification of creditor rights under Section 230(1)(a), the Tribunal possesses discretion to dispense with convening meetings of creditors or obtaining consent affidavits under Section 230(9). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict statutory threshold audit; objectors must conclusively establish via audited financial statements that they meet the minimum 10% equity or 5% debt percentage requirement at the time of challenging the scheme. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the objecting shareholders represented merely 0.0699% equity and the unsecured creditors accounted for only 0.04% of the debt, both appeals were completely barred for lack of locus standi, and the approved 15:1 swap ratio and amalgamation scheme were upheld.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 132 of 2021 and Company Appeal (AT) Nos. 150 & 151 of 2021 are dismissed without costs. All pending Interlocutory Applications are closed.
summary.summary: Appellants comprising minority shareholders (holding 0.0699% equity) and two unsecured creditors (holding 0.04% debt) challenged an NCLT Mumbai order approving the composite scheme of amalgamation of Tata Steel BSL Ltd. and Bamnipal Steel Ltd. into Tata Steel Ltd. Shareholders contested the 15:1 share swap ratio, while creditors argued that their meeting was unlawfully dispensed with without Section 230(9) consent affidavits. NCLAT dismissed both appeals, ruling that objectors failed to satisfy the mandatory thresholds under the proviso to Section 230(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 (10% shareholding or 5% debt). Creditor meetings could be dispensed with because the scheme did not modify or compromise creditor rights.

summary.case_title: M/s. Ambadi Investments Limited vs. Ms. Valli Arunachalam & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s Ambadi Investments Limited (Appellant / Holding Company of Murugappa Group); Ms. Valli Arunachalam and Ms. Vellachi Murugappan (Respondents No. 1 & 2 / Applicants / Legal Heirs of deceased 1st Petitioner); Mrs. M.V. Valli Murugappan (Deceased 1st Petitioner); M/s M.V. Murugappan HUF (Respondent No. 4 / 2nd Petitioner). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Management and shareholding affairs of Ambadi Investments Limited, a closely held family company wherein the branch of late M.V. Murugappan alleged systematic oppression, exclusion from board management, and denial of rights. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Oppression and mismanagement dispute under Section 241; Petitioners sought waiver under Section 244(1)(a) of the 10% shareholding threshold to maintain the main company petition. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CP/95/CHE/2021 (Waiver Application) filed on 09.08.2021; original 1st Petitioner died on 21.01.2022; substitution application IA/14/CHE/2022 filed on 09.02.2022; shares transmitted on 18.02.2022; Respondent No. 2 transferred transmitted shares to HUF on 04.03.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Deceased's Will dated 17.12.2015 and Codicil dated 10.04.2018 devolving shares on daughters; Benpos records showing transmission of 63,101 shares to Respondent No. 1 and 62,851 shares to Respondent No. 2 on 18.02.2022, and subsequent transfer of 62,851 shares by Respondent No. 2 to HUF on 04.03.2022 reducing her individual shareholding to zero. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai Division Bench-I allowed IA/14/CHE/2022 on 01.06.2022 under Rule 53 of NCLT Rules, permitting substitution of Respondents No. 1 & 2 in place of their deceased mother in the pending Section 244 waiver proceedings; Appellant appealed this substitution order.
summary.legal_issues: Whether legal representatives of a deceased petitioner can be substituted under Rule 53 of NCLT Rules, 2016 to continue a Section 241/244 petition when one legal representative has transferred all her transmitted shares post-demise and is no longer an individual registered member of the company; whether maintainability and member qualification under Section 241/244 must be judged at the date of presentation of the petition.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The estate of a deceased member vests immediately in their legal representatives upon demise, and such legal representatives are fully entitled to be substituted to continue a representative proceeding under Sections 241 and 242; the maintainability of a petition and shareholder qualification are determined strictly as on the date of original presentation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 53 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 provides that proceedings do not abate upon the death of a party and may be continued by or against the legal representatives; there is no statutory mandate under Sections 241 or 244 requiring that a legal representative must personally be an entered member on the register of members to continue a proceeding validly instituted by the deceased. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The doctrine laid down in Rajahmundry Electric Supply Corp. and World Wide Agencies applies; subsequent events, including transfer of shares by a legal representative or reduction in shareholding post-presentation, do not invalidate an originally maintainable petition. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The estate of the deceased was lawfully represented by her daughters, and the transfer of shares by one daughter to the family HUF did not divest her character as a legal representative under Rule 53; the order of substitution was free from legal error.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 53 of 2022 is dismissed without costs. IA No. 620 of 2022 for stay is closed. Parties are granted liberty to raise all factual and legal pleas before NCLT Chennai in pending CP/95/CHE/2021.
summary.summary: Appellant Ambadi Investments Ltd. appealed an NCLT Chennai order allowing the substitution of daughters (Respondents No. 1 & 2) in place of their deceased mother in a pending Section 244 waiver application and Section 241 company petition. Appellant contended that Respondent No. 2 ceased to be a member after transferring her transmitted shares to the family HUF and therefore could not maintain the action. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the estate of a deceased member devolves on the legal representatives under Rule 53 of the NCLT Rules and World Wide Agencies principles. The petition's validity must be determined at the date of presentation, and legal representatives need not be registered members to prosecute it.

summary.case_title: Arun Kumar vs. Sripriya Kumar & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Arun Kumar (Promoter / Suspended Director of Corporate Debtor Arun Shelters Pvt. Ltd. / Appellant); Ms. Sripriya Kumar (Resolution Professional / Respondent No. 1); Kotak Mahindra Bank Limited (Sole Financial Creditor in CoC / Respondent No. 2); Monitoring Committee (Respondent No. 3); Consortium of S.M. Kamal Pasha and Syed Fahad (Successful Resolution Applicant / Respondent No. 4). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan and credit facilities advanced by Kotak Mahindra Bank to Arun Shelters Private Limited for developing the residential real estate project 'Arun Auroville', restructured via a Settlement Agreement dated 22.05.2018 for Rs. 23.50 crores. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default committed under the Settlement Agreement; Kotak Bank filed a claim for Rs. 36,27,27,729, which was admitted by the RP at Rs. 34,27,27,729 (after adjusting Rs. 2 crores paid pendente lite); the claim grew to Rs. 53,51,00,000 as of 30.04.2021 inclusive of contractual and 3% monthly compounded penal interest. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 31.01.2020; Moratorium declared under Section 14; Resolution Plan approved by CoC on 21.07.2021; NCLT approved the plan on 04.11.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Settlement Agreement dated 22.05.2018 stipulating 3% p.m. compounded penal interest on default; Karnataka High Court writ order dated 12.06.2019 restoring the active DIN status of the resolution applicants; Form H and minutes of 20 CoC meetings reflecting unanimous CoC approval. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru Bench vide order dated 04.11.2022 in IA No. 252/2021 approved the Resolution Plan of Respondent No. 4 valued at Rs. 53.42 crores and dismissed objections preferred by the promoter.
summary.legal_issues: Whether project-wise CIRP and constitution of a CoC confined to a single real estate project is legally sustainable; whether a resolution applicant whose DIN is active following High Court intervention is disqualified under Section 29A read with Section 164(2)(a) of the Companies Act; whether accrual and capitalization of contractual penal interest during the moratorium period violates Section 14 or Section 30(2) of the IBC; whether an MSME promoter is entitled to statutory preference over a third-party resolution plan.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the CoC in approving a resolution plan providing for contractual and penal interest up to the date of settlement is non-justiciable under Section 31(1); Section 14 moratorium does not extinguish or freeze ongoing contractual liability for interest. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14 of the IBC merely stays enforcement actions and legal proceedings during the calm period but does not operate as an interest waiver or debt-reduction mechanism; Section 238 gives paramount effect to contractual recovery rights unless expressly barred; Section 29A ineligibility does not attach where a director's DIN is officially active and compliant pursuant to High Court judicial directives. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict compliance with Section 30(2) and financial records; resolution applicants whose DIN records are marked 'active' by the RoC cannot be treated as disqualified under Section 29A; liquidation value serves only as an internal benchmark to evaluate viability and the plan value need not match liquidation value. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The resolution plan settled 100% of admitted claims of all stakeholders (homebuyers, workers, creditors), received 100% CoC approval, and was legally valid, justifying dismissal of the promoter's appeal.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 431 of 2022 is dismissed without costs. All connected pending Interlocutory Applications are closed.
summary.summary: Appellant, promoter of Arun Shelters Pvt. Ltd., appealed the NCLT Bengaluru order approving a Resolution Plan submitted by a consortium for the real estate project 'Arun Auroville'. Appellant argued that project-wise CIRP was invalid, the SRA was disqualified under Section 29A, Kotak Bank impermissibly capitalized penal interest during moratorium in violation of Section 30(2), and the promoter was denied MSME preference. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that project-wise CIRP had attained finality, SRA was eligible with an active DIN under High Court orders, Section 14 does not freeze or waive contractual interest liabilities, and MSME promoters have no statutory priority over superior plans approved by the CoC's commercial wisdom.

summary.case_title: Dr. Ravi Shankar Vedam vs. Tiffins Barytes Asbestos and Paints Limited & Ors.
summary.appeal_number: TA (AT) No. 134/2021 & TA (AT) No. 135/2021 (Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 653/2019 & 803/2019)
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Dr. Ravi Shankar Vedam (Appellant / 38% Shareholder of Corporate Debtor); Tiffins Barytes Asbestos and Paints Limited (Corporate Debtor / Respondent No. 1); K. Vasudevan (Resolution Professional / Respondent No. 2); Embassy Property Developments Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant / SRA / Respondent No. 3); Udhyaman Investments Pvt. Ltd. (Financial Creditor / Respondent No. 1 in TA 135/2021); M. Poobalan and affiliated exporting entities (Respondents No. 4 to 8 in TA 135/2021). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor availed a loan facility of Rs. 11,50,00,000 from Udhyaman Investments Pvt. Ltd. pursuant to an MoU dated 16.04.2016 and a Joint Memorandum of Compromise settling a Section 138 NI Act proceeding before Judicial Magistrate Bellary. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose upon dishonour of Corporate Debtor's cheque dated 03.04.2014 for Rs. 8,82,68,439; Section 7 CIRP triggered on default of principal loan amount of Rs. 11.50 crores with 18% p.a. interest. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application CP/39/IB/2018 admitted on 12.03.2018; 270 days CIRP period expired on 07.03.2019; CoC approved SRA's Resolution Plan on 27.02.2019; NCLT approved the Plan on 12.06.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Registered valuation reports determining Corporate Debtor liquidation value; minutes of the 5th CoC meeting rejecting proposal for forensic audit by 91.90% vote; minutes of the 10th CoC meeting approving SRA plan with 96.45% voting share (VITPL competing bid rejected due to conditional non-renewal lease clauses); NCLT order in MA/573/2018 dated 27.03.2019 ruling Poobalan was an agent and not a related party. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai Bench dismissed Appellant's MA/120/2019 seeking a forensic audit and staying CIRP, and on 12.06.2019 passed order in MA/179/2019 approving the Resolution Plan submitted by Embassy Property Developments Pvt. Ltd.
summary.legal_issues: Whether an individual shareholder of a Corporate Debtor has locus standi under Section 61 of the IBC to challenge the approval of a Resolution Plan sanctioned by the CoC; whether an erstwhile director or shareholder can demand an independent forensic audit after the CoC in its commercial wisdom explicitly voted against it; whether non-reconstitution of the CoC invalidates plan approval where the CoC approved the plan by a decisive majority under alternate voting configurations.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In the creditor-in-control framework of the IBC, equity shareholders of a corporate debtor lack locus standi to challenge a resolution plan approved by the requisite majority of the Committee of Creditors; the corporate entity's representation vests exclusively in the Resolution Professional. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(2) read with the Explanation thereto establishes a statutory deemed approval by shareholders for all implementation steps in an approved resolution plan, rendering shareholder objections legally redundant; shareholders have no statutory seat, participation, or voting rights in the CoC during CIRP, and their economic interests are restricted to the waterfall mechanism under Section 53 in the event of liquidation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Commercial wisdom doctrine as enunciated in K. Sashidhar and Kalparaj Dharamshi; the decisions of the CoC regarding forensic audits, evaluation of risks between competing bids, and commercial feasibility are non-justiciable unless a patent violation of Section 30(2) is established. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CoC approved the resolution plan with 96.45% majority voting share, SRA infused necessary upfront funds, and the appellant shareholder had no legal standing or valid ground under Section 61(3) to overturn the approval.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 653 of 2019 [TA (AT) No. 134/2021] and Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 803 of 2019 [TA (AT) No. 135/2021] are dismissed without costs. All connected pending Interlocutory Applications are closed.
summary.summary: Appellant, a 38% shareholder of Tiffins Barytes Asbestos and Paints Ltd., appealed NCLT Chennai orders dismissing his application for a forensic audit and approving Embassy Property Developments Pvt. Ltd.'s Resolution Plan. Appellant alleged undervaluation, collusion, and related-party vitiation of the CoC. NCLAT dismissed both appeals, ruling that under the creditor-in-control model of the IBC, shareholders lack locus standi to challenge an approved resolution plan. Section 30(2) incorporates deemed shareholder consent, and the CoC's business decisions regarding the refusal of forensic audits and selection of resolution plans are protected under non-justiciable commercial wisdom.

summary.case_title: Nirej Vadakkedathu Paul & Ors. vs. Sunstar Hotels and Estates Private Limited & Anr.
summary.appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins.) No. 142 of 2022 & Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins.) No. 174 of 2022
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Nirej Vadakkedathu Paul and 8 other public shareholders holding ~15% equity (Appellants in Comp. App. 142/2022); Padrone Marketing Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant in Comp. App. 174/2022); Sunstar Hotels and Estates Pvt. Ltd. (Financial Creditor / Assignee / Respondent No. 1); McDowell Holdings Limited (Corporate Debtor / Respondent No. 2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor availed Inter Corporate Deposits (ICDs) from Zuari Fertilisers and Chemicals Limited (merged into Zuari Agro Chemicals Limited / ZACL); Corporate Debtor defaulted on settlement agreement dated 17.06.2019; Respondent No. 1 entered into a tripartite agreement on 19.11.2021 discharging ZACL, paying the outstanding liabilities, and taking assignment of the debt via subrogation, alongside disbursing a separate ICD of Rs. 1.50 crores on 20.10.2021. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default of financial debt amounting to Rs. 16,80,66,348 as of 30.11.2021. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand Notice issued by Financial Creditor on 10.12.2021; Corporate Debtor sought time on 15.12.2021; Section 7 petition CP (IB) No. 11/BB/2022 filed on 05.01.2022 / 06.01.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Tripartite assignment agreement dated 19.11.2021; bank payment receipts dated 20.11.2021 proving discharge of ZACL debt; audited financial results confirming debt and default; RBI deregistration letter dated 11.12.2017 confirming cancellation of Corporate Debtor's NBFC license. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru Bench vide order dated 08.04.2022 admitted Respondent No. 1's Section 7 application, initiated CIRP against McDowell Holdings Ltd., and dismissed shareholder intervention applications I.A. Nos. 86 and 87 of 2022.
summary.legal_issues: Whether equity shareholders have locus standi to intervene in or maintain an appeal against an admission order under Section 7 of the IBC; whether shareholders or third parties can compel a Financial Creditor to accept an out-of-court settlement from them to avoid CIRP; whether the Corporate Debtor qualifies as an NBFC/financial service provider exempt from CIRP under Section 3(17) of the IBC without holding a live RBI registration.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In a Section 7 insolvency proceeding, the lis is strictly between the Financial Creditor and the Corporate Debtor; individual equity shareholders have no locus standi to maintain derivative actions or oppose CIRP admission once financial debt and default are established. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7(5) mandates admission when the adjudicating authority is satisfied that a default has occurred and the application is complete; neither the IBC nor the Companies Act permits third-party shareholders to step in, tender unilateral payment of debt, and thwart statutory insolvency initiation without corporate debtor and creditor consent. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Objective ascertainment of debt and default under Section 7; status as a 'financial service provider' under Section 3(17) requires an active, subsisting registration or legal authorization from the financial sector regulator (RBI), which had been canceled in 2017. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt assignment and subsequent default were indisputable, the Corporate Debtor was not an operating NBFC, and the shareholder appellants lacked locus under Section 61(1), rendering the appeals non-maintainable.
summary.operative_order: Both Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins.) No. 142 of 2022 and Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins.) No. 174 of 2022 are dismissed without costs. Connected pending Interlocutory Applications are closed.
summary.summary: Appellants, equity shareholders holding ~15% of McDowell Holdings Ltd., appealed NCLT Bengaluru's order admitting Sunstar Hotels' Section 7 IBC petition for a default of Rs. 16.80 crores. Appellants contended that the petition was collusive, the CD was an exempt NBFC with assets over Rs. 1000 crores, and shareholders were willing to deposit funds to discharge the debt. NCLAT dismissed both appeals, ruling that third-party shareholders have no locus standi to intervene in Section 7 proceedings or file derivative appeals under Section 61. Debt and default were conclusively established, the CD lacked an active RBI financial services license, and the IBC provides no mechanism for shareholders to forcibly settle creditor debts.

summary.case_title: Satori Global Limited & Anr. vs. Ms. Shailja Krishna & Ors.
summary.appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) No. 379 of 2018 & Company Appeal (AT) No. 395 of 2018
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Satori Global Limited (Appellant No. 1 / Company in CA 379/2018); Ujjwal Agarwal (Appellant No. 2 in CA 379/2018); Mrs. Manjula Jhunjhunwala, mother-in-law (Appellant in CA 395/2018 / Respondent No. 4); Ms. Shailja Krishna (Respondent No. 1 / Original Petitioner); Mr. Ved Krishna, ex-husband (Respondent No. 2); Mr. Nirupam Mishra (Respondent No. 3). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Management and equity transfer dispute in Satori Global Ltd.; original 39,500 shares (out of 40,000 paid-up equity) held by Shailja Krishna transferred to Manjula Jhunjhunwala via an alleged Gift Deed and Share Transfer Form executed on 17.12.2010. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not an IBC default; petitioner alleged illegal dispossession of 39,500 equity shares (worth over 98% of paid-up capital) without consideration and unlawful removal from directorship. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Matrimonial rift and alleged execution of Gift Deed and resignation on 17.12.2010; share transfer approved by board on 10.11.2011 / 18.11.2011; company petition CP No. 107/ND/2013 filed before CLB/NCLT on 20.06.2013. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Notarized Gift Deed dated 17.12.2010; share transfer form with revalidation endorsement by RoC up to 12.11.2011; Form 32 showing resignation as director; three separate police final reports in Crime No. 105/2013 concluding no criminal fraud, threat, or coercion was established against the Jhunjhunwalas. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Allahabad Bench vide order dated 04.09.2018 allowed CP No. 107/ND/2013, setting aside board resolutions dated 15.12.2010 and 17.12.2010, canceling the share transfer of 39,500 shares, and restoring Shailja Krishna as shareholder and Executive Director.
summary.legal_issues: Whether NCLT exercising summary jurisdiction under Sections 397, 398, and 399 of the Companies Act, 1956 has the adjudicatory competence to determine complex questions of fraud, coercion, and cancel a registered Gift Deed; whether a petitioner whose name is not on the Register of Members and who has not instituted a civil suit for cancellation of a Gift Deed satisfies the locus standi requirements of Section 399(1).
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In an oppression and mismanagement petition under company law, the Company Tribunal exercising summary jurisdiction cannot adjudicate complex questions of title, fraud, or coercion regarding the validity of a transfer instrument; challenging and canceling a gift deed falls within the exclusive domain of a civil court under Sections 31 and 34 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Compliance with Section 399(1) of the Companies Act, 1956 is a mandatory jurisdictional prerequisite; the applicant must indisputably be an entered 'member' on the register of members at the time of presenting the petition under Section 397/398; where membership has ceased pursuant to an unchallenged gift deed, the petition is non-maintainable. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Summary jurisdiction boundary test established in Ammonia Supplies and Jai Mahal Hotels; where allegations of forged signatures, coercion, and validity of title documents require elaborate examination of conflicting evidence, the company court must relegate the parties to a civil suit. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The petitioner had not challenged the Gift Deed before a competent civil court and police investigations found no evidence of coercion; consequently, she was not an entered member holding the requisite share capital, and NCLT lacked jurisdiction to declare the transfer null and void.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 379 of 2018 and Company Appeal (AT) No. 395 of 2018 are allowed. The impugned order of NCLT Allahabad Bench dated 04.09.2018 and all consequential reliefs are set aside. No order as to costs.
summary.summary: Appellants challenged the NCLT Allahabad Bench order which allowed Shailja Krishna's company petition under Sections 397/398 of the Companies Act, 1956, declared the transfer of 39,500 shares to her mother-in-law void, and reinstated her as Executive Director. Appellants argued that the transfer occurred via a Gift Deed dated 17.12.2010, the petitioner ceased to be a member, and NCLT lacked jurisdiction to cancel the gift deed. NCLAT allowed the appeals and set aside the NCLT order, holding that under Section 399(1), a complainant must be a registered member. Serious allegations of coercion, fraud, and validity of gift deeds involve complex title disputes that cannot be adjudicated in summary company proceedings and must be resolved by a civil court under the Specific Relief Act.

summary.case_title: Adinath Jewellery Exports vs. Mr. Brijendra Kumar Mishra Liquidator & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Adinath Jewellery Exports (Occupant / Licensee / Appellant); Mr. Brijendra Kumar Mishra, Liquidator of Shrenuj & Co. Ltd. (Liquidator / Respondent No. 1); Rexnord Electronics And Controls Limited (Successful Auction Purchaser / Respondent No. 2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Leave and Licence Agreement dated 03.08.2016 leasing commercial premises at Plot No. A-7, MIDC, Andheri (E), Mumbai (6000 sq. ft.) to Appellant for 3 years at Rs. 2,00,000 monthly licence fee, expressly barring creation of any tenancy or sub-tenancy rights. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not an IBC debt default against the Corporate Debtor; default involved non-payment of licence fees from June 2021 onwards; outstanding licence fees quantified at Rs. 18,83,520 (paid by cheque on 08.02.2022) and illegal overstay following expiry of licence. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 12.03.2019; RP extended licence agreement till 02.07.2020; liquidation order passed on 12.07.2021; property successfully auctioned on 06.04.2022; Letter of Intent issued to R-2 on 13.04.2022; vacation notice issued requiring handover by 22.05.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Leave and Licence Agreement containing explicit non-tenancy clause 23; Appellant's admission letter dated 26.04.2022 confirming occupancy on 'Leave and Licence basis' and requesting time till 31.07.2022 to vacate; R.A.D. Suit No. 259/2022 filed by Appellant before Small Causes Court obtaining an ex-parte status quo order on 28.06.2022 by concealing pending NCLT proceedings. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Liquidator filed I.A. No. 1635/2022 under Section 33(5) and Section 35 of the IBC before NCLT Mumbai seeking eviction and possession; NCLT on 06.07.2022 directed the Liquidator to place lock and seal on the property with police assistance.
summary.legal_issues: Whether an occupant whose Leave and Licence Agreement expired during liquidation becomes a statutory 'tenant' under the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999 or remains an illegal occupant; whether NCLT has exclusive jurisdiction under Section 60(5)(c) and Section 33(5) read with Section 238 of the IBC to direct eviction and take custody of liquidation estate property, prevailing over Small Causes Court proceedings.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An occupant under an expired Leave and Licence Agreement does not acquire tenancy rights by merely paying monthly use-and-occupation charges; the Adjudicating Authority under the IBC possesses overriding jurisdiction under Section 238 to evict unauthorized occupants from the corporate debtor's liquidation assets to effectuate timely liquidation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 35(1)(b), (d), and (n) read with Section 33(5), the liquidator is statutorily mandated to take physical custody and preserve the assets of the corporate debtor; Section 60(5)(c) confers comprehensive jurisdiction on NCLT to dispose of questions of law and fact relating to the liquidation estate; the non-obstante mandate of Section 238 overrides state rent control enactments where the occupant is merely a licensee holding over illegally. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Documentary admission test; when an occupant executes a written leave and licence agreement containing non-tenancy covenants and expressly admits in correspondence that it occupies premises on a leave and licence basis seeking shifting time, it cannot recharacterize itself as a tenant. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Small Causes Court status-quo order obtained by suppressing material liquidation proceedings was non-binding on the insolvency process, and NCLT acted within its lawful jurisdiction in directing the liquidator to lock and seal the property.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 748 of 2022 is dismissed without costs. The impugned order of NCLT Mumbai Bench dated 06.07.2022 directing lock, seal, and police assistance is upheld.
summary.summary: Appellant, an occupant of commercial premises belonging to corporate debtor Shrenuj & Co. Ltd. (in liquidation), challenged NCLT Mumbai's order directing the liquidator to lock and seal the property to hand over vacant possession to the successful e-auction purchaser. Appellant argued that it was a protected tenant under the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999 and that an ex-parte status-quo order from the Small Causes Court barred NCLT from directing eviction. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the appellant was merely an overstaying licensee under an expired leave-and-licence agreement. Under Sections 33(5), 35, 60(5)(c), and 238 of the IBC, NCLT has overriding jurisdiction to secure liquidation estate assets free from state rent control interference.

summary.case_title: Ramesh Shantilal Modi & Anr. vs. Modi Landscape Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
