summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Ramesh Shantilal Modi and Bharat Shantilal Modi (Modi Group / Appellants); Modi Landscape Pvt. Ltd. through Liquidator Anagha Anasingaraju (Respondent No. 1 / Company); Ramesh Nanji Thakkar, Nandubala Mahesh Thakkar, and Rohan Mukesh Thakkar (Thakkar Group / Respondents No. 2, 3, and 5); Chandrakant Shivajirao Ghule (Ghule Group / Respondent No. 4). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Real estate development business and land acquisition, including two Development Agreements dated 16.08.2013 executed with Saakaar Corporation (comprising Respondent No. 4 as a partner) for developing a commercial amenity space and a residential plot at Manjri, Pune. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Saakaar Corporation paid advance deposits of Rs. 10,00,00,000 (Rs. 5 crores for each agreement); Saakaar failed to transfer an amount of Rs. 4,75,17,171 into the designated Escrow Account pursuant to the Consent Terms. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Company Petition No. 29 of 2016 filed under Sections 241 and 242; Consent Terms executed and disposed of by NCLT on 24.08.2017; M.A. No. 291 of 2018, M.A. No. 1046 of 2019 (contempt applications), and M.A. No. 3186 of 2019 (winding-up application) filed; NCLT passed winding-up order on 08.06.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Consent Terms dated 21.08.2017; report of Observer-cum-Facilitator Justice Dilip Karnik (Former Bombay High Court Judge) and Chartered Accountant N.D. Desai stating that settlement efforts failed; financial statements un-audited since 2015-2016; RoC strike-off notice under Section 248(1). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CP No. 29/2016 filed under Sections 241/242 was initially disposed of via consent order on 24.08.2017; due to non-compliance, contempt and winding-up applications were filed; NCLT Mumbai Bench (Court-II) on 08.06.2021 disposed of M.A. Nos. 291/2018, 1046/2019, and 3186/2019 and ordered winding up of Modi Landscape Pvt. Ltd.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT) was legally justified in ordering the winding up of a company under Section 242 read with Section 273 of the Companies Act, 2013 upon the complete breakdown of a consent settlement, lack of statutory compliance, and a management deadlock.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When shareholders are embroiled in prolonged litigation, mutual trust and confidence are completely uprooted, statutory compliance and accounts are neglected for years, and mediation efforts fail to resolve a management deadlock, the Tribunal is legally empowered under Section 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 to order the winding up of the company on just and equitable grounds. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 242 grants wide plenary powers to the Tribunal to make any order it thinks fit, including winding up, with a view to bringing to an end the matters complained of or addressing an irretrievable corporate impasse where alternative remedies are exhausted. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Failure of court-appointed mediation (Observer-cum-Facilitator) coupled with un-audited accounts for over five years, lack of active business operations, and active breach of consent terms establish that the company's substratum is lost and a management deadlock exists. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since all attempts at amicable settlement and revival failed and the parties were deadlocked with unequal shareholding groups unable to function, ordering the winding up of the company was just, equitable, and necessary in the interest of justice.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 92 of 2021 is dismissed without costs. The impugned order dated 08.06.2021 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench (Court-II) winding up Modi Landscape Pvt. Ltd. and appointing Ms. Anagha Anasingaraju as Liquidator is affirmed. The interim order dated 01.10.2021 is vacated.
summary.summary: Appellants (Modi Group) challenged the NCLT Mumbai order directing the winding up of Modi Landscape Pvt. Ltd. and appointing a liquidator, following the failure of a consent decree and a prolonged management deadlock between the Modi, Thakkar, and Ghule shareholder groups. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that where mutual trust is completely destroyed, accounts have not been audited since 2015-2016, and court-mandated mediation via an Observer-cum-Facilitator fails, ordering the winding up of the company on just and equitable grounds under Section 242 is fully justified.

summary.case_title: M/s. RBG Trading Corporation Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. vs. Sulochana Gupta & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: RBG Trading Corporation Pvt. Ltd., RBG Enterprises Pvt. Ltd., RBG Retail Pvt. Ltd., Rajkumar Gupta, and Vishnukant Gupta (Appellants); Sulochana Gupta, Minakshi Gupta, and Mahesh Kumar Gupta (Respondents No. 1 to 3). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Family-owned trading, retail, and enterprise companies engaged in agricultural/non-agricultural commodity imports and exports, involving related-party loans, rental transactions, and salary payments to spouses. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not an IBC default; minority shareholders (Sulochana Gupta and Minakshi Gupta) alleged oppression and mismanagement involving non-convening of AGMs for FY 2015-16, 2016-17, and 2017-18, unauthorized related-party transactions under Section 188, and siphoning of funds. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Company petitions C.P. No. 114, 119, and 125/KOB/2019 filed before NCLT Kochi Bench; NCLT passed common impugned order on 31.12.2021; Review Application 02/KOB/2022 filed and allowed by NCLT on 16.03.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Financial statements for FY 2015-18, missing attendance registers for board/general meetings, auditor reports detailing related-party loans to Sri Rubber Industries and family members, and review order granting sweeping consequential reliefs. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kochi Bench via common order dated 31.12.2021 found that AGMs were not convened properly and related-party transactions were invalid, but did not make specific findings of oppression or impose penalties; subsequently, via review order dated 16.03.2022, NCLT entertained a review application and granted substantive consequential relief (director disqualifications and replacements); Appellants appealed both orders.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the NCLT has the inherent power to review or recall its own final order under Section 420(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 or Rule 154 of NCLT Rules, 2016 to grant substantive consequential reliefs not originally adjudicated; whether related-party transactions and failure to hold AGMs constitute oppression and mismanagement warranting penal or corrective directions.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under the Companies Act, 2013, neither the Tribunal nor the Appellate Tribunal possesses an inherent power of review or recall; Section 420(2) and Rule 154 of NCLT Rules, 2016 are strictly restricted to rectifying clerical or arithmetical mistakes or errors arising from an accidental slip or omission. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: A review application cannot be utilized as an appeal in disguise or a vehicle to introduce substantive consequential reliefs or re-argue matters on merits when the original order contained no specific findings of oppression and mismanagement or penal directions. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict construction of statutory review powers; where an order lacks specific adjudicatory findings on core charges, subsequent modification to introduce severe corporate penalties under the garb of an 'accidental slip' is legally impermissible. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since NCLT exceeded its summary rectification jurisdiction by granting sweeping consequential reliefs through a review application, the review order was set aside and the matter remanded back for fresh adjudication on whether the proven infractions constituted oppression and mismanagement.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) Nos. 18, 19, 20, and 31 of 2022 are disposed of. The review order dated 16.03.2022 is set aside, and the matters are remanded back to the NCLT Kochi Bench to hear and decide afresh on whether the proven acts fall within the ambit of oppression and mismanagement and to pass a reasoned speaking order.
summary.summary: Appellants challenged the NCLT Kochi common order dated 31.12.2021 and subsequent review order dated 16.03.2022 passed in company petitions alleging oppression and mismanagement. NCLT had initially found violations regarding unconvend AGMs and invalid related-party transactions but ordered no penalties or specific reliefs; subsequently, via a review application, NCLT granted sweeping consequential relief including director disqualifications and board reconstitution. NCLAT held that NCLT lacks an inherent power of review under Section 420(2) to grant substantive consequential reliefs not originally adjudicated. Consequently, the review order was set aside and the matter remanded for fresh determination on oppression and mismanagement.

summary.case_title: Mr. P. Eswaramoorthy, Liquidator of M/s. Senthil Papers and Boards Private Limited vs. The Deputy Commissioner of Income Tax (Benami Prohibition)
summary.appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS) No. 188 of 2022 & Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS) No. 189 of 2022
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. P. Eswaramoorthy, Liquidator of M/s. Senthil Papers and Boards Private Limited (Appellant); The Deputy Commissioner of Income Tax (Benami Prohibition) (Respondent)[cite: 22]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor availed term loans and credit facilities through consortium arrangements, creating mortgages over movable and immovable assets in 2009 and 2013[cite: 22]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor underwent CIRP and was ordered into liquidation on 14.02.2019 following rejection of resolution plans[cite: 22]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 14.11.2017; Liquidation ordered on 14.02.2019; Income Tax Department (Benami Prohibition) issued show cause notice and provisional attachment order on 01.11.2019 under the Prohibition of Benami Property Transactions (PBPT) Act, 1988 regarding alleged cash transactions of Rs. 400 crores during demonetization[cite: 22]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Provisional attachment orders dated 01.11.2019 under Section 24(3) of the PBPT Act, 1988; audited balance sheets, income tax returns, and bank statements showing no cash inflows; mortgages created in 2009 and 2013 in favor of secured creditors[cite: 22]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Liquidator filed MA/1372/2019 and MA/1373/2019 under Section 60(5) before NCLT Chennai to set aside the provisional attachments; NCLT Chennai Division Bench-II dismissed the applications via order dated 29.03.2022, holding that NCLT lacked jurisdiction over PBPT Act matters and that proceedings under the PBPT Act did not violate moratorium or IBC provisions; Liquidator appealed[cite: 22].
summary.legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT) under Section 60(5) of the IBC has jurisdiction to entertain an application to set aside a provisional attachment order issued against a corporate debtor's assets under the Prohibition of Benami Property Transactions Act, 1988; whether proceedings under the PBPT Act, 1988 override or conflict with the IBC[cite: 22].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Section 60(5) of the IBC is not an all-pervasive provision conferring jurisdiction on the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT) to determine disputes or set aside attachments falling under the exclusive statutory purview and hierarchy of another specialized statute like the Prohibition of Benami Property Transactions Act, 1988[cite: 22]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The Prohibition of Benami Property Transactions Act, 1988 and the IBC operate in distinct fields; an aggrieved party seeking to challenge a provisional attachment under the PBPT Act must resort to the effective and efficacious appellate hierarchy established under the PBPT Act rather than taking umbrage under Section 60(5) of the IBC[cite: 22]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Jurisdictional competence test; where a specialized public law enactment (PBPT Act) provides its own adjudicatory and appellate mechanism for confiscation and attachment of benami property, NCLT cannot bypass or usurp that jurisdiction[cite: 22]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The provisional attachment orders passed by the tax authorities under the PBPT Act cannot be challenged or set aside under Section 60(5) of the IBC, and the NCLT correctly dismissed the liquidator's applications for lack of maintainability, leaving the liquidator to pursue remedies under the PBPT Act hierarchy[cite: 22].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS.) Nos. 188 and 189 of 2022 are dismissed without costs[cite: 22]. Connected pending interlocutory applications are closed, with liberty granted to the appellant liquidator to approach the appropriate competent forum under the PBPT Act[cite: 22].
summary.summary: Mr. P. Eswaramoorthy, liquidator of M/s. Senthil Papers and Boards Private Limited, appealed NCLT Chennai orders dismissing applications filed under Section 60(5) of the IBC to set aside provisional attachment orders issued on 01.11.2019 by the Deputy Commissioner of Income Tax (Benami Prohibition) under the Prohibition of Benami Property Transactions Act, 1988[cite: 22]. NCLAT dismissed the appeals, holding that Section 60(5) of the IBC does not confer jurisdiction on the NCLT to entertain challenges against attachments made under the PBPT Act[cite: 22]. The PBPT Act operates in its own specialized field with an independent appellate hierarchy, and the liquidator must pursue remedies under that statute[cite: 22].

summary.case_title: Rajeev Gupta vs. Standard Chartered Bank (Singapore) Ltd. & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Rajeev Gupta, Suspended Director of Corporate Debtor RCI Industries & Technologies Ltd. (Appellant); Standard Chartered Bank (Singapore) Ltd., Operational Creditor / Assignee (Respondent No. 1); Brijesh Singh Bhadauriya, Resolution Professional (Respondent No. 2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supplier M/s. Sizer Metals Pte Limited entered into a Receivables Purchase Agreement (RPA) dated 11.07.2017 (executed 01.08.2017) with Standard Chartered Bank Singapore assigning present and future receivables from supply of base metals to the corporate debtor; notice of assignment acknowledged by the corporate debtor on 03.05.2018. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default of USD 2,997,506.93 (equivalent to INR 21,05,65,569.56) based on unpaid invoices. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 8 demand notice issued on 18.05.2019 (unreplied); Section 9 application filed on 15.10.2019; NCLT New Delhi admitted Section 9 application on 25.11.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Receivables Purchase Agreement executed in Singapore; email correspondence acknowledging debt and assignment; invoices issued between September 2018 and January 2019. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 9 application admitted by NCLT on 25.11.2022; corporate debtor raised stamp duty objections via IA No. 1408 of 2022 after final arguments concluded, which NCLT and NCLAT previously dismissed on 21.04.2022 and 05.05.2022 respectively; subsequent Delhi High Court Article 227 petition disposed of; appeal filed against admission order.
summary.legal_issues: Whether an assignment deed executed outside India (Singapore) and brought into India is inadmissible in evidence under Sections 33 and 35 of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899 for want of proper stamping, thereby vitiating a Section 9 IBC application; whether a corporate debtor who failed to raise stamp objections in pleadings and permitted a document to be relied upon can subsequently challenge its admissibility under Section 36 of the Stamp Act.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 36 of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899, once a document has been admitted in evidence and relied upon in proceedings without timely objection raised during pleadings, its admissibility cannot be called into question at a belated stage on the ground that it was not duly stamped. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 36 acts as a 'stand alone' clause prohibiting courts from reopening issues regarding the sufficiency of stamp duty once an instrument has been accepted and acted upon; failure to object to admissibility at the earliest opportunity results in waiver of the objection. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Procedural waiver and estoppel test; parties must object to the admissibility of insufficiently stamped instruments at the appropriate stage in their pleadings; sitting back and raising objections post-arguments constitutes an abuse of process designed to delay resolution. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The corporate debtor admitted the debt and failed to object to the stamping of the Assignment Deed in its reply or additional affidavit; hence, Section 36 barred any subsequent challenge to its admissibility under Section 35, rendering the Section 9 admission order unassailable.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1513 of 2022 is dismissed. No order as to costs.
summary.summary: Appellant, a suspended director of RCI Industries & Technologies Ltd., appealed against the NCLT New Delhi order admitting a Section 9 IBC application filed by Standard Chartered Bank Singapore for a default of over Rs. 21 crores. Appellant contended that the underlying Receivables Purchase Agreement (Assignment Deed) executed in Singapore was unstamped under Section 18 of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899, making it inadmissible under Section 35. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the corporate debtor failed to raise any stamp duty objection in its initial replies or additional affidavits, and under Section 36 of the Stamp Act, a document admitted in evidence cannot be challenged at a belated stage.

summary.case_title: GVR Consulting Services Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. vs. Ms. Pooja Bahry & Ors. (with Dyna Rasayan Udyog Pvt. Ltd. vs. Pooja Bahry & Anr. and Praveen Gupta & Ors. vs. Pooja Bahry)
summary.appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 405 of 2022, 369 of 2022 & 412 of 2022
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: GVR Consulting Services Pvt. Ltd. & GVR Electronics Pvt. Ltd. (Appellants in CA 405/2022 / Unrelated Creditors); Dyna Rasayan Udyog Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant in CA 369/2022 / Unrelated Creditor); Praveen Gupta, Arun Gupta, and Keshika Exports Pvt. Ltd. (Appellants in CA 412/2022 / Managing Directors and Related Party); Ms. Pooja Bahry, Erstwhile Resolution Professional of NTL Electronics India Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 1). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor (NTL Electronics India Ltd.) had availed unsecured loans and commercial transactions from various related and non-related parties; during the lookback period under Section 43(4) of the IBC, the Corporate Debtor repaid antecedent liabilities amounting to Rs. 2,80,99,338 to related parties and Rs. 3,56,29,987 to non-related parties (totaling Rs. 6,37,29,325). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default leading to CIRP admission. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced against Corporate Debtor on 27.08.2019; Resolution Professional appointed on 30.10.2019; Transaction Auditor (Pipara & Co.) appointed on 09.09.2020; Avoidance application (IA No. 5768 of 2020) filed by RP under Section 43 on 24.09.2020; Resolution plan approved by NCLT on 28.01.2021; NCLT allowed avoidance application on 02.03.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Transaction Audit Report detailing repayments of unsecured loans to related parties (Arun Gupta, Praveen Gupta, Keshika Exports) and non-related parties (Dyna Rasayan Udyog, GVR Electronics, GVR Consulting Services) within the lookback period of 1 to 2 years preceding the insolvency commencement date. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench-V vide order dated 02.03.2022 in IA No. 5768 of 2020 allowed the RP's application under Section 43, declared the repayments as preferential transactions, and directed the respondents to refund the respective amounts to be distributed among eligible creditors.
summary.legal_issues: Whether repayments of antecedent unsecured loans made by a corporate debtor to related and unrelated creditors during the lookback period qualify as preferential transactions under Section 43 of the IBC; whether such repayments are exempt as transfers made in the 'ordinary course of business or financial affairs' under Section 43(3)(a); whether a composite avoidance application covering Sections 43, 45, and 66 is maintainable.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 43 of the IBC, if a transfer of property or interest is made for the benefit of a creditor on account of an antecedent debt within the specified lookback period, and has the effect of putting that creditor in a more beneficial position than under Section 53 distribution, a legal fiction of preferential transaction applies automatically, irrespective of the corporate debtor's intent or motive. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The exception under Section 43(3)(a) for transfers made in the 'ordinary course of business or financial affairs' requires a purposive conjunctive reading ('corporate debtor and transferee') as established in Anuj Jain; routine borrowing and repayment of unsecured loans outside the undistinguished common flow of the corporate debtor's commercial operations do not qualify as ordinary course of business. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Statutory deeming fiction test; fulfilment of twin conditions under Section 43(2) during the lookback period specified in Section 43(4) triggers the legal fiction of preference, and pressure or threat of legal action by lenders does not remove the preferential character of the transaction. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The repayments of antecedent unsecured loans made to both related and non-related parties during the lookback period met all statutory criteria for preferential transactions under Section 43, and the Adjudicating Authority correctly directed the refund of those amounts for distribution in accordance with Section 53.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 405, 369, and 412 of 2022 are dismissed[cite: 20]. Appellants are granted a further period of three months from the date of judgment to refund the respective amounts as directed by the Adjudicating Authority[cite: 20].
summary.summary: Appellants, comprising related and unrelated creditors, appealed against the NCLT New Delhi order holding that repayments of unsecured loans made by corporate debtor NTL Electronics India Ltd. during the lookback period constituted preferential transactions under Section 43 of the IBC. Appellants argued that the payments were made under lender pressure, in the ordinary course of business, and that a composite avoidance application was invalid. NCLAT dismissed the appeals, holding that Section 43 relies on a statutory deeming fiction where intent and motive are irrelevant, loan repayments do not qualify as ordinary course of business under the Anuj Jain standard, and composite avoidance applications are permissible as long as separate pleadings are maintained.

summary.case_title: Vinod Kothari vs. Vikas Gupta
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant was Vinod Kothari (Promoter/Shareholder and Member of the Suspended Board of Directors of M/s. Kamachi Industries Limited), and the Respondent was Vikas Gupta (Resolution Professional of M/s. Kamachi Industries Limited). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Corporate Debtor was primarily engaged in manufacturing sponge iron, billets, PMT Bars, and generating power at Gummidipoondi, Tamil Nadu, having sought term loans and facilities from banks to the tune of Rs. 1,489,54,11,615. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default occurred when the account of the Corporate Debtor was declared as a Non-Performing Asset (NPA) on 02.01.2013. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: State Bank of India filed a Section 7 application under the IBC, which was admitted on 19.02.2020 initiating Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP), followed by Company Appeal (AT) (INS.) No. 328 of 2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Committee of Creditors (CoC) unanimously rejected two resolution plans on the ground of value and resolved to liquidate the Corporate Debtor under Section 33 of the IBC. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed an Intervening Application (Ivn.P(IBC)/1(CHE)/2022) in IA(IBC)/1213/CHE/2021 seeking to intervene in the liquidation proceedings, which the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT, Division Bench I, Chennai) dismissed via order dated 09.12.2022.
summary.legal_issues: Whether a promoter/shareholder and member of the suspended board of directors has the locus standi as an 'aggrieved person' under Section 61 of the IBC to challenge a liquidation order or intervene in liquidation proceedings when the CoC has unanimously resolved to liquidate the Corporate Debtor in its commercial wisdom.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The decision of the Committee of Creditors to liquidate a corporate debtor, taken in its commercial wisdom, cannot be called into question by the Adjudicating Authority or appellate forums, and promoters ineligible under Section 29A cannot bypass statutory bars to propose schemes under Section 230 of the Companies Act during liquidation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61 of the IBC restricts appeals to 'persons aggrieved'; erstwhile promoters and shareholders holding equity who are excluded from the CoC do not qualify as aggrieved persons in strict sense to challenge liquidation decisions backed by the CoC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The commercial wisdom of the CoC regarding the viability and feasibility of resolution plans and the necessity of liquidation must be respected, and judicial intervention by tribunals should be kept to a bare minimum. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the CoC unanimously passed a resolution for liquidation under Section 33 of the IBC, the Adjudicating Authority was left with no other option than to order liquidation, making the appellant's intervention application non-maintainable.
summary.operative_order: The appeal (Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS.) No. 442 of 2022) is dismissed with no orders as to costs, and the interim stay application (IA No. 1117 of 2022) is closed.
summary.summary: The Appellant, a suspended director and shareholder of M/s. Kamachi Industries Limited (Corporate Debtor), challenged an order dated December 9, 2022, passed by the NCLT Chennai Bench, which dismissed his intervention application and ordered the liquidation of the Corporate Debtor. The Committee of Creditors (CoC) had unanimously rejected all resolution plans and resolved to liquidate the company. The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) held that the CoC's commercial wisdom regarding liquidation is supreme and cannot be arbitrarily challenged by promoters who are ineligible under Section 29A of the IBC. Furthermore, the Appellant lacked status as an aggrieved person under Section 61 of the IBC to obstruct the liquidation process. Consequently, the appeal was dismissed.

summary.case_title: Hotel City Plaza Private Limited vs. Union of India
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants were Hotel City Plaza Private Limited (Transferor Company) and Trivandrum Apollo Towers Pvt. Ltd. (Transferee Company), and the Respondent was the Union of India through the Regional Director, Southern Region, Ministry of Corporate Affairs. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The appellant companies proposed a Scheme of Amalgamation under Sections 391-394 of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to Sections 230-232 of the Companies Act, 2013) to merge the transferor company into the transferee company to run hotel businesses. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The transferor company retained unsecured loans/deposits exceeding Rs. 14 crores compared to a share capital of around Rs. 2.5 crores, including specific non-repaid amounts taken from directors and shareholders without complying with deposit rules. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Original company petitions (CP Nos. 36 and 38 of 2016) were filed before the Kerala High Court, transferred to NCLT Chennai Bench as TP(HC)/112 & 113(Kerala)/2019, and later reassigned to NCLT Kochi Bench as TCAA 4 & 5/KOB/2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Registrar of Companies (ROC) and Regional Director reported severe statutory violations, including illegal acceptance and retention of deposits under Sections 73 and 74 of the Companies Act, 2013, non-disclosure in financial statements, manipulation of member counts to evade restrictions, and misleading disclosures in balance sheets. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Kochi Bench dismissed the applications for sanctioning the Scheme of Amalgamation via order dated 05.02.2021 due to blatant statutory non-compliances and violations.
summary.legal_issues: Whether a Scheme of Amalgamation under the Companies Act can be sanctioned by the Tribunal when the applicant companies have committed gross statutory violations, illegal acceptance of deposits, and material misstatements in financial records.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A Tribunal will decline to sanction a scheme of compromise or amalgamation if it involves blatant statutory violations, tax evasion, fraudulent non-disclosures, or non-compliance with provisions governing public/shareholder deposits. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 230 and 232 of the Companies Act, 2013 require the Tribunal to ensure that a proposed arrangement is lawful, fair, and not contrary to public policy or designed to circumvent statutory mandates like deposit regulations. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where official reports from the Registrar of Companies and Regional Director establish material misstatements, illegal deposit retention under Section 73/74, and falsification of accounts, the scheme lacks bona fides and cannot be rubber-stamped. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the appellant companies failed to controvert widespread statutory breaches and maintained misleading disclosures in their balance sheets, the NCLT correctly exercised its supervisory jurisdiction to reject the scheme.
summary.operative_order: The appeal (Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 28 of 2021) is dismissed with no order as to costs.
summary.summary: The Appellants, Hotel City Plaza Private Limited and Trivandrum Apollo Towers Pvt. Ltd., filed an appeal against the order of the NCLT Kochi Bench dated February 5, 2021, which dismissed their petitions for sanctioning a Scheme of Amalgamation. The Regional Director and Registrar of Companies strongly objected to the scheme, citing severe violations of Sections 73 and 74 of the Companies Act, 2013, regarding unauthorized deposit collections from directors and shareholders, failure to repay, and material misstatements/misleading disclosures in financial statements. The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) affirmed the NCLT's order, ruling that the Tribunal is not a rubber stamp and must reject schemes tainted by illegality, fraud, and non-compliance with statutory mandates. The appeal was consequently dismissed.

summary.case_title: Galaxy Enterprise vs. Indiraben W/O Shri Vinodrai Kansagara
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant was Galaxy Enterprise (a partnership firm and purchaser of the land), Respondent No. 1 was Indiraben W/O Shri Vinodrai Kansagara (shareholder of the vendor company), and Respondent No. 2 was Galaxy Cinema Private Limited (the Corporate Vendor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Respondent No. 2 sold a piece of land (former site of Galaxy Cinema, Jamnagar measuring 5701.18 sq. mtr.) to the Appellant via a registered sale deed dated 13.07.2020 for a total consideration of Rs. 6 crores. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (dispute pertains to a corporate oppression and mismanagement petition regarding asset disposal rather than a financial default). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The land sale deed was executed on 13.07.2020 with a rectification deed on 02.02.2021; Respondent No. 1 filed Company Petition No. CP/1/(AHM)/2023 under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 in January 2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Following the purchase, the Appellant constructed a 3-storeyed commercial complex named 'Star Galaxy' comprising 302 units (investing over Rs. 16.62 crores, creating third-party rights for 61 transferred units, and securing bank mortgages), which was established prior to the filing of the NCLT petition. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Ahmedabad Bench, via interim order dated 06.03.2023 in CP/1/(AHM)/2023, directed respondents to maintain status quo on the remaining 227 units and prohibited further construction beyond 302 units, prompting the aggrieved purchaser to file the present appeal.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the NCLT was justified in granting an interim status quo order restraining a third-party bona fide purchaser from creating further third-party rights or completing construction on a property acquired years prior, pending the final adjudication of a petition under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An interim injunction or status quo order affecting a third party who acquired property in good faith should not be granted when the balance of convenience heavily favors the third party and the project is already substantially completed. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: While Sections 241 and 242 empower the Tribunal to regulate company affairs and set aside transactions under specific conditions, interim relief must be just and equitable and cannot disproportionately harm innocent third parties who are unconnected to internal management disputes. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where records demonstrate that land was purchased via a registered sale deed, construction was completed, and third-party rights were established long before the petition was filed without concrete proof of a sham transaction, interim restraint is unwarranted. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT committed an error in granting an interim status quo order against the appellant purchaser, as it caused irreparable loss to the appellant and unrepresented third-party unit buyers; hence, the interim order must be set aside.
summary.operative_order: The appeal is allowed, and the interim status quo order dated 06.03.2023 passed by the NCLT, Ahmedabad Bench in CP/1/(AHM)/2023 is set aside, with no order as to costs.
summary.summary: The Appellant, Galaxy Enterprise, purchased a vacant plot of land from Galaxy Cinema Private Limited via a registered sale deed in July 2020 and subsequently constructed a commercial complex comprising 302 units. In January 2023, a shareholder (Respondent No. 1) filed a petition under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act alleging oppression and mismanagement, leading the NCLT to issue an interim status quo order restricting further transfers and construction. The NCLAT allowed the appeal and set aside the interim order, holding that the balance of convenience favored the bona fide purchaser and third-party unit holders who had completed construction and invested heavily long before the petition was filed.

summary.case_title: T.V. Sandeep Kumar Reddy vs. State Bank of India
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant was T.V. Sandeep Kumar Reddy (Suspended Director of M/s. Gayatri Projects Limited / Corporate Debtor), Respondent No. 1 was State Bank of India (Financial Creditor), and Respondent No. 2 was M/s. Gayatri Projects Limited through its Interim Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: State Bank of India along with a consortium of lenders sanctioned various term loans, short-term loans, equipment loans, demand loans, ECB loans, and working capital facilities (fund-based and non-fund-based) to the Corporate Debtor, which were later restructured under a Master Restructuring Agreement dated 23.01.2015. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The aggregate amount of default claimed by the financial creditor as on 30.09.2022 was Rs. 242,33,00,269/-, with the account classified as a Non-Performing Asset (NPA) on 30.04.2022. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Section 7 application was filed on 17.10.2022, registered on 18.10.2022, notice was ordered on 21.10.2022, the corporate debtor was set ex-parte on 04.11.2022, matters were reserved on 10.11.2022, and the petition was admitted on 15.11.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The corporate debtor explicitly acknowledged the debt and default through a balance confirmation letter dated 10.05.2021 as on 31.03.2021, a reply under Section 13(3-A) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002 dated 08.10.2022, and its Annual Report for 2021-2022. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT, Hyderabad Bench II) admitted CP(IB) No. 308/7/HDB/2022 on 15.11.2022, while subsequent applications filed by the corporate debtor to set aside the ex-parte order (IA Nos. 1338 & 1339 of 2022) were not taken up prior to the final order, leading to the present appeal.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority committed a procedural illegality or violated principles of natural justice by proceeding ex-parte and admitting the Section 7 application without affording a prolonged opportunity to file a counter, and whether overwhelming evidence of debt and default justified the admission.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a financial debt and default are established through overwhelming documentary evidence such as balance confirmations and statutory reports, and proper service of notice is effected, the Adjudicating Authority is duty-bound to admit a Section 7 application under the IBC without entertaining hyper-technical procedural objections. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Procedural rules under the NCLT Rules or practice directions must be evaluated on the touchstone of prejudice; where statutory notice requirements under IBC rules are fulfilled and service is successfully delivered via email and speed post, an ex-parte order passed due to non-appearance is legally sustainable. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Facts admitted in writing, including balance confirmation letters and annual reports, do not require separate formal proof under Section 58 of the Indian Evidence Act, conclusively establishing the existence of a default. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the corporate debtor failed to displace the clear evidence of debt and default and was given sufficient notice of the proceedings, the admission of the Section 7 application by the Adjudicating Authority warranted no appellate interference.
summary.operative_order: The appeal (Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS.) No. 414 of 2022) is dismissed with no orders as to costs, and connected interlocutory applications (IA Nos. 1009, 1010, and 1011 of 2022) are closed.
summary.summary: The Appellant, a suspended director of M/s. Gayatri Projects Limited (Corporate Debtor), challenged an order dated November 15, 2022, passed by the NCLT Hyderabad Bench, which admitted a Section 7 application filed by the State Bank of India and initiated the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP). The Appellant argued that the Adjudicating Authority acted with undue haste, set the company ex-parte prematurely, and violated natural justice. The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) dismissed the appeal, holding that notices were duly served through email and speed post, and that the corporate debtor had unequivocally admitted its debt and default across multiple documents, including balance confirmations and annual reports. Consequently, the admission order was affirmed.

summary.case_title: Yash Vardhan Mall vs. Indrapuri Studios Pvt. Ltd.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant was Yash Vardhan Mall (shareholder/guardian), Respondent No. 1 was Indrapuri Studios Pvt. Ltd. (film studio company), and Respondents No. 2 to 7 included directors and managing directors such as Tejash Doshi and Dhirendra Kumar Doshi. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Appellant claimed shareholding ownership of 8050 shares (comprising 3890 shares held via minor nominee guardianship and 4160 shares transferred by R-2), constituting 61.92% of the total share capital in R-1 Company. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (dispute involves corporate oppression, mismanagement, and reduction of shareholding to 0%). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CP No. 189/KB/2015 was filed before NCLT, Kolkata; R-1 to R-4 and R-7 filed a demurrer application (CA No. 1755 of 2015) challenging maintainability, which was allowed via the impugned order dated 17.09.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: R-2 unilaterally cancelled the transfer of 4160 shares and refunded Rs. 4,16,000/- via RTGS on 17.09.2015 without stating reasons, and disputed a nomination deed of 3890 shares by producing a subsequent nomination deed dated 15.01.2013. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata dismissed CP No. 189/KB/2015 via the impugned order on 17.09.2019 after concluding that the appellant lacked maintainability under Section 244 due to non-ownership of shares, prompting the current appeal.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the issue of maintainability of a petition under Sections 241-242 of the Companies Act, 2013 can be decided as a preliminary threshold issue when the alleged reduction and cancellation of shareholding itself forms the core subject matter of oppression and mismanagement.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where a petitioner alleges that their shareholding has been illegally brought down below the statutory threshold requirement of 10% through acts of oppression and mismanagement, the question of maintainability and the merits of the case form a mixed question of fact and law that must be decided together at the time of final hearing, rather than at the threshold. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 59 of the Companies Act, 2013 provides that a company's register of members serves as prima facie evidence of ownership, and a company cannot unilaterally delete or cancel a valid share transfer without showing sufficient cause or following principles of natural justice. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Summary dismissal of a company petition at the preliminary stage is erroneous when the cancellation of shares lacks transparent reasons or documented statutory justification, and when multiple allegations of mismanagement are raised. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT committed an error by deciding the demurrer application separately and dismissing the main company petition without rigorous examination on merits; hence, the impugned order must be set aside and the matter remanded for a comprehensive trial.
summary.operative_order: The appeal is allowed, the impugned order dated 17.09.2019 passed in CA No. 1755 of 2015 is set aside, the cancellation of 4160 shares is held null and void, and CP No. 189/KB/2015 is remanded back to the NCLT for fresh adjudication on merits with all contentions open, with no order as to costs.
summary.summary: The Appellant, Yash Vardhan Mall, appealed against the NCLT Kolkata Bench order which dismissed his company petition (CP No. 189/KB/2015) alleging oppression and mismanagement, based on a preliminary demurrer application questioning his shareholding maintainability. The NCLAT held that issues of maintainability linked to the alleged illegal cancellation of shares cannot be decided at the threshold as a preliminary issue. The Appellate Tribunal set aside the impugned order, ruled that the unilateral cancellation of 4160 shares was void without sufficient cause, and remanded the matter back to the NCLT for a fresh trial on its merits.

summary.case_title: Assistant Commissioner of Commercial Taxes vs Mr. Alok Kailash Saksena
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant was the Assistant Commissioner of Commercial Taxes, LGSTO-150, Bengaluru. The Corporate Debtor was Associate Décor Limited, represented in the appeal by Resolution Professional Mr. Alok Kailash Saksena. Punjab National Bank, Union Bank of India, Bank of Baroda, Mohammed Enterprises (Tanzania) Ltd. and Svamitva Landmarks were other respondents. The Appellant was a statutory tax authority and not a Financial or Operational Creditor in the conventional IBC sense. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Corporate Debtor was engaged in manufacture and sale of products of wood, cork, straw and plating materials and effected taxable supplies in Karnataka, giving rise to statutory GST/KVAT tax liabilities. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant claimed Rs.54,46,13,819/- towards GST liability after adjustment of receipts; the PDF does not state a specific date of default for this tax claim. The claim was based on estimates/Best Judgment Assessment orders. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Appellant filed its Form-F claim on 21.12.2018. The Information Memorandum was prepared on 17.10.2019. The Karnataka High Court subsequently set aside the assessment orders on 02.07.2021 and directed processing of the Corporate Debtor's returns. IA No.134/2020 had earlier been dismissed with a direction to submit only an ascertained/crystallised demand. IA No.393/2022 was subsequently filed under Section 60(5) read with Rule 11. No Section 8 demand notice was applicable because this was a statutory tax claim rather than a Section 8 operational-creditor proceeding. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The claim relied upon Best Judgment Assessment orders, Form-F claim documents, the Information Memorandum, tax returns and statutory tax provisions. The High Court had set aside the assessment orders for September 2017 to December 2018, and the Tribunal found that no regular assessment had thereafter crystallised the disputed demand. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CP(IB) No.51/BB/2018 was the underlying CIRP proceeding; its filing date is not stated in the PDF. IA No.134/2020 seeking admission of the tax claim was dismissed, with directions concerning only an ascertained crystallised demand. IA No.393/2022 challenged the treatment of the claim and the resolution process. NCLT Bengaluru dismissed the application, and the Appellant filed the present Section 61 appeal. NCLAT dismissed the appeal on 27.09.2023.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the Appellant's disputed statutory GST/KVAT demand of Rs.54,46,13,819/- could be treated as a secured/first-charge claim in the CIRP; whether the Supreme Court's decision in State Tax Officer v. Rainbow Papers Ltd. applied; whether the Resolution Professional could reject the claim based on unascertained Best Judgment Assessment orders; whether the Appellant was barred by res judicata and estoppel from re-agitating the same claim; and whether the Information Memorandum and resolution process were legally defective because the disputed claim was not included in full.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A statutory tax claim must be ascertained and legally enforceable before it can be required to be considered as a crystallised claim in an insolvency resolution process. Statutory provisions creating a charge must be read together with their express exceptions and the overriding framework of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 82 of the KGST Act and CGST Act and Section 20 of the IGST Act contain provisions affecting the alleged first charge but also operate with specific exceptions relating to the IBC. The Tribunal held that the Rainbow Papers ruling could not be extended to the present statutory framework and facts. Section 238 IBC gives the Code overriding effect where applicable. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The tax demand had to be an ascertained and crystallised demand supported by a valid assessment. A demand founded on Best Judgment Assessment orders that had been set aside by the High Court, without a subsequent regular assessment, was not sufficiently crystallised. The same claim could not be repeatedly re-agitated after an earlier determination. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellant's Rs.54,46,13,819/- demand was not an ascertained crystallised demand and could not be treated as a first-charge secured claim overriding the IBC. Rainbow Papers did not assist the Appellant, the res judicata/estoppel findings were sustained, and the appeal therefore failed.
summary.operative_order: The Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No.302/2023 was dismissed. No costs were awarded. Connected pending IA No.968/2023 was closed.
summary.summary: The Assistant Commissioner of Commercial Taxes challenged the NCLT Bengaluru decision concerning a Rs.54.46 crore GST claim against Associate Décor Limited during CIRP. The tax authority argued that its statutory dues carried a first charge and that the Supreme Court's Rainbow Papers ruling protected the claim. The Tribunal noted that the claim was founded on Best Judgment Assessment orders, while the Karnataka High Court had set those assessment orders aside and directed processing of the Corporate Debtor's returns. A previous NCLT proceeding had also directed the department to place only an ascertained and crystallised demand before the Resolution Professional. NCLAT held that the disputed demand remained uncrystallised, Rainbow Papers was distinguishable, and res judicata/estoppel applied. The appeal was dismissed without costs and the connected IA was closed.

summary.case_title: D. Srinivasa Rao vs Stressed Assets Stabilisation Fund
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: D. Srinivasa Rao was the promoter and suspended Vice Chairman and Director of M/s. Priyaranjani Fibres Limited and the Appellant. Stressed Assets Stabilisation Fund was the Financial Creditor and Respondent No.1. M/s. PriyaranjaniFiber Limited was the Corporate Debtor in insolvency resolution and was represented by its Interim Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The dispute arose from financial debt owed by the Corporate Debtor to the Financial Creditor, involving recovery proceedings originally pursued before the DRT and a Debt Recovery Certificate. The record also contains repeated One Time Settlement proposals and part-payments by the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Tribunal recorded that the Corporate Debtor committed default on 01.04.1997. A revised date of default before BIFR was stated as 01.03.2000. A Debt Recovery Certificate was issued by the DRT on 19.11.2009. The PDF does not state the total principal-plus-interest default amount. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: OA No.222/2000 was filed on 01.02.2000. The Corporate Debtor approached BIFR on 13.09.2001. BIFR appointed IDBI as Operating Agency on 17.09.2002 and declared the company sick on 27.12.2004. A Section 13(2) SARFAESI notice was issued on 29.08.2006. The DRT issued the Recovery Certificate on 19.11.2009. A demand letter was sent on 30.06.2010. BIFR dismissed the application on 22.11.2011 and AIFR granted stay on 21.02.2012. SICA was repealed on 01.12.2016. The Section 7 application was filed on 19.08.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Key evidence included the DRT Recovery Certificate, OTS letters and part-payments. The Corporate Debtor made OTS-related payments including Rs.19,00,000/- on 17.12.2008, Rs.20,00,000/- as a down payment, Rs.76,00,000/- towards part payment, Rs.37,50,000/- on 16.02.2010, and later part payments of Rs.10 lakh amounts in April 2013 and Rs.20 lakh in 2017. OTS proposals included a promise to pay Rs.9,00,00,000/- in 2019. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Financial Creditor filed the Section 7 application on 19.08.2019. NCLT Hyderabad Bench-I admitted the application by order dated 24.03.2023, holding it within limitation. The suspended Director challenged the admission before NCLAT, primarily arguing that the application was barred by limitation because the original default occurred in 1997. NCLAT held the limitation period was affected by the SICA statutory bar and subsequent acknowledgements of debt, and dismissed the appeal.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the Section 7 IBC application filed on 19.08.2019 was barred by limitation; whether the period during which the Financial Creditor's enforcement rights were suspended under Section 22(1) SICA could be excluded; whether the 19.11.2009 Debt Recovery Certificate gave rise to a fresh cause of action; and whether OTS proposals, promises to pay and part-payments constituted acknowledgements of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where enforcement of a financial creditor's right is legally suspended by Section 22(1) SICA, the period of suspension is excluded while computing limitation under Section 22(5) SICA. A Recovery Certificate can give rise to a fresh cause of action for Section 7 IBC proceedings, and written acknowledgements of subsisting liability made within the applicable limitation period can restart limitation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 22(1) SICA created a statutory bar against recovery proceedings while the relevant BIFR/AIFR proceedings were pending. Section 22(5) excluded the period of suspension. The Tribunal held that February 2017 was the relevant fresh cause-of-action point because enforcement of the 19.11.2009 Recovery Certificate remained suspended until the SICA proceedings abated after repeal. Section 18 of the Limitation Act applied to written acknowledgements of debt, while a Recovery Certificate itself could generate a fresh right to initiate Section 7 proceedings. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal examined the OTS correspondence, promises to pay and actual part-payments to determine whether they established a jural relationship and acknowledgement of subsisting debt. An OTS proposal containing a promise to pay and followed by part-payment was treated as positive evidence of acknowledgement. The Tribunal also recognised that an acknowledgement need not be accompanied by an unconditional promise to pay. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The period during which the Financial Creditor was legally prevented from enforcing the Recovery Certificate had to be excluded, the Recovery Certificate provided a fresh cause of action, and the Corporate Debtor's OTS correspondence and payments evidenced continuing acknowledgement of debt. Therefore, the Section 7 application was within limitation and the NCLT's admission order was upheld by dismissal of the appeal.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins.) No.159/2023 was dismissed. There was no order as to costs. All connected pending Interlocutory Applications were closed.
summary.summary: D. Srinivasa Rao, promoter and suspended director of Priyaranjani Fibres Limited, challenged NCLT Hyderabad's admission of a Section 7 IBC application filed by Stressed Assets Stabilisation Fund. The principal issue was limitation because the original default was recorded as 01 April 1997. The Corporate Debtor had undergone BIFR/AIFR proceedings, during which enforcement rights were statutorily suspended. A DRT Recovery Certificate was issued on 19 November 2009, followed by repeated OTS proposals, acknowledgements and part-payments. NCLAT held that the statutory suspension period under SICA had to be excluded and that the Recovery Certificate created a fresh cause of action. It further found continuing acknowledgements of debt through OTS communications and payments. The Section 7 application was therefore within limitation. The appeal was dismissed without costs.

summary.case_title: Vijaya Hospitality and Resorts Limited & Anr vs Tony P.A & Ors
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Vijaya Hospitality and Resorts Limited was Appellant No.1 and its Chairman and Managing Director Mr. K.C. Baboo @ K.C. Babu was Appellant No.2. Tony P.A., Sijo Tony, Manju Sudhesh and Sudhesh Thankappan were Respondents 1-4 and minority shareholders. The Registrar of Companies was Respondent No.5. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: In 2016, Appellant No.2 and Mr. C.K. Sibi sought permission to infuse funds into the company as share capital to repay Federal Bank dues and save the company's assets, including The Elephant Court Hotel, from enforcement proceedings. NCLT permitted infusion of funds and directed preferential private-placement allotment of shares. Mr. K.C. Baboo subsequently infused Rs.11,00,00,000/- and the company allotted shares at Rs.10 face value per share. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The underlying financial distress concerned Federal Bank dues, but the PDF does not provide the exact principal-plus-interest default amount or a specific default date. The relevant investment was Rs.11,00,00,000/- infused as share capital. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT passed its interim order on 12.01.2017 permitting infusion and preferential private-placement allotment. The order became part of the final order dated 18.04.2017. A General Meeting was held on 15.06.2017 to increase authorised share capital. The Board resolved on 11.07.2017 to allot shares at face value without valuation. The original company petition CP/122/KOB/2019 was filed under Sections 59 and 62; the filing date is not expressly stated in the PDF. NCLT passed the impugned order on 10.03.2021 cancelling the allotment. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The NCLT orders of 12.01.2017 and 18.04.2017 directed preferential private-placement allotment. The Appellants relied on the Attendance Register of the 15.06.2017 General Meeting, but the Tribunal found that it only evidenced consent to increase authorised share capital, not consent to allot shares at face value. The 11.07.2017 Board decision allotted the shares at Rs.10 each without a registered valuation report. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Earlier shareholder disputes were addressed through TCP No.185/2016 and CA No.1/2016. The NCLT permitted fund infusion and preferential allotment, and its directions were affirmed by NCLAT in Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No.168/2017 and by dismissal of Supreme Court Civil Appeal No.4482/2019 on 06.05.2019. Minority shareholders thereafter pursued CP/122/KOB/2019 under Sections 59 and 62. NCLT cancelled the allotment on 10.03.2021. The Appellants challenged that order under Section 421, and NCLAT dismissed the appeal on 15.09.2023.
summary.legal_issues: Whether shares allotted on preferential basis through private placement pursuant to an NCLT order under Sections 241-242 of the Companies Act, 2013 still had to comply with Section 62(1)(c) and the applicable rules requiring valuation by a registered valuer; whether the allotment could be challenged through Section 59 rectification proceedings; and whether the earlier NCLT, NCLAT and Supreme Court orders made the allotment and its procedure immune from further challenge.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An NCLT direction to allot shares under Sections 241-242 does not by itself dispense with mandatory statutory requirements governing the manner of allotment. Preferential allotments must comply with Section 62(1)(c) and applicable rules unless the relevant statutory requirements have specifically been dispensed with. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 62(1)(c) requires shares issued to persons through the relevant preferential route to have their price determined through a valuation report of a registered valuer. Rule 13(g) similarly requires valuation for preferential issues. Section 59 permits rectification of the Register of Members where shares have been entered without sufficient cause. Rule 11 inherent powers cannot be used contrary to mandatory statutory provisions. The earlier orders attained finality as to the allotment itself, but not as to the procedure for making that allotment. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal required documentary proof of compliance with the statutory valuation procedure. The Attendance Register only established consent to increase authorised share capital and did not prove consent to allot shares at face value. No valuation report existed, and the shares were allotted at Rs.10 each. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The allotment pursuant to the earlier NCLT directions remained subject to mandatory Section 62(1)(c) and Rules 13(g)/12(7) requirements. Since the shares were allotted at face value without valuation, the dispute fell within Section 59 rectification jurisdiction and the Appellants' contention that statutory procedures could be ignored was rejected. The appeal was dismissed.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No.18/2021 was dismissed as devoid of merit. There was no order as to costs. All connected pending Interlocutory Applications were closed.
summary.summary: Vijaya Hospitality and Resorts Limited and its Managing Director K.C. Baboo challenged an NCLT order cancelling 1.10 crore equity shares allotted to Baboo. Earlier NCLT orders had permitted fund infusion as share capital to repay Federal Bank dues and directed preferential private-placement allotment. Baboo infused Rs.11 crore, and shares were allotted at face value of Rs.10 each without a registered valuation. The appellants argued that the earlier NCLT directions had attained finality and therefore statutory allotment procedures did not apply. NCLAT rejected this argument. It held that Section 62(1)(c) and the applicable rules remained mandatory, and Section 59 permitted rectification of the Register of Members. The earlier orders were final regarding the allotment, not the procedure. The appeal was dismissed without costs.

summary.case_title: Mist Avenue Private Limited vs Nitin Batra & Ors
summary.appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 127 of 2023; Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1478 of 2022; Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1506 of 2022
summary.material_facts: PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. Nitin Batra and other allottees were the Financial Creditors/applicants under Section 7. The Corporate Debtors were Anand Infoedge Pvt. Ltd., Mist Avenue Private Limited and Mist Direct Sales Private Limited. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Anand Infoedge obtained land at Sector 143 Noida and entered collaboration arrangements for development of the Festival City real estate project. Mist Avenue developed the project and allotted units to allottees under Builder Buyer Agreements; a later collaboration arrangement involved Mist Direct Sales Pvt. Ltd. DEFAULT METRICS: The judgment records the claimed date of default as 16.10.2016 and explains that the Section 7 threshold was satisfied because there was a default of at least Rs.1 crore; the exact aggregate default amount of all 115 applicants is not specified in the judgment. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Section 7 application was filed on 11.10.2021. No Section 8 demand notice was involved because this was a Section 7 financial-creditor application. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Builder Buyer Agreements, collaboration agreements, allotment records, the cancellation of the first collaboration agreement on 27.07.2017, the second collaboration arrangement, and the communication by Mist Direct taking over sold inventories were considered. UPRERA cancelled the project registration on 07.12.2019. The Tribunal also considered the claims of 115 allottees and held that 103 valid allottees fulfilled the statutory threshold. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT New Delhi Bench-VI passed an order dated 21.10.2022 holding the joint Section 7 application maintainable and listing it for further hearing. The three Corporate Debtors appealed. NCLAT held that the joint application was maintainable and that the statutory threshold was satisfied.
summary.legal_issues: Whether a joint Section 7 application could be maintained against three closely connected Corporate Debtors involved in the same real estate project; whether the second proviso to Section 7(1) required every applicant to individually satisfy the Rs.1 crore threshold and limitation requirements; and whether claims of some allottees being time-barred or settled invalidated the statutory threshold.
summary.ratio_decidendi: ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In a real estate insolvency application filed jointly by allottees, the statutory threshold under the second proviso to Section 7(1) does not require every individual applicant to have a separate default of Rs.1 crore or an individually timely claim where the required default threshold is otherwise established. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7(1) second proviso was interpreted in light of Manish Kumar so that a qualifying default of Rs.1 crore by some applicants can satisfy the threshold; claims of other applicants being time-barred do not automatically defeat the application. A continuing obligation concerning possession/delay compensation can also affect limitation. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal examined the Builder Buyer Agreements, collaboration arrangements, project structure and individual claims to determine whether the statutory threshold was met. It found 103 valid allottees and a qualifying default. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 7 application was maintainable and the objections based on misjoinder, limitation of some claims and insufficient threshold were rejected.
summary.operative_order: All three appeals challenging the NCLT order dated 21.10.2022 were dismissed. The NCLT finding that the Section 7 application filed by the allottees was maintainable was upheld.
summary.summary: Nitin Batra and other allottees of the Festival City real estate project filed a joint Section 7 application against Anand Infoedge, Mist Avenue and Mist Direct Sales. The project had been developed through collaboration arrangements and units had been allotted to buyers under Builder Buyer Agreements, but the project remained incomplete and UPRERA cancelled its registration in 2019. The Corporate Debtors challenged the insolvency application mainly on grounds of misjoinder, limitation and failure to satisfy the 100-allottee threshold. NCLAT held that the three companies were closely connected to the same project and could be proceeded against jointly. It further held that all applicants need not individually satisfy the Rs.1 crore threshold or limitation requirements. The appeals were dismissed and the NCLT order was upheld.

summary.case_title: Sanjay D. Kakade vs HDFC Ventures Trustee Company Limited & Ors
summary.material_facts: PARTY IDENTITIES: HDFC Ventures Trustee Company Ltd. on behalf of HDFC Investment Trust and Edward Mauritius Ltd. were the Financial Creditors. Kakade Estate Developers Pvt. Ltd. was the Corporate Debtor. Sanjay D. Kakade was a promoter and suspended director. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A Share Subscription and Shareholders Agreement dated 14.05.2008 provided investment of Rs.72,86,65,720 towards equity and compulsorily convertible preference shares. A Supplementary Agreement dated 11.07.2008 provided a further Rs.15 crore. The project was not developed and the parties subsequently entered into a Binding Term Sheet providing an exit to the investors. An arbitration dispute ended in Consent Terms and a Consent Award dated 19.01.2021. DEFAULT METRICS: The Corporate Debtor failed to pay the first tranche of Rs.72,85,71,429 due on 25.08.2021. The Consent Award made the entire Rs.120 crore payable with 15% interest after default. The Section 7 application claimed total default of Rs.133,75,89,041 calculated up to 31.05.2022. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Legal notices demanding payment were issued on 27.08.2021. The Section 7 application was filed on 16.06.2022. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Share Subscription and Shareholders Agreements, Supplementary Agreement, Binding Term Sheet, Consent Terms, Consent Award dated 19.01.2021, legal notices dated 27.08.2021, and acknowledgements/failure to make payments were considered. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: HDFC Ventures Trustee Company Ltd. and Edward Mauritius Ltd. filed the Section 7 application against Kakade Estate Developers. NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV admitted the application on 29.03.2023 and appointed an Interim Resolution Professional. The suspended director challenged the admission before NCLAT. During the appeal several opportunities were given for settlement, but no settlement was completed. NCLAT ultimately upheld the admission.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the investors were Financial Creditors despite the debt having crystallised through Consent Terms and an Arbitration Award; whether the underlying investment transactions had the commercial effect of borrowing and constituted financial debt under Section 5(8); and whether the Section 7 application could be maintained on the basis of the Consent Award.
summary.ratio_decidendi: ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A debt does not cease to be financial debt merely because it has subsequently crystallised through a settlement, decree or arbitration award when the underlying transaction itself qualifies as financial debt. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8) focuses on the nature of the underlying transaction, including whether money was disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money and whether the transaction had the commercial effect of borrowing. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal examined the original subscription agreements, supplementary funding, term sheet, consent terms, consent award, payment obligations and subsequent acknowledgements. The repeated failure to pay despite opportunities was treated as acknowledgement of debt and default. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The underlying transactions constituted financial debt and the Consent Award did not destroy the Financial Creditors' right to invoke Section 7. The NCLT was correct in admitting the insolvency application.
summary.operative_order: The appeal challenging the NCLT order dated 29.03.2023 was dismissed. No order as to costs. The NCLT admission of the Section 7 application was not interfered with.
summary.summary: HDFC Ventures Trustee Company and Edward Mauritius invested substantial amounts in Kakade Estate Developers through share subscription agreements for a real estate project. The project was not developed and the investors were promised an exit. Following disputes, the parties entered Consent Terms and an Arbitration Award requiring payment of Rs.120 crore in two tranches. The Corporate Debtor failed to pay the first tranche of Rs.72.85 crore due on 25 August 2021, resulting in the full amount becoming payable with interest. A Section 7 application claiming Rs.133.75 crore was admitted by NCLT Mumbai. The suspended director argued that the investors were shareholders rather than Financial Creditors and that the award could not itself create financial debt. NCLAT rejected these arguments, upheld the financial-debt character of the underlying transactions and dismissed the appeal.

summary.case_title: Hindalco Industries Ltd. vs Hirakud Industrial Works Ltd. & Ors; H.I.W. Workers' Union vs Nandakini Contractors Pvt. Ltd. & Ors
summary.appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 42 of 2022, 43 of 2022, 52 of 2022 & 53 of 2022
summary.material_facts: PARTY IDENTITIES: Nandakini Contractors Pvt. Ltd. claimed to be the Financial Creditor and Hirakud Industrial Works Ltd. was the Corporate Debtor. Hindalco Industries Ltd. and the H.I.W. Workers' Union were appellants challenging the insolvency process. Regus Impex Pvt. Ltd. was the Successful Resolution Applicant and Mr. Anand Rao Korada was the Resolution Professional. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Nandakini claimed that it had advanced a loan to Hirakud Industrial Works Ltd. under a purported loan agreement dated 14.03.2016. The alleged principal was Rs.14,51,047 with interest at 18% per annum. DEFAULT METRICS: The Section 7 application showed principal debt of Rs.14,51,047 and a claimed financial debt of Rs.24,11,975 including interest. The judgment found that the application did not establish a reliable documentary date of default. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Nandakini sent demand letters including letters dated 15.04.2018, 31.12.2018 and 09.02.2019. Hirakud sent confirmation/repayment-related letters dated 16.02.2019 and 22.02.2019. The Section 7 application was filed on 06.03.2019 and admitted on 04.06.2019. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The alleged loan agreement was not produced. No reliable proof of disbursement, banker-book entry, or corresponding financial-creditor balance-sheet entry was produced. The Corporate Debtor's balance sheet contained an entry relied upon as evidence, but Nandakini's own financial records did not corroborate the alleged loan. The Corporate Debtor's letter dated 22.02.2019 acknowledged an outstanding amount, but the Tribunal held that such indirect evidence could not cure the absence of basic loan and disbursement records. The workers' dues had been quantified at Rs.45,66,67,133. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Nandakini filed CP(IB) No.1/CTB/2019 under Section 7 on 06.03.2019. NCLT Cuttack admitted it on 04.06.2019. During CIRP, a CoC was constituted and a resolution plan submitted by Regus Impex was approved by NCLT on 22.12.2021. The appeals challenged the admission, CoC constitution and resolution plan. NCLAT found the initiation of CIRP fraudulent and malicious and set aside the entire process.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the alleged loan qualified as financial debt; whether the Section 7 admission was legally valid despite lack of loan and disbursement documents; whether the CoC was improperly constituted with related parties; whether the CIRP was fraudulently initiated to obstruct recovery of workers' dues; and whether the resolution plan could survive after the foundational Section 7 admission was found invalid.
summary.ratio_decidendi: ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A Section 7 CIRP cannot be sustained merely on an admission of debt where the foundational financial debt, disbursement and default are unsupported by adequate documentary evidence. A fraudulent or collusive initiation of CIRP invalidates the subsequent insolvency structure built upon it. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 requires the Financial Creditor to furnish evidence of financial debt and default. Section 65 prohibits fraudulent or malicious initiation of insolvency proceedings. The proviso to Section 21(2) prevents related parties from improperly controlling the CoC. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal required documentary support such as the loan agreement, proof of disbursement, banker-book records and corresponding financial records. Bare letters and an unsupported balance-sheet entry were insufficient to establish the alleged loan. The surrounding corporate relationships and conduct were also examined to determine collusion. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The alleged Section 7 initiation was fraudulent and in serious infringement of Section 65. The CoC constitution was a nullity and the resolution plan could not survive because its foundation was legally invalid.
summary.operative_order: The Section 7 admission order was set aside and the CIRP was abated; the Corporate Debtor was freed from the CIRP and moratorium. The resolution plan of Regus Impex was quashed. Penalty of Rs.50 lakh each was imposed on Nandakini Contractors Pvt. Ltd. and Hirakud Industrial Works Ltd. Rs.40 crore paid by the Successful Resolution Applicant to the Financial Creditor was directed to be returned to the Successful Resolution Applicant within one month. Other payments/assets transferred under the resolution plan were directed to be reverted. IBBI was directed to investigate the conduct of the erstwhile Resolution Professional Anand Rao Korada. The workers were left at liberty to pursue their claims.
summary.summary: Nandakini Contractors claimed that Hirakud Industrial Works had defaulted on a loan of Rs.14.51 lakh allegedly advanced under a 2016 loan agreement. NCLT admitted the Section 7 application and CIRP followed. Hindalco Industries and the H.I.W. Workers' Union challenged the process, alleging that the loan was unsupported and had been created through collusion to stop auction of the Corporate Debtor's assets for payment of workers' dues. NCLAT found that the alleged loan agreement and proof of disbursement were absent, while the Financial Creditor's own financial records did not corroborate the transaction. The Tribunal concluded that the CIRP had been fraudulently and maliciously initiated. It set aside the Section 7 admission, abated the CIRP, quashed the resolution plan, imposed Rs.50 lakh penalties on the Financial Creditor and Corporate Debtor, and directed an IBBI investigation.

summary.case_title: Nandamuri Meenalatha vs M/s. Quality Steels and Wire Products & Anr
summary.material_facts: PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s. Quality Steels and Wire Products was the Operational Creditor. Vantage Machine Tools Private Limited was the Corporate Debtor. Nandamuri Meenalatha was an erstwhile director/promoter/shareholder and appellant. Mr. Immaneni Eswara Rao was the Interim Resolution Professional. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Quality Steels supplied structural steel to Vantage Machine Tools under 18 invoices between 20.09.2017 and 24.10.2017. The total value of supplied steel was Rs.1,83,16,611. The Corporate Debtor made payments of Rs.10 lakh on 03.10.2017 and Rs.20 lakh on 13.12.2017. DEFAULT METRICS: Principal outstanding was Rs.1,53,16,611. The Section 8 demand notice stated total debt of Rs.3,04,76,004 as on 22.07.2021, including interest of Rs.1,51,59,393. The precise legally determined date of default is not separately stated; the last invoice was dated 24.10.2017. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Legal notice under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act was issued on 27.04.2019 and replied to on 12.05.2019. A Section 8 IBC demand notice was issued on 30.07.2021. The Section 9 petition was filed on 28.09.2021. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Purchase orders, 18 invoices, part-payment records, emails dated 26.09.2017 and 04.10.2017 seeking test certificates, the 02.11.2017 debt-confirmation email, the 19.04.2019 communication alleging inferior quality of steel, and the 12.05.2019 reply denying legally enforceable debt were considered. The Corporate Debtor also alleged that poor-quality material caused loss of Rs.82,60,000. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Section 9 petition was filed before NCLT Amaravati Bench and admitted by order dated 28.11.2022. Nandamuri Meenalatha, as promoter/shareholder, sought leave and challenged the admission. NCLAT granted leave to appeal and considered whether a pre-existing dispute existed and whether the operational debt was established. It ultimately upheld the admission.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the Corporate Debtor had a genuine pre-existing dispute regarding quality of steel and test certificates before the Section 8 demand notice; whether interest claimed by the Operational Creditor was an uncrystallised damages claim; whether the operational debt exceeded the statutory threshold; and whether the promoter/shareholder could maintain the appeal after CIRP admission.
summary.ratio_decidendi: ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A dispute raised after the transaction or one that is stale, unsupported or not pursued before an appropriate forum does not necessarily constitute a genuine pre-existing dispute sufficient to defeat a Section 9 application. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9 requires consideration of whether operational debt is due and whether a genuine dispute existed before the Section 8 notice. The statutory threshold is concerned with the qualifying debt and does not require the exact final claim amount to be conclusively determined at admission. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal considered the invoices, payments, debt-confirmation email and correspondence concerning quality/test certificates. It found that the Corporate Debtor had accepted the goods, made part-payments and had not pursued its alleged quality/damages dispute before an appropriate forum. The alleged dispute was therefore not sufficient to defeat the Section 9 proceeding. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The operational debt and default were established, the alleged dispute did not qualify as a genuine pre-existing dispute concerning the amount legally payable, and the NCLT's admission was valid.
