summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS.) No.11 of 2023 was dismissed. No costs were imposed. IA No.24 of 2023 seeking stay and IA No.25 of 2023 seeking exemption were closed. IA No.23 of 2023 seeking leave to appeal was allowed.
summary.summary: Nandamuri Meenalatha, an erstwhile director and shareholder of Vantage Machine Tools, challenged the NCLT order admitting a Section 9 insolvency application filed by Quality Steels and Wire Products. The Operational Creditor had supplied structural steel worth Rs.1.83 crore under 18 invoices, against which the Corporate Debtor made Rs.30 lakh in part-payments. The Section 8 demand notice claimed Rs.3.04 crore including principal and interest. The Corporate Debtor argued that poor-quality steel, missing test certificates and damages created a pre-existing dispute. NCLAT examined the purchase orders, invoices, emails, part-payments and notices and found that the alleged dispute did not establish a genuine pre-existing dispute sufficient to defeat insolvency proceedings. The appeal was dismissed and the NCLT admission was upheld.

summary.case_title: Raiyan Hotels and Resorts Pvt. Ltd. vs Unrivalled Projects Private Limited; Aryan Mining & Trading Corporation Pvt. Ltd. vs KAIL Limited & Anr
summary.appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1071 of 2023 & Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 588 of 2023
summary.material_facts: PARTY IDENTITIES: This judgment concerns two separate appeals: Raiyan Hotels and Resorts Pvt. Ltd. vs Unrivalled Projects Private Limited, and Aryan Mining & Trading Corporation Pvt. Ltd. vs KAIL Limited & Anr. The matters concerned appellate challenges to NCLT orders, not a Section 7 or Section 9 creditor-default proceeding. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The judgment does not adjudicate the underlying commercial transaction because it was concerned with condonation of delay in filing the appeals. DEFAULT METRICS: No operative financial default was determined by NCLAT in this judgment. STATUTORY TIMELINES: In Raiyan Hotels, the NCLT order was pronounced on 08.05.2023 and the appeal was e-filed on 04.07.2023; the Registry calculated a 27-day delay beyond the prescribed period. In Aryan Mining, the NCLT order was pronounced on 12.01.2023 and the appeal was filed on 11.03.2023; the Tribunal found the delay beyond the maximum condonable period. No Section 8 demand notice was involved in the appellate issue. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Tribunal considered the dates of pronouncement, presence of counsel, filing dates, certified-copy applications and whether the appellants had applied for certified copies within the limitation period. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Both appeals challenged NCLT orders, but the immediate applications before NCLAT sought condonation of delay. NCLAT held that limitation under Section 61 begins from the date the NCLT order is pronounced and that its power to condone delay is restricted to the additional statutory period of 15 days. The delay applications were not allowed, preventing the delayed appeals from proceeding.
summary.legal_issues: Whether limitation for an appeal under Section 61 of the IBC begins from the date of pronouncement of the NCLT order or from the date the appellant obtains knowledge/receives a copy; whether time taken to obtain a certified copy can be excluded without a timely application; and whether NCLAT can condone delay beyond the additional 15-day period permitted by Section 61(2).
summary.ratio_decidendi: ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The limitation period for an appeal under Section 61 of the IBC commences from the date the NCLT order is pronounced, and NCLAT cannot extend the statutory limitation beyond the maximum additional period permitted by Section 61(2). STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61 is a special limitation provision and operates notwithstanding contrary provisions of the Companies Act. Section 12 of the Limitation Act permits exclusion of time required for obtaining a certified copy when the statutory requirements are satisfied, but a party must act diligently and apply for the certified copy. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal examined the actual pronouncement dates, presence of counsel, filing dates and certified-copy conduct. Constructive knowledge exists when the order is pronounced in open court in the presence of counsel. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Knowledge obtained later by email does not postpone commencement of Section 61 limitation, and NCLAT cannot condone delay beyond the statutory additional 15-day period. The delay applications therefore failed and the appeals could not proceed.
summary.operative_order: The applications seeking condonation of delay were rejected. The delayed appeals could not be entertained because the delay exceeded NCLAT's statutory power of condonation. Pending applications were disposed of. The judgment finally determined the limitation issue in the two appeals.
summary.summary: This NCLAT judgment dealt with two appeals involving applications for condonation of delay. In the Raiyan Hotels matter, the NCLT order was pronounced on 8 May 2023 and the appeal was filed on 4 July 2023, with the Registry calculating a 27-day delay beyond the normal limitation period. In the Aryan Mining matter, the NCLT order was pronounced on 12 January 2023 and the appeal was filed on 11 March 2023. The appellants argued that limitation should begin when they received or learned the contents of the orders. NCLAT rejected that argument, holding that Section 61 limitation begins from pronouncement of the NCLT order. NCLAT's power to condone delay is restricted to the additional 15 days permitted by Section 61(2).

summary.case_title: Chinar Steel Segments Centre Pvt. Ltd. vs Samir Kumar Agarwal, Liquidator of Bhaskar Shrachi Alloys Limited & Anr
summary.material_facts: PARTY IDENTITIES: Chinar Steel Segments Centre Pvt. Ltd. was the successful auction purchaser/appellant. Bhaskar Shrachi Alloys Limited was the Corporate Debtor, which was in liquidation. Samir Kumar Agarwal was the Liquidator. Damodar Valley Corporation (DVC) was the Operational Creditor supplying electricity. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: DVC supplied electricity to Bhaskar Shrachi Alloys under a contract dated 26.11.1996. Electricity dues accumulated and the supply was eventually disconnected. DEFAULT METRICS: DVC filed a Section 9 application claiming unpaid electricity dues of Rs.49,51,59,781. The electricity supply was disconnected on 11.08.2017 after a disconnection notice dated 25.07.2017. The exact principal-interest breakup was not specified in the judgment. STATUTORY TIMELINES: DVC's Section 9 application was admitted on 27.09.2019 and CIRP commenced. No resolution plan was approved and liquidation was ordered on 29.04.2020. The Liquidator fixed 23.12.2020 as the last date for claims. Chinar Steel purchased the Corporate Debtor as a going concern through e-auction and paid Rs.11.40 crore. The Adjudicating Authority's order dated 26.02.2021 directed restoration of electricity and water upon application and payment of required charges. Chinar requested reconnection in August 2021. DVC refused by letter dated 03.09.2021 unless pre-existing dues were paid. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: DVC's admitted claim of Rs.49,51,59,781, liquidation records, sale notice dated 23.11.2020, e-auction sale, sale certificate, the NCLT order dated 26.02.2021, Chinar's correspondence requesting reconnection, DVC's letter dated 03.09.2021, and Clause 4.6.4 of WBERC Regulations were considered. The liquidation process had already dealt with DVC's claim under Section 53. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Chinar filed IA No.984(KB)2021 under Section 60(5) seeking quashing of DVC's refusal and restoration/fresh electricity connection without payment of the Corporate Debtor's extinguished pre-CIRP arrears. NCLT Kolkata dismissed the application on 01.09.2022, reasoning that electricity had been disconnected before CIRP and therefore the dispute was not maintainable. Chinar appealed to NCLAT.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the successful auction purchaser of a Corporate Debtor sold as a going concern can be compelled to pay the Corporate Debtor's pre-CIRP electricity arrears as a condition for obtaining a fresh electricity connection, when those dues had already been dealt with in liquidation under Section 53; and whether the Section 60(5) application was maintainable before the NCLT.
summary.ratio_decidendi: ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A successful purchaser of a Corporate Debtor as a going concern cannot be compelled to pay the Corporate Debtor's pre-CIRP electricity arrears that have already been dealt with and extinguished through the insolvency or liquidation process merely to obtain a fresh electricity connection. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60(5) gives the NCLT jurisdiction over claims and questions arising out of or relating to insolvency or liquidation. Section 53 provides the waterfall mechanism through which claims are dealt with. The clean-slate principle prevents extinguished pre-sale liabilities from being indirectly revived against a successful purchaser. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal examined the admitted DVC claim, liquidation proceedings, Section 53 distribution, sale of the Corporate Debtor as a going concern, the NCLT's earlier direction for restoration of electricity and DVC's refusal based on WBERC Clause 4.6.4. It found that the pre-CIRP dues had already been dealt with in liquidation and could not be re-agitated against the purchaser. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 60(5) application was maintainable and Chinar was entitled to a fresh electricity connection without paying the Corporate Debtor's extinguished pre-CIRP electricity arrears, subject to payment of necessary charges for the fresh connection.
summary.operative_order: The NCLT order dated 01.09.2022 was set aside. IA No.984 of 2021 was allowed. DVC was directed to grant a fresh electricity connection after taking all necessary charges for the fresh connection, but excluding the outstanding dues of the Corporate Debtor that had been satisfied and extinguished through the liquidation proceedings.
summary.summary: Chinar Steel Segments Centre Pvt. Ltd. purchased Bhaskar Shrachi Alloys Limited as a going concern through a liquidation e-auction for Rs.11.40 crore. Before CIRP began, electricity supplied by Damodar Valley Corporation had been disconnected because of unpaid dues. DVC's claim of Rs.49.51 crore was admitted during the liquidation process and was dealt with under the Section 53 waterfall. After purchasing the Corporate Debtor, Chinar sought restoration of electricity. DVC refused unless the old electricity arrears were paid. NCLT dismissed Chinar's Section 60(5) application, but NCLAT held that the application was maintainable and that extinguished pre-CIRP liabilities could not be imposed on the successful purchaser. The appeal was allowed and DVC was directed to provide a fresh connection upon payment of necessary new-connection charges.

summary.case_title: Sudhir John Horo vs Ideaworks Design & Strategy Private Limited & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Sudhir John Horo, promoter-director and 45% shareholder (4500 shares of Rs.10 each) of Respondent No.1 Ideaworks Design & Strategy Pvt Ltd; Respondent No.2 Amit Shahi, co-founder and 55% shareholder; Respondent No.3 Shyam Santhakumari Vasudevan, director inducted in 2017; Respondent No.4 Rajiv Krishan Nanda; Respondent No.5 August Company Consulting Services; Respondent No.6 Alok Kumar Agrawal, CEO of ASC Group (alleged to have prepared the disputed transfer documents). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Not a lending/supply transaction; Ideaworks, incorporated 24.06.2011, provided communication design and brand strategy services; Appellant and Respondent No.2 held 45%/55% shareholding from incorporation. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (no financial default); dispute concerns transfer of Appellant's 4500 shares via Form SH-4 dated 24.04.2017 (4000 shares to Respondent No.2, 500 to Respondent No.3), alleged by Appellant to be forged. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Not applicable; no Section 8 demand notice involved as this is a Companies Act oppression/mismanagement and rectification petition, not an IBC matter. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Email chain dated 26.01.2019, 28.01.2019, 29.01.2019, 20.02.2019, 21.05.2019 and 06.06.2019 between Appellant and Respondent No.2 regarding the shareholding dilution; Form SH-4 dated 24.04.2017; Appellant's resignation letter as director dated 15.04.2017; Form DIR-11 filed under Section 168(1); Annual Returns for FY 2016-17/2017-18 showing Appellant's shareholding reduced to zero; a 31.07.2013 letter to Axis Bank regarding a signature-mismatch issue relied on by Respondents to authenticate the Appellant's signature on the transfer form. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed Company Petition No.118/241-242/ND/2019 before NCLT New Delhi Bench-VI on 30.07.2019 under Sections 59, 241 and 242, seeking to set aside the share transfer as oppression; NCLT dismissed the petition as not maintainable by order dated 03.05.2021, holding the Appellant must first establish his membership title before a competent forum, relying on Gulabrai Kalidas Naik v. Laxmidas Lallubhai Patel; Appellant filed Company Appeal (AT) No.98 of 2021 on 16.08.2021 before NCLAT.
summary.legal_issues: Whether a Section 241-242 oppression and mismanagement petition is maintainable where the petitioner's own title to membership (reduced below the Section 244 threshold) is itself disputed and arises from an allegedly illegal private share transfer in which the company had no role; whether such disputed transfer can be adjudicated incidentally under a composite Section 59/241/242 petition.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where a petitioner's title to membership is in dispute and he must first obtain rectification to be restored to the register of members, it is improper to permit him to simultaneously maintain a petition for oppression and mismanagement until that title dispute is first resolved. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 241 requires that the company itself be shown to be the instrument or means of the alleged oppression; a share transfer executed purely as a private transaction between shareholders, without the company's engagement, does not constitute oppression or mismanagement in the 'affairs of the company,' even if the transfer is alleged to be forged. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: A petitioner must first establish, before a competent forum, his subsisting right/title as a member before the Tribunal examines oppression allegations; disputed questions of forgery and fabrication concerning private share transfers are not incidental or peripheral to a Section 59 rectification claim and fall outside NCLT's summary jurisdiction. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellant, having ceased to hold any shares via a transfer not involving the company, was required to first establish his membership rights before a competent forum; the Company Petition was rightly held not maintainable.
summary.operative_order: Appeal dismissed; NCLT order dated 03.05.2021 dismissing Company Petition No.118/241-242/ND/2019 as non-maintainable affirmed; no order as to costs; Registry directed to upload the judgment and send a copy to NCLT, New Delhi Bench-VI.
summary.summary: Sudhir John Horo, a 45% shareholder-director of Ideaworks Design & Strategy Pvt Ltd, alleged that co-founder Amit Shahi and others fraudulently transferred his entire shareholding to themselves via a forged share transfer form, and filed a Section 241/242/59 petition alleging oppression and mismanagement. NCLT dismissed the petition as not maintainable, holding the Appellant must first establish his membership title before a competent forum since the transfer was a private transaction outside the company's involvement. NCLAT agreed, applying Gulabrai Kalidas Naik, and dismissed the appeal, holding the petitioner could not invoke Sections 241-242 while his title to membership remained disputed.

summary.case_title: Anand Infoedge Pvt. Ltd., Mist Avenue Pvt. Ltd. & Mist Direct Sales Pvt. Ltd. vs Nitin Batra & Ors.
summary.appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 127 of 2023 & IA No. 463 of 2023; Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1478 of 2022; Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1506 of 2022 & IA No. 4895 of 2022 (heard together)
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditors are Nitin Batra and 114 other allottees of the 'Festival City' real estate project; Corporate Debtors/Appellants are Anand Infoedge Pvt. Ltd. (leaseholder of the project land), Mist Avenue Pvt. Ltd. (first developer/collaborator), and Mist Direct Sales Pvt. Ltd. (second developer/collaborator, in which Anand Infoedge held 99.99% shares at the time of the second collaboration agreement). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Anand Infoedge held leasehold rights over Plot No.1, Sector 143, Noida (100,980 sq. mtrs.) under a Lease Deed dated 21.08.2008 from NOIDA, with possession from 28.08.2008. It entered a Collaboration Agreement with Mist Avenue effective 26.10.2012 (85% developer/15% owner revenue share) for development; Mist Avenue allotted units to allottees via Builder Buyer Agreements between 2012-2017. The first Collaboration Agreement was cancelled on 27.07.2017, and on the same date Anand Infoedge entered a second Collaboration Agreement with Mist Direct (same 85:15 share); Mist Direct informed allottees by letter dated 02.12.2017 that it had taken over the inventories, buyer records and payment accounts. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default was pleaded from varying dates depending on each allottee's Builder Buyer Agreement possession timeline, with one date of default cited as 16.10.2016 and subsequent staggered possession dates; the project was never completed and UPRERA revoked its registration by order dated 07.12.2019. Of 115 claimed allottees, NCLT found 103 to be valid for threshold purposes, against Appellants' contention that only 55 were valid (excluding 18 as time-barred, 11 as hit by Section 10A, 8 as settled, and 5 as premature). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Not applicable in the Section 8/9 sense; this is a Section 7 financial creditor application, filed jointly by the allottees on 11.10.2021, with no separate statutory demand notice required. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Collaboration Agreement dated 26.10.2012/executed 28.07.2014 between Anand Infoedge and Mist Avenue; cancellation deed dated 27.07.2017; second Collaboration Agreement dated 27.07.2017 between Anand Infoedge and Mist Direct; sample Builder Buyer Agreement (allottee Gaurav Bhardwaj) with possession/delay-compensation clauses; letter dated 02.12.2017 from Mist Direct acknowledging takeover of inventories and buyer accounts; UPRERA order dated 07.12.2019 revoking project registration. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 application filed 11.10.2021 before NCLT, New Delhi Bench-VI (CP IB-682/(ND)/2021) by 115-unit allottees against all three corporate entities jointly; NCLT by order dated 21.10.2022 held the joint application maintainable and the 100-allottee/10% threshold under the second proviso to Section 7(1) satisfied; Anand Infoedge, Mist Avenue and Mist Direct each filed separate appeals against this maintainability order, heard and decided together by NCLAT on 17.11.2023.
summary.legal_issues: (i) Whether a joint Section 7 application against three separate corporate debtors involved in a single real estate project is maintainable; (ii) whether the threshold of 100 allottees (or 10%) under the second proviso to Section 7(1) IBC was satisfied; (iii) whether claims alleged to be time-barred, settled, premature, or hit by Section 10A must be excluded from that threshold count.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where two or more corporate debtors jointly collaborate to develop a single real estate project and are intrinsically interwoven in its development, sale, and delivery of units, a joint Section 7 application by allottees against all such corporate debtors is maintainable, since the project cannot be resolved without all of them being before the Tribunal. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The second proviso to Section 7(1), requiring joinder of not less than 100 allottees (or 10%), is satisfied so long as a default of Rs. 1 crore is established qua any applicant allottee (or even a non-applicant financial creditor) and that default is not time-barred; it is not necessary that every joined applicant's individual claim be within limitation, unsettled, or otherwise flawless. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The threshold must be tested as on the date of filing of the application; allottees whose claims are alleged settled, premature, or time-barred are not excluded from the numerical count so long as a qualifying default is established and within limitation, applying continuing-breach principles (Section 22, Limitation Act) given the developer's ongoing obligation to pay delay compensation until possession. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT correctly held the joint Section 7 application maintainable against all three corporate debtors and that the threshold under the second proviso to Section 7(1) was fulfilled; the appeals challenging the maintainability order were dismissed.
summary.operative_order: All three connected appeals dismissed; NCLT order dated 21.10.2022 holding the Section 7 application maintainable is affirmed; matter to proceed before NCLT for further consideration of the Section 7 application on merits (admission/rejection stage not yet reached).
summary.summary: Allottees of the 'Festival City' project in Noida filed a joint Section 7 application against Anand Infoedge (landowner), Mist Avenue (first developer) and Mist Direct (second developer), all closely linked through successive collaboration agreements, after the project stalled and UPRERA revoked its registration. NCLT held the joint application maintainable and the 100-allottee threshold satisfied. The three corporate debtors appealed separately, challenging both joinder and threshold compliance. NCLAT, relying on precedent on group real estate insolvencies and the Supreme Court's ruling in Manish Kumar, held the joint application maintainable and the threshold met, and dismissed all three appeals.

summary.case_title: M/s Morepen Laboratories Ltd. & Ors. vs Union of India
summary.appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) No. 04 of 2022 with Company Appeal (AT) No. 05 of 2022
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant No.1 Morepen Laboratories Ltd. (public listed pharmaceutical company), with Appellant Nos.2-5 being its Chairman/Managing Director and Whole-time/other Directors (Sushil Suri, Sanjay Suri, Arun Kumar, Manoj Joshi); Respondent is Union of India. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Not a lending transaction; Morepen, a pharmaceutical manufacturer, defaulted on repayment of matured Fixed Deposits after a 2002 collapse in the price of its key drug Loratadine (from ~USD 8,000/kg to USD 1,800/kg after US FDA reclassified it over-the-counter), leading to CLB proceedings and a Section 391 scheme to convert FD dues into equity shares. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total outstanding due to FD holders as on 30.09.2003 was Rs.156.19 crores; as of the appeal, only ~Rs.18.84 crores had been repaid to 4953 of 32,927 eligible FD holders who came forward, the balance FD holders retaining and largely trading their allotted shares. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Not applicable in Section 8/9 IBC sense; this is a Companies Act contempt/modification matter arising from CLB order dated 01.07.2005 directing appointment of two Government Directors, upheld by Himachal Pradesh High Court (17.05.2007) and Supreme Court (09.07.2019, with liberty to agitate subsequent events before the concerned forum). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: CLB order dated 01.07.2005; High Court order dated 17.05.2007; Supreme Court status quo orders dated 16.07.2007 and 07.09.2007, and final order dated 09.07.2019; NCLT order dated 12.03.2018 dismissing the Section 391 Revival Scheme and directing cancellation of shares issued to FD holders (except already-traded shares) with refund within three months; public notices dated 15.08.2019, 27.07.2020 and 28.07.2021; zero-debt certificate dated 22.10.2021; share price data showing appreciation from Rs.7.79 (2005) to Rs.54.70-66.60 (2019-2021). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant No.1 filed CA No.785/2019 before NCLT Chandigarh (pursuant to Supreme Court's 09.07.2019 liberty) seeking modification of the 01.07.2005 order; Union of India filed CA No.1207/2019 seeking contempt proceedings for non-compliance; NCLT Chandigarh by common order dated 06.10.2021 dismissed CA 785/2019 and issued contempt notice in CA 1207/2019; both orders were appealed to NCLAT as Company Appeal (AT) No.05/2022 and No.04/2022 respectively, heard together and decided on 25.04.2023.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the CLB order dated 01.07.2005 (directing appointment of two Government Directors), having been upheld through the High Court and finally by the Supreme Court on 09.07.2019, could be modified by the NCLT based on subsequent financial turnaround of the company; whether the doctrine of merger ousted NCLT's jurisdiction to entertain contempt proceedings for disobedience of the 2005 order; whether non-compliance amounted to wilful civil contempt.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where an order of a subordinate authority has been challenged up to and finally decided by the Supreme Court, that authority (or its successor tribunal) cannot thereafter modify or cancel the order on the ground of subsequent events, even where the Supreme Court has granted liberty to 'agitate' such subsequent events before the concerned forum, unless the Supreme Court's own language contemplates modification. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: A Supreme Court observation granting liberty to 'agitate subsequent events before the concerned forum', combined with a direction to conclude proceedings 'within one year', is to be read as a direction for proper compliance with the original order rather than as an empowerment to modify or set it aside. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: For civil contempt, disobedience must be 'wilful' — deliberate flouting rather than a bona fide or plausible misinterpretation of a court order; an action based on a plausible reading of an order does not amount to wilful disobedience. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT correctly refused to modify the 2005 CLB order (as upheld by the Supreme Court) and the appeals against both the refusal to modify and the issuance of contempt notice were dismissed; the contempt proceedings themselves were directed to continue before NCLT Chandigarh for further consideration in light of the subsequent developments.
summary.operative_order: Both appeals (Company Appeal (AT) Nos.04 and 05 of 2022) dismissed; NCLT Chandigarh's common order dated 06.10.2021 affirmed; no order as to costs. Appellants in Company Appeal (AT) No.04 of 2022 directed to appear before NCLT Chandigarh and file reply to the Contempt Application, with NCLT Chandigarh to consider the Supreme Court's order and subsequent developments and pass appropriate orders in accordance with law — i.e., the underlying contempt proceeding (CA 1207/2019) continues at NCLT following this disposal.
summary.summary: Morepen Laboratories, after a 2002 collapse in its key drug's price caused it to default on Fixed Deposit repayments, was directed by the Company Law Board in 2005 to appoint two Government Directors, an order upheld up to the Supreme Court in 2019 with liberty to raise subsequent events before the appropriate forum. Citing its financial turnaround, Morepen sought modification of the 2005 order before NCLT, which was dismissed, while the Union of India's parallel contempt application against Morepen for non-compliance was allowed to proceed via issuance of notice. NCLAT dismissed both of Morepen's appeals, holding that the Supreme Court's order did not empower modification and that the doctrine of merger did not oust NCLT's jurisdiction, while remitting the contempt proceeding for further consideration at NCLT Chandigarh.

summary.case_title: Chalasani Udaya Shankar & Ors. vs M/s. Lexus Technologies Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
summary.appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 44 of 2021 & I.A. No. 548/2021
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants Chalasani Udaya Shankar, Sripathi Sreevana Reddy and Yalamanchilli Manjusha, claiming to be shareholders holding 94.80% of Respondent No.1 M/s Lexus Technologies Pvt. Ltd. (a software solutions company incorporated 28.03.2000); Respondent No.2 Mantena Narasa Raju (alleged transferor and director), Respondent Nos.3-4 other Directors, Respondent No.5 a Chartered Accountant, Respondent Nos.6-7 RoC/Regional Director. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Alleged purchase by the Appellants of 10,51,933 equity shares (94.8% of paid-up capital) from Respondent No.2 via Securities Transfer Form SH-4 dated 18.04.2015, for a claimed consideration of Rs.14,67,41,557/-, following an alleged pre-emption offer letter dated 29.12.2014 from Respondent No.2 to the Board. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (share-transfer dispute, not a debt default); the Tribunal found the Appellants had remitted Rs.14,66,39,400/- (leaving an unexplained difference of Rs.1,02,157/- from the claimed Rs.14,67,41,557/-), with the funds actually routed through one Mr. Lingamaneni Ramesh, who received back Rs.9 crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Not applicable; this is a Section 59/241/242/244 rectification and oppression petition, not an IBC Section 7/9 matter. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Photocopies of Securities Transfer Forms (SH-4) dated 18.04.2015 with blank 'for office use' columns (indicating non-delivery to the company); photocopy share certificates dated 27.04.2015 alleged by Respondents to be fabricated (wrong format, non-matching distinctive numbers); bank transfer records showing Rs.14,66,39,400/- remitted via three individuals on 17.04.2015 and Rs.9 crores returned on 18.04.2015 to different persons; Respondent No.2's claim that he still held the original share certificates and never sold his shares; Registrar's strike-off of the company under Section 248 for non-filing of returns for FY2014-15 to 2016-17, later restored. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed Company Petition No.667/59 & 241/HDB/2018 before NCLT Amaravati Bench, Hyderabad on 09.11.2018 (with the alleged transfer dated 18.04.2015, i.e., beyond the 3-year limitation under Article 113 of the Limitation Act); NCLT dismissed the petition by order dated 21.08.2021 on grounds of limitation, non-compliance with the Companies Act share-transfer procedure, non-genuine consideration, and fabricated share certificates; Appellants filed Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No.44 of 2021 before NCLAT Chennai, decided on 10.04.2023.
summary.legal_issues: Whether a Section 59 rectification petition (with consequential relief under Sections 241, 242 and 244) filed more than three years after the alleged date of share transfer is barred by limitation under Article 113 of the Limitation Act; whether the petitioners, having failed to establish a valid transfer of shares in compliance with Sections 56 and 58 of the Companies Act and the Articles of Association, had locus standi as 'members' to maintain an oppression and mismanagement petition.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A petition seeking rectification of the register of members under Section 59, with consequential relief for oppression and mismanagement under Sections 241-242, is barred by the three-year limitation period under Article 113 of the Limitation Act where filed more than three years from the date of the alleged share transfer. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: For a valid transfer of shares under Section 56, a duly executed instrument of transfer must be delivered to the company within the prescribed period along with the share certificate; transfer forms with blank 'for office use' columns (no transfer number, no approval date, no signature verification by the company) indicate the forms were never lodged with or processed by the company, and such non-compliance defeats a claim of valid transfer. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Only a 'member' has locus to maintain a petition under Section 241; claimants relying on photocopy share certificates and transfer deeds bearing discrepancies from the company's genuine format, and unable to produce originals despite a Tribunal direction to do so, fail to discharge the burden of establishing bona fide membership; remittance of funds through third parties without direct correspondence between transferor and transferee does not establish that the funds constituted consideration for share transfer. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellants failed to establish valid share transfer in compliance with Sections 56, 58 and 59 and the Articles of Association, and consequently lacked locus to invoke Sections 241-242; the petition was rightly dismissed both as time-barred and on merits.
summary.operative_order: Appeal dismissed as devoid of merit; NCLT order dated 21.08.2021 dismissing the Company Petition affirmed. No costs.
summary.summary: Three individuals claimed to have purchased 94.8% of the shares of Lexus Technologies Pvt. Ltd. from a director in 2015 via signed share transfer forms and share certificates, and filed a petition under Sections 59, 241, 242 and 244 alleging oppression when the company was later struck off the register for non-filing of returns. The respondent company and the alleged transferor denied any such sale, calling the share certificates fabricated and the transfer forms never lodged with the company. NCLT dismissed the petition as time-barred (filed beyond the three-year limitation period) and for want of genuine evidence of transfer. NCLAT affirmed, holding the appellants failed to establish valid share transfer under the Companies Act and Articles of Association and therefore lacked locus as members to maintain the oppression petition, and dismissed the appeal.

summary.case_title: Mahmod Alam Khan & Mustafa Alam Khan vs Ahmed Alam Khan & Anr.
summary.appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS.) No. 30 of 2023 with Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS.) No. 38 of 2023
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants Mahmod Alam Khan and Mustafa Alam Khan, shareholders and suspended directors of M/s. Golconda Textiles Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor, a family-run business of three brothers each holding equal shareholding); Respondent No.1 Ahmed Alam Khan, the third brother and Financial Creditor/Petitioner; Respondent No.2 Mr. Prasanna Shenoy, Interim Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Ahmed Alam Khan advanced unsecured loans totalling Rs.13,84,72,064/- to the family-run Corporate Debtor over several years, including a specific sum of Rs.3,97,85,000/- disbursed on 25.01.2021 to enable the Corporate Debtor to honour a One-Time Settlement offered by State Bank of India (erstwhile State Bank of Hyderabad) on its bank loans; the Rs.3.97 crore portion was itself funded via a personal term loan of Rs.4 crore Ahmed Alam Khan obtained from Adarsh Co-operative Urban Bank Ltd. on 24.01.2021. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total claimed default amount was Rs.18,28,95,628/- (Rs.13,84,72,064/- principal plus Rs.4,44,23,565/- interest at 14% per annum computed to 21.02.2022); date of default stated in Form-I as 01.02.2022. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Not a Section 8/9 operational creditor matter (no statutory demand notice under Section 8); a demand letter dated 17.11.2021 was sent by the Financial Creditor to the Board of Directors requesting repayment or conversion of the unsecured loans into equity shares within 30 days, to which no reply was received. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor's Audited Balance Sheets for FY2019-20 (total unsecured loans Rs.12,50,34,119/-, of which Rs.9,37,87,064/- from the Financial Creditor) and FY2020-21 (total unsecured loans Rs.16,64,47,049/-, of which Rs.13,84,72,064/- from the Financial Creditor), both containing a Note 4.1 stating loans from directors were treated as long-term with no fixed repayment terms; Statutory Auditor's Certificate dated 08.05.2022 confirming the unsecured loan was advanced by the Financial Creditor; No Due Certificate from State Bank of India dated 30.01.2021; Adarsh Co-operative Urban Bank sanction letter dated 24.01.2021 for a Rs.4 crore personal loan to Ahmed Alam Khan for 'investment on Group Businesses and Units'. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Ahmed Alam Khan filed CP (IB) No.94/07/HDB/2022 under Section 7 before NCLT Hyderabad Bench-II; NCLT admitted the petition by order dated 24.01.2023, initiating CIRP and appointing an IRP; Mahmod Alam Khan and Mustafa Alam Khan (as shareholders/suspended directors and 'aggrieved persons' under Section 61(1)) separately appealed as Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS.) No.30 of 2023 and No.38 of 2023 respectively before NCLAT Chennai, both decided together on 02.08.2023.
summary.legal_issues: Whether unsecured, interest-bearing-on-demand funds advanced by a director/shareholder to a family-run corporate debtor, to ease its liquidity crisis and enable repayment of bank dues, constitute a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC in the absence of a formal loan agreement, board resolution, or fixed repayment term; whether such advances instead represent capital infusion by a family member not amounting to commercial borrowing.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A director's or shareholder's advance of funds to a company to improve its financial health or rescue it from financial distress has the commercial effect of a borrowing and constitutes a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC, even where no interest is claimed and no formal loan tenure is fixed. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The absence of an express agreement fixing a repayment term does not exclude a sum from being a 'financial debt'; in the absence of any agreed tenure, such a loan becomes due and payable 'on demand' made by the creditor, applying ordinary commercial practice. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Acknowledgment of the disbursed sum as an 'unsecured loan'/'long-term borrowing' in the corporate debtor's audited balance sheets, corroborated by a statutory auditor's certificate and traceable bank transaction records, establishes the existence of financial debt exceeding the statutory threshold; the classification of such sums as 'long-term borrowings' under non-current liabilities in the balance sheet does not, by itself, indicate the sums are not repayable. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Financial Creditor established a financial debt exceeding Rs.1 crore that was due and payable and had been defaulted upon following a demand notice that went unanswered; the Section 7 application was correctly admitted, and the appeals challenging admission were dismissed.
summary.operative_order: Both Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS.) No.30 of 2023 and Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS.) No.38 of 2023 dismissed. No costs. Connected pending interlocutory applications (IA Nos.108, 109, 111 of 2023 in Appeal No.30; IA Nos.134, 135, 137 of 2023 in Appeal No.38) closed.
summary.summary: In a family-run textile company where three brothers held equal shareholding, one brother (Ahmed Alam Khan) advanced over Rs.13.84 crore in unsecured loans over several years to ease the company's liquidity crisis, including funds used to settle bank dues under a One-Time Settlement. When the company failed to repay despite a demand notice, he filed a Section 7 application, which NCLT Hyderabad admitted, triggering CIRP. The other two brothers, as suspended directors, appealed, arguing there was no loan agreement, no board resolution, and that intra-family capital infusion lacked the 'commercial effect of borrowing' required for financial debt. NCLAT dismissed both appeals, holding that director advances to rescue a company from financial distress constitute financial debt under Section 5(8) IBC regardless of the absence of interest or fixed tenure, and that the balance sheet entries and auditor's certificate sufficiently established the debt and default.

summary.case_title: Dr. C. Vinod Hayagriv & Ors. vs C. Ganesh Narayan & Mrs. C. Valli Narayan
summary.appeal_number: Contempt Case (AT) No. 13 of 2023 in Company Appeal (AT) No. 65 of 2019
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Complainants (Hayagriv family) — Dr. C. Vinod Hayagriv (Director/MD of C. Krishniah Chetty & Sons Pvt. Ltd., 'CKC & Sons'), C. V. Hayagriv, Mrs. C. Triveni Vinod, Mrs. C. Visala Hayagriv, Chaitanya V. Cotha and Shreyas V. Cotha — each holding, collectively with the Contemnors, 50% shareholding in CKC & Sons; Contemnors (Narayan family) — C. Ganesh Narayan and Mrs. C. Valli Narayan, who also wholly own a similarly-named competing entity, C. Krishniah Chetty & Co. Pvt. Ltd. ('CKC & Co.', formerly Deepali Co. Pvt. Ltd.). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Not a lending/supply transaction; both CKC & Sons (jewellery business incorporated 1979) and CKC & Co. (incorporated 1982, objects identical to CKC & Sons) trace to the same founding family and operate jewellery businesses from adjacent premises (A-Block and B-Block respectively) of the same redeveloped 'Touchstone' building in Bangalore, governed in part by a disputed Family Settlement Agreement (FSA). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (no financial default; dispute concerns alleged breach of NCLAT interim directions restraining coercive action/precipitating the matter, and alleged operation of a competing jewellery business). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Not applicable; the contempt petition invoked Section 425 of the Companies Act, 2013 read with Sections 10 and 12 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, alleging wilful breach of NCLAT orders dated 08.07.2021, 25.11.2021 and 24.02.2022 passed in the pending main appeal, Company Appeal (AT) No.65 of 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The three NCLAT orders alleged to be breached; a prior NCLT interim order in I.A. No.54/2018 (TP No.65/2016) restraining the Contemnors from starting a competing jewellery business in B-Block; tax invoices from CKC & Co. dated as early as 04.03.2021 (before the first alleged order of 08.07.2021) showing it was already operating from the Touchstone B-Block under its changed name; a Commercial Court Bangalore order dated 20.02.2021 dismissing CKC & Sons' injunction application (affirmed by Karnataka High Court on 27.05.2021, and the underlying suit rejected 17.02.2022, unappealed); an NCLT order dated 24.01.2019 in the underlying CP 54/2014 (TP 65/2016) dismissing Mrs. Valli Narayan's original oppression petition. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Contempt Case (AT) No.13 of 2023 was filed within the pending main Company Appeal (AT) No.65 of 2019 (itself an appeal against NCLT's order dated 24.01.2019 dismissing CP 54/2014, still under hearing separately), alleging wilful breach of the three interim NCLAT orders; decided by NCLAT Principal Bench on 09.08.2023, without NCLAT expressing any view on the merits of the still-pending main appeal.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the Contemnors' continued operation of, and dealings by, a similarly-named competing jewellery business from adjacent premises constituted wilful, deliberate disobedience of NCLAT's interim orders directing the parties 'not to precipitate the matter' and 'not to take coercive action', where those orders were general in nature or specifically confined to a different, unrelated application (for permission to hold Board Meetings).
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: To establish civil contempt, two elements must be proved: (i) disobedience of a judgment, decree, direction or order of the court/tribunal, and (ii) that such disobedience was wilful, deliberate and intentional — not merely a bona fide or technical breach; if the impugned order admits of more than one reasonable interpretation and the alleged conduct is not contumacious, contempt proceedings are not maintainable. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: A contempt court must apply the directions actually contained in the order allegedly violated, and must not go beyond it by expanding vague or general language (such as a direction 'not to precipitate the matter') into specific prohibitions (such as a bar on operating or opening a competing business) that the order's text does not itself impose; where an order's direction was addressed only to one specific party or governed a specific application (e.g., permission to hold Board Meetings), it cannot be read as a general restraint binding all parties on unrelated conduct. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Disobedience must be proved beyond reasonable doubt as contempt proceedings are quasi-criminal in nature; where documentary evidence (e.g., tax invoices) shows the allegedly contumacious conduct (operating from the disputed premises) predates the very order said to have been violated, no wilful breach can be made out. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: None of the three NCLAT orders relied upon contained specific, unambiguous directions restraining the Contemnors from operating their existing competing business from the Touchstone B-Block, and the evidence showed that business had been operating from that location well before the first order; accordingly, no wilful disobedience amounting to contempt was established.
summary.operative_order: Contempt Case (AT) No.13 of 2023 dismissed as devoid of merit; no costs. NCLAT clarified it did not adjudicate the still-pending main appeal, Company Appeal (AT) No.65 of 2019, which continues to be heard separately, and the present findings are confined to the contempt case alone.
summary.summary: Members of the Hayagriv family, 50% shareholders of jewellery business C. Krishniah Chetty & Sons, filed a contempt case against the Narayan family (the other 50% shareholders, who also wholly own a similarly-named competing entity, CKC & Co.) alleging wilful breach of three NCLAT interim orders restraining coercive action and directing the parties not to precipitate a pending oppression appeal, by continuing to operate and expand CKC & Co.'s competing jewellery business from adjacent premises. The Narayans denied any breach, pointing to evidence that CKC & Co. had been operating from that location well before the orders were passed and that the orders in question were either general in nature or specifically confined to an unrelated application about Board Meetings. NCLAT dismissed the contempt case, holding that none of the three orders contained clear, unambiguous directions the Contemnors could be shown to have wilfully violated, while leaving the underlying main appeal on oppression and mismanagement to be decided separately.

summary.case_title: Soneko Marketing Pvt. Ltd., The U.P. Glass Manufacturers Syndicate, H.N.G. Karamchari Union & Anr., Independent Sugar Corporation Ltd. vs Girish Sriram Juneja (RP of Hindusthan National Glass & Industries Ltd.) & Ors.
summary.appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 807 of 2023 & I.A. No. 2721 of 2023, with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 607 of 2023, Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 724 of 2023, and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 735 of 2023
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Corporate Debtor Hindustan National Glass & Industries Ltd. ('HNG'); Resolution Professional Girish Sriram Juneja; competing Resolution Applicants AGI Greenpac Ltd. (successful applicant, 98% CoC vote share) and Independent Sugar Corporation Ltd. ('ISC', 88% CoC vote share, and CCI approval obtained 30.09.2022); other Appellants — Soneko Marketing Pvt. Ltd. (unrelated appellant in a connected appeal), The U.P. Glass Manufacturers Syndicate (an industry body of UP-based glass manufacturers), and H.N.G. Karamchari Union & H.N.G. Mazdoor Union (workmen's trade unions of HNG's Bahadurgarh unit). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP against HNG commenced 21.10.2021 on a Section 7 application by DBS Bank; RP issued Invitation for EOI on 25.03.2022 with a mandatory CCI-approval clause; both AGI Greenpac and ISC submitted Resolution Plans in April 2022, each involving a 'combination' under Section 5 of the Competition Act requiring CCI approval. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (dispute concerns interpretation of the resolution-plan-approval process, not the underlying Section 7 default against HNG). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: AGI Greenpac filed its CCI Form-1 combination application on 27.09.2022 (declared invalid 22.10.2022, resubmitted as Form-II on 03.11.2022); ISC received CCI approval on 30.09.2022 (before CoC vote); CoC approved AGI Greenpac's Plan (98% votes) over ISC's Plan (88% votes) on 28.10.2022 — i.e., after ISC's CCI approval but before AGI Greenpac's; CCI granted approval to AGI Greenpac's combination proposal only on 15.03.2023, i.e., after the CoC vote. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: RFRP terms requiring CCI approval; RP's email clarification dated 25.08.2022 relaxing the requirement to allow CCI approval any time before filing the Plan with the Adjudicating Authority; CCI's approval letter dated 15.03.2023 for AGI Greenpac's combination; prior NCLAT precedents (Arcelor Mittal, Makalu Trading, Vishal Vijay Kalantri) holding the proviso to Section 31(4) IBC directory, both affirmed by the Supreme Court on appeal. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: ISC filed I.A. No.1497/KB/2022 before NCLT Kolkata seeking to set aside selection of AGI Greenpac's Plan; U.P. Glass Manufacturers Syndicate and the workmen's unions filed connected intervention/objection applications (I.A. Nos.628/KB/2023 and 701/KB/2023, and earlier interventions rejected 21.09.2022 and 16.01.2023); NCLT Kolkata by common order dated 28.04.2023 rejected ISC's I.A. No.1497/KB/2022, holding CCI's 15.03.2023 approval satisfied Section 31(4); four connected appeals (Nos.807, 607, 724 and 735 of 2023) were filed by Soneko Marketing, U.P. Glass Manufacturers Syndicate, the workmen's unions, and ISC respectively, heard together and decided by NCLAT on 18.09.2023.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the proviso to Section 31(4) of the IBC — requiring a resolution applicant whose plan involves a 'combination' under the Competition Act to obtain CCI approval 'prior to the approval of such resolution plan by the committee of creditors' — is mandatory (such that CCI approval obtained only after CoC approval invalidates the plan) or merely directory.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The requirement of CCI approval itself for a resolution plan involving a combination is mandatory, but the specific timing requirement in the proviso to Section 31(4) IBC — that such approval be obtained prior to CoC approval rather than merely prior to Adjudicating Authority approval — is directory, not mandatory. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Use of the word 'shall' in a statutory provision is not conclusive of mandatory character; the court must examine the provision's object, design and context, and whether non-compliance is coupled with a specified consequence; where no penalty or invalidating consequence is prescribed for obtaining CCI approval after (rather than before) CoC approval, and given the divergent statutory timelines under the IBC/CIRP Regulations (135-165 days for CoC decision) versus the Competition Act (up to 210 days for CCI to decide), reading the requirement as mandatory would produce an unworkable, indefinite freeze on the CIRP process contrary to the Code's object of time-bound resolution. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Consistent application of a settled interpretive test previously laid down in Arcelor Mittal India Pvt. Ltd. v. Guhathakurta and followed in Makalu Trading Ltd. and Vishal Vijay Kalantri (both affirmed by the Supreme Court on appeal, finding no substantial question of law), holding that CCI approval obtained any time prior to approval of the Plan by the Adjudicating Authority satisfies the statutory scheme. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: CCI approval for AGI Greenpac's Plan obtained on 15.03.2023, after CoC approval on 28.10.2022 but prior to approval by the Adjudicating Authority, satisfied Section 31(4) of the IBC; the NCLT's rejection of ISC's challenge to maintainability on this ground was upheld and the appeals were accordingly dismissed.
summary.operative_order: All four connected appeals (Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos.807, 607, 724 and 735 of 2023) dismissed; parties to bear their own costs. NCLT Kolkata's order dated 28.04.2023 rejecting I.A. No.1497/KB/2022 is affirmed on the sole question of interpretation of Section 31(4) proviso; NCLAT clarified it expressed no opinion on other issues raised by the parties, and the Adjudicating Authority was directed to proceed to consider the RP's separate application (I.A. No.1401 of 2022/2023) for approval of the Resolution Plan under Section 30(6), which had been kept pending.
summary.summary: In the CIRP of glass manufacturer Hindustan National Glass & Industries Ltd., the Committee of Creditors approved AGI Greenpac's resolution plan over a rival plan from Independent Sugar Corporation, even though AGI Greenpac's mandatory Competition Commission of India approval for the combination was obtained only months after the CoC vote (though before Adjudicating Authority approval). Independent Sugar Corporation, along with an industry body and workmen's unions, challenged this sequencing as a violation of the mandatory proviso to Section 31(4) of the IBC requiring CCI approval prior to CoC approval; NCLT Kolkata rejected the challenge. NCLAT, applying its own settled precedent (twice affirmed by the Supreme Court) that this timing requirement is directory rather than mandatory, dismissed all four connected appeals, holding that CCI approval obtained any time before Adjudicating Authority approval suffices, while leaving the RP's separate plan-approval application to proceed before NCLT.

summary.case_title: SMBC Aviation Capital Limited vs Go Airlines (India) Limited
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The corporate applicant is Go Airlines (India) Limited (Corporate Debtor / Corporate Applicant), and the appellants are aircraft lessors including SMBC Aviation Capital Ltd., SFV Aircraft Holdings IRE 9 DAC, GY Aviation Lease 1731 Co. Ltd., and Engine Leasing Finance B.V., with Abhilash Lal acting as the Interim Resolution Professional (IRP). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The appellants granted operating leases for aircraft to the corporate applicant, which operated low-cost airlines under the brand name 'Go Air'. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The corporate applicant defaulted on payments to operational creditors/vendors amounting to INR 1,202 Crores and default towards aircraft lessors aggregating to INR 2,660 Crores, as of the date of application. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The corporate applicant passed a resolution to file a Section 10 application on April 30, 2023, and officially filed the application before the NCLT on May 2, 2023. Prior to the petition's admission, lessors issued lease termination notices around May 2, 2023, and subsequently approached the DGCA for deregistration on May 5, 2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The corporate applicant faced financial distress due to defective engines supplied by Pratt & Whitney (P&W), resulting in 34% of its aircraft being grounded in 2022, leading to an emergency arbitration award by SIAC on February 3, 2023, and April 15, 2023, directing P&W to supply serviceable engines. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The original Section 10 petition was filed on May 2, 2023, and was admitted by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT, New Delhi Special Bench) via an order dated May 10, 2023, prompting the lessors to file these appeals.
summary.legal_issues: 1. Whether notice and an opportunity of hearing must be given to creditors prior to the admission of a Section 10 application. 2. Whether the Adjudicating Authority is bound to entertain and decide a Section 65 application alleging fraudulent and malicious intent prior to admitting a Section 10 application. 3. Whether the termination of lease agreements prior to the admission of a Section 10 application excludes the leased aircraft from the moratorium and asset pool of the corporate debtor.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory framework of Section 10 of the IBC does not mandate issuing pre-admission notices or hearings to creditors, and the decision to grant an opportunity to objectors rests on the sound discretion of the Adjudicating Authority depending on the facts of the case. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 10 and Section 65 must be read together harmoniously; however, there is no mandatory legal requirement to keep the admission of a Section 10 application pending or to pre-decide a prospective Section 65 application if sufficient grounds showing malicious intent are not made out at the pre-admission stage. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The allegation of fraudulent or malicious initiation requires clear proof of deceit resulting in injury or loss, and cannot be established merely by showing that the corporate applicant filed the petition to protect its assets from coercive repossession by lessors during ongoing operational viability efforts. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's admission order under Section 10, while granting liberty to the appellants to pursue appropriate remedies under Section 65 and Section 60(5) of the IBC before the Adjudicating Authority regarding lease terminations and asset possessions.
summary.operative_order: The order dated 10.05.2023 passed by the Adjudicating Authority admitting the Section 10 application is upheld. The appellants are granted liberty to file an application under Section 65 of the Code, and both the appellants and the IRP are granted liberty to file applications under Section 60(5) of the Code before the Adjudicating Authority for a declaration regarding the applicability of moratorium and claims to possession of the aircraft. Parties shall bear their own costs.
summary.summary: Four appeals were filed by aircraft lessors challenging the NCLT order dated May 10, 2023, which admitted a Section 10 application filed by Go Airlines (India) Limited for corporate insolvency resolution. The lessors argued that the petition was filed with malicious intent to frustrate lease terminations and that they were denied natural justice. The NCLAT held that Section 10 of the IBC does not mandate pre-admission notices to creditors and that the corporate applicant's filing was a genuine measure to handle operational crises caused by defective P&W engines rather than a fraudulent act. The appellate tribunal upheld the admission order while granting liberty to the lessors to approach the Adjudicating Authority under Sections 65 and 60(5) for specific reliefs regarding lease terminations and asset possession.

summary.case_title: Mr. Zubin Bharucha vs Reliance AIF Management Company Ltd. & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The appellant is Mr. Zubin Bharucha, former director of the Corporate Debtor (Bharucha & Motivala Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. / B & M Infra). Respondents No. 1 and 2 are Reliance AIF Management Company Ltd. and Reliance Nippon Life Asset Management Limited (Debenture Holders). Respondent No. 3 is the Corporate Debtor. The issuer company developing the residential project 'The Cove' is Lake District Realty Private Limited (LDRPL). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: LDRPL issued Non-Convertible Debentures (NCDs) worth Rs. 40,00,00,000/- on a private placement basis to raise funds for 'The Cove', subscribed by R1 and R2. B & M Infra executed a Deed of Irrevocable and Unconditional Guarantee and signed the Debenture Trust Deed as a Co-Obliger and Guarantor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Following project delays due to regulatory and NGT restrictions, an event of default occurred. A Demand Certificate dated 14.05.2019 was issued by the Debenture Trustee to B & M Infra demanding an amount of Rs. 37,51,64,939/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Debenture Trust Deed and Deed of Guarantee were executed on October 6, 2016. Event of Default notices were issued on January 2, 2019, and February 21, 2019. The Section 7 application was filed by the financial creditors on January 11, 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Transaction documents including the Debenture Trust Deed dated October 6, 2016, Deed of Irrevocable and Unconditional Guarantee, and the formal Demand Certificate dated May 14, 2019, established the debt and invocation of guarantee against the Co-Obliger. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The original Section 7 petition (C.P. (IB) No. 4108/MB/2019) was admitted by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT, Mumbai Bench, Court No. V) on May 6, 2021, initiating CIRP against the Corporate Debtor, which led to the present appeal.
summary.legal_issues: 1. Whether debenture holders (Respondents 1 and 2) qualify as 'Financial Creditors' under the IBC in light of the transaction documents and the Debenture Trust Deed. 2. Whether the Corporate Debtor, acting as a guarantor and co-obligor under a Deed of Guarantee, is liable for a 'Financial Debt' and subject to a Section 7 application under the IBC.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Subscribers to debentures and beneficiaries holding a direct guarantee or co-obligation status for repayment are recognized as financial creditors under Section 5(7) and Section 5(8) of the IBC, possessing independent statutory rights to initiate corporate insolvency resolution. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8)(c) and Section 5(8)(i) explicitly encompass amounts raised via debentures and liabilities arising from any guarantee or indemnity for such items within the definition of 'financial debt'. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: A corporate guarantor that signs a deed of guarantee as a primary obligor (co-obliger) and undertakes unconditional payment upon the issuance of a demand certificate by a debenture trustee has a direct, enforceable liability, distinguishing it from cases involving simple third-party collateral security or share pledges. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that the debenture holders are valid financial creditors and the corporate debtor's liability under the guarantee constitutes a financial debt, thereby justifying the NCLT's admission of the Section 7 application.
summary.operative_order: The appeal filed against the order dated 06.05.2021 passed by the Adjudicating Authority admitting the Section 7 application is dismissed as devoid of merit. Parties shall bear their own costs.
summary.summary: Mr. Zubin Bharucha, former director of Bharucha & Motivala Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor), filed an appeal under Section 61(1) of the IBC challenging the NCLT Mumbai order dated May 6, 2021, which admitted a Section 7 application filed by Reliance AIF Management Company and another. The debt arose from Non-Convertible Debentures (NCDs) issued by a group company, for which the Corporate Debtor acted as a co-obligor and guarantor. The appellant contended that no direct jural relationship or money disbursal existed between the debenture holders and the corporate debtor. The NCLAT ruled that debenture holders qualify as financial creditors and that a guarantee and co-obligation for debentures constitute a financial debt under Section 5(8) of the IBC. Finding no error in the Adjudicating Authority's judgment, the appellate tribunal dismissed the appeal and upheld the initiation of CIRP.

summary.case_title: Hotel and Restaurant Association of (Western India) & Anr. vs. Hotel and Restaurant Federation Association of Eastern India & Ors.
summary.appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) No. 162 of 2022 with Company Appeal (AT) No. 166 of 2022
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The appellants are the Hotel and Restaurant Association of Western India and the Hotel and Restaurant Association of Northern India along with other members, while Respondent No. 1 is the Hotel and Restaurant Association of Eastern India (HRAEI). Respondent No. 12 is the Federation of Hotel & Restaurant Associations of India (FHRAI). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The underlying dispute involves the internal corporate governance and election of the President of FHRAI, a company limited by guarantee without share capital, structured on a regional rotation basis among Eastern, Western, Southern, and Northern regional associations. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (corporate governance and election dispute under Sections 241-242 of the Companies Act, 2013). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Annual General Meeting and Executive Committee meeting for electing the President for the year 2018-19 took place on October 30, 2018. The company petition (CP No. 437/241-242/PB/2018) was subsequently filed before the NCLT, which passed its impugned order on August 30, 2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: During the Executive Committee meeting on October 30, 2018, alternative nominees declined the presidency or insisted on the Eastern Region's sole nominated candidate, Mr. Sudesh Kumar Poddar, whose appointment was blocked by a majority faction of Western and Northern region members, prompting allegations of minority oppression and high-handed procedural conduct by the sitting president, Mr. Garish Oberoi. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Company Petition No. 437/241-242/PB/2018 was filed alleging oppression and mismanagement, and the NCLT granted a waiver under Section 244 of the Companies Act, 2013, eventually ruling in favor of the petitioners via order dated August 30, 2022, which led to the present appeals.
summary.legal_issues: 1. Whether the petitioners in the original company petition were entitled to maintain the action under Sections 241-242 and whether the grant of waiver under Section 244 of the Companies Act, 2013 was valid. 2. Whether the blockage of the regional nominee for the presidency and the procedural conduct during the Executive Committee meeting constitute acts of oppression and mismanagement. 3. Whether a sole regional nominee can be elected unopposed under Article 52 of the Articles of Association as a valid election.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Exceptional circumstances and a continuous pattern of prejudicial conduct impacting corporate democracy justify the grant of a waiver under Section 244 of the Companies Act to enable minority members or regional associations to maintain a petition for oppression and mismanagement. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The term 'election' under Article 52 of the Articles of Association does not exclude an uncontested or unopposed election of a single eligible candidate proposed by the entitled region pursuant to established rotational traditions. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Coordinated efforts by a majority faction to block a qualified regional candidate without rational legal justification, combined with high-handed continuation of meetings by retiring office bearers, constitute continuous acts of oppression and mismanagement rather than mere directorial complaints. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT dismissed the appeals, upholding the NCLT's order granting waiver and finding the election obstruction to be oppressive, and directed the completion of the election process for the year 2018-19 within 30 days.
summary.operative_order: The appeals (Company Appeal (AT) No. 162 of 2022 and Company Appeal (AT) No. 166 of 2022) are dismissed, and the NCLT order dated August 30, 2022, is upheld. The election for the post of President of FHRAI for the year 2018-19 shall be completed within 30 days of the judgment. There is no order as to costs.
summary.summary: Appeals were filed against the NCLT order dated August 30, 2022, which held that the majority faction of the Executive Committee of the Federation of Hotel & Restaurant Associations of India (FHRAI) acted oppressively by blocking the appointment of the Eastern Region's nominated candidate, Mr. Sudesh Kumar Poddar, as President for 2018-19. The appellants argued that the petition was not maintainable, lacked proper waiver under Section 244, and involved only a directorial dispute. The NCLAT held that the waiver was correctly granted due to exceptional circumstances, that the coordinated obstruction of the rotational election constituted oppression and mismanagement, and that an uncontested election of a sole eligible regional candidate is fully valid under the Articles of Association. The appellate tribunal dismissed the appeals and directed the election process to be concluded within 30 days.

summary.case_title: M/s. GVK Energy Limited & Anr. vs. Axis Bank Limited & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The 1st appellant is M/s. GVK Energy Limited (100% shareholder of the corporate debtor), the 2nd appellant is Mr. Palicherla Venkata Prasanna Reddy (suspended director), the 1st respondent is Axis Bank Limited (Financial Creditor), and the 2nd respondent is Mr. Ravi Sethia (Interim Resolution Professional of GVK Power (Goindwal Sahib) Limited). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The corporate debtor availed multiple term loan facilities and working capital facilities starting from February 1, 2010, aggregating to a total debt of over INR 3,000 Crores from a consortium of 13 financial institutions to part-finance a 540 MW coal-fired thermal power plant in Punjab, alongside priority facilities extended by priority lenders. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The corporate debtor committed defaults in repayments, and its loan account was classified as a Non-Performing Asset (NPA) on November 29, 2017. The claimed default amount by the 1st respondent as of November 30, 2019, stood at Rs. 442,20,14,321.40/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: An Inter-Creditor Agreement (ICA) was executed on July 6, 2019, following RBI directions dated June 7, 2019. The 1st respondent issued a loan recall notice on December 17, 2019, and filed the Section 7 application on December 20, 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The corporate debtor issued a revival letter on June 13, 2019, acknowledging the debt, and a record of default was filed with NeSL. Disputes also arose concerning project capital cost approvals from the Punjab State Electricity Regulatory Commission (PSERC) and priority payments under the Trust and Retention Account (TRA) agreement. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT, Hyderabad Bench-I) admitted the Section 7 petition via an order dated October 10, 2022 (CP (IB) No. 43/7/HDB/2020), placing the corporate debtor under CIRP, which was challenged in this appeal.
summary.legal_issues: 1. Whether the Section 7 application filed by the financial creditor was premature and barred by the standstill clauses of the Inter-Creditor Agreement (ICA) and RBI Directions of 2019. 2. Whether the existence of priority financing arrangements and priority repayment obligations to priority lenders acts as a legal bar against the initiation of CIRP by senior lenders. 3. Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in exercising its discretion to admit the Section 7 application despite pending tariff appeals before APTEL.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory right of a financial creditor to initiate corporate insolvency resolution under Section 7 of the IBC cannot be curtailed, overridden, or made subservient to any inter-creditor agreement or RBI circular framework once a debt and default are established. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Extension of the standstill period beyond the initial 30 days under the regulatory framework and ICA requires a positive decision by lenders to implement a resolution plan; in the absence of a submitted or approved resolution plan, the standstill period does not expand to 180 days. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Inter se priority distribution arrangements among lenders and trust and retention account (TRA) mechanisms do not absolve the corporate debtor from its independent payment obligations to senior lenders or extinguish an established financial debt and default. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that the financial creditor successfully proved the existence of financial debt and default exceeding the threshold limit, justifying the admission of the Section 7 application and dismissing the appeal.
summary.operative_order: The appeal (Comp. App (AT) (CH) (INS.) No. 385 of 2022) is dismissed with no order as to costs, and all pending interlocutory applications are closed. The Adjudicating Authority's order admitting the Section 7 petition and initiating CIRP is upheld, with instructions to the registry to ensure accurate certified copy issuance.
summary.summary: M/s. GVK Energy Limited and its suspended director filed an appeal against the NCLT Hyderabad order dated October 10, 2022, which admitted a Section 7 application filed by Axis Bank Limited and initiated CIRP against GVK Power (Goindwal Sahib) Limited. The appellants argued that the petition was premature under the Inter-Creditor Agreement and RBI circulars, and that priority lenders had superior repayment rights over cash flows. The NCLAT ruled that an Inter-Creditor Agreement cannot override the statutory right of a financial creditor under Section 7 of the IBC, and that the failure to formulate a resolution plan within the initial review period ended any standstill protection. Finding no legal error in the proof of debt and default, the appellate tribunal dismissed the appeal and upheld the initiation of corporate insolvency resolution.

summary.case_title: SREI Industrial Finance Ltd. vs. Satish Kumar Gupta, R.P. of Essar Steel Ltd. & Ors.
summary.appeal_number: I.A. No. 647 of 2023 in Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 242 of 2019
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The applicants in I.A. No. 647 of 2023 are SREI Industrial Finance Ltd. (Applicant No. 1, represented through an Administrator) and Ms. Limalemla Longkumer, a shareholder of Applicant No. 1 (Applicant No. 2, claiming derivative rights). Respondents include Satish Kumar Gupta (Resolution Professional of Essar Steel Ltd.), the Committee of Creditors (CoC), ArcelorMittal India Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant), and Standard Chartered Bank. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate insolvency resolution process (CIRP) was triggered against Essar Steel India Ltd. following applications filed by Standard Chartered Bank and State Bank of India, leading to the approval of a resolution plan submitted by ArcelorMittal India Pvt. Ltd. with total admitted claims exceeding Rs. 54,549 Crores. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The corporate debtor defaulted on financial debts owed to financial creditors, resulting in the admission of Section 7 petitions under the IBC on August 2, 2017. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The NCLT approved the resolution plan on March 8, 2019. The NCLAT delivered its detailed final judgment on the appeals on July 4, 2019. Subsequently, the Supreme Court delivered a comprehensive judgment on November 15, 2019, settling the matter. The recall application (I.A. No. 647 of 2023) was filed in February 2023, more than 3.5 years later. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The applicant alleged that the 2019 NCLAT judgment was obtained by fraud and suppression of material facts—specifically regarding affidavits filed before the Sealdah Civil Court and stances taken by the OSPIL resolution professional concerning pipeline asset ownership and right-to-use charges. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Standard Chartered Bank and other entities previously filed appeals against the NCLT resolution plan approval, which were adjudicated by the NCLAT on July 4, 2019, and later merged with the Supreme Court's judgment on November 15, 2019. In February 2023, the applicants filed I.A. No. 647 of 2023 seeking intervention and recall of the NCLAT's July 4, 2019 judgment, which the NCLAT heard and dismissed on maintainability grounds on March 31, 2023.
summary.legal_issues: 1. Whether an application for the recall of a final judgment passed by the Appellate Tribunal is maintainable under Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016, in the absence of provisions for review or recall under the IBC. 2. Whether the doctrine of merger applies to extinguish the Appellate Tribunal's judgment once it has been adjudicated and merged with the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court. 3. Whether a shareholder can maintain a recall application claiming derivative rights when the company is under the control of an appointed administrator, and whether allegations of fraud bypass the doctrine of merger and locus standi requirements.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In the absence of explicit statutory provisions for review or recall under the IBC or NCLAT Rules—save for correcting clerical or typographical errors—a final and binding judgment of the Appellate Tribunal cannot be recalled or reviewed under inherent powers (Rule 11). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Once an appeal is preferred against an order of a tribunal and is decided by the Hon'ble Supreme Court, the subordinate forum's decision merges completely into the superior forum's decision by operation of the doctrine of merger, leaving the latter as the only subsisting and enforceable order. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: General allegations of fraud and suppression cannot be used by a third-party shareholder lacking locus standi—without any foundational order under Section 340 of the CrPC or prior party status—to bypass the doctrine of merger and reopen settled, final litigation years after the Supreme Court's adjudication. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT dismissed the recall application as completely non-maintainable due to lack of locus standi, absence of a review/recall power, and the operation of the doctrine of merger with the Supreme Court's judgment, while reserving the right to order an in-depth investigation if further evidence of malicious motives arises.
summary.operative_order: The intervention and recall application (I.A. No. 647 of 2023 in Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 242 of 2019) is dismissed on the ground of maintainability and lack of locus standi, with an indication that the tribunal may consider initiating an in-depth investigation by an appropriate agency if further evidence regarding ulterior motives is brought forward.
summary.summary: An interlocutory application (I.A. No. 647 of 2023) was filed by SREI Industrial Finance Ltd. through a shareholder claiming derivative rights, seeking to recall the NCLAT's detailed final judgment dated July 4, 2019, concerning the Essar Steel insolvency resolution. The applicants argued that the judgment was obtained through fraud and concealment of material facts regarding pipeline ownership and contempt issues. The respondents vehemently challenged the maintainability of the application, citing a lack of statutory review powers, the absence of locus standi, and the operation of the doctrine of merger following the Supreme Court's final verdict dated November 15, 2019. The NCLAT held that it possesses no inherent power under Rule 11 to review or recall a final judgment, that general allegations of fraud cannot override the doctrine of merger with the Apex Court's ruling, and that a shareholder cannot bypass an appointed administrator to initiate such proceedings. The application was accordingly dismissed.

summary.case_title: State Bank of India vs. Dharmraj Aluminium Industries Private Limited
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The appellant is the State Bank of India (Financial Creditor), and the respondent is Dharmraj Aluminium Industries Private Limited (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The bank sanctioned a Cash Credit Facility of Rs. 7 crores and a Forward Contract of Rs. 0.2 crores on February 1, 2013, which were renewed and advanced from time to time. 3.
