DEFAULT METRICS: Default occurred on January 30, 2016, and the account was classified as a Non-Performing Asset (NPA) on April 29, 2016, with an outstanding claim amount of Rs. 22,52,02,115.61/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The bank issued a notice under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act on May 2, 2016, and filed O.A. No. 762 of 2017 before the DRT. A winding up petition filed by a third party (M/s Oswal Minerals Limited) was allowed by the Bombay High Court on January 25, 2018. The bank filed its Section 7 application on January 13, 2022. The Corporate Debtor subsequently submitted a One Time Settlement (OTS) offer letter on July 8, 2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The corporate debtor did not appear or file a reply before the Adjudicating Authority. The appellant introduced an OTS offer letter dated July 8, 2021, for the first time during the appeal proceedings to claim an extension of limitation under Section 25(3) of the Contract Act. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT, Mumbai Bench, Court-IV) dismissed the Section 7 application on November 29, 2022, as barred by limitation, holding that the bank could not claim the benefit of Section 14 of the Limitation Act based on a third-party winding-up petition, which led to the present appeal.
summary.legal_issues: 1. Whether the appellant is entitled to the exclusion of time under Section 14 of the Limitation Act on account of a third-party winding-up petition and pending DRT/SARFAESI proceedings. 2. Whether a One Time Settlement (OTS) offer letter can serve as a valid promise to pay a time-barred debt under Section 25(3) of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, extending the period of limitation.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The benefit of Section 14(2) of the Limitation Act is restricted to situations where the same party has been prosecuting another civil proceeding with due diligence in good faith for the same relief, and cannot be claimed based on a winding-up petition or proceedings initiated by a third party. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 25(3) of the Contract Act allows a debtor to enter into a written and signed agreement to pay a time-barred debt wholly or in part, which constitutes a valid contract and fresh basis for limitation, provided certain statutory conditions are met. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: A written OTS proposal submitted by a debtor acknowledging the debt and offering a settlement amount satisfies the preliminary elements of Section 25(3) of the Contract Act, requiring the adjudicating forum to afford an opportunity to the parties to examine its effect on limitation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT upheld the rejection of the benefit under Section 14 of the Limitation Act, but partly allowed the appeal by setting aside the dismissal of the Section 7 application and remanding the matter back to the Adjudicating Authority to decide afresh solely on the effect and consequence of the One Time Settlement offer dated July 8, 2021.
summary.operative_order: The appeal is partly allowed, the order dated November 29, 2022, passed by the Adjudicating Authority is set aside, and the Section 7 application is revived. The Adjudicating Authority is directed to decide afresh the claim of the bank based on the One Time Settlement offer dated July 8, 2021, after granting the Corporate Debtor one month's time to file a reply restricted to the OTS offer. The appellant's claim to the benefit of Section 14 of the Limitation Act stands finally rejected. No order as to costs.
summary.summary: State Bank of India filed an appeal against an NCLT Mumbai order dismissing its Section 7 application against Dharmraj Aluminium Industries Private Limited as barred by limitation. The appellant argued for the exclusion of time under Section 14 of the Limitation Act due to pending DRT and winding-up proceedings, and alternatively claimed an extension of limitation based on a One Time Settlement (OTS) letter dated July 8, 2021, under Section 25(3) of the Contract Act. The NCLAT rejected the applicability of Section 14 based on third-party winding-up proceedings, but agreed that the effect of the OTS offer under Section 25(3) required examination. Consequently, the appellate tribunal set aside the dismissal order, revived the Section 7 petition, and remanded the matter back to the Adjudicating Authority to determine limitation specifically regarding the OTS proposal after granting the corporate debtor an opportunity to reply.

summary.case_title: V. Ganesan, Erstwhile Liquidator of Kamachi Industries Ltd. vs. Prudent ARC Limited
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The appellant is V. Ganesan, erstwhile liquidator of Kamachi Industries Ltd., and the respondent is Prudent ARC Limited[cite: 8]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Prudent ARC Limited filed an application before the Adjudicating Authority under Regulation 31A(6) of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016 read with Section 60(5) of the IBC seeking to convene a stakeholders consultation committee meeting to replace the liquidator[cite: 8]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (liquidation governance and liquidator replacement dispute). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Adjudicating Authority passed the order replacing the liquidator on September 20, 2023[cite: 8]. The appellant filed a writ petition on September 25, 2023, which was dismissed on November 1, 2023, followed by a dismissed SLP on November 9, 2023, leading to the NCLAT appeal filed on November 14, 2023 (53rd day). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Adjudicating Authority found that inter se discord and vacillation by the liquidator caused a stalemate and detriment to the liquidation estate[cite: 8]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT allowed the application and replaced the liquidator on September 20, 2023[cite: 8]. After unsuccessful writ and SLP proceedings, the appellant filed this appeal under Section 61 of the IBC[cite: 8].
summary.legal_issues: 1. Whether the appellant is entitled to the exclusion of time under Section 14 of the Limitation Act, 1963 for prosecuting a writ petition and an SLP. 2. Whether the appeal filed on the 53rd day is barred by limitation under Section 61 of the IBC.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A party claiming the benefit of Section 14 of the Limitation Act must establish that prior proceedings were prosecuted with due diligence and in good faith. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61 of the IBC mandates a 30-day limitation period extendable by a maximum of 15 days, and cannot be extended beyond 45 days. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: A liquidator with full knowledge of statutory appeal options who bypasses an alternative efficacious remedy to engage in protracted writ proceedings and unmaintainable SLPs against a relegation order cannot be deemed to be prosecuting with due diligence or in good faith. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that the appellant was not entitled to Section 14 benefits, rendering the appeal barred by limitation and subject to dismissal.
summary.operative_order: The appeal (Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 396 of 2023) is dismissed as barred by limitation. No order as to costs.
summary.summary: V. Ganesan, the erstwhile liquidator of Kamachi Industries Limited, appealed an NCLT order dated September 20, 2023, which replaced him with an Insolvency Professional Entity due to a stalemate in the liquidation process[cite: 8]. Having spent time pursuing a writ petition in the Madras High Court and an SLP in the Supreme Court, the appellant filed the NCLAT appeal on the 53rd day, seeking time exclusion under Section 14 of the Limitation Act[cite: 8]. The NCLAT ruled that the appellant did not act with due diligence or in good faith given his legal standing as a liquidator and knowledge of statutory remedies. Consequently, the benefit of Section 14 was denied, and the appeal was dismissed as barred by limitation[cite: 8].

summary.case_title: Indiabulls Housing Finance Ltd. vs. Kalpataru Properties Pvt. Ltd. and Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Indiabulls Housing Finance Ltd. (Financial Creditor), Respondent No. 1 is Kalpataru Properties Pvt. Ltd. (Decree Holder/Purchaser), and the Corporate Debtor is Shree Ram Urban Infrastructure Ltd., with SREI Equipment Finance Ltd. acting as an intervening Financial Creditor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: On June 28, 2004, a Memorandum of Understanding was executed between the Corporate Debtor, its sister concern Vijay Infrastructure Technology Pvt. Ltd., and Respondent No. 1 for the transfer of a 20,955.40 sq. mts. property at Plot No. 5A, Lower Parel Division, for a total consideration of Rs. 30 Crores. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Corporate Debtor failed to complete the sale transaction and sought to resile from the agreement in 2005, prompting arbitration. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: An Arbitral Award was passed on August 29, 2016, directing specific performance. Following the initiation of corporate insolvency, Respondent No. 1 sent a compliance letter on October 12, 2018, offering the balance consideration of Rs. 75,30,00,000/- upon conveyance execution. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The core evidence included the MoU dated June 28, 2004, the Arbitral Tribunal Award dated August 29, 2016, and subsequent Bombay High Court rulings under Section 34 and Section 37 upholding the award. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: A Section 7 petition was filed by SREI Equipment Finance Ltd., and the Corporate Debtor was admitted into CIRP on November 6, 2019. Respondent No. 1 filed I.A. No. 1921 of 2021 before the NCLT Mumbai, which allowed the application on October 8, 2021, directing execution of the conveyance deed upon payment of the balance consideration, leading to the current appeal.
summary.legal_issues: Whether an intervener who has not filed an independent appeal can challenge or prevent the withdrawal of an appeal by the appellant, and whether the execution of an arbitral award for specific performance during CIRP is barred by Section 14 of the IBC.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An intervenor in an appellate proceeding is limited to addressing arguments in support of or against existing parties and cannot claim independent relief or prevent the primary appellant from withdrawing the appeal without having filed an independent challenge within statutory limitation periods. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The strict timelines under Section 61 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code preclude third parties from riding piggyback on active appeals to bypass limitation bars. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Proceedings governed by special statutes like the IBC must respect prescribed procedural diligence, rendering intervenor objections secondary to active party settlements. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the appellant sought to withdraw the appeal pursuant to statements recorded before the Supreme Court and the intervener failed to file an independent appeal, the appeal was dismissed as withdrawn and the intervention application was rejected.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 880 of 2021 is dismissed as withdrawn, and I.A. No. 2623 of 2021 filed by SREI Equipment Finance Ltd. for intervention and setting aside the NCLT order is rejected.
summary.summary: This case involves an appeal filed by Indiabulls Housing Finance Ltd. against an NCLT Mumbai order directing the Resolution Professional to execute a conveyance deed in favor of Kalpataru Properties Pvt. Ltd. pursuant to a binding 2016 arbitral award. SREI Equipment Finance Ltd. sought to intervene and oppose the execution during CIRP under Section 14 of the IBC. The NCLAT held that an intervenor who fails to file an independent appeal within statutory timelines cannot prevent the primary appellant from withdrawing its appeal. Consequently, the appellate tribunal dismissed the appeal as withdrawn and rejected the intervention application, allowing the transfer to proceed upon deposit of the balance consideration.

summary.case_title: Sanchit Kumar Agarwal vs. APG Logistics Private Limited
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Sanket Kumar Agarwal and Sanchit Kumar Agarwal, and the Respondent is APG Logistics Private Limited. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: An appeal filed under Section 61 of the IBC against the order passed by the Adjudicating Authority in CP/IB/113/CHE/2021. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable, as the proceedings relate to a limitation and delay condonation issue. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The impugned order was pronounced on August 26, 2022. The certified copy was provided on September 15, 2022, and the appeal was filed via the E-Portal on October 10, 2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: E-portal filing records and transaction reference numbers establishing that the online filing occurred on October 10, 2022, which was the 46th day from the pronouncement date. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Chennai dismissed the original petition on August 26, 2022. The Appellants filed Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins.) No. 418 of 2022 along with IA No. 1025 of 2022 seeking to condone a 5-day delay, which the Respondent opposed as being barred by time beyond the 45-day statutory limit.
summary.legal_issues: Whether an appeal filed under Section 61 of the IBC on the 46th day from the pronouncement of the impugned order can be entertained when the Appellate Tribunal's power to condone delay is strictly restricted to a maximum of 15 days beyond the initial 30-day period.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 61 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, the limitation period for filing an appeal is 30 days from the date of order pronouncement, with a maximum condonable extension of 15 days upon sufficient cause, beyond which the tribunal lacks jurisdiction. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61 of the IBC operates as a special self-contained code that overrides general limitation provisions and does not permit extension beyond the 45-day outer ceiling. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The appellant must file the appeal within the absolute statutory limit of 45 days (30 days plus 15 days); filing on the 46th day or later extinguishes the tribunal's discretionary power to condone delay. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the appeal was filed on the 46th day, exceeding the statutory outer limit of 45 days under Section 61(2) of the IBC, the delay condonation application was dismissed and the appeal was rejected as time-barred.
summary.operative_order: IA No. 1025 of 2022 is dismissed, and Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS.) No. 418 of 2022 is rejected as barred by time.
summary.summary: This case involves an appeal filed by Sanchit Kumar Agarwal and another against APG Logistics Private Limited, challenging an order dated August 26, 2022, passed by NCLT Chennai. The Appellants filed the appeal on October 10, 2022, which marked the 46th day from the date of pronouncement, along with an application to condone a 5-day delay. The NCLAT Chennai held that the 30-day limitation period under Section 61 of the IBC commences from the date of order pronouncement, and the tribunal's power to condone delay is strictly capped at an additional 15 days (total 45 days). Because the appeal was filed on the 46th day, exceeding the statutory outer limit, the delay condonation application was dismissed and the appeal was rejected as time-barred.

summary.case_title: Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. vs. HSA Traders & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. (power distribution company), Respondent No. 1 is HSA Traders (successful auction purchaser), Respondent No. 2 is Ezwaste Recycling Private Limited, and Respondent No. 3 is Chanchal Dua (erstwhile liquidator of Shashi Oils and Fats Private Limited). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The corporate debtor underwent liquidation, and an e-auction notice dated August 12, 2020, was published to sell its assets on an 'as is where is, as is what is, whatever there is and without recourse basis'. Respondent No. 1 emerged as the highest bidder for Rs. 3,78,00,000/- and was issued a sale and possession certificate after paying the full consideration and GST. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: There were outstanding pre-CIRP electricity dues amounting to Rs. 39,15,625/- owed by the erstwhile corporate debtor. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The liquidation order was passed on February 21, 2020; the e-auction was held on August 29, 2020; full payment and sale certificate issuance occurred by September 28, 2020; and the Adjudicating Authority passed the impugned order on February 21, 2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: E-auction terms specifying sale on an 'as is where is' basis, along with the appellant's refusal letter demanding payment of arrears prior to granting a new electricity connection. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The liquidator never filed a claim for electricity dues during liquidation. After the appellant rejected the application for a new electricity connection due to pending pre-CIRP dues, Respondent No. 1 filed I.A. No. 219 of 2022 under CP (IB) No. 140/ALD/2017 before NCLT Allahabad, which allowed the application on February 21, 2023, directing the appellant to energize the connection without insisting on pre-CIRP dues.
summary.legal_issues: Whether a power distribution company can legally insist upon the payment of pre-CIRP electricity arrears of an erstwhile corporate debtor as a pre-condition for granting a new electricity connection to a successful auction purchaser under the IBC.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The clean slate principle under the IBC prevents power distribution companies from insisting on the payment of pre-CIRP arrears of a corporate debtor as a condition for granting a new electricity connection to a successful auction purchaser. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60(5) of the IBC grants the Adjudicating Authority full jurisdiction to entertain applications arising out of or in relation to insolvency resolution or liquidation proceedings, such as disputes concerning utility connections demanded by auction purchasers. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Pre-CIRP operational debts or utility dues must be claimed and satisfied strictly through the liquidation waterfall mechanism under Section 53 of the IBC, and unsubmitted claims stand extinguished. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the appellant failed to file its claim during the liquidation process and the corporate debtor's past liabilities stood extinguished, the appellant cannot refuse a new electricity connection or burden the successful auction purchaser with pre-CIRP arrears.
summary.operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, and the impugned order dated February 21, 2023, passed by the Adjudicating Authority is upheld, requiring the appellant to energize the electricity connection without insisting on pre-CIRP dues.
summary.summary: This case involves an appeal filed by Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. against an NCLT Allahabad order directing it to grant a new electricity connection to a successful auction purchaser without demanding pre-CIRP dues of Rs. 39,15,625/- owed by the erstwhile corporate debtor, Shashi Oils and Fats Private Limited. The NCLAT held that since the appellant failed to file its claim during the liquidation process, its pre-CIRP dues stood extinguished under the clean slate principle, and it could not refuse a fresh electricity connection to the auction purchaser based on past unpaid liabilities. Consequently, the appeal was dismissed.

summary.case_title: GRI Towers India Pvt. Ltd. vs. Inox Wind Limited
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is GRI Towers India Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor), and the Respondent is Inox Wind Limited (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Three purchase orders were issued on February 23, 2013, October 23, 2013, and August 28, 2017. Under the first two purchase orders, 65 invoices amounting to Rs. 3,61,40,025/- were issued, of which Rs. 2,88,84,623/- was paid, leaving an unpaid principal of Rs. 72,55,402/-. Under the third purchase order, three invoices totaling Rs. 21,91,122/- were issued. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The total principal claimed in default was Rs. 94,46,524/- plus interest, with the date of default stated as April 30, 2015, for Stage 1 and October 23, 2018, for Stage 2. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: A civil recovery suit (Suit No. 67 of 2017) was filed on October 3, 2017, and withdrawn on July 18, 2022. A demand notice was issued on July 27, 2022, claiming Rs. 1,78,78,390/-. The Section 9 application was filed on December 5, 2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The civil court order permitting the withdrawal of Suit No. 67 of 2017 subject to a cost of Rs. 5,000/- without granting liberty to file a fresh suit. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh dismissed the Section 9 application via an order dated May 22, 2023, holding that the claim was barred by limitation and failed to meet the statutory threshold of Rs. 1 Crore without valid interest calculations, leading to the present appeal.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the time spent prosecuting a civil recovery suit that was subsequently withdrawn voluntarily without liberty to file a fresh suit can be excluded under Section 14 of the Limitation Act to bring a Section 9 IBC application within the limitation period.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The benefit of Section 14 of the Limitation Act requires that the prior proceeding failed due to a defect of jurisdiction or other cause of a like nature resulting in the court's inability to entertain it, and cannot be invoked when a party voluntarily withdraws its suit without obtaining liberty to institute a fresh proceeding. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14 and Section 5 of the Limitation Act cannot be stretched to save time lost in voluntary withdrawals or to bypass the strict three-year limitation period from the date of default under Article 137 of the Limitation Act read with Section 238A of the IBC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: To claim exclusion under Section 14, the cumulative statutory conditions—specifically that the prior proceeding failed due to jurisdictional defects—must be strictly satisfied. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the appellant withdrew its civil suit voluntarily without liberty and without any jurisdictional defect, the time spent during the suit cannot be excluded, rendering the Section 9 application time-barred.
summary.operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, upholding the Adjudicating Authority's order dated May 22, 2023, which dismissed the Section 9 application as barred by limitation.
summary.summary: This case involves an appeal filed by GRI Towers India Pvt. Ltd. against an NCLT Chandigarh order dismissing its Section 9 application under the IBC against Inox Wind Limited. The operational creditor had previously filed a civil recovery suit in 2017, which it voluntarily withdrew in July 2022 without liberty to file a fresh suit, before initiating corporate insolvency proceedings in December 2022. The NCLAT held that the time spent prosecuting the civil suit could not be excluded under Section 14 of the Limitation Act because the suit did not fail due to a defect of jurisdiction. Consequently, since the default occurred in 2015 for Stage 1, the Section 9 application was barred by limitation, and the appeal was dismissed.

summary.case_title: Exide Industries Ltd. vs. Jitender Kumar Jain, Resolution Professional of Morakhia Copper & Alloys Pvt. Ltd.
summary.appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1169 of 2022 & I.A. No. 3522 of 2022
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Exide Industries Ltd. (an aggrieved creditor/entity); Respondent is Jitender Kumar Jain, Resolution Professional of the Corporate Debtor Morakhia Copper & Alloys Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 6] 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying corporate insolvency proceedings involving Morakhia Copper & Alloys Pvt. Ltd. wherein the impugned order was rendered by the Adjudicating Authority[cite: 6]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Monetary default sums and specific underlying default dates are not specified in the appellate order[cite: 6]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The impugned order of the Adjudicating Authority was pronounced on 06.07.2022[cite: 6]. Appellant received a free certified copy on 27.07.2022[cite: 6]. The appeal was e-filed on 30.08.2022 and physical copies were submitted on 05.09.2022[cite: 6]. An application for condonation of delay (I.A. No. 3522 of 2022) was preferred[cite: 6]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Free certified copy received on 27.07.2022 alongside filings establishing the dates of pronouncement and electronic/physical presentation[cite: 6]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Aggrieved by an order dated 06.07.2022 passed by the Adjudicating Authority, Appellant filed the appeal beyond the 30-day period plus the 15-day condonable limit calculated from the date of pronouncement, contending limitation ran from receipt of the free certified copy[cite: 6].
summary.legal_issues: Whether the limitation period for preferring an appeal under Section 61 of the IBC commences from the date of pronouncement of the impugned order or from the date of receipt of a free certified copy, and whether the Appellate Tribunal has jurisdiction to condone a delay exceeding fifteen days beyond the initial thirty-day period[cite: 6].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The limitation clock for filing an appeal under the IBC begins running from the date the order is pronounced, not when a free certified copy is received; an appellant cannot stop limitation from running by awaiting a free certified copy, and the appellate tribunal's jurisdiction to condone delay is strictly limited to fifteen days beyond the initial thirty-day timeline[cite: 6]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(1) and (2) of the IBC consciously omit the phrase 'order is made available to the aggrieved party' (in contrast to Section 421(3) of the Companies Act, 2013)[cite: 6]. In terms of the Supreme Court's ruling in V. Nagarajan v. SKS Ispat and Power Ltd., an aggrieved party must exercise due diligence by applying for a certified copy upon pronouncement, and the proviso to Section 61(2) restricts condonation jurisdiction strictly to a maximum of 15 days[cite: 6]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Date of pronouncement of the order versus the date of presentation/e-filing of the appeal, without allowing the date of receipt of a free copy to extend the statutory timeline[cite: 6]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the appeal was filed beyond the condonable threshold of fifteen days from the expiry of the thirty-day limitation running from pronouncement (06.07.2022), the delay condonation application is non-maintainable and must be dismissed, necessitating rejection of the appeal[cite: 6].
summary.operative_order: I.A. No. 3522 of 2022 (application for condonation of delay) is dismissed; consequently, the Memo of Appeal is rejected[cite: 6].
summary.summary: Exide Industries Ltd. appealed against an order of the Adjudicating Authority pronounced on 6th July 2022[cite: 6]. The appeal was e-filed on 30th August 2022 and physically filed on 5th September 2022, accompanied by an application for condonation of delay arguing that limitation should run from 27th July 2022, when a free certified copy was received[cite: 6]. Applying the Supreme Court's precedent in V. Nagarajan v. SKS Ispat and Power Ltd., the NCLAT held that limitation begins running from the date of order pronouncement and cannot be arrested by awaiting a free copy[cite: 6]. Given the delay exceeded the maximum 15-day condonable period under Section 61(2), the delay application was dismissed and the appeal rejected[cite: 6].

summary.case_title: Puneet Kaur & Ors. vs. K V Developers Private Limited & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants (Puneet Kaur, Mayukh Chakraborthy, Mahesh Chandra Sahu, Shruti Anand, Ravi Raghavachary, and Shabnam) are homebuyers/allottees of real estate Corporate Debtor K V Developers Private Limited (Respondent No. 1); Respondent No. 2 is Pankaj Narang, Resolution Professional; Respondent No. 3 is the Committee of Creditors; Respondent No. 4 is the Consortium of Sumit Kumar Khanna and M/s Brij Kishore Trading Pvt. Ltd., the Successful Resolution Applicant[cite: 7]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Allotment of residential apartments/flats by Corporate Debtor under allotment letters and builder-buyer agreements, against which substantial advance purchase considerations were collected[cite: 7]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose following admission of Section 7 petition by LIC Housing Finance Ltd. on 28.10.2020[cite: 7]. Claims submitted by Appellants were: Puneet Kaur (Rs. 23,18,422/-); Mayukh Chakraborthy (Rs. 34,00,000/-); Mahesh Chandra Sahu & Shruti Anand (Rs. 27,57,259/-); Ravi Raghavachary (Rs. 18,63,489/-); Shabnam (Rs. 38,55,267/-)[cite: 7]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Public announcement in Form-A issued on 30.10.2020 setting cut-off date as 11.11.2020[cite: 7]. Resolution Plan submitted by SRA on 09.04.2021 and approved by CoC on 20.07.2021[cite: 7]. Appellants filed claims belatedly between 14.07.2021 and 09.11.2021, and subsequent IAs before NCLT were dismissed between 26.10.2021 and 04.01.2022[cite: 7]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor's audited books of accounts, builder-buyer agreements, allotment letters, and payment receipts clearly reflecting homebuyers' identity, allotments, and received consideration[cite: 7]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench-III rejected Appellants' interim applications (I.A. Nos. 5146/2021, 4864/2021, 5119/2021, 4863/2021, and 5602/2021) seeking admission of claims, holding that claims filed after an eight-month delay cannot be entertained once CoC has approved the Resolution Plan[cite: 7].
summary.legal_issues: Whether the claims of homebuyers stand extinguished upon approval of a Resolution Plan by the CoC prior to its approval by the Adjudicating Authority, and whether the Resolution Professional is statutorily obligated under Regulation 36 of the CIRP Regulations to include liabilities towards all homebuyers reflected in the Corporate Debtor's books in the Information Memorandum even if they failed to submit timely claims[cite: 7].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Claims of creditors do not stand extinguished upon the Committee of Creditors approving a resolution plan; extinguishment occurs only when the Adjudicating Authority approves the plan under Section 31(1) of the IBC[cite: 7]. Furthermore, the Resolution Professional is mandated to reflect all known corporate liabilities—including allottee advance payments found in company records—in the Information Memorandum so that resolution applicants can comprehensively address them[cite: 7]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 31(1) read with the Supreme Court doctrine in Ghanashyam Mishra confirms that statutory finality and extinguishment of unprovided claims operate only upon approval by the Adjudicating Authority[cite: 7]. The term 'liabilities' under Regulation 36(2)(a) and 'other information' under Regulation 36(2)(l) of the CIRP Regulations encompasses all binding financial and contractual obligations reflected in corporate books, requiring their inclusion to avoid inequitable resolution[cite: 7]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Presence of undisputed allottee records, executed agreements, and payment entries within the books and records of the corporate debtor[cite: 7]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Although the NCLT did not err in refusing belated addition into the List of Creditors after CoC plan approval, justice requires that reflected liabilities towards non-claimant homebuyers must not be discarded; the RP must supply all reflected records to the SRA to prepare an addendum for CoC consideration prior to Section 31 approval[cite: 7].
summary.operative_order: Appeals disposed of with directions: (1) RP shall provide all details and claims of omitted homebuyers reflected in Corporate Debtor records to the SRA within one month; (2) SRA shall prepare an addendum to the Resolution Plan within one month and place it before CoC; (3) CoC shall deliberate and decide on the addendum within one month; (4) NCLT shall consider the addendum and CoC minutes while adjudicating IA No. 3447 of 2021 for final plan approval; parties to bear their own costs[cite: 7].
summary.summary: Multiple homebuyers of KV Developers Private Limited appealed against NCLT New Delhi orders rejecting their belated claim applications after the Committee of Creditors had already voted to approve a Resolution Plan[cite: 7]. The Resolution Professional and Successful Resolution Applicant argued that these claims were extinguished upon CoC approval[cite: 7]. The NCLAT held that under Section 31(1), claim extinguishment takes effect only upon Adjudicating Authority approval, not CoC approval[cite: 7]. It ruled that under Regulation 36, the RP must include all known liabilities reflected in corporate records in the Information Memorandum[cite: 7]. The Tribunal directed the RP and SRA to submit an addendum covering recorded homebuyers for CoC reconsideration before final plan approval[cite: 7].

summary.case_title: Prashant Agarwal vs. Vikash Parasrampuria & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Prashant Agarwal is a suspended director of Corporate Debtor Bombay Rayon Fashions Limited; Respondent No. 1 Vikash Parasrampuria is the Sole Proprietor of Chiranjilal Yarns Trading (Operational Creditor); Respondent No. 2 Santanu T. Ray is the Interim Resolution Professional[cite: 8]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Operational supply of various types of yarns under nine commercial invoices raised between March 2017 and January 2020 totaling Rs. 2,02,26,017/-[cite: 8]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Principal outstanding operational debt was Rs. 97,87,220/-; contractual interest stipulated at 18% per annum plus GST on delayed payments aggregated the total default claim to Rs. 1,60,87,838/-; invoices spanned March 2017 to January 2020, with the last invoice dated 01.02.2020[cite: 8]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Invoices raised March 2017 to January 2020; last invoice dated 01.02.2020; Section 9 application filed on 31.12.2020; Adjudicating Authority admitted the application on 07.06.2022[cite: 8]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Nine invoices expressly stipulating 'interest will be charged @ 18% plus GST P.A after due date of the bill', which terms were accepted without objection, and full payment was made on three invoices and part payment on one invoice[cite: 8]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed CP (IB) No. 1443/MB-IV/2020 under Section 9; NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV admitted the application on 07.06.2022; the suspended director appealed challenging limitation and maintainability below the Rs. 1 crore threshold under Section 4[cite: 8].
summary.legal_issues: Whether contractually agreed interest on delayed payments stipulated on commercial invoices forms part of the 'operational debt' to determine the minimum pecuniary threshold of Rs. 1 crore mandated under Section 4 of the IBC[cite: 8].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where commercial invoices or agreements clearly stipulate the payment of interest on delayed payments and such term has not been disputed, the interest component constitutes a legally enforceable claim and must be aggregated with the principal amount to compute the minimum default threshold under Section 4 of the IBC[cite: 8]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Reading the definition of 'debt' under Section 3(11) together with 'claim' under Section 3(6) of the IBC, an entitlement to contractual interest constitutes a right to payment arising from breach of contract and forms part of the operational debt[cite: 8]. Consequently, the threshold under Section 4 encompasses both principal and agreed interest[cite: 8]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Clear, uncontradicted stipulation of an 18% per annum interest clause printed on the face of the accepted invoices, coupled with absence of any pre-existing dispute regarding such term[cite: 8]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Adding the accrued contractual interest to the principal operational debt of Rs. 97,87,220/- elevated the total default to Rs. 1,60,87,838/-, thereby satisfying the revised Rs. 1 crore threshold under Section 4; the petition was also filed within three years of the last invoice (01.02.2020) and is within limitation[cite: 8].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 690 of 2022 is dismissed; the admission order of the Adjudicating Authority initiating CIRP is affirmed[cite: 8].
summary.summary: Prashant Agarwal, suspended director of Bombay Rayon Fashions Limited, appealed against an NCLT Mumbai Bench order admitting a Section 9 application filed by operational creditor Vikash Parasrampuria, proprietor of Chiranjilal Yarns Trading[cite: 8]. The appellant argued that the principal debt was only Rs. 97.87 lakhs, falling below the Section 4 threshold of Rs. 1 crore introduced on 24.03.2020, and that the petition was barred by limitation[cite: 8]. The NCLAT held that because all invoices explicitly stipulated 18% annual interest on delayed payments without dispute, such interest qualifies as operational debt under Sections 3(6) and 3(11)[cite: 8]. The aggregated default of Rs. 1.60 crores satisfied Section 4, and the appeal was dismissed[cite: 8].

summary.case_title: Damodar Valley Corporation vs. Dimension Steel and Alloys Private Limited & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Damodar Valley Corporation (DVC) is a statutory electricity distribution company/Operational Creditor; Respondent No. 1 Dimension Steel and Alloys Private Limited is the Corporate Debtor; Respondent No. 2 Bijoy Murmuria is the Resolution Professional; Respondent No. 3 C.P. Ispat Private Limited is the Successful Resolution Applicant[cite: 9]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Power Purchase Agreement dated 30.11.2012 executed between DVC and Corporate Debtor for electrical power supply[cite: 9]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor defaulted on electricity bills resulting in power disconnection on 07.06.2019; Appellant lodged a pre-CIRP claim of Rs. 36,35,64,214/-, against which the resolution plan allocated Rs. 7,45,608/- (0.19% recovery)[cite: 9]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Electricity disconnected on 07.06.2019; Section 9 CIRP initiated on 18.10.2019; Form-G published on 21.06.2020; NCLT condoned delay and allowed consideration of SRA's plan on 16.03.2021; CoC approved plan on 22.04.2021 with 80.93% votes; NCLT approved plan on 08.10.2021[cite: 9]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Power Purchase Agreement dated 30.11.2012; disconnection notices; West Bengal Electricity Regulatory Commission Regulations, 2013 (Regulations 4.6.1 and 4.6.4 requiring clearance of past arrears for new/restored connection); audited CIRP claims[cite: 9]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In CP (IB) No. 832/KB/2019, NCLT Kolkata Bench allowed I.A. (IB) No. 479/KB/2021 on 08.10.2021 approving C.P. Ispat's Resolution Plan and directing DVC to restore power upon receipt of allocated sums; DVC appealed challenging plan approval, 330-day timeline breaches, and dilution of statutory electricity dues[cite: 9].
summary.legal_issues: Whether consideration and approval of a resolution plan beyond the 330-day timeline vitiates its validity, and whether state electricity supply regulations conditioning power restoration on full payment of pre-CIRP arrears override the IBC under Section 238 or render the plan contrary to law under Section 30(2)(e)[cite: 9].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Statutory electricity regulations that condition power supply or restoration upon the payment of pre-insolvency arrears are inconsistent with the IBC and are overridden by Section 238; once a resolution plan is approved under Section 31, all pre-CIRP claims are extinguished and the utility cannot condition service on cleared historical arrears[cite: 9]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 238 accords overriding effect to the IBC over inconsistent state regulations such as Regulations 4.6.1 and 4.6.4 of the WBERC Supply Code, 2013[cite: 9]. Section 30(2)(b) requires payment of at least liquidation value to operational creditors, and commercial wisdom allows differential percentage distributions across creditor classes so long as equitable treatment within the same class is maintained[cite: 9]. The 330-day timeline under Section 12 is directory, not mandatory[cite: 9]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification that the operational creditor received at least its statutory liquidation entitlement under Section 53 and that the resolution plan was validly approved by over 66% CoC voting share[cite: 9]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The resolution plan satisfies Section 30(2), and pre-CIRP electricity dues stand extinguished pursuant to Ghanashyam Mishra; the direction compelling restoration of power without clearance of pre-CIRP dues is legally valid[cite: 9].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 62 of 2022 is dismissed; approval of the Resolution Plan is affirmed; no order as to costs; copy of order forwarded to MCA and IBBI for review regarding operational creditor statutory distributions[cite: 9].
summary.summary: Damodar Valley Corporation appealed an NCLT Kolkata Bench order approving a Resolution Plan submitted by C.P. Ispat Private Limited for Corporate Debtor Dimension Steel and Alloys Private Limited[cite: 9]. DVC, owed Rs. 36.35 crores in pre-CIRP electricity dues, was allocated Rs. 7.45 lakhs under the plan[cite: 9]. DVC argued that the plan violated Section 30(2) and West Bengal Electricity Regulatory Commission Regulations requiring full clearance of arrears before power restoration, and breached the 330-day CIRP timeline[cite: 9]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that Section 238 overrides state electricity regulations, pre-CIRP claims stand extinguished upon Section 31 plan approval, and differential payout to operational creditors does not invalidate the plan[cite: 9].

summary.case_title: Jet Aircraft Maintenance Engineers Welfare Association vs. Ashish Chhawchharia, Resolution Professional for Jet Airways (India) Ltd. & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Jet Aircraft Maintenance Engineers Welfare Association (Trade Union of aircraft maintenance engineers); Respondent No. 1 is Ashish Chhawchharia, Resolution Professional for Jet Airways (India) Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 2 is the Committee of Creditors; Respondent No. 3 is HDFC Bank; Respondent No. 4 is M/s Vrihis Properties Pvt. Ltd., the auction purchaser[cite: 10]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor held six Boeing 777 aircraft under finance lease charged to US Exim Bank requiring USD 13 million settlement to transfer absolute title, against which corporate debtor had already paid USD 881 million[cite: 10]. Separately, Corporate Debtor owned encumbered premises (floors 3 and 4 of BKC building) mortgaged to HDFC Bank against admitted dues of INR 425 crores[cite: 10]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Following default on financial facilities, Section 7 CIRP was initiated against Jet Airways; Appellant trade union had an admitted claim of INR 1,525,859,239/-[cite: 10]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 20.06.2019; CoC approved BKC sale resolution on 24.04.2020 with 74.45% voting; NCLT approved sale in IA 998/2020 on 11.06.2020; public auction held on 26.06.2020; assignment deeds executed on 10.07.2020 and 13.07.2020; appeal filed on 17.07.2020[cite: 10]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Registered Deeds of Assignment dated 10.07.2020 and 13.07.2020 for INR 490 crores; HDFC's registered release of mortgage upon receiving INR 360 crores; minutes of the 8th and 10th CoC meetings classifying BKC property as non-core asset[cite: 10]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In CP(IB)-2205/MB/2019, NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi allowed RP's IA-998/2020 on 11.06.2020 granting approval to auction BKC premises; Appellant appealed alleging the sale and payoff to HDFC violated the Section 14 moratorium[cite: 10].
summary.legal_issues: Whether the statutory moratorium under Section 14(1)(b) prohibits the Resolution Professional and Committee of Creditors from selling non-core assets to protect corporate value, and whether paying an encumbered creditor to release its charge to facilitate value maximization violates Section 14(1)(c) when CIRP subsequently culminates in an approved resolution plan[cite: 10].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The prohibition against transferring or encumbering corporate assets under Section 14(1)(b) of the IBC restricts the corporate debtor itself, and does not divest the Resolution Professional or the Committee of Creditors of statutory powers under Section 28 and Regulation 29 to dispose of assets outside the ordinary course of business for value maximization[cite: 10]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14(1)(b) operates to shield corporate assets from external attack and management dissipation, but must be harmoniously construed with Sections 20, 25, and 28, which empower the RP, with CoC approval (minimum 66%), to take protective actions to maximize asset values[cite: 10]. Although Section 14(1)(c) bars individual enforcement of security interests during CIRP, completed commercial transactions approved by NCLT that yield significant asset accretion (acquiring unencumbered aircraft title) will not be unwound once CIRP achieves final resolution plan approval[cite: 10]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Approval of the sale by over 66% CoC vote (74.45%), proof that real estate auction proceeds exceeded liquidation value, and tangible value accretion via acquisition of title to six long-haul aircraft[cite: 10]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The RP acted within statutory powers with CoC approval; given that the auction was fully consummated, proceeds utilized to preserve valuable aircraft assets, and the overarching CIRP successfully concluded with plan approval, reversing the sale is impermissible[cite: 10].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 628 of 2020 is dismissed; no order as to costs[cite: 10].
summary.summary: Jet Aircraft Maintenance Engineers Welfare Association appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order permitting the Resolution Professional of Jet Airways (India) Ltd. to auction encumbered floors of its BKC premises for INR 490 crores during the moratorium[cite: 10]. The proceeds were used to pay INR 360 crores to HDFC Bank to release its mortgage and allocate INR 130 crores to acquire unencumbered title to six Boeing 777 aircraft from US Exim[cite: 10]. The NCLAT held that the moratorium under Section 14(1)(b) restricts the debtor, not the RP and CoC exercising value-maximizing statutory powers under Section 28 and Regulation 29[cite: 10]. Recognizing that the sale significantly increased overall asset value and that the CIRP had since culminated in an approved plan, the Tribunal dismissed the appeal[cite: 10].

summary.case_title: V.R. Ashok Rao & Ors. vs. TDT Copper Ltd.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants include V.R. Ashok Rao & Ors. (in CA 780/2022), Stressed Assets Stabilization Fund (in CA 823/2022), A'XY Kno Capital Services Pvt. Ltd. (in CA 913/2022), and Bhagwati Singh (in CA 914/2022); Respondents are respective Corporate Debtors including TDT Copper Ltd., Delta International Ltd., Rattan India Power Ltd., and Incab Industries Ltd.[cite: 11] 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying insolvency petitions filed under the IBC (such as Section 7 in CP (IB) No. 1093/(ND)/2022 dismissed by NCLT New Delhi Bench-V on 11.03.2022)[cite: 11]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Monetary default sums are not specifically detailed in the reference order[cite: 11]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: In CA 780/2022, NCLT order passed on 11.03.2022; appeal originally presented on 13.04.2022; defects notified on 19.04.2022; refiled on 08.06.2022 resulting in a 43-day refiling delay[cite: 11]. In companion appeals, refiling delays were 35 days (CA 823/2022), 40 days (CA 913/2022), and 105 days (CA 914/2022)[cite: 11]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Filing stamps, registry endorsements, notices of defect under Rule 26(2), and applications for condonation of refiling delay[cite: 11]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Three-Member Bench doubted earlier decisions in Jitendra Virmani and Arul Muthu Kumaara Samy and referred the issue of refiling delay beyond 7 days to a five-member Larger Bench for determination[cite: 11].
summary.legal_issues: Whether an appeal re-presented after curing defects beyond the 7-day period under Rule 26 of NCLAT Rules must be treated as a fresh appeal, and whether statutory limitation under Section 61 of the IBC or Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013 governs and restricts the condonation of delay in refiling/re-presentation[cite: 11].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory limitation prescribed for the initial institution of an appeal does not govern the subsequent cure of defects and re-presentation; curing defects beyond the seven-day administrative window does not transform the re-presentation into a fresh appeal, and appellate tribunals possess inherent jurisdiction to condone refiling delay upon sufficient cause shown[cite: 11]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(2) of the IBC and Section 421(3) of the Companies Act govern original presentation of appeals; Rule 26 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016 provides an administrative procedure where the 7-day period is directory and contains no penal consequence or deeming fiction creating a fresh institution[cite: 11]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of whether the original presentation was timely and whether the appellant provided justifiable and sufficient cause explaining the delay in curing defects upon re-presentation[cite: 11]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Jitendra Virmani and Arul Muthu Kumaara Samy do not lay down correct law and are overruled; re-presentation beyond 7 days is merely refiling, and delays exceeding statutory appeal limitation periods can be condoned on sufficient justification[cite: 11].
summary.operative_order: Reference answered: (a) Overruled Jitendra Virmani and Arul Muthu Kumaara Samy, holding re-presentation beyond 7 days is not a fresh appeal; (b) Held that limitation under Section 61 IBC or Section 421 Companies Act does not govern refiling delays, which may be condoned on sufficient cause; directed appeals to be listed before the regular bench on 01.09.2022 for condonation of delay[cite: 11].
summary.summary: A five-member Larger Bench of NCLAT resolved a reference regarding whether an appeal refiled after curing defects beyond seven days constitutes a fresh appeal subject to the strict limitation period under Section 61 of the IBC or Section 421 of the Companies Act[cite: 11]. Overruling its previous rulings in Jitendra Virmani and Arul Muthu Kumaara Samy, the NCLAT held that initial presentation and re-presentation stand on entirely distinct legal footings[cite: 11]. The seven-day timeline under Rule 26 of NCLAT Rules is directory, not mandatory, and contains no deeming fiction of fresh institution[cite: 11]. Consequently, statutory appeal filing deadlines do not limit the tribunal's power to condone refiling delay upon sufficient justification[cite: 11].

summary.case_title: Jaipur Trade Expocentre Private Limited vs. M/s Metro Jet Airways Training Private Limited
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Jaipur Trade Expocentre Private Limited is the Licensor/Operational Creditor; Respondent M/s Metro Jet Airways Training Private Limited is the Licensee/Corporate Debtor[cite: 12]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: License Agreement dated 15.04.2017 granting license of a 31,000 sq. ft. warm shell administrative building with corporate fittings and fixtures for five years to run an educational establishment at a monthly license fee of Rs. 4,00,000/- plus applicable taxes (GST)[cite: 12]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor defaulted on license fees; two cheques of Rs. 20,00,000/- each dated 07.05.2018 and 08.10.2018 dishonoured; total default claimed in statutory demand notice was Rs. 1,31,20,788/-[cite: 12]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 8 issued on 03.05.2019 (served on 07.05.2019); unreplied by Debtor who initiated civil suit on 09.05.2019; Section 9 petition filed in 2019 and rejected on 04.03.2020[cite: 12]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: License Agreement dated 15.04.2017, dishonoured cheques, bank return memos, Section 8 demand notice, and GST invoice covenants[cite: 12]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In Company Petition No. (IB)/176/9/JPR/2019, NCLT Jaipur Bench dismissed the Section 9 application on 04.03.2020 holding license fees do not constitute goods or services; on appeal, a reference was made to a five-member Larger Bench[cite: 12].
summary.legal_issues: Whether the previous decisions in M. Ravindranath Reddy and Promila Taneja lay down the correct law, and whether a licensor's claim for unpaid license fees/rent for use and occupation of commercial premises constitutes an 'operational debt' under Section 5(21) of the IBC[cite: 12].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The licensing or leasing of immovable property for commercial or business operations constitutes a provision of 'services', and outstanding license fees or lease rentals arising therefrom qualify as an 'operational debt' under Section 5(21) of the IBC[cite: 12]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The term 'services' under Section 5(21) is not confined to essential goods and services under Section 14(2); relying on the Bankruptcy Law Reforms Committee Report (2015) affirmed in Mobilox Innovations, lessors and licensors providing operational space are operational creditors, and licensing commercial premises attracting GST constitutes a taxable supply of services[cite: 12]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification of an agreement granting commercial occupation for business operations, accrual of unpaid license fees, and tax covenants contemplating statutory indirect taxes (GST/Service Tax) on services rendered[cite: 12]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The contrary view expressed in M. Ravindranath Reddy and Promila Taneja is erroneous and overruled; unpaid commercial license fees constitute operational debt, and the petition warrants admission[cite: 12].
summary.operative_order: Appeal allowed; NCLT Jaipur Bench order dated 04.03.2020 set aside; Section 9 application held deserving of admission; NCLT directed to pass an admission order within one month, granting parties time to explore settlement; parties to bear own costs[cite: 12].
summary.summary: Jaipur Trade Expocentre Private Limited licensed commercial premises to Metro Jet Airways Training Private Limited to operate an educational institute[cite: 12]. Following default and cheque dishonour exceeding Rs. 1.31 crores, the licensor filed a Section 9 application, which NCLT Jaipur dismissed relying on precedent holding that immovable property rentals do not constitute 'goods or services'[cite: 12]. Resolving the reference, a five-member Larger Bench of NCLAT overruled M. Ravindranath Reddy and Promila Taneja[cite: 12]. The Tribunal held that leasing or licensing premises for commercial use constitutes a 'service' under Section 5(21) of the IBC and GST laws, rendering unpaid license fees an operational debt[cite: 12]. The dismissal was set aside and admission directed[cite: 12].

summary.case_title: Kiran Shah, Resolution Professional of KSL and Industries Ltd. vs. Enforcement Directorate, Kolkata
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Kiran Shah is the Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor KSL and Industries Ltd. (a Tayal Group company); Respondent is the Directorate of Enforcement (ED), Kolkata[cite: 13]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Tayal Group entities availed credit facilities aggregating Rs. 524.61 crores from a consortium of banks, which funds were allegedly laundered through fictitious entities, prompting registration of ECIR No. KLZO/14/2016 under PMLA[cite: 13]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate loan default led to Section 7 CIRP initiation; proceeds of crime under investigation were valued at Rs. 483,16,35,696/-, matching the value of the attached single asset 'Express Mall' / 'Empress Mall' in Nagpur[cite: 13]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Provisional Attachment Order (PAO) issued on 08.05.2019; Section 7 CIRP admitted against Corporate Debtor on 06.09.2019; PAO confirmed by PMLA Adjudicating Authority on 24.10.2019; RP filed PMLA Appeal No. 3387/2019 on 27.12.2019; RP filed IA 81/2020 before NCLT in 2020; NCLT dismissed IA on 31.12.2020[cite: 13]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bank FIRs, ECIR records, PAO dated 08.05.2019, confirmation order dated 24.10.2019, conveyance deeds dated 07.02.2005, and mortgage documentation with Bank of India[cite: 13]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In CP(IB) No. 397/NCLT/AHM/2018, NCLT Ahmedabad Bench Court No. 2 dismissed RP's IA 81/2020 on 31.12.2020 as not maintainable, holding NCLT lacks jurisdiction to quash attachment orders passed by PMLA authorities; RP appealed[cite: 13].
summary.legal_issues: Whether the NCLT has jurisdiction under Section 60(5) or Section 32A of the IBC to quash or set aside a provisional attachment order confirmed by the PMLA Adjudicating Authority over corporate assets alleged to be proceeds of crime during the pendency of CIRP[cite: 13].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC does not bar criminal or penal proceedings under special penal statutes like the PMLA regarding the attachment of proceeds of crime; the NCLT lacks supervisory jurisdiction under Section 60(5) to quash or interfere with attachment orders passed by authorities under the PMLA[cite: 13]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14 shields corporate assets from civil pecuniary recoveries, but does not override statutory confiscation of proceeds of crime by the State, which acts as a sovereign authority rather than a creditor[cite: 13]. Section 32A(2) immunity applies strictly after a resolution plan is approved under Section 31; prior to such approval, NCLT cannot invoke Section 32A to discharge attached properties[cite: 13]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Existence of a valid confirmation of provisional attachment by the PMLA Adjudicating Authority and the absence of an approved Section 31 resolution plan[cite: 13]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The RP cannot bypass the specialized statutory appellate mechanism established under Sections 26 and 42 of the PMLA by approaching NCLT under Section 60(5); the NCLT correctly dismissed the application as non-maintainable[cite: 13].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 817 of 2021 is dismissed; connected I.A.s dismissed; Corporate Debtor left with liberty to pursue statutory remedies before the PMLA Appellate Tribunal in Appeal No. 3387/2019 or other appropriate legal fora; no costs[cite: 13].
summary.summary: The Resolution Professional of KSL and Industries Ltd. appealed an NCLT Ahmedabad Bench order dismissing an interim application seeking to set aside a PMLA provisional attachment order covering the company's flagship Empress Mall property[cite: 13]. The attachment was confirmed after Section 7 CIRP had commenced[cite: 13]. The RP argued that the Section 14 moratorium and Section 238 non-obstante clause barred PMLA attachments during CIRP[cite: 13]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that Section 14 does not apply to penal confiscations of proceeds of crime and that Section 32A immunity is unavailable prior to final plan approval[cite: 13]. The NCLT lacks jurisdiction under Section 60(5) to quash PMLA orders, and the RP must seek relief before the PMLA Appellate Tribunal[cite: 13].

summary.case_title: Regional Provident Fund Commissioner vs. Ashish Chhawchharia & Anr. [and Connected Appeals]
summary.appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 752, 643, 792, 801 & 915 of 2021, and 361, 771 & 987 of 2022
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants include Trade Unions/Workmen Associations (Jet Aircraft Maintenance Engineers Welfare Association, Association of Aggrieved Workmen, Bhartiya Kamgar Sena, All India Jet Airways Officers Association, individual engineers), Regional PF Commissioner, Department of State Tax, and Concor Air Ltd.; Respondents are Ashish Chhawchharia (RP for Jet Airways (India) Ltd.), CoC, and Jalan Fritsch Consortium (SRA)[cite: 14]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Insolvency resolution of Corporate Debtor Jet Airways (India) Ltd. following airline suspension in April 2019[cite: 14]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Massive admitted claims included Rs. 578.7 crores for workmen, Rs. 674.9 crores for employees, Rs. 24,40,65,594/- under Section 14B EPF Act, and Rs. 56.85 crores state tax dues[cite: 14]. SRA offered Rs. 52 crores for workmen/employees, later adjusted[cite: 14]. Liquidation value was Rs. 2,555 crores, with workmen's minimum liquidation value calculated at Rs. 113 crores in Form-H[cite: 14]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 CIRP admitted 20.06.2019; CoC approved plan 03.10.2020; NCLT approved plan 22.06.2021; multiple appeals filed challenging the plan[cite: 14]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Form-H compliance certificate, 17th CoC minutes, EPFO assessment orders, Section 14B penalty orders, and scheme of demerger of workforce into subsidiary AGSL[cite: 14]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-I approved Jalan Fritsch Consortium's Resolution Plan on 22.06.2021 in IA No. 2081/2020 in CP (IB) No. 2205/MB/2019; workmen, EPFO, State Tax Department, and operational creditors appealed[cite: 14].
summary.legal_issues: Whether workmen and employees are entitled to 100% payment of unpaid provident fund and gratuity dues up to the insolvency commencement date outside the Section 53 waterfall under Section 36(4)(a)(iii), and whether statutory damages under Section 14B of the EPF Act must be satisfied in full[cite: 14].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Unpaid provident fund and gratuity dues accrued up to the insolvency commencement date are statutorily protected welfare entitlements that do not form part of the liquidation estate under Section 36(4)(a)(iii) of the IBC; they cannot be curtailed or subjected to the Section 53 waterfall, and a resolution plan failing to pay them in full violates Section 30(2)(e)[cite: 14]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: In accordance with Sunil Kumar Jain and Rainbow Papers, Section 36(4)(a)(iii) gives absolute protection to workmen's PF and gratuity dues, placing them outside liquidation assets[cite: 14]. Where the employer failed to maintain a separate fund, the statutory obligation persists and must be fully discharged by the Successful Resolution Applicant[cite: 14]. Damages assessed under Section 14B of the EPF Act also enjoy priority under Section 11 of the 1952 Act[cite: 14]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Admitted statutory dues reflected in the RP's list of claims regarding unpaid employee PF and accrued gratuity prior to the insolvency commencement date[cite: 14]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Resolution Plan must pay the full unpaid PF and pre-CIRP gratuity to workmen and employees, plus the minimum liquidation value of Rs. 113 crores to workmen under Section 30(2)(b); EPFO's Section 14B claim must also be paid in full[cite: 14].
summary.operative_order: Appeals of workmen/employees and Regional PF Commissioner allowed in part; SRA directed to pay full unpaid provident fund and pre-CIRP gratuity dues after adjusting sums paid under the plan, pay Rs. 113 crores minimum liquidation value to workmen, and pay EPFO's admitted Section 14B claim; demerger to AGSL upheld; appeals of State Tax and Concor Air dismissed; Resolution Plan approval upheld subject to these mandatory modifications[cite: 14].
summary.summary: Multiple appeals challenged the NCLT Mumbai Bench order approving the Resolution Plan submitted by Jalan Fritsch Consortium for Jet Airways (India) Ltd.[cite: 14] Workmen and the Regional PF Commissioner argued that the plan unlawfully capped workmen dues at Rs. 52 crores, failed to pay full provident fund and gratuity, and ignored Rs. 24.4 crores in Section 14B EPF damages[cite: 14]. The NCLAT held that under Section 36(4)(a)(iii) and Section 30(2)(e), provident fund and gratuity dues do not form part of the liquidation estate and must be paid in full by the SRA up to the insolvency commencement date[cite: 14]. The Tribunal also directed payment of Rs. 113 crores minimum liquidation value to workmen and full satisfaction of EPFO dues, while upholding the rest of the plan[cite: 14].

summary.case_title: Bank of Maharashtra vs. Videocon Industries Limited & Ors. [and Connected Appeals]
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Dissenting Financial Creditors (Bank of Maharashtra, IFCI Ltd., SIDBI), trademark licensor Electrolux Home Products Inc., and suspended director Venugopal Dhoot; Respondents are 13 consolidated Videocon Group Corporate Debtors, Resolution Professional Abhijit Guhathakurta, CoC led by SBI, and Successful Resolution Applicant Twin Star Technologies Limited[cite: 15]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Consolidated CIRP of 13 Videocon Group entities across consumer electronics, telecom, and energy sectors under a syndicated loan structure[cite: 15]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Massive default where total claims were Rs. 71,433.75 crores, admitted claims were Rs. 64,838.63 crores, and SRA's plan offered a nominal Rs. 2,962.02 crores, imposing an unprecedented haircut of over 95.85% (creditors receiving ~4.15%, operational creditors ~0.72%)[cite: 15]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP consolidated on 08.08.2019; CoC approved Twin Star's plan on 11.12.2020 by 95.09%; NCLT approved plan on 08.06.2021; NCLAT stayed implementation on 19.07.2021[cite: 15]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Form-H compliance certificate showing discrepancies in liquidation value entitlements of DFCs, offer of deferred Non-Convertible Debentures instead of cash, lack of prior approval from the Competition Commission of India under Section 31(4) proviso, and affidavit of Assenting Financial Creditors (94.98%) seeking reconsideration[cite: 15]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-II approved Twin Star's Resolution Plan on 08.06.2021 in IA No. 196/2021 while making adverse observations regarding the 95% haircut, potential leak of liquidation value, and directing cash payments to DFCs; DFCs, licensor, and promoter appealed[cite: 15].
summary.legal_issues: Whether a resolution plan offering Non-Convertible Debentures to dissenting financial creditors complies with Section 30(2)(b), whether the Adjudicating Authority can unilaterally modify payment terms to cash without remitting the plan to the CoC, and whether prior approval of the Competition Commission of India under the proviso to Section 31(4) is mandatory prior to CoC approval[cite: 15].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A resolution plan providing payment to dissenting financial creditors in the form of long-term debentures or securities rather than upfront cash violates Section 30(2)(b); the Adjudicating Authority has no jurisdiction to rewrite commercial terms by ordering cash payments, and must remand a non-compliant plan back to the Committee of Creditors[cite: 15]. Additionally, obtaining prior approval from the Competition Commission of India under the proviso to Section 31(4) before CoC approval is mandatory for combinations[cite: 15]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(2)(b) read with Jaypee Kensington dictates that 'payment' to dissenting creditors must strictly be in monetary terms (cash) and cannot force them to accept securities; the proviso to Section 31(4) establishes a mandatory statutory condition precedent requiring CCI combination approval prior to CoC voting[cite: 15]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of plan clauses proposing NCDs to DFCs, absence of CCI clearance prior to the 19th CoC meeting approval, and recorded discrepancies between Form-H and distribution models[cite: 15]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Resolution Plan failed to meet Section 30(2)(b) and Section 31(4); given the 95% haircut and the CoC's own request to reconsider, the approval must be quashed and the matter remitted to the CoC[cite: 15].
summary.operative_order: Appeals CA(AT) (Ins.) Nos. 503, 505, 529 & 545 of 2021 allowed; appeal of Venugopal Dhoot (CA 650/2021) dismissed; approval of the Resolution Plan by CoC and Adjudicating Authority set aside; matter remitted back to the Committee of Creditors to complete CIRP afresh in accordance with law; no order as to costs[cite: 15].
summary.summary: Appellants, including dissenting financial creditors Bank of Maharashtra, IFCI, and SIDBI, challenged an NCLT Mumbai Bench order approving Twin Star Technologies' Resolution Plan for 13 consolidated Videocon entities[cite: 15]. The plan offered Rs. 2,962 crores against admitted claims of Rs. 64,838 crores (a 95.85% haircut) and proposed discharging dissenting creditors through deferred debentures[cite: 15]. In its approval order, NCLT altered the plan by directing upfront cash payments to DFCs[cite: 15]. During appeal, 94.98% of the CoC sought reconsideration in the public interest[cite: 15]. The NCLAT held that offering NCDs violated Section 30(2)(b) under the Jaypee Kensington doctrine, NCLT lacked power to modify payment terms, and prior CCI approval under Section 31(4) had been omitted[cite: 15]. The approval was set aside and remitted to the CoC[cite: 15].

summary.case_title: S.M. Ghogbhai vs. Schedulers Logistics India Pvt. Ltd.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant S.M. Ghogbhai is the Operational Creditor; Respondent Schedulers Logistics India Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor[cite: 16]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Provision of transport and logistics services between the operational creditor and corporate debtor[cite: 16]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed outstanding unpaid debt was Rs. 76,04,050/- based on 174 commercial invoices issued during 2015–2016; the last payment received from the corporate debtor was on 26.09.2016, and the last invoice dates were 29.09.2016 and 10.10.2016[cite: 16]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Last payment received 26.09.2016; corporate debtor sought account reconciliation via email on 10.10.2017; Section 8 demand notice issued on 08.03.2019 and replied to on 26.03.2019 denying dues; Section 9 petition filed on 24.10.2019[cite: 16]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Operational creditor ledger account, bank statements, corporate debtor's reconciliation email dated 10.10.2017, Section 8 demand notice, and 174 unpaid invoices from 2015–2016[cite: 16]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In C.P. No. 3857/I&B/2019, NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-III dismissed the Section 9 application on 16.11.2021 as time-barred, holding all invoices were issued beyond the three-year limitation period preceding filing; operational creditor appealed arguing Article 1 for mutual accounts applied[cite: 16].
summary.legal_issues: Whether the limitation period for initiating corporate insolvency resolution under Section 9 of the IBC on running commercial accounts is governed by Article 1 of the Limitation Act, 1963 (suits relating to mutual, open, and current accounts) or by Article 137 (three years from the date default/right to apply accrues)[cite: 16].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application for initiation of corporate insolvency resolution under Section 9 of the IBC is not a suit relating to accounts; its period of limitation is governed strictly by Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963, commencing from the date when the default occurs and the right to apply accrues, which cannot be extended by importing Article 1[cite: 16]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Applying Section 238A of the IBC and the Supreme Court precedents in B.K. Educational Services and Babulal Vardharji Gurjar, applications under Sections 7 and 9 fall under Article 137 of the Limitation Act[cite: 16]. Article 1 applies specifically to suits relating to accounts, whereas Section 9 proceedings are summary insolvency initiation processes triggered by non-payment of mature debt[cite: 16]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Ascertainment of whether individual invoices forming the basis of default occurred within three years prior to the date of filing the Section 9 petition[cite: 16]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: All 174 invoices and the last credit payment (26.09.2016) fell beyond three years prior to the filing of the Section 9 petition on 24.10.2019; hence, the right to apply was barred under Article 137, rendering the dismissal valid[cite: 16].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) Insolvency No. 281 of 2022 is dismissed; the impugned order of the Adjudicating Authority is affirmed[cite: 16].
summary.summary: S.M. Ghogbhai appealed against an NCLT Mumbai Bench order rejecting his Section 9 insolvency application against Schedulers Logistics India Pvt. Ltd. as time-barred[cite: 16]. The operational debt claim of Rs. 76.04 lakhs was based on 174 invoices dating from 2015 to October 2016, with the last partial payment made on 26.09.2016[cite: 16]. The appellant contended that the parties maintained an open, mutual running account governed by Article 1 of the Limitation Act, 1963, running from the close of the financial year[cite: 16]. The NCLAT held that Section 9 applications are governed solely by Article 137, where the right to apply accrues on invoice defaults[cite: 16]. Because the application was filed on 24.10.2019, beyond three years from the invoices and last payment, the appeal was dismissed[cite: 16].

summary.case_title: Koncentric Investments Limited & Anr. vs. Standard Chartered Bank & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant No. 1 is Koncentric Investments Ltd. (promoter/shareholder of Corporate Debtor Khubchandani Hospitals Pvt. Ltd.); Appellant No. 2 Prakash Khubchandani is a suspended director; Respondent No. 1 is Standard Chartered Bank, London (Financial Creditor); Respondent No. 2 Anshuman Chaturvedi is the IRP[cite: 17]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Facility Agreement dated 22.05.2013 and Supplemental Agreement dated 19.08.2013 for External Commercial Borrowings disbursed in three tranches of USD 5 million each (total USD 15 million) on 30.08.2013, 31.10.2013, and 31.12.2013, secured by a Registered Indenture of Mortgage dated 26.06.2013[cite: 17]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in interest payment occurred on 30.06.2015; first principal instalment of USD 0.45 million fell due on 30.11.2015 (27 months post first drawdown); entire facility accelerated on 05.01.2017 following RBI NOC dated 07.12.2016; total claim in Section 7 petition was USD 18,194,742.69 as on 31.10.2018[cite: 17]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Interest default on 30.06.2015; first principal default on 30.11.2015; RBI acceleration approval on 07.12.2016; Acceleration Notice issued on 05.01.2017; Default Notice issued on 11.06.2018; Section 7 petition filed on 28.11.2018; NCLT admitted CIRP on 06.10.2021[cite: 17]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Facility agreements, Registered Indenture of Mortgage dated 26.06.2013, RBI NOC letter, Acceleration Notice dated 05.01.2017, and Part-IV computation schedule commencing from 30.11.2015[cite: 17]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-III admitted Standard Chartered Bank's Section 7 petition CP No. 4468/IBC/MB/2018 on 06.10.2021, holding the petition was within limitation from the principal default of 30.11.2015; suspended management appealed alleging limitation began on initial interest default (30.06.2015) and facility agreements were insufficiently stamped[cite: 17].
summary.legal_issues: Whether the failure of a financial creditor to initiate Section 7 proceedings on the occurrence of the very first default in interest payment forecloses its right to trigger CIRP for subsequent defaults on principal instalments or loan acceleration within three years, and whether insufficient stamping of underlying facility agreements vitiates Section 7 admission when debt and default are independently evidenced by registered mortgage instruments[cite: 17].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Section 7(1) of the IBC does not mandate that a financial creditor must rush to initiate insolvency upon the very first fractional default of interest; a creditor's election not to trigger CIRP on an initial interest default does not foreclose its statutory right to initiate Section 7 proceedings for subsequent defaults on principal instalments or loan recall within three years[cite: 17]. Furthermore, insufficient stamping of financing contracts does not bar Section 7 admission if the financial debt and default are proven through other credible evidence, such as registered mortgage deeds[cite: 17]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7(1) employs the word 'default' and courts cannot read the restrictive word 'first' before it; under Section 3(12), default encompasses non-payment of whole, part, or instalment of debt[cite: 17]. Under Innoventive Industries, the NCLT only needs to satisfy itself that default occurred on a debt legally due and payable within three years of filing under Article 137[cite: 17]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of registered mortgage documentation, undisputed disbursement records of USD 15 million, and computation showing the petition was presented within three years of the first principal instalment default (30.11.2015) and acceleration (05.01.2017)[cite: 17]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 7 application filed on 28.11.2018 was within three years of the principal default of 30.11.2015, and the registered mortgage independently proved the transaction dehors the unstamped facility agreement[cite: 17].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 911 of 2021 is dismissed; order of admission of CIRP dated 06.10.2021 is affirmed[cite: 17].
summary.summary: Suspended directors of Khubchandani Hospitals Pvt. Ltd. challenged an NCLT Mumbai Bench order admitting Standard Chartered Bank's Section 7 petition for defaulting on an ECB facility of USD 15 million[cite: 17]. Appellants argued that the petition filed on 28.11.2018 was time-barred because the first interest default occurred on 30.06.2015, and that the underlying loan agreements were inadmissible due to deficient stamping under Maharashtra stamp laws[cite: 17]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that Section 7 does not restrict initiation strictly to the 'first' default; lenders may initiate proceedings upon subsequent principal defaults or acceleration notices[cite: 17]. The petition was within three years of the first principal default (30.11.2015), and a registered mortgage established debt and default independent of the unstamped loan document[cite: 17].

summary.case_title: Union Bank of India (Erstwhile Corporation Bank) vs. Dinkar T. Venkatasubramanian & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Union Bank of India (formerly Corporation Bank) is a dissenting secured financial creditor; Respondent No. 1 Dinkar T. Venkatasubramanian is the Resolution Professional of Amtek Auto Limited (Corporate Debtor); Respondents No. 2 and 3 are DVI PE (Mauritius) Ltd. and Deccan Value Investors LP, the joint Successful Resolution Applicants[cite: 18]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor required procurement of steel and alloys to maintain operations as a going concern, for which the RP instructed Appellant Bank to continue extending and revolving Non-Fund Based (NFB) Letter of Credit and Bank Guarantee facilities at pre-CIRP levels[cite: 18]. 3.
