DEFAULT METRICS: Appellant had an admitted financial claim of Rs. 836.80 crores; during CIRP, Appellant honoured devolving LCs/BGs by paying third-party raw material suppliers directly, debiting Rs. 33.34 crores from the CD's collection/current account[cite: 18]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated under Section 7 in 2017; LHG resolution plan approved on 25.07.2018 and subsequently failed; RP instructed continuation of NFB limits; in the 30th and 31st CoC meetings (05.02.2020 and 07.02.2020), CoC decided to deduct Rs. 34 crores from Appellant's plan allocation; IA 222/2020 filed on 12.03.2020 and dismissed on 09.07.2020[cite: 18]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: RP's written instructions dated 08.08.2017, 30.10.2018, 21.11.2018, and 26.11.2018 requesting continuation of NFB facilities; bank payment records showing direct disbursements to external steel/alloy suppliers; CoC minutes of 30th and 31st meetings[cite: 18]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh Bench dismissed Appellant's IA No. 222/2020 on 09.07.2020, holding CoC approved the plan and distribution deducting Rs. 34 crores with requisite majority which binds all creditors; Appellant appealed[cite: 18].
summary.legal_issues: Whether payments made by a financial creditor to honour Letters of Credit issued at the request of the Resolution Professional to procure essential raw materials to run the Corporate Debtor as a going concern constitute CIRP costs, and whether the CoC can deduct such amounts from the creditor's allocated share under an approved resolution plan by characterizing the debits as unauthorized post-moratorium recoveries[cite: 18].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Payments made by a lender to third-party suppliers to honour letters of credit maintained during CIRP at the express request and instruction of the Resolution Professional to preserve the corporate debtor as a going concern constitute Insolvency Resolution Process Costs under Section 5(13)(c); such operational payments do not constitute unauthorized recovery or unjust enrichment, and the Committee of Creditors has no jurisdiction under Section 30(4) to deduct these costs from the lender's final plan distribution[cite: 18]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 20 and 25, the RP must protect going-concern value; continuation of NFB facilities constitutes interim finance/CIRP costs[cite: 18]. Section 17(1)(d) does not empower the RP to compel financial institutions to extend credit lines without contractual backing, nor does paying vendors violate Section 14 when funds go directly to suppliers of raw materials consumed during CIRP[cite: 18]. Under Section 53(1)(a), CIRP costs enjoy first priority and cannot be penalized by plan deductions[cite: 18]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Concrete proof that debits from the corporate debtor's account went entirely to pay external suppliers under devolved LCs for goods delivered to and utilized by the debtor during CIRP[cite: 18]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Rs. 34 crores paid to raw material vendors were legitimate CIRP costs necessary to maintain going-concern operations; the CoC and RP acted illegally in deducting this sum from the Appellant's approved resolution plan payout[cite: 18].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 729 of 2020 is partly allowed; order of the Adjudicating Authority dated 09.07.2020 is set aside; Resolution Professional is directed not to deduct the amount of Rs. 34 crores from the final payment to be made to the Appellant under the approved Resolution Plan; no order as to costs[cite: 18].
summary.summary: Union Bank of India (erstwhile Corporation Bank) appealed against an NCLT Chandigarh Bench order dismissing its application to restrain the RP and CoC from deducting Rs. 34 crores from its resolution plan entitlement in the CIRP of Amtek Auto Limited[cite: 18]. At the RP's express request to keep the debtor running as a going concern, the bank continued non-fund based LC facilities for raw material supplies, and subsequently debited the debtor's account to pay steel vendors upon LC devolvement[cite: 18]. The RP and CoC treated this debit as an illegal recovery during the moratorium and deducted it from the bank's plan distribution[cite: 18]. The NCLAT held that payments made to operational suppliers to maintain going-concern status constitute CIRP costs under Section 5(13)(c), which cannot be deducted from plan distributions[cite: 18]. The deduction was quashed[cite: 18].

summary.case_title: Union Bank of India vs. Kapil Wadhawan & Ors. [and Connected Appeals]
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Union Bank of India acts on behalf of the CoC of Corporate Debtor Dewan Housing Finance Corporation Ltd. (DHFL); connected appeals filed by the Administrator (R. Subramaniakumar) and Successful Resolution Applicant Piramal Capital & Housing Finance Ltd.; Respondent No. 1 Kapil Wadhawan is the erstwhile promoter/director; Respondent No. 3 is the Reserve Bank of India[cite: 19]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP of Financial Service Provider DHFL initiated by RBI under Section 227 read with FSP Rules, 2019[cite: 19]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate debtor had massive outstanding liabilities of approximately Rs. 87,247 crores; CoC approved Piramal's resolution plan of Rs. 37,250 crores by 93.65% vote share; promoter submitted an uninvited second settlement proposal offering Rs. 91,158 crores[cite: 19]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 03.12.2019; CoC approved Piramal's plan in January 2021; RBI granted NOC on 16.02.2021; Plan Approval Application (IA 449/2021) heard and reserved for orders by NCLT; while reserved, NCLT passed impugned order on 19.05.2021 directing CoC to consider promoter's settlement proposal within 10 days; NCLAT heard appeals[cite: 19]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Letter dated 29.12.2020 containing promoter's second settlement proposal, Piramal's CoC-approved resolution plan, RBI approval letters, and voting sheets of CoC approving the plan by 93.65%[cite: 19]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In IA No. 2431 of 2020 in CP (IB) No. 4258/MB/C-II/2019, NCLT Mumbai Bench-II on 19.05.2021 directed the Administrator to place promoter Kapil Wadhawan's second settlement proposal before the CoC for consideration and voting within 10 days; CoC, Administrator, and Piramal appealed[cite: 19].
summary.legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has jurisdiction under Section 60(5) of the IBC or Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 to direct the CoC to convene and consider an unsolicited settlement proposal submitted by an erstwhile promoter when a compliant resolution plan has already been approved by the CoC and is reserved for approval under Section 31[cite: 19].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a resolution plan has been approved by the Committee of Creditors by the requisite statutory majority and is submitted for approval under Section 31, the Adjudicating Authority possesses no jurisdiction under Section 60(5) or inherent powers under Rule 11 to compel the CoC to entertain, negotiate, or vote upon an unsolicited settlement proposal submitted by an erstwhile promoter[cite: 19]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: In terms of the Supreme Court's ruling in Ebix Singapore v. CoC of Educomp Solutions Ltd., a CoC-approved resolution plan creates binding statutory obligations governed strictly by the IBC framework; there is no scope for renegotiation or entertaining parallel settlement proposals outside Section 12A once the plan is before the Adjudicating Authority[cite: 19]. The NCLT's jurisdiction under Section 31(1) is strictly circumscribed to examining compliance with Section 30(2) and possesses no unchartered equity powers to interfere with commercial wisdom[cite: 19]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Established compliance of the resolution plan with Section 30(2), valid CoC approval by 93.65% majority, and receipt of statutory regulatory approvals (RBI NOC) prior to the impugned order[cite: 19]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The promoter's settlement offer complied neither with the RFRP nor with Section 12A; the Adjudicating Authority exceeded its statutory jurisdiction in directing the CoC to vote on the offer, rendering both orders dated 19.05.2021 unsustainable[cite: 19].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeals (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 370, 376-377, and 393 of 2021 are allowed; impugned orders dated 19.05.2021 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench-II in IA No. 2431 of 2020 are set aside[cite: 19].
summary.summary: Union Bank of India (for the CoC), the Administrator of DHFL, and Successful Resolution Applicant Piramal Capital & Housing Finance Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Mumbai Bench order directing the Administrator to place an unsolicited settlement offer of Rs. 91,158 crores from erstwhile promoter Kapil Wadhawan before the CoC for voting within 10 days[cite: 19]. The order was passed after the CoC had already approved Piramal's resolution plan by a 93.65% vote and the plan approval application was reserved for orders[cite: 19]. Applying the Supreme Court doctrine in Ebix Singapore and Pratap Technocrats, the NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority has no equity-based jurisdiction under Section 60(5) or Rule 11 to reopen negotiations or compel the CoC to consider non-statutory promoter offers once a compliant plan has been approved[cite: 19]. The impugned orders were set aside[cite: 19].

summary.case_title: Aditya Kumar Tibrewal vs. Om Prakash Pandey & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Aditya Kumar Tibrewal is the Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor M/s Sri Balaji Forest Products Pvt. Ltd.; Respondents No. 1 and 2 (Om Prakash Pandey and Dhiraj Pandey) are suspended directors; Respondents No. 3 to 5 are Imax Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. and its directors; Respondents No. 6 and 7 are related entities (Shree Ram Saw Mill Pvt. Ltd. and Shova Properties Pvt. Ltd.)[cite: 20]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor executed a 29-year Lease Deed dated 30.11.2016 leasing out all factory land, plants, and machinery to Respondent No. 3 at a nominal rent; additionally, related-party preferential transfers totaling Rs. 16,60,000/- were made between 2017 and 2019[cite: 20]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Bank of India issued a SARFAESI Section 13(2) notice on 11.02.2015 and took symbolic possession on 09.08.2016; lease executed thereafter without lender consent; preferential related-party payments were Rs. 11,10,000/- to Respondent No. 6 and Rs. 5,50,000/- to Respondent No. 7[cite: 20]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 CIRP initiated on 18.10.2019; Section 19(2) compliance order passed 09.12.2019; lease deed disclosed on 15.01.2020; contempt notice issued 04.02.2020; Transaction Audit Report finalized on 14.08.2020; IA No. 742/KB/2020 filed beyond the 135th day[cite: 20]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Lease Deed dated 30.11.2016, Transaction Audit Report dated 14.08.2020, SARFAESI possession notices, corporate hypothecation letters dated 30.03.2013, and bank transfer records[cite: 20]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench dismissed RP's IA No. 742/KB/2020 on 26.02.2021 holding the application was barred by the 135-day timeline under Regulation 35A of CIRP Regulations and the lease fell outside the two-year lookback period under Section 46; RP appealed[cite: 20].
summary.legal_issues: Whether the timelines prescribed under Regulation 35A of the CIRP Regulations for filing avoidance applications are mandatory or directory, and whether applications under Sections 49 (transactions defrauding creditors) and 66 (fraudulent trading) are subject to the two-year lookback period prescribed under Section 46 of the IBC[cite: 20].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The timelines prescribed under Regulation 35A of the CIRP Regulations for forming an opinion, making a determination, and applying to the Adjudicating Authority are directory, not mandatory; applications for avoiding transactions cannot be dismissed solely for exceeding the 135-day timeline[cite: 20]. Furthermore, the statutory lookback period of one/two years under Section 46 applies strictly to avoidance of undervalued transactions under Section 45, and has no application to transactions defrauding creditors under Section 49 or fraudulent trading under Section 66[cite: 20]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Employing the Supreme Court doctrine in Surendra Trading Company, procedural rules governing public duties without statutory invalidation clauses are directory[cite: 20]. Sections 49 and 66 contain no lookback time limitations, which is supported by Section 69, which criminalizes fraudulent acts committed up to five years prior to CIRP[cite: 20]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of concrete pleadings alleging fraudulent diversion of hypothecated mortgaged factory assets for 29 years to defraud creditors, alongside adverse inference drawn from respondents' failure to file replies[cite: 20]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The application contained substantial pleadings under Sections 49 and 66; neither Regulation 35A nor Section 46 barred the application, and the Adjudicating Authority erred in dismissing it[cite: 20].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) Insolvency No. 583 of 2021 is allowed; impugned order dated 26.02.2021 is set aside; I.A. No. 742/KB/2020 is revived and remitted to the Adjudicating Authority to decide on merits in accordance with law; parties to bear their own costs[cite: 20].
summary.summary: The Resolution Professional of Sri Balaji Forest Products Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Kolkata Bench order dismissing his application under Sections 43, 45, 49, and 66 of the IBC[cite: 20]. The application challenged a 29-year lease of the company's mortgaged plant and machinery to a related entity and preferential cash transfers[cite: 20]. The NCLT rejected the application as barred by the 135-day deadline under Regulation 35A and outside the two-year lookback period under Section 46[cite: 20]. The NCLAT reversed the decision, holding that Regulation 35A timelines are directory and that the lookback limits under Section 46 do not apply to fraudulent transactions under Sections 49 and 66[cite: 20]. The application was revived for adjudication on merits[cite: 20].

summary.case_title: Indian Bank vs. Charu Desai, Erstwhile Resolution Professional & Chairman of Monitoring Committee of GB Global Ltd. & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Indian Bank is a dissenting secured financial creditor holding an 11.11% voting share in the CoC; Respondent No. 1 Charu Desai is the Erstwhile Resolution Professional and Monitoring Committee Chairman of Corporate Debtor GB Global Limited (formerly Mandhana Industries Limited); Respondent No. 2 Dev Land & Housing Private Limited is the Successful Resolution Applicant; Respondent No. 3 represents the CoC[cite: 21]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP was initiated against the Corporate Debtor on 29.09.2017; an initial resolution plan by Formation Textiles LLC (FTL) was approved on 30.11.2018 but failed during implementation, prompting NCLT on 05.02.2020 to authorize fresh resolution plan invitations[cite: 21]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Original CIRP liquidation value on 29.09.2017 was INR 307.08 crores; fresh liquidation valuation obtained as on 31.07.2020 was INR 184.92 crores (fair value INR 379.65 crores)[cite: 21]. Under the approved plan, total secured financial creditor payout was INR 151 crores against admitted claims of INR 1180.95 crores; Appellant was allocated INR 40.39 crores (~19% recovery)[cite: 21]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced 29.09.2017; FTL plan approved 30.11.2018 and possession retaken 08.01.2020; CoC resolved on 27.08.2020 to procure fresh valuation as of 31.07.2020; plan approved by 67.01% CoC vote ending 31.12.2020; NCLT approved plan on 19.05.2021[cite: 21]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Valuation reports of Kakode & Associates and Garg & Associates as on 31.07.2020, minutes of 32nd, 34th, 35th, 36th, 38th, and 39th CoC meetings, and lender-wise distribution matrices under Revised Scenario 1[cite: 21]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In IA No. 19 of 2021 in CP (IB) No. 1399/MB/2017, NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-I approved Respondent No. 2's Resolution Plan on 19.05.2021; Appellant appealed challenging the fresh valuation and allocation under Section 30(2)(b)[cite: 21].
summary.legal_issues: Whether the Committee of Creditors has statutory authority under the IBC to commission a fresh valuation report during CIRP when an earlier approved resolution plan fails, and whether the distribution mechanism allocating 19% pro-rata value to dissenting secured financial creditors based on the updated liquidation value complies with Section 30(2)(b)[cite: 21].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: While Regulation 35 of the CIRP Regulations prescribes the initial procedure for determining fair and liquidation values, there is no statutory prohibition in the IBC preventing the Committee of Creditors from obtaining an updated, realistic valuation to inform its commercial judgment where business disruptions or failed prior plans cause severe asset erosion; distribution among creditors based on such commercial assessment is non-justiciable so long as minimum liquidation thresholds under Section 30(2)(b) are observed[cite: 21]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Following the Supreme Court rulings in Essar Steel and Amit Metaliks, Section 30(2)(b) refers to Section 53 only to establish a minimum quantitative floor for dissenting creditors; it does not confer a right on a dissenting secured creditor to demand recovery corresponding to the full value of its encumbered security interest over and above its pro-rata entitlement within its class[cite: 21]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Unanimous CoC resolution adopting the updated 31.07.2020 valuation, participation without recorded contemporaneous dissent by the appellant during valuation deliberations, and proof that all dissenting financial creditors received uniform pro-rata treatment (19%)[cite: 21]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CoC's adoption of the updated valuation and the approved distribution scheme conformed to Section 30(2)(b); commercial wisdom exercised without statutory infraction cannot be disturbed on appeal[cite: 21].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 644 of 2021 is dismissed; the Adjudicating Authority's approval order dated 19.05.2021 is affirmed; no order as to costs[cite: 21].
summary.summary: Indian Bank, a dissenting secured financial creditor with an 11.11% vote share in GB Global Limited, appealed against the NCLT Mumbai Bench's order approving a Resolution Plan submitted by Dev Land & Housing Private Limited[cite: 21]. After an earlier approved plan collapsed, the CoC resolved to commission a fresh valuation as of 31.07.2020, which lowered the corporate debtor's liquidation value from INR 307.08 crores to INR 184.92 crores, resulting in a reduced allocation of INR 40.39 crores (19%) to the appellant[cite: 21]. The NCLAT held that the IBC does not prohibit the CoC from procuring an updated valuation when justified by extraordinary circumstances[cite: 21]. Affirming Essar Steel and Amit Metaliks, the Tribunal held that dissenting secured creditors are not entitled to the full value of their security interest, and dismissed the appeal[cite: 21].

summary.case_title: Krishan Kumar Basia vs. State Bank of India & Anr. [and Connected Appeals]
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are personal guarantors (Krishan Kumar Basia, Ankit Kumar Gupta, and Dinesh Kumar Basia) of Corporate Debtor M/s Gee Ispat Private Limited; Respondent No. 1 is State Bank of India (Financial Creditor); Respondent No. 2 is the proposed Resolution Professional Chanchal Dua[cite: 22]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Personal guarantees executed by Appellants in favour of State Bank of India securing credit facilities advanced to the Corporate Debtor[cite: 22]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by the Corporate Debtor and invocations of personal guarantees; monetary default figures not specifically quantified in the order[cite: 22]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: SBI e-filed its Section 95(1) petition on 01.10.2021 (assigned filing number 07101020/7186/2021) and it was registered/numbered on 18.02.2022 as CP-IB 111/2022; Personal Guarantor filed a Section 94 application on 25.10.2021 (filing number 07101020/7885/2021) which was registered/numbered earlier on 22.12.2021 as CP-IB 788/2021; NCLT passed the impugned order on 06.06.2022[cite: 22]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Electronic filing receipts, filing dates generated by the portal, and subsequent registry numbering logs[cite: 22]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Special Bench (Court-II) on 06.06.2022 in (IB)111(ND)/2022 held SBI's Section 95 application was filed prior in time (01.10.2021) and appointed an RP under Section 97; Guarantors appealed contending their Section 94 petition was numbered first, triggering the Section 96 interim moratorium against SBI[cite: 22].
summary.legal_issues: Whether an insolvency application under Section 94 or 95 of the IBC is considered 'filed' for the triggering of the interim moratorium under Section 96 upon electronic presentation at the registry counter, or only upon scrutiny, removal of defects, and formal numbering by the registry[cite: 22].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under the IBC and attendant procedural rules, an insolvency application is legally 'filed' on the date it is presented and registered in electronic form at the registry, rather than the date it is formally numbered after defect curation; the statutory interim moratorium under Section 96 operates from the date of presentation[cite: 22]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 2(14) of the NCLT Rules defines 'filed' as filed in the office of the registry, and Rule 10(2) of the 2019 Personal Guarantor Rules mandates electronic filing; tying the legal date of filing to registry numbering would generate unacceptable uncertainty regarding the enforcement of the statutory moratorium, which takes immediate effect upon presentation[cite: 22]. In accordance with the Supreme Court ruling in Vidyawati Gupta, procedural curation of defects relates back to the initial date of presentation[cite: 22]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Comparison of the official electronic filing receipts establishing that SBI presented its application on 01.10.2021, prior to the debtor's presentation on 25.10.2021[cite: 22]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: SBI's Section 95 petition was prior in time; the debtor's subsequently filed Section 94 petition could not interdict it via Section 96 moratorium, validating the appointment of the RP[cite: 22].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 721, 722 & 724 of 2022 are dismissed; impugned orders dated 06.06.2022 affirmed; no order as to costs[cite: 22].
summary.summary: Personal guarantors of Gee Ispat Private Limited challenged an NCLT New Delhi order appointing a Resolution Professional in Section 95 applications filed by State Bank of India[cite: 22]. The guarantors argued that their self-initiated insolvency applications under Section 94, though filed electronically after SBI's applications, were scrutinized and numbered earlier by the registry, thereby triggering the Section 96 interim moratorium to bar SBI's petitions[cite: 22]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeals, holding that under Rule 2(14) of the NCLT Rules and Rule 10 of the 2019 Personal Guarantor Rules, an application is 'filed' upon electronic submission[cite: 22]. Tying the Section 96 moratorium to registry numbering would create administrative uncertainty; since SBI e-filed first on 01.10.2021, its petition had legal precedence[cite: 22].

summary.case_title: Avantha Holdings Limited & Anr. vs. Abhilash Lal, Resolution Professional for Jhabua Power Limited & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant No. 1 Avantha Holdings Limited is the promoter/shareholder (holding 17.9% through an intermediate entity) of Corporate Debtor Jhabua Power Limited; Appellant No. 2 Anil Bhargava is a suspended director; Respondent No. 1 Abhilash Lal is the Resolution Professional; Respondent No. 2 is the CoC; Respondent No. 3 NTPC Limited is the Successful Resolution Applicant[cite: 23]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP was initiated against the thermal power project Corporate Debtor under Section 9 on 27.03.2019; NTPC and Adani Power submitted resolution plans[cite: 23]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellants submitted an unaccepted OTS/Section 12A restructuring proposal offering INR 100 crores upfront payment and deferred payments over 19 years; NTPC submitted four plan iterations culminating in an approved offer featuring INR 905 crores upfront cash[cite: 23]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated 27.03.2019; initial plan submitted by NTPC on 30.12.2019; Canara Bank classified NTPC joint ventures (RGPPL and KLL) as NPA on 21.05.2018 (retrospectively effective 01.04.2009); lenders issued no due certificates to KLL in March 2020 and RGPPL in January 2021; CoC rejected Section 12A proposal on 05.03.2021 and 21.04.2021; NTPC's revised plan approved by 100% CoC vote on 27.06.2021; NCLT dismissed Appellants' challenge on 08.03.2022[cite: 23]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Section 29A eligibility reports by Mazars Business Advisors, bank NPA declarations, no due certificates from lenders of RGPPL and KLL, and CoC minutes[cite: 23]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In IA(IB) No. 537/KB/2021 in CP (IB) No. 634/KB/2017, NCLT Kolkata Bench rejected Appellants' application seeking NTPC's disqualification under Section 29A and challenging CoC's rejection of their Section 12A offer on 08.03.2022; Appellants appealed[cite: 23].
summary.legal_issues: Whether the one-year grace period under Section 29A(c) of the IBC is computed from the actual date a bank declares an NPA or from a retrospective effective date assigned by the bank, and whether suspended promoters can challenge the CoC's rejection of an uninvited Section 12A settlement proposal[cite: 23].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: For assessing disqualification under Section 29A(c) of the IBC, the statutory period of one year from NPA classification until CIRP commencement runs from the actual date the classification is made by the financial institution, and cannot be antedated to a retrospective effective date; otherwise, the statutory one-year cure period would be rendered illusory[cite: 23]. Furthermore, promoters cannot utilize Section 12A as a backdoor mechanism to submit non-compliant restructuring proposals, and the CoC's commercial rejection of such proposals is non-justiciable[cite: 23]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 29A(c) grants a one-year period from the date of classification during which an account is treated as a substandard asset before doubtful asset status triggers disqualification; permitting retrospective antedating would subvert the legislative policy explained in Swiss Ribbons[cite: 23]. Additionally, Section 12A permits withdrawal only upon an application approved by a 90% CoC vote, which cannot be compelled by the tribunal[cite: 23]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of Canara Bank's classification letter issued on 21.05.2018, proving that one year had not elapsed before CIRP commenced on 27.03.2019, alongside unanimous CoC minutes rejecting the promoters' Section 12A offer[cite: 23]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: NTPC was fully eligible under Section 29A at all relevant times; CoC was within its commercial rights to negotiate and accept improved revisions of the plan and reject the promoters' restructuring proposal[cite: 23].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 304 of 2022 is dismissed; Adjudicating Authority order dated 08.03.2022 is affirmed; no order as to costs[cite: 23].
summary.summary: Avantha Holdings Limited, promoter of Jhabua Power Limited, appealed against an NCLT Kolkata Bench order dismissing its application to disqualify NTPC Limited under Section 29A(c) and challenging the CoC's rejection of its Section 12A settlement proposal[cite: 23]. The appellant argued that two NTPC joint ventures were NPAs backdated to 2009, disqualifying NTPC when it submitted its initial plan, and that the CoC acted arbitrarily in rejecting the promoter's settlement offer[cite: 23]. The NCLAT held that the one-year lookback period under Section 29A(c) runs from the actual date of classification (21.05.2018) rather than retrospective backdates, meaning one year had not elapsed prior to CIRP initiation on 27.03.2019[cite: 23]. The Tribunal affirmed NTPC's eligibility and held that the CoC's commercial rejection of an uninvited Section 12A offer is non-justiciable[cite: 23].

summary.case_title: Eastern Power Distribution Company of Andhra Pradesh Limited vs. Maithan Alloys Limited & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Eastern Power Distribution Company of Andhra Pradesh Limited (APEPDCL) is a state electricity distribution licensee; Respondent No. 1 Maithan Alloys Limited is the Successful Auction Purchaser of Corporate Debtor Impex Metal & Ferro Alloys Ltd. (in liquidation); Respondent No. 2 Samir Bhattacharya is the Liquidator[cite: 24]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor availed electricity connections from the Appellant; following failure to pay power bills, electricity was disconnected on 24.12.2018; liquidation was ordered on 12.02.2019 and the debtor was sold as a going concern via e-auction for Rs. 74.22 crores[cite: 24]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellant asserted electricity dues of Rs. 52,44,85,882/-, comprising pre-CIRP arrears of Rs. 28,34,90,801/- and CIRP-period consumption dues of Rs. 20,72,84,722/-; Liquidator admitted an operational claim of Rs. 36.51 crores[cite: 24]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated 09.03.2018; power disconnected 24.12.2018; liquidation ordered 12.02.2019; joint settlement between liquidator and purchaser approved on 21.06.2021; Sale Certificate issued 16.09.2021; NCLT directed reconnection on 05.10.2021[cite: 24]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: E-auction notice for going concern sale on 'as is where is' basis without mentioning past electricity liabilities; Sale Certificate dated 16.09.2021; Regulation 8.4 of General Terms and Conditions of Supply[cite: 24]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In IA (IBC)/748 (KB) 2021 in CP (IB)/176 (KB) 2018, NCLT Kolkata Bench on 05.10.2021 directed Appellant to energize the 24 MW connection to the Corporate Debtor, retain requisite security deposit, refund the balance of Rs. 24.50 crores deposited ad-interim, and claim past arrears from the liquidator under Section 53; APEPDCL appealed[cite: 24].
summary.legal_issues: Whether an electricity distribution licensee can refuse to restore power supply or demand payment of pre-CIRP and CIRP electricity arrears from a successful auction purchaser who acquired the corporate debtor as a going concern in liquidation proceedings under the IBC, relying on statutory supply regulations[cite: 24].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An entity purchasing a corporate debtor as a going concern in a liquidation sale under the IBC acquires the enterprise on a clean slate and cannot be saddled with past pre-CIRP or CIRP liabilities; statutory electricity regulations conditioning reconnection on the payment of past arrears are inconsistent with the priority distribution waterfall under Section 53 and are overridden by Section 238 of the IBC[cite: 24]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 53 establishes an exhaustive, non-obstante scheme for distributing liquidation assets; pre-CIRP electricity dues constitute operational debt, while CIRP consumption constitutes insolvency process costs, both of which must be satisfied strictly through the Section 53 waterfall from the liquidation estate[cite: 24]. By virtue of Section 238, these provisions override state electricity terms and conditions of supply (such as Regulation 8.4)[cite: 24]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the e-auction notice and sale certificate establishing a going-concern sale without any clause imposing past operational liabilities onto the buyer, alongside the claim lodged by the utility with the liquidator[cite: 24]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The utility must seek its recoveries solely from the Liquidator under Section 53; it cannot withhold power or compel the auction purchaser to clear historical corporate debts[cite: 24].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 961 of 2021 is dismissed; NCLT order dated 05.10.2021 is upheld, with liberty granted to the Appellant to move the Adjudicating Authority for its pre-CIRP and post-CIRP entitlements under Section 53[cite: 24].
summary.summary: APEPDCL appealed against an NCLT Kolkata Bench order directing it to restore a 24 MW electricity connection to Impex Metal & Ferro Alloys Ltd., which had been purchased as a going concern in a liquidation sale by Maithan Alloys Limited[cite: 24]. The utility demanded payment of over Rs. 52 crores in pre-CIRP and CIRP electricity arrears pursuant to Regulation 8.4 of its supply conditions[cite: 24]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that purchasers acquiring companies as going concerns under the IBC start on a clean slate[cite: 24]. Pre-CIRP and CIRP electricity arrears must be recovered through the Section 53 waterfall, and under Section 238, the IBC overrides inconsistent state electricity regulations[cite: 24].

summary.case_title: Praful Nanji Satra vs. Vistra ITCL (India) Limited & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Praful Nanji Satra is the personal guarantor and promoter of Corporate Debtor Satra Properties (India) Ltd. (SPIL); Respondent No. 1 Vistra ITCL (India) Limited is the Debenture Trustee; Respondents No. 2 and 3 (Mayank J. Shah and Shruti Mayank Shah) are Debenture Holders/Financial Creditors; Respondent No. 4 is the IRP[cite: 25]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor issued 5,600 secured redeemable Non-Convertible Debentures (NCDs) of face value Rs. 1 lakh each aggregating Rs. 56 crores under a Debenture Subscription Agreement and Debenture Trust Deed dated 01.03.2014 to finance real estate projects in Borivali and Jodhpur, secured by a mortgage over a Jodhpur commercial plot and personal guarantee of the Appellant[cite: 25]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate debtor failed to redeem debentures per the original schedule; 4,330 NCDs remained outstanding (Rs. 43.30 crores principal plus accrued interest); redemption dates were extended into 5 tranches from April 2019 to December 2019, but were defaulted on[cite: 25]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Agreements executed 01.03.2014; corporate debtor alleged an all-encompassing settlement on 31.01.2018; debtor sought interest reset from 12% to 9% on 14.02.2018; events of default notices issued on 12.04.2019; Section 7 petition admitted on 03.08.2020; Third Member opinion rendered 10.02.2022[cite: 25]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: NCD Subscription Agreement, Debenture Trust Deed, Standalone Audited Balance Sheet for the year ended 31.03.2018 acknowledging NCD debts, escrow bank statements, and default demand notices[cite: 25]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In CP (IB) No. 1632/MB/2019, NCLT Mumbai Bench admitted the Section 7 petition on 03.08.2020 but the bench split on whether the NCD agreements should be impounded for insufficient stamping under the Maharashtra Stamp Act; Third Member held impounding unnecessary; suspended director appealed alleging novation and inadmissible unstamped documents[cite: 25].
summary.legal_issues: Whether an alleged tripartite corporate settlement regarding other group liabilities novated the underlying NCD subscription agreement, and whether insufficient stamping under the Maharashtra Stamp Act renders debenture agreements inadmissible to prove financial debt and default in a summary Section 7 proceeding[cite: 25].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In summary proceedings under Section 7 of the IBC, where the execution of underlying debt documents and disbursement of funds are admitted and acknowledged in corporate financial statements, an objection regarding insufficient stamping of the agreements does not bar admission of the petition, as stamping is a curable technical defect and financial debt can be evidenced by other sources recognized under Rule 4 and Part V of Form 1[cite: 25]. Furthermore, an overarching business settlement does not novate specific debenture contracts unless the contracts and their underlying securities are expressly extinguished or superseded by the parties[cite: 25]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 requires the Adjudicating Authority to ascertain default from information utilities or other evidence specified in Form 1; under Innoventive Industries, debt is due and payable unless interdicted by substantive law, and procedural deficiencies in stamping do not extinguish the commercial debt[cite: 25]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Balance sheet entries as of 31.03.2018 acknowledging 9% redeemable NCD liabilities, letters dated 14.02.2018 requesting interest reductions post-dating the alleged settlement, and uncontradicted evidence of bank disbursements[cite: 25]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCD subscription agreement was not novated, and default was conclusively established; the Section 7 petition was properly admitted[cite: 25].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 713 of 2020 is dismissed; NCLT order admitting Section 7 application is affirmed; no order as to costs[cite: 25].
summary.summary: Praful Nanji Satra, promoter of Satra Properties (India) Ltd., appealed against an NCLT Mumbai Bench order admitting a Section 7 petition filed by debenture holders and trustee Vistra ITCL for defaulting on 4,330 Non-Convertible Debentures worth Rs. 43.30 crores[cite: 25]. The appellant argued that the NCD debt had been novated under an overall settlement dated 31.01.2018, and that the Debenture Subscription Agreement and Trust Deed were inadmissible as evidence under Section 34 of the Maharashtra Stamp Act due to insufficient stamping[cite: 25]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the settlement never referenced the NCDs, which were subsequently acknowledged in the debtor's audited balance sheet[cite: 25]. The Tribunal further ruled that insufficient stamping is a curable technical defect that does not prevent establishing debt and default in summary Section 7 proceedings[cite: 25].

summary.case_title: Damodar Valley Corporation vs. Kharkia Steels Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Damodar Valley Corporation (DVC) is a statutory electricity distribution company/Operational Creditor; Respondent No. 1 Kharkia Steels Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor; Respondent No. 2 Uday Narayan Mitra is the Resolution Professional; Respondent No. 3 Amritvani Exim Private Limited is the Successful Resolution Applicant[cite: 26]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Power Purchase Agreement dated 28.07.2009 for industrial power supply to the Corporate Debtor's manufacturing facilities[cite: 26]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in power bills led to disconnection notice on 12.08.2015; Appellant's admitted claim was Rs. 18.71 crores (later asserted at Rs. 39.08 crores after WBERC tariff revision); resolution plan offered Rs. 0.14 crore for operational creditors, allocating Rs. 0.03 crore (approx. 0.16%) to Appellant[cite: 26]. Corporate Debtor's liquidation value was Rs. 6.52 crores against admitted financial debts of Rs. 411.16 crores (operational creditor liquidation value was NIL)[cite: 26]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Power disconnected 12.08.2015; Section 7 CIRP initiated on 26.09.2019; CoC approved resolution plan in 7th meeting on 05.03.2020; NCLT approved plan on 21.09.2020; SRA sought reconnection on 12.10.2020[cite: 26]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: PPA dated 28.07.2009, disconnection notices, proof of claim dated 17.10.2019, WBERC supply regulations, and the approved Resolution Plan[cite: 26]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In IA (IB) No. 680/KB/2020 in CP IB No. 1440/KB/2018, NCLT Kolkata Bench approved Respondent No. 3's resolution plan on 21.09.2020; DVC appealed challenging inadequate payout and extinguishment of pre-CIRP electricity claims[cite: 26].
summary.legal_issues: Whether the allocation of a negligible percentage (0.16%) towards pre-CIRP electricity dues in a resolution plan violates Section 30(2)(b) of the IBC, and whether an electricity distributor can condition reconnection on payment of extinguished pre-CIRP arrears pursuant to state electricity regulations[cite: 26].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where the liquidation value payable to operational creditors under Section 53 is nil, an allocation of an amount in the resolution plan satisfying the minimum requirements of Section 30(2)(b) is statutorily valid and deemed fair and equitable; once approved under Section 31, all pre-CIRP claims stand extinguished and the utility cannot demand past arrears for supplying electricity, though fresh connection charges and tariffs may be governed by applicable electricity regulations[cite: 26]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(2)(b) mandates a minimum floor based on Section 53 liquidation value; in line with Essar Steel, Ghanashyam Mishra, and Pratap Technocrats, the commercial wisdom of the CoC governs distribution and NCLT holds no equity-based jurisdiction to enhance payouts to operational creditors[cite: 26]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Demonstration that the liquidation value for operational creditors was nil and that the distribution was approved by the requisite majority of the CoC[cite: 26]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The approved plan meets Section 30(2)(b) requirements and extinguishes past DVC liabilities; while DVC cannot demand pre-CIRP arrears, the SRA must apply for a fresh connection complying with current WBERC tariffs and security deposit rules[cite: 26].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1111 of 2020 is dismissed; approval of the Resolution Plan is upheld with modification that terms of fresh power supply shall be in accordance with prevailing WBERC tariffs and regulations at the time of entering the fresh agreement; no order as to costs[cite: 26].
summary.summary: Damodar Valley Corporation appealed an NCLT Kolkata Bench order approving a Resolution Plan submitted by Amritvani Exim Private Limited for Corporate Debtor Kharkia Steels Private Limited[cite: 26]. DVC, with an admitted pre-CIRP claim of Rs. 18.71 crores, received Rs. 3 lakhs (0.16%) under the plan and argued that WBERC Regulations barred reconnection without clearing historical dues[cite: 26]. The NCLAT held that because the corporate debtor's liquidation value was insufficient to cover financial debt, the operational creditors' liquidation entitlement was nil, rendering the allocation compliant with Section 30(2)(b)[cite: 26]. Confirming that pre-CIRP dues stand extinguished under Ghanashyam Mishra, the Tribunal dismissed the appeal, subject to the SRA paying standard security deposits and prevailing tariffs for a fresh connection under WBERC Regulations[cite: 26].

summary.case_title: Standard Surfa Chem India Pvt. Ltd. vs. Kishore Gopal Somani, Liquidator of Advanced Surfactants India Ltd.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Standard Surfa Chem India Pvt. Ltd. (formerly Portia Ventures Pvt. Ltd.) is the successful auction purchaser; Respondent Kishore Gopal Somani is the Liquidator of Advanced Surfactants India Ltd. (Corporate Debtor in liquidation)[cite: 27]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: E-auction sale of the Corporate Debtor's Pondicherry unit in liquidation conducted in March 2021[cite: 27]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellant emerged as the highest bidder with a bid of Rs. 3.3 crores; Letter of Intent dated 05.03.2021 required full payment within 90 days (expiring 03.06.2021)[cite: 27]. Due to the second COVID-19 lockdown, payment was delayed, but the full sum of Rs. 3,48,04,548/- (including 12% interest) was paid on 08.09.2021 and 09.09.2021[cite: 27]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: LOI issued 05.03.2021; complete lockdown imposed in Tamil Nadu on 10.05.2021; Appellant filed IA No. 3377/2021 for extension on 25.05.2021; NCLT dismissed IA as infructuous on 09.08.2021; Liquidator terminated bid and forfeited EMD on 13.08.2021[cite: 27]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bank RTGS receipts dated 08.09.2021 and 09.09.2021, terms of E-Auction Process Information Document empowering the Liquidator to extend timelines (Clause 17.2), and Tamil Nadu lockdown orders[cite: 27]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In (IB)-922(PB)/2018, NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi dismissed IA No. 3377 of 2021 on 09.08.2021 via an unreasoned one-line order stating the application had become infructuous; Appellant appealed[cite: 27].
summary.legal_issues: Whether the 90-day model timeline for payment of auction consideration under the IBBI Liquidation Process Regulations is mandatory or directory, and whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in dismissing an extension application without reasons despite delays caused by COVID-19 lockdown disruptions[cite: 27].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The model timelines prescribed in the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016 for payment of auction sale consideration are directory, not mandatory deadlines; where force majeure events such as pandemic lockdowns impede timely compliance, the Liquidator and Adjudicating Authority possess discretion to extend time to achieve asset maximization[cite: 27]. Furthermore, judicial orders rejecting extension applications must be reasoned[cite: 27]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 47 provides model guidance; applying the Supreme Court ruling in Surendra Trading Company and Pioneer Urban Land, procedural timelines devoid of statutory default consequences are directory[cite: 27]. Clauses in the process document empowering the liquidator to adjust timelines must be exercised harmoniously with the overarching IBC objective of asset value maximization[cite: 27]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Proof of diligent application for extension prior to expiry of the 90-day window, disruption caused by lockdown, and subsequent payment of the entire balance consideration with 12% interest[cite: 27]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The dismissal of IA 3377/2021 via an unreasoned one-line order was erroneous; the delay stood regularized by full payment with interest[cite: 27].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 684 of 2021 is allowed; impugned order dated 09.08.2021 and the Liquidator's termination and forfeiture letter dated 13.08.2021 are set aside; the Appellant's bid is declared valid and subsisting[cite: 27].
summary.summary: Standard Surfa Chem India Pvt. Ltd. was declared the successful auction purchaser of the Pondicherry unit of Advanced Surfactants India Ltd. for Rs. 3.3 crores[cite: 27]. Due to COVID-19 second wave lockdowns in Tamil Nadu, the appellant filed IA 3377/2021 before the expiry of the 90-day payment period seeking an extension[cite: 27]. NCLT New Delhi dismissed the application through a one-line order as infructuous, prompting the liquidator to cancel the sale and forfeit the EMD[cite: 27]. During the appeal, the purchaser paid the entire bid amount along with 12% interest[cite: 27]. The NCLAT held that the liquidation timelines under Regulation 47 are directory, not mandatory, and that procedural delays caused by force majeure should not override asset maximization[cite: 27]. The termination was set aside and the sale upheld[cite: 27].

summary.case_title: Amit Goel vs. Piyush Shelters India Private Ltd. & Ors. [and Connected Appeals]
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are suspended director Amit Goel (CA 700/2021) and homebuyers/allottees Harjeet Kaur and Bala Pareek & Ors. (CAs 761 & 925 of 2021); Respondents are Corporate Debtor Piyush Shelters India Pvt. Ltd. (through RP Swami Deen Gupta), the CoC, and Successful Resolution Applicant Consortium led by Naveen Kumar Gupta (including Maya Buildcon Pvt. Ltd. and Geotech Homz Pvt. Ltd.)[cite: 28]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Real estate development of residential projects in Faridabad, Haryana, wherein homebuyers/allottees executed MOUs/allotment agreements and deposited substantial considerations[cite: 28]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: 222 homebuyers filed timely claims, while 251 homebuyers (approx. 53% of total 473 allottees) either failed to file or submitted belated claims; approved plan created two classes: timely claimants received flat possession, while non-claimants received only 10% of their verified booking amounts after which their claims were abandoned[cite: 28]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated 03.12.2018; 4th EOI issued 01.10.2019; Maya Buildcon withdrew earlier plan and filed CA 282/2019 to submit revised plan; RP placed revised consortium plan for e-voting on 06/07.11.2019; NCLT Allahabad approved plan on 14.07.2021[cite: 28]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Newspaper publications in Jansatta and Financial Express (Delhi editions only, despite offices in Meerut/Faridabad being closed); e-voting notices sent barely 25.5 hours prior; records of simultaneous CoC and class voting[cite: 28]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In CA No. 371/2019 in CP No. 322/ALD/2018, NCLT Allahabad Bench approved the Resolution Plan on 14.07.2021; suspended director and homebuyers appealed[cite: 28].
summary.legal_issues: Whether holding simultaneous e-voting of the class of financial creditors (homebuyers) alongside the Committee of Creditors without prior consultation by the Authorized Representative violates Section 25A of the IBC, and whether a resolution plan can unlawfully discriminate within the same class of homebuyers by awarding flat possession to timely claimants while providing only 10% refunds to non-claimants[cite: 28].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Authorized Representative of financial creditors in a class must strictly comply with Section 25A of the IBC and Regulation 16A of the CIRP Regulations by seeking prior instructions and circulating agendas before CoC meetings; conducting simultaneous voting alongside the CoC creates a legal fiction that vitiates the statutory process[cite: 28]. Furthermore, a resolution plan cannot discriminate within the same class of financial creditors by allotting property possession to timely claimants while extinguishing the rights of belated claimants with a 10% payout[cite: 28]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 25A(1) and (3) requires the AR to act exclusively upon 'prior instructions' of creditors in a class; failure to provide adequate notice and holding simultaneous voting infringes Section 30(2)(e)[cite: 28]. In line with Rajputana Properties, similarly situated creditors within the same class cannot be meted unequal, discriminatory treatment[cite: 28]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Evidence showing simultaneous voting windows, notification to the AR barely 25.5 hours before voting, and exclusion of 53% of total allottees due to inadequate notice[cite: 28]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The voting process was fundamentally flawed and the plan discriminatory; CIRP must be recommenced from the stage of inviting fresh claims[cite: 28].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) Nos. 700, 761 & 925 of 2021 are allowed; impugned approval order dated 14.07.2021 is set aside; process ordered to be started afresh with RP accepting all allottee claims with realistic timelines, issuing a revised Information Memorandum, seeking fresh EOIs, and completing the exercise within 90 days; no costs[cite: 28].
summary.summary: Appeals were filed by a suspended director and excluded homebuyers challenging the NCLT Allahabad Bench's approval of a Resolution Plan for real estate debtor Piyush Shelters India Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 28] The plan provided flat possession to 222 timely claimant homebuyers, while relegating 251 non-claimant homebuyers (53% of allottees) to an arbitrary 10% refund[cite: 28]. Moreover, the Authorized Representative conducted voting for the homebuyers simultaneously with the CoC vote rather than obtaining prior voting instructions[cite: 28]. The NCLAT held that simultaneous voting violated Section 25A and that discriminating between homebuyers of the same class violates the IBC[cite: 28]. Setting aside the approval, the Tribunal ordered a fresh CIRP process giving all allottees an opportunity to submit claims[cite: 28].

summary.case_title: Rushabh Civil Contractors Pvt. Ltd. vs. Centrio Lifespaces Ltd.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Rushabh Civil Contractors Pvt. Ltd. is the purported Financial Creditor; Respondent Centrio Lifespaces Ltd. (formerly Satra Realty and Builders Limited - SRBL) is the Corporate Debtor, taken over by the MJ Shah Group[cite: 29]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Alleged Loan Agreement dated 02.12.2015 for an unsecured credit facility of Rs. 12 crores at 12% annual interest repayable on demand, entered into when both companies were under the common management of the Satra Group[cite: 29]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellant claimed outstanding financial debt of Rs. 12,39,06,879/-; disbursement occurred on 07.11.2015 prior to the loan agreement dated 02.12.2015, with circular day-to-day fund movements between Satra Group entities and write-offs of Rs. 7 crores transferred to third parties[cite: 29]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Purported loan agreement executed 02.12.2015; MOU executed 23.03.2018; management transferred to MJ Shah Group on 09.04.2018; Demand Notices issued 06.05.2019 and 13.05.2019; Section 7 petition filed 28.05.2019[cite: 29]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bank statements revealing simultaneous circular fund transfers between group entities, audited accounts reflecting related-party transactions, MOU dated 23.03.2018, and Section 226(3) Income Tax garnishee notices[cite: 29]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In C.P. No. (IB) 2161/MB/C-IV/2019, NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV dismissed Appellant's Section 7 application on 06.05.2020 holding the transactions were collusive, lacked proper authorization, and predated the loan agreement; purported creditor appealed[cite: 29].
summary.legal_issues: Whether circular, undocumented money transfers executed between related sister companies under common promoter management qualify as a genuine 'financial debt' disbursed against consideration for the time value of money under Section 5(8) of the IBC[cite: 29].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Sham, circular, or collusive transactions engineered between interconnected sister entities under common management do not constitute a 'financial debt' disbursed against consideration for the time value of money under Section 5(8); such arrangements do not confer the status of a 'financial creditor' under Section 5(7) of the IBC[cite: 29]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Applying the Supreme Court doctrine in Phoenix ARC v. Spade Financial Services, the Adjudicating Authority must pierce the veil to determine whether transactions are genuine financial borrowings or collusive book entries intended to defraud external buyers or manipulate credit positions; summary admission under Innoventive Industries does not apply to collusive transactions[cite: 29]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Review of ledger entries and bank statements showing circular same-day fund flows, loan disbursals predating agreement execution, violation of Section 186 lending limits under the Companies Act, and common directorship[cite: 29]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The transaction was a collusive internal arrangement within the Satra Group rather than an arm's length commercial loan, disentitling the Appellant from triggering Section 7[cite: 29].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 715 of 2020 is dismissed; impugned order dated 06.05.2020 of the Adjudicating Authority is affirmed; no order as to costs[cite: 29].
summary.summary: Rushabh Civil Contractors Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Mumbai Bench order dismissing its Section 7 petition against Centrio Lifespaces Ltd. (formerly Satra Realty and Builders Limited) claiming default on an alleged Rs. 12 crore loan[cite: 29]. The corporate debtor demonstrated that the loan agreement was executed after purported disbursements and constituted circular, internal transactions between entities controlled by the Satra Group before management transferred to the MJ Shah Group[cite: 29]. Applying the Supreme Court's ruling in Phoenix ARC v. Spade Financial Services, the NCLAT held that collusive transactions entered into between sister concerns do not qualify as financial debt under Section 5(8)[cite: 29]. Finding no genuine financial borrowing with time value of money, the Tribunal affirmed the dismissal[cite: 29].

summary.case_title: Damodar Valley Corporation vs. Karthik Alloys Limited & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Damodar Valley Corporation (DVC) is a statutory electricity supply corporation/Operational Creditor; Respondent No. 1 Karthik Alloys Limited is the Corporate Debtor; Respondent No. 2 is the Resolution Professional[cite: 30]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Power Supply Agreement dated 01.01.1997 for supply of industrial power (10,000 KVA contract demand) to Corporate Debtor's Durgapur factory[cite: 30]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in electricity charges prompted disconnection on 14.09.2019; DVC filed a pre-CIRP operational claim of Rs. 27,78,95,386/- with the RP; Durgapur factory was operating on diesel generators[cite: 30]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Power disconnected on 14.09.2019; Section 9 CIRP initiated on 17.12.2019; RP requested restoration under Section 14(2) on 12.02.2020; DVC refused on 24.02.2020; NCLT Mumbai ordered reconnection on 08.12.2020[cite: 30]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Power Supply Agreement dated 01.01.1997, disconnection notices, proof of claim accepted by RP, and WBERC Supply Regulations[cite: 30]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In IA No. 1203/2020 in CP(IB) 2119/MB/C-IV/2019, NCLT Mumbai Bench ordered DVC on 08.12.2020 to reconnect power supply within 15 days upon deposit of current electricity dues from the CIRP initiation date, without demanding past arrears or security deposits; DVC appealed[cite: 30].
summary.legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the jurisdiction under Section 14(2) and 14(2A) of the IBC to direct an electricity licensee to restore power disconnected prior to CIRP initiation without insisting on the payment of pre-CIRP arrears or a fresh security deposit[cite: 30].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where an electricity supply agreement has not undergone deemed termination under relevant supply codes prior to the commencement of insolvency, the moratorium under Section 14(2) and 14(2A) prevents deemed termination from occurring during CIRP; the Adjudicating Authority possesses jurisdiction to direct reconnection to preserve going-concern value and facilitate resolution, without requiring upfront payment of pre-CIRP arrears[cite: 30]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Clause 4.6.1 of the WBERC Regulations prescribes a 180-day period post-disconnection before deemed termination occurs; as CIRP intervened before the 180 days expired, Section 14 statutorily froze termination[cite: 30]. Under Section 14(2A), critical supplies needed to preserve value cannot be interrupted, provided current post-moratorium consumption charges are met as CIRP costs, while pre-CIRP dues remain payable solely under a final resolution plan or liquidation[cite: 30]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Disconnection occurred on 14.09.2019, meaning the 180-day period had not elapsed when CIRP commenced on 17.12.2019, combined with the fact that electricity was necessary to replace diesel generation and preserve debtor viability[cite: 30]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: DVC cannot demand pre-CIRP arrears as a condition precedent for power reconnection; the direction to restore supply upon receiving current CIRP dues was lawful[cite: 30].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 13 of 2021 is dismissed; NCLT order dated 08.12.2020 directing reconnection of power without demanding past arrears or security deposits is upheld; no order as to costs[cite: 30].
summary.summary: Damodar Valley Corporation appealed against an NCLT Mumbai Bench order directing it to restore electricity supply to Karthik Alloys Limited's Durgapur plant without requiring pre-CIRP arrears or fresh security deposits[cite: 30]. DVC had disconnected power three months prior to the Section 9 CIRP admission and argued that Section 14(2) does not mandate reconnection of already-severed lines[cite: 30]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that because the 180-day threshold for deemed contract termination under WBERC Regulations had not elapsed before CIRP commenced, the agreement remained alive[cite: 30]. Under Section 14(2A), the RP was entitled to restoration of critical power to maintain going-concern operations, with pre-CIRP debts to be satisfied solely through the eventual resolution plan[cite: 30].

summary.case_title: Bharat Heavy Electricals Ltd. vs. Anil Goel, Resolution Professional, Ideal Energy Projects Ltd. & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Bharat Heavy Electricals Ltd. (BHEL) is an operational creditor/payee; Respondent No. 1 Anil Goel is the Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor M/s Ideal Energy Projects Ltd.[cite: 32] 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor owed an outstanding liability of Rs. 8,00,00,000/- to BHEL, against which it paid Rs. 4,50,00,000/- and issued 4 post-dated cheques of Rs. 87,50,000/- each dated 18.02.2020, 18.03.2020, 18.04.2020, and 18.05.2020 on 17.01.2020 to discharge the remaining Rs. 3,50,00,000/-[cite: 32]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose in loan facilities of Rs. 492 Crores owed by the Corporate Debtor to Corporation Bank leading to CIRP admission; the disputed transaction involved the encashment of one post-dated cheque for Rs. 87,50,000/- on 18.02.2020[cite: 32]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Hearing reserved on Section 7 petition on 16.12.2019; post-dated cheques handed over on 17.01.2020; Section 7 CIRP admitted and Section 14 moratorium imposed on 28.01.2020; first post-dated cheque encashed on 18.02.2020; public announcement made on 19.02.2020; NCLT ordered reversal on 10.08.2021[cite: 32]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Post-dated cheques dated 18.02.2020 to 18.05.2020, bank debit statement of 18.02.2020 showing transfer of Rs. 87.50 lakhs from the debtor's account, and CIRP admission order dated 28.01.2020[cite: 32]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In IA No. 191 of 2021, the Adjudicating Authority directed BHEL to reverse the transaction of Rs. 87.50 lakhs dated 18.02.2020 and submit its claim before the IRP; BHEL appealed contending the cheque was handed over prior to CIRP admission and Section 74 penalties did not justify transaction reversal[cite: 32].
summary.legal_issues: Whether encashing a post-dated cheque and receiving funds from the bank account of a corporate debtor after the declaration of moratorium violates Section 14(1)(b) of the IBC, and whether the Adjudicating Authority possesses the power to order the reversal and refund of such post-moratorium transfers[cite: 32].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The encashment of a post-dated cheque and resultant transfer of funds from the bank account of a corporate debtor during the currency of a statutory moratorium violates Section 14(1)(b) of the IBC, even if the instrument was handed over prior to the insolvency commencement date; the Adjudicating Authority has full jurisdiction to nullify such prohibited transfers and order a complete refund to the corporate debtor's estate[cite: 32]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14 takes effect immediately upon the pronouncement of the admission order; Section 14(1)(b) creates an absolute statutory freeze prohibiting transferring, encumbering, alienating, or disposing of any corporate assets[cite: 32]. The fact that penal provisions under Section 74 exist does not preclude the tribunal from granting civil restitution to undo transactions executed in contravention of the moratorium[cite: 32]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Comparing the date of pronouncement of the Section 14 moratorium (28.01.2020) against the date of presentation and bank debit of the post-dated cheque (18.02.2020)[cite: 32]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The encashment on 18.02.2020 directly breached the Section 14 moratorium; BHEL was legally bound to refund the sum and lodge its claim with the IRP[cite: 32].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 965 of 2021 is dismissed; impugned order dated 10.08.2021 directing BHEL to reverse the Rs. 87.50 lakh transaction is affirmed; no order as to costs[cite: 32].
summary.summary: Bharat Heavy Electricals Ltd. (BHEL) appealed against an NCLT order directing it to refund Rs. 87.50 lakhs encashed from the bank account of Corporate Debtor Ideal Energy Projects Ltd. during CIRP[cite: 32]. Prior to the initiation of insolvency, the debtor had issued four post-dated cheques to BHEL on 17.01.2020[cite: 32]. After Section 7 CIRP was admitted and a moratorium imposed on 28.01.2020, BHEL presented the first cheque on its due date, 18.02.2020[cite: 32]. BHEL argued that it had received the instrument before CIRP commenced and before the public announcement[cite: 32]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the statutory moratorium under Section 14 takes effect upon order pronouncement, prohibiting all asset transfers[cite: 32]. Encashing cheques post-moratorium is illegal, and ordering restitution is proper[cite: 32].

summary.case_title: Damodar Valley Corporation vs. Kharkia Steels Private Limited & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Damodar Valley Corporation (DVC) is the electricity distribution licensee; Respondent No. 1 Kharkia Steels Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor, represented by Successful Resolution Applicant Amritvani Exim Private Limited; Respondent No. 2 Uday Narayan Mitra is the Resolution Professional[cite: 33]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Power Purchase Agreement dated 28.07.2009 for supply of industrial power; electricity disconnected due to non-payment on 12.08.2015; resolution plan of Amritvani Exim Private Limited approved by NCLT on 21.09.2020[cite: 33]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: DVC claimed substantial pre-CIRP electricity arrears (Rs. 18.71 crores admitted); SRA applied for a new temporary power connection offering the statutory security deposit[cite: 33]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated 26.09.2019; resolution plan approved by NCLT on 21.09.2020; SRA applied for reconnection on 12.10.2020; DVC appealed plan approval in CA 1111/2020; while CA 1111/2020 was pending, SRA filed IA 119/KB/2021; NCLT directed temporary connection on 25.11.2021[cite: 33]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Approved Resolution Plan extinguishing pre-CIRP DVC liabilities, SRA application for temporary connection, and WBERC Supply Regulations[cite: 33]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In IA(IB) No. 119/KB/2021 in CP (IB) No. 1440/KB/2018, NCLT Kolkata Bench on 25.11.2021 directed DVC to process SRA's application and provide a new temporary electricity connection within 10 days of receiving the requisite security deposit; DVC appealed contending final relief was granted while its appeal against the plan approval was pending[cite: 33].
summary.legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in directing an electricity utility to provide a new temporary connection upon deposit of statutory security charges during the pendency of an appeal challenging the approval of the resolution plan[cite: 33].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An approved resolution plan takes binding effect under Section 31(1) upon sanction by the Adjudicating Authority, and its implementation cannot be stalled merely because an appeal against plan approval is pending without a stay; the Adjudicating Authority has full jurisdiction to enforce the provisions of the plan by directing essential service providers to grant power connections in accordance with statutory supply regulations on a clean slate[cite: 33]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Once a resolution plan is approved, pre-CIRP statutory claims not included therein stand extinguished pursuant to Ghanashyam Mishra; the utility cannot withhold connection on grounds of past dues, and directions ordering supply upon receipt of standard security deposits under WBERC regulations are fully lawful[cite: 33]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Compliance by the Successful Resolution Applicant with the terms of the approved plan and willingness to deposit requisite security amounts as per state electricity regulations[cite: 33]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The dismissal of companion appeal CA 1111/2020 reaffirmed the plan's legality; NCLT's direction to provide a new temporary connection upon payment of security deposit was valid, subject to tariff application under current WBERC regulations[cite: 33].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 119 of 2022 is dismissed; impugned order dated 25.11.2021 is upheld with modifications that the SRA shall pay statutory security deposits and charges under WBERC Regulations and electricity supply shall be billed at current prevailing tariffs; no order as to costs[cite: 33].
summary.summary: Damodar Valley Corporation appealed against an NCLT Kolkata Bench order directing it to provide a new temporary power connection within ten days to Successful Resolution Applicant Amritvani Exim Private Limited for Corporate Debtor Kharkia Steels Pvt. Ltd., upon payment of the requisite security deposit[cite: 33]. DVC argued that granting such relief was impermissible while its appeal challenging the approval of the resolution plan was pending before the NCLAT[cite: 33]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, noting that the companion appeal upholding the plan approval had since been decided[cite: 33]. The Tribunal held that an approved plan is legally binding and enforceable, and DVC must provide power without demanding extinguished pre-CIRP dues, subject to the SRA paying standard security deposits and prevailing tariffs under WBERC Regulations[cite: 33].

summary.case_title: Nidhi Rekhan vs. M/s. Samyak Projects Private Limited
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Nidhi Rekhan is a purported allottee/financial creditor; Respondent M/s Samyak Projects Private Limited is the real estate Corporate Debtor[cite: 34]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Agreement dated 20.07.2016 for allotment of two flats (Nos. A-1201 and E-1301) measuring 4,476 sq. ft. in project 'Ansal Heights 86', Gurugram, against an upfront down payment of Rs. 1,00,00,000/- (out of Rs. 1,11,90,000/- total price) promising an assured return of 24% per annum until termination, with absolute unilateral cancellation rights after one year[cite: 34]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellant surrendered the flats and demanded principal plus assured return totaling Rs. 2,19,56,000/-; debtor issued 40 post-dated cheques between November 2018 and January 2020 which were not realized[cite: 34]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Agreement executed 20.07.2016; debtor acknowledged continued assured returns on surrender on 15.06.2019; Section 7 petition filed on 16.03.2020; NCLT dismissed petition on 20.10.2020[cite: 34]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Agreement dated 20.07.2016 lacking standard construction milestones or delay penalty covenants, 40 dishonoured refund cheques, and letters confirming 24% assured returns[cite: 34]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In CP(IB) No. 784(ND)/2020, NCLT New Delhi dismissed Appellant's Section 7 petition on 20.10.2020 holding that the applicant was not a financial creditor and the investment was not a financial debt; Appellant appealed[cite: 34].
summary.legal_issues: Whether a speculative investor who enters into an agreement for allotment of flats featuring an unusually high assured return (24% per annum) and an unconditional exit/cancellation clause after one year qualifies as a genuine 'allottee' and 'financial creditor' under Section 5(7) read with Explanation (i) of Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC[cite: 34].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A speculative investor who deposits funds with a real estate developer primarily to earn an abnormally high assured financial return coupled with an unconditional right to rescind the allotment and claim a refund does not qualify as a genuine homebuyer/allottee; such an investor cannot claim the status of a 'financial creditor' under Section 5(7) or invoke Explanation (i) to Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC to initiate CIRP[cite: 34]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Explanation (i) to Section 5(8)(f) deems amounts raised from allottees under real estate projects to have the commercial effect of a borrowing, but as held in Pioneer Urban Land and Mansi Brar Fernandes, the protection is intended solely for genuine flat buyers interested in possession; Section 65 bars the use of insolvency proceedings by speculative investors seeking debt recovery through coercive measures[cite: 34]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of contractual terms showing an absence of standard builder-buyer covenants (construction schedules, delivery milestones, delay penalties), the presence of an exorbitant 24% return, and unilateral exit clauses[cite: 34]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appellant entered the project as an investor seeking speculative interest rather than residential possession; the claim does not constitute a financial debt under Section 5(8)(f)[cite: 34].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1035 of 2020 is dismissed; impugned order dated 20.10.2020 of the Adjudicating Authority is affirmed; no order as to costs[cite: 34].
summary.summary: Nidhi Rekhan appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order dismissing her Section 7 application against developer Samyak Projects Private Limited[cite: 34]. The appellant deposited Rs. 1 crore under an agreement dated 20.07.2016 booking two apartments, which assured a 24% annual return and gave her the unilateral right to cancel after one year and obtain a full refund[cite: 34]. After the developer defaulted on refund cheques totaling Rs. 2.19 crores, she triggered CIRP as a financial creditor[cite: 34]. Applying the Supreme Court precedents in Pioneer Urban Land, Anuj Jain, and Mansi Brar Fernandes, the NCLAT held that the agreement lacked essential features of a genuine builder-buyer contract and served merely as a speculative investment vehicle[cite: 34]. The appellant was held not to be an allottee or financial creditor under Section 5(8)(f), and the appeal was dismissed[cite: 34].

summary.case_title: Kalinga Allied Industries India Private Limited vs. Committee of Creditors (Bindals Sponge Industries Limited) & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Kalinga Allied Industries India Private Limited is the Successful Resolution Applicant; Respondent No. 1 is the Committee of Creditors of Corporate Debtor Bindals Sponge Industries Limited (represented by Punjab National Bank); Respondent No. 2 Dinesh Sood is the Resolution Professional[cite: 35]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP initiated against the Corporate Debtor on 11.05.2018; modified resolution plan submitted by Appellant offering Rs. 45.11 crores was approved by CoC in its 13th meeting on 11.11.2019[cite: 35]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default under CIRP; while the plan approval application under Section 31 was pending, third-party entities (Hindustan Coils Limited - HCL offering higher amounts, KEPL, etc.) sought intervention[cite: 35]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced 11.05.2018; CoC approved Appellant's plan on 11.11.2019; NCLT initially allowed HCL to submit a plan on 27.02.2020; NCLAT set aside that order on 11.01.2021; on remand, CoC filed IA No. 999/2021 seeking to withdraw its approval and invite fresh plans; NCLT allowed CoC's application on 26.07.2021[cite: 35]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: CoC voting resolution dated 11.11.2019 approving the plan, NCLAT final judgment dated 11.01.2021 in CA (AT) (Ins) No. 518/2020 barring non-participants, and IA No. 999(PB)/2021 filed by CoC[cite: 35]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In IA No. 999(PB)/2021 in IB-60(PB)/2018, NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi on 26.07.2021 permitted the CoC to withdraw its approval of Appellant's plan, order fresh valuations, and solicit fresh EOIs; Successful Resolution Applicant appealed[cite: 35].
summary.legal_issues: Whether the Committee of Creditors has the legal authority to withdraw its approval of a resolution plan submitted to the Adjudicating Authority after the lapse of several years, and whether the Adjudicating Authority can direct the CoC to entertain fresh plans or EOIs from third parties who did not participate in the CIRP to achieve asset value maximization[cite: 35].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A resolution plan approved by the Committee of Creditors and submitted to the Adjudicating Authority under Section 31 is binding and irrevocable between the CoC and the Successful Resolution Applicant; the CoC possesses no authority to withdraw its approval or invite fresh resolution plans from third parties who failed to participate in the CIRP within statutory timelines, nor can the Adjudicating Authority order fresh EOIs merely because a third party subsequently offers a higher value[cite: 35]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Applying the Supreme Court doctrine in Ebix Singapore v. CoC of Educomp Solutions Ltd., the IBC framework provides no scope for open-ended renegotiation, modifications, or withdrawals of CoC-approved plans; residuary powers under Section 60(5)(c) cannot be exercised to bypass statutory timelines or create unregulated extra-statutory procedures[cite: 35]. The objective of 'maximization of value' must be realized strictly within statutory timelines and not through indefinite delays[cite: 35]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Concluded approval of the plan by the CoC on 11.11.2019, combined with the finality of the earlier NCLAT order dated 11.01.2021 which barred non-participating bidders[cite: 35]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CoC cannot withdraw approval after more than two years to consider belated third-party offers; the NCLT order reopening the CIRP was contrary to law[cite: 35].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 689 of 2021 is allowed; impugned order dated 26.07.2021 passed by the Adjudicating Authority in IA No. 999(PB)/2021 is set aside; no order as to costs[cite: 35].
summary.summary: Kalinga Allied Industries India Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order allowing an application by the CoC of Bindals Sponge Industries Limited to withdraw its approval of Kalinga's resolution plan, conduct fresh asset valuations, and solicit fresh bids from non-participating entities offering higher amounts[cite: 35]. The CoC's application was filed more than two years after it had approved Kalinga's plan on 11.11.2019[cite: 35]. Applying the Supreme Court ruling in Ebix Singapore v. CoC of Educomp Solutions Ltd., the NCLAT held that once a plan is approved by the CoC and placed before the Adjudicating Authority, it becomes binding and irrevocable between the CoC and the resolution applicant[cite: 35]. The Tribunal held that asset value maximization cannot be pursued outside statutory timelines by entertaining third parties who bypassed the CIRP, and set aside the NCLT order[cite: 35].

summary.case_title: Mr. Rakshit Dhirajlal Doshi vs. IDBI Bank Ltd. & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1.
