PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor/Lender is IDBI Bank Limited (member of Bank of Baroda Consortium); Corporate Debtor/Corporate Guarantor is Fivebro International Private Limited (FIPL); Principal Borrower is Doshion Veolia Water Solutions Private Limited (Doshion); IL&FS Trust Company Limited acted as Security Trustee; Appellant is Rakshit Dhirajlal Doshi, suspended director of FIPL. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Consortium of banks led by Bank of Baroda (Union Bank of India, Standard Chartered Bank, IDBI Bank) sanctioned and restructured credit facilities to Doshion up to Rs. 422.11 crores (actual disbursement Rs. 408.64 crores). FIPL executed a Deed of Guarantee dated 27.06.2014 in favor of IL&FS Trust Company Limited as Security Trustee acting for the consortium. Relevant Inter-se Agreement and Security Trustee Agreement were executed on 26.11.2013. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: IDBI Bank claimed an outstanding default of Rs. 72.32 crores due as of 20.09.2016 in respect of its individual disbursed facility. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: IDBI Bank issued loan recall notice to Doshion on 20.09.2016 demanding payment within 15 days; IDBI Bank issued guarantee invocation notice directly to FIPL on 04.11.2016 demanding Rs. 72.32 crores forthwith. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Inter-se Agreement dated 26.11.2013 (clauses 4, 5, 7.1, 7.2, 7.3, 7.5), Security Trustee Agreement dated 26.11.2013 (clauses 2.1.2, 2.2.5, 4), Deed of Guarantee dated 27.06.2014 (clauses 1, 7, 20), recall notice dated 20.09.2016, and demand notice dated 04.11.2016 showing that IDBI Bank acted unilaterally without giving written intimation to the Security Trustee or convening a consortium meeting. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 petition was filed by IDBI Bank on 11.10.2018; Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Ahmedabad) admitted the Section 7 petition and initiated CIRP against FIPL vide order dated 10.05.2022 in CP (IB) No. 570/2018 relying on clause 7.5 of the Inter-se Agreement.
summary.legal_issues: Whether an individual member bank of a consortium has the locus standi to unilaterally declare an Event of Default, invoke a corporate guarantee executed in favor of a Security Trustee, and file a Section 7 IBC application without following the mandatory procedure prescribed under the Inter-se Agreement and Security Trustee Agreement; and whether the non-disbursement of restructured funds by a consortium member discharged the corporate guarantor.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where credit facilities and securities are governed by consortium agreements requiring collective decision-making, an individual participating lender lacks locus standi to unilaterally declare an event of default and enforce a guarantee in an insolvency proceeding under Section 7 of the IBC bypassing the mandatory contractual mechanisms established under the inter-se and security trustee agreements. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 of the IBC requires the establishment of a legally valid and enforceable 'default'; a default predicated on an 'Event of Default' declared in contravention of binding multi-party transaction agreements does not constitute a valid default enforceable by an individual lender. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Harmonious contractual construction test—clauses governing specific enforcement actions and declarations of default (such as clauses 7.1, 7.2, and 7.3 of the Inter-se Agreement and clause 4 of the Security Trustee Agreement) override general residuary empowerment clauses (such as clause 7.5 of the Inter-se Agreement); strict adherence to prescribed written notice and consortium approval thresholds must be demonstrated. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: IDBI Bank failed to notify the Security Trustee or Lead Bank before declaring an event of default and recalling the loan, rendering its unilateral declaration invalid and depriving it of the locus standi to maintain the Section 7 application against the guarantor.
summary.operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the impugned order dated 10.05.2022 passed by NCLT Ahmedabad in CP (IB) No. 570/2018 is set aside, and the Corporate Debtor Fivebro International Private Limited is freed from the rigours of CIRP, moratorium, and all other related provisions of the IBC. No order as to costs.
summary.summary: Rakshit Dhirajlal Doshi, suspended director of corporate guarantor Fivebro International Private Limited (FIPL), appealed the NCLT Ahmedabad order admitting IDBI Bank's Section 7 IBC application for an alleged default of Rs. 72.32 crores under a restructured consortium loan granted to Doshion Veolia Water Solutions Pvt. Ltd. FIPL had executed a Deed of Guarantee in favor of IL&FS Trust Company Limited as Security Trustee for the Bank of Baroda-led consortium. NCLAT held that IDBI Bank acted unilaterally in violation of mandatory clauses in the Inter-se and Security Trustee Agreements requiring consortium consultation and trustee action to declare default and enforce security. Finding IDBI Bank lacked locus standi, NCLAT allowed the appeal and quashed the CIRP.

summary.case_title: M/S. Ahluwalia Contracts (India) Ltd. vs. Logix Infratech Pvt. Ltd.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor is M/S Ahluwalia Contracts (India) Ltd.; Corporate Debtor is Logix Infratech Private Limited. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Award of contract by Corporate Debtor to Operational Creditor for civil and structural construction work of 'Logix Group Blossom Green' Project and a subsequent award on 11.07.2014 for balance work of the non-tower area of the same project. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total claimed default amount under Section 9 application is Rs. 7,72,00,000/- arising out of an agreed final settlement sum of Rs. 11 crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Section 9 application was filed following a breach of payment terms agreed in a Memorandum of Understanding dated 30.09.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Award of contracts dated 11.07.2014; final bill certificate duly signed by both parties certifying an outstanding amount of Rs. 11 crores; and Memorandum of Understanding / Settlement Agreement dated 30.09.2019 stipulating the mode and manner of payment of the certified Rs. 11 crores debt. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 9 application filed by the Appellant before NCLT New Delhi registered as CP (IB) No. 882/ND/2022; dismissed by Adjudicating Authority on 03.06.2022 holding that an application under Section 9 is not maintainable for breach of a settlement agreement as dues arising out of settlement do not constitute an operational debt.
summary.legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 9 of the IBC is maintainable when filed for default in payment under a Memorandum of Understanding / Settlement Agreement that merely restructures the payment mode of undisputed operational dues certified under signed final construction bills.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An operational debt does not lose its intrinsic character under the IBC merely because the parties enter into a settlement agreement or Memorandum of Understanding that governs only the mode, timeline, and manner of payment for underlying works or services rendered. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9 read with Section 5(21) encompasses unpaid dues stemming from the execution of civil and structural construction contracts; a subsequent payment restructuring agreement linked directly to certified final bills remains an actionable operational debt rather than a non-maintainable settlement claim. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the underlying commercial transaction and final bill certificates; when services/works have been executed and the final bill is mutually signed, the subsequent MoU is treated as an agreement on mode of discharge rather than novation altering the nature of the debt. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in rejecting the Section 9 application, as the claim arose directly from structural construction contracts and certified final bills, with the Corporate Debtor conceding its inability to pay.
summary.operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the order dated 03.06.2022 passed by the Adjudicating Authority in CP (IB) No. 882/ND/2022 is set aside; the Adjudicating Authority is directed to pass an order of admission under Section 9 and other consequential orders within a period of four weeks from the receipt of this order.
summary.summary: Ahluwalia Contracts (India) Ltd. appealed against the NCLT New Delhi order rejecting its Section 9 IBC application for recovery of Rs. 7.72 crores against Logix Infratech Pvt. Ltd. The NCLT had held that default arising from a settlement agreement/MoU did not constitute an operational debt. NCLAT set aside the rejection, observing that the debt originated from civil and structural construction work executed by the appellant, supported by a mutually signed final bill certificate of Rs. 11 crores. The MoU merely fixed the mode and schedule of payment. NCLAT held that the dues maintained their operational character and remanded the matter directing NCLT to admit the Section 9 petition within four weeks.

summary.case_title: V-Con Integrated Solutions Pvt. Ltd. vs. Argos Technology Resources Pvt. Ltd.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor is V-Con Integrated Solutions Pvt. Ltd.; Corporate Debtor is Argos Technology Resources Pvt. Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Provision of operational goods/services giving rise to an unpaid operational debt. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed operational default of Rs. 20,27,659/-; date of default occurred prior to 24.03.2020. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice issued under Section 8 of the IBC; Section 9 application filed before the Adjudicating Authority on 27.03.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Operational invoices and default records demonstrating that the default occurred prior to 24.03.2020, along with the MCA Notification dated 24.03.2020 enhancing the pecuniary threshold under Section 4 of the IBC. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Application under Section 9 filed on 27.03.2021; dismissed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT) vide order dated 26.04.2022 on the ground of non-fulfilment of the minimum pecuniary threshold of Rs. 1 Crore under Section 4 of the IBC.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the MCA Notification dated 24.03.2020 enhancing the minimum threshold of default under Section 4 of the IBC to Rs. 1 Crore applies to an application under Section 9 filed after 24.03.2020 where the underlying default occurred prior to 24.03.2020.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The date of filing the insolvency application, not the date of default, determines the applicable threshold under Section 4 of the IBC; any insolvency petition filed after the publication of the statutory amendment notification must fulfill the enhanced pecuniary threshold. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The notification dated 24.03.2020 issued under Section 4 of the IBC is prospective in operation; it exempts only those insolvency applications that were already pending before the Adjudicating Authority prior to 24.03.2020 and strictly governs all fresh applications filed subsequent to that date. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Threshold compliance test at the time of presentation/filing of the petition before the registry; the date of default prior to the notification does not confer a vested right to institute insolvency proceedings under the unamended pecuniary threshold. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 9 application was filed on 27.03.2021 for an amount of Rs. 20,27,659/-, which fell below the mandatory statutory limit of Rs. 1 Crore; the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in rejecting the application.
summary.operative_order: The appeal is dismissed; the order dated 26.04.2022 passed by the Adjudicating Authority rejecting the Section 9 application is affirmed. No order as to costs.
summary.summary: V-Con Integrated Solutions Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the NCLT order dated 26.04.2022 dismissing its Section 9 application against Argos Technology Resources Pvt. Ltd. for failing to meet the enhanced Section 4 pecuniary threshold. The appellant contended that because the default of Rs. 20,27,659/- occurred prior to the 24.03.2020 notification, the pre-amendment threshold of Rs. 1 Lakh should apply. The NCLAT rejected this contention, holding that the notification enhancing the threshold to Rs. 1 Crore operates prospectively and governs all applications filed after 24.03.2020, regardless of when the default occurred. Because the petition was filed on 27.03.2021, the appeal was dismissed.

summary.case_title: M/s. Aswathi Agencies vs. Bijoy Prabhakaran Pulipra & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor and Appellant is M/s. Aswathi Agencies (supplier of life-saving medicines); Respondent No. 1 is Bijoy Prabhakaran Pulipra (Resolution Professional/Monitoring Agent); Respondent No. 2 is Dr. N.P. Kamalesh representing Successful Resolution Applicant M/s. Lissie Medical Institutions (a registered Charitable Public Trust under the Indian Trusts Act, 1882); Respondent No. 3/Corporate Debtor is PVS Memorial Hospital Private Limited. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of life-saving medicines and hospital pharmaceuticals by the Appellant to the Corporate Debtor between June 2017 and April 2019, resulting in accumulated unpaid invoices and dishonored cheques, as well as an unrefunded GST payment of over Rs. 12 Lakhs. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational debt claimed by Appellant for unpaid supplies and GST liability; total claims admitted during CIRP comprised average Fair Value of Rs. 162,22,78,150/- and average Liquidation Value of Rs. 122,90,59,890/-, while the CoC-approved resolution plan consideration was Rs. 126 Crores (plus Rs. 1 Crore dedicated under Clause 5.1.18.3 for unsecured financial and operational creditors). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated under TIBA/11/KOB/2019; CoC approved the final Resolution Plan with 100% voting share on 26.12.2020; plan approval application IA (IBC)/13/KOB/2021 was filed and subsequently allowed by NCLT Kochi Bench on 16.03.2021 (modifying order dated 22.02.2021). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Valuation reports by two IBBI-registered independent valuers (Mr. Jigar Shah and Mr. Ruben George Joseph) averaging Fair Value at Rs. 162.23 Crores and Liquidation Value at Rs. 122.90 Crores; Clause 5.1.18.3 offering Rs. 1 Crore pro-rata distribution to operational and unsecured creditors; trust deed and 12A registration certificate of Lissie Medical Institutions confirming its status as a charitable institution under the Indian Trusts Act, 1882 and Income Tax Act, 1961. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Corporate Debtor was admitted to CIRP; CoC approved the Resolution Plan of Lissie Medical Institutions with 100% voting share; Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Kochi Bench) approved the plan on 16.03.2021 in IA (IBC)/13/KOB/2021; Appellant filed Section 61(3) appeal alleging illegality in SRA's eligibility, valuation defects, and inadequate payment to operational creditors.
summary.legal_issues: Whether a registered Charitable Public Trust is legally competent to act as a Resolution Applicant under Section 5(25) read with Section 3(23)(d) of the IBC; and whether an approved resolution plan can be challenged under Section 61(3) on grounds of inadequacy of distribution to operational creditors or valuation irregularities when the plan has been approved by 100% CoC voting share within its commercial wisdom.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 5(25) read with Section 3(23)(d) of the IBC, the statutory definition of 'person' includes a 'trust', thereby conferring unambiguous legal competency on a registered charitable public trust to participate as a resolution applicant; further, the commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors regarding allocation and valuation is non-justiciable provided the statutory minimum floors under Section 30(2) are preserved. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 3(23)(d) read with Section 5(25) contains no prohibition or disqualification barring a public charitable trust from submitting a resolution plan or acquiring a corporate debtor to revive healthcare operations; Section 30(2)(b) mandates only a minimum payment floor linked to liquidation value and does not require mathematical equality between financial and operational creditors. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict conformity review under Section 30(2) and Section 61(3); where two independent IBBI-registered valuers provide proximate estimates and CoC exercises informed commercial judgment, courts cannot substitute subjective notions of equity or market value. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Resolution Plan strictly conformed with Section 30(2) and CIRP Regulations 38 and 39; the SRA trust was fully qualified under Section 29A; and the CoC exercised unassailable commercial wisdom, warranting dismissal of the operational creditor's appeal.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS.) No. 179 of 2021 is dismissed. The approval of the Resolution Plan passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Kochi Bench) is affirmed. No order as to costs. All connected pending Interlocutory Applications are closed.
summary.summary: Operational creditor M/s. Aswathi Agencies appealed against the NCLT Kochi Bench order approving the resolution plan of M/s. Lissie Medical Institutions for reviving PVS Memorial Hospital Pvt. Ltd. The appellant contended that the SRA, being a registered charitable public trust, was legally ineligible to submit a commercial resolution plan, and that the valuation was suppressed while operational creditors were paid a meager share compared to financial creditors. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT held that Section 3(23)(d) read with Section 5(25) expressly defines a 'person' to include a 'trust', entitling it to submit a plan. The Tribunal reaffirmed that CoC's commercial wisdom regarding asset valuation and fund allocation is non-justiciable under Section 61(3).

summary.case_title: Santanu T. Ray, RP of Zicom SAAS Pvt. Ltd. vs. Tata Capital Financial Services Ltd. & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Santanu T. Ray, Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor Zicom SAAS Private Limited; Respondent No. 1 is Tata Capital Financial Services Limited (lessor/claimant); Respondents Nos. 2 to 5 are members of the Committee of Creditors (Central Bank of India, Union Bank of India, PNB, Khemani Distributors). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Master Lease Agreement dated 14.05.2015 executed between Corporate Debtor and Respondent No. 1 for operating lease facility of Honeywell security systems across 23 lease schedules with stipulated tenors expiring between June 2017 and June 2020. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose from unpaid lease rentals; Respondent No. 1 originally filed Form B on 13.01.2021 for Rs. 1.05 Crores (out of which Rs. 95 Lakhs was admitted), and later submitted an unverified additional claim on 23.04.2021 after a 256-day delay, totaling Rs. 11.79 Crores (comprising Rs. 8.65 Crores pre-CIRP arrears and Rs. 3,14,81,158/- CIRP period charges). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 18.03.2020; public announcement made on 13.08.2020 with claim submission deadline of 25.08.2020; outer 90-day window under CIRP Regulation 12(2) expired on 09.11.2020; CoC approved the final Resolution Plan with 98.85% vote share on 11.06.2021; plan approval application IA No. 1300 of 2021 was filed on 15.06.2021; Respondent No. 1 filed IA No. 1511 of 2021 on 05.07.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Master Lease Agreement dated 14.05.2015 requiring periodic invoices under Clause 2(g); lease summary schedules showing that equipment lifespans had expired by June 2020; lack of any CIRP-period rental revenue generated by the Corporate Debtor; absence of valid invoices raised during moratorium; and prior admission of Rs. 43.54 Lakhs fair market value within the admitted Rs. 95 Lakhs claim. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench vide order dated 02.09.2021 in IA No. 1511 of 2021 directed the RP, CoC, and SRA to include the belated claim of Rs. 3,14,81,158/- as CIRP costs in the CoC-approved resolution plan; RP appealed against this direction.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the jurisdiction to unilaterally direct the inclusion of a belated, unverified claim as CIRP cost under Section 5(13) and Regulation 31 after the approval of the Resolution Plan by the CoC; and whether claims submitted after the expiry of the mandatory 90-day window under Regulation 12(2) can disrupt an approved plan.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Adjudicating Authority cannot usurp the administrative verification role of the Resolution Professional or the commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors by directing payment of an unverified, belated claim as CIRP cost, particularly after the CoC has approved a resolution plan; entertaining surprise claims beyond the outer statutory limit of Regulation 12(2) disrupts the clean-slate principle of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(13)(c) read with CIRP Regulation 31 requires expenses to be actual costs incurred by the RP in running the business as a going concern or specifically ratified/approved by the CoC; lease rental claims for expired assets where no invoices were raised during CIRP and no business revenue was generated cannot be classified as CIRP costs. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict timeline and verification standard under CIRP Regulations 12(2), 13, and 14; a creditor must produce contemporaneous invoices and substantiate that the expenditure was directly incurred to run the corporate debtor as a going concern. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The lease schedules had expired by June 2020, fair market value was already factored into the admitted claim, no invoices were raised, and the claim was filed after an impermissible delay of 256 days following CoC approval; the NCLT's direction to pay Rs. 3,14,81,158/- was illegal.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 951 of 2021 is allowed. The impugned order dated 02.09.2021 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench in IA No. 1511 of 2021 is set aside. Pending applications and interim orders stand disposed of with no order as to costs.
summary.summary: The Resolution Professional of Zicom SAAS Pvt. Ltd. challenged the NCLT Mumbai Bench order directing him, the CoC, and the SRA to incorporate a belated, unverified claim of Rs. 3.14 Crores by lessor Tata Capital Financial Services Ltd. as CIRP cost into a CoC-approved Resolution Plan. Tata Capital had filed its revised claim after a delay of 256 days, well beyond the 90-day outer window under Regulation 12(2), without raising invoices during the CIRP period. Setting aside the NCLT order, the NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority lacks jurisdiction to adjudicate or impose unverified claims as CIRP costs without RP verification or CoC ratification. Entertaining such belated surprise claims impermissibly derails the time-bound resolution process and violates the clean-slate doctrine.

summary.case_title: Sahara India vs. Shri Nandkishor Vishnupant Deshpande & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sahara India (Appellant/Claimant), an operational creditor converted to purported unsecured financial creditor; Royal Refinery Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/Respondent No. 2, in CIRP/Liquidation); Shri Nandkishor Vishnupant Deshpande (Resolution Professional/Respondent No. 1), later replaced by Liquidator Arihant Nenawati. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Under an MoU dated 07.03.2017, Sahara India advanced funds to the Corporate Debtor for future supply of gold coins/ornaments after January 2019 without interest, with a 2% discount and no making/delivery charges. Due to the Corporate Debtor's inability to supply the requested gold, the parties executed a Loan Agreement dated 15.04.2019 converting the advance into an unsecured loan carrying 10% interest per annum with a 5-year tenure. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Advance principal paid was Rs. 39,95,00,000/- remitted in tranches between April 2018 and February 2019; total claim filed was Rs. 42,61,33,333/- (inclusive of interest). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand for supply made on 04.02.2019 and 28.02.2019; refund demand sent on 05.03.2019; CD proposed conversion to loan on 11.03.2019; Loan Agreement executed on 15.04.2019; Section 9 petition by Raksha Bullion admitted on 13.11.2019; claim Form-C submitted on 03.03.2020; RP rejected financial debt categorization on 06.05.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: MoU dated 07.03.2017, correspondence dated February-March 2019, Loan Agreement dated 15.04.2019, books of accounts, and claim Form-C. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Corporate Debtor was admitted into CIRP on 13.11.2019. After the RP refused to treat the claim as financial debt, Sahara India filed I.A. No. 991 of 2020 before NCLT Mumbai Bench. On 07.01.2021, NCLT dismissed the application, suo motu holding the conversion to be a preferential transaction under Section 43(2)(a) within a two-year lookback period and treating the creditor as a related party.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority possessed the jurisdiction to suo motu declare a debt conversion transaction preferential under Section 43 in the absence of an avoidance application under Section 43(1) read with Section 44 by the RP/Liquidator, and whether an unrelated party transaction beyond the one-year lookback period could be invalidated.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Adjudicating Authority exceeds its statutory jurisdiction by suo motu declaring a transaction preferential under Section 43 of the Code without an explicit avoidance application filed by the Resolution Professional or Liquidator under Section 43(1) and Section 44. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 43(1) mandates an application by the RP or Liquidator as a sine qua non for avoidance. Furthermore, under Section 43(4)(b), the lookback period for unrelated parties is strictly one year preceding the insolvency commencement date, and transfers executed in the ordinary course of business are excluded under Section 43(3)(a). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: To avoid a transaction as preferential qua an unrelated party, evidence must establish that the transaction occurred within the one-year suspect period and that the statutory twin conditions of Section 43(2) are met, rather than relying on unsupported assumptions of related-party status. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority acted ultra vires in treating the creditor as a related party without evidence, applying an erroneous two-year lookback period, and suo motu declaring the transaction preferential without an application under Section 43(1).
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 368 of 2021 is allowed; the impugned order dated 07.01.2021 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench in I.A. No. 991 of 2020 is set aside; the matter is remanded back to the Adjudicating Authority to reconsider afresh on merits in accordance with law during liquidation proceedings without being influenced by any prior remarks; no order as to costs.
summary.summary: Sahara India advanced Rs. 39.95 crores to Royal Refinery Pvt. Ltd. under a 2017 MoU for gold supply, which was converted into an unsecured loan at 10% interest via an agreement dated 15.04.2019 after delivery failures. In CIRP, the RP and NCLT Mumbai rejected Sahara's Form-C financial debt claim, with NCLT suo motu declaring the loan agreement a preferential transaction under Section 43. On appeal, NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority exceeded its jurisdiction by declaring a preference suo motu without an avoidance application under Section 43(1) by the RP/Liquidator and wrongly applied a two-year lookback period to unrelated entities. NCLAT set aside the impugned order and remanded the matter for fresh adjudication.

summary.case_title: Raghu KS & Ors. vs. R. Subramaniakumar, Administrator of Dewan Housing Finance Corporation Ltd. & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Raghu KS & 34 other Fixed Deposit Holders (Appellants/Dissenting Financial Creditors); Dewan Housing Finance Corporation Limited (DHFL/Corporate Debtor/FSP); R. Subramaniakumar (Respondent No. 1/Administrator); Committee of Creditors of DHFL (Respondent No. 2); Piramal Capital & Housing Finance Limited (Respondent No. 3/Successful Resolution Applicant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor, a Housing Finance Company/NBFC, offered public fixed deposit schemes backed by AAA credit ratings. Appellants deposited funds under these retail deposit schemes. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total admitted claims of public deposit holders were approximately Rs. 5,375 Crores (representing ~6.18% of total admitted claims); the approved distribution mechanism allocated Rs. 1,243 Crores (23.08% payout) to FD holders, whereas secured financial creditors received approx. 40%. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: RBI superseded the Board on 20.11.2019 and appointed the Administrator; RBI filed Section 227 insolvency petition on 29.11.2019; NCLT Mumbai admitted the petition and imposed moratorium on 03.12.2019; resolution plan approved by CoC on 15.01.2021 by 93.65% majority and distribution by 86.95%; NCLT approved plan on 07.06.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Terms of FD schemes, credit rating certificates, Form C claims, minutes of the 18th CoC meeting dated 24-25 December 2020 and 20th meeting dated 17.06.2021. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed I.A. No. 625/2021 in C.P. (IB) No. 4258/MB/C-II/2019 seeking full repayment under the NHB Act or parity with secured lenders. On 07.06.2021, NCLT requested CoC reconsideration but approved the plan. CoC reconsidered and rejected higher payout by 89.19% on 17.06.2021.
summary.legal_issues: Whether a resolution plan providing a haircut to fixed deposit holders of an FSP violates the NHB Act or RBI Act, whether individual deposit holders represented by an Authorized Representative have locus to independently challenge an approved plan, and whether Section 238 of the IBC overrides the NHB Act.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Fixed deposit holders in an insolvent Financial Service Provider are financial creditors whose recovery is governed exclusively by the Code; they are entitled only to the minimum statutory liquidation value under Section 30(2)(b) and cannot claim full repayment outside the commercial wisdom of the CoC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 238 of the IBC overrides provisions of earlier enactments including the NHB Act and RBI Act. The non-obstante clause in Section 238 grants primacy to the Code's distribution waterfall over any statutory full refund provisions under housing finance regulations. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Compliance of a resolution plan is measured strictly against Section 30(2) requirements; so long as dissenting financial creditors are allocated their requisite liquidation value, judicial review cannot interfere with CoC's commercial determinations regarding haircuts or inter-class distribution. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The approved resolution plan and distribution mechanism fully complied with the Code, binding the dissenting fixed deposit holders, and the impugned order required no interference.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 538 of 2021 is dismissed following the precedent set in Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) Nos. 506, 507 & 516 of 2021; no order as to costs.
summary.summary: Fixed deposit holders of Dewan Housing Finance Corporation Ltd. (DHFL) appealed against the NCLT Mumbai Bench order approving the resolution plan submitted by Piramal Capital & Housing Finance Ltd. The Appellants challenged the 23.08% payout allocation decided by the CoC, contending that the NHB Act and RBI Act mandate 100% repayment of public deposits and that Section 238 of the Code should not override depositor protections. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that Section 238 of the IBC overrides the NHB and RBI Acts, fixed deposit holders are financial creditors bound by the commercial wisdom of the CoC, and dissenting creditors are only entitled to liquidation value under Section 30(2)(b).

summary.case_title: Vineet Khosla vs. Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. & Ors.
summary.appeal_number: I.A. Nos. 190, 191, 192 & 337 of 2022 and Contempt Case (AT) No. 06 of 2022 in Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) Nos. 1124-1125 of 2020
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Vineet Khosla (Suspended Director of Corporate Debtor/Applicant); Margra Industries Ltd. (Corporate Debtor, ordered into liquidation); Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. (Financial Creditor/Assignee of EXIM Bank/Respondent No. 1). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor availed a credit facility from EXIM Bank in 1996. EXIM Bank filed O.A. No. 177/2001 before DRT, which issued a recovery certificate on 12.09.2011 for Rs. 6.58 Crores pursuant to consent terms. EXIM Bank assigned the debt to Edelweiss on 02.01.2014, which entered into OTS agreements with extensions. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default date was 29.07.2000; Section 7 application claimed Rs. 44,20,38,989.20/-; balance settlement debt under OTS was Rs. 5,92,26,120/- payable by 12.09.2012. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Recovery certificate issued 12.09.2011; OTS extension letters exchanged up to 17.12.2015 extending validity to 31.03.2016; OTS revoked on 05.04.2016; Section 7 petition filed on 12.06.2018; Section 7 admitted on 15.03.2019; NCLAT dismissed original appeal on 06.09.2019; liquidation ordered on 15.10.2020; recall application CA No. 307/2020 dismissed on 10.11.2020; NCLAT dismissed appeals 1124-1125/2020 on 07.01.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Recovery Certificate No. 67/2011, OTS extension letters dated 01.11.2014, 17.03.2015, 01.12.2015, and 27.02.2016 by Corporate Debtor acknowledging debt. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Applicant filed CA No. 307/2020 seeking recall of the 15.03.2019 admission order for fraud and limitation bar. NCLT dismissed it on 10.11.2020, and ordered liquidation on 15.10.2020. NCLAT dismissed appeals on 07.01.2022. Applicant subsequently filed I.A. Nos. 190, 191, 192, 337 of 2022 and Contempt Case No. 06 of 2022 alleging fraud on the Appellate Tribunal.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the judgment dated 07.01.2022 dismissing the appeal was obtained by fraud or misrepresentation concerning limitation pleadings, thereby warranting recall under inherent powers, and whether contempt and criminal perjury proceedings should be initiated against the Respondent and its advocates.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A court or tribunal retains inherent jurisdiction to recall an order obtained by fraud, but 'fraud' requires establishing deliberate deception designed to secure an unfair advantage. Where material correspondence was properly placed on record during appellate proceedings without false representations that they were annexed to the original petition, no fraud is committed. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: 'Fraud' under IBC proceedings imports the definition from Section 17 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 pursuant to Section 3(37) of the Code, requiring proof of intentional deception, false representation, or active concealment. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Fraud cannot be inferred when the initial Section 7 petition contained foundational pleadings of debt acknowledgment and extensions, and full underlying correspondence was subsequently submitted via reply affidavits in appeal to counter fresh allegations. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Respondent No. 1 practiced no fraud, concealment, or misrepresentation before the Appellate Tribunal; impleadment of advocates was reckless, and all recall applications and contempt petitions were devoid of merit.
summary.operative_order: I.A. Nos. 190, 191, 192, and 337 of 2022 are dismissed; names of Respondent Nos. 16 to 21 (advocates) are deleted from the array of parties; Contempt Case (AT) No. 06 of 2022 is dismissed.
summary.summary: Vineet Khosla, suspended director of Margra Industries Ltd., filed applications to recall NCLAT's judgment dated 07.01.2022, which had dismissed his challenge against the liquidation and admission orders. The Applicant alleged that Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Co. played fraud by falsely portraying that documents evidencing Section 18 Limitation Act acknowledgments were part of the original Section 7 petition, and initiated contempt proceedings against Edelweiss and its advocates. NCLAT dismissed all applications, holding that Edelweiss fully pleaded the extensions in Form-1 and merely produced the supporting letters in its appellate reply affidavit without misrepresentation, failing the legal test of fraud under Section 17 of the Indian Contract Act.

summary.case_title: IDBI Trusteeship Services Ltd. & Anr. vs. Abhinav Mukherji & Ors.
summary.appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 356 of 2022 with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 358 of 2022
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: IDBI Trusteeship Services Ltd. (Debenture Trustee/Appellant in Comp App 356/2022); ECL Finance Ltd. & Assets Care & Reconstruction Enterprises Ltd. (Debenture Holders/Assignee/Appellants in Comp App 358/2022); Palm Developers Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/Corporate Guarantor); Saha Infratech Pvt. Ltd. (Principal Borrower/Issuer); Abhinav Mukherji (Respondent No. 1/Homebuyer/Financial Creditor holding 4.43% voting share); Krit Narayan Mishra (Respondent No. 2/RP). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Saha Infratech issued 110 Non-Convertible Debentures (NCDs) of Rs. 1 Crore each (aggregate Rs. 110 Crores) subscribed by ECL under a Debenture Trust Deed dated 01.07.2016, with IDBI as Trustee. Palm Developers executed an irrevocable Corporate Guarantee, Mortgage on 'Project Encore', and Revenue Escrow Agreement on 02.07.2016. Articles of Association (AoA) were amended conferring extensive governance rights on the debenture holders. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed since 2017; Form C claim filed for Rs. 1,26,96,88,698/- as of 27.01.2020. Overdue interest claimed on 03.02.2020 was Rs. 9,16,66,666/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated against Palm Developers on 27.01.2020; public announcement on 31.01.2020; Form-C submitted on 10.02.2020; CoC initially constituted on 20.02.2020; Homebuyer filed IA 1610/2020 on 25.02.2020; debenture redemption recall issued on 25.03.2020; corporate guarantee invoked on 07.04.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Debenture Trust Deed dated 01.07.2016, Guarantee Agreement dated 02.07.2016, irrevocable Power of Attorney dated 22.09.2017 granting operational control, AoA Clauses 4.1, 5.4, 7.1, 7.2, and Forensic Audit Report showing Rs. 28 Crores fund diversion. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: First Respondent filed I.A. No. 1610/2020 challenging admission of Appellants' claim. NCLT New Delhi Bench-II on 14.03.2022 held Appellants were not Financial Creditors (guarantee uninvoked prior to CIRP) and were Related Parties under Section 5(24), ordering CoC reconstitution.
summary.legal_issues: Whether an individual homebuyer has locus standi to challenge the admission and CoC membership of a financial creditor without acting through an Authorized Representative, whether a corporate guarantee uninvoked prior to CIRP commencement gives rise to an admissible claim, and whether extensive affirmative governance and operational veto rights render a lender a related party under Section 5(24).
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An individual financial creditor in a class has independent locus standi under Section 60(5) to challenge the inclusion or classification of competing creditors in the CoC. Furthermore, a claim under a corporate guarantee does not accrue as a matured debt if the guarantee was not invoked prior to the commencement of CIRP and moratorium under Section 14. Entitles possessing positive, proactive control over a debtor's management and policy decisions are related parties under Section 5(24) and must be excluded from the CoC under Section 21(2). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 21(6A) restricts the role of an Authorized Representative to attending CoC meetings and voting; it does not divest an individual financial creditor of the right to invoke Section 60(5). 'Debt' under Section 3(11) and 'claim' under Section 3(6) require a right to payment to have accrued; an uninvoked guarantee cannot mature post-moratorium under Section 14. 'Control' under Section 5(24) aligns with Section 2(27) of the Companies Act, encompassing de facto positive control. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The test of control is whether the entity is in the 'driving seat'—possessing proactive authority to manage escrow accounts, direct sales, veto board decisions, and alter management, regardless of whether nominee directors were formally appointed. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Guarantee was uninvoked prior to CIRP, barring right to payment, and the Appellants exercised positive, pervasive control over Palm Developers under the AoA and PoA, making them related parties rightfully excluded from the CoC under Section 21(2).
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 356 and 358 of 2022 are dismissed; the Adjudicating Authority's direction excluding Appellants from the CoC is upheld; connected I.A. No. 1118 of 2022 is dismissed; no order as to costs.
summary.summary: IDBI Trusteeship and ECL Finance challenged the NCLT New Delhi order disqualifying them as financial creditors and excluding them from the CoC of Corporate Guarantor Palm Developers Pvt. Ltd. upon an application by a homebuyer. NCLAT dismissed the appeals, holding that an individual allottee has locus to challenge creditor admissions. On merits, NCLAT held that because the corporate guarantee was not invoked prior to the CIRP commencement and Section 14 moratorium, no matured debt accrued. Furthermore, under extensive powers in the Articles of Association and an irrevocable Power of Attorney over project operations and escrow funds, the Appellants held positive de facto control, qualifying as Related Parties under Section 5(24) excluded under Section 21(2).

summary.case_title: (Capt.) Vadlamannati Jaya Pushpakumar vs. Madras Race Club & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: (Capt.) Vadlamannati Jaya Pushpakumar (Appellant/Petitioner claiming to be legal heir/grandson of original lessor); Madras Race Club (Respondent No. 1/Company under Companies Act); A.C. Muthiah (President/Secretary) & Devanathan Yadav (Director/Respondent No. 2); State of Tamil Nadu, Tax Authorities & DLF entities (Proforma Respondents). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: An ancestral lease agreement dated 27.07.1927 (extended to 26.10.1936) executed between late grandfather of the Appellant and the Madras Race Club for 12.53 acres of land in Guindy/Velachery. Appellant claimed Respondent No. 1 retained possession, failed to pay lease rentals, grabbed 160 acres of Government land, and fraudulently sub-leased/alienated portions to third-party developers (DLF) and Madras School of Equitation. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed unpaid lease rentals of approx. Rs. 55 to 150 Crores due to the Appellant; Rs. 1386.13 Crores claimed unpaid lease rentals to State Government; alleged tax evasion of Rs. 250 Crores in Service Tax/GST and Rs. 75 Crores in Income Tax. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Lease executed 27.07.1927 and expired 26.10.1936; Supreme Court judgment in Dr. K.R. Lakshmanan delivered in 1996; Company Petition CP/46(CHE)/2021 filed before NCLT Chennai in 2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Lease deed of 1927, Will dated 24.02.1960, revenue records (Patta Chitta Adangal), RTI applications/replies, balance sheets showing alienation to DLF in FY 2018-19 for Rs. 360 Crores. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed CP/46(CHE)/2021 before NCLT Chennai Bench-II under Section 213 of the Companies Act, 2013 seeking investigation by Central Government inspectors, appointment of an Administrator/Receiver, and recovery of rent arrears. On 17.11.2021, NCLT dismissed the petition in limine for lack of prima facie evidence, lack of locus, and delay/laches.
summary.legal_issues: Whether a stranger/non-member asserting private tenancy and lease rental disputes has locus standi to maintain an application under Section 213(b) of the Companies Act, 2013 for investigation into a company's affairs, and whether claims based on causes of action arising decades prior are barred by delay and laches under Section 433.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An investigation under Section 213(b) of the Companies Act, 2013 cannot be ordered at the behest of an unconnected stranger or non-member seeking to enforce private civil or tenancy claims under the guise of corporate fraud, especially where the petition is afflicted by gross delay and laches. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The words 'any other person' in Section 213(b) must be interpreted as a person having a legitimate legal grievance or tangible interest in the corporate affairs, not an alien party. Section 433 incorporates the Limitation Act, 1963, rendering stale claims subject to the doctrine of delay and laches. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: To invoke Section 213(b), the applicant must establish prima facie tangible circumstances suggesting intent to defraud or unlawful conduct; bare assertions, private title disputes, and uncorroborated allegations of tax evasion are legally insufficient. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellant had no locus standi as a member or creditor under company law, and the petition arose from ancient civil disputes dating prior to 1996, warranting summary dismissal.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 17 of 2022 is dismissed; the dismissal order dated 17.11.2021 passed by NCLT Chennai Bench-II is confirmed; connected I.A. No. 185 of 2022 is closed; no costs.
summary.summary: The Appellant, claiming to be the grandson of a landowner who leased property to Madras Race Club in 1927, filed a petition under Section 213(b) of the Companies Act, 2013 alleging corporate fraud, land grabbing, non-payment of rent arrears, and tax evasion, seeking an investigation and the appointment of an Administrator. NCLT Chennai dismissed the petition in limine. On appeal, NCLAT Chennai Bench affirmed the dismissal, ruling that the Appellant was an alien stranger with no stake or standing as a member or creditor, that private tenancy and title disputes cannot justify ordering an investigation under Section 213, and that the petition was barred by gross delay and laches under Section 433.

summary.case_title: S. Chandriah vs. Sunil Kumar Agarwal, Resolution Professional of Digjam Limited & Ors.
summary.appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) Insolvency No. 22 of 2022 & Company Appeal (AT) Insolvency No. 21 of 2022
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: S. Chandriah is the Appellant (prospective buyer/claimant); Digjam Limited is the Corporate Debtor; Sunil Kumar Agarwal is Respondent No. 1 (Resolution Professional); Committee of Creditors of Digjam Limited is Respondent No. 2; M/s Finquest Financial Solutions Pvt. Ltd. is Respondent No. 3 (Successful Resolution Applicant); Suspended Board of Directors is Respondent No. 4. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellant submitted an offer letter dated 14.09.2018 proposing to purchase surplus mill land of approximately 10 acres at Jamnagar on an 'as is where is' basis for Rs. 2.25 Crores per acre, offering an interest-free advance of up to Rs. 10 Crores to be adjusted against sale consideration or refunded if rejected. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Between 26.09.2018 and 08.04.2019, Appellant remitted Rs. 7 Crores via RTGS/NEFT as earnest money/advance. No agreement to sell was executed, and the land was never transferred. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated against Corporate Debtor on 26.04.2019 under Section 9 IBC (filed by M/s Oman Inc. for Rs. 21,74,626/-). Appellant filed Form F on 22.05.2019, followed by Form C claim as Financial Creditor on 02.07.2019 for Rs. 7 Crores. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Offer letter dated 14.09.2018; RTGS payment confirmations for Rs. 7 Crores; Annual Reports of Corporate Debtor for FY 2018-19 and 2019-20 recording the earnest money under 'other Financial Liability'; RP communications declining financial debt status; approved Resolution Plan providing NIL payment to other creditors. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP admitted the Rs. 7 Crore claim under 'other creditors' rather than financial debt. Appellant filed IA No. 658 of 2019 before NCLT Ahmedabad Bench seeking admission as Financial Creditor and CoC member, which was dismissed on 07.02.2020. CoC approved Finquest's Resolution Plan on 11.02.2020, which NCLT approved via IA No. 144 of 2020 on 27.05.2020. Appellant filed Appeal No. 22/2022 against the 07.02.2020 dismissal and Appeal No. 21/2022 against the 27.05.2020 plan approval.
summary.legal_issues: 1. Whether payment of earnest money/advance of Rs. 7 Crores under an unaccepted proposal for the purchase of surplus land constitutes a 'financial debt' disbursed against consideration for the time value of money under Section 5(8) of the IBC. 2. Whether classification of an advance as a 'Financial Liability' in balance sheets converts it into a 'financial debt'. 3. Whether a resolution plan approved by the CoC allocating NIL payment to 'other creditors' violates Section 30(2) of the IBC or Regulation 38(1-A) of CIRP Regulations.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Advance earnest money paid towards the purchase of immovable property to be adjusted against final sale consideration does not constitute a borrowing or disbursal against consideration for the time value of money under Section 5(8) of the IBC. Furthermore, the commercial wisdom of the CoC to provide NIL payment to 'other creditors' is valid so long as mandatory priority distribution requirements under Section 30(2) read with Section 53 are met. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8) requires an indispensable element of 'disbursal against consideration for the time value of money'. Accounting treatment of earnest money as a 'Financial Liability' under Ind AS does not equate to a 'financial debt' under IBC. Under Section 30(2) and Regulation 38(1-A), the resolution plan must demonstrate how interests of all stakeholders were considered, but there is no statutory mandate that every class must receive monetary payout. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: In the absence of a borrowing transaction, interest stipulations, or financing arrangement, an earnest money deposit cannot satisfy the legal standard of Section 5(8). 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Appellant's claim was properly classified under 'other creditors', and the approved Resolution Plan allocating NIL payment to other creditors was legally compliant and non-interferable.
summary.operative_order: Both Company Appeal (AT) Insolvency No. 22 of 2022 and Company Appeal (AT) Insolvency No. 21 of 2022 are dismissed. The impugned orders dated 07.02.2020 and 27.05.2020 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Ahmedabad Bench) are affirmed. No order as to costs.
summary.summary: Appellant S. Chandriah challenged orders of NCLT Ahmedabad Bench rejecting his claim as a Financial Creditor and approving Digjam Limited's Resolution Plan. The Appellant paid Rs. 7 Crores as earnest money under an unaccepted proposal to purchase surplus mill land. The Resolution Professional admitted the claim under 'other creditors' rather than financial debt, and the approved plan provided nil recovery to this class. NCLAT held that advance earnest money lacks the indispensable element of disbursal against consideration for the time value of money under Section 5(8) IBC. Categorization as a financial liability in balance sheets does not constitute financial debt. The CoC's commercial wisdom offering nil payment to other creditors complied with Section 30(2). Both appeals were dismissed.

summary.case_title: Sumit Binani, RP of KSK Mahanadi Power Company Ltd. vs. V. Venkatachalam, RP of KSK Water Infrastructures Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
summary.appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Insolvency) No. 234 of 2021 & Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Insolvency) No. 239 of 2021
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sumit Binani is the Resolution Professional of KSK Mahanadi Power Company Ltd. (KMPCL, Corporate Debtor 1/Appellant); Committee of Creditors of KMPCL is Co-Appellant; V. Venkatachalam is the Resolution Professional of KSK Water Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. (KWIPL, Corporate Debtor 2/Respondent No. 1); Committee of Creditors of KWIPL is Respondent No. 2. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: KMPCL and KWIPL entered into a Water Transport Agreement (WTA) on 14.03.2014 for piped water supply to KMPCL's 1800 MW power plant, containing a minimum take-or-pay obligation of 6 MCM/month effective from 01.04.2016 onwards. A two-year Amendment Agreement dated 01.03.2015 temporarily revised the take-or-pay quantity to 2.55 MCM/month until 31.03.2017. Lenders entered an amended Common Loan Agreement (CLA) in October 2016 restricting water charges to O&M expenses pending a merger that aborted. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: RP of KWIPL issued post-CIRP invoices for April 2021 (Rs. 11,32,80,000), May 2021 (Rs. 11,32,80,000), and July 2021 (Rs. 9,13,54,845) based on the 6 MCM take-or-pay clause, totaling Rs. 31,79,14,845 billed against Rs. 12,09,48,880 for actual water consumed. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated against KMPCL on 03.10.2019; CIRP initiated against KWIPL on 01.01.2021. Letter dated 30.03.2017 sent by KWIPL stating expiry of the 2015 amendment and reviving 2014 WTA. RP of KWIPL issued invoice on 17.05.2021 and suspended water supply on 01.06.2021 due to unpaid dues. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: WTA dated 14.03.2014; Amendment Agreement dated 01.03.2015; CLA dated 22.11.2016; letter dated 30.03.2017; invoices dated 17.05.2021, 25.06.2021, and 02.08.2021; minutes of KWIPL's 4th CoC meeting approving water supply under WTA pursuant to Section 28(1)(f). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP of KMPCL filed IA No. 270 of 2021 before NCLT Hyderabad Bench in CP (IB) No. 492 of 2019 seeking uninterrupted water supply under the 2016 O&M arrangement. On 17.06.2021, NCLT directed KWIPL to restart water supply subject to KMPCL paying water transportation charges as claimed under the 2014 WTA and raised invoices pursuant to Section 14(2A) IBC. Appellants challenged this order.
summary.legal_issues: 1. Whether the Adjudicating Authority or Appellate Tribunal exercising summary jurisdiction under the IBC can adjudicate complex contractual disputes regarding contract interpretation, novation under Section 62 of the Contract Act, and pricing terms of pre-CIRP agreements. 2. Whether under Section 14(2A) of the IBC a Corporate Debtor undergoing CIRP can compel continuation of critical services while altering contractual billing terms to pay only for actual supplies rather than contractual take-or-pay charges.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Adjudicating Authorities and Appellate Tribunals operating under summary jurisdiction cannot adjudicate complex contractual disputes relating to the interpretation, novation, or enforcement of commercial contracts. When critical supplies are mandated during CIRP under Section 14(2A) of the IBC to preserve the debtor as a going concern, the debtor must pay the charges arising under the existing valid contract, and the tribunal cannot rewrite contract terms. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14(2A) IBC dictates that supplies of critical goods and services cannot be suspended during moratorium except where the debtor fails to pay dues arising from such supply during moratorium. The statutory phrase 'such supply' refers to supply under subsisting contractual terms and cannot be judicially rewritten to mean 'actual supply' at altered rates. Ratification of contracts by the CoC under Section 28(1)(f) constitutes commercial wisdom that cannot be overturned. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Relying on Supreme Court precedents in Tata Consultancy Services and Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam, tribunals must respect contractual rights unless termination arises solely out of insolvency and threatens corporate death. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT rightly directed water supply resumption conditioned upon payment of invoices raised under the 2014 WTA.
summary.operative_order: Both Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Insolvency) No. 234 of 2021 and Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Insolvency) No. 239 of 2021 are dismissed. The interim order dated 01.10.2021 stands vacated. All pending applications are closed. No order as to costs.
summary.summary: Appellants, the Resolution Professional and Committee of Creditors of KSK Mahanadi Power Company Ltd. (KMPCL), appealed NCLT Hyderabad's order directing KMPCL to pay water transport charges to KSK Water Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. (KWIPL) under a 2014 agreement to ensure uninterrupted water supply. Both entities were undergoing CIRP. KMPCL claimed water charges should be restricted to actual consumption and operational expenses under subsequent 2015 and 2016 understandings rather than a 6 MCM take-or-pay condition. NCLAT dismissed the appeals, holding that tribunals exercising summary jurisdiction cannot rewrite contracts or adjudicate contractual novation. Under Section 14(2A) IBC, uninterrupted supply of critical services requires the debtor to pay the corresponding contractual dues arising during moratorium.

summary.case_title: Raj Singh Gehlot vs. Vistra (ITCL) India Ltd. & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Raj Singh Gehlot is Appellant/Promoter of Ambience Pvt. Ltd. (Developer/Corporate Debtor); Vistra (ITCL) India Ltd. (formerly IL&FS Trust Company Ltd.) is Respondent No. 1 (Investor/Financial Creditor); Sandeep Chandana is Respondent No. 2 (IRP); Ambience Projects and Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. is the Joint Venture SPV. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: On 28.05.2011, parties entered into a Share Subscription cum Shareholders Agreement (SSHA) to develop a 17.63-acre real estate project in Gurgaon. Investor infused funds directly into the SPV by subscribing to 49% equity, optionally convertible debentures (OCDs) of Rs. 134.93 Crores, and unsecured loans of Rs. 65.05 Crores. No disbursal was made directly to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Investor issued an Event of Default Notice on 31.03.2016 and invoked put-option on 06.09.2016. In conciliation, parties entered a Settlement Agreement dated 07.04.2017 where SPV/Corporate Debtor agreed to pay Rs. 200 Crores in three tranches with 6% interest against transfer/redemption of securities. After the first tranche of Rs. 65 Crores (totaling Rs. 85.10 Crores with interest) was paid by the SPV and an affiliate, defaults occurred on subsequent tranches on 30.09.2017 and 28.02.2018, leading to a claimed default of Rs. 234,69,62,791 as of 31.10.2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Put option exercised 06.09.2016; Settlement Agreement/Arbitral Consent Award dated 07.04.2017; defaults on 30.09.2017 and 28.02.2018; Section 7 petition CP (IB)-1600/ND/2018 filed in late 2018. Parallel execution petition filed before Delhi High Court. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: SSHA dated 28.05.2011 and amendments; Settlement Agreement dated 07.04.2017 under Part III of the Arbitration Act; banking records establishing that all funds were disbursed to the SPV and zero to the Corporate Debtor; Delhi High Court execution proceedings where SPV earmarked 59 apartments valued over Rs. 260 Crores. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent No. 1 filed a Section 7 IBC petition against Corporate Debtor Ambience Pvt. Ltd. On 21.12.2020, NCLT New Delhi Bench-III admitted the application and initiated CIRP, holding that the conciliation settlement had the status of an arbitral award under Section 74 of the Arbitration Act and evidenced financial debt. Promoter appealed.
summary.legal_issues: 1. Whether investment infused into a Joint Venture SPV via share subscription, optionally convertible debentures, and unsecured loans constitutes a 'financial debt' owed by a co-shareholder/developer (Corporate Debtor) to whom no funds were disbursed. 2. Whether an arbitral consent award or conciliation settlement agreement can form the foundation for initiating CIRP under Section 7 of the IBC against a non-recipient of the disbursement.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: To qualify as a financial creditor under Section 5(7) read with Section 5(8) of the IBC, there must be an actual disbursal of funds to the Corporate Debtor against consideration for the time value of money. An equity or debenture investment into an SPV governed by profit-sharing does not establish a financial debt against a co-promoter/developer. Furthermore, Section 7 cannot be utilized as an executing mechanism to enforce an arbitral award or conciliation decree in the absence of an underlying financial debt disbursed to the corporate debtor. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The core requirement of Section 5(8) is 'disbursal against the consideration for the time value of money' flowing to the corporate debtor. Although Section 3(10) includes a decree-holder as a 'creditor', Part II of the Code specifically limits Section 7 triggers to 'financial creditors'; hence, a decree or arbitral settlement cannot independently generate a financial debt without underlying disbursal. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under the principles of Anuj Jain v. Axis Bank, the genesis of the liability must reveal direct disbursal and the commercial effect of a borrowing. Since funds were disbursed exclusively to the SPV, the evidentiary standard was not met. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Vistra was not a Financial Creditor of Ambience Pvt. Ltd., and Section 7 could not be invoked to execute the arbitral settlement.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 06 of 2021 is allowed. The impugned order dated 21.12.2020 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT New Delhi Bench-III) admitting the Section 7 petition and initiating CIRP against Ambience Pvt. Ltd. is set aside. Interim orders stand vacated. No order as to costs.
summary.summary: Appellant Raj Singh Gehlot, promoter of Ambience Pvt. Ltd., appealed the NCLT New Delhi order admitting a Section 7 IBC petition filed by Vistra (ITCL) India Ltd. Vistra had infused funds into a Joint Venture SPV via equity, debentures, and unsecured loans. Following project disputes, parties executed a conciliation Settlement Agreement for Rs. 200 Crores, treated as an arbitral award. When subsequent tranches defaulted, Vistra filed under Section 7 against the promoter entity. Setting aside CIRP admission, NCLAT held that direct disbursal against time value of money is mandatory for establishing financial debt under Section 5(8). Investments in an SPV do not create financial debt against the developer, nor can IBC be invoked to execute an arbitral award.

summary.case_title: Budhpur Buildcon Pvt. Ltd. vs. Abhay Narayan Manudhane, Resolution Professional of Housing Development and Infrastructure Limited
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Budhpur Buildcon Pvt. Ltd. (BBPL, an Adani Group company, formerly Adani Developers Pvt. Ltd.) is the Appellant/Developer; Housing Development and Infrastructure Limited (HDIL) is the Corporate Debtor; Abhay Narayan Manudhane is the Respondent/Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Parties executed Project Agreements between 24.02.2007 and 09.04.2018 (including Supplemental Agreement dated 20.03.2012) for Slum Rehabilitation Authority projects in Mumbai. Appellant agreed to pay staged considerations totaling Rs. 1,192 Crores to enable HDIL to construct rehabilitation tenements in exchange for transferring free-sale development rights/saleable area of 12,12,171 sq. ft. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Clause 4 of Supplemental Agreement dated 20.03.2012 stipulated that upon HDIL's failure to meet construction timelines, it had 60 days to cure, failing which it was liable to pay interest at 2% per month on paid consideration. Appellant disbursed Rs. 721.03 Crores and claimed penal interest of Rs. 14,391 Crores accruing from default. Claim excluded principal repayment. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced against HDIL on 20.08.2019; claims cut-off date under Regulation 12(2) was 20.11.2019; Appellant filed Form C claim four months late on 08.01.2020; RP issued clarification query on 28.03.2020 and formally rejected claim on 28.09.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Development Agreements dated 24.02.2007, 01.03.2008, 05.04.2018 and Supplemental Agreements dated 14.10.2008 and 20.03.2012; Form C dated 08.01.2020; RP's rejection letter dated 28.09.2020; evidence of forfeiture of Rs. 340 Crores security deposit; absence of any pure borrowing or loan documents. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP rejected BBPL's claim as a financial debt. BBPL filed IA No. 2129 of 2020 before NCLT Mumbai Bench in CP No. 27 of 2019. On 02.08.2021, NCLT dismissed the application, holding that the claim was for penal interest/damages for breach of contract and did not constitute financial debt. BBPL appealed to NCLAT.
summary.legal_issues: 1. Whether an interest stipulation of 2% per month imposed as a penalty/liquidated damages for breach of construction timelines under a real estate joint development agreement constitutes a 'financial debt' disbursed against consideration for the time value of money under Section 5(8) of the IBC. 2. Whether a commercial developer partner under a joint development agreement qualifies as a 'financial creditor' under Section 5(7) or Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A claim arising from a contractual penalty or liquidated damages clause under Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 for delayed performance of reciprocal obligations in a commercial development agreement does not constitute a financial debt under Section 5(8) of the IBC. Financial debt requires that funds be disbursed as a borrowing against consideration for the time value of money, rather than as milestone advances in a collaborative commercial venture. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8) mandates that the genesis of the debt must be a borrowing transaction. While Section 5(8)(f) captures transactions with the commercial effect of a borrowing, it does not encompass ordinary joint development agreements where default triggers penal interest. The word 'interest' in a commercial agreement does not create financial debt where it represents liquidated damages or penalty under Section 74 of the Contract Act. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying Pioneer Urban and Anuj Jain, tribunals assess whether advances were made for temporary use as a borrowing with return on time value. Advances tied to reciprocal construction and land-sale obligations fail this standard. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Rs. 14,391 Crore claim represented penal damages for contractual breach rather than a financial debt. RP rightly rejected the claim.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 589 of 2021 is dismissed. The impugned order dated 02.08.2021 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Mumbai Bench) is affirmed. Interim orders stand vacated. All pending applications are disposed of. No order as to costs.
summary.summary: Appellant Budhpur Buildcon Pvt. Ltd. challenged the NCLT Mumbai order upholding the Resolution Professional's rejection of its claim of Rs. 14,391 Crores as a Financial Creditor of Corporate Debtor Housing Development and Infrastructure Limited (HDIL). The claim was grounded entirely on a 2% monthly interest clause stipulated under a 2012 Supplemental Development Agreement as liquidated damages for HDIL's failure to meet construction timelines. Affirming NCLT's dismissal, NCLAT held that penal interest or liquidated damages arising from breach of reciprocal obligations under Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act does not constitute a financial debt under Section 5(8) IBC. The underlying transaction was a commercial real estate development venture lacking the essential character of borrowing disbursed for time value of money.

summary.case_title: Dolphin Vintrade Private Limited vs. Ashray Vyapaar Private Limited & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Gourepore Company Limited is the Corporate Debtor (in liquidation since 26.11.1997); Ashray Vyapaar Private Limited is Respondent No. 1 (alleged assignee claiming status as Financial Creditor); Dolphin Vintrade Private Limited is the Appellant (unsecured creditor and intervenor); Official Liquidator represents the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor availed credit facilities prior to 1993 from four secured banks (Allahabad Bank, Indian Bank, United Bank of India, and IIBI). Between 2007 and 2008, Respondent No. 1 acquired assignments of debts aggregating roughly Rs. 50 Crores for an outlay of approximately Rs. 9 Crores, with Allahabad Bank executing a registered indenture of assignment on 14.09.2015 confirming the 2008 assignment. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor was ordered wound up on 26.11.1997. DRT Recovery Certificates were issued in 1996 for Allahabad Bank (Rs. 26,20,41,281) and 2002 for Indian Bank (Rs. 16,92,08,930). In its Section 7 petition, Respondent No. 1 claimed a default amount of Rs. 2486,44,80,162.85 with the default date asserted as 19.12.2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Winding up order passed 26.11.1997; winding up petition CP No. 355/1997 dismissed for non-prosecution on 19.12.2019 and restored on 28.02.2020; Section 7 petition filed on 18.02.2020; Appellant filed intervention IA No. 1069/2021 on 12.12.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Calcutta High Court orders dated 14.07.2014 holding the bank debt assignments dubious and Division Bench order dated 09.08.2017 characterizing Respondent No. 1 as a passerby attempting to hijack liquidation assets and restraining further proceedings without disclosure; dismissal of SLP by Supreme Court on 18.09.2017; complete concealment of the Division Bench restraint order in the Section 7 petition. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent No. 1 filed CP (IB) No. 572/KB/2020 under Section 7 IBC before NCLT Kolkata Bench. Appellant filed IA No. 1069/KB/2021 seeking dismissal of the petition. On 31.01.2022, NCLT rejected IA 1069/KB/2021 and admitted the Section 7 petition. Appellant appealed to NCLAT.
summary.legal_issues: 1. Whether a Section 7 IBC application filed in 2020 on the basis of bank debts decreed by DRT in 1996 against a company ordered wound up in 1997 is barred by limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963. 2. Whether an applicant who conceals adverse High Court and Division Bench orders characterizing debt assignments as dubious and restraining undisclosed applications can maintain a Section 7 application. 3. Whether an unsecured creditor has locus standi under Section 61(1) of the IBC to challenge the fraudulent admission of a Section 7 application.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963, a petition under Section 7 of the IBC must be filed within three years from the date default occurs or fresh cause of action arises from a recovery certificate or decree; the dismissal of a pending winding-up petition for default cannot create an artificial date of default. A party guilty of material concealment of binding court orders and employing IBC proceedings to hijack the assets of a company in liquidation is disentitled to equitable and statutory relief. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: 'Debt' under Section 3(11) of the IBC requires a subsisting liability due from a person; where a corporate debtor has been in liquidation for decades with assets in custodia legis, default cannot be pegged to the procedural dismissal of a winding-up case. Section 3(1) of the Limitation Act mandates dismissal of time-barred applications regardless of whether limitation is pleaded in defence. Section 61(1) IBC confers locus standi on any person aggrieved by an order of the Adjudicating Authority. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict scrutiny applies to limitation and the bona fides of debt assignments. When DRT recovery certificates date back to 1996, the three-year limitation period under Dena Bank v. C. Shivakumar Reddy expired decades ago, rendering the 2020 petition time-barred on the face of the record. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt claimed was hopelessly barred by limitation, the date of default fictitious, and material Division Bench orders suppressed; hence, the Section 7 petition was dismissed with costs of Rs. 10 Lakhs.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 320 of 2022 is allowed. The impugned order dated 31.01.2022 passed by NCLT Kolkata Bench is set aside, and Section 7 Application in C.P. (IB) No. 572/KB/2020 is dismissed with costs assessed at Rs. 10 Lakhs to be paid by Respondent No. 1 to the Official Liquidator within one month for use in the liquidation process. Parties shall bear their own costs.
summary.summary: Appellant Dolphin Vintrade Pvt. Ltd., an unsecured creditor, challenged the NCLT Kolkata Bench order admitting a Section 7 IBC petition filed by Respondent No. 1, Ashray Vyapaar Pvt. Ltd., against Gourepore Company Limited (in liquidation since 1997). Respondent No. 1 claimed Rs. 2,486 Crores based on pre-1997 bank loan assignments deemed dubious by the Calcutta High Court, citing an artificial default date of 19.12.2019 when the winding-up petition was briefly dismissed for non-prosecution. NCLAT held that the petition was hopelessly barred by limitation under Article 137, as DRT recovery certificates were issued in 1996. Additionally, Respondent No. 1 fraudulently suppressed adverse Division Bench orders. NCLAT allowed the appeal, set aside admission, and dismissed Section 7 with Rs. 10 Lakhs costs.

summary.case_title: Davinder Kumar Singhal vs. Sanjay Kumar Chetwani & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s Medinnbelle Herbalcare Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor (manufacturer of 'Endura Mass'); Davinder Kumar Singhal is the Suspended Director/Appellant; Sanjay Kumar Chetwani is Respondent No. 1 (Operational Creditor/proprietor); Santanu Kumar Samanta is Respondent No. 2 (IRP). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Parties executed an Assignment Deed dated 19.01.2018 whereby Respondent No. 1 assigned the trademark 'NPD Endura Mass' to the Corporate Debtor for a full and final sale consideration of Rs. 4.40 Crores, which was paid in full via two demand drafts less 10% TDS. A post-dated cheque of Rs. 52,80,000 dated 15.03.2018 was handed over as security to an intermediary with an endorsement regarding GST payment. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational Creditor claimed a default of Rs. 52,80,000/- towards 12% IGST on invoice No. NPDTM001 dated 06.02.2018. The post-dated cheque was presented and dishonoured on 12.06.2018 due to 'Stop Payment' instructions. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: On 12.03.2018, Corporate Debtor issued a letter repudiating GST liability and intimating stop payment; stop payment executed 13.03.2018; criminal complaint filed with EOW on 21.05.2018; GST demand email sent by Respondent on 19.10.2018 and refuted on 24.10.2018; Section 8 notice issued 11.09.2019 and replied 26.09.2019; Section 9 petition filed in late 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Assignment Deed dated 19.01.2018 declaring Rs. 4.40 Crores as full and final consideration without tax additions; stop-payment letter dated 12.03.2018; bank memo dated 12.06.2018; criminal complaint dated 21.05.2018 alleging conspiracy and fraud; reply dated 24.10.2018 refuting GST claims; detailed reply to Section 8 notice dated 26.09.2019. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent No. 1 filed C.P. (IB)-2681/ND/2019 under Section 9 IBC. On 14.12.2021, NCLT New Delhi Bench IV admitted the application, holding that the issuance of the cheque proved admission of liability to pay GST. Suspended Director appealed to NCLAT.
summary.legal_issues: 1. Whether issuance of a post-dated cheque that was countermanded prior to its due date by written notice constitutes an unequivocal admission of operational debt under Section 9 of the IBC. 2. Whether written repudiations, stop payment instructions, and criminal complaints disputing additional tax liability prior to the service of Section 8 demand notice constitute a pre-existing dispute under Section 9(5)(ii)(d) of the IBC.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 9(5)(ii)(d) of the IBC, an application for corporate insolvency must be rejected if the Corporate Debtor demonstrates a plausible, non-spurious pre-existing dispute raised prior to the issuance of a Section 8 demand notice. The statutory presumption under Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act in criminal cheque dishonour proceedings does not displace proof of a genuine pre-existing dispute in summary IBC proceedings. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Applying Mobilox Innovations, the Adjudicating Authority must determine whether the defense is not a patently feeble legal argument and whether a dispute truly exists in fact. Where the underlying contract fixes full and final consideration, subsequent unilateral demands for indirect taxes that are disputed prior to demand notice fall within the realm of pre-existing disputes. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Contemporaneous written letters dated 12.03.2018 and 24.10.2018 expressly denying GST liability, supported by bank stop-payment instructions dated 13.03.2018 and criminal fraud complaints dated 21.05.2018, satisfy the evidential threshold demonstrating a pre-existing dispute prior to the Section 8 notice dated 11.09.2019. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: A bona fide pre-existing dispute existed between the parties regarding liability for GST; hence, the NCLT committed an error in admitting the application.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1088 of 2021 is allowed. The impugned order dated 14.12.2021 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench IV is set aside, and the Section 9 Application filed by Respondent No. 1 is rejected. The sum of Rs. 52,80,000/- deposited by the Appellant pursuant to interim orders is directed to be returned to the Appellant. Parties shall bear their own costs.
summary.summary: Appellant Davinder Kumar Singhal, Suspended Director of Medinnbelle Herbalcare Pvt. Ltd., appealed the NCLT New Delhi order admitting a Section 9 IBC application filed by Sanjay Kumar Chetwani. Chetwani claimed unpaid GST of Rs. 52.80 Lakhs on an assignment of the 'NPD Endura Mass' trademark for Rs. 4.40 Crores, relying on a stopped post-dated cheque. NCLAT set aside the admission, finding clear evidence of a genuine pre-existing dispute under Section 9(5)(ii)(d) IBC. Prior to the Section 8 demand notice, the Corporate Debtor had issued written disclaimers of GST liability, stopped cheque payment, and lodged criminal fraud complaints against the creditor. Applying Mobilox Innovations, NCLAT held the dispute was plausible and rejected the Section 9 petition.

summary.case_title: Deepak Vegpro Pvt. Ltd. vs. Shree Hari Agro Industries Ltd.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Deepak Vegpro Pvt. Ltd. (controlled by Niranjan Lal Data Group) is Appellant/alleged Financial Creditor; Shree Hari Agro Industries Ltd. (controlled by Babu Lal Data Group) is Corporate Debtor; IDBI and SASF are original lender and assignor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor obtained a term loan of Rs. 4.50 Crores from IDBI on 11.07.1996 with interest at 21% p.a., secured by hypothecation and mortgage. IDBI assigned the loan to SASF, which subsequently assigned it to Appellant on 17.01.2007 for consideration of Rs. 2.50 Crores pursuant to Corporate Debtor's NOC dated 09.01.2007. 3.
