DEFAULT METRICS: Default occurred on the first installment on 01.04.1998. IDBI issued a recall notice on 26.04.2000 and filed DRT Jaipur recovery proceedings on 22.09.2000 (withdrawn 16.10.2007). In its Section 7 petition, Appellant claimed Rs. 412.52 Crores (principal, interest, and liquidated damages) as of 02.02.2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: First default 01.04.1998; loan recall 26.04.2000; BIFR declared sickness 13.06.2001; assignment to Appellant 17.01.2007; Section 7 petition CP(IB) No. 265/KB/2018 filed on 10.04.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Loan agreement dated 11.07.1996; Assignment Deed dated 17.01.2007; Balance sheets for FY 2006-07 to 2007-08 reflecting Rs. 4.50 Crores, and FY 2008-09 to 2015-16 reflecting Rs. 1.35 Crores without interest or repayment terms; Notes to Accounts for FY 2008-09 showing one-time settlement and interest waivers credited to Capital Reserve; family settlement records dividing Data family businesses. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed Section 7 petition before NCLT Kolkata Bench claiming Rs. 412.52 Crores. On 05.09.2019, NCLT dismissed the petition as time-barred, finding material discrepancies in debt figures and a lack of unequivocal acknowledgment. Appellant appealed to NCLAT.
summary.legal_issues: 1. Whether balance sheet entries reflecting a reduced sum of Rs. 1.35 Crores with explanatory notes showing settlement and waiver constitute an unequivocal acknowledgment of a claimed debt of Rs. 412.52 Crores under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963. 2. Whether an assigned amount lacking interest stipulations and repayment schedules constitutes a financial debt under Section 5(8) of the IBC. 3. Whether the Adjudicating Authority possesses discretion under Section 7(5)(a) of the IBC to decline admission when default is unproven and disputed.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An entry in a company's balance sheet can extend limitation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 only if it amounts to an unequivocal and conscious acknowledgment of a subsisting jural relationship and liability qua the specific debt claimed. A balance sheet entry reflecting a reduced sum accompanied by notes of waiver and devoid of repayment schedules cannot extend limitation for an unacknowledged claim. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Applying Bishal Jaiswal, balance sheets must be construed alongside accompanying notes and auditor caveats; where notes reflect settlement and waiver credited to Capital Reserve, acknowledgment of debt is negated. Under Section 5(8) of the IBC, financial debt requires disbursal against consideration for the time value of money; without interest or a repayment schedule, capital entries cannot qualify as financial debt. Under Section 7(5)(a) read with Vidarbha Industries, the Adjudicating Authority retains discretion to refuse admission where debt and default are not conclusively established. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying J.C. Budhiraja and Tilak Ram, there must be conscious admission of a subsisting liability. The discrepancy between the claimed Rs. 412.52 Crores and the balance sheet entry of Rs. 1.35 Crores, coupled with a ten-year absence of demand notices, fails the evidentiary test. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt was neither established as a financial debt nor shown to be within limitation; hence, dismissal of the Section 7 petition was valid.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1085 of 2019 is dismissed. The impugned order dated 05.09.2019 passed by NCLT Kolkata Bench in CP(IB) No. 265/KB/2018 is affirmed. No order as to costs.
summary.summary: Appellant Deepak Vegpro Pvt. Ltd. appealed the NCLT Kolkata Bench order dismissing its Section 7 IBC application against Corporate Debtor Shree Hari Agro Industries Ltd. for an alleged default of Rs. 412.52 Crores. The claim originated from an IDBI term loan assigned to Appellant in 2007 following a family partition. The Appellant relied on balance sheet entries from 2006 to 2016 to claim extended limitation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act. NCLAT held that the balance sheets reflected a settled, reduced sum of Rs. 1.35 Crores with notes indicating complete waiver of interest and absence of repayment schedules. Consequently, there was no unequivocal acknowledgment of the claimed debt, rendering the Section 7 petition time-barred and devoid of financial debt attributes.

summary.case_title: Raghavendra G. Kundangar & Ors. vs. Shashi Agarwal, Liquidator of Bharat NRE Coke Ltd. & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Raghavendra G. Kundangar and 115 others are Appellants (shareholders of Corporate Debtor); Bharat NRE Coke Ltd. is Corporate Debtor (in liquidation); Shashi Agarwal is Respondent No. 1 (Liquidator); Jindal Steel and Power Limited is Respondent No. 2 (original petitioner/creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Respondent No. 2 supplied materials under a contract to Corporate Debtor Bharat NRE Coke Ltd. and subsequently initiated corporate insolvency proceedings under Section 7 claiming unpaid invoices constituted financial debt. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose on commercial supply dues under CP(IB) No. 1340 of 2018, which was admitted under Section 7 on 11.03.2019 and affirmed as financial debt through appellate proceedings up to the Supreme Court. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Kolkata admitted Section 7 application on 11.03.2019; NCLAT dismissed appeal on 23.07.2019; Supreme Court dismissed Civil Appeal No. 7029 of 2019 in limine on 16.08.2019; Supreme Court rendered Anuj Jain judgment on 26.02.2020; Appellants filed recall IA No. 1340 of 2020 in 2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Section 7 admission order dated 11.03.2019; Supreme Court dismissal orders dated 16.08.2019 in Arun Kumar Jagatramka and Suraksha ARC; Supreme Court judgment in Anuj Jain v. Axis Bank; Corporate Debtor's liquidation records. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 admission against Corporate Debtor attained finality upon dismissal of appeals by the Supreme Court. Following the subsequent decision in Anuj Jain holding that material suppliers are operational and not financial creditors, Appellants filed IA No. 1340 of 2020 under Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules to recall the 11.03.2019 admission order. NCLT Kolkata Bench dismissed IA No. 1340 of 2020 on 06.05.2022. Appellants appealed to NCLAT.
summary.legal_issues: 1. Whether an order admitting a Section 7 IBC application that has attained finality upon affirmation by the Supreme Court can be recalled by the Adjudicating Authority under Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules based on a subsequent judgment of the Supreme Court overruling the underlying legal principle. 2. Whether entertaining a Section 7 application for supply dues constitutes a patent lack of inherent jurisdiction justifying recall of a concluded judgment.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A court or tribunal cannot recall an order that has attained finality merely because the legal principle upon which it was decided was subsequently overruled in another case by a superior court. Concluded judgments can only be recalled under the four narrow grounds laid down in Sri Budhia Swain: patent lack of inherent jurisdiction, fraud or collusion, mistake of court prejudicing a party, or ignorance of an unserved or deceased necessary party. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules does not confer jurisdiction to sit in appeal over concluded orders. The doctrine of constructive res judicata applies to proceedings under the IBC (Ebix Singapore), precluding collateral challenges to concluded admission orders. The doctrine of prospective overruling validates actions taken under prior prevailing law to maintain judicial finality. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Adjudicating Authority possesses statutory subject-matter jurisdiction to adjudicate insolvency petitions under Part II of the IBC; entertaining a Section 7 petition for a supply transaction does not constitute a patent lack of inherent jurisdiction. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Reopening concluded proceedings upon subsequent changes in law is legally impermissible; NCLT rightly dismissed the recall application.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 886 of 2022 is dismissed. The impugned order dated 06.05.2022 passed by NCLT Kolkata Bench in I.A. No. 1340 of 2020 in C.P. (IB) No. 1340 of 2018 is affirmed. No costs.
summary.summary: Appellants, shareholders of Bharat NRE Coke Ltd. (in liquidation), appealed the NCLT Kolkata Bench's dismissal of their recall application under Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules. The Corporate Debtor had been admitted into CIRP under Section 7 IBC by Jindal Steel and Power Limited for unpaid supplies, an order affirmed by NCLAT and the Supreme Court in 2019. Appellants argued that the Supreme Court's subsequent ruling in Anuj Jain, which held suppliers are operational creditors, rendered the admission void for lack of jurisdiction. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that subsequent overruling of law does not invalidate orders that have attained finality. Principles of res judicata apply to IBC, and misclassification does not constitute patent lack of inherent jurisdiction.

summary.case_title: Urvashi Infrastructure Limited vs. Registrar of Companies, Delhi & Haryana
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Urvashi Infrastructure Limited (formerly Beriwal Chemicals Limited) through Director Mrs. Deepa Kansal is Appellant; Registrar of Companies, Delhi & Haryana is Respondent. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellant was incorporated on 01.06.1992 to carry on infrastructure and real estate works. After finishing projects in 2014-15, its funds remained locked with trade debtors, leading it to pursue eight criminal complaints under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act to recover Rs. 18,12,500/-. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Company failed to submit financial statements for FY 2016-17 through FY 2020-21 and annual returns for FY 2018-19, leading RoC to presume cessation of business for two consecutive years. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: RoC issued show cause notice on 20.07.2019; STK-5 public notice issued 09.08.2019 (Sl. No. 8709); STK-7 striking off notice issued 29.10.2019 (Sl. No. 7503); restoration Appeal No. 215/252(ND)/2020 filed before NCLT in 2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Successive deaths of the Director's sons in Feb 2018 and Jan 2020 and co-director Raja Beriwal on 17.09.2019; filed Income Tax Returns for AY 2017-18 to 2020-21 showing active revenue; bank statements showing employee salary payments from 2015-16 to 2020-21; court records of eight pending Section 138 NI Act recovery complaints. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RoC struck off Appellant's name under Section 248(5). Appellant appealed to NCLT New Delhi Bench (Court II) under Section 252(3). On 04.01.2021, NCLT dismissed the appeal, holding that the company failed to prove significant business operations at the time of striking off. Appellant appealed to NCLAT.
summary.legal_issues: 1. Whether it is 'just' under Section 252(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 to order restoration of a struck-off company that actively maintains pending litigations for debt recovery, turnover in income tax returns, and justifiable family tragedies explaining non-filing defaults. 2. Whether statutory lapses in filing annual returns can be cured by imposing costs while ordering restoration of the company's name.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 252(3) of the Companies Act, 2013, the tribunal possesses equitable discretion to restore a struck-off company if it is 'otherwise just', even if the company was not actively carrying on business at the time of striking off. The active pursuit of recovery suits to preserve company assets and substratum satisfies the test of justness, as striking off would cause irreparable harm by frustrating pending legal proceedings. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The words 'or otherwise' in Section 252(3) establish an independent, equitable head of jurisdiction distinct from carrying on business. The right to seek restoration persists for 20 years from the date of publication in the Official Gazette. Default in filing statutory returns under Section 92 should be penalized by costs rather than corporate death. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Bank records demonstrating ongoing salary disbursements, filed income tax returns with turnover, and records of eight pending Section 138 NI Act recovery complaints establish sufficient evidence to justify restoration in the interest of justice. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: NCLT's refusal to restore the company was unsustainable in law; restoration was ordered subject to filing compliances and payment of costs.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 28 of 2021 is allowed. The impugned order dated 04.01.2021 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench (Court II) and STK-7 striking off notice dated 29.10.2019 are set aside. Appellant's name is restored to the Register of Companies subject to filing all pending statutory documents/fees and paying costs of Rs. 60,000/- to the Prime Minister Relief Fund within two weeks.
summary.summary: Appellant Urvashi Infrastructure Limited appealed against the NCLT New Delhi order dismissing its petition under Section 252(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 for restoration of its company name. The Registrar of Companies struck off the company under Section 248(5) for failure to file statutory financial statements and annual returns for consecutive years. The Appellant demonstrated that filing defaults were caused by successive deaths in the directors' family, and produced evidence of ongoing salary disbursements, filed income tax returns, and eight pending criminal complaints to recover debts totaling Rs. 18.12 Lakhs. NCLAT held that maintaining pending recovery litigations and corporate substratum makes restoration 'otherwise just' under Section 252(3). The appeal was allowed subject to Rs. 60,000 costs.

summary.case_title: M/s AVS Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. vs. Registrar of Companies, Delhi & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s AVS Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. is Appellant Company (incorporated 25.08.1995); Registrar of Companies, Delhi & Haryana is Respondent No. 1; Income Tax Office, Circle 1(1) Delhi is Respondent No. 2. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellant held a commercial lease from RIICO dated 22.03.2002 for an industrial plot in Shahpura, Rajasthan, operating a hotel and restaurant business that suffered disruption due to adjacent flyover construction and the pandemic. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellant failed to file statutory Annual Returns and Balance Sheets after FY 2005-06, prompting the RoC to treat the entity as defunct and inoperative for two consecutive years. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: STK-1 notice issued March 2017; STK-5 public notice issued 13.06.2017; STK-7 striking off notice issued 21.08.2017 (gazetted 01.09.2017); Appeal No. 350/252(ND)/2020 filed before NCLT in 2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Lease deed dated 22.03.2002 executed by RIICO for Shahpura plot; audited balance sheets from FY 2006-07 to FY 2018-19 showing ongoing asset/liability substratum; Allahabad Bank statements from 2010 to 2019; Income Tax Department report confirming no objection to revival; RoC report expressing no objection to revival subject to filing defaults. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RoC struck off Appellant's name under Section 248(5). NCLT New Delhi Special Bench (Court-II) dismissed Appeal No. 350/252(ND)/2020 on 31.12.2020, holding that financial statements were compiled post-striking off and continuous operation prior to striking off was not established beyond doubt. Appellant appealed to NCLAT.
summary.legal_issues: 1. Whether it is just and proper under Section 252(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 to order restoration of a company struck off by the RoC when it owns valuable leasehold immovable property and neither the RoC nor the Income Tax Department objects to revival. 2. Whether non-filing of statutory annual returns for several years justifies permanent dissolution when the corporate substratum remains intact.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 252(3) of the Companies Act, 2013, the existence of valuable immovable property, an intact asset-liability substratum, and the absence of objections from regulatory authorities make it 'otherwise just' to restore a struck-off company. The statutory right of restoration endures for twenty years, and administrative omissions in filing annual returns should be remedied through costs and compliance directions rather than irrevocable corporate dissolution. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 252(3) sets out three alternative grounds: carrying on business, being in operation, or it being 'otherwise just'. The phrase 'otherwise just' confers wide equitable discretion on the tribunal to prevent irreparable harm to the company, its shareholders, and public interest. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Ownership of a valid industrial plot leased from RIICO, supported by audited balance sheets and no-objection reports from the RoC and Income Tax Department, satisfies the evidential threshold of justness under Section 252(3). 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: NCLT's refusal to restore the company was unsustainable in law; restoration was ordered subject to completing statutory filings and paying costs.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 47 of 2021 is allowed. The impugned order dated 31.12.2020 passed by NCLT New Delhi Special Bench Court-II and the STK-7 striking off notice dated 21.08.2017 are set aside. Appellant's name is restored to the Register of Companies subject to filing all pending statutory documents, paying applicable statutory fees, and depositing costs of Rs. 40,000/- with the Prime Minister Relief Fund within the prescribed timeframe.
summary.summary: Appellant M/s AVS Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the NCLT New Delhi order dismissing its application under Section 252(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 for restoration of its company name. The Registrar of Companies struck off the company under Section 248(5) after it failed to file annual returns and financial statements following FY 2005-06. Appellant demonstrated that it held valuable immovable leasehold land from RIICO in Shahpura, Rajasthan, operating a hotel and restaurant. Neither the RoC nor the Income Tax Department opposed revival. NCLAT held that the existence of immovable assets and commercial substratum made restoration 'otherwise just' under Section 252(3), setting aside the striking-off order subject to filing compliances and Rs. 40,000 costs.

summary.case_title: Mrs. Jayanthi G. Ravi vs. M/s Chemizol Additives Pvt. Ltd.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mrs. Jayanthi G. Ravi is the Appellant (erstwhile Director and Financial Creditor); M/s Chemizol Additives Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor (99.99% owned by OnChamp Investments Ltd.). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellant advanced unsecured loans totaling Rs. 4.10 Crores to Corporate Debtor to fund operational expenses and employee salaries across two tranches: Rs. 2.50 Crores on 01.12.2016 and Rs. 1.60 Crores on 18.01.2017 directly from her bank account. Board meetings on 23.02.2017 and 06.04.2017 ratified the borrowing at 7.5% per annum interest, agreeing to repayment within 60 days of the April meeting. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total debt claimed was Rs. 4,70,50,000/- (Rs. 4.10 Crores principal plus Rs. 60,50,000/- interest at 7.5% p.a. through 31.11.2018). Default occurred on 05.06.2017. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Amounts disbursed on 01.12.2016 and 18.01.2017; Board ratifications on 23.02.2017 and 06.04.2017; repayment deadline expired 05.06.2017; Appellant resigned as Director on 25.07.2017; Advocate issued mischaracterized legal notice on 26.06.2018; corrected Section 7 demand notice issued 26.09.2018; Corporate Debtor acknowledged liability in letters dated 05.07.2018, 25.10.2018, and 12.03.2019; Section 7 petition filed in December 2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Board Minutes dated 23.02.2017 and 06.04.2017 signed by director Ooi Boon Aun; Ledger voucher dated 01.12.2016 signed 06.04.2017; Balance Sheets for FY 2016-17 and 2017-18 recording Rs. 4.10 Crores under liabilities; written correspondence from Corporate Debtor admitting liability and requesting extensions to repay principal and interest. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed CP (IB) No. 1/BB/2019 under Section 7 IBC before NCLT Bengaluru Bench. NCLT dismissed the application on 28.01.2020 holding that funds advanced unilaterally by an interested Director to meet company expenses without a prior formal loan agreement lacked the character of financial debt under Section 5(8), and that the solvent company should not be pushed into CIRP. Appellant appealed to NCLAT.
summary.legal_issues: 1. Whether money advanced by an executive director to a company to meet operational expenses, which is subsequently ratified by the Board of Directors with interest and reflected in balance sheets, constitutes a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC despite the absence of a prior formal written loan agreement. 2. Whether an initial demand notice inadvertently describing a debt as an operational debt bars a financial creditor from maintaining a petition under Section 7 of the IBC. 3. Whether the solvency and net worth of a corporate debtor are valid grounds for an Adjudicating Authority to reject a Section 7 petition when financial debt and default are established.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 5(8) of the IBC, funds advanced by a director to a company to meet operational liquidity requirements and keep the company operational have the commercial effect of a borrowing and constitute a financial debt, particularly where post-facto board resolutions ratify the borrowing with interest and the liability is recorded in balance sheets. The absence of a formal prior written loan agreement does not negate the character of a financial debt where bank disbursal and terms are proven. Furthermore, the solvency or asset-rich status of a corporate debtor is irrelevant once debt and default are proved. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8) provides an inclusive definition of financial debt that encompasses interest-bearing advances; under Section 179(3)(d) of the Companies Act, 2013, subsequent ratification of borrowing by the board relates back to the original disbursal. Under Section 7(5), where the Adjudicating Authority is satisfied that a financial debt is due and default has occurred, the application must be admitted. An inadvertent misdescription of financial debt in an initial legal notice does not extinguish the creditor's statutory right to proceed under Section 7. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Signed board minutes, ledger vouchers, balance sheet entries, and repeated written admissions of liability requesting extensions of time satisfy the legal test of debt and default under Innoventive Industries. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Financial debt and default having been conclusively established by written evidence and party admissions, NCLT's dismissal was erroneous and CIRP admission was warranted.
summary.operative_order: TA No. 117/2021 [Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 553 of 2020] is allowed. The impugned order dated 28.01.2020 passed by NCLT Bengaluru Bench is set aside. The Adjudicating Authority is directed to restore CP(IB) No. 1/BB/2019 to its file, admit the petition, and proceed in accordance with law. No order as to costs.
summary.summary: Appellant Mrs. Jayanthi G. Ravi appealed against the NCLT Bengaluru Bench's dismissal of her Section 7 IBC petition against Chemizol Additives Pvt. Ltd. seeking recovery of Rs. 4.70 Crores. The Appellant, while serving as Director, advanced Rs. 4.10 Crores to the company to meet operational expenses. The borrowing was subsequently ratified in board meetings at 7.5% per annum interest and acknowledged in balance sheets and letters. NCLT dismissed the petition, ruling the advance lacked a prior loan contract and noting the company's solvency. Reversing the order, NCLAT held that loans from directors ratified with interest constitute financial debt under Section 5(8) IBC, and financial solvency cannot preclude CIRP once debt and default are established.

summary.case_title: New Okhla Industrial Development Authority vs. Nilesh Sharma, Resolution Professional of Dream Procon Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: New Okhla Industrial Development Authority (NOIDA) is the Appellant (Lessor/Statutory Authority); Nilesh Sharma is Respondent No. 1 (Resolution Professional of Dream Procon Pvt. Ltd., Corporate Debtor); Victory Ace Social Welfare Society is Respondent No. 2 (Association of 234 Homebuyers/Allottees); M/s Logix City Developers Pvt. Ltd. is the Lessee. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: NOIDA leased 1,00,080.98 sq. mtrs. at Plot No. GH-02, Sector 143, Noida to Logix on 08.06.2011 for 90 years for a premium of Rs. 235.69 Crores. On 08.03.2013, Logix entered into a Joint Development Agreement (JDA) with the Corporate Debtor, assigning development and marketing rights over 6,00,000 sq. ft. FSI for a Group Housing Project named 'Victory Ace', in exchange for Rs. 70.04 Crores security deposit and proportionate lease premium/rent liabilities. Logix executed a GPA on 23.10.2013 in favour of the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor defaulted on its obligations, leading to admission under CIRP. Project 'Victory Ace' was 80% constructed for over 500 homebuyers. CoC approved a resolution plan submitted by Respondent No. 2 with a 90% majority on 07.05.2021, allocating Rs. 10 Crores toward NOIDA's proportionate lease dues. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Lease Deed executed 08.06.2011; JDA executed 08.03.2013; Building plan approval granted by NOIDA on 08.01.2014; UPRERA registration granted 18.03.2019; Section 7 CIRP initiated against Corporate Debtor on 06.09.2019; RP representation to NOIDA sent 23.10.2020; NOIDA filed IA 5050/2020 on 12.11.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Registered Lease Deed dated 08.06.2011; JDA dated 08.03.2013 and GPA dated 23.10.2013; NOIDA's written building plan approval dated 08.01.2014 explicitly naming 'Victory Ace'; UPRERA certificate dated 18.03.2019; accepted payment of lease premiums by NOIDA without invoking lease cancellation under Clause 12 for 7 years. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In CIRP, Respondent No. 2 filed IA 4538 of 2020 seeking NOIDA's participation. NOIDA filed IA 5050 of 2020 seeking to exclude the project land from the Corporate Debtor's asset pool, arguing the JDA was non-est. On 02.03.2021, NCLT New Delhi Bench III allowed IA 4538/2020 directing NOIDA to lodge its claim and participate in CIRP, and dismissed IA 5050/2020. NOIDA appealed to NCLAT.
summary.legal_issues: 1. Whether development rights accrued under an unregistered Joint Development Agreement constitute 'property' and an asset of the Corporate Debtor under Section 3(27) and Section 18(1)(f) of the IBC protected from alienation under Section 14(1)(d). 2. Whether a statutory land authority (NOIDA) that granted building plan approvals, accepted lease payments, and took no steps to cancel the underlying lease for seven years can challenge the validity of a JDA during CIRP to exclude the project land to the detriment of homebuyers.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Development rights acquired by a developer under a Joint Development Agreement constitute proprietary rights and 'property' within the meaning of Section 3(27) of the IBC. Consequently, an Interim Resolution Professional or Resolution Professional is statutorily mandated under Section 18(1)(f) to take control and custody of such rights as assets of the corporate debtor. Furthermore, where a statutory authority tacitly assents to project construction, approves building plans, and accepts lease dues over several years without invoking contractual forfeiture clauses, it is estopped from treating the JDA as void during insolvency proceedings. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Applying Rajendra K. Bhutta v. MHADA, Section 14(1)(d) applies to actual physical occupation under development agreements. Under Section 18(1)(f) and Section 3(27), property includes every description of interest, present or future, vested or contingent. The Adjudicating and Appellate Authorities lack equity jurisdiction under Section 61(3) to derail a CoC-approved resolution plan balancing homebuyer interests (Ebix Singapore, Pratap Technocrats). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Documentary proof establishing statutory building plan approvals from NOIDA, registration with UPRERA, and uninterrupted 80% construction over seven years disproved NOIDA's claim of having no knowledge of the development. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The project's development rights were valid assets of the Corporate Debtor; NOIDA was rightly directed to submit its claims and participate in CIRP.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 288 of 2021 is dismissed. The impugned common order dated 02.03.2021 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench III in IAs 4538 and 5050 of 2020 is affirmed. No order as to costs.
summary.summary: Appellant New Okhla Industrial Development Authority (NOIDA) challenged the NCLT New Delhi order dismissing its application to exclude a housing project plot from the asset pool of Corporate Debtor Dream Procon Pvt. Ltd. NOIDA had leased land to M/s Logix, which entered into a Joint Development Agreement (JDA) transferring development rights of 6,00,000 sq. ft. to the Corporate Debtor for the 'Victory Ace' project. NOIDA contended the JDA was non-est as prior permission was not obtained. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that development rights constitute 'property' under Section 3(27) and Section 18(1)(f) IBC. Having sanctioned building plans, accepted lease rentals, and permitted 80% project completion over seven years, NOIDA was estopped from disputing the JDA to the detriment of homebuyers.

summary.case_title: Writer Business Services Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. vs. Ashutosh Agrawala, Resolution Professional for Cox & Kings Ltd.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Writer Business Services Pvt. Ltd. (successor via court-approved demerger to Writer Information Management Services, a division of P.N. Writer & Co. Pvt. Ltd.) is Appellant No. 1; Writer Information Management Services Pvt. Ltd. is Appellant No. 2; Ashutosh Agrawala is the Respondent (Resolution Professional of Cox & Kings Ltd., Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor entered into a Record Management Agreement on 15.01.2007 with Appellant's predecessor to provide document storage, management, and retrieval services with monthly invoicing payable within 15 days. Appellants continued providing record storage during CIRP, but payments ceased after February 2020. Appellants demanded advance payment for additional packing and carton services. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellant filed Form-B claim of Rs. 24,60,525/- for pre-CIRP dues. During CIRP, Corporate Debtor made payments until 31.01.2020 and defaulted on invoices from 01.02.2020 to 30.06.2020. RP claimed Rs. 6.22 Crores in damages for disruption of critical records access. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Agreement executed 15.01.2007; CIRP initiated against Cox & Kings Ltd. on 22.10.2019; RP appointed 10.01.2020; payments stopped after 31.01.2020; RP filed IA 1239/2020 and IA 484/2021 in 2020-2021; Appellant filed IA 1628/2021; NCLT passed impugned order 29.10.2021; liquidation of Corporate Debtor ordered 06.12.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Record Management Agreement dated 15.01.2007; Bombay High Court demerger order dated 23.10.2015; unpaid CIRP invoices from 01.02.2020 onwards; RP correspondence demanding records access and packing work without paying storage invoices; lack of any statutory complaint filed under Section 236 IBC. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP filed IA 1239/2020 seeking directions to Appellants to provide continuous services and documents, and IA 484/2021 seeking refund of post-CIRP payments and Rs. 6.22 Crores damages. Appellant filed IA 1628/2021 seeking payment of unpaid and advance storage charges. On 29.10.2021, NCLT Mumbai Bench Court III directed Appellants to continue services, refund all payments received during CIRP, and imposed a fine of Rs. 20 Lakhs under Section 235A IBC. Appellants appealed to NCLAT.
summary.legal_issues: 1. Whether the Adjudicating Authority possesses jurisdiction under Section 235A of the IBC to directly impose a penal fine on a party in an interlocutory application, or whether offences punishable with fine must be tried by a Special Court under Section 236 of the IBC. 2. Whether record management and retrieval services qualify as 'critical services' under Section 14(2A) of the IBC during the moratorium period. 3. Whether a service provider that continues to provide critical services during CIRP can be ordered to refund fees received for services rendered during the CIRP period.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Section 235A of the IBC is a penal provision prescribing punishment with fine for contravention of the Code where no specific penalty is provided, and constitutes an 'offence' under Section 3(38) of the General Clauses Act, 1897. The Adjudicating Authority lacks jurisdiction to directly impose a penal fine under Section 235A on an application; cognizance and trial of such offences lie exclusively within the jurisdiction of the Special Court under Section 236 upon a formal complaint by the Board or Central Government. Furthermore, a vendor rendering critical services during CIRP cannot be ordered to refund payments received for actual services rendered. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 235A uses the phrase 'punishable with fine' (denoting a criminal sentence for an offence), distinct from civil 'penalty' provisions like Section 65. Under Section 236, all offences under the Code must be tried by Special Courts following criminal procedure to ensure the accused receives an opportunity to answer specific charges. Section 14(2A) protects critical services necessary to run the corporate debtor as a going concern, but does not disentitle service providers from receiving payments for CIRP services. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Absence of a formal complaint by the Central Government or IBBI under Section 236 vitiates the imposition of a criminal fine under Section 235A. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The imposition of the Rs. 20 Lakh fine and the direction to refund CIRP service fees were ultra vires and unsustainable, whereas the classification of record management as critical services was affirmed.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 956 of 2021 is allowed in part. The directions in paragraph 15(B) (directing refund of payments received during CIRP) and paragraph 15(C) (imposing a fine of Rs. 20 Lakhs under Section 235A) of the impugned order dated 29.10.2021 are set aside. The direction in paragraph 15(A) directing continuation of services during CIRP is affirmed. Parties shall bear their own costs.
summary.summary: Appellants Writer Business Services Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. appealed against the NCLT Mumbai Bench order which directed them to provide record management services to Corporate Debtor Cox & Kings Ltd. under Section 14(2A) IBC, refund all payments received for services during CIRP, and pay a fine of Rs. 20 Lakhs under Section 235A. NCLAT partly allowed the appeal, holding that Section 235A is a penal provision for offences and cannot be invoked by the Adjudicating Authority to impose fines in summary proceedings. Under Section 236 IBC, trials for offences punishable with fine lie exclusively before Special Courts on a complaint by IBBI or the Central Government. The refund direction was also set aside, while the classification of record management as critical services was upheld.

summary.case_title: M.K. Resely & Ors. vs. Union Bank of India & Ors.
summary.appeal_number: IA No. 990/2022 in Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 337/2022
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M.K. Resely and 7 others are Appellants/Petitioners (shareholders/guarantors of Corporate Debtor); Union Bank of India (Erattupetta Branch) is Respondent No. 1 (Financial Creditor); Meenachil East Urban Co-operative Bank Ltd. is Respondent No. 2; C.A. Mahalingam Suresh Kumar is Respondent No. 3 (Liquidator of Raihan Healthcare Pvt. Ltd., Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Liquidator in the liquidation process of Raihan Healthcare Pvt. Ltd. filed MA/76/KOB/2020 in IBA/240/KOB/2019 seeking directions to incorporate personal properties of the Appellants into the liquidation estate of the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose in liquidation proceedings where NCLT allowed inclusion of personal assets of promoters into the Corporate Debtor's liquidation estate. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned order passed on 21.01.2022 and uploaded on NCLT website on 25.01.2022; Appellants filed WP No. 2832/2022 before Kerala High Court on 26.01.2022 (dismissed 22.04.2022); Appellants filed Writ Appeal No. 537/2022 (dismissed 22.06.2022 with interim protection extended for two weeks to file NCLAT appeal); two-week deadline expired on 05.07.2022; Appellants e-filed appeal before NCLAT on 06.07.2022 at 22:07 hrs and filed physical papers on 14.07.2022; Supreme Court dismissed SLP (C) No. 12357/2022 on 29.07.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: NCLT order dated 21.01.2022; Kerala High Court Division Bench judgment in WA No. 537/2022 dated 22.06.2022 extending interim stay for two weeks; NCLAT e-portal filing timestamp showing filing on 06.07.2022 at 22:07 hrs. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kochi Bench allowed the Liquidator's application MA/76/KOB/2020 on 21.01.2022. Following dismissal of writ proceedings, Appellants filed Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 337 of 2022 along with IA No. 990 of 2022 seeking exclusion of 147 days under Section 14 of the Limitation Act, 1963. NCLAT excluded the writ litigation period, but evaluated maintainability regarding the subsequent filing.
summary.legal_issues: 1. Whether an appeal filed under Section 61 of the IBC that is lodged one day after the expiry of the specific extension period granted by the High Court can be entertained by the Appellate Tribunal. 2. Whether compliance with the strict statutory limitation framework under Section 61(2) of the IBC is a jurisdictional condition precedent mandating rejection of delayed appeals under Section 3 of the Limitation Act, 1963.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Limitation is an issue of jurisdiction. Under Section 3 of the Limitation Act, 1963, courts and tribunals are barred from entertaining an appeal instituted after the expiration of the prescribed period of limitation, even if limitation is not pleaded as a defense. When a litigant is granted a specific protective window by a constitutional court under Section 14 principles to approach the statutory appellate forum, failure to scrupulously file within that window renders the appeal time-barred and un-entertainable. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(2) of the IBC mandates filing an appeal within 30 days, extendable by no more than 15 days upon sufficient cause; this special statutory limitation period cannot be routinely extended. Applying V. Nagarajan v. SKS Ispat, the strict timelines of the IBC cannot be defeated by liberal procedural interpretations. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Electronic time-stamping on the NCLAT e-filing portal conclusively establishes the date and time of institution. Where the two-week period granted by the High Court expired on 05.07.2022, an e-filing recorded on 06.07.2022 at 22:07 hrs proves a delay of one day beyond the sanctioned period. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal was filed beyond the prescribed period permitted by the High Court, depriving the tribunal of jurisdiction to entertain it; hence, the appeal was rejected.
summary.operative_order: IA No. 990/2022 is disposed of having excluded the 147 days spent in High Court proceedings. Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 337 of 2022 is rejected as time-barred. Connected applications IA/907/2022, IA/758/2022, and IA/759/2022 are closed. No costs.
summary.summary: Appellants M.K. Resely and others filed Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 337 of 2022 challenging an NCLT Kochi Bench order that allowed the Liquidator to include personal properties into Raihan Healthcare Pvt. Ltd.'s liquidation estate. Appellants pursued writ proceedings before the Kerala High Court, which ultimately dismissed their writ appeal on 22.06.2022 while extending interim protection for two weeks to enable an appeal before NCLAT. Although NCLAT permitted exclusion of the 147 days spent before the High Court under Section 14 of the Limitation Act, it noted that the two-week period expired on 05.07.2022. The e-filing portal recorded the appeal as filed on 06.07.2022. Holding that limitation goes to jurisdiction under Section 61 IBC and Section 3 of the Limitation Act, NCLAT rejected the appeal as time-barred.

summary.case_title: Hasan Shafiq vs. CT Technologies ApS & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: B.Y. Agro & Infra Limited is Corporate Debtor; Hasan Shafiq is Suspended Director/Appellant; CT Technologies ApS (Denmark) is Respondent No. 1 (Operational Creditor); Hajali Lal Saini is Respondent No. 2 (IRP)[cite: 21]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Contract executed on 25.03.2012 for design, supply, and installation of PUF panels, PRV, and doors for a fruit/vegetable processing unit in Nagpur for Euros 275,410[cite: 21]. Materials delivered in July 2012; installation finished in April 2013[cite: 21]. Corporate Debtor issued a provisional installation certificate on 02.03.2013[cite: 21]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational Creditor claimed Euros 245,451 (INR 1,91,28,631) plus interest[cite: 21]. Part payments of Euros 5,000 (09.06.2015), Euros 5,000 (28.07.2015), and Euros 19,960 (04.01.2016) were made, totaling Euros 29,960[cite: 21]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Letter acknowledging debt sent 15.06.2013[cite: 21]; repeated payment assurances sent via emails up to 31.10.2017[cite: 21]; legal notice issued 06.11.2017 and replied 02.01.2018[cite: 21, 22]; Section 8 notice issued 26.02.2018 and replied 13.03.2018[cite: 22]; Section 9 petition CP(IB) 4270/MB/C-IV/2018 filed in 2018[cite: 21]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Provisional installation certificate dated 02.03.2013[cite: 21]; written debt acknowledgments dated 15.06.2013, 03.04.2015, 14.07.2015, 09.10.2015, 31.10.2017, and 02.01.2018[cite: 21, 22]; belated allegation of freezer room leakage referencing an unproduced 05.08.2014 email[cite: 22, 23]; failure of Corporate Debtor to file a reply before NCLT[cite: 22, 23]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 9 petition was admitted by NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV on 26.05.2020 after closing Corporate Debtor's right to reply on 15.07.2019[cite: 21, 22]. Suspended Director appealed to NCLAT[cite: 22].
summary.legal_issues: 1. Whether an international arbitration clause providing for dispute resolution under Swiss law bars an Operational Creditor from maintaining an application under Section 9 of the IBC in view of Section 238 of the Code and Section 45 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996[cite: 22]. 2. Whether an isolated communication regarding a defect (leakage) constitutes a plausible pre-existing dispute under Section 9(5)(ii)(d) of the IBC when followed by multiple unconditional acknowledgments of debt and requests for payment extension[cite: 22, 23, 24]. 3. Whether a solvent company with claims of Rs. 50 Crores can resist Section 9 CIRP admission when operational debt and default are established[cite: 22, 24].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 238 of the IBC, the provisions of the Code override any inconsistent terms in contracts or other laws, including Section 45 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996; hence, the existence of an international or domestic arbitration clause does not impede an Adjudicating Authority from admitting an insolvency petition once debt and default are established[cite: 22, 23]. Additionally, a pre-existing dispute must be genuine, supported by evidence, and not a spurious moonshine defense raised to evade admitted liabilities[cite: 23, 24]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 238 confers overriding supremacy to IBC proceedings in rem over private dispute resolution agreements[cite: 22, 23]. Applying Indus Biotech and Macquarie Bank, a foreign operational creditor is entitled to invoke Section 9, and the Adjudicating Authority has no duty to refer parties to foreign arbitration under Section 45 when default is clear[cite: 22, 23]. Under Mobilox Innovations, a dispute raised belatedly without substantiation after successive acknowledgments cannot satisfy Section 9(5)(ii)(d)[cite: 23, 24]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Unconditional admissions of debt in writing across multiple years (2013-2018), accompanied by part payments and absence of formal dispute notices, establish clear default and defeat illusory assertions of pre-existing disputes[cite: 23, 24]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Registered office of Corporate Debtor falls within NCLT jurisdiction, operational debt and default were proved, and the arbitration defense was untenable; hence CIRP admission was valid[cite: 22, 23, 24].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 802 of 2020 is dismissed[cite: 24]. The impugned judgment dated 26.05.2020 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV admitting the Section 9 application is affirmed[cite: 21, 24]. No order as to costs[cite: 24].
summary.summary: Appellant Hasan Shafiq, Suspended Director of B.Y. Agro & Infra Limited, challenged NCLT Mumbai's order admitting a Section 9 application filed by Danish entity CT Technologies ApS for default of Euros 245,451[cite: 21, 22]. The Appellant contended the petition was barred by an international arbitration clause governed by Swiss law, and that an earlier email citing freezer leakage evidenced a pre-existing dispute[cite: 22, 23]. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that under Section 238 IBC, the Code overrides Section 45 of the Arbitration Act, and an arbitration clause cannot oust IBC jurisdiction once default is established[cite: 22, 23]. Furthermore, under Mobilox Innovations, successive written acknowledgments of liability and debt restructuring promises rendered the alleged dispute spurious[cite: 23, 24].

summary.case_title: Srei Multiple Asset Investment Trust vs. IDBI Bank Ltd. & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Srei Multiple Asset Investment Trust (via IGOF scheme) is Appellant (69.8% equity shareholder of Corporate Debtor); Odisha Slurry Pipeline Infrastructure Limited (OSPIL) is Respondent No. 2 (Corporate Debtor); IDBI Bank Ltd. is Respondent No. 1 (Financial Creditor); ArcelorMittal India Private Limited (AMIPL) is Respondent No. 3 (Successful Resolution Applicant); Committee of Creditors of OSPIL is Respondent No. 4; Essar Steel India Ltd. (ESIL) is shareholder (30.2%) and debenture holder[cite: 22, 23]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: OSPIL's primary asset was a slurry pipeline acquired under a Business Transfer Agreement with Essar, which generated revenues via a Right to Use (RTU) Agreement[cite: 22, 23]. Appellant invested Rs. 60 Crores for 60 lakh equity shares[cite: 22]. Essar subscribed to Compulsorily Convertible Debentures (CCDs) of Rs. 50.01 Crores[cite: 22]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: IDBI Bank initiated Section 7 CIRP against OSPIL on 14.05.2019[cite: 22]. AMIPL submitted a resolution plan offering 100% of admitted principal debt to financial creditors, including Rs. 501.01 Crores to ESIL for its CCDs, while allocating NIL to equity shareholders[cite: 23, 24]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated 14.05.2019[cite: 22]; AMIPL declared successful bidder for ESIL in March 2019, but Supreme Court stayed plan implementation until 15.11.2019[cite: 23, 24]; AMIPL submitted OSPIL plan on 30.11.2019[cite: 24]; CoC approved plan unanimously on 06.12.2019[cite: 23, 24]; AMIPL acquired management of ESIL on 16.12.2019[cite: 23, 24]; NCLT Cuttack approved OSPIL plan on 02.03.2020[cite: 22]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Eligibility affidavit dated 29.11.2019 submitted by AMIPL under Section 29A[cite: 22, 23]; minutes of 8th CoC meeting dated 06.12.2019 approving the plan by 100% vote[cite: 23, 24]; shareholding registers confirming AMIPL took control of ESIL on 16.12.2019 after plan approval[cite: 23, 24]; RP's claim collation treating CCDs as financial debt[cite: 24, 25]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP filed CA No. 188 of 2019 in CP No. 352 of 2018 seeking plan approval[cite: 22, 24]. On 02.03.2020, NCLT Cuttack approved AMIPL's resolution plan under Section 31(1)[cite: 22, 24]. Appellant, an equity shareholder who filed no objections before NCLT, appealed to NCLAT[cite: 23, 24].
summary.legal_issues: 1. Whether a Resolution Applicant is disqualified under Section 29A(a) read with Section 29A(j) of the IBC as a connected person to an 'undischarged insolvent' merely because it acquired another corporate entity undergoing CIRP[cite: 23, 24]. 2. Whether the ineligibility under Section 29A attaches to a resolution applicant when the takeover of the connected entity is implemented subsequent to the submission and CoC approval of the resolution plan[cite: 23, 24]. 3. Whether a resolution plan is discriminatory for paying 100% principal to holders of Compulsorily Convertible Debentures (treated as financial debt) while allocating NIL payment to equity shareholders[cite: 23, 25].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The term 'undischarged insolvent' under Section 29A(a) of the IBC applies to natural persons and partnership firms governed by Part III of the Code (via Section 79(3)), and does not apply to a corporate entity undergoing Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process under Part II[cite: 24]. A resolution applicant acquiring a corporate debtor under an approved plan is protected under the second proviso to Section 29A(c) and cannot be barred as an undesirable or connected person[cite: 23, 24, 25]. Furthermore, treating Compulsorily Convertible Debentures as financial debt entitled to payout while providing nil return to equity shareholders does not constitute unlawful discrimination[cite: 25]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 29A(a) read with Section 79(3) restricts undischarged insolvency to individuals/firms adjudged bankrupt[cite: 24]. Section 29A(j) cannot be invoked where the applicant did not exercise control or management of the connected company on the date of plan submission[cite: 24, 25]. Under the IBC, debentures represent debt, not equity, and equity shareholders have no statutory entitlement to payouts under Section 30[cite: 24, 25]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Review of corporate filings established that AMIPL took management of ESIL on 16.12.2019, after submitting the OSPIL plan on 30.11.2019 and after CoC approval on 06.12.2019; hence no connection existed at the material statutory milestone[cite: 23, 24, 25]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: AMIPL was fully eligible under Section 29A, and the approved plan conformed to statutory requirements; appeal was dismissed[cite: 24, 25].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 593 of 2020 is dismissed[cite: 22, 25]. The order dated 02.03.2020 passed by NCLT Cuttack Bench approving the Resolution Plan of Respondent No. 3 is affirmed[cite: 22, 25]. No order as to costs[cite: 25].
summary.summary: Appellant Srei Multiple Asset Investment Trust, a 69.8% shareholder of Corporate Debtor Odisha Slurry Pipeline Infrastructure Limited (OSPIL), challenged NCLT Cuttack's approval of ArcelorMittal India Private Limited's (AMIPL) resolution plan[cite: 22]. Appellant argued AMIPL was disqualified under Section 29A(a) and (j) IBC as a connected person to Essar Steel, an alleged undischarged insolvent shareholder of OSPIL, and that the plan unfairly paid Essar's debentures while giving nil to equity holders[cite: 22, 23]. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that 'undischarged insolvent' under Section 29A(a) applies only to individuals under Part III, not corporate entities[cite: 24]. Furthermore, AMIPL assumed control of Essar only after plan submission and CoC approval[cite: 24, 25]. Payout to debenture holders as financial debt was non-discriminatory[cite: 25].

summary.case_title: Raju Chappakal Pappu & Anr. vs. Arunava Sikdar, Interim Resolution Professional of Dugal Projects Development Company Private Limited & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s Sima Hotels and Resorts Ltd. is Principal Borrower; M/s Dugal Projects Development Company Pvt. Ltd. is Corporate Debtor/Guarantor; Raju Chappakal Pappu and Chitranjan Kumar are Suspended Directors/Appellants; Arunava Sikdar is Respondent No. 1 (IRP); Alchemist Asset Reconstruction Company Pvt. Ltd. (AARC) is Respondent No. 2 (Financial Creditor/Assignee)[cite: 23]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Lenders (IFCI/IDBI/ICICI) extended loans to Principal Borrower under Loan Agreement dated 04.11.1987 to set up a five-star hotel in Goa[cite: 23]. Corporate Debtor executed a deed of guarantee on 06.11.1987 and leased the project land[cite: 23]. Lenders subsequently assigned their debts to AARC[cite: 23]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default occurred on 13.03.1989[cite: 23, 24]. Loans were recalled on 29.11.1989 and guarantee was invoked on 05.01.1990 for Rs. 5,43,94,687/-[cite: 23]. DRT Mumbai decreed the recovery suit (O.A. No. 224/2002) on 06.05.2011 for Rs. 6,04,77,858/- plus 12% interest, issuing recovery certificates on 22.12.2011[cite: 23]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: DRT decree passed 06.05.2011; recovery certificates issued 22.12.2011; Corporate Debtor's appeal before DRAT dismissed as withdrawn on 14.02.2017; parallel Section 7 petition against Principal Borrower (CP-2528/MB/2018) dismissed as time-barred and affirmed by Supreme Court on 07.02.2020; Section 7 petition CP-2527(IB)/MB/2018 against Corporate Debtor filed on 10.07.2018[cite: 23, 24]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: DRT decree dated 06.05.2011 and recovery certificates dated 22.12.2011[cite: 23]; withdrawal order of DRAT dated 14.02.2017 noting defect in appeal numbering[cite: 23, 25]; unpleaded OTS proposals of Principal Borrower dated 11.02.2014 and 04.03.2016[cite: 24]; NCLAT judgment dated 18.12.2019 in CA (AT) Ins. No. 650 of 2019 holding the same debt barred by limitation[cite: 23, 24]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: AARC filed Section 7 petitions against both Principal Borrower and Corporate Guarantor[cite: 23]. On 08.05.2019, NCLT Mumbai dismissed the petition against Principal Borrower but admitted the petition against Corporate Guarantor without addressing limitation objections[cite: 23, 24]. Suspended Directors appealed to NCLAT[cite: 23].
summary.legal_issues: 1. Whether an application under Section 7 of the IBC filed against a corporate guarantor is governed by the three-year limitation period under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963 running from the DRT decree/recovery certificate, or by the 12-year period under Article 136 or Article 62[cite: 24, 25]. 2. Whether the withdrawal of a defective appeal before the Debt Recovery Appellate Tribunal (DRAT) extends limitation or creates a fresh cause of action under Section 18 of the Limitation Act[cite: 24, 25]. 3. Whether an Adjudicating Authority can admit a Section 7 application without determining an objection that the application is barred by limitation under Section 3 of the Limitation Act[cite: 24, 25].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application under Section 7 of the IBC is governed by Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963, which prescribes a three-year limitation period running from the date of default or from the date of a court decree or DRT recovery certificate establishing fresh cause of action under Dena Bank. Article 136 (12-year period for decree execution) and Article 62 (mortgage enforcement) are inapplicable to Section 7 petitions. Furthermore, the withdrawal and dismissal of a defective appeal by an appellate tribunal without adjudication on the merits does not merge the decree or extend the period of limitation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 3(1) of the Limitation Act imposes a mandatory obligation on the Adjudicating Authority to dismiss any application instituted after the expiration of the prescribed period of limitation, irrespective of whether limitation is set up as a defense[cite: 24, 25]. Under Dena Bank v. C. Shivakumar Reddy, a DRT recovery certificate grants a fresh cause of action of three years under Article 137, which cannot be artificially stretched by subsequent voluntary withdrawal of appellate proceedings[cite: 24, 25]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The limitation period flowing from the DRT decree dated 06.05.2011 and recovery certificates dated 22.12.2011 expired in December 2014[cite: 25]. The Section 7 application filed on 10.07.2018 was time-barred on the face of the record[cite: 23, 25]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 7 petition was barred by limitation under Article 137, and the Adjudicating Authority erred in failing to dismiss it under Section 3(1)[cite: 24, 25].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 681 of 2019 is allowed[cite: 25]. The impugned order dated 08.05.2019 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench in CP 2527(IB)/MB/2018 is set aside, and the Section 7 petition is dismissed as barred by limitation[cite: 23, 25]. Parties shall bear their own costs[cite: 25].
summary.summary: Appellants, Suspended Directors of Dugal Projects Development Company Pvt. Ltd., appealed the NCLT Mumbai order admitting a Section 7 IBC application filed by Alchemist Asset Reconstruction Company Pvt. Ltd. (AARC)[cite: 23]. Corporate Debtor had guaranteed financial facilities extended to Sima Hotels and Resorts Ltd. in 1987, which defaulted in 1989 and were decreed by DRT Mumbai on 06.05.2011 with recovery certificates issued on 22.12.2011[cite: 23]. AARC filed Section 7 petitions against both borrower and guarantor in July 2018; the borrower petition was dismissed as time-barred[cite: 23]. Setting aside the admission against the guarantor, NCLAT held that Section 7 petitions are governed by the three-year period under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, not the 12-year execution period[cite: 24, 25]. Withdrawal of a defective DRAT appeal did not extend limitation, rendering the 2018 petition time-barred[cite: 25].

summary.case_title: Abhishek Gupta vs. Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Limited & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Uday Estates Private Limited is Corporate Debtor; Abhishek Gupta is Director/Appellant; Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Limited (ARCIL) is Respondent No. 1 (Assignee/Financial Creditor); Nilesh Sharma is Respondent No. 2 (IRP)[cite: 24]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Bank of Baroda sanctioned Term Loan-I (Rs. 60 Crores, 28.07.2009) and Term Loan-II (Rs. 13 Crores, 08.01.2011) to Corporate Debtor[cite: 24]. Account became NPA on 31.12.2011[cite: 24]. Bank issued Section 13(2) SARFAESI notice on 11.06.2012 for Rs. 79,93,84,596/- and assigned the debt to ARCIL via deed of assignment on 13.03.2013 under Section 5 SARFAESI[cite: 24]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default occurred on 31.12.2011[cite: 24]. Corporate Debtor made a part-payment of Rs. 15 Crores pursuant to DRT directions[cite: 24, 25]. In settlement correspondence dated 11.08.2018, Corporate Debtor admitted dues based on DRT orders charging 11% interest on Rs. 81.60 Crores less Rs. 15 Crores paid[cite: 25]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account declared NPA on 31.12.2011; balance sheet signed on 03.09.2012; balance sheet signed on 04.09.2013; DRT-III judgment rendered 29.04.2016; DRAT dismissed appeal on 29.01.2018; Corporate Debtor sent settlement letters on 03.07.2018 and 11.08.2018; Section 7 petition CP (IB) No. 393/ND/2021 filed on 28.07.2021[cite: 24, 25]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Audited balance sheets for FY 2011-12 and FY 2012-13 acknowledging the loans and assignment; DRT-III final orders dated 29.04.2016 and 27.07.2016; letter dated 03.07.2018 offering floor-wise property sale; letter dated 11.08.2018 admitting crystallized liability under DRT orders marked 'Without Prejudice'[cite: 24, 25]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: ARCIL filed CP (IB) No. 393/ND/2021 under Section 7 IBC before NCLT New Delhi[cite: 24]. Corporate Debtor argued the claim was time-barred and that letters marked 'Without Prejudice' could not be relied upon under Section 23 Evidence Act[cite: 24]. On 15.11.2021, NCLT admitted the petition and initiated CIRP[cite: 24]. Director appealed to NCLAT[cite: 24].
summary.legal_issues: 1. Whether correspondence marked 'Without Prejudice' proposing a debt settlement and admitting liability constitutes an acknowledgment of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963, or is barred from admission under Section 23 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872[cite: 24, 25]. 2. Whether a chain of acknowledgments in balance sheets, DRT recovery judgments, and settlement letters continuously extends the three-year limitation period under Article 137 of the Limitation Act for filing a Section 7 IBC petition[cite: 24, 25].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The inclusion of the phrase 'Without Prejudice' in correspondence containing an admission of liability or settlement proposal does not negate an acknowledgment of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963. Section 23 of the Indian Evidence Act does not bar the use of such a document when it is relied upon directly as the statutory acknowledgment of a debt rather than secondary evidence of negotiation admissions. Successive acknowledgments in balance sheets, decrees of the DRT granting fresh causes of action under Dena Bank, and written settlement proposals serve to continuously extend the period of limitation under Section 18. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Applying ITC Ltd. v. Blue Coast Hotels Ltd., the 'without prejudice' rule has no application when a statement is itself the acknowledgment of an existing, undisputed liability under Section 18(2)(a)[cite: 24, 25]. Under Dena Bank v. C. Shivakumar Reddy, an order or decree of the DRT creates a fresh cause of action of three years to initiate Section 7 CIRP[cite: 24]. An assignee under a valid assignment deed is a 'Financial Creditor' under Section 5(7) of the IBC[cite: 24, 25]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Chronological tracking showed the limitation extended from NPA date (31.12.2011) to 30.12.2014, then via FY 2011-12 balance sheet to 02.09.2015, via FY 2012-13 balance sheet to 03.09.2016, via DRT order (29.04.2016) to 28.04.2019, and via the admission letter dated 11.08.2018 to 10.08.2021[cite: 25]. Section 7 petition filed on 28.07.2021 was well within time[cite: 25]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 7 application was timely and properly initiated by a financial creditor; admission of CIRP was sustained[cite: 25].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1094 of 2021 is dismissed[cite: 24, 25]. The impugned order dated 15.11.2021 passed by NCLT New Delhi admitting CP (IB) No. 393/ND/2021 is affirmed[cite: 24, 25]. No order as to costs[cite: 25].
summary.summary: Appellant Abhishek Gupta, Director of Uday Estates Pvt. Ltd., appealed the NCLT New Delhi order admitting a Section 7 IBC application filed by Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Ltd. (ARCIL)[cite: 24]. ARCIL had acquired Bank of Baroda's term loans that became NPA in 2011[cite: 24]. The Appellant contended the claim was time-barred, asserting that two 2018 settlement letters marked 'Without Prejudice' were protected under Section 23 of the Evidence Act and could not extend limitation[cite: 24, 25]. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT followed the Supreme Court's ruling in ITC Ltd. v. Blue Coast Hotels, holding that the words 'Without Prejudice' do not negate debt admissions under Section 18 of the Limitation Act[cite: 25]. The chain of acknowledgments across balance sheets, DRT judgments, and settlement letters kept the debt within limitation[cite: 25].

summary.case_title: Sun Pharmaceutical Industries Limited & Anr. vs. Sumit Binani, Liquidator of Gujarat NRE Coke Limited & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Gujarat NRE Coke Ltd. is Corporate Debtor (in liquidation); Sumit Binani is Respondent No. 1 (Liquidator); State Bank of India represents Respondent No. 2 (Monitoring Committee/Creditors); Sun Pharmaceutical Industries Limited is Appellant No. 1; Unimed Technologies Limited is Appellant No. 2[cite: 25]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Under a Master Restructuring Agreement (MRA) dated 18.09.2014 and supplemental MRA dated 02.03.2015, SBI was authorized by the Joint Lenders Forum (JLF) to sell non-core windmill assets of the Corporate Debtor by private treaty[cite: 25]. Appellants were declared successful bidders for 62 windmills for Rs. 180 Crores (Rs. 154 Crores and Rs. 26 Crores respectively)[cite: 25]. Appellants paid 25% advance (Rs. 45 Crores) into a No-Lien Account and furnished bank guarantees for the balance 75% (Rs. 135 Crores)[cite: 25]. Agreements for sale executed 01.04.2017[cite: 25]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor was admitted to Section 10 CIRP on 07.04.2017[cite: 25]. On 22.08.2017, NCLT allowed CA (IB) No. 326/KB/2017 permitting completion of the windmill sale outside CIRP[cite: 25]. Appellants attempted to cancel the deal via email dated 18.08.2017 and filed Civil Suit No. 39 of 2019 in Calcutta High Court seeking refund of advances and injunction against bank guarantees[cite: 25]. The High Court Division Bench permitted SBI to invoke the bank guarantees, yielding the entire Rs. 180 Crores into SBI's account[cite: 25]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Sale agreement 01.04.2017; CIRP admitted 07.04.2017; NCLT approved sale outside CIRP 22.08.2017; liquidation ordered 11.01.2018; High Court Division Bench allowed bank guarantee encashment 04.09.2019; Liquidator filed IA No. 1001/KB/2020 in 2020; NCLT passed order 18.03.2021 and corrigendum 23.03.2021[cite: 25]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: MRA dated 02.03.2015; LOI dated 07.10.2016; Sale Agreement dated 01.04.2017; NCLT order dated 22.08.2017; Calcutta High Court Division Bench judgment dated 04.09.2019 holding issues of contractual breach, frustrative termination, and title sub-judice in the civil suit; deposit of entire Rs. 180 Crores in SBI lien account[cite: 25]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Liquidator filed IA (IB) No. 1001/KB/2020 seeking to exclude the windmill assets from the liquidation estate and seek leave to intervene in the civil suit[cite: 25]. On 18.03.2021, NCLT Kolkata Bench permitted exclusion of the windmill assets from the liquidation estate and allowed the Liquidator to intervene, while rejecting distribution of proceeds[cite: 25]. A corrigendum dated 23.03.2021 removed a sentence regarding sale proceeds distribution[cite: 25]. Appellants appealed to NCLAT[cite: 25].
summary.legal_issues: 1. Whether the Adjudicating Authority has jurisdiction to exclude assets from the liquidation estate under Section 36(4)(a) and (e) of the IBC when their ownership, transfer of title, and underlying pre-CIRP contractual validity are sub-judice before a competent civil court[cite: 25]. 2. Whether the Adjudicating Authority has authority to permit the Liquidator to intervene and represent the Corporate Debtor in a pending civil suit concerning assets tied to the debtor[cite: 25]. 3. Whether rectifying an accidental slip or ministerial observation in an order under Rule 154 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 constitutes an impermissible review of an order[cite: 25].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where the ownership and passage of title of assets are the subject matter of an active pre-CIRP contractual dispute pending adjudication before a competent civil court, such assets fall within the statutory exclusions under Section 36(4) of the IBC and may be kept outside the liquidation estate to avoid complicating the liquidation of the corporate debtor as a going concern. An Adjudicating Authority has the jurisdiction to permit a liquidator to intervene in pending civil proceedings to protect the corporate debtor's interests. Rectification of an inadvertent clerical observation under Rule 154 of the NCLT Rules does not constitute an unlawful review of a judgment. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 36(4)(a) and (e) of the IBC, assets owned by third parties or assets subject to set-off and mutual commercial dealings do not form part of the liquidation estate. Under Tata Consultancy Services v. Vishal Ghisulal Jain, NCLT lacks jurisdiction under Section 60(5)(c) to determine pre-CIRP contractual disputes arising aliunde the insolvency. Under Rule 154 of the NCLT Rules, 2016, tribunals possess inherent power to correct accidental slips or omissions. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Appellants' own counter-affidavits conceded that title over the windmill assets was sub-judice in Civil Suit No. 39 of 2019 before the Calcutta High Court and expressed no objection to keeping the assets outside the liquidation process. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The order excluding the disputed windmills from the liquidation estate and allowing the Liquidator to apply for impleadment was lawful, and the corrigendum under Rule 154 was valid[cite: 25].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 334 of 2021 is dismissed[cite: 25]. The impugned orders dated 18.03.2021 and corrigendum dated 23.03.2021 passed by NCLT Kolkata Bench in IA (IB) No. 1001/KB/2020 are affirmed[cite: 25]. No order as to costs[cite: 25].
summary.summary: Appellants Sun Pharmaceutical Industries Ltd. and Unimed Technologies Ltd. appealed against NCLT Kolkata Bench's order permitting the Liquidator of Gujarat NRE Coke Ltd. to keep windmill assets outside the liquidation estate and intervene in a pending civil suit[cite: 25]. Prior to CIRP, Appellants agreed to purchase 62 windmills for Rs. 180 Crores, paying 25% advance with the balance secured by bank guarantees[cite: 25]. Post-moratorium, Appellants sought to terminate the transaction and filed a civil suit in the Calcutta High Court for refund, where the bank guarantees were subsequently encashed by SBI[cite: 25]. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that since passage of title and contractual validity were sub-judice before the High Court, the assets were properly excluded from the liquidation estate under Section 36(4) IBC[cite: 25]. The corrigendum rectifying an accidental slip under Rule 154 was also valid[cite: 25].

summary.case_title: The Registrar of Companies, Kerala vs Bhagyodayam Company & 12 Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is the Registrar of Companies, Kerala, the 1st Respondent is M/s Bhagyodayam Company (a charitable company with 57 members), and Respondents 2 to 12 include members, directors, and the court-appointed administrator. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The company was incorporated for charitable purposes, holding financial statements up to March 31, 2017, with a net worth of Rs. 1,23,87,566.43 and turnover of Rs. 15,49,421/-. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Allegations involved statutory non-compliances, financial irregularities, and non-cooperation by former management with the administrator. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The administrator filed an interim application leading to the NCLT order dated March 11, 2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: A preliminary audit report by a Chartered Accountant listed numerous financial irregularities and diversion of funds. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Kochi Bench admitted IA No. 29/KOB/2020 on March 11, 2020, directing an SFIO investigation, which the ROC appealed against.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the Registrar of Companies is a competent aggrieved person to challenge an order directing SFIO investigation under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013, and whether the NCLT can directly order an SFIO investigation without Central Government sanction.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Only a person who has suffered a direct legal grievance qualifies as an 'aggrieved person' under Section 421(1) of the Companies Act, 2013. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 212 mandates that SFIO investigations are initiated at the instance and opinion of the Central Government, not straightway by the Adjudicating Authority. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The appellant ROC failed to establish a direct legal injury conferring standing, as the Central Government / SFIO is the primary competent authority. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal filed by the Registrar of Companies is not maintainable in law because the ROC is not an aggrieved person for an SFIO investigation order, leaving liberty to the Central Government to challenge it.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT)(CH) No. 11/2022 is dismissed with no orders as to costs, clarifying that the dismissal does not preclude the Central Government or SFIO from challenging the impugned order before a competent forum.
summary.summary: This appeal was filed by the Registrar of Companies, Kerala, assailing an NCLT Kochi Bench order dated March 11, 2020, which directed a Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO) probe into Bhagyodayam Company. The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal evaluated whether the ROC possessed legal standing as an aggrieved person under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013. The Appellate Tribunal held that the Central Government, acting through the SFIO, is the proper authority to feel aggrieved by such investigation directives, making the ROC's appeal non-maintainable. Consequently, the appeal was dismissed, with explicit clarification preserving the Central Government's right to challenge the order independently.

summary.case_title: Tejas Khandhar vs Bank of Baroda
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Tejas Khandhar (suspended director of the Corporate Debtor) and the Respondent is Bank of Baroda (Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Bank of Baroda extended various term loans totaling Rs. 9,91,00,000/- to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The loan account was declared NPA on September 22, 2013, with a total default amount exceeding Rupees One Lakh. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: A loan recall notice under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act was issued on October 8, 2013, demanding Rs. 6,11,42,097/-. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: One-Time Settlement (OTS) proposals were submitted by the Corporate Debtor on August 1, 2016, and March 7, 2018, which were accepted by the Bank. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Financial Creditor filed a Section 7 application on July 11, 2019, which the NCLT Mumbai Bench admitted on January 10, 2020.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the Section 7 application filed by the Financial Creditor was barred by limitation, and whether subsequent One-Time Settlement proposals constitute an acknowledgement of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An offer of One-Time Settlement made within the limitation period constitutes a valid acknowledgement of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, extending the limitation period by a fresh three years. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 triggers upon default of debt, and successive acknowledgements in writing renew the limitation period under Section 18 for initiating insolvency proceedings. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Documented OTS proposals signed by the debtor clearly admit liability to pay, satisfying Section 18 requirements. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT correctly admitted the Section 7 application because the OTS proposals revived the limitation period prior to its expiration.
summary.operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no order as to costs, confirming the admission of the Section 7 application and the continuation of the corporate insolvency resolution process.
summary.summary: This appeal challenged an NCLT Mumbai order admitting a Section 7 application filed by Bank of Baroda against the Corporate Debtor. The suspended director argued that the application was barred by limitation since the default date and NPA classification occurred in 2013, while the application was filed in 2019. The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal examined subsequent One-Time Settlement proposals made by the corporate debtor in 2016 and 2018. Applying Supreme Court precedents such as Dena Bank v. C. Shivkumar Reddy, the Appellate Tribunal held that the OTS proposals operated as valid acknowledgements of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, successfully extending the limitation period. Consequently, the appeal was dismissed.

summary.case_title: Deputy Commissioner State Taxes & Excise vs Sh. Sanjay Gupta Liquidator
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is the Deputy Commissioner of State Taxes & Excise, Himachal Pradesh, and the Respondent is Sh. Sanjay Gupta, Liquidator of M/s Case Cold Roll Forming Limited (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Corporate Debtor manufactured telecom towers and incurred pending tax assessments under the HP VAT Act, 2005, and CST Act, 1956. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: A tax demand of Rs. 12,27,77,844/- was levied against the Corporate Debtor on April 25, 2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP was admitted on December 11, 2018, assessment was finalized on April 25, 2019, and liquidation was ordered on November 5, 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Assessment orders and tax demand notices were issued post-CIRP admission, followed by the creation of a statutory first charge lien on property on May 14, 2019. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Principal Bench vacated the tax lien via order dated October 1, 2020, prompting the State tax authorities to appeal.
summary.legal_issues: Whether statutory first charge dues owed to the State under state VAT enactments override provisions of the IBC, and whether the NCLT erred in vacating the tax lien.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Statutory dues owed to the State and government authorities under state tax enactments constitute secured debt, creating a first charge that ranks equally under Section 53 of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 48 of the GVAT Act / Section 26 of the HP VAT Act are not inconsistent with Section 53 of the IBC, as the State qualifies as a secured creditor by operation of law. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Assessment orders creating statutory charges establish the government as a secured creditor entitled to priority distribution under Section 53. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Following the Supreme Court ruling in State Tax Officer v. Rainbow Papers Limited, the NCLT incorrectly set aside the tax demand and vacated the lien.
summary.operative_order: The appeal is allowed, the impugned order dated October 1, 2020 passed by the Adjudicating Authority is set aside, and the Adjudicating Authority is directed to proceed in accordance with law.
summary.summary: This appeal was filed by the Deputy Commissioner of State Taxes & Excise, Himachal Pradesh, against an NCLT Principal Bench order that had set aside a tax demand assessment and vacated a statutory lien on the corporate debtor's property. The State authorities contended they held a statutory first charge under Section 26 of the HP VAT Act, 2005. The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal noted that the Adjudicating Authority failed to consider the Supreme Court's ruling in State Tax Officer v. Rainbow Papers Limited. The Appellate Tribunal held that government authorities are secured creditors under the IBC with valid statutory claims. Consequently, the appeal was allowed and the impugned order was set aside.

summary.case_title: Central Bank of India vs Himmat Steel Foundry Limited
