summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Central Bank of India (Financial Creditor) and the Respondent is Himmat Steel Foundry Limited (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Financial Creditor extended multiple credit facilities, including overdraft, term loans, and working capital loans to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Accounts were declared NPA on October 1, 1994, with a principal default amount of Rs. 8,68,64,184.29/- and substantial accumulated interest. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: DRT passed a recovery decree in favor of the Bank on April 10, 2000, while the Section 7 application was filed on March 16, 2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: One-Time Settlement proposals and financial statement acknowledgements occurred after the expiration of the original limitation period. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Cuttack Bench dismissed the Section 7 application on February 3, 2022, as barred by time.
summary.legal_issues: Whether a Section 7 application filed decades after an NPA declaration and DRT decree is barred by limitation, and whether subsequent acknowledgements can revive expired limitation.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An acknowledgement of liability under Section 18 of the Limitation Act must occur before the expiration of the prescribed period of limitation to be effective. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: A DRT decree provides a fresh three-year limitation period, after which any subsequent acknowledgement of debt is legally inconsequential for saving limitation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Acknowledgments made in financial statements or OTS proposals after limitation has expired cannot revive the dead claim. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority correctly held that the application filed in 2020, long after the limitation period expired in April 2003, was hopelessly barred by time.
summary.operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no order as to costs, upholding the rejection of the Section 7 application.
summary.summary: This appeal challenged an NCLT Cuttack Bench order that dismissed a Section 7 application filed by Central Bank of India as barred by time. The bank's accounts were declared NPA in 1994, and a DRT recovery decree was obtained on April 10, 2000. The bank argued that subsequent One-Time Settlement proposals and balance sheet entries extended limitation. The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal held that a DRT decree grants a fresh limitation period of three years ending on April 9, 2003. Since all alleged acknowledgements occurred after this date, they could not revive the expired limitation period under Section 18 of the Limitation Act. The appeal was accordingly dismissed.

summary.case_title: Entegra Ltd & Ors vs Shree Maheshwar Hydel Power Corp Ltd & Ors
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Entegra Ltd & Ors, and the Respondents include Shree Maheshwar Hydel Power Corp Ltd and lender financial institutions. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Parallel legal proceedings involved a company petition alleging oppression and mismanagement alongside a financial creditor's petition under Section 7 of the IBC. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Financial defaults by the corporate debtor triggered lender action and loan recall notices issued on January 17, 2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CP No. 175/2017 was filed under Section 241/242 in August 2017, while CP (IB) No. 111/2018 under Section 7 of the IBC was filed on February 16, 2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Record showed multiple hearings, bench re-constitutions, and a split verdict requiring reference to a third member in the IBC proceedings. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT adjourned CP 175/2017 on July 28, 2022, prompting an appeal against the adjournment order.
summary.legal_issues: Whether an appeal lies against a procedural adjournment order passed by the NCLT, and whether proceedings under the IBC take precedence over company petitions.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013 is not maintainable against a simple procedural order of adjournment. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 238 of the IBC provides an overriding effect, requiring the Adjudicating Authority to prioritize and conclude insolvency resolution proceedings. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where multiple parallel proceedings are pending, deferring a company law petition while concluding an advanced IBC matter involves no legal error. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT committed no error in deferring the company petition when the Section 7 IBC matter had reached conclusion and final judgment stage.
summary.operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, affirming the NCLT's procedural adjournment of the company petition.
summary.summary: This appeal was filed under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013, challenging an NCLT order that adjourned a company petition regarding oppression and mismanagement (CP 175/2017). The appellants argued that the NCLT improperly deferred their petition while prioritizing a lender's Section 7 IBC petition. The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal observed that the impugned order was a simple adjournment order and noted that proceedings under the IBC carry overriding statutory priority. Since the Section 7 matter had already concluded its final hearings and awaited judgment, the Appellate Tribunal found no ground to interfere with the adjournment. The appeal was consequently dismissed.

summary.case_title: Steel Strips Wheels Ltd. vs Shri Avil Menezes, Resolution Professional of AMW Autocomponent Ltd. & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Steel Strips Wheels Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant), Respondent No. 1 is Shri Avil Menezes (Resolution Professional), Respondent No. 2 is the Committee of Creditors (CoC), and Respondent No. 3 is Triton (joint resolution applicant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) was initiated against AMW Auto Component Ltd. on September 1, 2020. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant's resolution plan was approved by the CoC with a 98.55% majority voting share on September 21, 2021. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The application for approval of the plan (I.A. No. 692 of 2021) was filed by the RP on September 24, 2021, and remained pending before the Adjudicating Authority. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: On December 13, 2021, Respondent No. 3 submitted a late expression of interest/joint resolution plan, which the CoC initially rejected on December 18, 2021. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent No. 3 filed I.A. No. 43 of 2022, which the NCLT Ahmedabad allowed on January 18, 2022, directing the CoC to consider Respondent No. 3's plan, leading to the current appeal.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority can direct the Committee of Creditors to consider a late, unsolicited resolution plan submitted after the approval of a successful resolution plan and the close of the CIRP period.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a resolution plan is duly approved by the Committee of Creditors and submitted for approval to the Adjudicating Authority, the finality of the process cannot be disturbed by entertaining late or unsolicited bids. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The IBC mandates strict adherence to timelines to prevent commercial uncertainty and value degradation of the corporate debtor. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Adjudicating authorities cannot suo motu direct the CoC to reconsider already approved plans or entertain fresh bids from parties who were not part of the active CIRP. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in entertaining the application of Respondent No. 3 and directing the CoC to consider a new plan after the statutory timeline and CoC approval had concluded.
summary.operative_order: The appeal is allowed, the impugned order dated January 18, 2022 is set aside, and Application I.A. No. 43 of 2022 is rejected with no order as to costs.
summary.summary: This appeal challenged an NCLT Ahmedabad order that directed the Committee of Creditors to consider a late resolution plan submitted by a third party (Respondent No. 3) after the appellant's resolution plan had already been approved by a 98.55% majority vote and filed for judicial approval. The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal held that entertaining unsolicited, late bids after the conclusion of the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process and CoC approval violates the strict timelines and finality mandated by the IBC. Citing Supreme Court precedents such as Ebix Singapore and Essar Steel, the Appellate Tribunal set aside the Adjudicating Authority's order and allowed the appeal.

summary.case_title: IDBI Bank Limited vs Ms. Mamta Binani & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is IDBI Bank (dissenting financial creditor), Respondent No. 1 is Ms. Mamta Binani (Resolution Professional), Respondent No. 2 is Vision India Fund, and Respondent No. 3 is the Committee of Creditors represented by Canara Bank. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP was initiated against Deccan Chronicle Holdings Limited, which had availed credit facilities and executed hypothecation deeds over trademarks. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The total admitted claims of financial creditors amounted to Rs. 8,180.65 Crores, with IDBI holding an admitted claim of Rs. 549,08,19,434/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The resolution plan was approved by the CoC in the 20th meeting on December 10, 2018, and later approved by the Adjudicating Authority on June 3, 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The resolution plan arbitrarily categorized financial creditors into categories A and B and distributed upfront cash disproportionately, allocating only 3.86% to IDBI while granting higher pro-rata shares to other lenders despite IDBI holding exclusive security over trademarks. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: IDBI's application challenging the plan's discrimination was dismissed by the NCLT Hyderabad Bench on May 9, 2019, leading to the current appeal.
summary.legal_issues: Whether a resolution plan can discriminate among similarly situated secured financial creditors in the distribution of resolution funds without a sound principle, and whether an exclusive security holder can be paid less than its pro-rata or priority entitlement.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A resolution plan must provide fair and equitable treatment to creditors of the same class and cannot arbitrarily discriminate between similarly situated secured financial creditors. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(4) and Regulation 38 require that the manner of distribution must take into account the order of priority and value of security interests of secured creditors. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Unsubstantiated categorization and arbitrary allocation of funds that ignore a creditor's exclusive charge over core assets violate the provisions of the IBC. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in dismissing the challenge against a discriminatory resolution plan that failed to respect the priority and value of the dissenting financial creditor's security interest.
summary.operative_order: The appeal is allowed, the impugned order dated May 9, 2019 and the subsequent order dated June 3, 2019 approving the resolution plan are set aside, and the matter is remitted back to the CoC to distribute the resolution amount in conformity with Section 30(4) and Regulation 38.
summary.summary: This appeal was filed by IDBI Bank as a dissenting financial creditor challenging an NCLT Hyderabad order that dismissed its application against an approved resolution plan. IDBI argued that the plan arbitrarily discriminated against it by allocating a disproportionately low share of upfront cash despite its exclusive hypothecation charge over valuable corporate trademarks. The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal evaluated the distribution methodology, found it discriminatory and contrary to amended Section 30(4) and Regulation 38 of the CIRP Regulations, and held that security priority must be respected. Consequently, the Appellate Tribunal set aside both the impugned order and the plan approval order, remanding the matter back to the CoC.

summary.case_title: M/s. Rana Saria Poly Pack Pvt. Ltd. & Simbhaoli Sugars Ltd. vs. Uniworld Sugars Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
summary.appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 422 of 2021 with No. 741 of 2021
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are M/s Rana Saria Poly Pack Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor) and Simbhaoli Sugars Ltd., while respondents include the Resolution Professional, CoC, and M/s NCIRCLE Exim LLP (Successful Resolution Applicant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP was initiated against Uniworld Sugars Pvt. Ltd. following a Section 9 application, with initial registered valuations of liquidation value conducted on May 28, 2018. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Initial valuations estimated liquidation value at approximately Rs. 123.66 crores, whereas a later third valuation obtained on October 8, 2020, arbitrarily lowered it to Rs. 52.69 crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Adjudicating Authority approved the resolution plan via an impugned order dated March 17, 2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The third valuation report, which severely reduced operational creditor payouts to nil, was procured outside the framework of Regulation 35 without a valid basis for significant disparity, and pending recovery applications worth Rs. 85 crores were ignored. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Allahabad Bench approved the resolution plan and summarily disposed of pending avoidance and recovery applications, prompting these appeals.
summary.legal_issues: Whether a third valuation report for liquidation value obtained outside the scope of CIRP Regulations can form the valid basis for a resolution plan, and whether operational creditors can be deprived of minimum payouts based on flawed valuations.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The procurement of a third liquidation valuation report must strictly adhere to the procedure and conditions stipulated under Regulations 27 and 35 of the CIRP Regulations. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(2)(b) mandates that operational creditors receive payments not less than what they would get in liquidation under Section 53, making accurate liquidation valuations critical. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: A drastic, unexplained reduction in liquidation value from a third valuation procured irregularly without proper justification cannot prejudice stakeholder entitlements. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in relying on an irregular third valuation report and approving a resolution plan that bypassed statutory payment protections for operational creditors.
summary.operative_order: The impugned order and resolution plan are set aside to the extent of allocation of payments to stakeholders, with directions for the SRA to revise payments based on a liquidation value of Rs. 123.66 crores within two months, and pending recovery applications (CA 235, 236, 237 of 2018) are ordered to be disposed of.
summary.summary: These cross-appeals challenged an NCLT Allahabad order approving a resolution plan for Uniworld Sugars Pvt. Ltd. The appellants contended that the resolution plan was formulated using a deeply flawed and drastically reduced third liquidation valuation report obtained in violation of CIRP Regulations, which wrongly resulted in nil payouts to operational creditors. The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal agreed, holding that the third valuation must be discarded in favor of the average of the first two valid valuations (Rs. 123.66 crores). The Appellate Tribunal set aside the plan approval regarding payment allocations, directed a revision based on the correct liquidation value, and ordered the swift adjudication of pending recovery applications.

summary.case_title: Amit Wadhwani vs M/s Global Advertisers & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Amit Wadhwani (suspended director and shareholder of Sai Estate Consultants Chembur Pvt. Ltd.), Respondent No. 1 is M/s Global Advertisers (Operational Creditor), and Respondent No. 2 is the Interim Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Operational Creditor provided outdoor billboard and hoarding advertisement services to the Corporate Debtor under various confirmation letters and invoices. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The operational creditor claimed an outstanding principal sum of Rs. 1,98,47,520/- along with interest based on unpaid invoices raised between February 2018 and June 2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: A demand notice under Section 8 was issued on June 12, 2020, followed by the filing of a Section 9 application, which was admitted by the NCLT on August 2, 2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Prior to the Section 8 notice, the corporate debtor repeatedly demanded account reconciliation, noting that invoices bore endorsements like 'received (not checked)', and letters dated February 20, 2020, and March 14, 2020, explicitly disputed the claims. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Mumbai Bench admitted the Section 9 application and initiated CIRP, leading to this appeal by the suspended director.
summary.legal_issues: Whether there was a pre-existing dispute between the parties regarding the reconciliation of accounts and verification of services prior to the issuance of the Section 8 demand notice.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a corporate debtor raises a plausible, pre-existing dispute regarding debt verification and account reconciliation that is not illusory, a Section 9 application under the IBC must be rejected. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9(5)(2)(d) mandates the dismissal of an operational creditor's application if a notice of dispute was received or a pre-existing dispute is evident from correspondence. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Documented exchanges showing requests for reconciliation, unverified invoices bearing 'not checked' endorsements, and unresolved discrepancies establish a genuine pre-existing dispute. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority incorrectly entertained the Section 9 application despite clear documentary evidence of a pre-existing dispute between the operational creditor and the corporate debtor.
summary.operative_order: The appeal is allowed, and the order dated August 2, 2021 passed by the Adjudicating Authority initiating CIRP is set aside, with liberty for the operational creditor to pursue other remedies in accordance with law.
summary.summary: This appeal was filed by a suspended director of Sai Estate Consultants Chembur Pvt. Ltd. against an NCLT Mumbai order admitting a Section 9 application filed by M/s Global Advertisers and initiating CIRP. The appellant argued that there was a genuine pre-existing dispute concerning account reconciliation and unverified invoice amounts, which was raised in correspondence prior to the Section 8 notice. The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal examined the letters and invoice endorsements, confirming that the corporate debtor had consistently demanded reconciliation and verification of services. Applying the principles from Mobilox Innovations, the Appellate Tribunal held that a genuine pre-existing dispute existed. Consequently, the impugned order initiating CIRP was set aside.

summary.case_title: Axis Bank Limited vs Naren Seth & State Bank of India
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Axis Bank Limited (mortgagee/creditor), Respondent No. 1 is Naren Seth (Resolution Professional), and Respondent No. 2 is State Bank of India (Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: State Bank of India extended term loans and credit facilities to Shreem Corporation Limited (Corporate Debtor), secured by equitable mortgages and various agreements. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The corporate debtor's account was classified as a Non-Performing Asset (NPA) on June 28, 2013, with default amounts exceeding Rs. 681.87 crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: SBI issued a SARFAESI notice in July 2013, initiated DRT recovery proceedings in 2014, obtained a Section 14 possession order in March 2017, and filed a Section 7 application on January 22, 2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The corporate debtor acknowledged its debt liability in its balance sheet for the financial year ending March 31, 2015, and later approached the bank with a settlement offer on May 16, 2019. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Mumbai Bench condoned the delay under Section 5 of the Limitation Act and admitted SBI's Section 7 application via order dated September 22, 2021.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the Section 7 application was barred by limitation, and whether the Adjudicating Authority rightly condoned the delay after factoring in debt acknowledgement under Section 18 of the Limitation Act.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An acknowledgement of debt liability in a corporate debtor's balance sheet operates as a valid acknowledgement under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, extending the limitation period. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 238A makes the Limitation Act applicable to IBC proceedings, and courts may condone delays under Section 5 upon establishing sufficient cause and active prosecution of remedies. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Continuous legal actions under the SARFAESI Act and DRT, combined with balance sheet acknowledgements, negate claims of creditor negligence or laches. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority correctly computed the delay as 662 days after accounting for the balance sheet acknowledgement and rightly exercised its discretion to condone it in public interest.
summary.operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no order as to costs, upholding the Adjudicating Authority's order admitting the Section 7 application.
summary.summary: This appeal was filed by Axis Bank Limited, a mortgagee of the corporate debtor, challenging an NCLT Mumbai order that admitted a Section 7 application filed by State Bank of India. Axis Bank contended that the application was barred by limitation and that the delay was incorrectly computed and inadequately explained. The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal noted that the corporate debtor had acknowledged its debt in its balance sheet as of March 31, 2015, which extended the limitation period under Section 18 of the Limitation Act. The Appellate Tribunal also observed that SBI had been actively prosecuting recovery proceedings under the SARFAESI and DRT Acts, thereby showing sufficient cause. Finding no error in the Adjudicating Authority's discretion to condone the delay, the appeal was dismissed.

summary.case_title: Indus Motor Company Private Limited vs. Tp Anilkumar
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants were the original Respondents (including Indus Motor Company Pvt. Ltd. and its majority directors/shareholders), and the Respondents were the original Petitioners (minority shareholders holding 5% shares each, viz., T.P. Anilkumar and others) before the NCLT. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Appellant No. 1 Company operates as a premier automobile dealership for Maruti Suzuki Vehicles, depending heavily on working capital credit facilities from various financial institutions, with a cumulative sanctioned credit limit of Rs. 427.11 Crores as of January 17, 2020. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable, as the underlying proceeding pertains to allegations of oppression and mismanagement rather than a debt default. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: On January 17, 2020, the NCLT Kochi Bench passed an omnibus status quo order; subsequently, the Appellant company held its 245th Board Meeting on February 10, 2021, filed an ECLGS Affidavit on March 3, 2021, and the minority shareholders filed C.A. No. 44 of 2021 shortly thereafter. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellants produced board meeting records showing utilization of the Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme (ECLGS) of the Government of India to reorganize existing credit limits down to Rs. 312 Crores as of February 2, 2021, to restart operations post-lockdown, alongside minutes documenting minority dissension. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The original company petition (CP/02/KOB/2020) was filed alleging oppression and mismanagement, under which the NCLT passed an interim status quo order on January 17, 2020, and subsequently via the impugned order dated June 18, 2021 (CA No. 44/KOB/2021), made the status quo absolute while restricting the company from raising additional debt.
summary.legal_issues: Whether an omnibus interim status quo order can be stretched to prohibit a board-managed company from availing a beneficial government-backed credit restructuring scheme (ECLGS) in the ordinary course of business without explicit statutory restriction.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An interim order of status quo granted without specific qualifications or context leads to ambiguity and injustice; it must not be interpreted in a sweeping manner so as to bring the day-to-day operations and commercial running of a going concern to a grinding halt. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The NCLT's broad phrasing of a status quo order cannot override the core mandate of a company's Board of Directors to manage daily commercial affairs and make business-critical financial decisions in the paramount interest of the company. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The test of whether a status quo order has been violated depends strictly on evaluating whether the disputed action fundamentally alters the structural baseline or constitutes a legitimate reorganization of existing credit limits within pre-existing financial parameters. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appellate tribunal concluded that availing the ECLGS scheme to restructure existing credit lines does not violate a general status quo order, and an adjudicating authority cannot interfere with the commercial and operational day-to-day decisions of a company.
summary.operative_order: The impugned order dated June 18, 2021 passed by the NCLT, Kochi Bench in C.A. No. 44 of 2021, specifically from paragraph 11 third sentence onwards restricting the raising of additional debt, is quashed and set aside, and the appeal is allowed.
summary.summary: Indus Motor Company Private Limited and its directors filed an appeal against the NCLT Kochi Bench's order making an interim status quo order absolute and restraining the company from raising additional debt through the Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme (ECLGS). The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal at Chennai held that the omnibus status quo order could not be interpreted to paralyze the day-to-day business operations and commercial management of a company supporting thousands of employees. Finding that the ECLGS was merely a reorganization of existing credit limits rather than prohibited additional debt, the Appellate Tribunal allowed the appeal and set aside the restrictions placed on the company's financial operations.

summary.case_title: Mr. Abhay Narendra Lodha vs. Bank of Baroda and Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Mr. Abhay Narendra Lodha (Suspended Board Director of the Corporate Debtor, Topworth Urja and Metals Ltd.); Respondent No. 1 is Bank of Baroda; Respondent No. 2 is Topworth Urja and Metals Limited (through Resolution Professional Mr. Alok Kailash Saksena). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Bank of Baroda and consortium lenders extended multiple credit facilities (term loans, working capital, cash credit, and letters of credit) which were restructured via a Master Restructuring Arrangement (MRA) dated 30.03.2015 and a Supplemental Working Capital Consortium Agreement dated 14.05.2015. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total claimed default amount of Rs. 218,14,20,222.95 as of 30.04.2018, with specific facility default dates occurring between September 2015 and January 2016 (e.g., 30.01.2016 for Term Loan I). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Bank issued a recall notice on 01.02.2016 revoking the MRA and demanding Rs. 174.61 crores; froze the account on 23.02.2016; and subsequently filed the Section 7 application on 17.05.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: CIBIL report dated 01.08.2017, CRILC report dated 01.09.2017, entries in bankers' books under the Bankers Books Evidence Act 1891, the recall notice dated 01.02.2016, and the Corporate Debtor's Annual Report for FY 2015-16 acknowledging debt. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The original Section 7 application (C.P. (IB) No. 1807/MB/2018) was filed on 17.05.2018 before the NCLT Mumbai Bench-I, which admitted the application via order dated 12.08.2022, leading to the present appeal.
summary.legal_issues: 1. Whether the date of default for initiating CIRP under Section 7 of the IBC must be reckoned from the date of Non-Performing Asset (NPA) classification or from the actual dates of default under the restructured repayment schedule. 2. Whether the Section 7 application was barred by limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The trigger for initiating Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) by a financial creditor under Section 7 of the IBC is the date of actual 'default' (non-payment of debt when due) and not the date when the account is classified as a Non-Performing Asset (NPA). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 3(12) defines 'default' as non-payment of debt when due and payable, and Section 7 consciously uses 'default' rather than the date of NPA notification; furthermore, Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 applies, ensuring written acknowledgments of liability renew the limitation period. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The existence of financial debt and default can be validated through multiple statutory sources including CIBIL and CRILC reports, bankers' book entries under the Bankers Books Evidence Act 1891, recall notices, and corporate financial statements. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appellate tribunal concluded that the Section 7 application was filed within the limitation period reckoned from the actual dates of default and continuous acknowledgments, affirming the Adjudicating Authority's admission order.
summary.operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no orders as to cost, confirming the Adjudicating Authority's order dated 12.08.2022 admitting the CIRP application.
summary.summary: Mr. Abhay Narendra Lodha, suspended director of Topworth Urja and Metals Ltd., appealed against the NCLT Mumbai Bench order admitting a Section 7 insolvency application filed by Bank of Baroda for defaults exceeding Rs. 218 crores. The Appellant argued that the application was barred by limitation, asserting that limitation should be computed from the date the account was declared NPA (27.03.2015) following the revocation of a Master Restructuring Arrangement. The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal Principal Bench held that the trigger for CIRP under Section 7 is the actual date of default under the repayment terms rather than the NPA classification date, and that financial acknowledgments in annual reports successfully attract Section 18 of the Limitation Act. Finding no legal infirmity, the Tribunal dismissed the appeal.

summary.case_title: Innoventive Ventures Limited vs. Trupal J. Patel (Liquidator of Innoventive Industries Limited) and Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Innoventive Ventures Limited (shareholder/creditor); Respondent No. 1 is Mr. Trupal J. Patel (Liquidator of the Corporate Debtor, Innoventive Industries Limited, succeeding Mr. Dhinal Shah); Respondent No. 2 is Innoventive Americas, Inc. (IAI, wholly-owned subsidiary of the Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 3 is Mr. Chandu Laxman Chavan (Promoter and Shareholder). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Corporate Debtor availed working capital facilities from SBI and RBL in 2013, for which the Appellant provided shares as security; upon invocation and sale of those shares by the banks in 2014, a past liability arose, leading to the execution of a share pledge agreement on 10.06.2014 for 85% shares of Respondent No. 2 against an advance loan of Rs. 2,56,00,000/-, followed by a subsequent share pledge agreement on 25.11.2016 for 100% shares of Respondent No. 2 and other assets to secure Rs. 12,14,86,020/-. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant filed a claim (Form-D) for a principal amount of Rs. 32,14,86,020/- along with interest of Rs. 48,71,938/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP was admitted on 17.01.2017; liquidation was ordered on 08.12.2017; the Appellant invoked the pledge on 04.01.2018 and filed its proof of claim on 05.01.2018; subsequently, the Liquidator filed an avoidance application under Section 43 on 22.03.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The 2016 share pledge agreement lacked board resolutions, statutory registrations, RBI approvals, or lender no-objection certificates, and the purported 2014 agreement surfaced for the first time during the proceedings through a scanned copy without original records. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT, Mumbai Bench) allowed the Liquidator's application (M.A. No. 253 of 2018) on 29.10.2020, declaring the 2016 pledge a preferential transaction under Section 43, and subsequently dismissed the Appellant's recall application (IA No. 2444 of 2020) on 06.01.2021, leading to the present consolidated appeals.
summary.legal_issues: 1. Whether the share pledge agreement dated 25.11.2016 executed by the Corporate Debtor in favor of a related party constitutes a preferential transaction under Section 43 of the IBC. 2. Whether the 2016 pledge was a valid continuation of an alleged 2014 pledge agreement outside the look-back period or created in the ordinary course of business.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A transaction transferring property or an interest thereof to a related party for an antecedent debt within the look-back period satisfies the deeming fiction of a preferential transaction under Section 43 of the IBC, irrespective of commercial intentions or lack of subjective dishonesty. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 43 creates an objective statutory filter distinct from the old 'fraudulent preference' regime under Section 531 of the Companies Act, 1956, where furnishing security to secure past liabilities for related entities outside the ordinary course of business is invalid. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The ordinary course of business exception requires that the transaction fall within the undistinguished common flow of business operations rather than arising from special distress situations, supported by contemporaneous statutory compliance, board approvals, and authentic documentation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appellate tribunal concluded that the 2016 pledge agreement was a preferential transaction favoring a related party for an antecedent debt within the statutory look-back period, thereby upholding the Adjudicating Authority's orders.
summary.operative_order: The appeals (Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 102-104 of 2021) are dismissed, and the impugned orders dated 29.10.2020 and 06.01.2021 passed by the Adjudicating Authority are upheld with no order as to costs.
summary.summary: Innoventive Ventures Limited appealed against two NCLT Mumbai Bench orders that set aside a November 2016 share pledge agreement over the shares of its subsidiary, Innoventive Americas Inc., as a preferential transaction under Section 43 of the IBC. The Appellant contended that the 2016 agreement was merely an extension of an authentic 2014 pledge agreement executed outside the look-back period to support a distressed corporate debtor and keep workers employed. The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal Principal Bench held that the transaction met all statutory elements of a preferential transfer to a related party for an antecedent debt without qualifying as an ordinary course of business transaction. Finding no validity in the belatedly produced 2014 agreement or commercial justification, the Tribunal dismissed the appeals and upheld the avoidance order.

summary.case_title: Small Industries Development Bank of India (SIDBI) vs. Vivek Raheja (Resolution Professional) and Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Small Industries Development Bank of India (SIDBI, a dissenting financial creditor); Respondent No. 1 is Vivek Raheja (Resolution Professional of the Corporate Debtor, M/s. Gupta Exim (India) Pvt. Ltd.); Respondent No. 2 is Punjab National Bank (CoC member); Respondent No. 3 is Lotus Textiles and Vijayant Mittal (Successful Resolution Applicant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Oriental Bank of Commerce initiated a Section 7 insolvency application against the Corporate Debtor, which was admitted on 29.10.2019, during which SIDBI held a security interest (first charge) over two properties of the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Resolution Plan distribution proposed for SIDBI was Rs. 1,65,47,078/- based on its 2.03% voting share, whereas SIDBI claimed entitlement of Rs. 5,64,97,893/- (6.93%) based on the liquidation value of its exclusive security interest. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The revised resolution plan was approved by the CoC with a 97.97% majority via e-voting conducted between 07.08.2021 and 16.08.2021; SIDBI sent objections on 16.08.2021 and subsequently filed I.A. No. 581 of 2021 before the Adjudicating Authority. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Committee of Creditors approved distribution of resolution plan proceeds based on voting shares and admitted claims, which was challenged through SIDBI's application seeking priority distribution matching its security value. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Chandigarh Bench) rejected SIDBI's I.A. No. 581 of 2021 via an order dated 17.03.2022, upholding the CoC's distribution methodology, which led to the filing of the present appeal.
summary.legal_issues: Whether a dissenting financial creditor is entitled to claim distribution of resolution plan proceeds based on the value of its security interest or in accordance with its voting share/admitted debt proportion under Section 30(2)(b) of the IBC.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A dissenting financial creditor under a resolution plan is entitled to receive distribution based on the proportion of its admitted debt/voting share rather than claiming a higher amount referenced to the independent value of its security interest. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(2)(b) and Section 53 of the IBC utilize the concept of 'debts owed to a secured creditor' corresponding to admitted claims in the CIRP, and Section 53 reference is only meant to establish a minimum threshold floor rather than mandate security-wise priority distribution. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in determining the allocation and distribution framework among financial creditors cannot be overridden by individual dissenting creditors demanding quantitative security valuation adjustments. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appellate tribunal concluded that the CoC's decision to distribute resolution plan proceeds in proportion to voting shares does not contravene Section 30(2)(b) of the IBC, thereby affirming the Adjudicating Authority's rejection of the dissenting creditor's application.
summary.operative_order: The appeal (Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 570 of 2022) is dismissed, confirming the Adjudicating Authority's order dated 17.03.2022.
summary.summary: Small Industries Development Bank of India (SIDBI), a dissenting financial creditor of M/s. Gupta Exim (India) Pvt. Ltd., filed an appeal against the NCLT Chandigarh Bench order which rejected its application for priority distribution of resolution plan proceeds. SIDBI argued that it was entitled to receive funds equivalent to the liquidation value of its exclusive security interest rather than its lower voting share proportion (2.03%). The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal Principal Bench held that a dissenting secured creditor cannot demand higher payouts based on security interest values, as distribution under Section 30(2)(b) is governed by admitted debt values and the commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors. Finding no statutory violation, the Tribunal dismissed the appeal.

summary.case_title: Mr. M. Appayya and Ors. vs. Mr. M. Chandra Sekhar Rao and Ors.
summary.appeal_number: TA No. 10 of 2021 (Company Appeal (AT) No. 184 of 2019)
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Mr. M. Appayya, Mrs. M. Mrinalini, Mr. M. Sai Sudhakar, Mrs. M. Srilatha, and another; Respondents include Mr. M. Chandra Sekhar Rao and other family members along with M/s Polygon Refractories Private Limited. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The company is a family-owned unlisted private company engaged in the manufacture of refractories, which experienced working capital deficits and required capital advances from directors/shareholders. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable, as the dispute pertains to corporate governance, oppression, and share allotments rather than financial debt default. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The company held an Extraordinary General Meeting (EOGM) on March 23, 2017, to increase its authorized share capital, followed by board meetings on February 28, 2017, and March 25, 2017, which allotted 30,000 equity shares exclusively to certain family members. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate records demonstrated that notices for the EOGM and AGM meetings were not served on the contesting respondent group, and no letters of offer or proportionate rights were extended to existing shareholders under Section 62. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The contesting respondents filed C.P. No. 217/241/HDB/2018 before the NCLT Hyderabad Bench, which allowed the petition via order dated June 6, 2019, setting aside the EOGM and share allotments, leading to the present appeal.
summary.legal_issues: Whether an exclusive allotment of further equity shares to certain members by excluding other existing shareholders and without issuing formal statutory notices or letters of offer under Section 62 of the Companies Act, 2013 constitutes an act of oppression and mismanagement in a family-owned company.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Even in closely held or family-owned companies structured as quasi-partnerships, mandatory statutory requirements governing the issuance of meeting notices and the pre-emptive offer of further shares to existing members in proportion to their shareholdings cannot be bypassed. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 62 of the Companies Act, 2013 strictly mandates that any further issue of share capital must be offered to existing equity shareholders via a letter of offer in proportion to their holdings unless specific exceptions are met, and failure to do so renders exclusive allotments illegal. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The validity of corporate meetings and share allotments depends on affirmative documentary proof demonstrating service of proper meeting notices and compliance with principles of natural justice and pre-emptive rights. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appellate tribunal concluded that the exclusive allotment of shares without serving statutory notices or offering shares proportionately to all members violated mandatory provisions of law and constituted oppressive conduct against the minority group, thereby affirming the NCLT's order.
summary.operative_order: The appeal (TA No. 10 of 2021 / Company Appeal (AT) No. 184 of 2019) is dismissed with no order as to costs, and the interim order dated July 29, 2019, stands vacated.
summary.summary: Mr. M. Appayya and other appellants challenged the NCLT Hyderabad Bench order dated June 6, 2019, which had set aside an EOGM held on March 23, 2017, and subsequent board resolutions allotting 30,000 equity shares exclusively to the appellant group in M/s Polygon Refractories Private Limited. The Respondents (minority/equal faction) contended that they received no notice of the meetings and were illegally squeezed out through share dilution. The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal at Chennai held that the company failed to comply with mandatory provisions under Section 62 and Section 100 of the Companies Act, 2013, regarding pre-emptive share offers and meeting notices. Emphasizing that law prevails over informal family practices, the Tribunal dismissed the appeal and upheld the cancellation of the preferential share allotments.

summary.case_title: M/s Shiv Shakti Inter Globe Exports P Ltd vs. M/s K.T.C Foods Private Limited
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is M/s Shiv Shakti Inter Globe Exports (P) Ltd. (successful e-auction purchaser); Respondent No. 1 is M/s K.T.C Foods Private Limited (Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 2 is Mr. Anup Kumar Singh (Liquidator). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process was initiated against the Corporate Debtor upon an application by M/s Ashok Kumar & Brother under Section 9 of the IBC; subsequently, due to no resolution plan, liquidation was ordered, and the Liquidator invited expressions of interest for the e-auction of the Corporate Debtor as a going concern under Regulation 32(e) of the Liquidation Process Regulations, 2016. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant successfully bid an amount of Rs. 18,45,86,646/-, representing 100% of the reserve price during the e-auction conducted on 19.11.2019, which was distributed under Section 53 of the IBC covering 13.17% of the admitted debt of the sole financial creditor, Oriental Bank of Commerce. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The application for liquidation was approved; the public announcement for claims was set with a deadline of 30.06.2019; the e-auction was held on 19.11.2019; the sale certificate was issued on 26.11.2019; and an unexpected claim notice of Rs. 81,34,157/- was subsequently issued by Uttar Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam on 18.06.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Liquidator formed the liquidation estate after security interest relinquishment by Oriental Bank of Commerce; valuation reports fixed fair value at Rs. 24.63 Crores and liquidation value at Rs. 18.45 Crores; sale proceeds were distributed under Section 53; and possession of all assets was handed over to the Appellant without inclusion of the belated electricity dues in the sale notice or claims. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Liquidator filed CA No. 1189/2019 in CP(IB) No. 136/Chd/Hry/2018 before the NCLT Chandigarh Bench under Regulation 45(3)(a) for closure of the liquidation process; the Adjudicating Authority partially allowed the application on 18.05.2020 by directing the closure of the liquidation process without dissolution but denying prayers for the extinguishment of past liabilities and waivers from non-compliances, leading to the present appeal.
summary.legal_issues: Whether a successful auction purchaser of a corporate debtor as a going concern during liquidation proceedings is entitled to immunity from past/contingent unpaid liabilities and past non-compliances after the sale proceeds have been distributed in accordance with Section 53 of the IBC.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once the sale proceeds of a corporate debtor sold as a going concern in liquidation are duly distributed in the order of priority under Section 53 of the IBC, no creditor or government entity can claim past unpaid or outstanding dues against the auction purchaser. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The statutory architecture of the IBC aims to ensure that a liquidation purchaser taking over a company as a going concern starts on a 'clean slate' without being burdened by surprise or unsubmitted historical claims. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Claims that were never submitted in the prescribed form during CIRP or the liquidation stage cannot be foisted upon the auction purchaser subsequent to the going concern sale. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appellate tribunal concluded that the purchaser of a corporate debtor as a going concern during liquidation cannot be burdened with past liabilities not mentioned in the sale notice, thereby allowing the appeal and granting the extinguishment of past unpaid liabilities.
summary.operative_order: The appeal is allowed, and the impugned order dated 18.05.2020 passed by the Adjudicating Authority in CA No. 1189 of 2019 is modified to the extent that the prayers for extinguishment of past/remaining unpaid outstanding liabilities including contingent liabilities, prior to the going concern sale, after payment of sale proceeds distributed under Section 53 of the IBC, are granted.
summary.summary: M/s Shiv Shakti Inter Globe Exports (P) Ltd. appealed against the NCLT Chandigarh Bench order which partially allowed the Liquidator's application for closing the liquidation process of M/s K.T.C Foods Private Limited after it was sold as a going concern for Rs. 18.45 crores. While the Adjudicating Authority ordered the closure of the liquidation process without dissolution, it refused to extinguish the corporate debtor's past unpaid liabilities and contingent claims, subsequently resulting in a surprise utility demand notice. The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal held that under the IBC framework, a going concern purchaser in liquidation is entitled to start on a clean slate and cannot be saddled with past liabilities that were not part of the sale notice or submitted during the liquidation process. The Appellate Tribunal allowed the appeal and granted the extinguishment of past unpaid liabilities.

summary.case_title: Hyline Mediconz Private Limited vs. Anandaloke Medical Centre Private Limited
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Hyline Mediconz Private Limited (Operational Creditor); the Respondent is Anandaloke Medical Centre Private Limited (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Appellant rendered services relating to the installation of Modulation Operation Theatre and General Operation Theatre along with the supply of related equipment, raising invoices between 24.07.2018 and 31.03.2019. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The total claimed default amount was Rs. 41,10,166/- (inclusive of principal and interest). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: A demand notice under Section 8 of the IBC was issued on 05.03.2020 and delivered on 11.03.2020, and the application under Section 9 was filed by the Operational Creditor on 18.01.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Invoices showing unpaid dues and delivery proofs of the Section 8 demand notice prior to the enactment of the one crore threshold. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Kolkata Bench) dismissed the Section 9 application via order dated 10.06.2021 on the ground that the claimed amount of Rs. 41,10,166/- fell below the enhanced statutory threshold of Rupees One Crore, leading to the present appeal.
summary.legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 9 of the IBC filed after 24.03.2020 is maintainable for a default amount below Rupees One Crore if the default occurred and the Section 8 demand notice was issued prior to the notification enhancing the threshold limit.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The threshold requirement of Rupees One Crore under Section 4 of the IBC applies prospectively to all applications filed on or after 24.03.2020, irrespective of the date when the default was committed or when the Section 8 demand notice was served. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Part II of the IBC and its applicability depend on the minimum amount of default on the 'initiation date' (the date of filing the application), meaning no right to initiate CIRP exists after 24.03.2020 if the default is less than Rupees One Crore. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The crucial determinant for threshold compliance is the date on which the application to initiate CIRP is formally presented to the Adjudicating Authority. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appellate tribunal concluded that the Section 9 application filed on 18.01.2021 for an amount below Rupees One Crore was barred by the enhanced threshold requirement, thereby affirming the dismissal order.
summary.operative_order: The appeal (Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1036 of 2022) is dismissed, confirming the Adjudicating Authority's order dated 10.06.2021.
summary.summary: Hyline Mediconz Private Limited, an operational creditor, appealed against the NCLT Kolkata Bench order dismissing its Section 9 insolvency application against Anandaloke Medical Centre Private Limited for an unpaid debt of Rs. 41,10,166/-. The Appellant argued that since the default occurred and the Section 8 demand notice was served prior to the Ministry of Corporate Affairs notification dated 24.03.2020 (which raised the default threshold from Rupees One Lakh to Rupees One Crore), the application should be governed by the unamended threshold. The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal Principal Bench held that the enhanced threshold of Rupees One Crore applies to all applications filed on or after 24.03.2020, regardless of the earlier default date. Finding the application non-maintainable, the Tribunal dismissed the appeal.

summary.case_title: Alok Kailash Saksena (Resolution Professional for Associate Décor Limited) vs. Associate Décor Ltd. and Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Alok Kailash Saksena (Resolution Professional of Associate Décor Limited); Respondent No. 5 is Mohammed Enterprises (Tanzania) Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant); Respondents No. 6 to 8 are Swamitva Landmarks and Shankeshwar Landmarks (consortium applicants); Respondents No. 2 to 4 and 9 to 10 are banks and government tax departments. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) was initiated against Associate Décor Limited on 26.10.2018, during which the RP invited Expressions of Interest via Form-G and provided information memoranda and VDR access to prospective resolution applicants. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable, as the appeal involves the approval and consideration of competing resolution plans rather than a debt default computation. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The deadline for submitting resolution plans expired on 07.12.2019; the CIRP 330-day period expired on 16.03.2020; Respondent No. 5's plan was approved by the CoC with 100% voting after e-voting concluded on 06.03.2020; the RP filed I.A. No. 161 of 2020 on 16.03.2020; and the consortium (Respondents No. 6 to 8) submitted a belated plan on 27.05.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Respondents No. 6 to 8 participated in the initial provisional list but backed out on 06.11.2019 citing lack of audited financial statements, whereas Respondent No. 5 successfully submitted and revised its plan, furnishing a Performance Bank Guarantee of Rs. 30 crores. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Bengaluru Bench) disposed of I.A. No. 161 of 2020 via a common order dated 28.05.2021 without considering it on merits, instead directing the CoC to re-consider a belated plan submitted by Respondents No. 6 to 8, which led to the present appeal.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority can bypass a CoC-approved resolution plan and direct the Committee of Creditors to consider a belated resolution plan submitted by applicants who backed out of the CIRP process after the expiry of the statutory timeline.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Adjudicating Authority possesses limited powers of judicial scrutiny under Section 31 of the IBC restricted to Section 30(2) parameters, and cannot trespass upon the commercial wisdom of the CoC or direct re-bidding/consideration of plans from entities who remained outside the CIRP. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Once a resolution plan is approved by the CoC with the requisite statutory majority, it becomes binding and irrevocable, leaving no scope for the Adjudicating Authority to reopen the resolution process or entertain fresh bids. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The outer limit of 330 days under the IBC is paramount, and courts cannot permit entities that failed to participate within the timelines to derail a time-bound resolution process under the guise of asset value maximization. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appellate tribunal concluded that the Adjudicating Authority erred in disposing of I.A. No. 161 of 2020 without merits and directing consideration of a belated plan, thereby setting aside the impugned order and restoring the application for prompt approval.
summary.operative_order: The appeal (Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins.) No. 172 of 2021) is allowed; the impugned common order dated 28.05.2021 in I.A. No. 161 of 2020 is set aside; I.A. No. 161 of 2020 is restored to the file of the Adjudicating Authority with a direction to consider the CoC-approved resolution plan of Respondent No. 5 within 4 weeks; and the interim order dated 03.08.2021 is made absolute.
summary.summary: Alok Kailash Saksena, Resolution Professional of Associate Décor Limited, appealed against a common order passed by the NCLT Bengaluru Bench that disposed of his application for approval of a 100% CoC-approved resolution plan (submitted by Mohammed Enterprises (Tanzania) Ltd.) without deciding it on merits, while instead directing the CoC to consider a belated plan filed by a consortium that had earlier backed out. The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal Chennai Bench held that the Adjudicating Authority exceeded its jurisdiction by circumventing the commercial wisdom of the CoC and attempting to revive a concluded CIRP timeline for non-participating parties. The Appellate Tribunal allowed the appeal, set aside the impugned order, and directed the Adjudicating Authority to approve the successful resolution plan within four weeks.

summary.case_title: PNC Infratech Limited vs. Deepak Maini and Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is PNC Infratech Limited (unsuccessful prospective resolution applicant / H2 bidder); Respondent No. 1 is Deepak Maini (Resolution Professional); Respondent No. 2 is Central Bank of India (sole financial creditor holding 100% CoC voting right); Respondent No. 3 is Shree Metals (Mujbi) Private Limited (Successful Resolution Applicant / H1 bidder). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) was initiated against the Corporate Debtor (Era T&D Ltd.) on 03.12.2018, during which the RP published an Expression of Interest (EoI) and Request for Resolution Plan (RFRP). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The 3rd Respondent's approved resolution plan involved an infusion of Rs. 11.5832 crores to be paid within 12 months, whereas the Appellant submitted a revised bid of Rs. 12.06 crores with 100% upfront payment within 30 days. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The RFRP was issued on 07.03.2019; the Appellant submitted its plan on 27.04.2019 and a revised plan on 30.05.2019; the CoC declared the 3rd Respondent as the highest bidder in its 9th meeting on 26.07.2019; the Appellant sent a further revised plan on 25.07.2019/27.07.2019; and the Adjudicating Authority approved the resolution plan on 02.01.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Evaluation matrix scores awarded by the CoC rated the 3rd Respondent at 58/100 and the Appellant at 56/100, ranking the 3rd Respondent as H1 and the Appellant as H2. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed an application under Section 60(5)(c) of the IBC challenging the CoC's decision, which was dismissed upon the Adjudicating Authority approving the resolution plan on 02.01.2020, leading to the present appeal.
summary.legal_issues: Whether an unsuccessful resolution applicant can challenge the commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors and the scoring under the evaluation matrix when the resolution plan complies with Section 30(2) of the IBC and is approved with 100% voting share.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in evaluating, comparing, and approving a resolution plan is paramount and non-justiciable, and neither the Adjudicating Authority nor the Appellate Tribunal can substitute its own views or interfere with evaluation matrix scoring unless express provisions of law or public interest are violated. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 31(1) of the IBC limits the scope of judicial review by the Adjudicating Authority to verifying compliance with the mandatory requirements set out under Section 30(2) of the Code. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Technical issues regarding the evaluation matrix and scoring parameters fall within the exclusive commercial domain of the CoC and cannot be re-litigated by unsuccessful resolution applicants. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appellate tribunal concluded that the CoC meticulously evaluated the plans and approved the 3rd Respondent's plan in its commercial wisdom with 100% voting without any statutory contravention or material irregularity, thereby affirming the approval order.
summary.operative_order: The appeal (Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 143 of 2020) is dismissed with no order as to costs, and pending applications stand closed.
summary.summary: PNC Infratech Limited, an unsuccessful resolution applicant, appealed against an NCLT Principal Bench order approving the resolution plan submitted by Shree Metals (Mujbi) Private Limited for the Corporate Debtor, Era T&D Ltd. The Appellant contended that its financial bid was higher and offered 100% upfront payment, and argued that errors existed in the evaluation matrix scoring. The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal Principal Bench held that the evaluation matrix and scoring fall within the exclusive commercial domain of the Committee of Creditors, whose commercial wisdom is paramount and non-justiciable under the IBC framework. Finding no statutory contravention or material irregularity, the Tribunal dismissed the appeal.

summary.case_title: Sudip Dutta @ Sudip Bijoy Dutta vs. State Bank of India and Anr.
summary.appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 807 of 2021 and No. 740 of 2022
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Sudip Dutta @ Sudip Bijoy Dutta (personal guarantor and former director of the Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1 is State Bank of India; Respondent No. 2 is Prashant Jain (Resolution Professional). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Appellant executed a Deed of Guarantee on 19.10.2015 to secure credit facilities up to Rs. 50 crores extended by State Bank of India to the Corporate Debtor, M/s Ess Dee Aluminum Limited. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default occurred under the credit facilities, following which a recall notice was issued on 05.03.2018, and insolvency proceedings under Section 7 against the Corporate Debtor were admitted on 14.02.2020. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Appellant acquired Singapore citizenship on 18.06.2018; State Bank of India filed an application under Section 95(1) of the IBC against the Appellant on 01.12.2020; the Adjudicating Authority appointed a Resolution Professional on 03.08.2021; and subsequently admitted the Section 95(1) application on 16.06.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Original Deed of Guarantee dated 19.10.2015 produced before the Adjudicating Authority, alongside records establishing default and the Corporate Debtor's registered office location. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Kolkata Bench) passed orders dated 03.08.2021 (appointing the RP) and 16.06.2022 (admitting the Section 95(1) insolvency application), which were challenged by the Appellant in Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 807 of 2021 and Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 740 of 2022 respectively.
summary.legal_issues: 1. Whether a personal guarantor can escape liability or jurisdiction under the IBC by acquiring foreign citizenship (Singapore) subsequent to executing a Deed of Guarantee. 2. Whether Section 234 and 235 of the IBC restrict the initiation of insolvency proceedings against a personal guarantor who has become a foreign citizen. 3. Whether Section 60(1) confers territorial jurisdiction on the NCLT where the corporate debtor's registered office is located, irrespective of the personal guarantor's current residence or nationality.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A personal guarantor cannot evade financial and legal obligations incurred under a personal guarantee executed in India merely by subsequently acquiring foreign citizenship and residing outside the country. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60(1) of the IBC mandates that insolvency proceedings against a personal guarantor shall be filed before the National Company Law Tribunal having territorial jurisdiction over the corporate debtor's registered office, without requiring the guarantor to be an Indian citizen or residing within India. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Sections 234 and 235 of the IBC apply exclusively to overseas assets or properties situated in foreign countries with reciprocal arrangements, and do not bar domestic insolvency proceedings against guarantors whose assets are not shown to be exclusively overseas. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appellate tribunal concluded that the Appellant remains fully bound by the Deed of Guarantee and that the NCLT Kolkata Bench possessed valid jurisdiction under Section 60(1) to initiate and admit the Section 95 insolvency resolution process, thereby dismissing both appeals.
summary.operative_order: Both Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 807 of 2021 and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 740 of 2022 are dismissed with no orders as to costs.
summary.summary: Sudip Dutta, a personal guarantor and former director of M/s Ess Dee Aluminum Limited, filed two appeals against NCLT Kolkata Bench orders appointing a resolution professional and admitting an insolvency application under Section 95(1) of the IBC filed by State Bank of India. The Appellant contended that he had obtained Singapore citizenship in 2018, making him a foreign national outside the jurisdictional reach of the IBC and necessitating reciprocal agreements under Sections 234 and 235. The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal Principal Bench held that a personal guarantor cannot escape contractual obligations by renouncing Indian citizenship and moving abroad. The Tribunal ruled that territorial jurisdiction under Section 60(1) is determined by the corporate debtor's registered office, making the insolvency proceedings legally valid. Both appeals were dismissed.

summary.case_title: Whispering Towers Flat Owners Welfare Association vs. Abhay Narayan Manudhane, RP of Housing Development and Infrastructure Ltd. & Ors.
summary.appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 896 of 2021 (with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 980 & 1045 of 2021)
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Bank of India is the Financial Creditor; Housing Development and Infrastructure Limited (HDIL) is the Corporate Debtor (a real estate company undertaking multi-storied housing projects); Abhay Narayan Manudhane is the Resolution Professional; Whispering Towers Flat Owners Welfare Association, Majestic Towers Flat Owners Association, and Galaxy Apartment F Wing Welfare Association are associations representing homebuyers/allottees (holding ~10% voting share in the CoC); and Sarang Kumar Wadhawan is the Ex-Promoter/Director. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Homebuyers purchased and financed flats across various multi-storied projects of the Corporate Debtor (such as Whispering Towers, Majestic Towers, and Galaxy Apartments), and credit facilities were provided by financial institutions including Bank of India. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose on financial credit facilities availed by the Corporate Debtor, triggering a Section 7 IBC insolvency application by Bank of India (specific claimed default figures not detailed in judgment). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Section 7 CIRP application was admitted by the Adjudicating Authority on 20.08.2019/29.08.2019; the CIRP timeline with prior extensions expired on 15.09.2021 / 30.09.2021, having exceeded the 330-day statutory mark (~730 days elapsed). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: During the initial CIRP under Form-G, no resolution plans were received for the Corporate Debtor as a single going concern; in its 18th meeting on 08.09.2021, the CoC passed a resolution with requisite voting to divide assets into 8 projects for project-wise resolution and re-run the CIRP; subsequent to this, 25 Expressions of Interest (EOIs) were received for project-wise resolution. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The RP filed I.A. No. 2118 of 2021 in C.P. (IB)-27(MB)/2019 before NCLT Mumbai Bench-III seeking extension of the CIRP period; on 29.09.2021, NCLT rejected the extension application on grounds that over 730 days had elapsed without resolution in sight and the CoC agreed to project-wise resolution merely under pressure from homebuyers.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in rejecting the application for extension of the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) beyond the 330-day limit despite the Committee of Creditors having approved project-wise resolution and receipt of 25 Expressions of Interest.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The primary objective of the IBC is corporate resolution over liquidation, which should remain a remedy of last resort; where the commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors resolves to pursue project-wise resolution and viable interest is demonstrated, reasonable extension beyond 330 days ought to be granted if delay is not solely attributable to litigant fault. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 12 outer timeline of 330 days is directory rather than mandatory in exceptional circumstances where short extensions preserve stakeholder interest and enable resolution instead of forced liquidation (following Essar Steel principles). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Concrete viability and bona fide progress toward resolution, evidenced by the receipt of multiple Expressions of Interest (25 EOIs) following the CoC's commercial decision to divide assets project-wise. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority failed to give due weight to the commercial wisdom of the CoC and the interests of thousands of middle-class homebuyers; therefore, an extension of 90 days is warranted to complete the project-wise resolution process.
summary.operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the impugned order of the Adjudicating Authority dated 29.09.2021 is set aside; I.A. No. 2118 of 2021 in C.P. (IB)-27(MB)/2019 is allowed; an extension of 90 days from the date of the order (04.01.2022) is granted to the RP and CoC to complete the project-wise CIRP; no order as to costs.
summary.summary: Appellants, comprising homebuyers' associations and an ex-promoter of Housing Development and Infrastructure Limited (HDIL), appealed the NCLT Mumbai Bench's dismissal of an application filed by the Resolution Professional seeking an extension of the CIRP period beyond the statutory 330 days. Although no resolution plans were received for HDIL as a whole, the CoC resolved on 08.09.2021 to undertake a project-wise resolution across 8 project verticals, which subsequently drew 25 Expressions of Interest. Relying on Supreme Court precedent prioritizing revival over liquidation, the NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority erred in ignoring the CoC's commercial wisdom and granted a 90-day CIRP extension to conclude project-wise resolution.

summary.case_title: Sumat Kumar Gupta vs. Committee of Creditors of M/s Vallabh Textiles Company Ltd.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sumat Kumar Gupta is the Appellant (erstwhile Resolution Professional); Committee of Creditors of M/s Vallabh Textiles Company Ltd. (through Punjab National Bank, Financial Creditor) is the Respondent; M/s Vallabh Textiles Company Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP was initiated against the Corporate Debtor M/s Vallabh Textiles Company Ltd. under CP(IB) No. 391/Chd/Pb/2018, during which the Appellant was appointed as the Resolution Professional. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose under the credit facilities extended by Punjab National Bank / financial creditors to the Corporate Debtor (quantum and exact date of default not specified in the order). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: On 04.06.2022, the CoC held a meeting and resolved with a 100% majority vote to replace the Appellant as Resolution Professional. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The CoC passed a formal resolution with 100% voting share resolving to replace the RP and propose Mr. Rajiv Khurana as the new RP, obtaining the requisite written consent from the proposed RP in terms of Section 27(2). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Punjab National Bank filed I.A. No. 682 of 2022 in CP(IB) No. 391/Chd/Pb/2018 before NCLT Chandigarh Bench seeking replacement of the RP under Section 27; on 11.07.2022, NCLT allowed the application and appointed Mr. Rajiv Khurana without issuing notice or affording a hearing to the Appellant.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority is required to observe principles of natural justice and afford an opportunity of hearing to the incumbent Resolution Professional before passing an order for their replacement under Section 27 of the IBC, 2016.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The scheme of replacement of an insolvency professional under Section 27 of the IBC is founded upon the confidence of the Committee of Creditors; replacement is complete upon a resolution passed with the requisite statutory majority (66%), and principles of natural justice are impliedly excluded, leaving no scope for an adversarial lis by the outgoing professional. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 27 does not require the CoC to record reasons or grounds for replacement, nor does it mandate the Adjudicating Authority to issue notice or provide an opportunity of being heard to the outgoing Resolution Professional. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Ascertainment of whether the statutory threshold under Section 27(2) was met, namely the passing of a resolution by at least 66% voting share of the CoC along with the written consent of the proposed Resolution Professional. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the CoC resolved by 100% majority to replace the Appellant, the replacement was legally complete and the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in approving it without issuing prior notice or hearing to the Appellant.
summary.operative_order: The appeal is dismissed; the order dated 11.07.2022 passed by NCLT Chandigarh Bench in I.A. No. 682 of 2022 is upheld; no order as to costs.
summary.summary: The Appellant, erstwhile Resolution Professional of M/s Vallabh Textiles Company Ltd., appealed an order of NCLT Chandigarh Bench allowing an application under Section 27 of the IBC filed by Punjab National Bank replacing him with a new RP, contending that the order violated natural justice as no hearing or notice was granted. The NCLAT held that Section 27 does not contemplate any opportunity of hearing to an outgoing RP, as the relationship between the RP and CoC is based on confidence. The decision to replace the RP is complete once approved by a 66% majority vote of the CoC, and the appeal was accordingly dismissed.

summary.case_title: Akshar Plastchem Investment Private Limited vs. Bijay Murmuria, RP of M/s Kitply Industries Ltd. & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Akshar Plastchem Investment Private Limited is the Appellant/unregistered Operational Creditor; Bijay Murmuria is the RP (Respondent No. 1); SREI Multiple Asset Investment Fund is the Successful Resolution Applicant (Respondent No. 2); IDBI Bank Ltd. is the Financial Creditor (Respondent No. 3); and M/s Kitply Industries Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor (Respondent No. 4). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of industrial solvents, dyes, and chemicals (Phenol and Melamine) by the Appellant to the Corporate Debtor between 03.02.2010 and 28.08.2010. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total goods invoiced worth Rs. 1,41,85,730 against which part payment of Rs. 19,99,104 was made, leaving an outstanding default balance of Rs. 1,21,86,626 plus interest. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Two statutory winding up notices were served by the Appellant, followed by Company Petition No. 11 of 2011 before the Gauhati High Court (kept in abeyance on 20.07.2012 due to BIFR proceedings); IDBI Bank filed Section 7 IBC petition admitted on 01.05.2018; IRP published Form-A on 04.05.2018 setting claims deadline as 18.05.2018; CoC approved SREI's Resolution Plan on 22.10.2018; NCLT approved plan on 07.12.2018; Appellant filed I.A. No. 46 of 2020 after withdrawing High Court proceedings on 07.01.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: IRP published Form-A public announcements in Financial Express (English, Kolkata) and The Sentinel (English, Guwahati/Shillong/Itanagar) and Amar Asom (Regional, Guwahati/Jorhat/Lakhimpur), and uploaded it on websites of the Corporate Debtor, IBBI, and stock exchanges; Appellant did not submit a claim during CIRP and filed I.A. 46/2020 twenty months past the claims deadline. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Guwahati Bench admitted IDBI Bank's Section 7 petition on 01.05.2018 and approved the resolution plan on 07.12.2018; Appellant filed I.A. No. 46 of 2020 seeking to recall the approval order or direct payment of Rs. 1,21,86,626; NCLT Guwahati rejected the I.A. on 27.11.2020.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the public announcement made under Section 15 of the IBC read with Regulation 6 of the CIRP Regulations was invalid for not being published in the state where the creditor carried on business, and whether an operational creditor who failed to submit a claim during CIRP can challenge an approved resolution plan.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Regulation 6(2)(b)(i) mandates publication where the corporate debtor's registered office, principal office, and material business operations are located, not everywhere its creditors reside or supply goods; furthermore, once a resolution plan is approved under Section 31(1), all omitted or unfiled claims stand extinguished under the doctrine of clean slate. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 6(2)(b)(i) cannot be expanded to require publication at every location where creditors maintain offices or supply goods; Section 31(1) makes the approved resolution plan final and binding on all stakeholders, extinguishing non-included claims. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Compliance with publication in registered/corporate office regions and areas of operation as verified through newspaper publications and website uploads; strict enforcement of claim submission timelines. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The IRP satisfied all statutory publication requirements; the Appellant, having failed to lodge a claim prior to approval, lacked locus standi to challenge the approved plan, and its claims stood extinguished.
summary.operative_order: The appeal is dismissed; the order of the Adjudicating Authority dated 27.11.2020 rejecting I.A. No. 46 of 2020 is affirmed; no order as to costs.
summary.summary: The Appellant, an operational creditor who supplied chemicals to Corporate Debtor M/s Kitply Industries Ltd. in 2010, challenged the NCLT Guwahati Bench's rejection of its application to set aside an approved resolution plan or secure payment of Rs. 1.21 crores. The Appellant argued that the IRP's public announcement was invalid because it was not published in Maharashtra where the Appellant carried on business. The NCLAT held that Regulation 6 of the CIRP Regulations only requires publication where the corporate debtor has its registered/corporate offices or material operations.
