Because the Appellant failed to file a claim within the stipulated period, all such claims stood extinguished upon plan approval under Section 31(1), and the appeal was dismissed.

summary.case_title: K.L.J. Resources Ltd. & Anr. vs. Rajendra Mulchand Varma & Ors.
summary.appeal_number: IA No. 3303 of 2022 in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 359 of 2020
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: K.L.J Resources Ltd. and K.L.J Plasticizers Ltd. are the Applicants (Creditors/Petitioners); Rajendra Mulchand Varma, Gaurav Vishnu Kumar Gupta, Babulal Mulchand Varma, Kamalkishore Gupta Gokalchand, Rahul Maroo, Mohan Subramanian, M/s Omkar Realtors & Developers Pvt. Ltd., M/s Anatomy Realtors Pvt. Ltd., and M/s Surana Developers (Wadala) LLP are the Respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Commercial lending/debt transaction between the parties that initially culminated in settlement/consent terms before the NCLT. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Breach of consent terms and failure to honour settlement amounts by the Corporate Debtor/Respondents (specific default sums not stated in the IA order). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: On 18.09.2019, NCLT passed an order recording settlement; on 20.01.2020, NCLT passed an order in MA No. 3564/2019 in CP(IB) No. 1084 of 2019; NCLAT disposed of the main appeal on 20.07.2022; IA No. 3303 of 2022 was decided on 11.10.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Following breach of consent terms, the Applicant filed a contempt petition before NCLT rather than an application for revival/restoration; NCLAT's final judgment dated 20.07.2022 observed that filing a contempt petition instead of a fresh Section 7 petition was totally uncalled for and unwarranted as the contempt petition was not maintainable. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In CA (AT) (Ins.) No. 359 of 2020, NCLAT set aside NCLT's order dated 20.01.2020 on 20.07.2022 and made remarks on the non-maintainability of the contempt petition; the Applicant subsequently filed I.A. No. 3303 of 2022 under Rule 11 of NCLAT Rules, 2016 seeking clarification and recall of those specific observations.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the NCLAT possesses the jurisdiction under Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016 to review, recall, or substantively modify observations made in its own final judgment in the absence of an express review provision in the IBC, 2016.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In the absence of an express statutory provision conferring powers of review or recall under the IBC, an appellate tribunal cannot invoke its inherent powers under procedural rules to review, recall, or effect substantive modifications to its conclusive and binding final judgments. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The scheme of IBC provides appellate remedies exclusively under Section 61 (to NCLAT) and Section 62 (to Supreme Court); Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules cannot create a substantive review jurisdiction or bypass statutory appellate remedies. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Distinction between procedural abuse of court process and substantive modification of findings; an application seeking alteration of findings in a final order constitutes an impermissible substantive review. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The tribunal lacks jurisdiction under Rule 11 to alter its final order dated 20.07.2022, and the applicant's remedy lies solely in an appeal before the Supreme Court under Section 62.
summary.operative_order: IA No. 3303 of 2022 in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 359 of 2020 is rejected; no order as to costs.
summary.summary: The Applicants filed an interlocutory application under Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016 seeking clarification and recall of observations made in NCLAT's final judgment dated 20.07.2022, which had noted that a contempt petition filed by the Applicant before the NCLT for breach of consent terms was unwarranted and unmaintainable. The NCLAT held that the IBC contains no statutory provision for review or recall of final orders. Inherent powers under Rule 11 cannot be utilized to alter or modify substantive findings once a judgment has attained finality, leaving the applicant the sole remedy of an appeal before the Supreme Court under Section 62. The application was rejected.

summary.case_title: Manoj Majumder vs. Registrar of Companies, West Bengal & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Manoj Majumder is the Appellant (shareholder of MPH Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd.); Registrar of Companies, West Bengal is Respondent No. 1; MPH Infrastructure Private Limited is Respondent No. 2 (Proforma Respondent, struck-off company). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: MPH Infrastructure Private Limited was incorporated on 26.12.2012 under the Companies Act, 1956 to carry on business in real estate, development, and construction work, with an authorized share capital of Rs. 15,00,000/- and paid-up share capital of Rs. 3,00,000/-. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Complete failure to file statutory annual returns and audited financial statements/balance sheets since incorporation across an eight-year period (FY 2012-13 to FY 2017-18). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Public Notice in Form STK-5 (ROC/WB/STK/2017/1) was issued on 07.04.2017; Notice of Striking Off and Dissolution in Form STK-7 (ROC/WB/STK/2017/2) was issued on 30.06.2017 with effect from 09.06.2017; notification was published in the Official Gazette on 15.07.2017; Appellant discovered the strike-off in March 2019 and filed Appeal No. 729/KB/2019 under Section 252(3) before NCLT Kolkata Bench. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Financial statements for financial years ending 31.03.2013 to 31.03.2018 demonstrated zero revenue from operations since incorporation, no profits earned, and no fixed assets held by the company; no application had been submitted to obtain dormant company status under Section 455. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed Appeal No. 729/KB/2019 before NCLT Kolkata Bench under Section 252(3) seeking restoration of the company's name to the Register of Companies; NCLT Kolkata Bench dismissed the appeal on 15.10.2019 on finding the company was neither carrying on business nor in operation.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the NCLT was justified in refusing to restore the struck-off name of the company under Section 252(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 when the company had failed to file statutory returns since incorporation and demonstrated no operational revenue or fixed assets.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: To warrant an order of restoration of a struck-off company under Section 252 of the Companies Act, 2013, the applicant must satisfy the tribunal that the company was at the time of strike-off carrying on business or in active commercial operation, or that it is otherwise just and equitable to restore it; passive existence without operational revenue or fixed assets is insufficient. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 248 authorizes the Registrar to strike off a company where there is reasonable cause to believe it is not carrying on business or in operation for two consecutive financial years without seeking dormant status under Section 455; restoration under Section 252 requires objective proof of ongoing commercial operations. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Scrutiny of audited financial statements across multiple fiscal years to verify the generation of operational revenue, active profit-earning endeavors, and possession of fixed assets. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The company failed to demonstrate any business operations, revenue generation, or asset creation from its inception in 2012 through 2018; hence, the ROC's strike-off action was valid and no grounds for restoration under Section 252 were established.
summary.operative_order: The appeal is dismissed; the impugned order dated 15.10.2019 passed by the NCLT Kolkata Bench in Appeal No. 729/KB/2019 is affirmed; no order as to costs.
summary.summary: The Appellant, a shareholder of MPH Infrastructure Private Limited, appealed the order of NCLT Kolkata Bench dismissing his application under Section 252(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 seeking restoration of the company's name after it was struck off by the Registrar of Companies, West Bengal. The ROC struck off the entity under Section 248 following non-filing of statutory returns and balance sheets since incorporation in 2012. The NCLAT affirmed the NCLT's finding that financial records revealed zero revenue from operations, no profit generation, and an absence of fixed assets across all operating years, thus justifying the strike-off and dismissal of the restoration plea.

summary.case_title: Nirmal Kumar Agarwal vs. State Bank of India & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Nirmal Kumar Agarwal is the Appellant; State Bank of India is the Financial Creditor (Respondent No. 1); Sungrowth Share and Stocks Limited is the Corporate Guarantor; M/s Adhunik Alloys & Power Limited is the principal Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: State Bank of India extended financial credit facilities to principal borrower M/s Adhunik Alloys & Power Limited, for which Sungrowth Share and Stocks Limited executed a Deed of Guarantee dated 23.09.2011 securing debt up to Rs. 30 Crores. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by the principal borrower in repaying financial debt of Rs. 63,04,53,226/- against total outstanding creditor claims of Rs. 324.73 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP against principal debtor Adhunik Alloys & Power Limited was admitted on 23.08.2017 and its resolution plan was approved on 07.12.2018; Section 7 application against the Corporate Guarantor was filed on 08.06.2018; RBI Certificate of Registration as NBFC (No. B.05.03435 issued 28.03.2001) held by Sungrowth was cancelled prospectively by RBI on 09.07.2018 (communicated on 11.07.2018); NCLT admitted Section 7 on 04.09.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Certificate of Registration No. B.05.03435 issued by RBI under Section 45-IA of RBI Act on 28.03.2001 established that Sungrowth was an operating Non-Banking Financial Institution on the date the Section 7 petition was filed; cancellation took effect only prospectively thereafter. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: State Bank of India filed a Section 7 IBC application against Sungrowth Share and Stocks Limited before NCLT Kolkata Bench; on 04.09.2019, NCLT Kolkata admitted the application and initiated CIRP against the Corporate Guarantor.
summary.legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 7 of the IBC is maintainable against an entity registered as a Non-Banking Financial Company (Financial Service Provider) under the RBI Act on the date of filing of the application, prior to the notification of FSP insolvency rules under Section 227.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An entity registered as a Financial Service Provider by a financial sector regulator on the date an insolvency application is presented is expressly excluded from the definition of a 'corporate person' under Section 3(7) and cannot be treated as a 'corporate debtor' or 'corporate guarantor' amenable to Section 7 CIRP; subsequent cancellation of registration does not retroactively validate a petition instituted without subject-matter jurisdiction. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 3(7) explicitly excludes financial service providers from the definition of 'corporate person'; by extension, Section 3(8) and Section 5A mandate that a corporate debtor or corporate guarantor must be a corporate person, thereby depriving the Adjudicating Authority of jurisdiction over entities holding valid NBFC registration on the date of presentation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification of the legal status and registration certificate granted by the financial sector regulator (RBI) subsisting on the date of institution of the CIRP application. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 7 application filed on 08.06.2018 was non est in law as Sungrowth was a registered NBFC on that date; proceedings conducted without inherent jurisdiction are nullities.
summary.operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the impugned order of NCLT Kolkata Bench dated 04.09.2019 admitting Section 7 against the Corporate Guarantor is set aside as non est; State Bank of India granted liberty to initiate proceedings in accordance with law; no order as to costs.
summary.summary: The Appellant challenged the order of NCLT Kolkata Bench admitting an application under Section 7 of the IBC filed by State Bank of India against Sungrowth Share and Stocks Limited (Corporate Guarantor for M/s Adhunik Alloys & Power Limited). The Appellant contended that on the date the Section 7 application was filed (08.06.2018), Sungrowth held a valid NBFC registration from the Reserve Bank of India, which was cancelled only subsequently on 09.07.2018. The NCLAT held that financial service providers are statutorily excluded from the definition of a corporate person under Section 3(7) of the IBC. Consequently, the Adjudicating Authority lacked subject-matter jurisdiction on the date of filing, rendering the proceedings non est and void ab initio, and the admission order was set aside.

summary.case_title: Ramachandra D. Choudhary, Liquidator of M/s Oasis Tradelink Ltd. vs. Bansal Trading Company & Ors.
summary.appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 810 of 2020 (with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 811, 812 & 815 of 2020)
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Ramachandra D. Choudhary is the Appellant (Liquidator of M/s Oasis Tradelink Ltd.); Bansal Trading Company is Respondent No. 1 (Sundry Debtor); Snehal Patel, Olga Vinchentpaul Menezes, and Rajasekharan Krishnan Nair are Respondents No. 2 to 4 (Suspended Directors of Corporate Debtor M/s Oasis Tradelink Ltd.). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Contract for the supply of goods, namely Crude Edible Oil and Palm Oil, by the Corporate Debtor to Respondent No. 1. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed outstanding debt of Rs. 4,25,90,475/- reflected in the statutory audit of the Corporate Debtor as unpaid sundry debtor dues (specific date of default not stated). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced against the Corporate Debtor on 26.02.2019; liquidation order passed and Liquidator appointed on 04.12.2019; Liquidator filed I.A. No. 319 of 2020 under Section 60(5)(b) before NCLT Ahmedabad Bench; NCLT dismissed the application on 26.06.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Liquidator relied on the statutory audit and ledger accounts showing Rs. 4,25,90,475/- outstanding; the Sundry Debtor raised disputes regarding non-supply and inferior quality of goods resulting in financial losses and claimed amounts were squared off/adjusted, supported by the suspended directors' disclosures. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Liquidator filed I.A. No. 319 of 2020 in C.P. (IB) No. 433 of 2018 under Section 60(5)(b) seeking direction against Bansal Trading Company for recovery of dues; NCLT Ahmedabad Bench Court-I dismissed the application on 26.06.2020 holding it non-maintainable as summary recovery cannot bypass civil proceedings or regular Section 7/9 filings.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the jurisdiction under Section 60(5)(b) of the IBC to pass summary orders for the recovery of disputed commercial debts owed by sundry debtors to a Corporate Debtor in liquidation.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority exercising summary jurisdiction under Section 60(5) of the IBC cannot be utilized as a recovery court to adjudicate disputed commercial contractual claims owed to a corporate debtor; the liquidator must pursue regular civil suits, arbitration, or independent insolvency proceedings rather than short-circuiting judicial fora. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60(5)(c) confers jurisdiction only over disputes arising solely from or related to the insolvency of the corporate debtor; it does not expand to broad contractual disputes with third parties falling under the realm of general civil or commercial law. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where sundry debtors raise bona fide contractual defenses requiring examination of complex evidence (such as non-delivery, substandard goods, or debt adjustment), the claim cannot be resolved summarily under Section 60(5). 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The application filed by the Liquidator under Section 60(5)(b) for debt recovery was not maintainable, and the Liquidator was correctly directed to pursue recovery through appropriate civil or statutory legal remedies.
summary.operative_order: The appeals are dismissed; the impugned orders dated 26.06.2020 passed by NCLT Ahmedabad Bench in I.A. Nos. 319, 318, 316, and 317 of 2020 are affirmed; no order as to costs.
summary.summary: The Liquidator of M/s Oasis Tradelink Ltd. appealed an order of NCLT Ahmedabad Bench dismissing an application filed under Section 60(5)(b) of the IBC seeking recovery of Rs. 4.25 crores from a sundry debtor, Bansal Trading Company. The sundry debtor raised disputes regarding failure to supply goods and loss adjustments. The NCLAT upheld the dismissal, ruling that Section 60(5) cannot be exploited as a summary recovery mechanism for commercial contractual debts owed to the corporate debtor. Relying on Supreme Court precedent in Embassy Property, the Tribunal held that disputed claims require regular trial/evidence in a civil court or appropriate forum, and the liquidator cannot bypass ordinary legal proceedings under the guise of insolvency adjudication.

summary.case_title: Uttar Pradesh Awas Evam Vikas Parishad (UP Housing and Development Board) vs. M/s JNC Construction Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Uttar Pradesh Awas Evam Vikas Parishad is the Appellant (Statutory Authority/Operational Creditor); M/s JNC Construction Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor (Respondent No. 1); Prabhjeet Singh Soni is the Resolution Professional (Respondent No. 2); and M/s Gautam Builders in consortium with M/s Rapid Contracts Pvt. Ltd. is the Successful Resolution Applicant (Respondent No. 3). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Allotment of land for group housing development via Allotment Letters dated 11.04.2008 and 02.12.2009, followed by a Hire-Purchase Agreement dated 14.12.2009 entered into between the Appellant and Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in payment of 21 quarterly installments of Rs. 2,07,83,225/- each, with a total operational debt claimed by the Appellant under Form B of Rs. 124,37,16,022/- (admitted claim of Rs. 123,07,52,746/-, with principal dues of Rs. 17,06,69,446/-). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notices issued on 27.09.2011, 09.01.2012, and 31.12.2012; Section 7 CIRP initiated on 30.05.2019; Appellant filed Form B on 08.08.2019; CoC approved the Resolution Plan by 96.07% majority in its 11th/12th meeting on 17.03.2020; NCLT approved the plan on 04.08.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Hire-Purchase Agreement dated 14.12.2009 created possessory interest in favor of the Corporate Debtor; the Appellant never terminated or cancelled the agreement prior to CIRP initiation; Appellant filed its claim as an Operational Creditor in Form B; Resolution Plan allocated Rs. 12,30,75,276/- (10% of admitted claim) despite liquidation entitlement under Section 53 being NIL. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP filed I.A. No. 2201(PB)/2020 in CP (IB)-272(PB)/2019 under Section 30(6) seeking approval of the Resolution Plan; NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi approved the plan on 04.08.2020.
summary.legal_issues: Whether property held by a corporate debtor under an uncanceled hire-purchase agreement can be included in the resolution plan, and whether an operational creditor whose liquidation value is nil can challenge the commercial wisdom of the CoC for approving a 10% payout on its admitted claim.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in determining haircuts and distribution among classes of creditors is non-justiciable provided statutory requirements under Section 30(2) are satisfied; additionally, possessory rights created under an agreement not terminated through due process prior to CIRP form part of the resolution estate. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Judicial review under Sections 30(2) and 31(1) of the IBC is strictly circumscribed to examining compliance with mandatory minimum statutory payouts and priorities; the adjudicating authority cannot evaluate commercial viability or quantitative fairness. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Confirmation that the claimant filed Form B as an operational creditor and received an amount exceeding the liquidation value entitlement under Section 30(2)(b) read with Section 53. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Hire-Purchase Agreement created possessory rights that remained in force as it was never terminated; the approved plan satisfied all Section 30(2) requisites, and the CoC's business decision to pay 10% of the operational debt is unimpeachable.
summary.operative_order: The appeal is dismissed; the impugned order dated 04.08.2020 passed by NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi in I.A. No. 2201(PB)/2020 is affirmed; no order as to costs.
summary.summary: The Appellant, UP Awas Evam Vikas Parishad, challenged an order of NCLT New Delhi approving a resolution plan for M/s JNC Construction Pvt. Ltd. submitted by Gautam Builders consortium. The Appellant contended that the housing land could not be included in the CIRP pool because the corporate debtor breached the 2009 Hire-Purchase Agreement, and further argued that receiving only a 10% payout on its admitted claim of Rs. 123.07 crores was discriminatory. The NCLAT held that because the agreement was never revoked prior to the insolvency commencement date, possessory rights remained with the debtor. Furthermore, the liquidation entitlement of the Appellant was nil, and the CoC's commercial wisdom regarding haircuts under Section 30(2) is non-justiciable. The appeal was dismissed.

summary.case_title: Rahul Khilnani & Anr. vs. Atul Kumar Jain, RP & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Rahul Khilnani and H&R Enterprises are the Appellants (Operational Creditors); Atul Kumar Jain is the Resolution Professional (Respondent No. 1); Committee of Creditors through M/s SM Finlease is Respondent No. 2 (holding 82% voting rights); M/s Ranjit Fin Trade Pvt. Ltd. is the Successful Resolution Applicant (Respondent No. 3). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of goods/services by the Appellants to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellants claimed total unpaid operational dues amounting to Rs. 51,91,935/- (initial claim of Rs. 11,05,850/- submitted on 14.03.2020). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 18.02.2020; Appellants lodged Form B on 14.03.2020; Appellants issued notices demanding dues and valuation reports on 20.01.2021 and 22.01.2021; CoC unanimously approved the revised Resolution Plan on 17.01.2021; NCLT approved the plan and dismissed Appellants' objections on 08.04.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor's liquidation value was determined at Rs. 308.14 Lakhs; Successful Resolution Applicant offered Rs. 655.21 Lakhs; under Section 53 priority distribution, operational creditors' entitlement was NIL; the plan proposed an ex-gratia payout of 2% of admitted operational claims; no formal operational creditor representative was designated to receive Section 24 notices. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed I.A. No. 641/2021 in CP (IB) No. 2413(ND)/2019 before NCLT New Delhi Bench Court-V objecting to the plan on grounds of non-notice of CoC meetings and discriminatory 2% payout; NCLT dismissed the application on 08.04.2021.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the failure to serve notice of CoC meetings to operational creditors under Section 24(3)(c) invalidates the CIRP proceedings, and whether an approved resolution plan providing a 2% payout to operational creditors is discriminatory when their liquidation value is nil.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 24(4) of the IBC, the absence of an operational creditor's representative does not invalidate CoC proceedings; furthermore, operational creditors have no voting rights, and where their statutory liquidation value is nil, an allocation of nominal recovery does not violate Section 30(2)(b) or taint the CoC's commercial wisdom. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 35 restricts disclosure of fair value and liquidation value exclusively to CoC members under confidentiality undertakings, conferring no statutory right on operational creditors to access such reports; Section 24(4) expressly cures any defect in meeting notices. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Confirmation that the resolution plan value exceeds liquidation value and meets the mandatory minimum distribution required under Section 30(2)(b) read with Section 53 waterfall priorities. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: No prejudice was suffered by the Appellants since their liquidation value was NIL and they possessed no voting rights; the plan satisfied Section 30(2) and the CoC acted within its unassailable commercial wisdom.
summary.operative_order: The appeal is dismissed; the order dated 08.04.2021 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench Court-V in IA No. 641/2021 is affirmed; no order as to costs.
summary.summary: Appellants, operational creditors of the corporate debtor, appealed against an order of NCLT New Delhi Bench dismissing their objections to an approved resolution plan submitted by M/s Ranjit Fin Trade Pvt. Ltd. The Appellants contended that they were denied notices of CoC meetings under Section 24(3)(c), denied access to the liquidation valuation, and subjected to discrimination by receiving only a 2% payout while workmen received 100%. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that Section 24(4) expressly provides that absence of operational creditors does not invalidate CoC proceedings. Moreover, Regulation 35 maintains confidentiality of liquidation values, operational creditors hold no voting rights, and their liquidation entitlement under Section 53 was NIL, rendering the CoC's approval legally compliant and conclusive.

summary.case_title: Raj Singhania, Liquidator of Gontermann-Peipers (India) Ltd. vs. Chinar Steel Segment Centre Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
summary.appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 465 of 2022 (with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 264 of 2022)
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Raj Singhania is the Appellant in CA 465/2022 (Official Liquidator of Gontermann-Peipers India Ltd.); Snaefell Heights LLP is the Appellant in CA 264/2022 (Highest Bidder); Chinar Steel Segment Centre Pvt. Ltd., HR Commercials Pvt. Ltd., JSW Steel Ltd., Rahul Roy Chowdhary, and DTC Projects Pvt. Ltd. are the Respondents (Participating/Prospective Bidders and Employee Representatives); Gontermann-Peipers (India) Limited is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Public e-auction sale of the Corporate Debtor and its assets as a 'going concern' during liquidation proceedings. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose under Section 9 IBC proceedings initiated by Balaji Metals, resulting in CIRP admission on 11.12.2019 and liquidation order on 30.04.2021 (debt quantum not stated). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Auction notice published on 24.08.2021 fixing Reserve Price at Rs. 86 Crores, EMD at Rs. 8.6 Crores, inspection on 07.09.2021, and e-auction on 09.09.2021; corrigendum published on 08.09.2021 extending EMD to 11.09.2021 and auction to 13.09.2021; e-auction conducted on 13.09.2021; NCLT set aside the auction on 02.03.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corrigendum extended bid submission deadlines but failed to provide any fresh dates or opportunity for physical inspection of the Corporate Debtor's assets; during bidding on 13.09.2021, Chinar Steel faced severe internet connectivity issues at Rs. 87.75 Crores; Snaefell Heights LLP placed H1 bid of Rs. 88 Crores; JSW Steel offered Rs. 90 Crores and Chinar Steel offered Rs. 93 Crores upon re-bidding. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Prospective and participating bidders filed I.A. Nos. 830, 848, 962, 963, and 969 of 2021 in C.P. (IB) No. 1542/KB/2018 before NCLT Kolkata Bench seeking cancellation of the auction; NCLT Kolkata Bench set aside the entire e-auction on 02.03.2022 due to material irregularity and ordered a fresh bidding process.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the Liquidator's failure to provide a revised inspection period in a corrigendum extending auction deadlines constitutes a material irregularity that vitiates the public e-auction under the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In public auction sales conducted by a liquidator, offering prospective bidders a reasonable opportunity for physical inspection is an essential prerequisite; issuing an extension corrigendum without granting a corresponding inspection window constitutes a fatal material irregularity that deprives creditors of asset value maximization. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 33 read with Schedule I and Regulation 32A of the Liquidation Process Regulations mandates fair and open competitive bidding designed to achieve maximization of value; compliance with the 90-day/one-year liquidation period under Regulation 32A(4) is directory and cannot supersede procedural fairness. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Establishing whether a procedural omission in auction scheduling caused substantial prejudice to market participation and prevented realization of the highest possible price for the liquidation estate. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The failure to designate an inspection window prevented interested bidders from inspecting the unit and participating effectively, leading to suppressed bidding (Rs. 88 Crores vs subsequent bids exceeding Rs. 93 Crores); the auction was rightly set aside for material irregularity.
summary.operative_order: The appeals are dismissed; the order of NCLT Kolkata Bench dated 02.03.2022 setting aside the e-auction dated 13.09.2021 and directing fresh bidding is affirmed; no order as to costs.
summary.summary: The Liquidator and the successful highest bidder (Snaefell Heights LLP) appealed against an order of NCLT Kolkata Bench setting aside the public e-auction of Gontermann-Peipers (India) Limited held on 13.09.2021. The NCLT had cancelled the sale because the Liquidator's corrigendum extended the EMD and auction dates without fixing fresh inspection dates, coupled with network glitches that prevented higher bids from competing parties like Chinar Steel. The NCLAT affirmed the cancellation, holding that depriving prospective bidders of the right to physical inspection is a serious material irregularity that violates Regulation 33 and Schedule I of the Liquidation Process Regulations, undermining the fundamental IBC objective of asset value maximization.

summary.case_title: Punjab National Bank vs. Animesh Mukhopadhyay, RP of Zenith Finesse (India) Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Punjab National Bank (into which United Bank of India merged) is the Appellant/Financial Creditor; Animesh Mukhopadhyay is the Resolution Professional (Respondent No. 1); Loka Properties Pvt. Ltd. is the Successful Resolution Applicant (Respondent No. 2); State Bank of India is an Intervenor/CoC Member; M/s Zenith Finesse (India) Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor (Corporate Guarantor for M/s Purple Advertising Services Pvt. Ltd.). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities extended by United Bank of India to M/s Purple Advertising Services Pvt. Ltd., secured by a corporate guarantee furnished by M/s Zenith Finesse (India) Pvt. Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by the principal borrower resulting in invocation of corporate guarantee against Corporate Debtor (specific claim value not quantified in the order; acceptance of claim would increase PNB's voting share from 20.56% to 42.96%). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 20.11.2019; 90-day claim period expired on 29.12.2020; PNB filed claim on 08.03.2020; RP rejected claim on 18.03.2021; NCLT condoned delay on 08.04.2021 in I.A. 391/2021; RP requested proof on 10.04.2021; 270-day CIRP period expired on 12.04.2021; PNB submitted proof on 20.04.2021; PNB filed I.A. 1078/2021 on 13.12.2021; NCLT ordered voting on 14.12.2021; CoC approved plan on 24.12.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: RP rejected PNB's claim proof because it was received on 20.04.2021, eight days after the 270-day CIRP period lapsed on 12.04.2021; conversely, the Adjudicating Authority excluded 245 days from CIRP on an application by a prospective resolution applicant while leaving PNB's delay condonation application (I.A. 1078/2021) undecided. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: PNB filed I.A. No. 1078/KB/2021 seeking directions to the RP to verify proof and admit its claim; while pending, NCLT Kolkata Bench passed an order on 14.12.2021 in I.A. Nos. 912 & 988 of 2021 directing CoC to vote on the resolution plan based on its existing composition as of 14.12.2021, effectively freezing PNB's voting share at 20.56%.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in directing the CoC to proceed with voting on a resolution plan while keeping an application for condonation of an 8-day delay in submitting claim verification documents pending, especially after granting a 245-day general CIRP exclusion.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Principles of natural justice and equity require that where an Adjudicating Authority grants extensive exclusions of time to preserve the CIRP, a minor, bona fide delay by a financial creditor in submitting claim verification documents must be condoned so that its voting share and claim are properly accounted for prior to plan finalization. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The statutory timelines under Section 12 and Regulation 12/12A of the CIRP Regulations are designed to facilitate resolution; when substantive time exclusions (245 days) are granted, such extensions must equitably accommodate the verification of legitimate financial debts owed to public sector banks. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Demonstration of due diligence, prior court condonation, and negligible procedural delay (8 days) during an active CIRP extension. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Excluding PNB's corporate guarantee claim while granting time extensions to other parties was arbitrary; the 8-day delay is condoned, and the RP is mandated to verify the claim and adjust the plan accordingly.
summary.operative_order: The appeal is allowed; delay in submission of proof of claim by PNB is condoned; RP directed to verify PNB's proof of claim within 15 days and revise claim if found meritorious; CoC directed to consider the revised claim for payment under the resolution plan and obtain approval; the entire exercise to be completed within 45 days; no order as to costs.
summary.summary: Punjab National Bank appealed an order of NCLT Kolkata Bench directing the CoC to complete voting on a resolution plan without deciding PNB's pending application (I.A. No. 1078/2021) for condonation of an 8-day delay in submitting proof of claim under a corporate guarantee. The RP had refused to verify PNB's documents because they arrived eight days after the 270-day CIRP period, even though NCLT subsequently excluded 245 days from the CIRP. The NCLAT allowed the appeal and condoned the 8-day delay, holding that it was unjust to shut out a public financial creditor's legitimate claim when substantial time exclusions were granted to other participants. The RP was directed to verify PNB's claim within 15 days and revise the resolution plan accordingly within 45 days.

summary.case_title: Ankit Patni vs. State Bank of India & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Ankit Patni is the Appellant (Suspended Director of Corporate Debtor Rohit Ferro Tech Limited); State Bank of India is Respondent No. 1 (Financial Creditor); the Resolution Professional is Respondent No. 2; and Tata Steel Mining Limited is Respondent No. 3 (Successful Resolution Applicant / H-1). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Lending and credit facilities extended by State Bank of India and other consortium financial creditors to Rohit Ferro Tech Limited. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default committed by the Corporate Debtor leading to initiation of Section 7 CIRP (exact quantum of debt and date of default not specified in judgment). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application admitted on 07.02.2020; Form-G published on 10.12.2020 setting EOI deadline as 31.12.2020; provisional list of PRAs issued on 26.12.2020 and updated on 25.01.2021; Tata Steel Mining Limited submitted delayed EOI on 16.03.2021; CoC condoned delay on 18.03.2021 (e-voting concluded 20.03.2021); CoC extended revised plan submissions to 25.03.2021; CoC approved Tata Steel Mining Limited's plan by 100% majority on 01.06.2021; Appellant filed I.A. (IB) No. 644/KB/2021 on 17.07.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Minutes of the 18th CoC meeting (02.03.2021) and 19th CoC meeting (08.03.2021) showed existing resolution plans were deliberated but never put to vote; CoC resolved to condone the delay of Respondent No. 3 to maximize asset value; a prior Scheme of Arrangement under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 was rejected as creditors (except SBI) did not attend and SBI communicated non-tenability via email dated 09.12.2020. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed I.A. (IB) No. 644/KB/2021 in C.P. (IB) No. 1214/KB/2018 before NCLT Kolkata Bench seeking to set aside the CIRP, remove Respondent No. 3, and revive Section 230 proceedings; NCLT Kolkata Bench rejected the application on 25.11.2021.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the Committee of Creditors has the jurisdiction and commercial wisdom to condone the delay in submission of an Expression of Interest and include a prospective resolution applicant after reviewing prior plans, and whether a suspended director disqualified under Section 29A can seek revival of a Section 230 scheme of arrangement during CIRP.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors to condone delays in the submission of Expressions of Interest to maximize asset value is paramount and non-justiciable when done prior to voting on any plan; furthermore, suspended directors ineligible under Section 29A of the IBC cannot seek backdoor entry into company management through Section 230 schemes of arrangement. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 29A read with Section 35(1)(f) applies across the insolvency continuum, barring defaulting promoters and suspended management from proposing compromises or arrangements under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 during ongoing insolvency proceedings. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Review of CoC minutes to verify that prior plans were not yet voted upon or finalized when delay was condoned, and verification of statutory disqualification under Section 29A. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Inclusion of Respondent No. 3 was a lawful exercise of the CoC's commercial wisdom aimed at value maximization, and the Appellant as an ineligible suspended director had no right to stall CIRP or revive an unapproved Section 230 compromise scheme.
summary.operative_order: The appeal is dismissed; the order dated 25.11.2021 passed by NCLT Kolkata Bench in I.A. (IB) No. 644/KB/2021 is affirmed; no order as to costs.
summary.summary: The Appellant, a suspended director of Rohit Ferro Tech Limited, appealed against an order of NCLT Kolkata Bench dismissing his application to set aside the CIRP and disqualify Tata Steel Mining Limited (H-1 bidder), whose delayed EOI was admitted by the CoC. The Appellant also sought revival of a compromise scheme under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the CoC acted well within its commercial wisdom to condone the delay in EOI submission to achieve value maximization before voting had occurred. Additionally, the Tribunal affirmed that under Section 29A of the IBC, ineligible ex-promoters cannot circumvent statutory bars through Section 230 schemes.

summary.case_title: Kotak Mahindra Bank Limited vs. Rohit Sehgal, Liquidator of R.S. Ajit Singh and Co. (Automotives) Pvt. Ltd.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Kotak Mahindra Bank Limited is the Appellant (Secured Financial Creditor holding 10.69% voting share); Rohit Sehgal is the Respondent (Liquidator); R.S. Ajit Singh and Co. (Automotives) Private Limited is the Corporate Debtor (commercial vehicle dealer). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Dealer finance credit facility extended by Appellant to the Corporate Debtor sanctioned on 28.09.2015, secured via Deed of Hypothecation dated 28.01.2019 covering vehicle inventory and receivables. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose under operational and financial debts; Appellant claimed an outstanding default amount of Rs. 1,62,42,003.20/- against 12 specific vehicles. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated under Section 9 on 31.07.2019; CoC decided to sell BS-IV inventory back to manufacturers on 08.01.2020; 57 vehicles sold for Rs. 6,91,53,381/-; liquidation order passed on 26.06.2020; Appellant submitted Form 'D' on 24.07.2020 marking 'No' for relinquishment of security interest; Appellant sent representation identifying 12 chassis numbers on 19.08.2020; Appellant received its pro-rata share of liquidation distribution on 01.03.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: RoC charge registration Form CHG-1 and Deed of Hypothecation described a general floating charge on inventory and receivables without specific vehicle chassis numbers; Appellant consented to the sale of inventory in CoC meetings without objection; vehicles had already been liquidated and ceased to exist prior to the liquidation order; Appellant furnished an undertaking affidavit dated 23.02.2021 and received pro-rata proceeds on 01.03.2021. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed CA 3955(PB)/2020 in C.P. (IB) No. 1499(PB)/2019 before NCLT New Delhi Principal Bench seeking exclusive release of sale proceeds from 12 vehicles under Section 52; NCLT New Delhi dismissed the application on 20.11.2020.
summary.legal_issues: Whether a secured creditor who consented to the sale of hypothecated inventory during CIRP can subsequently opt under Section 52 during liquidation to realize exclusive security interest over proceeds of already-sold assets whose charge was registered only generally without itemized identification.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A secured creditor cannot enforce or realize a security interest under Section 52 of the IBC against assets that have already been converted into cash proceeds during CIRP with the creditor's consent; such proceeds form part of the liquidation estate and must be distributed pro-rata under Section 53. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 52(2) mandates that a secured creditor seeking realization outside the liquidation estate must specifically identify subsisting physical assets subject to security interest; it cannot be invoked retrospectively over generic cash proceeds from assets already liquidated with creditor participation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of RoC charge documentation (Form CHG-1) and company accounts to verify whether an exclusive identifiable charge existed over specific assets, and conduct evidencing estoppel through acceptance of pro-rata distribution. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellant had a generic charge over inventory, consented to the sale of vehicles during CIRP, and accepted its pro-rata share of proceeds; therefore, it is legally estopped from claiming exclusive appropriation under Section 52.
summary.operative_order: The appeal is dismissed; the order dated 20.11.2020 passed by NCLT New Delhi Principal Bench in CA 3955(PB)/2020 is affirmed; no order as to costs.
summary.summary: Kotak Mahindra Bank appealed against an order of NCLT New Delhi dismissing its application under Section 52 of the IBC seeking exclusive recovery from sale proceeds of 12 commercial vehicles hypothecated to it. The vehicles had been sold back to the manufacturer during CIRP with CoC approval to avoid value loss from BS-IV phase-out. After the Corporate Debtor entered liquidation, the Bank filed Form 'D' opting not to relinquish its security interest. The NCLAT held that because the vehicles were already sold during CIRP with the Bank's consent, no identifiable physical assets remained at liquidation commencement. Having accepted its pro-rata distribution under Section 53, the Bank was estopped from claiming exclusive rights, and the appeal was dismissed.

summary.case_title: Vipul Himatlal Shah & Anr. vs. Teco Industries & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Vipul Himatlal Shah and Tushar Himatlal Shah are Appellants (Suspended Directors/Shareholders of Corporate Debtor); Teco Industries is Respondent No. 1 (Financial Creditor partnership firm); Dilipkumar Natvarlal Jagad is Respondent No. 2 (Interim Resolution Professional); M/s Superdrawn Wire Industries Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Disbursement of loan funds carrying 14% interest per annum by Respondent No. 1 to the Corporate Debtor, which the Appellants disputed as an alleged part-advance toward a promised Rs. 50 crore equity investment for 49% shareholding. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default committed in repayment of financial debt of Rs. 19,40,81,000/- principal plus accrued interest totaling Rs. 26,49,46,085/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 8 issued prior to petition, corporate debtor replied refuting loan on 11.01.2020; Section 7 application filed on 04.02.2020; NCLT admitted Section 7 on 16.03.2022; NCLAT final order passed on 18.05.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: NeSL Information Utility records recorded debt of Rs. 19,40,81,000/- at 14% interest with yellow 'Deemed Authenticated' status following three unresponded email reminders delivered to director emails; corporate debtor's own ledger designated Teco Industries' balance as a loan account; authorized share capital was only Rs. 2 crores (Rs. 1,99,95,540 paid-up), rendering an equity investment of Rs. 50 crores legally impossible without capital expansion; pending Civil Suit No. 977 of 2018 before City Civil Court Ahmedabad filed by debtor. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent No. 1 filed CP(IB) No. 177/NCLT/AHM/2020 under Section 7 before NCLT Ahmedabad Bench; NCLT admitted the application and initiated CIRP on 16.03.2022.
summary.legal_issues: Whether debt registered with an Information Utility and deemed authenticated under Regulation 21 of the IBBI (Information Utilities) Regulations, 2017 establishes default under Section 7 of the IBC, and whether an uncorroborated defense of equity investment in excess of authorized share capital can displace a recorded financial debt.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where a debt and default are authenticated or deemed authenticated in the records of an Information Utility and corroborated by the corporate debtor's ledger accounts, the Adjudicating Authority is not required to look beyond such records to admit a Section 7 petition; self-serving defenses unsupported by documentary evidence cannot defeat admission. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Regulation 21(3) of the IBBI (Information Utilities) Regulations, 2017, the failure of a corporate debtor to respond to three consecutive reminders results in 'deemed authentication' of the default, satisfying the definition of financial debt under Section 5(8). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Deemed authenticated NeSL records combined with ledger entries classifying advances as loan accounts, weighed against the structural legal impossibility of an equity claim exceeding statutory authorized capital limits. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt was a disbursed financial debt carrying interest for the time value of money; default was conclusively established through Information Utility records and ledger accounts, making Section 7 admission unimpeachable.
summary.operative_order: The appeal is dismissed; the order dated 16.03.2022 passed by NCLT Ahmedabad Bench in CP(IB) No. 177/NCLT/AHM/2020 is affirmed; no order as to costs.
summary.summary: Suspended directors of M/s Superdrawn Wire Industries Pvt. Ltd. appealed an order of NCLT Ahmedabad Bench admitting a Section 7 IBC application filed by Teco Industries for default on a financial debt exceeding Rs. 26.49 crores. The Appellants contended that the disbursed Rs. 19.40 crores was a non-debt part-investment for a 49% stake and that Information Utility notices were misdirected. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that NeSL records had attained deemed authentication after three unanswered notices sent to director emails. Furthermore, the debtor's ledgers classified the account as a loan, and the debtor's authorized capital of Rs. 2 crores contradicted the assertion of a Rs. 50 crore equity transaction, fully establishing financial debt and default.

summary.case_title: One City Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. vs. Haryana Telecom Limited & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: One City Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. is the Appellant (Unsuccessful Resolution Applicant / H-3); Haryana Telecom Limited is Respondent No. 1 (Corporate Debtor through RP Sanyam Goel); Parivartan Investment and Finance Company is Respondent No. 2 (Financial Creditor and sole CoC member). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Respondent No. 2 held 5,50,000; 12% non-convertible debentures of Rs. 100 each issued by the Corporate Debtor with redemption due date extended to 31.12.2020. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default occurred upon non-redemption of non-convertible debentures carrying 12% per annum interest, leading to initiation of Section 7 proceedings (exact default quantum not quantified in order). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Letter demanding NCD redemption issued on 01.01.2019; Director Sunaina Singh resigned from Corporate Debtor board on 25.03.2019; Section 7 application filed on 25.09.2019 and admitted on 07.12.2020; Appellant declared H-3 on 19.09.2020; CoC approved H-1 resolution plan in 9th CoC meeting; Appellant filed I.A. No. 728 of 2020 on 19.10.2020; NCLT disposed of I.A. 728/2020 on 02.11.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellant challenged CoC constitution alleging Ms. Sunaina Singh (Director in Respondent No. 2) was the granddaughter of Mrs. Sita Chaudhary (Director in Corporate Debtor) and had resigned only six months prior to the Section 7 filing; no evidence or pleadings demonstrated that the resignation was a collusive contrivance or intended to sabotage CIRP. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed I.A. No. 728 of 2020 in C.P. No. 515/CHD/2019 before NCLT Chandigarh Bench seeking reconstitution of the CoC; NCLT dismissed I.A. 728/2020 on 02.11.2021 adopting the reasoning of an earlier order dated 05.03.2021 passed in I.A. No. 344 of 2020.
summary.legal_issues: Whether a financial creditor is disqualified under the first proviso to Section 21(2) of the IBC from participating in the CoC as a related party when its common director resigned from the corporate debtor's board six months prior to filing the Section 7 petition.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The disqualification of a financial creditor as a 'related party' under the first proviso to Section 21(2) operates in praesenti; a financial creditor is not barred from the CoC merely because a former director was once on the corporate debtor's board, unless it is proven that the relationship was formally severed as a fraudulent contrivance to infiltrate the CoC and sabotage the CIRP. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 21(2) proviso read with Section 5(24) employs the present tense ('is a related party'); familial grandmother-granddaughter relationship between directors of distinct entities without evidence of mutual acting on advice/directions does not satisfy Section 5(24) disqualification. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The exception test established in Phoenix ARC requiring specific averments and evidence demonstrating that the creditor divested its role with the fraudulent intention of sabotaging CIRP and diluting voting share. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because Ms. Sunaina Singh resigned six months prior to the Section 7 filing and no evidence of collusive divestment was established, Respondent No. 2 was not a related party in praesenti and was lawfully constituted as the CoC.
summary.operative_order: The appeal is dismissed; the order dated 02.11.2021 passed by NCLT Chandigarh Bench in I.A. No. 728 of 2020 is affirmed; no order as to costs.
summary.summary: The Appellant, an unsuccessful resolution applicant (H-3) for Haryana Telecom Limited, appealed against an order of NCLT Chandigarh Bench rejecting its application to reconstitute the CoC. The Appellant alleged that the sole CoC member, Parivartan Investment and Finance Company, was an ineligible related party under Section 21(2) because its director, Ms. Sunaina Singh, was the granddaughter of the Corporate Debtor's director and had previously served on the debtor's board. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that related party disqualification applies in praesenti. Since the director resigned six months prior to the Section 7 petition and no evidence proved a collusive intent to infiltrate the CoC, the financial creditor was fully eligible to constitute the CoC.

summary.case_title: Prayag Polytech Private Limited vs. Bon Lon Petrochem LLP
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Prayag Polytech Private Limited acted as the alleged Financial Creditor (Appellant), and Bon Lon Petrochem LLP was the alleged Corporate Debtor (Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Appellant disbursed an aggregate amount of Rs. 1,60,00,000 to the Respondent across three tranches between May 8, 2017 and May 12, 2017 under an oral agreement, claiming it to be a short-term loan carrying 15% interest per annum payable on demand; conversely, the Respondent maintained the funds were received as a 10-year long-term borrowing to be converted into an equity investment in the firm. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The claimed default amounted to Rs. 1,88,33,978 (comprising principal of Rs. 1,60,00,000 and accrued interest of Rs. 28,33,978 net of TDS up to December 25, 2018), with the alleged date of default asserted as January 9, 2019 following non-compliance with a recall notice. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Appellant issued a loan recall notice on January 2, 2019 demanding repayment by January 9, 2019; postal tracking records indicated the notice was returned as 'Not Delivered Unclaimed' due to incorrect addressing, and no reply was issued. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Core evidence comprised bank disbursement entries, Form 26AS records showing 11% TDS deduction by the Respondent on interest credited towards long-term borrowings, postal tracking reports displaying non-delivery of the recall notice, and the Respondent's balance sheet reflecting the remittance classified under 'Long Term Borrowings' for a 10-year tenure to be converted into an investment, without any written loan agreement or statutory registers produced under Section 186 of the Companies Act, 2013. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed an application under Section 7 of the IBC [CP (IB) No. 383 (ND) of 2019] before the NCLT, New Delhi Bench-III, which was dismissed on June 14, 2019 on the grounds that the funds were provided for a 10-year period as an investment and default was not established in summary proceedings.
summary.legal_issues: Whether an oral remittance classified in the balance sheet as long-term borrowings for ten years to be converted into an investment constitutes a financial debt with an established default payable on demand, and whether complex oral arrangements can be determined in summary proceedings under Section 7 of the IBC without documentary proof.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application for initiation of corporate insolvency resolution process under Section 7 cannot be maintained in the absence of documentary evidence proving that the disbursement constitutes a financial debt that has become due and payable, and disputed terms grounded entirely on oral understandings requiring elaborate trial evidence cannot be resolved in summary proceedings before the insolvency tribunal. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The statutory expression 'default' under Section 7 of the IBC necessitates proof of non-payment of a debt that has become legally due and payable; where an amount is reflected in financial records as a long-term borrowing/investment with a ten-year tenure, it cannot be construed as a debt in 'default' prior to the expiry of the stipulated term merely on the basis of a unilateral oral loan assertion. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The financial creditor must substantiate the commercial terms of the borrowing, including tenure, interest rate, and maturity, through contemporaneous documentary proof; deduction of tax at source or generic balance sheet entries indicating long-term borrowings without corroborating loan agreements or statutory filings fail to prove a debt payable on demand. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellant failed to establish default by documentary evidence, and because the balance sheet demonstrated the remittance was intended as a long-term tenure investment of 10 years, no actionable default occurred under Section 7.
summary.operative_order: The impugned order dated 14.06.2019 passed by the NCLT New Delhi Bench-III in CP (IB) No. 383 (ND) of 2019 is affirmed, and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 705 of 2019 is dismissed without any order as to costs.
summary.summary: Prayag Polytech Private Limited appealed against an order of the NCLT New Delhi dismissing its Section 7 IBC application against Bon Lon Petrochem LLP. The Appellant claimed that a disbursement of Rs. 1.60 Crore was an oral loan payable on demand with 15% interest per annum, defaulted upon issuance of an unclaimed recall notice. The Respondent established that the funds were accepted as a ten-year long-term borrowing to be converted into an investment. The NCLAT held that summary proceedings under the IBC cannot resolve disputed oral agreements lacking documentary proof. Finding no debt fell due as default, the Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal.

summary.case_title: Mukesh N. Desai vs. Piyush Patel & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mukesh N. Desai was the Appellant (alleged sole Financial Creditor and CoC member), Piyush Patel was Respondent No. 1 (Promoter of the Corporate Debtor), M/s Shipraj Developers Private Limited was Respondent No. 2 (Corporate Debtor), Sunil Kumar Agarwal was Respondent No. 3 (Resolution Professional), and Nuvoco Vistas Corporation Limited was the original Operational Creditor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: An MoU dated May 26, 2014 was executed whereby 25% ownership of project land for a real estate project named 'Coconut' was agreed to be transferred to the Appellant in exchange for funding construction costs up to the sample flat stage, entitling the Appellant to a 25% share in the net profits from flat sales as a joint development partner. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant claimed a financial debt of Rs. 4,41,82,071 disbursed between May 22, 2014 and August 25, 2014; no specific default date or loan interest schedule was established under the MoU. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Section 9 application filed by the Operational Creditor was admitted on July 24, 2019; the IRP made a public announcement on July 30, 2019; the first CoC meeting was held on September 16, 2019; an application under Section 12A for withdrawal was submitted following settlement on March 24, 2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The registered MoU dated May 26, 2014 stipulating profit-sharing terms and joint ownership; audited balance sheet of the Corporate Debtor for the year ending March 31, 2019 reflecting Rs. 4,41,82,071 under 'Long Term Borrowings'; pending arbitral proceedings between the parties concerning agreement covenants; and Section 12A withdrawal settlement documentation between the Corporate Debtor and operational creditors. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In CP (IB) No. 178/NCLT/AHM/2018 initiated under Section 9, the promoter filed IA No. 752 of 2019 to de-recognize the Appellant as a Financial Creditor, dissolve the single-member CoC, and close CIRP upon settling the Operational Creditor's debt; the NCLT Ahmedabad allowed the IA on July 10, 2020.
summary.legal_issues: Whether a joint venture partner entitled to land ownership and net profit sharing under an MoU qualifies as a Financial Creditor under Section 5(7) read with Section 5(8) of the IBC, and whether the Adjudicating Authority can close CIRP after operational debt settlement where the sole surviving CoC member is excluded as a Financial Creditor.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An investment made by a joint development partner in a real estate project with rights to share in the net profits of the venture does not constitute a financial debt, as the transaction represents an equity-type commercial risk for residual return rather than a loan disbursed against consideration for the time value of money. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8) requires a disbursement against consideration for the time value of money; reciprocal joint venture obligations to fund construction in exchange for 25% project land and profit sharing do not create a debtor-creditor relationship or a financial debt owed under Section 5(7). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Balance sheet classification of funds as 'Long Term Borrowings' is not conclusive evidence of financial debt when the governing underlying contract demonstrates that the funding was made towards partnership capital and profit-sharing equity in a real estate venture. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellant is a profit-sharing development partner and not a Financial Creditor; consequently, the constitution of the CoC was void ab initio, and CIRP was rightly closed upon settlement of the initiating Operational Creditor's claims under Section 12A.
summary.operative_order: The impugned order dated 10.07.2020 passed by the NCLT Ahmedabad Bench in IA No. 752 of 2019 is upheld, and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 780 of 2020 is dismissed with no order as to costs.
summary.summary: Mukesh N. Desai appealed against an NCLT Ahmedabad order disqualifying him as a Financial Creditor and closing the CIRP of Shipraj Developers Private Limited following settlement with the operational creditor. The Appellant claimed financial debt status based on advancing Rs. 4.41 Crores recorded as 'Long Term Borrowings' in balance sheets. The NCLAT examined the underlying MoU dated May 26, 2014 and held that the Appellant was a joint venture development partner entitled to a 25% share in project profits and land ownership, rather than a creditor disbursing funds for the time value of money. Confirming the CoC was void ab initio, the Tribunal dismissed the appeal.

summary.case_title: E to E Transportation Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. vs. Zephyr Peacock India & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: E to E Transportation Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. was the Appellant company; Zephyr Peacock India (Mauritius-based foreign investor) was Respondent No. 1; the Registrar of Companies, Bangalore was Respondent No. 2; and the Reserve Bank of India was Respondent No. 3. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Respondent No. 1 was allotted Series-A and Series-B Compulsorily Convertible Preference Shares (CCPS) alongside equity shares between 2012 and 2014 under FEMA pricing regulations; upon conversion on March 20, 2019, the Appellant erroneously applied the conversion-date fair value of Rs. 2,195 per share instead of the historical issuance fair values (Rs. 8,112 for Series-A and Rs. 4,826 for Series-B), resulting in the mistaken issuance of 80,347 equity shares instead of 28,458 equity shares. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (the dispute pertained to corporate share rectification, involving an inadvertent over-allotment of 51,889 equity shares of Rs. 10 each). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: FC-GPR forms filed on April 28, 2012 and July 3, 2014; CCPS converted on March 20, 2019; representation sent to RBI on October 10, 2019; RBI response issued on November 26, 2019 directing approach to RoC; Board resolution and NOC from Respondent No. 1 executed on December 13, 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Independent valuation reports dated March 15, 2012 and December 24, 2013; correspondence with RBI; Board Resolution and written No Objection Certificate dated December 13, 2019 from Respondent No. 1 consenting to cancellation of the 51,889 excess shares; and statutory filings reflecting the error. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed Company Petition CP No. 38/BB/2020 under Section 59 of the Companies Act, 2013 before the NCLT Bengaluru Bench seeking rectification of the Register of Members by cancelling the excess shares, which the NCLT dismissed on February 5, 2021 on the ground of non-maintainability for not approaching the ROC first.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the National Company Law Tribunal has original statutory jurisdiction under Section 59 of the Companies Act, 2013 to rectify a company's register of members by cancelling excess shares issued due to inadvertent valuation errors without requiring prior adjudication by the Registrar of Companies.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 59 of the Companies Act, 2013, the National Company Law Tribunal is vested with primary statutory authority to entertain petitions for rectification of the register of members—including cancellation of shares erroneously allotted without sufficient cause—and the exercise of this jurisdiction is not contingent upon the petitioner first obtaining an order or approaching the Registrar of Companies. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 59(1) and 59(2) confer wide statutory powers upon the Tribunal to hear aggrieved persons, direct rectification of records, or order cancellation of entries where names or shares are entered without sufficient cause, making the NCLT the competent forum to direct statutory authorities to reflect rectified capital structures. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where an erroneous share allotment in breach of regulatory pricing guidelines is demonstrated to be an inadvertent, bona fide mistake supported by valuation reports, regulator advice, and an explicit No Objection Certificate via Board Resolution from the affected shareholder, sufficient cause is established for rectification. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT failed to exercise its statutory jurisdiction under Section 59 by wrongly dismissing the petition as non-maintainable, and the matter warranted restoration for cancellation of the excess shares.
summary.operative_order: The impugned order dated 05.02.2021 in CP No. 38/BB/2020 passed by NCLT Bengaluru is set aside; the company petition is restored to file and remanded to NCLT Bengaluru with directions to consider cancellation of 51,889 equity shares allotted to Respondent No. 1 and direct the ROC to effect necessary rectifications in share capital and securities premium records expeditiously; appeal allowed with no order as to costs.
summary.summary: E to E Transportation Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the dismissal of its Section 59 Companies Act petition by NCLT Bengaluru, which held the petition non-maintainable because the company had not first approached the ROC. The Appellant had mistakenly allotted 51,889 excess equity shares to foreign investor Zephyr Peacock India due to an erroneous valuation price applied during CCPS conversion. Respondent No. 1 consented to the cancellation via Board resolution. The NCLAT held that Section 59 directly vests original jurisdiction in the NCLT to rectify the register of members and cancel shares. The Appellate Tribunal allowed the appeal and remanded the matter to NCLT for rectification.

summary.case_title: M/s. Ashish Ispat Pvt. Ltd. vs. Primuss Pipes & Tubes Ltd.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s. Ashish Ispat Pvt. Ltd. was the Operational Creditor (Appellant in Comp. App. 892/2021); Primuss Pipes & Tubes Ltd. was the Corporate Debtor represented by its Resolution Professional Mr. Nitin Jain; Ajay Kumar Jain was the Suspended Director of the Corporate Debtor (Appellant in Comp. App. 893/2021); Kotak Mahindra Bank (83% voting share) and M/s. Anjali Capfine Pvt. Ltd. (17% voting share) were Financial Creditors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Operational debts arising from supply of goods/materials by the Operational Creditor to the Corporate Debtor leading to initiation of insolvency proceedings. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational debt settled for Rs. 63,74,000 comprising two Demand Drafts of Rs. 19,00,000 and Rs. 6,00,000, and an initial cheque of Rs. 38,74,000 subsequently honored in full via RTGS on September 17, 2021. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Admission of Section 9 application occurred on August 4, 2021; public announcement made on August 6, 2021; MoU for amicable settlement and Form-FA executed on August 25, 2021; IRP filed withdrawal application IA No. 267/2021 on August 25, 2021; CoC constituted subsequently on August 27, 2021; first CoC meeting held on September 3, 2021; final RTGS payment cleared on September 17, 2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Settlement Memorandum of Understanding dated August 25, 2021; Form-FA submitted to the IRP; RTGS remittance receipts and Addendum to MoU dated September 17, 2021 confirming complete liquidation of operational dues; record of CoC constitution dated August 27, 2021 showing Kotak Mahindra Bank supporting withdrawal. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Following settlement, the IRP filed IA No. 267/2021 under Section 12A read with Regulation 30A(1)(a) before NCLT Allahabad; on September 29, 2021, the NCLT refused to consider the withdrawal application without 90% CoC approval due to dissent from a 17% financial creditor.
summary.legal_issues: Whether an application for withdrawal of CIRP under Section 12A of the IBC read with Regulation 30A(1)(a) filed prior to the constitution of the Committee of Creditors requires the approval of 90 percent voting share of the Committee of Creditors.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory mandate requiring ninety percent voting share approval from the Committee of Creditors under Section 12A of the IBC is applicable solely to withdrawal applications filed post-constitution of the CoC, and cannot be imposed on withdrawal applications filed through the Interim Resolution Professional prior to the constitution of the CoC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 12A pre-supposes the existence of a Committee of Creditors; when read harmoniously with Regulation 30A(1)(a) and 30A(3), an application moved prior to CoC constitution must be submitted directly to the Adjudicating Authority without placing it before or obtaining approval from the CoC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Once the operational debt is fully satisfied under a binding settlement agreement and Form-FA is filed before the formal constitution of the CoC, the Adjudicating Authority must exercise inherent powers under Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules to evaluate the settlement on its merits without conditioning it on subsequent CoC voting thresholds. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because IA No. 267/2021 was filed on August 25, 2021 before the CoC was formed on August 27, 2021, and the entire operational claim was fully satisfied, the Adjudicating Authority erred in refusing withdrawal.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 892 & 893 of 2021 are allowed; the impugned order dated 29.09.2021 in IA No. 267/2021 and the CIRP admission order dated 04.08.2021 passed by NCLT Allahabad are set aside; withdrawal application IA No. 267/2021 is allowed without costs.
summary.summary: M/s. Ashish Ispat Pvt. Ltd. and the suspended director of Primuss Pipes & Tubes Ltd. challenged an NCLT Allahabad order refusing to approve a Section 12A withdrawal of CIRP without 90% CoC consent. The Operational Creditor and Corporate Debtor had settled all claims under an MoU and submitted Form-FA on August 25, 2021, prior to the constitution of the CoC on August 27, 2021. The NCLAT held that the requirement of 90% CoC approval applies strictly to applications filed after CoC formation. Because the application preceded CoC constitution and all operational dues were discharged, the Appellate Tribunal allowed the appeals and terminated the CIRP.

summary.case_title: Valency International Pte Ltd. vs. Vasudevan & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Valency International Pte Ltd. was the Applicant/Appellant (Resolution Applicant), and Vasudevan alongside two others were Respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate insolvency resolution process involving an order passed in miscellaneous application MA/179/2019 arising out of CP/39/IB/CB/2018. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (appeal arose from an interlocutory/miscellaneous insolvency order subject to a condonation of delay challenge). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned order passed by NCLT Chennai on June 12, 2019; the statutory 30-day appeal timeline expired on July 28, 2019; Supreme Court decision in connected matter delivered on December 3, 2019; appeal initially lodged at Principal Bench New Delhi on November 30, 2021 and subsequently presented before the Chennai Bench resulting in an overall delay of 1027 days; IA No. 460 of 2022 filed seeking condonation of delay. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Non-receipt of certified copy of the impugned order; records showing the applicant failed to apply for a certified copy within the limitation period; Supreme Court suo motu limitation extension order dated January 10, 2022 covering the COVID-19 period from March 15, 2020 to February 28, 2022. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed an appeal under Section 61 of the IBC challenging the NCLT Chennai Bench order dated June 12, 2019 accompanied by IA No. 460/2022 seeking condonation of 1027 days of delay; Respondent No. 1 and No. 2 opposed maintainability under Section 61(2) of the Code.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the NCLAT possesses jurisdiction under Section 61(2) of the IBC to condone an appeal delay of 1027 days that accrued nine months prior to the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic and exceeded the statutory outer ceiling of 45 days (30 days plus 15 days condonation).
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal constituted under a special statute with an express and mandatory limitation regime lacks statutory power or inherent jurisdiction to condone any delay in preferring an appeal beyond the prescribed outer condonable period. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(2) mandates that appeals must be filed within 30 days, with the tribunal's discretionary power to condone delay on sufficient cause strictly restricted to a maximum subsequent period not exceeding 15 days (total 45 days); this statutory ceiling functions as an absolute bar to appeals filed thereafter. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Following the Supreme Court ruling in V. Nagarajan v. SKS Ispat and Power Ltd., an appellant cannot claim exclusion of time or pandemic relaxation where the prescribed limitation period lapsed prior to March 15, 2020 and where no timely application for a certified copy was made within the initial statutory limitation window. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The delay of 1027 days far exceeded the statutory maximum of 45 days permitted under Section 61(2), leaving the Tribunal without legal authority to condone the delay.
summary.operative_order: IA No. 460/2022 seeking condonation of 1027 days of delay is dismissed; consequently, Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 209 of 2022 is rejected, and connected interlocutory applications IA Nos. 458/2022, 459/2022, and 461/2022 are closed without costs.
summary.summary: Valency International Pte Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Chennai order dated June 12, 2019, seeking condonation of a 1027-day delay via IA No. 460 of 2022. The Appellant cited non-receipt of a certified copy, connected Supreme Court proceedings, and COVID-19 disruptions. The Respondents objected under Section 61(2) of the IBC. The NCLAT Chennai Bench held that Section 61(2) sets an unalterable deadline of 30 days plus a maximum condonable window of 15 days upon sufficient cause. Because the statutory limitation period expired nine months prior to COVID-19 and the delay exceeded statutory limits, the Tribunal dismissed the condonation application and rejected the appeal.

summary.case_title: Mr. Prateek Gupta & Ors. vs. Kotak Mahindra Bank Limited & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. Prateek Gupta and others were the Appellants (Promoters and Suspended Directors of the Corporate Debtor); Kotak Mahindra Bank Limited was Respondent No. 1 (Financial Creditor and Mortgagee); and the Liquidator of the Corporate Debtor was Respondent No. 2. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities extended by Kotak Mahindra Bank secured by a mortgage over 1400 square yards of land owned by the Promoters, alongside contiguous land admeasuring 260 square yards owned by the Corporate Debtor situated at Nangloi. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default details are not specified in the order; the proceeding arose during the liquidation phase of the Corporate Debtor regarding asset realization. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act issued by the Bank on September 28, 2017; measures under Section 13(4) executed subsequently; Securitisation Application No. 396 of 2019 filed by the Appellants before the DRT under Section 17; liquidation IA No. 6014 of 2021 filed before NCLT; impugned order passed on January 4, 2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: SARFAESI Section 13(2) notice and Section 13(4) possession records; pendency of S.A. No. 396/2019 before DRT; submissions by the Liquidator stating that the 260 sq. yards (liquidation estate asset) and 1400 sq. yards (promoters' mortgaged asset) formed an inseparable single composite property yielding maximum realization value only through a joint sale. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In the Corporate Debtor's liquidation proceedings, Kotak Mahindra Bank filed IA No. 6014/2021 before NCLT New Delhi (Court-III) seeking physical possession of the 260 sq. yards plot to conduct a joint e-auction under SARFAESI along with the mortgaged 1400 sq. yards and remit pro-rata proceeds to the liquidation estate; NCLT allowed the application on January 4, 2022.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the jurisdiction during liquidation proceedings to permit a secured creditor to conduct a joint composite sale under the SARFAESI Act of contiguous land parcels comprising both the Corporate Debtor's liquidation estate and the promoters' mortgaged property, with pro-rata sale proceeds remitted to the liquidator.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Adjudicating Authority supervising liquidation proceedings may legitimately authorize the composite sale of an inseparable parcel of land belonging to the liquidation estate together with adjacent mortgaged land of promoters under the SARFAESI Act to maximize asset realization value for stakeholders, provided the proportionate proceeds of the liquidation asset are returned to the liquidation estate. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Permitting a composite sale under the SARFAESI Act does not prejudice the liquidation estate under the IBC where the properties are functionally and physically inseparable and the liquidator himself would have been required to follow analogous public auction procedures. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where commercial and physical realities demonstrate that land parcels are contiguous and inseparable, maximizing revenue realization through a consolidated public auction benefits the liquidation estate rather than causing prejudice or financial loss to the corporate debtor. 4.
