DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT committed no error in permitting the joint e-auction under SARFAESI subject to the liquidator receiving the proportionate proceeds of the 260 sq. yards parcel; the promoter's remedy lies in their Section 17 application pending before the DRT.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 147 of 2022 is dismissed without costs, leaving it open for the Appellants to pursue their pending Section 17 application before the Debt Recovery Tribunal.
summary.summary: The Promoters and Suspended Directors of the Corporate Debtor appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order allowing Kotak Mahindra Bank to conduct a composite public e-auction under the SARFAESI Act for a total of 1660 square yards. The property comprised 260 square yards owned by the Corporate Debtor in liquidation and 1400 square yards mortgaged by the Promoters. The Appellants argued that the liquidation estate asset had to be sold independently under the IBC. The NCLAT held that because the contiguous parcels were inseparable, a joint composite sale maximized realization for the liquidation estate. Affirming the order, the Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal.

summary.case_title: Oriental Bank of Commerce (Now Punjab National Bank) vs. Anil Anchalia & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Oriental Bank of Commerce, now Punjab National Bank, was the Appellant (Secured Financial Creditor); Anil Anchalia was Respondent No. 1 (Liquidator of Bala Techno Industries Ltd.); and UCO Bank was Respondent No. 2 (Member of the Stakeholders Consultation Committee). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial assistance extended in 2014 by the Appellant to the Corporate Debtor, secured by a registered exclusive charge over factory land, buildings, and plots situated at Ramnagar, West Bengal. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Upon liquidation, the Liquidator sold the secured assets for Rs. 1,68,00,000 and distributed the proceeds on a pro-rata basis among creditors under Section 53 of the IBC. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on October 15, 2019; liquidation order passed on February 15, 2021; Appellant relinquished its security interest to the liquidation estate under Section 52; Appellant sent an email demanding exclusive entitlement to the realization proceeds on October 28, 2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Charge registration certificate with ROC Kolkata demonstrating exclusive security charge; written relinquishment of security interest under Section 52 of the IBC; Liquidator's pro-rata distribution schedule prepared in terms of the Section 53 waterfall mechanism. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed IA (I.B.C)/101(KB)2022 before NCLT Kolkata Bench seeking directions to the Liquidator to pay over the entire sale proceeds of Rs. 1,68,00,000 exclusively to the Appellant; NCLT Kolkata rejected the application on March 4, 2022.
summary.legal_issues: Whether a secured financial creditor who exercises the option under Section 52 of the IBC to relinquish its security interest to the liquidation estate is entitled to receive the entire sale proceeds realized from those specific secured assets on the strength of its exclusive charge, or whether distribution must strictly follow the pro-rata waterfall mechanism under Section 53.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A secured creditor who voluntarily elects to relinquish its security interest to the liquidation estate under Section 52 of the Code loses any preferential or exclusive right over the proceeds realized from those assets and is bound strictly by the collective, pro-rata waterfall distribution mechanism stipulated under Section 53. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 52 provides an election either to enforce security outside liquidation or relinquish it to the estate; once relinquished under Section 52, the assets merge into the common pool, and Section 53 does not permit a dissenting or exclusive secured creditor to demand payment up to the specific value of its relinquished security to the exclusion of other creditors in the same class. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Relying on the Supreme Court ruling in India Resurgence ARC Pvt. Ltd. v. Amit Metaliks Ltd., the distribution of realization proceeds must be in the same proportion and percentage as provided to other secured financial creditors, and an exclusive charge cannot confer priority beyond the statutory waterfall priority. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Liquidator acted in accordance with law in distributing the realization proceeds of Rs. 1.68 Crore on a pro-rata basis under Section 53, and the Appellant's claim of exclusive distribution was rightly rejected.
summary.operative_order: The impugned order dated 04.03.2022 passed by NCLT Kolkata Bench in IA (I.B.C)/101(KB)2022 is affirmed, and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 547 of 2022 is dismissed without costs.
summary.summary: Punjab National Bank (formerly Oriental Bank of Commerce) challenged an NCLT Kolkata order rejecting its application for exclusive distribution of Rs. 1.68 Crore realized from the sale of its mortgaged factory assets during the liquidation of Bala Techno Industries Ltd. The Appellant argued that having held an exclusive registered charge, it was entitled to the entire realization proceeds. The NCLAT held that once a secured creditor voluntarily relinquishes its security interest to the liquidation estate under Section 52 of the IBC, it is bound by the collective waterfall mechanism of Section 53 on a pro-rata basis. Affirming the NCLT order, the Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal.

summary.case_title: Bank of India vs. Mr. Vinod Kumar P. Ambavat
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Bank of India was the Appellant (Financial Creditor), and Mr. Vinod Kumar P. Ambavat was the Respondent (Resolution Professional of the Corporate Debtor, Actif Corporation Ltd.). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan and credit facilities extended by Bank of India to the Corporate Debtor, followed by a proposed One-Time Settlement (OTS) under which the Corporate Debtor deposited Rs. 1,00,00,000 via a cheque sourced from a third party (M/s Avazy Realcom Private Limited) into a designated 'no lien account'. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The dispute concerned custody of an earnest deposit of Rs. 1,00,00,000 held in a 'no lien account' pending OTS approval; CIRP was initiated on November 26, 2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Cheque for Rs. 1,00,00,000 deposited on July 12, 2017 / July 15, 2017; CIRP admitted against Corporate Debtor on November 26, 2019; RP requested release during the 3rd CoC meeting on September 8, 2020; IA No. 653/2020 filed by RP leading to the impugned order dated January 19, 2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor's letter dated July 12, 2017 stating the Rs. 1 Crore was deposited in a 'No Lien Account' solely to show bona fides, instructing that it was not to be adjusted towards principal, interest, or charges until OTS approval; bank ledger entries showing the failed OTS was never sanctioned and funds remained parked without appropriation. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In CP (IB) No. 272/NCLT/AHM/2019, the RP filed IA No. 653/2020 before NCLT Ahmedabad Bench seeking directions to Bank of India to release the Rs. 1 Crore to the CIRP account; NCLT allowed the IA on January 19, 2021 holding the funds were assets of the Corporate Debtor.
summary.legal_issues: Whether money deposited by a corporate debtor into a 'no lien account' to establish bona fides for an unapproved One-Time Settlement proposal constitutes an asset of the corporate debtor under Section 18(f) of the IBC which the Resolution Professional is entitled to take custody of, or whether the bank possesses a statutory banker's lien to retain the funds.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Monies deposited into a designated 'no lien account' earmarked exclusively for an proposed settlement that fails to materialize remain the property of the depositor corporate debtor and cannot be unilaterally appropriated by a lending bank under a general banker's lien, especially after the onset of the statutory moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 18(f) read with Section 3(27) of the IBC, 'property' includes money, and the Resolution Professional is under a statutory obligation to take custody and control of all assets belonging to the Corporate Debtor; funds held in a 'no lien account' do not become the property of the bank without an approved settlement. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The express terms of the deposit letter dated July 12, 2017 established a conditional deposit prohibiting appropriation towards principal or interest pending OTS sanction; following the Supreme Court precedent in Kut Energy Pvt. Ltd. v. PNB, earnest money deposited to show bona fides for a settlement offer is not a payment towards debt satisfaction. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Rs. 1 Crore lying unappropriated in the 'no lien account' at the time of CIRP commencement constitutes an asset of the Corporate Debtor, and the bank cannot assert a banker's lien over it post-moratorium.
summary.operative_order: The impugned order dated 19.01.2021 passed by NCLT Ahmedabad Bench in IA No. 653/2020 in CP (IB) No. 272/NCLT/AHM/2019 is affirmed, and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 214 of 2021 is dismissed without costs.
summary.summary: Bank of India appealed against an NCLT Ahmedabad order directing it to release Rs. 1 Crore lying in a 'no lien account' to the Resolution Professional of Actif Corporation Ltd. The Bank asserted that the funds, provided by a third party for a failed One-Time Settlement in 2017, were subject to a statutory banker's lien. The NCLAT held that the deposit was made under an express condition that it would only be utilized upon OTS approval and not adjusted against loan balances. Since the OTS never materialized, the money remained property of the Corporate Debtor under Section 18(f) of the IBC. The Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal.

summary.case_title: Vikram Puri & Anr. vs. Universal Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Vikram Puri and Raman Puri were the Appellants (Suspended Directors of the Corporate Debtor); Universal Buildwell Private Limited was Respondent No. 1 (Corporate Debtor); Atul Kansal was Respondent No. 2 (Resolution Professional); and Ms. Pallavi Joshi Bakhru was the original Financial Creditor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Real estate development and insolvency proceedings initiated under Section 7 of the IBC by a financial creditor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default details arose under Section 7 petition admitted on July 3, 2018; the dispute directly concerned persistent non-cooperation and failure of suspended management to hand over records and documents under Section 19. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application filed on April 18, 2018 and admitted on July 3, 2018; Section 19(2) application CA No. 400/2018 filed by RP; notices issued to Appellants on August 2, 2018; bailable warrants issued on August 29, 2018 and October 17, 2018; non-bailable warrants issued on October 19, 2018 and renewed on July 16, 2021; recall application dismissed on August 3, 2021; IA No. 3221/2021 filed for exemption and cancellation of warrants rejected on September 30, 2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Registrar's compliance report showing failure of the Suspended Directors to surrender or appear in court; repeated show-cause notices and warrant execution reports; records detailing non-supply of requisite corporate books and documents to the RP under CA No. 400/2018. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: During CIRP, the RP filed CA No. 400/2018 under Section 19(2) of the Code due to non-cooperation; following repeated non-appearance, NCLT New Delhi (Court-II) issued Non-Bailable Warrants and on September 30, 2021, dismissed IA No. 3221/2021 filed by the Appellants seeking cancellation of the Non-Bailable Warrants.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the National Company Law Tribunal exercising jurisdiction under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code possesses statutory power under Rule 77 of the NCLT Rules read with Order XVI Rule 10 of the CPC to issue Non-Bailable Warrants to enforce the personal attendance and surrender of suspended directors who fail to cooperate under Section 19.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An insolvency adjudicating authority is vested with full statutory power to enforce the personal attendance of defaulting parties—including the issuance of bailable and non-bailable warrants—when persons fail to obey summonses or refuse to cooperate with an officer of the tribunal in supplying essential documents. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 19(2) and 19(3) of the IBC empower the tribunal to issue mandatory directions to management to cooperate with the resolution professional; read with Rule 77 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 and Section 424 of the Companies Act, the enforcement mechanism under Order XVI Rule 10 of the CPC is fully applicable to IBC proceedings. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where notices and bailable warrants have been repeatedly ignored without lawful excuse and court orders dictated in open court are deliberately evaded, the statutory preconditions for issuing Non-Bailable Warrants under Order XVI Rule 10(3) CPC are satisfied, and the tribunal is not required to proceed ex parte. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT acted within its jurisdiction in issuing and refusing to recall the Non-Bailable Warrants against the non-cooperative suspended directors to compel production of corporate records.
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1018 of 2021 is dismissed without costs; the Adjudicating Authority is also granted liberty to recommend initiation of criminal prosecution under Chapter VII of the IBC against the Suspended Directors.
summary.summary: Suspended directors of Universal Buildwell Private Limited appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order rejecting their application to cancel Non-Bailable Warrants issued against them for failure to surrender and supply corporate records under Section 19 of the IBC. The Appellants contended that the NCLT lacked jurisdiction to issue arrest warrants and ought to have proceeded ex parte. The NCLAT held that under Rule 77 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 read with Order XVI Rule 10 of the Civil Procedure Code, the Tribunal is fully empowered to issue Non-Bailable Warrants to secure personal attendance and enforce cooperation. Finding no jurisdictional error, the Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal.

summary.case_title: Mascot Petrochem Private Limited vs. Midaas Construction Company Private Limited
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mascot Petrochem Private Limited was the Operational Creditor (Appellant) and Midaas Construction Company Private Limited was the Corporate Debtor (Respondent)[cite: 11]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of bitumen, Light Density Oil (LDO), and allied products delivered across sites for road construction and civil engineering projects between February 22, 2016 and June 22, 2016 based on verbal purchase orders[cite: 11]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total supply value of Rs. 48,76,136 against which Rs. 34,72,214 was paid, leaving a claimed principal outstanding amount of Rs. 14,03,922 along with 18% interest per annum; last payment received was on April 10, 2017[cite: 11]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 8 of the IBC issued on October 9, 2018 and served on October 10, 2018; Section 8 reply issued by Corporate Debtor on October 18, 2018 disputing receipt of goods except for an admitted amount of Rs. 2,17,438[cite: 11]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Three contentious invoices comprising Invoice No. MPPL/405/15-16 dated March 7, 2016 (discrepancy between handwritten proforma and computerized invoice rates), Invoice No. MPPL/062/16-17 dated June 1, 2016 (disputed delivery, unconfirmed lorry consignment note from Siddhi Vinayak Road Carriers, unaccepted reliance on VAT quarterly returns), and Invoice No. MPPL/080/16-17 dated June 22, 2016 for bitumen worth Rs. 4,65,990 (disputed forged signature of receipt)[cite: 11]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed CP(IB) No. 1692/KB/2018 under Section 9 before NCLT Kolkata Bench, which was dismissed on August 20, 2019 due to material discrepancies in the claim and genuine disputes regarding delivery and pricing[cite: 11].
summary.legal_issues: Whether a dispute concerning non-delivery of goods, discrepant invoice rates, and alleged forged acknowledgment signatures raised for the first time in reply to a Section 8 demand notice constitutes a pre-existing bona fide dispute under the IBC sufficient to reject a Section 9 application[cite: 11].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An operational debt claim under Section 9 cannot be admitted where the operational creditor fails to furnish unimpeachable proof of actual physical delivery of goods and where genuine, non-spurious disputes regarding invoice rates and receipt authenticity are raised by the corporate debtor, as the summary mechanism under the IBC cannot serve as a debt recovery substitute[cite: 11]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The statutory expression 'existence of a dispute' under Section 8 and Section 9 encompasses bona fide defenses regarding non-receipt of goods raised in reply to a statutory demand notice where the corporate debtor had no prior notice or knowledge of the purported invoices[cite: 11]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: In the absence of signed delivery receipts or unimpeachable consignment acknowledgments by the corporate debtor, indirect evidence such as statutory VAT filings or unilateral internal ledger accounts maintained by the operational creditor cannot establish delivery of materials[cite: 11]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because legitimate disputes existed regarding the actual supply of goods and discrepancies in billing rates for the invoices, the application under Section 9 was rightly rejected[cite: 11].
summary.operative_order: The impugned judgment dated 20.08.2019 of the NCLT Kolkata Bench in CP(IB) No. 1692/KB/2018 is upheld, and Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1399 of 2019 is dismissed without costs[cite: 11].
summary.summary: Mascot Petrochem Private Limited appealed against an order of NCLT Kolkata dismissing its Section 9 IBC petition against Midaas Construction Company Private Limited[cite: 11]. The Appellant claimed an outstanding default of Rs. 14,03,922 plus interest for bitumen supplies under three specific invoices[cite: 11]. The Respondent disputed liability in its Section 8 reply, citing divergent prices between handwritten and computerized invoices, lack of delivery receipts, and forged acknowledgments[cite: 11]. The NCLAT held that internal ledgers and VAT returns do not constitute unimpeachable evidence of delivery and that genuine factual disputes over delivery and rates bar summary insolvency proceedings[cite: 11]. Confirming the NCLT order, the Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal[cite: 11].

summary.case_title: Kalptaru Steel Rolling Mills Ltd. vs. Southern Power Distribution Company of Andhra Pradesh Ltd. & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Kalptaru Steel Rolling Mills Ltd. acted through its Monitoring Committee/Resolution Applicant (Appellant in CA 866/2020 and Respondent in CA 914/2020), and Southern Power Distribution Company of Andhra Pradesh Ltd. was the electricity distribution licensee (Appellant in CA 914/2020 and Respondent in CA 866/2020)[cite: 12]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: High Tension power supply connections (HT Service No. 328 and HT Service No. 375) provided to the manufacturing plant of the Corporate Debtor by the electricity utility under state supply codes[cite: 12]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Pre-CIRP electricity dues claimed by the discom via a belated claim submitted on June 23, 2020; resolution plan already approved on February 14, 2020 without accommodating the unsubmitted past dues[cite: 12]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on August 14, 2018; Resolution Plan approved by NCLT on February 14, 2020; discom submitted post-approval claim on June 23, 2020; Chairman of Monitoring Committee filed IA No. 2477/2020; impugned order passed on September 8, 2020[cite: 12]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Approved Resolution Plan extinguishing all past liabilities; records showing the discom lodged its claim only after approval of the resolution plan; statutory requirement under electricity codes demanding a security deposit for high tension connection sanction[cite: 12]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Monitoring Committee filed IA No. 2477/2020 in CP (IB)/563(PB)/2018 before NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi seeking reconnection without paying past dues or fresh security deposit; on September 8, 2020, NCLT held that past dues stood extinguished but security deposit was mandatory for restoration; both parties appealed[cite: 12].
summary.legal_issues: Whether an electricity distribution company can condition the restoration of power connections on the payment of extinguished pre-CIRP arrears pursuant to state electricity regulations, and whether a successful resolution applicant is legally exempted from furnishing a standard statutory security deposit for ongoing high-tension power supply[cite: 12].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a resolution plan is approved by the Adjudicating Authority, all pre-CIRP liabilities of the corporate debtor stand extinguished and state regulatory provisions demanding clearance of past arrears yield to the non-obstante provisions of Section 238 of the IBC; however, the resolution applicant must fulfill mandatory statutory preconditions, including security deposits, for obtaining prospective essential utility supplies[cite: 12]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 238 overrides inconsistent state electricity supply code regulations requiring settlement of previous dues before granting reconnection; nevertheless, regulations imposing prospective security deposits for high tension consumption operate independently as standard operational requirements to adjust future bill defaults[cite: 12]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Extinguishment of past dues is governed strictly by the approved resolution plan and statutory timelines; prospective compliance obligations for continuous commercial operations require strict adherence to extant regulatory frameworks[cite: 12]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The discom cannot claim past dues after plan approval, but the resolution applicant is legally required to furnish the security deposit to obtain power restoration[cite: 12].
summary.operative_order: Both Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 866 of 2020 and Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 914 of 2020 are dismissed, affirming the NCLT order dated 08.09.2020 in IA/2477/2020 without costs[cite: 12].
summary.summary: Cross-appeals were preferred by the Monitoring Committee of Kalptaru Steel Rolling Mills Ltd. and Southern Power Distribution Company of AP Ltd. against an NCLT Principal Bench order[cite: 12]. The NCLT directed the discom to restore power connections without insisting on extinguished past pre-CIRP dues, but mandated payment of a fresh security deposit[cite: 12]. The discom contested the extinguishment of arrears under state supply codes, while the resolution applicant challenged the security deposit requirement[cite: 12]. The NCLAT held that Section 238 overrides state regulations demanding past dues, but the discom is entitled to a security deposit to secure future consumption[cite: 12]. Both appeals were dismissed[cite: 12].

summary.case_title: Vishal Ghisulal Jain vs. Amar Universal Pvt. Ltd.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Vishal Ghisulal Jain was the Resolution Professional of S.K. Wheels Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant), and Amar Universal Pvt. Ltd. was the Landowner/Lessor (Respondent)[cite: 13]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Lease agreement dated August 7, 2015 leasing an RCC industrial shed of 39,100 sq. ft. and open space at MIDC Sanpada to the Corporate Debtor for five years from September 1, 2015 to August 31, 2020 at a monthly rent of Rs. 13,68,500 with a security deposit of Rs. 82,11,000[cite: 13]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Outstanding lease claim filed by Respondent on June 4, 2019 in Form-B for Rs. 2,30,92,536[cite: 13]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application admitted on March 29, 2019; Form-B claim filed on June 4, 2019; MA No. 2319/2019 allowed on October 16, 2019; NCLT contempt directions issued on November 13, 2019 and November 25, 2019; NCLAT appellate modification order issued on November 20, 2019 in CA No. 1324/2019; clarification order passed on December 18, 2019[cite: 13]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Prior order of NCLAT dated November 20, 2019 ruling that only current CIRP-period rent was payable by the RP and setting aside a Rs. 1 Lakh cost; court records of November 13, 2019 and November 25, 2019 noting the RP was present in court premises but did not enter until the bench was rising; compliance report showing subsequent surrender of possession to the lessor[cite: 13]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai ordered immediate vacation, payment of full claim, and Rs. 1 Lakh cost on October 16, 2019, followed by orders deprecating the RP's conduct on November 13 and 25, 2019, and ordering full rent payment on December 18, 2019; the RP appealed to expunge adverse remarks and set aside the full payment directive[cite: 13].
summary.legal_issues: Whether judicial remarks regarding a Resolution Professional's conduct can be expunged when not objected to before the recording bench, and whether the NCLT can direct payment of pre-CIRP lease dues contrary to the moratorium and previous appellate directives[cite: 13].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Judicial observations regarding conduct in court, as recorded in an order, are conclusive of what transpired and cannot be expunged by an appellate tribunal if the aggrieved party failed to move the recording bench at the earliest instance; however, directions instructing an insolvency professional to pay pre-CIRP claims violate statutory moratorium provisions[cite: 13]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14 of the IBC bars payment of pre-CIRP debts to individual operational creditors during resolution; the Resolution Professional is only responsible for administrative costs incurred during the CIRP period to keep the entity a going concern[cite: 13]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under the rule laid down in State of Maharashtra v. Ramdas Shriniwas Nayak, statements in a judgment as to court proceedings are unassailable unless prompt rectification is sought before the same bench[cite: 13]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The refusal to expunge adverse conduct remarks is affirmed due to uncontradicted contemporaneous records, but the directive requiring payment of pre-CIRP rent arrears is set aside as contrary to Section 14 and binding appellate orders[cite: 13].
summary.operative_order: The appeal is allowed exclusively to the extent of setting aside the NCLT order dated 18.12.2019 directing payment of entire historical rent dues; prayers seeking expunction of adverse judicial observations against the Appellant in orders dated 13.11.2019 and 25.11.2019 are rejected[cite: 13].
summary.summary: The Resolution Professional of S.K. Wheels Pvt. Ltd. challenged orders of NCLT Mumbai directing him to pay entire lease arrears to Amar Universal Pvt. Ltd. and recording adverse remarks against his professional conduct[cite: 13]. The NCLAT had earlier held in appeal that only post-CIRP lease amounts were payable as resolution costs[cite: 13]. In the present appeal, the NCLAT refused to expunge the adverse conduct remarks, holding that statements of judges regarding courtroom behavior are conclusive where no correction was sought before the trial bench[cite: 13]. However, the Tribunal set aside the direction compelling payment of entire historical rent, confirming it violated Section 14 moratorium rules[cite: 13].

summary.case_title: Regen Powertech Pvt. Ltd. vs. M/s. Wind Construction Private Limited & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Regen Powertech Pvt. Ltd. represented by its Erstwhile Resolution Professional Ebenezar Inbaraj was the Appellant; M/s Wind Construction Private Limited was Respondent No. 1; and Madhusudhan Khemka, Sundaresh Ramanathan, and Varahatu Rao Kavala (suspended/erstwhile directors) were Respondents Nos. 2, 3, and 4[cite: 14]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Turnkey agreement dated January 24, 2018 for supply, erection, and commissioning of 33 wind turbine generators (49.5 MW) at Onamakulam, Tirunelveli, with a contractual 18% annual interest clause for delayed payment[cite: 14]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor issued invoices for Rs. 286,19,78,856 against which Rs. 206,90,45,531.50 was remitted; an amount of Rs. 70,82,13,056 was remitted back to Respondent No. 1's Yes Bank account between April and June 2018; claimed fraudulent diversion/contribution sought was Rs. 75.63 Crore plus 18% interest[cite: 14]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Turnkey contract executed on January 24, 2018; account remittances executed April-June 2018; Resolution Plan approved by NCLT on February 1, 2022; impugned dismissal order passed on July 1, 2022[cite: 14]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Transaction Audit Report by Khicha & Prabhu Kesavan; banking statements across Karur Vysya Bank, HDFC Bank, and YES Bank showing transactions; contractual provisions regarding liquidated damages adjustments of Rs. 43.33 Crore and direct third-party vendor disbursements of Rs. 130 Crore[cite: 14]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Erstwhile RP filed IA(IBC)/489(CHE)/2021 under Section 66(1) and Section 65 before NCLT Chennai alleging fraudulent trading and diversion of receivables; NCLT dismissed the application on July 1, 2022 for failure to establish dishonest intention with documentary proof[cite: 14].
summary.legal_issues: Whether commercial fund remittances and project cost reconciliation adjustments between contracting entities constitute fraudulent or wrongful trading under Section 66(1) of the IBC without specific pleadings and evidence establishing a dishonest intent to defraud creditors[cite: 14].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application for fraudulent trading under Section 66 of the IBC requires strict pleading and a very high standard of proof establishing actual dishonest intent to defraud creditors, which cannot be sustained through generalized allegations arising out of complex contractual reconciliations or project adjustments[cite: 14]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 66(1) requires proof that the business was carried on with intent to defraud creditors; bona fide business decisions made under the belief of resolving commercial distress do not constitute fraudulent trading, and isolated contractual defaults remain civil tort or contract remedies[cite: 14]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Relying on the Supreme Court standard in Anuj Jain v. Axis Bank, material facts and distinct allegations must be specifically substantiated by convincing documentary evidence demonstrating deliberate fraud, rather than routine transaction audit notations of disputed accounts[cite: 14]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellant failed to substantiate dishonest fraudulent intention behind the account adjustments, and the NCLT rightly dismissed the application under Section 66(1)[cite: 14].
summary.operative_order: The impugned order dated 01.07.2022 passed by NCLT Chennai Bench-II in IA(IBC)/489(CHE)/2021 is affirmed, and Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 349 of 2022 is dismissed without costs[cite: 14].
summary.summary: The Erstwhile Resolution Professional of Regen Powertech Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Chennai order dismissing a Section 66 application alleging fraudulent trading against Wind Construction Private Limited and former directors[cite: 14]. The RP claimed that Rs. 70.82 Crores in windmill project receivables was fraudulently diverted back to the buyer and sought contribution of Rs. 75.63 Crores[cite: 14]. The Respondents proved that payments involved mutual adjustments for direct vendor disbursements and liquidated damages under the turnkey contract[cite: 14]. The NCLAT held that invoking Section 66 requires a high degree of proof demonstrating dishonest intent to defraud creditors, which was not established[cite: 14]. The appeal was dismissed[cite: 14].

summary.case_title: Tricounty Premier Hearing Service Inc. vs. State Bank of India & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Tricounty Premier Hearing Service Inc. (acting through Indian subsidiary Tri County Holding Pvt. Ltd.) was the Successful Resolution Applicant (Appellant); State Bank of India was Respondent No. 1 (Lead Financial Creditor, 66.76% vote); Axis Bank was Respondent No. 2; and Sundaresh Bhat was Respondent No. 3 (Erstwhile RP/Monitoring Committee Member)[cite: 15]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Approved Resolution Plan for revival and acquisition of Corporate Debtor BSR Diagnostic Limited, operating diagnostic centers across four states[cite: 15]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Restructured financial debt payable was Rs. 45 Crores, including Rs. 12 Crores upfront within 60 days, Rs. 26 Crores by March 31, 2019, Rs. 3 Crores by March 31, 2020, and Rs. 4 Crores by March 31, 2021; Appellant paid Rs. 15 Crores to Financial Creditors and over Rs. 20 Crores total, defaulting on the remaining balance of Rs. 30 Crores[cite: 15]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Plan approved by CoC on November 12, 2018 and NCLT on January 22, 2019; extension CA No. 58/2020 filed February 2020; conditional order dated April 12, 2021; order granting extension till October 31, 2021 passed on September 20, 2021; IA No. 115/2021 filed October 29, 2021; impugned dismissal on November 24, 2021[cite: 15]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Term loan sanction in-principle offer dated November 11, 2021 from Kotak Mahindra Bank for Rs. 20 Crores; overseas bank accounts holding USD 1,000,000; flight itinerary dated November 16, 2021 demonstrating principal travel to execute security documents; proof of Rs. 15 Crore payment to lenders and full payment of Rs. 4.6 Crore CIRP costs[cite: 15]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed IA No. 115/2021 before NCLT Cuttack Bench seeking a 30-day extension to execute loan financing and discharge the remaining Rs. 30 Crores; NCLT rejected the application on November 24, 2021 citing past defaults and disregard of timelines[cite: 15].
summary.legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the jurisdiction to grant a reasonable 30-day extension to a Successful Resolution Applicant to implement financial obligations under an approved plan where substantial payments have been made and funding has been secured, or whether such extension is barred under the Supreme Court ruling in Ebix Singapore[cite: 15].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A procedural extension of time sought by a successful resolution applicant to discharge outstanding payments under an approved resolution plan does not constitute an impermissible modification or withdrawal of the plan, and the tribunal possesses jurisdiction to grant reasonable extensions where bona fide efforts and verified financing are demonstrated to avoid liquidation[cite: 15]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The ruling in Ebix Singapore v. CoC of Educomp prohibits unilateral withdrawal or substantive restructuring of plan terms; it does not eliminate the tribunal's discretionary power to grant procedural time extensions for completing financial closures[cite: 15]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where substantial plan compliance is shown (e.g., Rs. 15 Crores paid to lenders, full CIRP costs settled) and credible documentary evidence shows an in-principle loan sanction and liquid bank funds for the balance, granting time avoids corporate death without causing prejudice to lenders[cite: 15]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in refusing a 30-day extension without evaluating the secured funding sources; an extension of 30 days is warranted to enable full satisfaction of dues[cite: 15].
summary.operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the impugned order dated 24.11.2021 passed by NCLT Cuttack Bench in IA No. 115/2021 is set aside; the Appellant is granted 30 days up to 20.02.2022 to deposit the remaining Rs. 30 Crores, failing which liquidation shall proceed[cite: 15].
summary.summary: Tricounty Premier Hearing Service Inc., the Successful Resolution Applicant of BSR Diagnostic Limited, appealed against an NCLT Cuttack order refusing a 30-day extension to pay the outstanding Rs. 30 Crores under an approved plan[cite: 15]. State Bank of India opposed the plea, arguing that timelines cannot be modified under the Ebix Singapore ruling[cite: 15]. The NCLAT held that seeking a procedural time extension to fulfill commitments is not an impermissible plan modification[cite: 15]. Because the Appellant had already paid Rs. 15 Crores, settled CIRP costs, and secured an in-principle loan of Rs. 20 Crores from Kotak Mahindra Bank, the Appellate Tribunal allowed the appeal and granted 30 days to complete payment[cite: 15].

summary.case_title: Pooja Finelease Ltd. vs. Auto Needs (India) Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Pooja Finelease Ltd. was the Financial Creditor (Appellant), and Auto Needs (India) Pvt. Ltd. alongside another were the Corporate Debtor and respondents (Respondents)[cite: 17]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan financing facility leading to initiation of Section 7 insolvency proceedings, followed by bilateral settlement during CIRP under executed Consent Terms dated January 27, 2020 providing for payment through 12 post-dated cheques[cite: 17]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default details arose from dishonor or breach of the settlement installments under the Consent Terms dated January 27, 2020, entitling revival under Clause 8 thereof[cite: 17]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated under Section 7 on December 20, 2019; Consent Terms executed on January 27, 2020; withdrawal allowed under Rule 11 of NCLT Rules on February 5, 2020; default committed under Consent Terms; revival application rejected by NCLT on November 10, 2021[cite: 17]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Consent Terms dated January 27, 2020 containing Clause 8 explicitly stipulating that the Financial Creditor shall be entitled to revive the Section 7 petition IB-2340(ND)/2019 upon default; withdrawal order dated February 5, 2020 recording the settlement and receipt of 12 cheques[cite: 17]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Following default by the Corporate Debtor under the Consent Terms, the Appellant filed an application seeking revival of CP (IB) No. 2340/ND/2019; NCLT New Delhi (Bench-IV) dismissed the application on November 10, 2021 on the ground that the dismissal order did not explicitly grant liberty to revive[cite: 17].
summary.legal_issues: Whether a Financial Creditor is entitled to seek revival of an admitted Section 7 application withdrawn on the basis of consent terms taken on record by the Adjudicating Authority where the consent terms contain an explicit revival clause in the event of default, notwithstanding the absence of an express reservation of liberty in the operative withdrawal order[cite: 17].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where an insolvency petition is withdrawn pursuant to a settlement agreement and the consent terms are formally taken on record and allowed by the Adjudicating Authority, the terms of the settlement (including explicit clauses reserving the right to revive the insolvency process upon subsequent payment default) form an integral part of the court order and confer an actionable right on the creditor to seek revival of the original proceedings without requiring an independent express grant of liberty in the operative order[cite: 17]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 11 inherent powers exercised to dispose of an application on the basis of consent terms incorporate the covenants of those consent terms into the judicial record; distinguishable from cases where settlements are reached outside the record without filed terms[cite: 17]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Production of on-record consent terms embodying an unambiguous default-revival clause distinguishes the case from precedents where oral or unfiled settlements precluded revival without explicit liberty[cite: 17]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed an error in rejecting the revival application, and the Section 7 company petition stood revived for determination on merits[cite: 17].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 103 of 2022 is allowed; the impugned order dated 10.11.2021 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench-IV is set aside; C.P. (IB) No. 2340 of 2019 under Section 7 of the IBC is revived before the Adjudicating Authority to be heard in accordance with law[cite: 17].
summary.summary: Pooja Finelease Ltd. appealed against an order of NCLT New Delhi rejecting its application to revive a Section 7 IBC petition against Auto Needs (India) Pvt. Ltd. following default under settlement terms[cite: 17]. The Section 7 petition had previously been withdrawn under Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules based on Consent Terms dated January 27, 2020, wherein Clause 8 expressly reserved the creditor's right to revive the petition upon payment default[cite: 17]. The NCLT declined revival because explicit liberty was absent from the operative order[cite: 17]. The NCLAT reversed the order, holding that because the Consent Terms were formally taken on record, the revival clause formed part of the order itself[cite: 17]. The appeal was allowed and the petition was revived[cite: 17].

summary.case_title: Amitabh Roy vs. Master Development Management (India) Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Amitabh Roy was the Appellant (Suspended Director of the Corporate Debtor); Master Development Management (India) Pvt. Ltd. was Respondent No. 1 (Operational Creditor)[cite: 18]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Services rendered leading to the filing of four Company Petitions by the Operational Creditor; followed by a comprehensive Settlement Agreement dated October 4, 2019 resolving all pending petitions[cite: 18]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Original petition claimed default of Rs. 9,48,997; all principal settlement dues were fully satisfied, leaving only unpaid Tax Deducted at Source (TDS) amounts of Rs. 66,884 and Rs. 1,10,820 claimed as default[cite: 18]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CP (IB) No. 1686/KB/2018 filed on December 13, 2018; petition disposed of on October 3, 2019 granting liberty to revive if settlement talks failed; bilateral Settlement Agreement executed on October 4, 2019; supplementary affidavit filed on January 24, 2022; impugned admission order passed on February 25, 2022[cite: 18]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Settlement Agreement dated October 4, 2019 covering four petitions; Supplementary Affidavit dated January 24, 2022 establishing complete liquidation of operational dues and documenting unpaid TDS liabilities of Rs. 66,884 and Rs. 1,10,820[cite: 18]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Following complete payment of underlying settlement dues, the Operational Creditor filed an IA for revival of CP (IB) No. 1686/KB/2018 based on non-deposit of statutory TDS amounts; NCLT Kolkata Bench admitted the Section 9 petition on February 25, 2022 holding that the Corporate Debtor remained liable for TDS sums[cite: 18].
summary.legal_issues: Whether the non-deposit or non-payment of Tax Deducted at Source (TDS) amounts to income tax authorities constitutes an operational debt or an actionable default under Section 9 of the IBC sufficient to justify reviving and admitting an insolvency application where all underlying commercial settlement dues to the creditor have been paid in full[cite: 18].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The failure of a corporate debtor to remit statutory Tax Deducted at Source (TDS) to the revenue authorities does not constitute an operational debt due to the operational creditor, nor does it provide an actionable ground of default for initiating or reviving corporate insolvency resolution process under Section 9 of the IBC[cite: 18]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9 insolvency proceedings cannot be invoked or revived as an instrument of debt recovery or tax compliance where the operational debt owed to the creditor stands completely discharged; non-compliance with TDS statutory provisions is governed exclusively by the penal and recovery framework of the Income Tax Act, 1961[cite: 18]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where contemporaneous record evidence establishes full satisfaction of all contractual claim amounts and the sole subsisting grievance pertains to tax deduction remittances, reviving a Section 9 petition constitutes an abuse of the statutory process[cite: 18]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT committed serious error in admitting the Section 9 petition for unpaid TDS balances; the order was unsustainable and warranted imposition of costs for misuse of the Code[cite: 18].
summary.operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the impugned order dated 25.02.2022 passed by NCLT Kolkata Bench admitting Section 9 in CP (IB) No. 1686/KB/2018 is set aside; a cost of Rs. 1,00,000 is imposed on the Operational Creditor (Respondent No. 1) to be paid to the Corporate Debtor within one month[cite: 18].
summary.summary: Amitabh Roy, Suspended Director of the Corporate Debtor, appealed against an NCLT Kolkata order admitting a Section 9 application filed by Master Development Management (India) Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 18] Following an earlier disposal of the petition, the parties entered into a Settlement Agreement on October 4, 2019 under which all substantive dues were discharged[cite: 18]. The Operational Creditor sought revival exclusively on the ground that statutory TDS amounts of Rs. 66,884 and Rs. 1,10,820 were not deposited[cite: 18]. The NCLAT held that non-payment of TDS does not constitute an operational debt under the IBC and is punishable exclusively under the Income Tax Act[cite: 18]. The Appellate Tribunal set aside the admission order and imposed Rs. 1 Lakh cost on the creditor[cite: 18].

summary.case_title: TUF Metallurgical Pvt. Ltd. vs. Wadhwa Glass Processors Pvt. Ltd.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: TUF Metallurgical Pvt. Ltd. was the Financial Creditor (Appellant), and Wadhwa Glass Processors Pvt. Ltd. was the Corporate Guarantor (Respondent); alongside the Principal Borrower against whom CIRP was already initiated[cite: 19]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan or financial accommodation extended by the Financial Creditor to the Principal Borrower backed by a corporate guarantee furnished by the Respondent[cite: 19]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default occurred on the guaranteed debt, leading to two Section 7 applications for the same financial default[cite: 19]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Insolvency Act amendment inserting Section 60(2) enacted on June 6, 2018 (Act 26 of 2018); CIRP admitted against Principal Borrower; subsequent Section 7 petition filed against Corporate Guarantor dismissed by NCLT on March 27, 2019; appeal disposed on July 21, 2022[cite: 19]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate guarantee executed by the Respondent; Section 7 petition CP (IB) 356/PB/2019 against the Corporate Guarantor; record showing CIRP admission and CoC approval of a resolution plan against the Principal Borrower[cite: 19]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Financial Creditor filed CP (IB) 356/PB/2019 under Section 7 against the Corporate Guarantor before NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi, which dismissed the petition on March 27, 2019 relying on the Piramal precedent barring simultaneous proceedings for the same claim[cite: 19].
summary.legal_issues: Whether a Financial Creditor can simultaneously initiate and maintain CIRP proceedings under Section 7 of the IBC against both the Principal Borrower and the Corporate Guarantor before the NCLT for the same set of financial claims in light of the 2018 amendment to Section 60(2) of the Code[cite: 19].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 60(2) of the IBC, a financial creditor is entitled to initiate and proceed with simultaneous or parallel insolvency resolution proceedings against both the principal borrower and the corporate guarantor before the National Company Law Tribunal for the same financial claim and default[cite: 19]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The 2018 amendment to Section 60(2) deliberately expanded the adjudicatory remit of the NCLT to encompass corporate guarantors alongside principal corporate debtors, overturning the prior restrictive interpretation in Dr. Vishnu Kumar Agarwal v. Piramal Enterprises Ltd.[cite: 19] 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: In accordance with the binding Supreme Court rulings in Lalit Kumar Jain v. Union of India and SBI v. Athena Energy Ventures, the contractual liability of a guarantor is independent and co-extensive, and parallel resolution proceedings under Section 60(2) do not constitute an impermissible double claim[cite: 19]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The dismissal of the Section 7 petition against the Corporate Guarantor was contrary to settled statutory law and warranted remand for adjudication on merits[cite: 19].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 611 of 2019 is allowed; the impugned order dated 27.03.2019 passed by NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi is set aside; CP (IB) 356/PB/2019 is remanded to the Adjudicating Authority to decide the Section 7 application on merits in accordance with law; parties directed to appear on 10.08.2022[cite: 19].
summary.summary: TUF Metallurgical Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Principal Bench order dismissing its Section 7 IBC petition against Wadhwa Glass Processors Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Guarantor)[cite: 19]. The NCLT dismissed the application on the ground that CIRP had already been initiated against the Principal Borrower for the same debt, relying on the Piramal precedent[cite: 19]. The NCLAT held that the issue is fully settled by the 2018 amendment to Section 60(2) and Supreme Court rulings in Lalit Kumar Jain and Athena Energy, which establish that simultaneous insolvency proceedings against both principal borrower and corporate guarantor are legally maintainable[cite: 19]. The Appellate Tribunal allowed the appeal and remanded the case to the NCLT[cite: 19].

summary.case_title: M/s. Brand Realty Services Ltd. vs. M/s. Sir John Bakeries India Pvt. Ltd.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s. Brand Realty Services Ltd. was the Operational Creditor (Appellant), and M/s. Sir John Bakeries India Pvt. Ltd. was the Corporate Debtor (Respondent)[cite: 20]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Commercial services rendered under agreements dated November 28, 2014 and June 15, 2018 conferring reciprocal rights and payment entitlements on the Appellant[cite: 20]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed operational debt of Rs. 54,94,874 following alleged partial payments and default under the agreements[cite: 20]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 8 issued on April 30, 2019 and served on May 4, 2019; reply to demand notice issued by Corporate Debtor on May 25, 2019; Section 9 petition filed on June 3, 2019; impugned dismissal order passed on July 22, 2020[cite: 20]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Agreements dated November 28, 2014 and June 15, 2018; Section 8 demand notice and reply dated May 25, 2019 asserting execution fraud and police complaints regarding stolen cheques; Information Utility dispute records[cite: 20]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed IB 1677(ND)/2019 under Section 9 before NCLT New Delhi (Bench-V); NCLT dismissed the petition on July 22, 2020 on two grounds: that the Section 8 reply was not served within 10 days, and that default of an installment of a settlement agreement does not constitute an operational debt[cite: 20].
summary.legal_issues: Whether default under a commercial contract establishing operational obligations constitutes an operational debt under the IBC, and whether a Corporate Debtor's failure to reply to a Section 8 demand notice within ten days statutorily precludes it from raising a pre-existing dispute before the Adjudicating Authority under Section 9(5)[cite: 20].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Failure of a corporate debtor to issue a reply to a Section 8 demand notice within the stipulated ten-day statutory window does not extinguish its right to establish the existence of a pre-existing bona fide dispute before the Adjudicating Authority in Section 9 proceedings[cite: 20]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8(2) read with Section 9(1) and Section 9(5)(ii) establishes that the Adjudicating Authority is statutorily mandated to reject a Section 9 application if a notice or record of dispute is brought before it, whether via information utility, reply to petition, or contemporaneous evidence, irrespective of a delayed Section 8 reply[cite: 20]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal must evaluate the substantive nature of the underlying contract; an agreement defining operational service rights cannot be erroneously characterized as a mere 'installment settlement agreement' to summarily reject an operational debt claim[cite: 20]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred both in treating the commercial contract as a settlement installment and in holding that the Corporate Debtor was barred from raising pre-existing disputes due to a delayed Section 8 reply; the application warranted fresh determination[cite: 20].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 958 of 2020 is allowed to the extent that the impugned order dated 22.07.2020 in IB 1677(ND)/2019 is set aside, and the Section 9 application is revived and remitted to NCLT New Delhi Bench-V for fresh consideration on merits in accordance with law[cite: 20].
summary.summary: Brand Realty Services Ltd. appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order dismissing its Section 9 IBC petition claiming Rs. 54.94 Lakhs against Sir John Bakeries India Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 20] The NCLT rejected the petition holding that default of a settlement agreement installment is not an operational debt and that the Corporate Debtor's reply to the Section 8 notice was barred because it was not sent within 10 days[cite: 20]. The NCLAT reversed the decision, ruling that the underlying contract was a commercial service agreement rather than a settlement installment[cite: 20]. Furthermore, the Appellate Tribunal held that failure to reply within 10 days does not extinguish the debtor's statutory right to demonstrate a pre-existing dispute[cite: 20]. The petition was revived and remanded[cite: 20].

summary.case_title: Sherbahadur D. Yadav vs. M/s. Rohan Dyes and Intermediates Ltd.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sherbahadur D. Yadav is the Operational Creditor (Appellant), and M/s. Rohan Dyes and Intermediates Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor (Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: In the financial year 2017-2018, the Corporate Debtor awarded fabrication work to the Operational Creditor, pursuant to which invoices totaling Rs. 32,10,781.50 were raised. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The claimed default operational debt amount was Rs. 17,83,642, arising from alleged non-payment/part payment of invoices issued in 2017-2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Operational Creditor issued a legal notice on 17.03.2018, a Section 8 demand notice, and subsequently filed an application under Section 9 of the IBC on 31.07.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Prior to the Section 9 filing, cross criminal complaints were filed: the Operational Creditor filed a police complaint on 02.04.2018 at Vatva Police Station alleging criminal breach of trust, cheating, and intimidation; the Corporate Debtor filed police complaints on 11.12.2018 and 28.08.2019 at Vatva Police Station and on 20.08.2019 at Khambat Police Station alleging incorrect GST invoices without particulars, billing for work done by factory laborers, threats, and intimidation. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Operational Creditor filed a Section 9 application on 31.07.2019 before the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT), which dismissed the application on 13.05.2021 on the ground of a pre-existing dispute evidenced by the cross criminal complaints.
summary.legal_issues: Whether cross criminal police complaints lodged by both parties prior to the filing of a Section 9 application constitute sufficient evidence of a 'pre-existing dispute' under the IBC, and whether IBC proceedings can be utilized to adjudicate disputed claims.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Mutual and contentious cross police complaints between parties alleging fraud, inflated billing, and criminality prior to the initiation of Section 9 proceedings substantiate a genuine pre-existing dispute, barring insolvency admission. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9 read with Section 8 mandates that insolvency proceedings cannot be invoked as debt recovery mechanisms where serious allegations regarding billing validity and execution of work exist prior to the demand notice/petition. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The existence of contemporaneous, pre-litigation cross criminal complaints constitutes prima facie, tangible proof of an acrimonious and substantial pre-existing dispute that cannot be treated as a spurious afterthought. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT correctly dismissed the Section 9 petition as the dispute between the parties predated the insolvency proceedings and the IBC is not a recovery mechanism for contested claims.
summary.operative_order: The Appellate Tribunal upheld the order dated 13.05.2021 passed by the Adjudicating Authority and dismissed Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 472 of 2021.
summary.summary: Operational Creditor Sherbahadur D. Yadav appealed the NCLT's dismissal of his Section 9 petition against Corporate Debtor Rohan Dyes and Intermediates Ltd. for an unpaid debt of Rs. 17,83,642. The NCLT dismissed the application due to a pre-existing dispute evidenced by mutual police complaints filed before the petition, where the Corporate Debtor disputed GST invoices and alleged intimidation. The NCLAT held that contemporaneous cross criminal complaints demonstrate a genuine pre-existing dispute over the invoices. Emphasizing that IBC proceedings are not intended to serve as debt recovery proceedings for disputed claims, the Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal, affirming the rejection of the Section 9 application.

summary.case_title: Printland Digital (India) Pvt. Ltd. vs. Nirmal Trading Company
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Printland Digital (India) Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor (Appellant), and Nirmal Trading Company is the Creditor (Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying operational/financial transaction in CP No. IB 1105/ND/2020 pending before NCLT New Delhi. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default details stem from CP No. IB 1105/ND/2020 pending before the Adjudicating Authority. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Adjudicating Authority closed the Corporate Debtor's right to file a reply on 22.07.2021; the Corporate Debtor filed I.A. No. 5064/ND/2021 for recall of that order on 16.09.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Adjudicating Authority dismissed the recall application citing lack of power to review/recall its own orders and noting that multiple opportunities to file the reply were granted but not availed. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In CP No. IB 1105/ND/2020, the NCLT (Court-IV, New Delhi) dismissed Corporate Debtor's I.A. No. 5064/ND/2021 on 10.03.2022, holding that it lacked jurisdiction to recall its order closing the right to reply, prompting the present appeal.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT) possesses the jurisdiction under Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 to recall an interlocutory procedural order closing a party's right to file a reply, as distinguished from reviewing an order on merits.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Adjudicating Authority lacks the jurisdiction to review its substantive orders decided on merits, but retains inherent power to recall purely procedural orders—such as closing the right to file a reply—to advance substantial justice. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 preserves the inherent power of the Tribunal to make such orders as may be necessary for meeting the ends of justice, which encompasses procedural recalls of orders closing pleadings. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Distinction between substantive review on merits (prohibited without express statutory empowerment) and procedural recall of an order closing pleadings to afford an opportunity of being heard. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in holding it lacked jurisdiction to recall the order dated 22.07.2021 closing the right to file reply, as procedural recall falls squarely within Rule 11 powers.
summary.operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the impugned order dated 10.03.2022 is set aside; the matter is remanded to the Adjudicating Authority to consider the recall application on its merits in accordance with law. The parties were directed to appear before the NCLT on 09.06.2022.
summary.summary: Corporate Debtor Printland Digital (India) Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the NCLT New Delhi order dated 10.03.2022 dismissing its application (I.A. No. 5064/ND/2021) to recall an earlier order dated 22.07.2021 that closed its right to file a reply. The NCLT had held it lacked review or recall powers. The NCLAT distinguished between a substantive review on merits and a procedural recall. Relying on Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016, the Appellate Tribunal held that the NCLT has inherent jurisdiction to recall procedural orders concerning pleadings. The NCLAT allowed the appeal and remanded the application for reconsideration on merits.

summary.case_title: Sumat Kumar Gupta, RP of M/S International Mega Food Park Ltd. vs. Chairman and Managing Director, Punjab State Power Corporation Ltd. & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sumat Kumar Gupta is the Resolution Professional of the Corporate Debtor, M/S International Mega Food Park Ltd. (Appellant); Punjab State Power Corporation Ltd. (PSPCL) is the contractual power purchaser/governmental authority (Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) was executed between the Corporate Debtor and PSPCL pursuant to permissions granted by the State of Punjab for the supply of wind energy. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Corporate Debtor committed continuous default in supplying wind energy to PSPCL under the PPA, which persisted from prior to the initiation of CIRP. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: PSPCL issued a cure notice on 20.05.2021 providing a 60-day period, but terminated the PPA on 28.05.2021; the RP passed an order under Section 20(2)(b) on 05.05.2021 regarding PPA amendment; I.A. No. 413 of 2021 was rejected by NCLT on 18.10.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Termination memo no. 1356/57IIPC-412 dated 28.05.2021; Cure notice dated 20.05.2021; High Court of Punjab & Haryana order in CWP-PIL-77-2021 direction (xi) extending compliance deadlines up to 30.06.2021; admitted inability of the Corporate Debtor to supply energy during the cure period. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The RP filed I.A. No. 413 of 2021 seeking declaration of the termination memo as void, revival of PPA, and restraint on adverse actions pending plan approval in IA No. 616/2020. The NCLT rejected the application on 18.10.2022, prompting the appeal.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the termination of a Power Purchase Agreement during CIRP prior to the expiry of a 60-day contractual cure notice can be invalidated under the IBC where the Corporate Debtor was incapable of remedying default, and whether general High Court COVID-19 timeline extension orders apply to contractual performance obligations.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Contractual termination cannot be invalidated merely because termination occurred before the contractual cure period expired if the defaulting party was demonstrably incapable of curing the underlying continuous performance default, nor do judicial administrative time extension orders protect purely contractual supply obligations. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 20(2)(b) powers of the RP to manage the Corporate Debtor as a going concern cannot compel a contractual counterparty to continue a contract where non-performance predated CIRP and continued unrectified. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Assessing whether the party challenging termination possessed the readiness and willingness/ability to perform within the cure window; in the absence of capacity to supply, premature termination causes no legal prejudice under insolvency jurisdiction. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT rightly refused to revive the terminated PPA or declare the termination void, as the Corporate Debtor was never in a position to restore supply, and the High Court order applied strictly to court-directed timelines.
summary.operative_order: The appeal is dismissed; the order of the Adjudicating Authority dated 18.10.2022 is affirmed, clarifying that rejection of the application does not preclude the Appellant from pursuing any other remedy/recourse permissible in law.
summary.summary: The Resolution Professional of M/s International Mega Food Park Ltd. challenged an NCLT order dismissing an application to declare Punjab State Power Corporation Ltd.'s (PSPCL) termination of a Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) premature and void. PSPCL issued a 60-day cure notice on 20.05.2021 but terminated the PPA eight days later on 28.05.2021 due to continuous non-supply of wind energy spanning pre-CIRP periods. The NCLAT held that because the Corporate Debtor admittedly could not supply power within the cure period, the termination could not be faulted. Furthermore, blanket judicial pandemic extensions did not cover contractual performance. The appeal was dismissed without prejudice to legal remedies.

summary.case_title: Bharat Sharma, Resolution Applicant vs. Reshma Mittal, RP (Now Liquidator) & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Bharat Sharma is the Resolution Applicant/Joint Applicant (Appellant); Reshma Mittal is the Resolution Professional turned Liquidator (Respondent No. 1); Monitoring Committee/Financial Creditors (Respondent No. 2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Joint resolution plan submitted during CIRP by the Appellant for resolution of the Corporate Debtor (an MSME entity). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose from failure to implement the previously approved resolution plan, leading to its cancellation by the Adjudicating Authority on 01.07.2021. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Monitoring Committee resolved to liquidate on 29.05.2021; plan cancelled on 01.07.2021; Appellant submitted revised plan on 23.10.2021; NCLT allowed liquidation and rejected plan reconsideration on 26.08.2022; auction fixed for 10.11.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Resolution of Monitoring Committee dated 29.05.2021 resolving for liquidation; NCLT order dated 01.07.2021 indicating viable plans could be placed before liquidation; auction notice issued by the Liquidator with earnest money deposits (EMD) received from prospective bidders. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Principal Bench allowed Monitoring Committee's I.A. No. 2479/2021 for liquidation and dismissed Appellant's I.A. No. 1151/2021 seeking directions to place the revised resolution plan before the CoC, against which this appeal was preferred.
summary.legal_issues: Whether, upon failure of an approved resolution plan and subsequent order of liquidation, a resolution applicant is entitled to liberty under Regulation 2B of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016 to submit a scheme of compromise or arrangement under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 prior to an asset auction.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Liquidation proceedings should facilitate corporate revival, and before proceeding with the public auction of a corporate debtor's assets, eligible parties must be afforded the statutory opportunity to explore a compromise or arrangement under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 in terms of Regulation 2B. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 2B of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016 read with Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 establishes a three-month window during which a compromise/arrangement should be completed before proceeding to auction liquidation assets. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Balancing the objective of maximizing asset value against ongoing liquidation processes; where the applicant seeks to propose a compromise scheme, auctions scheduled during the statutory window should be deferred. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Justice is served by deferring the auction and granting the applicant one month to submit a scheme under Section 230 to the Liquidator and Financial Creditors, to be concluded within the three-month period of Regulation 2B.
summary.operative_order: The appeal was disposed of by granting the Appellant liberty to submit a scheme of compromise/arrangement under Section 230 to the Liquidator and Financial Creditors within one month, to be completed within three months under Regulation 2B of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016. The Liquidator was directed to defer the auction scheduled for 10.11.2022 until the expiry of the three-month period.
summary.summary: Bharat Sharma, a joint resolution applicant, appealed an NCLT order directing the liquidation of the Corporate Debtor and rejecting his plea to reconvene the CoC to consider a revised resolution plan after the earlier approved plan failed implementation. The Liquidator had scheduled an auction for 10.11.2022. The NCLAT held that to serve the ends of justice and pursue corporate revival, the Appellant should be afforded liberty to submit a scheme of compromise or arrangement under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 read with Regulation 2B of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016. The NCLAT ordered the auction deferred for three months.

summary.case_title: The Janata Cooperative Bank Ltd. vs. Suresh Kumar Jain & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Janata Cooperative Bank Ltd. is the Appellant (Bank/Respondent No. 4 before NCLT), and Suresh Kumar Jain (Resolution Professional) & Anr. are the Respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Banking and financial transactions involving the Corporate Debtor that were audited and scrutinized for fraudulent trading during the CIRP. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Fraudulent/unexplained transactions adjudicated under Section 66 of the IBC, leading to an initial fine of Rs. 1,00,000 imposed on the Appellant Bank. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Adjudicating Authority decided I.A. No. 3135 of 2020 in CP (IB)-1731(ND)/2019 on 04.10.2021; interim deposit of Rs. 1,00,000 as FDR was made pursuant to NCLAT order dated 04.01.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: NCLT order dated 04.10.2021 finding suspended directors liable under Section 66 and directing complaints against the statutory auditor and the Bank before RBI/ICAI, along with a fine of Rs. 1,00,000 each to the Prime Minister's Relief Fund; deposit of Rs. 1,00,000 FDR with the NCLAT Registrar. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In I.A. No. 3135 of 2020 arising out of CP (IB)-1731(ND)/2019, the NCLT New Delhi penalized the Appellant Bank with a fine of Rs. 1,00,000. The Bank appealed solely to alter the terminology from 'fine' to 'cost'.
summary.legal_issues: Whether a monetary penalty of Rs. 1,00,000 imposed by the Adjudicating Authority under Section 66 proceedings on a regulated entity for shortcomings can be modified and substituted from a 'fine' to 'cost'.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In exercise of appellate review under insolvency proceedings, the appellate tribunal may modify punitive nomenclature from 'fine' to 'cost' while maintaining the monetary liability payable to a public welfare fund, considering the totality of facts. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 66 adjudications addressing fraudulent conduct allow the Adjudicating Authority to address shortcomings, but appellate courts maintain discretion to treat regulatory/oversight omissions under the character of costs rather than criminal-style fines. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Assessment of the nature of the alleged shortcoming on the part of the institutional party and compliance efforts (such as filing complaints before the regulator and depositing security). 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The totality of the circumstances warranted the modification of the term 'fine' of Rs. 1,00,000 to 'cost' of Rs. 1,00,000 to be deposited into the Prime Minister's Relief Fund.
summary.operative_order: The appeal is disposed of by modifying the order dated 04.10.2021: the word 'fine' of Rs. 1 lakh in paragraph 12 is substituted with 'cost' of Rs. 1 lakh. The Registrar of NCLAT, New Delhi was directed to encash and deposit the Rs. 1 lakh FDR in the Prime Minister's Relief Fund within four weeks.
summary.summary: The Janata Cooperative Bank Ltd. appealed an order of the NCLT New Delhi passed in an avoidance application under Section 66 of the IBC, which imposed a 'fine' of Rs. 1,00,000 on the Bank payable to the Prime Minister's Relief Fund for shortcomings related to fraudulent transactions of the Corporate Debtor. The Bank had deposited the amount via FDR with the NCLAT and prayed solely for converting the word 'fine' to 'cost'. Considering the totality of circumstances, the NCLAT allowed the prayer, modifying the order so that the penalty is categorized as 'cost' rather than 'fine', and directed the Registrar to transfer the deposited amount to the Fund.

summary.case_title: Suzlon Synthetics Ltd. vs. Stressed Asset Stabilization Fund & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Suzlon Synthetics Ltd. is an assignee of IFCI debts and claimed secured financial creditor (Appellant); Stressed Asset Stabilization Fund (SASF) is the Financial Creditor (Respondent No. 1); IC Textiles Limited is the Corporate Debtor (Respondent No. 2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying financial debt facilities extended to the Corporate Debtor, subsequently involving an OTS entered into between Corporate Debtor and SASF. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: SASF claimed a default of Rs. 39,30,00,000 in Part IV of Form 1 (and Rs. 10,82,94,94,335 as on 01.06.2019), whereas Corporate Debtor admitted liability to the extent of Rs. 88,75,000 following part-payments under the OTS. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CP (IB) No. 1567/KB/2019 was filed under Section 7; BIFR proceedings ran between 24.09.2004 and 01.12.2016; NCLT Kolkata Bench admitted the Section 7 petition on 14.03.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor balance sheets for FY 2003-04, 2012-13, 2015-16, and 2018-19 showing acknowledgment of debt; exclusion of BIFR period under limitation principles; Corporate Debtor's admission of Rs. 88.75 Lakhs outstanding under OTS. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench admitted Section 7 application on 14.03.2022 holding the debt exceeded the Section 4 threshold and was within limitation; Appellant (not an original party before NCLT) appealed against admission.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority at the stage of Section 7 admission is required to determine and quantify the exact default amount, and whether another financial creditor can challenge the admission of a Section 7 petition on the apprehension that a large claim admitted will dilute its voting share or claim value in CIRP.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: At the stage of adjudicating a Section 7 petition, the Adjudicating Authority is not required to quantify or crystalize the precise quantum of debt owed; it must only determine whether there is an existing financial debt and a default exceeding the statutory threshold prescribed under Section 4. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The statutory scheme under Section 25(2) and Chapter IV of the IBBI CIRP Regulations vests the power of claim reception, verification, and determination solely with the IRP/RP, rendering claim quantification by the Adjudicating Authority at the Section 7 stage unnecessary. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Threshold default test: As long as the admitted default amount exceeds the statutory minimum threshold under Section 4(1), disputes regarding the broader claimed amount do not impede admission under Section 7. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed no error in admitting the Section 7 petition without quantifying SASF's full claim, and a third-party creditor cannot maintain a frivolous appeal challenging CIRP initiation based on speculative voting share dilution.
summary.operative_order: The appeal is dismissed. Holding the litigation to be frivolous and a waste of judicial time, the Appellate Tribunal imposed a cost of Rs. 2,00,000 on the Appellant to be deposited in the Prime Minister's Relief Fund within 15 days.
summary.summary: Suzlon Synthetics Ltd., claiming to be a financial creditor of Corporate Debtor IC Textiles Ltd., challenged the NCLT Kolkata Bench's order admitting a Section 7 application filed by SASF. The Appellant contended that SASF inflated its claim beyond the OTS balance of Rs. 88.75 lakhs, threatening to dilute other creditors' voting share in the CIRP. The NCLAT held that Section 7 adjudication only requires establishing debt and default exceeding the Section 4 threshold, not quantifying the exact claim, which is statutorily delegated to the RP under CIRP Regulations. Finding the appeal to be a frivolous front for promoters, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal with costs of Rs. 2 lakhs.

summary.case_title: M/s. Genius Security and Allied Services vs. Shivadutt Bannanje, RP of M/s. Fortuna Urbanscape Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s Genius Security and Allied Services (Appellant in CA 110/2021) and M/s RCC Mix (Appellant in CA 225/2021) are Operational Creditors; Shivadutt Bannanje is the Resolution Professional (Respondent No. 1); M/s Koncept Shelters is the Successful Resolution Applicant (Respondent No. 2); M/s Fortuna Urbanscape Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of security and housekeeping services by Genius Security, and supply of materials/concrete by RCC Mix to the Corporate Debtor's real estate projects. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Genius Security claimed operational debt of Rs. 8,77,317 (admitted at Rs. 8,47,147); RCC Mix claimed operational debt of Rs. 1,08,55,500 (admitted at Rs. 1,08,55,500). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Claims submitted on 21.10.2019 and 08.02.2020; CoC approved resolution plan with 95.07% majority on 30.07.2020; NCLT Bengaluru Bench approved the plan in I.A. No. 334 of 2020 on 29.01.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Total admitted claims were: Secured Financial Creditors Rs. 123.05 Crores, Homebuyers Rs. 13.99 Crores, Employees/Workmen Rs. 47.16 Lakhs, Operational Creditors Rs. 99.50 Lakhs; Liquidation value was Rs. 18.06 Crores (between 17.58 and 18.55 Crores); Resolution plan infusion was Rs. 8.80 Crores. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In CP (IB) No. 132/07/BB/2017, the NCLT Bengaluru approved the Resolution Applicant's plan via order dated 29.01.2021 in I.A. No. 334 of 2020; Operational Creditors appealed against zero payout in the plan.
summary.legal_issues: Whether a resolution plan proposing nil payment to operational creditors violates Section 30(2)(b) of the IBC or constitutes unlawful discrimination when the liquidation value is insufficient to cover even secured financial creditors under the Section 53 waterfall mechanism.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1.
