ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A resolution plan providing nil payment to operational creditors is valid and non-discriminatory if, in the event of liquidation, the liquidation value is insufficient to cover secured financial creditors and operational creditors would receive zero under the Section 53 waterfall priority. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(2)(b) requires payment to operational creditors not less than the amount payable in a liquidation under Section 53(1); if the statutory liquidation entitlement is zero, a nil provision in the resolution plan satisfies Section 30(2)(b). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Commercial wisdom and liquidation value comparison test: Discrimination requires disparate treatment among similarly situated creditors of the same class. Where the entire class of operational creditors is uniformly allocated nil based on insufficient liquidation value, no hostile discrimination exists. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CoC approved the plan with 95.07% majority in its commercial wisdom, complying fully with Sections 30(2) and 31(1), rendering the approval valid and binding on all stakeholders including operational creditors.
summary.operative_order: Both Company Appeals (CA (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 110 of 2021 and CA (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 225 of 2021) are dismissed. No orders as to costs. Connected applications stand closed.
summary.summary: Operational Creditors M/s Genius Security and M/s RCC Mix appealed against an NCLT Bengaluru order approving a resolution plan submitted by M/s Koncept Shelters for Fortuna Urbanscape Pvt. Ltd., alleging illegal discrimination because their admitted operational debts received nil allocation. The total admitted secured financial debt was Rs. 123.05 Crores against a liquidation value of approximately Rs. 18.06 Crores. The NCLAT held that under Section 30(2)(b) read with Section 53(1) of the IBC, operational creditors are only entitled to what they would receive in liquidation, which was zero. Because all operational creditors were treated equally without disparity, the commercial wisdom of the CoC (95.07% vote) was upheld and appeals dismissed.

summary.case_title: Mr. Nitin Bharal & Ors. vs. Stockflow Express Private Limited Through Liquidator, Mr. Sanjay Gupta
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Nitin Bharal, Narendra Singh Bisht, Yashpal Arora, and Rajeev Sharma are Ex-Directors/Promoters (Appellants); Stockflow Express Private Limited (formerly Committed Worldwide Express Pvt. Ltd.) represented by Liquidator Sanjay Gupta is the Corporate Debtor (Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Courier service operations of Corporate Debtor, involving circuitous share transfers between the Corporate Debtor and related sister concern Committed Cargo Care Ltd., along with selective bad debt write-offs and cash settlements. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Fraudulent write-offs and siphoning amounting to Rs. 1,33,68,262 in written-off bad debts over FY 2016-17, 2017-18, and 2018-19, and settling receivables of Rs. 42,33,304 against Vyke Logistics/Vyke International for a mere Rs. 3 Lakhs cash. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: IRP appointed on 26.11.2019; Promoters resigned on 31.12.2018; Promoters continued operating bank accounts between 08.01.2019 and 19.10.2019; NCLT New Delhi Bench V allowed I.A. 2153 of 2020 under Section 66 on 21.01.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bank statements from Yes Bank, ICICI Bank, and Axis Bank proving Appellants acted as authorized signatories and transacted Rs. 19,98,602 post-resignation; balance sheet write-offs of Rs. 1,25,37,262 in FY 2017-18; non-cooperation by ex-directors preventing formal Transaction Audit. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In CP (IB) No. 2414(ND)/2019, the IRP filed I.A. 2153 of 2020 under Section 66. The NCLT allowed the application on 21.01.2022, ordering Appellants to contribute Rs. 1,33,68,262 and initiating Section 69 prosecution, which Appellants appealed.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the absence of a formal Transaction Audit Report precludes the Adjudicating Authority from finding fraudulent trading under Section 66 of the IBC when non-cooperation of ex-directors prevents an audit, and whether post-resignation banking operations establish continued financial control and intent to defraud creditors.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application under Section 66 for fraudulent trading does not mandate a formal Transaction Audit Report where ex-directors' refusal to cooperate impedes its preparation; the Adjudicating Authority can base findings on primary bank records, balance sheet entries, and independent analysis of the IRP/RP. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 18(1)(a) and Section 66(1), the IRP is empowered to collect financial intelligence, and any persons who knowingly carried on the business with intent to defraud creditors—even after formally resigning on paper while retaining banking control—are personally liable to contribute to the assets. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Circumstantial and forensic record analysis: Circuitous intra-group share transfers, arbitrary cash settlements of substantial debts for nominal sums, and sustained operation of bank accounts post-resignation establish culpability under Section 66. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT correctly held the ex-directors liable under Section 66 and properly ordered contributions alongside prosecution under Section 69.
summary.operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, affirming the Adjudicating Authority's order directing Appellants to contribute Rs. 1,33,68,262 to the Corporate Debtor within three months and upholding directions to initiate prosecution under Section 69 of the IBC.
summary.summary: Ex-promoters/directors of Stockflow Express Pvt. Ltd. appealed an NCLT New Delhi Bench V order holding them liable under Section 66 of the IBC for fraudulent trading and directing them to contribute Rs. 1,33,68,262, alongside Section 69 prosecution. Appellants argued that the findings were invalid without a formal Transaction Audit Report. The NCLAT rejected this contention, observing that the Appellants' deliberate non-cooperation prevented the audit. Relying on primary evidence—including bank statements showing post-resignation account operations, unjustified bad debt write-offs, and suspicious cash settlements of book debts—the NCLAT affirmed the NCLT's order and dismissed the appeal.

summary.case_title: Shaikh Mohammed Tariq vs. Aegis Forging Ltd.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Shaikh Mohammed Tariq is the Guarantor/Claimant (Appellant), and Aegis Forging Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor (Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Funds provided by creditor investors to the Corporate Debtor secured against the personal guarantee given by the Appellant, which led to arbitration. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Arbitral award rendered on 11.11.2013 directing payment of cash security of Rs. 3,64,58,785 with interest in favour of the Appellant. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Arbitral award passed on 11.11.2013, put into execution by the Appellant; subsequent Section 7 petition filed by the Appellant and rejected by the Adjudicating Authority. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Arbitral award dated 11.11.2013 for Rs. 3,64,58,785 with interest; pending execution proceedings instituted by the Appellant to enforce the arbitral award against the Corporate Debtor. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed a petition under Section 7 of the IBC seeking initiation of CIRP based on the arbitral award/personal guarantee claim; NCLT rejected the Section 7 petition, leading to the present appeal before NCLAT.
summary.legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority is mandatorily required to admit an application under Section 7 of the IBC upon proof of debt and default, or whether it possesses discretion to refuse admission where the claim arises from an arbitral award already pending execution.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Admission of a Section 7 petition is not mandatory merely upon establishing financial debt and default; the Adjudicating Authority retains statutory discretion to reject initiation of CIRP where appropriate circumstances exist, including pending execution of an arbitral award. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: As established by the Supreme Court in Vidarbha Industries Power Ltd. vs. Axis Bank Limited, the word 'may' in Section 7(5)(a) confers discretionary power rather than an obligatory mandate upon the Adjudicating Authority. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Discretionary assessment test: Evaluating whether the debtor-creditor relationship and surrounding circumstances, such as an arbitral award for cash security already under execution, warrant invoking the insolvency regime or pursuing execution remedies. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The existence of an arbitral award already put into execution was good and sufficient ground for the Adjudicating Authority to exercise discretion refusing Section 7 admission.
summary.operative_order: The Appellate Tribunal dismissed Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1342 of 2022 and closed pending interlocutory applications I.A. No. 4107 and 4165 of 2022.
summary.summary: Shaikh Mohammed Tariq appealed against an NCLT order rejecting his Section 7 IBC petition against Aegis Forging Ltd. The Appellant contended that funds given under his personal guarantee constituted a financial debt under Section 5(8)(i), crystallised by an arbitral award dated 11.11.2013 for Rs. 3,64,58,785 with interest, which was pending execution. The NCLAT affirmed the dismissal, holding that under the Supreme Court's ruling in Vidarbha Industries Power Ltd. vs. Axis Bank Ltd., admission under Section 7 is not obligatory merely upon establishing debt and default. The pending execution of the arbitral award provided sufficient ground to decline admission.

summary.case_title: Atharva Auto Logistics Pvt. Ltd. vs. Intec Capital Ltd. & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Atharva Auto Logistics Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor (Appellant); Intec Capital Ltd. is the Financial Creditor (Respondent No. 1). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan/credit facility extended by Intec Capital Ltd. to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default date mentioned in Part-IV of Form 1 was 25.08.2017; interim partial repayment of Rs. 2,00,000 made on 31.07.2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Date of default specified as 25.08.2017; last part payment made on 31.07.2018; Section 7 petition CP No. 1258/MB/I&B/2020 filed on 28.08.2020; NCLT Mumbai admitted petition on 18.02.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Record of default issued by National E-Governance Services Limited (NeSL); statement of account/ledger annexed to the Section 7 petition showing the last repayment of Rs. 2 Lakhs on 31.07.2018. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Intec Capital Ltd. filed CP No. 1258/MB/I&B/2020 before NCLT Court-5 Mumbai Bench under Section 7. The NCLT admitted the application on 18.02.2022, ruling that the application was within the limitation period from the last payment.
summary.legal_issues: Whether a Section 7 application is barred by limitation when filed more than three years from the original date of default stated in Part-IV, but within three years from the date of the last part-payment acknowledged in the annexed ledger accounts.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The limitation period of three years for initiating corporate insolvency under Section 7 is renewed and computed afresh from the date of the last part-payment or written acknowledgment of debt reflected in the supporting ledger documents annexed to the petition. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 read with general principles of the Limitation Act permits a financial creditor to compute limitation from the date of last payment, even if Part IV states an earlier initial default date, provided payment records are filed with the petition. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Reconciliation of Form Part-IV pleadings with annexed account statements: The date of default in Part-IV must be evaluated alongside NeSL records and ledger statements produced on record showing subsequent part payments. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the last repayment of Rs. 2 Lakhs was made on 31.07.2018, the petition filed on 28.08.2020 was well within the three-year limitation period.
summary.operative_order: The Appellate Tribunal dismissed Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 303 of 2022, affirming the NCLT Mumbai Bench order dated 18.02.2022 admitting the Section 7 petition.
summary.summary: Atharva Auto Logistics Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the NCLT Mumbai Bench order admitting Intec Capital Ltd.'s Section 7 petition. The Appellant contended that the petition was time-barred as the date of default mentioned in Part-IV was 25.08.2017 while the petition was filed on 28.08.2020 (beyond three years), relying on Babulal Vardharji Gurjar. The NCLAT held that the financial creditor had placed on record NeSL data and account statements evidencing a part-repayment of Rs. 2 Lakhs on 31.07.2018. The three-year limitation period was computed afresh from 31.07.2018, making the 28.08.2020 filing timely. The appeal was dismissed.

summary.case_title: Prafulla Purushottamrao Gadge vs. Narayan Mangal & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Prafulla Purushottamrao Gadge is the Suspended Director of the Corporate Debtor (Appellant)[cite: 12]; Narayan Mangal is the Financial Creditor (Respondent No. 1)[cite: 12]; PCS Lovkesh Batra/Navin Khandelwal is the Interim Resolution Professional (Respondent No. 2)[cite: 12]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying financial debt/loan facility extended by Respondent No. 1 to the Corporate Debtor, which was subject to an initial Section 7 petition and subsequent settlement terms[cite: 12]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Original petition claimed default of Rs. 63,20,388[cite: 12]; subsequent Section 7 petition CP (IB) No. 725 (MB) 2021 filed for an alleged default amount under Part-IV of Rs. 78,65,000 arising from breach of settlement terms. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: First Section 7 application filed on 12.10.2019 and withdrawn on consent terms on 13.12.2019[cite: 12]; restoration application I.A. 1128/2020 dismissed on 02.02.2021[cite: 13]; fresh Section 7 application CP (IB) No. 725 (MB) 2021 filed on 25.06.2021; admission order passed by NCLT Mumbai on 04.04.2022[cite: 12]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Consent terms taken on record on 13.12.2019 containing Clause 12 granting liberty to initiate fresh legal proceedings under Section 7 in the event of default; Ministry of Corporate Affairs Notification dated 24.03.2020 raising the Section 4 threshold to Rs. 1 Crore[cite: 13]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent No. 1 filed a fresh Section 7 petition on 25.06.2021 claiming Rs. 78,65,000. NCLT Mumbai Bench admitted the application on 04.04.2022[cite: 12]. The Suspended Director appealed against admission on the ground that the default failed to meet the revised Rs. 1 Crore threshold[cite: 13].
summary.legal_issues: Whether a fresh Section 7 application filed after 24.03.2020 pursuant to a default under settlement terms of a previously withdrawn petition can be treated as a continuation of the earlier 2019 petition to bypass the increased statutory threshold of Rupees One Crore under Section 4 of the IBC[cite: 13].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A fresh petition under Section 7 filed after the notification raising the threshold limit under Section 4 must independently satisfy the enhanced pecuniary threshold and cannot be treated as a continuation of an earlier withdrawn petition, especially where restoration of the earlier petition was specifically rejected[cite: 13]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The notification dated 24.03.2020 issued under Section 4 of the IBC mandating a minimum threshold limit of Rs. 1 Crore applies strictly to all independent Section 7 applications filed after the notification date[cite: 13]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Threshold compliance test at the date of presentation: Where consent terms stipulate liberty to initiate fresh proceedings upon default rather than automatic revival, any new petition filed post-notification is subject to the Rs. 1 Crore statutory threshold[cite: 13]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the fresh application claimed only Rs. 78,65,000, it failed to meet the mandatory threshold of Rs. 1 Crore, and the Adjudicating Authority committed an error in admitting it[cite: 13].
summary.operative_order: The appeal is allowed, and the NCLT Mumbai order dated 04.04.2022 is set aside on the threshold ground without entering into merits[cite: 13]. The IRP is directed to be paid fees of Rs. 1,00,000 (Rs. 50,000 each by Appellant and Respondent No. 1 within one month), with liberty to Respondent No. 1 to take fresh proceedings under Section 7 if conditions are fulfilled[cite: 13].
summary.summary: Prafulla Purushottamrao Gadge, Suspended Director of the Corporate Debtor, appealed an NCLT Mumbai order admitting a Section 7 application filed on 25.06.2021 by Financial Creditor Narayan Mangal for a default of Rs. 78,65,000 following non-compliance with earlier settlement terms. The Appellant contended that the petition failed to meet the Rs. 1 Crore threshold introduced on 24.03.2020[cite: 13]. The NCLAT rejected the Creditor's contention that the application was a continuation of an earlier 2019 petition, noting that restoration had been refused and the settlement granted liberty only to initiate fresh proceedings[cite: 13]. Holding the application non-compliant with the Section 4 threshold, the NCLAT allowed the appeal and set aside the admission order[cite: 13].

summary.case_title: Bharat Hotels Ltd. vs. Tapan Chakraborty, RP of RDG Interior Decoration Exterior Architecture Pvt. Ltd.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Bharat Hotels Ltd. is a Financial Creditor holding a 33.07% voting share in the CoC (Appellant); Tapan Chakraborty is the Resolution Professional of RDG Interior Decoration Exterior Architecture Pvt. Ltd., the Corporate Debtor (Respondent)[cite: 13]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying financial debt owed by the Corporate Debtor during the CIRP[cite: 13]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default details stem from CIRP initiated on 19.12.2019, culminating in liquidation resolution approved by 66.93% voting share. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 19.12.2019[cite: 14]; CoC in its 7th meeting on 28.06.2022 resolved to liquidate the Corporate Debtor with 66.93% vote share[cite: 13]; Appellant filed I.A. No. 656/KB/2022 on 29.06.2022[cite: 13]; NCLT Kolkata Bench-I rejected the application on 26.08.2022[cite: 13]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Voting results of the 7th CoC meeting dated 28.06.2022 approving liquidation by 66.93%; Interlocutory application prayers seeking item-wise CIRP costs disclosure, records inspection, and forensic audit before liquidation[cite: 13]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Following the CoC's liquidation resolution, Appellant filed I.A. No. 656/KB/2022 under Section 18 and Regulation 34A to direct cost disclosures and audits. NCLT Kolkata Bench-I dismissed the application on 26.08.2022 for lack of locus/merit under the cited provisions, which Appellant challenged.
summary.legal_issues: Whether a minority financial creditor in the CoC can maintain an application before the Adjudicating Authority under Section 18 and Regulation 34A to demand item-wise CIRP costs and forensic/valuation audits to challenge or stall a liquidation decision resolved by the CoC by statutory majority under Section 33(2).
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A minority financial creditor in the CoC cannot collaterally resist or derail a valid statutory resolution for liquidation passed by the requisite majority under Section 33(2) by filing applications for disclosure of CIRP costs or audit procedures. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 33(2) permits the CoC to resolve to liquidate at any time before resolution plan confirmation, and the Adjudicating Authority must pass a liquidation order upon intimation[cite: 14]; Regulation 34A cost approvals fall within the internal domain of the CoC rather than pre-emptive adjudication by the Tribunal. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Commercial autonomy of CoC: Grievances regarding CIRP costs, audits, and valuations are subject to CoC deliberations and do not grant locus to invoke Section 18 to thwart a 66% majority liquidation decision. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT rightly dismissed the application as CIRP cost determination lies with the CoC, and minority creditors cannot subvert Section 33(2) mandates.
summary.operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, affirming the NCLT order dated 26.08.2022, while observing that the Appellant remains free to raise cost issues in CoC meetings and request the Liquidator to obtain a valuation report if not already obtained[cite: 15].
summary.summary: Bharat Hotels Ltd., a minority financial creditor holding a 33.07% voting share, appealed against an NCLT Kolkata Bench order dismissing its application (I.A. No. 656/KB/2022)[cite: 13]. The application sought disclosure of item-wise CIRP costs and directions for forensic/valuation audits after the CoC approved the Corporate Debtor's liquidation with a 66.93% majority under Section 33(2) of the IBC. The NCLAT held that the CoC possesses the statutory authority to resolve liquidation at any time prior to plan approval, which minority creditors cannot collaterally obstruct[cite: 14]. Furthermore, CIRP cost approvals lie strictly within the CoC's domain rather than the Tribunal's. The appeal was dismissed[cite: 15].

summary.case_title: State Bank of India vs. Bhanwar Lal Jajodia & Mahendra Kumar Jajodia
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: State Bank of India (Stressed Asset Management Branch) is the Financial Creditor (Appellant); Bhanwar Lal Jajodia and Mahendra Kumar Jajodia are Personal Guarantors to the Corporate Debtor (Respondents)[cite: 14]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Personal guarantee facilities executed by the Respondents to secure credit facilities extended by State Bank of India to the Corporate Debtor[cite: 14]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default committed by the Corporate Debtor and invoked against Personal Guarantors forming the basis of petitions under Section 95(1)[cite: 14]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Creditor filed CP(IB)/230/KB/2021 under Section 95(1) after approval of a resolution plan in the Corporate Debtor's CIRP; NCLT Kolkata rejected petition as premature on 05.10.2021[cite: 14]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Approved resolution plan for the Corporate Debtor resulting in no ongoing CIRP or liquidation proceedings pending against the Corporate Debtor at the time of filing under Section 95(1). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: State Bank of India filed CP(IB)/230/KB/2021 under Section 95(1) before NCLT Kolkata Bench[cite: 14]. The NCLT dismissed the application on 05.10.2021 as premature, holding that under Section 60(2), an insolvency application against a personal guarantor requires a concurrent CIRP or liquidation proceeding pending against the corporate debtor. SBI appealed[cite: 14].
summary.legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 95(1) of the IBC for insolvency resolution against a personal guarantor is maintainable before the NCLT under Section 60(1) when no CIRP or liquidation proceeding is currently pending against the principal corporate debtor under Section 60(2).
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The pendency of a CIRP or liquidation proceeding against the principal corporate debtor is not a mandatory prerequisite for maintaining an insolvency application under Section 95(1) against a personal guarantor before the NCLT having territorial jurisdiction under Section 60(1)[cite: 15]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60(1) is the substantive jurisdictional provision designating the NCLT as the Adjudicating Authority for corporate persons and personal guarantors[cite: 15]. Section 60(2) uses 'without prejudice to sub-section (1)' and operates supplementally to ensure forum convergence before 'such' NCLT only when corporate proceedings are actively pending[cite: 15]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Textual harmonisation of Sections 60(1) and 60(2): The words 'a' and 'such' in Section 60(2) prevent forum fragmentation during concurrent proceedings, but do not bar Section 95 actions under Section 60(1) where corporate insolvency is not pending[cite: 15]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred in rejecting the Section 95(1) application as premature; the petition was maintainable before the NCLT having territorial jurisdiction over the corporate debtor's registered office[cite: 15].
summary.operative_order: Both appeals are allowed; the order dated 05.10.2021 is set aside; the Section 95(1) applications are revived before NCLT Kolkata to proceed in accordance with law[cite: 15].
summary.summary: State Bank of India appealed against the NCLT Kolkata Bench's order dismissing its Section 95(1) insolvency application against personal guarantors Mahendra Kumar Jajodia and Bhanwar Lal Jajodia as premature, because no CIRP or liquidation was actively pending against the principal debtor following resolution plan approval. Reversing the decision, the NCLAT held that Section 60(1) is the primary jurisdictional provision conferring authority on the NCLT over personal guarantors[cite: 15]. Section 60(2) operates 'without prejudice' to Section 60(1) merely to prevent parallel proceedings before different benches when corporate CIRP is pending, rather than barring independent guarantor actions[cite: 15]. The Section 95(1) applications were revived[cite: 15].

summary.case_title: Rishi Kapoor vs. Kashi Vishwanathan Sivaraman, RP of Kindle Developers Pvt. Ltd.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Rishi Kapoor, an advocate who rendered legal services, is the Appellant (Claimant/Allottee)[cite: 15]; Kashi Vishwanathan Sivaraman is the Resolution Professional of Kindle Developers Pvt. Ltd., the Corporate Debtor (Respondent)[cite: 15]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Legal services rendered by Appellant to the Corporate Debtor, followed by an alleged Memorandum of Understanding and Apartment Buyer Agreement dated 19.04.2018 allotting 20 real estate units in lieu of outstanding legal fees. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose in underlying Section 7 CP(IB) 470(ND)/2017 filed by Amit Kumar Malik, leading to admission; Appellant claimed status as Financial Creditor for 20 allotted units. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application admitted in court on 09.03.2018; MOU executed by Corporate Debtor on 19.04.2018; admission order uploaded on NCLT website on 22.06.2018; Appellant filed Form B claim on 09.07.2019; I.A. 445/2021 seeking amendment rejected on 16.08.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Cause list dated 09.03.2018 showing Item No. 1 for pronouncement; signed admission order dated 09.03.2018 imposing moratorium; MOU and Apartment Buyer Agreement dated 19.04.2018; Form CA submitted with amendment application. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 petition admitted on 09.03.2018. Appellant initially filed claim as an Operational Creditor in Form-B, but later moved I.A. No. 445/2021 to amend his earlier application (I.A. No. 1442/2020) to claim financial debt as an allottee under the MOU dated 19.04.2018. NCLT New Delhi Bench-II dismissed I.A. No. 445/2021 on 16.08.2021[cite: 15], leading to this appeal[cite: 15].
summary.legal_issues: Whether an order of the Adjudicating Authority admitting a Section 7 petition and declaring a moratorium under Section 14 takes effect from the date of its oral pronouncement in court or only from the date it is uploaded to the tribunal's website, and whether transactions entered into during the interim period are void.
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An order of the Adjudicating Authority takes effect immediately upon its formal delivery and pronouncement in open court under Rule 150 of the NCLT Rules, 2016; its statutory enforceability and the resultant Section 14 moratorium are not deferred until the date of website uploading. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 13 mandates declaration of moratorium immediately upon admission; holding that commencement remains suspended until website publication would cause severe legal vagueness and enable corporate debtors to dissipate assets in defiance of statutory objectives. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Validity of post-pronouncement alienations: Any transaction, agreement, or memorandum of understanding executed by a corporate debtor after the date of pronouncement violates the Section 14 moratorium and is void ab initio. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because CIRP commenced on 09.03.2018 upon pronouncement, the MOU dated 19.04.2018 was void, and the NCLT properly rejected the Appellant's application to amend his claim to financial creditor status.
summary.operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, affirming the Adjudicating Authority's order dated 16.08.2021 rejecting I.A. No. 445 of 2021.
summary.summary: Rishi Kapoor appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order rejecting his application (I.A. No. 445/2021) to amend a pending claim petition to convert his operational claim for legal fees into a financial debt as an allottee under an MOU dated 19.04.2018[cite: 15]. The Appellant contended that although the Section 7 petition was admitted on 09.03.2018, it was uploaded only on 22.06.2018, meaning the MOU was valid. The NCLAT held that under Rule 150 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 and Section 14 of the IBC, admission and moratorium take effect on the date of judicial pronouncement. Consequently, the subsequent MOU was void, and the dismissal of the amendment was affirmed.
